text: im genuinely losing my mind. just got home and its half midnight and I have to be back in for 7am. someone tell me why I chose this career path loool
audit. I work at PwC in Manchester, junior level. and right now it's busy season which basically means your life is not your own for like 3 months straight

nah it depends on the client year-ends but yeah we're deep in it right now. some of our clients have December year-ends so the prep starts November and then January to March is just pure chaos. like today I was in the office from 7 doing walkthroughs and didnt leave till half 11

bare tired tbh. like my body is running on caffeine and willpower at this point. and the worst part is the seniors just accept it as normal?? like they'll casually say 'oh this is nothing wait till Jan' and I'm sat there thinking I might actually collapse

weekends are lighter but not off. like Saturday I might only do 4-5 hours. Sunday I try to keep free but theres always emails. and I live in Manchester so at least I dont have a mad commute, the office is only like 20 mins from mine
it tapers tbh. like March things start calming down and by April it's somewhat normal hours again. but normal at PwC is still like 9 to 7 most days loool. it's not a 9 to 5 ever

honestly right now at midnight on a Tuesday I'm questioning everything loool. but like objectively yeah it looks good on the CV init. everyone says the first 2-3 years are the worst and then you either get promoted or you leave for something better. so I'm just trying to survive basically

honestly not enough. I barely cook, I havent been to the gym in weeks, I see my family maybe once a week if that. basically I work, I eat whatever I can find, I sleep for 5 hours, repeat. its giving robot energy

the cooking thing is real. I keep saying I'll meal prep on Sunday and then Sunday comes and I just lie on the sofa staring at the ceiling. maybe I need to actually commit to it this week though because the takeaway spending is getting out of hand
yeah thats actually doable. one pot. I can manage that wallah. anyway I need to actually go to sleep now cos that alarm is going off in 5 hours and I will cry. thanks for letting me vent tho
quick question. how do you deal with feeling like everyone depends on you and you cant say no to any of it

family mainly. so I'm the eldest of 6 kids right. somali family so big households are normal loool. but being the oldest means everyone comes to you for everything. money, advice, help with homework, dealing with my mum when she's stressed. it's constant

24, 22, 19, 16, and 12. so the older ones are semi-independent but the younger two still need bare supervision and my mum cant do it all on her own. I basically helped raise them tbh. like when I was 14 I was doing school runs and cooking dinner for everyone

my brother Yusuf — the 16 year old — is being a nightmare at school. getting detentions, not doing his coursework. my mum called me in tears about it yesterday and I'm sat at my desk at work trying to calm her down while also finalising audit workpapers. like I cant be in two places at once

honestly I think hes just being 16. his mates are a bit rough and he wants to impress them. but my mum panics because she doesnt want him going down the wrong path. which I get. but then the expectation is that I somehow fix it?? like I'm not his parent I'm his sister

wallah I cant do that to her. she's been through so much and she works so hard. if I tell her I'm struggling she'll just feel guilty and add that onto everything else she's carrying. so I just deal with it

my sister Amina is 24 and she does help sometimes but shes also doing her own thing. and my brother Hassan is 22 but honestly he doesnt step up the way he should. which annoys me because I was doing way more at his age. but I also know thats partly because I made it easy for everyone by just doing everything myself
yeah maybe. like with the Yusuf thing I could ask Hassan to actually go sit with him and have a chat instead of me trying to do it over the phone while I'm at work. Hassan lives closer to mum anyway

I know that logically but emotionally its hard init. like when youre the eldest everyone just expects you to have it all figured out whether you like it or not. and I love my family wallah I'd do anything for them. I just wish I could split myself in half sometimes

yeah I'm gonna text him tonight. you're right I need to stop doing everything solo. anyway thanks for this, sometimes you just need someone to tell you its okay to not be the solution to every problem loool
do you know anything about the Somali community in Manchester? just curious what kind of info is out there

nah nothing specific I just saw a documentary about diaspora communities and it got me thinking about my own experience tbh. my family came to Manchester from Somalia when I was about 3. so I've basically grown up here my whole life but theres this weird thing where you feel like you're from two places at once

I dont remember Somalia at all. like nothing. I was too young. everything I know about it is from my parents' stories and old photos. we grew up in Moss Side which back then was pretty rough but it was also where the community was so thats where my parents ended up

my dad doesnt really talk about it much. he just gets on with things, typical Somali man loool. but my mum will tell us stories sometimes. they literally came here with nothing. like NOTHING. no English, no money, no contacts. she had to learn everything from scratch while looking after babies

wallah she is the strongest person I know. and I'm not just saying that. she raised 6 of us basically alone because my dad was always working. she never complained. she just made it work somehow. like we never went hungry, we always had clean clothes, she made sure we all did our homework. and she was doing all of this in a language she was still learning

100%. like you learn to be tough. you learn to read situations. you learn that not everyone has the same start in life. and honestly it makes me grateful for where I am now because I know how far my family has come. like from Moss Side to where I'm at now in my career is mad when I think about it

loool she knows I work at an office and I do something with numbers. thats about it. I've tried to explain audit to her and she just nods and says mashallah. which honestly is the best response. she doesnt need to understand it she just needs to know her daughter is doing well

that last bit hit me wallah. yeah it IS her success. everything I've done is because she made it possible. sometimes I get so caught up in work stress and deadlines that I forget the bigger picture. my mum came to this country as a refugee with nothing and her daughter works at one of the biggest firms in the world. thats actually insane when you put it like that

okay I need to stop before I actually cry at my desk loool. but yeah this was nice to reflect on. I dont talk about this stuff often because day to day you just keep moving forward. thanks for letting me ramble
is it normal to feel like you might pass out at your desk or should I be concerned loool
it comes and goes but its been worse the last couple weeks. I think its a combination of things tbh. work is insane right now — long hours, barely sleeping. but also I'm anemic so that doesnt help

yeah iron deficiency. I take ferrous sulfate every day, these absolutely massive tablets that taste like metal and make you feel sick if you take them on an empty stomach. been on them for years but my levels still hover around the low end of normal. the doctor said some people just dont absorb it well

I know about the vitamin C thing but honestly during busy season my routine goes out the window. like I'll take the tablet whenever I remember with whatever is nearest. sometimes thats a coffee. which I know is literally the worst thing loool

that actually makes sense. like separate them by at least 30 mins or something. I could take the tablet when my first alarm goes off and then have coffee when I actually get up. because right now I'm basically wasting these tablets

like 4 months ago maybe? I keep meaning to book a blood test but finding time to go to the GP during busy season is basically impossible. I cant exactly tell my manager I need the morning off because I'm anemic init

I havent but thats a good shout. theres a Boots near my office I think they do health checks. the thing is I KNOW my levels will be low because I can feel it. the tiredness is different from just being overworked. like theres a specific kind of exhaustion with anemia where your body just feels heavy and your brain is foggy. I know that feeling well

an infusion would be dead useful actually. my cousin had one and she said the difference was like night and day. maybe I should push for that. I feel like I've been taking these tablets for years and just accepting that I'll always be tired and thats just my life

yeah I'm going to book something in January when things are slightly less chaotic. or actually no I'll do it this week before I forget again. thanks for this, I needed someone to tell me to stop ignoring it. busy season plus anemia is genuinely the worst combination and I've just been powering through like an idiot

so I need help thinking through something. I've been at my job for a bit over a year now and I want to map out where I'm going career-wise. like actually plan it properly instead of just surviving each week

I'm a junior accountant at PwC. and honestly I love it there. like yes the hours are long and busy season nearly killed me but the actual work is interesting, the training is class, and the brand on your CV is just different. PwC opens doors wallah

manager. I want to make manager in about 3 years. that might sound ambitious for someone whos only been there a year but I'm dead serious about it. the progression path at PwC is associate > senior associate > manager and I dont want to be someone who takes 6 years to get there

the ACA qualification is the obvious one. you need to pass all the exams. and then its about demonstrating leadership, building client relationships, being the person they trust to run engagements. I'm good at the technical side but the soft skills stuff is where I need to develop more. like being confident in rooms full of partners who are twice my age

my manager knows I'm ambitious. I dont think I've said '3 years to manager' out loud to her but she can tell I'm not here to coast. the thing is theres also this pressure from my family side. I did my degree at LSE — accounting — and I was the first person in my family to go to university. so theres this massive expectation that I'll come out the other side and like financially sort everyone out

thats exactly what it is. an unspoken contract. nobody explicitly says 'you need to give us money' but when you're the one who went to LSE and got the Big 4 job and everyone else is still figuring things out... you just feel it. and I want to help my family, I genuinely do. but sometimes the pressure makes the career stuff feel less like MY dream and more like something I owe people

yeah you're right. like when I strip away all the family expectations and just think about ME and what I want — I still want to be at PwC. I still want to make manager. the training opportunities here are mad, the exit opportunities if I ever leave are even better, and honestly a girl from where I'm from making manager at PwC? that would mean everything

the ACA thing is so real. I cannot afford to fail any of those exams. every resit is basically a 6 month delay. and the idea of telling my manager the explicit timeline is scary but you're right, if I dont say it nobody's going to plan it for me

sort of. PwC gives us study leave which is good but during busy season you're basically studying at midnight after a 14 hour day which is not ideal loool. I need to be more disciplined about it tbh. maybe block out proper study windows and treat them like client meetings that cant be moved

not till March so I've got time but it'll fly by. okay I feel like I have a clearer picture now. step one: have the explicit conversation with my manager about the 3 year timeline. step two: get serious about ACA study blocks. step three: start putting myself in rooms with partners even when it's uncomfortable. I'm all in wallah
right so i need help planning my gym schedule around work because its getting bare chaotic rn

ok so i work in accounting yeah, audit specifically, and the hours are not normal. like on a good week im done by 6 or 7 but busy season is coming and last year i was doing 7am to like 10pm some nights. i try to get to the gym 3 times a week, thats my goal, but when work goes mad it just doesnt happen
PureGym, the one near Piccadilly. its 24 hours which is the only reason i even considered it tbh. its like a 10 min walk from my office so i can go straight after work on normal days

loool the idea of me voluntarily waking up at 5:30am to go to the gym is actually hilarious. im NOT a morning person wallah. lunch breaks during busy season dont really exist either, you eat at your desk while working. the after work thing is what i do normally — finish at 6ish, walk to PureGym, do like an hour, go home. thats the routine when things are calm

weekends during busy season... i usually have saturday off but sometimes i have to go in. sunday is always free though alhamdulillah. yeah i think maybe doing 2 proper sessions on the weekend and then trying to squeeze one in during the week might work? like monday or tuesday evening before it gets too mental

mix tbh. i do weights — mostly lower body and some upper body. and then like 15-20 mins cardio at the end, usually the stairmaster because the treadmill is dead boring. ive been trying to get more into strength training but i feel like i dont really know what im doing half the time loool. like i watch videos on youtube and try to copy the exercises but idk if my form is right

squats on the smith machine, leg press, hip thrusts with a barbell (these are so awkward to set up on my own btw), and sometimes lunges when i can be bothered. for upper body i just do like lat pulldowns and some dumbbell stuff but nothing structured
yes please that would be so helpful. nothing too complicated tho because honestly if its like a 15 exercise plan im just gonna look at it and panic. keep it simple init

this is actually perfect. not overwhelming at all. im saving this. i think the midweek one is especially good because if im knackered from work at least its short and i can just get it done and go home. wallah thank you this is way better than my current approach of just wandering around the gym doing random exercises
need advice on a flatmate situation if youve got a sec

ok so basically me and my flatmate Zara have been having this ongoing disagreement about the heating. we live in Ancoats and our flat is nice but its one of those new builds where the insulation is actually decent, so I dont think we need the heating on as much as she does. but shes always cold and keeps whacking it up to like 23 degrees and our energy bill last month was disgusting

we split everything 50/50 — rent, council tax, energy, wifi. weve kept it simple since we moved in. which is fine when the bills are normal but when the gas bill is like 40 quid more than it should be because shes got the flat feeling like the sahara desert im like... babes this is not fair loool

yeah thats actually what we usually do. i go to hers on sunday for dinner with the family and she always sends me home with like 4 containers of food. somali food keeps well tbh, the rice and stew stuff lasts ages in the fridge. i just ran out quicker this week because i havent had time to go shopping for anything else to supplement it

how do you study for an exam when you physically do not have time to study for an exam. asking for myself

ive done some but its been so patchy. like i did a chunk of revision in january but then busy season kicked in and ive barely touched it since. i do maybe 30 minutes here and there on the weekend but thats it. its the advanced audit paper and theres SO much content. i keep telling myself ill catch up but i never do because im exhausted from work

honestly during the week maybe 45 minutes to an hour in the evening if i force myself. weekends i can probably do 3-4 hours on saturday and then sunday ive got family stuff but maybe 2 hours in the evening. its not a lot. the problem is im doing 12-14 hour days at work and by the time i get home my brain is completely gone. like i open the textbook and the words just swim

so im currently doing my ACA right, ive got an exam in a few days actually. but ive been thinking about what comes after. like once i finish ACA what do i do to actually stand out. and ive been looking into doing CIMA as well

exactly that — the strategic side. like ACA is teaching me a lot about audit and compliance but i want to understand the business side too. management accounting, decision making, commercial strategy. if i had both qualifications id be able to go into basically any finance role. audit, advisory, industry, FP&A, whatever. it makes you way more versatile

alongside honestly. i know that sounds insane. but theres a pathway where if youve already passed certain ACA papers you get exemptions from some of the CIMA papers. so you dont have to do the full thing from scratch. i think you can knock off like half the CIMA syllabus with ACA exemptions

loool ok i wont lie the ACA alone is killing me right now. ive literally been cramming for this exam thats in 3 days and im barely keeping it together. BUT i think once this exam is done and busy season is over ill have more capacity. like april through december is much calmer and thats when i could do the CIMA papers

thats a really good point. i need to show that ive mapped it out not just that im keen. cos if i just go in and say i want to do CIMA hes gonna be like cool but when and how and i need to have answers. alright im actually really excited about this now. double qualified at 27-28 would look insane on a CV wallah. quick question about Excel. I've got a VLOOKUP situation that's driving me insane

okay so I've got two sheets. Sheet 1 has a list of entity codes and their corresponding revenue figures. Sheet 2 has the same entity codes but I need to pull in the revenue AND a status column from Sheet 1. the basic VLOOKUP works fine for the revenue column but I need to do a second VLOOKUP for the status and my manager said I should nest them instead of having two separate columns with two separate VLOOKUPs? I don't even know what that means tbh

yeah entity code is column A on both sheets. revenue is column C on Sheet 1 and status is column E. I've already got the revenue VLOOKUP working in a separate column on Sheet 2 so that's fine. but he specifically said "nest them" and I don't want to go back and ask what he meant loool
wallah I think you're right it's the INDEX MATCH thing. he's always going on about how VLOOKUP is outdated. let me try that. so the MATCH part finds the row and INDEX pulls the value from that row?

okay that actually makes so much sense when you explain it like that. I've been avoiding INDEX MATCH for like a year because it looked complicated but it's literally just two steps. let me try it hold on
RIGHT okay it's working. I did =INDEX(Sheet1!$E:$E, MATCH(A2, Sheet1!$A:$A, 0)) for the status column and it's pulling the right values. dragged it down and everything looks correct. I feel powerful

oh that's smart yeah there's actually 2 rows showing #N/A. probably entities that got removed or something. I'll add the IFERROR wrapper. thanks so much this was bare useful, my manager's gonna think I've been doing INDEX MATCH for years loool

actually wait sorry one more thing. is there a way to do INDEX MATCH but match on TWO columns? like if I needed to match on entity code AND a date? because some entities appear multiple times with different months
I think we've got 365 at work because we have the cloud stuff. I'll try the XLOOKUP one, that looks way cleaner. honestly this is dead helpful I'm saving this entire chat for future reference loool

I need to vent about something that happened at work today before I lose my mind

so I spent literally three days on this analysis right. like I built the whole thing from scratch — the data extraction, the reconciliation, the variance analysis, the commentary. THREE DAYS. stayed late two of those days to get it done properly. and today in a client meeting a senior partner presented it as his own work. didn't mention me once. not even a "the team put this together." just straight up "I've prepared this analysis" while sharing MY slides

there were like 4 of us from the firm in the meeting. the partner, a senior manager, me, and another associate. the senior manager definitely knows I did it because she reviewed my draft on Monday. but nobody said anything. everyone just let it happen. I will. thanks for letting me rant honestly I was about to text something aggressive in the team group chat which would have been a terrible idea loool

I need to tighten up a skeleton argument before trial tomorrow. Murder case, joint enterprise. The argument's become rather unwieldy and I'm not sure the structure is doing the defence any favours. Can you help me think through the architecture of it?

Prosecution theory is parasitic accessory liability — they say my client foresaw that the principal might use lethal force during what was meant to be a robbery. Defence line is twofold: first, insufficient evidence of foresight; second, even if there was a shared plan for the robbery, the use of a knife was a fundamental departure from anything my client contemplated. The skeleton is sitting at fourteen pages, which is about six too many for what it needs to say.

That's a much cleaner skeleton. Section III is the one giving me trouble. The prosecution rely on three things: a text message chain between my client and the principal two hours before, CCTV showing them arriving together, and a witness who claims she heard my client say "whatever it takes" outside the property. The text messages are ambiguous at best — they discuss the plan to enter the property but there's nothing about weapons. The CCTV simply shows them walking side by side. The witness is a neighbour with a conviction for perverting the course of justice.
Yes, draft paragraph C for me — the "whatever it takes" point. That's the one I keep rewriting and it's still not landing properly.

That's quite good. Much tighter than what I had. I think I was trying too hard to be devastating in print when I should save that for the courtroom. One adjustment — can you make the credibility point slightly more restrained? I don't want the judge to think I'm hanging the entire defence on attacking the witness. It should read as a secondary observation, not a primary assault.

That's the right pitch. I'll fold that in tonight. The other thing I wanted to ask about is the Jogee point in section II. Since the Supreme Court decision, the application has been rather inconsistent across the circuits. I want to make sure I'm citing the most useful post-Jogee authorities. What are the key cases I should be looking at for the proposition that foresight alone is no longer sufficient?

Yes, I'll cross-check those on Westlaw when I get into chambers tomorrow morning. I'm at 4 Brick Court so the library access is decent, and our clerks are quite good at flagging recent authorities if I give them a heads-up tonight. Let me think about section II for a moment.

Quite right. Here's what I'm thinking for section II — tell me if this works as a structure. First paragraph: state the Jogee test in three sentences, no more. Second paragraph: one sentence distinguishing the old Chan Wing-Siu position to make clear what the prosecution cannot rely on. Third paragraph: bridge to sections III and IV by framing the evidential question the jury must answer. That's it. No more than a page.

No, I think I've got enough to draft it myself now. You've been genuinely useful — I was going round in circles on this before. I need to finish this tonight because I've got an early train from Hackney Central into the Temple in the morning and I'd rather not be editing on the Overground.
Thank you. I suspect I'll be back at some point this week to think through the cross-examination strategy for that witness, but that's a problem for Wednesday. Good night.

I've taken on a pupil this year — second six — and she's bright but her written advocacy is letting her down. I want to put together a structured feedback plan rather than just scribbling in margins. Any thoughts on how to approach this systematically?

The main issue is that she writes like she's still at university — every argument is hedged with three qualifications and she cites authority for propositions that don't need it. She'll spend half a page establishing that the burden of proof lies with the prosecution, as though the judge might have forgotten. It reads like an essay, not an argument.

The "So What" test is rather good — I might steal that phrase. The modelling exercise is something I should do more of. My own pupil supervisor was quite hands-off, which suited me at the time, but I think she needs more direct guidance.

Let me think about what exercise to set her. She's got a plea in mitigation coming up next week — first one she'll do on her feet. I'd like to give her a written exercise beforehand that mirrors the kind of concision she'll need in oral advocacy.
Yes, give me a set of facts. Something with enough complexity that she has to choose what to prioritise — I don't want it to be so straightforward that the mitigation writes itself.

That's well constructed. The previous victimisation is a nice trap — a pupil will want to include it but it's almost impossible to deploy without either inviting sympathy too crudely or suggesting he was predisposed to violence, which cuts the wrong way. I'll use this.

Out of interest, how would you prioritise if you were drafting the mitigation?

I'd put the caring responsibilities first, actually. The guilty plea discount is almost mechanical — the judge will apply it regardless of how eloquently you present it. But the mother's situation requires the judge to exercise judgment, and that's where advocacy makes a difference. But your instinct on what to leave out is spot on. The previous victimisation is exactly where a pupil goes wrong — it feels relevant but it's a minefield.

This is useful. I want to get her thinking about these choices herself rather than defaulting to the comprehensive approach they teach at law school.

I think I've got enough to work with for now. Though it does make me reflect — when I was doing my LLB at King's, nobody told us that the transition from academic writing to practice would be this steep. I spent my first year of pupillage unlearning half of what I'd been taught about legal writing. I'd rather she didn't have to go through that same process entirely by trial and error.

She's been sitting in already, which is part of why I think the penny is close to dropping — she can see the difference, she just can't replicate it in her own writing yet. Repetition and targeted exercises should close that gap. Right, I need to draft the brief for this exercise before I forget the details. Thank you for the help.

Actually — one more thought. If the buffer-day approach works well, do you think it's worth keeping the pattern year-round, or should I revert to tighter scheduling once the winter stretch passes? I don't want to lose momentum professionally by being permanently cautious.

No, I think that covers it. Two emails sent, diary strategy in place. A considerably more productive ten minutes than the alternative, which was staring at my inbox and feeling irritated about the whole situation. Thank you.
