iPhone 14 Pro. Since the last software update — I think it was iOS 18.2 or thereabouts — my notifications have gone erratic. Some come through immediately, others are delayed by ten, fifteen minutes. Text messages from solicitors, calendar reminders, the lot. For someone in my line of work that's not a minor inconvenience.
I hadn't looked at the Scheduled Summary. I'd never have turned that on deliberately — batching notifications defeats the entire purpose of having them. Let me check. Give me a moment.

Right. Scheduled Summary was on. I have no memory of enabling it. It had Messages, Mail, and my calendar app all bundled into it with delivery times at 8am and 6pm. That explains everything — things sent at 7am wouldn't come through until 8. Absurd.

I've switched it off and restarted. We'll see. It's rather alarming that an update can silently alter how your notifications work. I've had a solicitor ring me twice this week asking whether I'd seen his email — I had, just twenty minutes after it mattered.
I'll do that now. While I have you — is there any way to prevent future updates from resetting these preferences? Or am I going to have to audit my notification settings after every point release?

Turning off automatic updates is sensible. I'll do that. I'd rather spend two minutes reading release notes than discover mid-trial that my phone has decided to curate my notifications for me. One more thing — is there a way to test that the fix has actually worked, short of waiting for someone to message me and hoping it arrives promptly?
I'll do the calendar reminder test now. Straightforward enough. Thank you — this has been genuinely useful. I was half-convinced the phone was failing and I'd need to replace it.
I have a Crown Court trial starting on the tenth of February at Snaresbrook and I need to pressure-test my defence strategy. Can you help me think through some angles?

Client is charged with robbery — specifically robbery with a firearm, section 17 of the Firearms Act alongside the Theft Act offences. Prosecution says he entered a bookmaker's in Ilford on the fourteenth of September last year, produced a handgun, and left with just over four thousand pounds in cash. Their case rests on CCTV, a cell site analysis placing his phone in the area, and an identification by one witness — a customer who was in the shop.

The CCTV is their weakest link, which is partly why I'm cautiously optimistic. The footage shows a man in a dark hoodie with a face covering — balaclava, the prosecution says, though it could frankly be a pulled-up scarf. No facial features visible. They haven't instructed a facial mapping expert. They're essentially asking the jury to accept that because the build is similar and the phone was nearby, the man on the screen is my client.

The eyewitness is where it gets interesting. VIPER was conducted, and the witness picked my client out. But — and this is significant — the witness initially described the robber as being around five foot ten. My client is six foot one. The witness also said the robber had light brown skin. My client is dark-skinned. The description was given about forty minutes after the incident.

Cell site puts his phone within the coverage area of a mast that serves most of central Ilford. The radius is roughly a kilometre. He lives in Ilford, so being within range of that mast on a Saturday afternoon is entirely unremarkable. The prosecution expert concedes the data is consistent with normal daily movement in the area.

No weapon recovered. No forensic evidence linking him to the scene. No financial evidence. He was arrested three weeks later based on the VIPER identification. His flat was searched — nothing found. The four thousand pounds has never been traced.

I'm inclined to keep him out. His account is that he was at home watching football — Leyton Orient were playing that afternoon, he supports them. But he was alone, so there's no corroboration. Putting him in the box opens him to cross-examination and his previous convictions could come in through bad character if he attacks prosecution witnesses. He has a prior for a commercial burglary from 2019.

Two weeks feels tight but manageable. I've got most of my cross-examination prepared for the main witnesses. The eyewitness is the one I need to get right — it's the spine of their case, and if I can show the jury the description simply doesn't match, the rest falls apart. I'm working on the sequencing of my questions now.

Not today — I think I need to draft them myself first and then perhaps come back to refine. But this has been extremely useful for organising my thinking. The framework is clear: dismantle the identification, neutralise the cell site, highlight the absence of any corroborating evidence, and keep my client out of the box. That's the case.
Thank you. Snaresbrook isn't my favourite court but the case is sound. I'll be back before the trial starts.

I need a recommendation for somewhere to take a friend for her birthday dinner this Saturday. East London ideally, somewhere with good food and a decent atmosphere. She's turning forty so it should feel like an occasion.

Just the two of us. She eats everything, no restrictions. Budget — I'd say up to a hundred a head is fine for a fortieth. Hackney or Dalston area would be convenient. She loves Turkish and Middle Eastern food but I'm open to suggestions beyond that.
Berber & Q sounds promising. The cocktail list isn't relevant for me — I don't drink. Haven't touched alcohol in two years. But Sophie enjoys a good cocktail so that works in her favour.

Good to know about the non-alcoholic options. I get rather tired of places that treat not drinking as an afterthought — sparkling water and a shrug. If they've actually put thought into it, that's a point in their favour.

Actually yes — a gift. Sophie is a photographer. Not professionally, but she's quite serious about it. Shoots on film, mostly street photography. She's not the type for generic presents. Any ideas for something thoughtful in the fifty to eighty pound range?

The photography book is the right call. She's mentioned Saul Leiter before — quite taken with his colour work. I'll try Donlon Books this week. If they don't have anything suitable I'll try online.

Actually — should I have the book gift-wrapped, or is that the sort of thing where the presentation matters less than the choice?
Restraint over spectacle is rather my philosophy as well. I'll ask Donlon to wrap it. Thank you — this has been efficient and helpful.
Perfect. Much appreciated.

I need to think through my options on the flat situation. My lease expires at the end of March and the landlord has confirmed he won't be renewing — he's selling the property. So I have roughly six weeks to find somewhere to live in London, which as you can imagine is not filling me with joy.

Assured shorthold, yes. He's served a valid section 21 notice with the correct notice period — I've checked, believe me. I'm a barrister, I know what a properly served notice looks like. So no wriggle room there. I need to be out by the thirty-first of March.

I'd like to stay in Hackney. I've been here for years and my life is built around it — the park, the transport links, the neighbourhood. Moving to Zone 4 would add an hour to my commute and I simply can't afford that with my caseload.

I can stretch to about seventeen hundred a month for a one-bed. I know that's tight for Hackney but I'm not willing to go beyond that — I've seen what happens to people who overcommit on rent and then can't absorb an unexpected expense. Clapton or Homerton would be acceptable alternatives. I grew up nearby so I know the area well enough.

Court is the problem. I've just come out of a trial at Snaresbrook and I have another case listed in three weeks. Most viewings seem to be scheduled between ten and four, which is precisely when I'm unavailable. I could ask Sophie — she's a close friend and her schedule is more flexible. But it feels odd having someone else view a flat I'll be living in.

Ground floor is a dealbreaker — I won't take a ground floor flat. Security, mainly, but also the lack of light. I need a proper desk space, enough room for my papers and books. I work from home regularly so it can't be a box room with a kitchenette. I also need decent broadband — not negotiable when you're handling case files remotely.

I've been scrolling Rightmove in the evenings but without much structure. It's demoralising, frankly. Half the flats are clearly overpriced for what they are, and the decent ones vanish before I can enquire. I saw one in Clapton last Thursday that ticked every box — Victorian conversion, first floor, bay window — and by Friday morning it was gone.

You're right. I've been treating this as a passive scroll rather than an active campaign and that's why I'm falling behind. I'll visit agencies this Saturday. The pre-drafted message is a good idea — I should have thought of that. I do the same thing with skeleton arguments at work, having templates ready to adapt.
Yes, actually. Draft me something I can adapt. Keep it concise — agents don't want an essay.

That works. Clean and to the point. I'll adapt it tonight and have it ready to go. Right — I feel marginally less overwhelmed. Six weeks is not long but it's not impossible if I approach this with the same discipline I'd bring to a case. Thank you.
I need to think through something career-related, if you don't mind being a sounding board.

I've been doing more asylum and immigration defence work over the past year. It's become quite a significant part of my caseload, and frankly, it's the work I find most meaningful. But I keep running into the limits of my own expertise in international human rights frameworks.

Formal study, actually. I've been looking at doing an LLM in human rights law at UCL. Part-time, so I could keep practising. I haven't committed to anything yet, but the prospectus is sitting on my kitchen table and I keep coming back to it.

A bit of both. The practical side is obvious — time. I already work long hours and I'm not sure where I'd fit seminars and reading. But there's also the question of whether it would genuinely change my practice, or whether it's just an expensive credential.

The former. I had a case last month where I knew there was a stronger argument to be made under Article 3, but I couldn't quite marshal the Strasbourg case law as effectively as I wanted. I managed, but I was conscious of the gap. That's not a comfortable feeling when someone's deportation is at stake.

I've had a quick look. The international refugee law module is exactly what drew me in. There's also one on economic and social rights that could be useful for the housing cases I pick up through legal aid. Could you help me think about how to structure a conversation with my clerk about this? I'd need to manage my listing diary carefully if I'm doing it part-time.
That's rather helpful, actually. Yes, some bullet points I could take into the meeting would be good. Keep it concise — my clerk appreciates brevity as much as I do.
Perfect. One last thing — do you know when the application deadline typically is for UCL's part-time LLM? I want to make sure I haven't already missed it for a September start.
Good. I'll look into it this week. Thank you — this has been a useful exercise in organising my own thoughts.
I need to get my head around the current state of self-defence case law in England and Wales. Can you walk me through the key authorities?

The Williams direction is the one I'm most interested in. I have a client who says she believed she was about to be attacked, but the objective evidence for that belief is rather thin. Walk me through how Williams applies.

She says the complainant moved towards her aggressively after a verbal altercation. There were witnesses, but their accounts are inconsistent — some say the complainant was moving towards her, others say he was standing still. No CCTV.
She pushed him and he fell, hit his head on the kerb. He's sustained a head injury — not life-threatening, but significant. She's been charged with GBH under section 20.

Trial is in a few weeks. I'm drafting the defence case statement now and want to make sure my legal framework is tight. What about pre-emptive self-defence — is there anything useful on the point that she didn't have to wait to be struck first?
That would be useful. Keep it to the legal framework — I'll handle the factual narrative myself.

No, that's well put. I'll weave the factual narrative around it. One more thing — any thoughts on how to handle the witnesses whose accounts contradict my client? I'm not suggesting they're lying, but their vantage points were poor.
Quite right. Thank you — that's given me a solid foundation to work from.
So the CPS have just served three hundred pages of unused material at half four on a Friday. Trial is Monday. I am incandescent.

A drugs conspiracy, Crown Court. My client has been in custody for months. The unused material should have been with me weeks ago — my instructing solicitor chased them repeatedly. And now it arrives, all at once, with no time to review properly. Some of it may actually assist the defence, which makes the delay even more galling. My client has been sitting in custody while the prosecution sat on material that could help him.

Both, frankly. This particular office is notorious for it. But it's also systemic — the entire disclosure regime is buckling under the weight of underfunding and overwork. I have some sympathy for individual caseworkers who are drowning, but the institution has a legal obligation, and my client's right to a fair trial is not negotiable.

I'll be applying for an adjournment first thing Monday morning. But it makes my blood boil because the judge will probably grant it, the CPS will face no real consequences, and my client stays in custody for another few weeks while everyone pretends this is just how things work. It is not just how things work. It is a failure.
The wasted costs application is tempting. I've never actually done one — do you know how the threshold works?

I have five emails from my instructing solicitor chasing disclosure over the past six weeks, all met with vague assurances that it was "in hand." The schedule of unused material was only served on Friday alongside the documents themselves.

You're quite right about the tone. I save the outrage for conversations like this one. In court I'll be surgical about it. Though I confess I may allow myself one pointed observation about the prosecution's interpretation of the word 'continuing' in continuing duty of disclosure.
Indeed. Right, I'd better spend what's left of my weekend reading three hundred pages of material the CPS couldn't be bothered to send me on time. Thank you for the assist.
Slightly unusual request. I'm attempting to cook jollof rice for the first time in years and I'm already second-guessing myself.

I have my mum's recipe, written on the back of an envelope in handwriting that assumes I already know what I'm doing. "Blend the tomatoes and peppers, fry the base, add the rice, you know the rest." I do not, in fact, know the rest.

Most of it tracks. She does mention tomato paste specifically — "fry the tin tomato paste first until it's dark" — and she underlines "do not open the lid" twice with what I think is an angry exclamation mark. My question is about the rice. She says to use long grain but I've also seen people insist on basmati. Does it matter?

Long grain it is. Now, the scotch bonnets. I enjoy heat but I don't want to render this inedible. She's written "2 or 3" which in my experience with her cooking means the dish will be incendiary. What's a sensible starting point?

I've got them. There's a good greengrocer near me that always has them in stock. Right — one blended, one whole. That sounds like a reasonable compromise between flavour and being able to feel my tongue afterwards. What about the "party rice" smoky flavour I've tasted at gatherings? My mum's version has this slightly charred note at the bottom that I've never been able to replicate.
I do have a cast-iron pot, mercifully. One last question — timing. I'm having people round at seven. What time should I realistically start this to have it ready without rushing?
Rather a lot more structured than the envelope suggests. One more thing — I was thinking of doing a side of fried plantain. Any tips on getting it right, or is it as simple as it looks?
Perfect. I think I'm actually looking forward to this now rather than dreading it. Thank you — I feel considerably more confident about the whole enterprise than I did twenty minutes ago.

I've run out of things to listen to during my commute. Can you recommend some podcasts? I'm after legal commentary, possibly true crime if it's intelligent, or political analysis. Nothing that talks down to its audience.

I already listen to Law in Action and The Rest is Politics, so you've read me correctly. The Daniel Morgan one sounds interesting — I remember the case vaguely but never followed the detail. How long is the series?
That does sound right up my street. What about In the Dark — you said the second season is about prosecutorial misconduct. What's the outline?

Six trials for the same offence. I can't quite fathom the double jeopardy implications under their system, but that's a different conversation. Right, both of those are going on my list. What about something a bit more niche — anything good on sentencing policy or criminal justice reform specifically?

Ear Hustle is one I've heard mentioned before but never tried. The fact that it's produced inside a prison is genuinely interesting — I spend a great deal of time thinking about what happens to people after sentencing, and very little time hearing from them directly.
That's a rather good point about mitigation. Understanding the reality of what you're asking a judge to impose — or not impose — ought to be fundamental. I'll start with that one this week.
Quite sufficient. Actually, one last thing — do you know if any of these work well at 1.5x speed? I sometimes speed up podcasts when the pacing is slow, but some don't survive the treatment.
Sensible advice. Right, that's genuinely helpful. Thank you — a productive use of ten minutes.
I need you to help me make sense of something before I lose my composure entirely. The Ministry of Justice has just published the latest legal aid expenditure figures. Have you seen them?

Criminal legal aid spending has dropped in real terms again. We're now at roughly 40% below 2010 levels when you adjust for inflation. Forty percent. And the government has the audacity to talk about access to justice as though it's something they value.

Both. I do privately funded defence work primarily, but I still take legal aid cases — I always have, on principle. The rates are an insult. I had a solicitor ring me last week about a case, serious fraud matter, multi-handed. The legal aid rates on offer meant I'd effectively be working at less than minimum wage once you factor in preparation time. And this is specialist advocacy we're talking about, not shelf-stacking. No disrespect to anyone who stacks shelves, but the skill set is rather different.

Precisely. The juniors can't afford to do it because they're drowning in debt from training. The seniors won't do it because the rates are beneath them — and I understand that, even if I find it disheartening. So who's left? The people in the middle who still believe in something, grinding themselves down. I've watched colleagues leave the criminal Bar entirely. Good advocates. People who cared. Gone to commercial work or left law altogether.

Funding is the foundation. You can restructure all you like but if the money isn't there, it's rearranging furniture in a burning building. The CLAIR recommendations were a start but they didn't go far enough and implementation has been glacial. What I'd want to see is legal aid rates indexed to inflation at a minimum, with proper recognition of preparation time. The current system pretends that a barrister can prepare a complex case in a fraction of the time it actually takes. It's dishonest accounting.

The CBA has been vocal. They organised the action in 2022 which did produce some movement. But there's a limit to what industrial action achieves when the public doesn't fully understand the issue. People hear 'barristers on strike' and think we're all earning six figures complaining about champagne budgets. They don't see the junior tenant in a bedsit in Tottenham preparing a murder case for the equivalent of twelve pounds an hour. The narrative is broken and nobody in government has any incentive to fix it.

Bit of both, honestly. I've been asked to speak on a panel next month about the future of criminal defence and I want to have the numbers sharp. But yes, sometimes one simply needs to say it out loud to someone who'll listen without glazing over. Thank you for that.

A comparison with other jurisdictions would be quite useful, actually. I know Australia and Canada have had their own issues with legal aid funding, but I'd like to understand how England and Wales compares. Do we spend less per capita?

That is useful. The contrast between the constitutional guarantee in the US and the reality of public defenders carrying impossible caseloads is a rather damning illustration. We don't even have the constitutional guarantee, which makes the political will to fund it even more fragile. Right, I think I have enough to begin preparing my remarks. I may come back to you for help sharpening the statistics before the panel.
Quick question. If someone asks you what postgraduate qualifications are worth doing for a practising barrister, what would you say?

I was. Past tense. I'd been looking at the LLM in human rights law at UCL. Seemed like it might sharpen things up, give me an academic grounding in some of the policy questions I deal with daily. International criminal law modules looked interesting too.

I spoke to three people who actually did it. Two barristers and one solicitor-advocate, all criminal practitioners. The consensus was unanimous and rather deflating. They said the academic content was fine but it didn't translate to practice in any meaningful way. One of them described it as 'an expensive year of reading things I could have read anyway.' The other said the networking was the only real value, and you can network without paying fifteen thousand pounds for the privilege.

One thought it might have been a marginal factor in getting onto a Recorder panel, but she admitted she couldn't be sure. The other two said it made no difference whatsoever to their practice or their standing. And that was the nail in the coffin, really. I'm not interested in credentials for their own sake. If it doesn't make me a better advocate or open a door that's otherwise shut, it's dead. The whole idea is dead.

Quite. And it's not just the money, it's the opportunity cost. That's a year I could spend building my practice, taking on more complex cases, developing a genuine specialism through actual work rather than coursework. I'd rather invest that time in something that moves the needle.

I've been gravitating towards serious fraud and financial crime anyway. The cases are intellectually demanding, the preparation is intense, and frankly the fees are better which means I can continue to take legal aid work on the side without bankrupting myself. It feels like a more honest path than collecting letters after my name.

Now that's a sensible suggestion. Short courses I can manage. Something I can do over a weekend or a few evenings without derailing everything else. I'll look into the FLA. Do you know if the SFO runs any practitioner workshops?

Good. I'll have a look at what's available this autumn. Far more proportionate than committing to a full master's that three separate people have told me was a waste of their time. Right, I need to get back to a skeleton argument. Thank you.
I need to think through some logistics and you might be useful for this. I'm trying to book flights to Lagos for December and the prices are already eye-watering.

I'm flying out on the 20th of December. That's fairly fixed — I need to be there for Christmas with my family and my mother will have opinions if I arrive on Christmas Eve looking half-dead from a red-eye. The return is more flexible, probably early January.

Direct if at all possible. I've done the Addis Ababa connection before and the layover was grim — six hours in the transit lounge with nothing to show for it. BA from Heathrow is my preference. What sort of prices should I expect for the 20th?

I'll do economy. I'm not so grand that I need a flat bed for six hours. Though I will want an aisle seat — I refuse to be trapped by a stranger's sleeping arrangements. Can you remind me what the current baggage allowance is for BA economy to Lagos?

Good point about the gifts. My mother has a list that seems to grow every year. Last Christmas I brought half of John Lewis in my suitcase. I might need the second bag. What does BA typically charge for an additional checked bag on that route?

I'll add the second bag at booking. Posting things to Lagos is an adventure I'd rather not undertake — my cousin sent a parcel last year and it took three weeks and arrived looking like it had been through a war. I'd rather just pay the baggage fee and have everything with me.

Passport is fine, I renewed it last year. And I travel on my Nigerian passport for Lagos so no visa needed. I just need to sort the flights and then work out how to clear my diary for two weeks without everything falling apart. December is quieter in the courts at least.
That's the plan. Right, I'll book this evening before the prices climb any further. Thank you — this was more useful than I expected for what started as me complaining about airline pricing.

I'm trying to draft a short professional biography for a chambers website. I've never been good at writing about myself — it always comes out either too dry or faintly embarrassing. Can you help me structure one?

Criminal defence, primarily. Serious and complex crime — I've been doing a lot of fraud and financial crime work over the past couple of years, alongside the usual serious violence, drugs conspiracies, that sort of thing. Fifteen years at the Bar. I've just joined 7 Bedford Row as a senior tenant, so the biography needs to reflect that move.

Let's draft it. Keep it tight — I don't want three pages of self-congratulation. The Bedford Row website tends towards concise profiles. Called in 2010, Lincoln's Inn. I've led in a number of multi-handed fraud trials, several serious violence matters including attempted murder, and I've done a fair amount of appellate work in the Court of Appeal Criminal Division.

That's close. A few things — drop the "Solicitors value her accessibility" line. It reads like a reference letter. And can you add something about regulatory work? I've been picking up more of that at Bedford Row. Financial services regulatory matters, FCA investigations, that sort of thing.
Better. Though I'm second-guessing the "meticulous preparation" bit. Everyone says that. It's the legal equivalent of putting 'hardworking' on your CV.

I'm good at finding the weakness in the prosecution case. That's what I do — I pull the thread until it unravels. In fraud cases particularly, that means getting deep into the documents and the financial evidence, finding the gaps and inconsistencies that the prosecution has glossed over. In violence cases it's more about the witness evidence and testing the narrative.
Yes. That works. One more thing — should I mention my previous chambers or is that not done?

Include it. I was at Brick Court for a long time and there's no bad blood — I simply outgrew it. The move to Bedford Row was about the quality of fraud and regulatory work they attract. Better fit for where my practice is going.
No, that's right. Clean and honest. I'll send it to the clerks this afternoon. Thank you — you've saved me an hour of agonising over adjectives.

I'm working on a plea in mitigation for a sentencing on Wednesday and I want to make sure the structure is as tight as possible. The client has pleaded guilty to a section 20 GBH. Can you help me think through the framework?

Right. Client is 24, no previous convictions. The offence arose from a confrontation outside a pub. The complainant made remarks about the client's girlfriend, things escalated, and my client threw a single punch which caused a fractured cheekbone. There was drink involved on both sides. He pleaded guilty at the first opportunity at the magistrates' court before it was sent to the Crown Court.

I'd argue Category 3 harm, lesser culpability. The injury, while serious enough to cross the section 20 threshold, was from a single blow and the complainant has made a full recovery. No weapon, no kicking on the ground, no sustained assault. On culpability, there was provocation and a significant degree of it — the remarks were about his girlfriend's appearance and were sexually degrading.

Exactly. I'm not saying the remarks justified the punch. Nobody's saying that. But the context matters for understanding why a young man with no history of violence suddenly threw a punch. He's not someone who goes around hitting people. He reacted badly in a situation where he was provoked. That's qualitatively different from someone who attacks a stranger for no reason.

He works as an electrician, qualified, in steady employment for three years. Lives with his girlfriend in rented accommodation. No children. His employer has written a letter confirming his job will be held open. He's also done a voluntary anger management course since the incident, which I think is significant — it shows insight and a willingness to address the behaviour without being told to.

Good. That sequence works. I want to finish with a clear ask. I'm going to invite the court to impose a community order with unpaid work. I think a suspended sentence is unnecessary given the combination of factors we've discussed. What's your view on whether that's too ambitious?

That's well put. I'll use that framing. Actually, one thing I'm slightly uncertain about — the voluntary anger management course. Should I produce a certificate or letter from the course provider, or is it sufficient to refer to it in submissions?

Good point. I'll chase the solicitor for both documents today. One more question — what about a pre-sentence report? The court hasn't ordered one. Should I be requesting an adjournment for one, or does that risk losing momentum?

That's sensible. Prepare for the best outcome but have the PSR argument in reserve if needed. Right, I think I genuinely have what I need now. Structure is clear, the argument hangs together, and the ask is realistic. Thank you.

I need a reading list. Miscarriages of justice, wrongful convictions — that territory. Preferably well-researched rather than sensationalised. I'm a criminal defence barrister so I don't need the hand-holding introductions to how the system works, I want the substance.

Both, really, but if pressed I'd lean toward systemic analysis. I've read Stevenson — quite good, though the American sentencing landscape is rather alien. What about anything focused on the UK system specifically?

I've read Stafford Smith. Haven't read Naughton, which is rather embarrassing given I should know that work. The Cardiff 3 case is one I know well from a legal perspective but I haven't read Sekar's account of it. That's going on the list.

The Godsey one sounds particularly useful. Cognitive bias in investigation is something I see constantly — you get a detective who's decided on a theory in the first forty-eight hours and everything after that is just confirmation. It's maddening.
Actually, false confessions are quite relevant to something I'm dealing with at the moment. Is there a definitive text on that specifically?

It's a significant part of the prosecution's case, yes. The interview was conducted over several hours and my client's account changed quite substantially during that period, which the prosecution is presenting as evidence of guilt — 'he changed his story because he was caught out' — whereas I'd argue the changes are consistent with someone under extreme pressure gradually saying what they think the interviewing officers want to hear. The Gudjonsson work sounds directly applicable.

One more thought — are any of these available as audiobooks? I have a reasonable commute and it seems a better use of the time than listening to the Today programme work itself into a state about whatever the crisis of the morning is.

The Godsey is going on the list as well. I've got a case at the moment where exactly that dynamic is at play — the investigation locked onto my client early and everything since has been confirmation. Thank you, this is a proper list. I'll start with the Godsey for immediate practical purposes and work through the others.

Quick question — I've just set up a new Samsung Galaxy S25 and I'm trying to get my work email configured. The IT department at chambers sent instructions but they're clearly written for iPhone users and entirely useless to me. I need to set up Microsoft Outlook with our Exchange server. What's the best approach on Android?

Microsoft 365, I believe. We switched over last year. I'll go with the Outlook app — I used it on my old iPhone and it was perfectly adequate. The S25 is rather different to navigate but I'm getting the hang of it.

The notification control is actually one of the reasons I switched. On the iPhone everything was all or nothing — either an app could interrupt me or it couldn't. I need to be reachable for urgent matters from the court listing office but I don't need my phone buzzing every time someone sends a round-robin email about the chambers Christmas party. Android seems to handle that distinction rather well.

The Focused Inbox approach sounds ideal. I'll set that up. What about transferring my contacts and calendar from the iPhone? I've already moved the SIM across but I gather the data migration is a separate matter.

I do, yes. It's sitting on my desk looking rather forlorn. I'll try Smart Switch — that sounds like the least tedious option. One more thing: is there a good password manager that works well on the S25? I was using the iCloud Keychain which obviously doesn't carry over.

Bitwarden. Open source and independently audited appeals to the part of me that cross-examines everything. I'll export the passwords before I wipe the iPhone. The S25 is genuinely impressive, by the way — the screen is beautiful and I feel like I have far more control over how the phone actually works. I should have made this switch years ago.

I would not have thought of that. Solicitors send me text messages about case updates regularly — if those were vanishing into the ether that would be a genuine problem. I'll disable iMessage before I do anything else. One more thing — the S25 camera seems quite good. Is there a way to scan documents with it directly? I sometimes need to capture case documents quickly when I'm away from a proper scanner.
Microsoft Lens makes sense given the rest of the setup. Thank you — this has been considerably more useful than the IT department's instructions.

I have spent the last forty-five minutes standing on a platform at Mile End because of yet another signal failure on the Central line. Forty-five minutes. I had a conference with counsel at two o'clock and I am going to be catastrophically late. Is there a faster alternative route I can take from Mile End to Holborn right now?
It's twenty past one. The conference is at two at chambers. I'm getting a taxi. This is absurd. The Central line has had signal failures three times in the past fortnight. Three times.

It is genuinely unacceptable for a city of this size. I pay a not-insignificant amount for an annual Travelcard and the service I receive in return is, frankly, contemptuous. There are clients at Crown Court hearings, there are hearings at the Old Bailey, and I cannot reliably get to any of them because a signal built in 1993 has decided not to function.

I am not arriving at the Old Bailey on a bicycle in a wig and gown carrying three lever arch files, no. I appreciate the lateral thinking but the answer to a broken public transport system is not 'use a different mode of transport,' it's 'fix the system.' I'm in the taxi now. Driver says twenty minutes.

I do have Citymapper, actually, which is why I knew the Central line was down before I got to the station — but the District line was also showing delays, so there was no good option. The whole network seems to be held together with optimism and cable ties. We're coming through Aldgate now. Should be there in ten minutes.

Quite. Arriving flustered is not a good look when one is supposed to be the calm, authoritative voice in the room. I do wonder whether TfL has any concept of the cumulative economic cost of this unreliability. It's not just inconvenience — it's professional appointments missed, client relationships damaged, court time wasted. Multiply that across every commuter on the Central line and the figure must be staggering.

That analogy is rather uncomfortably apt. I suppose the question is whether anyone with actual authority is listening, or whether we're all just shouting into the void. The mayor's office puts out statements about 'record investment in transport' but the daily experience of using the network tells a rather different story.
Indeed. Right, we're pulling up now. Thank you for the route advice — and for letting me vent. Back to the day job.

I watched a documentary last night that has left me quite unsettled. It was about Andrew Malkinson — the man who spent seventeen years in prison for a rape he didn't commit. Are you familiar with the case?

Several things. The CCRC rejected his applications multiple times despite what now appears to be clear evidence of problems with the original identification procedure. The lineup was conducted in circumstances that were, at best, questionable. And the fact that GMP had DNA evidence sitting in storage that could have resolved the matter years earlier — it's unconscionable.

Yes, and that was perhaps the most affecting part. He was effectively punished for maintaining his innocence. The parole system requires you to demonstrate remorse and engage with offending behaviour programmes, which means an innocent person is faced with an impossible choice: lie about something you didn't do in order to secure release, or tell the truth and remain in prison indefinitely. He chose the truth and it cost him seventeen years.

Both, if I'm honest. I do criminal defence precisely because of cases like this. The system is capable of catastrophic failure, and when it fails, it destroys lives. I'd like recommendations for similar documentaries — well-made ones, not the sensationalised true crime variety.

I've seen Making a Murderer — the Dassey interrogation was appalling. I haven't seen The Phantom or The Innocence Files. I'll start with The Innocence Files given the structured approach to different types of failure. It's rather telling, isn't it, that most of the rigorous work in this area is American. There's a squeamishness in this country about confronting the possibility that the English criminal justice system gets it wrong. We're quite comfortable pointing at American injustices from a distance while being rather less willing to examine our own.

The complacency point is well made. I encounter it regularly — the quiet assumption that because the system has certain procedural safeguards, it must be producing just outcomes. But procedural correctness and substantive justice are not the same thing. You can follow every rule impeccably and still convict the wrong person.

A prosecution-led review unit would be fascinating, though I imagine the institutional resistance would be formidable. No organisation enjoys being told to look for its own mistakes. Still, if the alternative is another Malkinson — another seventeen years — then the discomfort seems a rather small price.

Quite right. The press can be maddening when it comes to criminal trials — the sensationalism, the presumption of guilt — but when investigative journalists turn their attention to systemic failure, they serve an essential function. Thank you for the recommendations and the discussion. I have some viewing to do.

I need to sort out a weekly schedule that accommodates a new gym routine. I've started boxing at a gym in Bethnal Green — classes are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday evenings at half six. The problem is that court days are unpredictable and I frequently don't leave chambers until gone six. How do other people manage fixed-time fitness commitments around demanding work?

About three weeks. So yes, still at the stage where if I miss too many sessions the whole thing could collapse. The gym does have morning sessions — seven o'clock on Tuesdays and Thursdays — but I am categorically not a morning person. The idea of being punched before breakfast is deeply unappealing.

They do have open gym time, actually. I could use the bags outside of class hours. That's a reasonable fallback.

As for why boxing — I'd been running three mornings a week, 5K round Victoria Park, but I've given it up. It stopped doing what I needed it to do. My mind would wander straight back to cases within the first kilometre. Boxing is entirely different. The focus required is absolute. You cannot think about a problematic cross-examination while someone is throwing combinations at you. It empties my head in a way the running never quite managed.

Open gym runs until nine, I think. So even if I left chambers at seven, I could get to Bethnal Green by half past and still get a decent session in. That's actually quite workable. The gym is only about fifteen minutes from where I live, which helps.

The sofa is indeed a formidable opponent. Taking the bag to chambers is a good suggestion. I'll need a locker at the gym for the wraps and gloves though — I can't have those in my bag at court. Rather undermines the professional image. The trainer, Kofi, is excellent by the way — demanding but encouraging. He's already noticed when I've missed a session and sent a message asking if I'm coming to the next one.

That's sensible. I'll speak to him. One last thing — any advice on recovery? I am thirty-seven and my body is letting me know about it after every session. My shoulders in particular are quite vocal in their objections.

I will say I'm already sleeping better on training days, which alone makes it worthwhile. The magnesium is a good suggestion — I'll pick some up. And I'll mention the shoulder to Kofi in case it is a form issue. Actually, one more thing — do I need to worry about hand injuries? I've heard boxing can be quite hard on the wrists and knuckles, and I rather need my hands to function for writing submissions.

Noted. I'll ask Kofi about the wrapping — I've been doing it myself based on a video I watched and I suspect it's not quite right. Thank you — this has been genuinely helpful. I feel like I have an actual plan now rather than just hoping I can make it work.
I need to think through something practical. I've been looking at flats in Islington and I want to weigh up whether it actually makes sense.

Commute, primarily. I work at chambers in Bedford Row and Islington would put me significantly closer. At the moment I'm in Hackney, which I love, but the journey in the mornings is starting to wear on me. I cycle when the weather cooperates, which is about twenty-five minutes, but otherwise it's the Overground and then the Tube — closer to forty-five with the changeover. From Islington I could walk to chambers in under half an hour.

One-beds and small two-beds, mostly around Barnsbury and Canonbury. Rent is higher than what I pay now, but not catastrophically so — perhaps two to three hundred more a month. I could absorb it. The issue isn't really financial. It's Hackney. I've lived there for years. I know the neighbourhood properly — the market, the coffee shops, the park. I've got a life there that isn't connected to work. Moving to Islington feels like letting chambers consume another piece of my geography. I'm not sure I could leave Hackney without losing something I can't quite name.

Canonbury is actually the area I'm most drawn to. It has a bit of a village quality. Trees, quieter streets. But then I walk past Broadway Market on a Saturday morning and think I'm mad for even considering leaving.

That's a fair point about the tenancy. I suppose I've been treating this as a permanent life decision when it needn't be. I've got two viewings booked next week — one on Canonbury Road and one off Alwyne Place. I'll go with an open mind rather than agonising about it in the abstract.
Quite. I'll see how the viewings go. Thank you for helping me untangle it — I think I was just going round in circles on my own.

One other thing before I go. Should I be looking at anything specific when I view a flat, beyond the obvious? I haven't moved in quite some time and I suspect I'll be distracted by whatever they've done with the staging.
Water pressure. I would never have thought to check that. Rather glad I asked. I'll make a mental checklist and try not to be swayed by a well-placed bookshelf.
Exploring is the right word. I'm still not certain Islington is the answer, but at least now I have a sensible way to find out. I'll report back.

I need to draft a thank-you email. We had a chambers dinner on Friday night and one of the silks hosted the whole thing at his house in Hampstead. I should write something to him before the week starts.

It was quite a good evening, actually. Charles — that's the silk — had the whole thing catered. About twenty of us from chambers, a mix of juniors and seniors. The food was excellent, and he'd chosen some rather fine wines to go with each course. I had a lovely Sancerre with the starter and a Burgundy with the main that was genuinely exceptional.

Warm but professional. He's been quite supportive of me within chambers — recommends me for cases occasionally. He's senior enough that I wouldn't be overly familiar, but we're past the stage of stiff formality. Brief and elegant is right. Three or four sentences at most.

That's right. I'll send it this evening. The dinner was well-timed, actually — we've had a rather intense few weeks in chambers. There's been some tension around clerking arrangements and it was good to have an evening where everyone was just being human with each other.

Almost certainly. Charles is many things but oblivious is not one of them. I think it was quietly intentional. He seated people rather carefully, now that I think about it — put some of the people who'd been clashing next to each other. It worked, as it happens. They were getting on perfectly well by the second course.
Temporary ceasefire, I suspect. But that's a problem for another day. For now I'll send the email and be grateful for the evening. The Burgundy alone was worth the trip to Hampstead.

Actually, while I'm thinking about it — do you think I should mention the clerking tension in the email at all? Not directly, but perhaps a line about how the evening brought everyone together. Or is that better left unsaid?
You're right. Less is more. I sometimes overthink these things — professional instinct, I suppose. I spend all day weighing every word in submissions and it bleeds into my personal correspondence.

Quite. I'll send it as drafted. Incidentally, Charles mentioned he might host something similar in the spring — a garden party, weather permitting. If the Friday dinner is anything to go by, that would be worth attending.
My parents' wedding anniversary is coming up in January and I need gift ideas. I always leave it too late and end up with something uninspired. Not this year.

It's their fortieth. Which is significant, obviously. They're not particularly materialistic — they don't need things. My mother appreciates anything with thought behind it. My father is harder to read but he's sentimental underneath the stoicism, so something meaningful would land well.

The memory book is lovely in theory, but coordinating messages from extended family in the next three weeks while I'm in the middle of a trial is not realistic. The experience idea interests me, though. They enjoy eating well — my mother is an excellent cook and my father has always appreciated good food. They don't go out enough. They'd never treat themselves to somewhere really good.
Warm and relaxed. My father gets uncomfortable in places that are too stiff — he doesn't like being fussed over. The River Cafe sounds right. Italian food is something they both love.

I'll write the card myself — some things ought to come from the hand, not a prompt. But I might see if my brother wants to go in on it and we can cover the whole bill including wine. Make it clear they're not to think about the cost.

Paying in advance is a good idea — if the bill arrives my father will insist on contributing, which defeats the purpose entirely. I'll call the restaurant tomorrow and ask about pre-payment. Do they usually accommodate that?

Good. I'll phone them first thing. Now, the only remaining question is the date. Their actual anniversary is the eighteenth of January, which is a Sunday. Should I book for the Saturday evening instead, or the day itself?

Sunday lunch on the day itself. That feels right. My brother lives outside London so he won't join the meal, but he'll want to be part of the gift. I'll ring him tonight and then call the restaurant in the morning.

I need to get my head around the current sentencing guidelines for supply of Class A drugs. I have a client facing a charge under section 5(3) of the Misuse of Drugs Act and I want to make sure I'm working from the right framework before the PTPH.

The quantity puts it in Category 3. The prosecution will push significant role because of the frequency of his involvement, but I think there's a strong argument for lesser. He's twenty-three, no previous convictions, was drawn into the operation by an associate. He was essentially doing the legwork — collecting and delivering. Two hundred pounds per delivery, roughly twice a week over three months.

None whatsoever. No evidence of him recruiting anyone, no decision-making role, no control over supply. His account is that the associate told him it was easy money and he didn't fully appreciate the scale of the operation. He's not sophisticated. The difficulty is the total sum — the prosecution will say five thousand pounds is not "very limited financial gain."

He's indicated he will plead guilty at the PTPH. So full credit, one-third. If I get lesser role, Category 3, with a starting point of three years, the one-third reduction brings it to approximately two years. That opens the door to a suspended sentence, which is what I'm aiming for.

I'll draft it myself — I know the client's circumstances better than anyone and the note needs to sound like me, not a template. But this has been useful for confirming the framework. I was fairly sure of the starting points but I wanted to pressure-test the lesser role argument before committing to it. It holds up. Thank you.
One more thing. If the judge does find significant role despite my submissions, what's the fallback position? I want to be prepared for that contingency rather than being caught flat-footed.

I've already requested a PSR. The probation officer seemed sympathetic when she interviewed him, which is encouraging. He's enrolled on a construction skills course since his arrest and has cut ties with the associate. Those are precisely the steps that tend to impress.

Agreed. I'll make sure the sentencing note dovetails with whatever the PSR says. The construction course is particularly useful because it gives the judge a tangible narrative — not just remorse, but a concrete alternative to the life that produced the offending. Right. I think I've got a clear picture now. Lesser role as the primary argument, significant role at the bottom of the range as the contingency. Thank you — this has sharpened my thinking considerably.
I've been roped into rather a lot of chambers admin this term and I need to get organised. Can you help me think through what needs doing and when?

Right. There's the marketing committee, which I somehow ended up chairing. We need to update the chambers website — the profiles are out of date and several members have changed practice areas. Then there's the equality and diversity training that needs to be arranged for the spring term. And I'm on the pupillage interview panel on 15 April, which means I need to review applications before then.

The web updates are done by a small external agency. I've drafted the circular but keep putting it off because I know I'll end up chasing half the members. There's a practice manager, Helen, who could help but I've been reluctant to delegate — the committee is technically my responsibility. For E&D, we don't have a preferred provider. Last year's was apparently mixed. And for pupillage — we're one of the better criminal sets, so we get a significant volume. Last year it was over three hundred applications. There are four of us on the panel.

Flexible within reason — chambers can absorb a few thousand. The Bar Council route makes sense. And you're right about Helen. I'll speak to her tomorrow. Now, the pupillage interviews are the thing I least want to be underprepared for. These are people's careers.
February. So the sift would happen in March. We divide applications among the four of us for the initial review and then meet to discuss before shortlisting.

The calendar is exactly what I needed. Seeing it laid out like that makes it feel achievable rather than overwhelming. I've been carrying it all as one amorphous burden rather than breaking it into stages.

One thing I wanted to ask about the pupillage sift specifically. We've had complaints in previous years that the criteria were too opaque. Candidates who were rejected at the paper stage felt they had no idea what we were looking for. I'd like to do better this time.

That's sensible. I'll draft a scoring sheet and circulate it to the panel before the applications close. It also gives us something to point to if anyone queries the outcome — we can show the process was structured rather than ad hoc. I rather wish someone had done this in previous years.
Right, I need cooking help. I'm attempting egusi soup and it's not going well.

I've got the egusi seeds ground up, the palm oil is heating, I've got spinach, stockfish, and some assorted meat already cooked. But the last time I tried this, the egusi went lumpy and the whole thing tasted flat. I'm determined to get it right this time.
I've got onions, salt, and a Maggi cube. I didn't use crayfish or locust beans. I suspect that's where the depth was missing last time as well.

There's one in Dalston that stocks everything. I should have gone there first rather than improvising with what I had in the cupboard. I can pause and go now, it's only ten minutes away. What else should I pick up while I'm there?

I've got scotch bonnets already. I'll get the crayfish, locust beans, and some uziza if they have it. One more thing — when I add the egusi paste to the oil, how long should I fry it before adding the stock? Last time I panicked and poured the stock in almost immediately.

Eight to ten minutes. Noted. I was definitely guilty of rushing it — probably gave it two minutes at most. Right, I'm heading to Dalston. If this works I may actually stop being embarrassed about my cooking. Thank you.
One last thing before I go — should I serve it with pounded yam or is that overly ambitious for someone who can barely manage the soup itself?
Poundo yam flour it is. Adding it to the list. Right, genuinely leaving now. I'll report back on how it turns out.
Have you been following the Andrew Malkinson situation? I know the original quashing was back in 2023 but the inquiry report has just come out and I am struggling to contain my anger.

The sheer catalogue of failures. The Greater Manchester Police failures with DNA evidence, the CCRC dragging its feet for years, the refusal to refer the case back to the Court of Appeal despite credible evidence of innocence. And now the inquiry lays it all out in meticulous detail and the response from the institutions involved is the usual performative contrition. 'Lessons will be learned.' That phrase should be struck from the English language.

Disclosure. It is always disclosure. The police had DNA evidence from the crime scene that didn't match Malkinson. They had it. And it wasn't properly disclosed to the defence. This is not a novel problem — disclosure failures have been at the heart of virtually every major miscarriage of justice in this country for decades. Judith Ward. The Birmingham Six. The Guildford Four. And here we are in the twenty-first century and the same fundamental failing is still destroying lives.

All three, but culture is the root of it. There is a mindset within certain parts of the police and prosecution that disclosure is an obstacle to conviction rather than a safeguard for justice. They see it as a bureaucratic burden. And when the pressure is on to get results, to close cases, to maintain conviction rates, the temptation to under-disclose or to fail to look for exculpatory material in the first place becomes overwhelming. The legal framework is adequate on paper. The Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act sets out clear obligations. But a framework is only as good as the people operating within it, and if the institutional culture treats disclosure as an afterthought, no amount of statutory language will fix it.

Regularly enough that it's become part of the job. I build time into every case for chasing disclosure that should have been provided unprompted. I've had cases where material emerged at trial that the prosecution had been sitting on for months. And the response is always the same — apologetic shrug, promise to look into it. Meanwhile my client has been preparing a defence without the full picture. It is corrosive. And the consequences fall entirely on the defendant. Nobody in the prosecution team faces sanctions. Nobody is disciplined. The asymmetry is obscene.

Judicial enforcement would help at the margins. Judges who take disclosure seriously and are willing to stay proceedings or exclude evidence when there have been failures — that sends a message. But you're right that there's a risk of driving it underground. What I'd really want is a cultural shift that starts in training. Every police officer and every prosecutor should understand from day one that their job is not to secure convictions. Their job is to ensure that justice is done. And sometimes justice means your case falls apart because the evidence points the other way. That should be seen as the system working, not as a failure.

Mainly the latter, if I'm honest. I read the report over breakfast and I've been simmering ever since. There's a junior member at chambers who's been asking me about doing innocence project work and I think I might take that conversation more seriously now. Seventeen years that man lost. Seventeen years. Sometimes this profession reminds you exactly why you went into it, and exactly how far there is still to go.

It does rather clarify things. I've been so caught up in the daily grind of case preparation and court appearances that I'd almost forgotten what drew me to criminal law in the first place. It wasn't the procedure. It was the principle that the state should not be able to take someone's liberty without meeting the highest standards of fairness. When that principle is betrayed, as it was with Malkinson, something has to be done about it.

I'll let you know. For now, I need to put the report down and go do something that doesn't make me want to write a furious letter to the Lord Chancellor. Which, for the record, I have drafted mentally three times this morning.
What is the appropriate professional response when an instructing solicitor has sent you the same incomplete bundle for the fourth time in a row?

I've been instructed on a GBH case — section 18, so serious. Trial is in three weeks. The instructing solicitor, whom I shall charitably decline to name, has been utterly impossible. I've asked for the full witness statements four times now. Four. Each time I get a partial bundle with pages missing, documents out of order, and no index.

A pattern. I've worked with them twice before and both times the preparation was slapdash. But they keep getting instructions because their firm has a large legal aid contract and they churn through cases. Volume over quality. The last time, I ended up essentially doing the solicitor's job as well as my own — chasing the CPS for materials, organising the bundle myself, even taking a conference with the client that should have been the solicitor's responsibility.

I have, in the most diplomatically firm terms I could manage. The response was a breezy 'sorry about that, we're stretched thin at the moment.' Stretched thin. As though that's an excuse when someone is facing a potential life sentence. I understand firms are under pressure — legal aid rates are what they are — but at some point, if you can't service the case properly, you shouldn't be taking it on.

That's the difficult part. The client trusts the solicitor — they've been with the firm for years, family connection or something. If I go over the solicitor's head to the client, it poisons the professional relationship and potentially destabilises the client's confidence right before trial. But if I don't, I'm compensating for someone else's inadequacy at the expense of my own preparation time for other cases. I'm rather stuck.

The paper trail is sensible. I should have been doing that from the start rather than relying on phone calls where everything evaporates. I'll send a detailed email today setting out every outstanding item with a deadline of end of this week. If I don't have a complete bundle by Friday, I'll escalate to the senior partner. Could you help me draft the email? I want it firm but not hostile — I still have to work with this person through trial.

That's quite good. I'd want to add a line about the conference with the client — I need one arranged for next week at the latest, and the solicitor should be there for it. But otherwise the tone is right. Professional, clear, and with enough subtext that they know I'm serious.

Perfect. I'll send it this afternoon. If Friday comes and goes without a proper bundle, the senior partner will be hearing from me. Thank you — I feel slightly less inclined to throw my laptop out of the window now.
I need gift ideas. My brother Chidi's birthday is coming up and I've left it far too late as usual.

It's in two weeks. He's in his early forties, quite practical, not particularly materialistic. He reads a lot — mostly non-fiction, history and politics. He's into cooking as well, better at it than I am, which isn't difficult. Budget-wise, I'd say up to about a hundred and fifty pounds. I don't want to go overboard but I don't want it to look like I grabbed something from the petrol station on the way over either.

The knife idea is interesting. He's been complaining about his kitchen knives for months — apparently they're all blunt and he hasn't got round to replacing them. A proper chef's knife could work well. Tell me more about the Tojiro.

A knife and a whetstone together. That's rather good — practical, high quality, and it shows I've actually thought about it rather than defaulting to a bottle of something. He'd appreciate the intentionality. Would he need anything else to maintain it properly?

I'll skip the honing rod — knowing Chidi, he'll research the entire subject exhaustively the moment he unwraps it and end up knowing more about Japanese metallurgy than I ever will. Knife and whetstone it is. Where's the best place to buy the Tojiro in the UK without getting a counterfeit?

CuttingEdgeKnives sounds right. I'll order from there this week. Thank you — this is the most organised I've been about Chidi's birthday in years. He's usually quite difficult to buy for but I think this will genuinely please him.

Now I just need to work out what to write in the card. I'm dreadful at that sort of thing. I always end up writing something stiff and formal, as though I'm drafting a skeleton argument rather than a birthday message to my own brother.

That is actually quite good. Direct, a bit sharp, sounds like something I'd say rather than something off a greetings card. I'll use that as a starting point. Right — knife, whetstone, card that doesn't read like a legal submission. I think we're done.
Do you ever have those moments where you look back on a decision and think, yes, that was exactly right? I'm having one of those today.

The move to Bedford Row. I was nervous about it — more than I admitted at the time. New colleagues, new clerks, different culture. Starting over in a sense, even though I brought my practice with me. But sitting here now, several months in, I can say with some confidence it was the right call.

The work, primarily. The quality of instructions coming in is materially better. I'm being briefed on cases that genuinely test me, which at this stage of my career is what I want. I don't need easy wins. I need cases that make me think. And the clerks here are exceptional — they understand the kind of work I want and they actively seek it out rather than just filling my diary with whatever comes through the door.

Better than I expected. There's a collegiate atmosphere that I wasn't sure I'd find. People actually discuss cases over lunch, bounce ideas off each other. Not in a competitive way — in a genuinely collaborative way. There's a senior silk here who specialises in fraud who's been incredibly generous with her time. We come at criminal defence from completely different angles but the conversations have been illuminating.

New connection entirely. We'd appeared against each other once, years ago — she was prosecuting, I was defending. I remembered her as formidable. Turns out she's equally formidable over a sandwich. She's been quite helpful on the financial aspects of some of my cases. Defence work increasingly involves following the money, and her expertise in that area has been invaluable.

Subtly, yes. I'm more thorough in certain areas — financial disclosure, digital evidence. Not because I wasn't thorough before, but because I'm now surrounded by people who think about those dimensions instinctively, and it's sharpened my own approach. There's also a higher expectation on written work here. The standard of skeleton arguments and written submissions is very high. It's pushed me to raise my own standard, which I didn't think had much room to rise, but apparently it did.

It has. I won't pretend there wasn't a period of adjustment — the first month or two I felt like the new girl, which is an odd sensation at thirty-seven with over a decade of practice behind me. But that passed. I feel at home now. The commute is marginally worse but I can live with that for everything else it offers.
Quite right. I'll bank this one. Thank you for listening — it's not often I'm in a reflective mood but when I am, it helps to articulate it rather than just let it pass.

hey i'm looking for advice on how to advocate for more cultural safety in a hospital birthing environment. i work in maternity care and i feel like institutional systems just steamroll over what families actually need

sure so i'm a community midwife based in christchurch and most of my mamas birth at christchurch women's hospital eh. i do about 45 births a year through there. the hospital has its own kaupapa around cultural safety but honestly it's mostly on paper. i try to bring tikanga into the space but the system pushes back in a hundred small ways

all of those things honestly. like wanting to do karakia before a birth and the staff rushing in to do their obs. or whānau being told there's too many people in the room when actually having your people around you is the whole point eh. and then simple things like keeping the whenua, the placenta, and the systems aren't set up for that. every time it's like starting from scratch explaining why these things matter

mostly one birth at a time if i'm being honest. i've raised things in team meetings but it kind of gets nodded at and then nothing changes. the written tikanga guide is a good idea though, something that sits in the notes so i'm not the one saying it every time. i could work on that

yeah i'd love that actually. and it's not just for māori whānau either eh, i've got mamas from all kinds of backgrounds who have their own practices around birth. but for me personally it comes from my own whakapapa. i'm ngāi tahu, through my māmā's side, banks peninsula. that whenua is in my bones and everything i bring to my midwifery practice traces back to that connection to place and tūpuna

that's really solid actually. i'd add something in the during birth section about skin to skin not being interrupted for weighing and measuring eh, because that's a massive one. staff come in with the scales two minutes after the pēpi arrives and it breaks that first connection. and in the after birth section maybe something about who does the first bath and when because that's culturally significant for a lot of people

yes please. and honestly this conversation has fired me up a bit. sometimes you just need someone to kōrero with about this stuff and suddenly it feels doable instead of overwhelming. i'm going to bring this to my next team meeting but this time with something concrete on paper

this is amazing thank you so much. i'm going to rework the language a bit so it sits right for our community and then print some copies off. really appreciate this kōrero, it's given me a clear path forward eh

i've been thinking a lot about visibility lately and what it means to carry your identity visibly in professional spaces. like how much of yourself do you bring into work versus how much do you leave at the door

bit of both eh. i had a moment last week with a new registrar at the hospital. she was staring at my face during handover and i could tell she wanted to ask but didn't know how. and it made me think about how my moko kauae shifts the energy in a room before i even open my mouth

honestly it depends on the day and the person. that registrar, she was young, probably just hadn't encountered moko kauae up close before. i don't mind genuine curiosity. what gets to me is when people treat it like it's decorative, like a tattoo you just chose for aesthetics. my moko is my whakapapa on my face eh. it carries my tūpuna with me into every room, every birth i attend. it's not something i can or would want to separate from my professional self

with my māori mamas absolutely. there's this moment of recognition sometimes, like a settling. they see my moko and something relaxes because they know i carry tikanga, it's not just something i talk about. i've had kuia in the room who touch their own faces and nod at me and that exchange holds so much without a single word being spoken

it varies eh. most are fine, some are curious in a respectful way. occasionally someone is a bit taken aback but honestly once i start talking and they feel my energy around their birth, it fades fast. my job is to make them feel safe and held and that comes through regardless. the moko is part of me not separate from me, and people feel that authenticity

usually the night before if i remember, but sometimes it's been two or three days since the last feed and i just use it anyway. nan never seemed to worry about timing, she'd just look at it and know if it was ready eh. i don't have that instinct yet

i do about 200 degrees for maybe 40 minutes but again that's a guess because nan never used a timer. she'd knock on the bottom and if it sounded hollow it was done. i do the knock test too but half the time i can't tell if it sounds hollow or not eh

i just need to vent for a minute because i've just seen the latest workforce survey results for midwifery in aotearoa and nothing has changed and i am tired of it

so the pay for community midwives like me is still sitting at about $55 an hour and it has not moved in years. years. and people hear fifty-five dollars and think oh that sounds alright but they don't understand what that actually means when you're self-employed and on call 24/7 and covering your own ACC levies and indemnity insurance and vehicle costs and phone and continuing education out of your own pocket eh

that's exactly right and there's more. we don't get paid for a lot of the admin either. you do a home visit that takes an hour but you also drove 30 minutes each way and spent 20 minutes writing up your notes afterwards and none of that travel or documentation time is covered. so your one hour visit is actually two hours and twenty minutes of your day but you bill for one. and when a mama calls at 2am because she's worried about her pēpi's breathing you pick up the phone because that's what you do but nobody is paying you for that call

it comes through the section 88 notice which is the funding framework that the ministry sets for maternity services. and technically it gets reviewed but every time it's reviewed the increase is insulting, like a dollar or two that doesn't even cover inflation. meanwhile the cost of insurance goes up every year, petrol goes up, ACC levies go up. so you're actually going backwards in real terms. and the midwives who negotiate this are doing their best but they're up against a government that just does not prioritise maternity care

absolutely. i know at least four midwives in canterbury who've either gone back to hospital employment or left the profession entirely in the last two years. and the ones who stay are exhausted because we're picking up the slack. you can't just say no to a mama who can't find a midwife, you take her on even if your caseload is already full because what's the alternative, she goes through pregnancy with no continuity of care?

i'm a member of the college of midwives and i go to the meetings when i can but honestly by the time i finish a day of clinical work the last thing i want to do is sit in another meeting talking about how broken the system is eh. and that's part of the problem too, they've made us so tired that we don't have the energy to fight for ourselves. it's designed that way whether they admit it or not

honestly if you costed it properly — the on-call component, the travel, the admin, the insurance, the fact that we're providing a service that literally brings humans into the world — it should be $85 to $90 minimum. that would let midwives actually sustain themselves without running a second job or having a partner subsidise their career. i know midwives who do meal deliveries on the side to make ends meet and that is a scandal in a country that says it values maternity care

it's been playing on my mind all week because the anniversary is coming up and even after all these years it still sits heavy. i want to talk through some thoughts about it if that's okay

the christchurch earthquake. february 22 2011. it'll be fourteen years next february but honestly every year around this time i start thinking about it again because the rebuild is still happening around us and the empty lots are still there in the CBD and it just never really goes away eh. you live with it

yeah i was. i was in my mid-twenties, just starting out in my career, living in the east side. our house was damaged, not destroyed but damaged enough that we couldn't live in it for months. the liquefaction came up through the floors and out in the garden and it was just this surreal grey sludge everywhere. and the sound, people always talk about the sound. this deep rumble that comes from underneath you, not around you. i still feel it in my body sometimes when a truck goes past and the ground shakes a little bit

about four months with whānau and then we went back once the repairs were done enough to live in. but the east side never really came back. some streets are just gone, they bought the houses out and turned the land into the red zone which is now this strange empty green space where neighbourhoods used to be. i drive through there sometimes and i can still picture where the houses were, the dairy on the corner, the park where the kids played. it's like a ghost suburb

a few things. they're doing some new memorial work in the city and there was a piece in the press about it which got people talking again. and then one of my mamas at work, she's young, early twenties, and she mentioned that she barely remembers the quake because she was only about ten when it happened. and it hit me that there's a whole generation now who don't carry it the way we do, which is good for them but it made me feel old and a bit alone with it eh

bit of both. the 185 chairs memorial is beautiful, each white chair representing someone who died, and that one i always stop at because it's honest. it doesn't dress it up. but some of the rebuild stuff feels like it's trying to make the city shiny and new and forgetting that for a lot of us the old city was home and we didn't want a new one we just wanted our one fixed. the new stuff is nice but it's not mine if that makes sense

i usually go to the civic memorial in the morning, they do a service at 12:51 which was the time the quake hit. two minutes silence. and then i go to the moana afterwards because that's where i went on the day itself when everything was chaos and there was no water or power and the ground kept shaking. the ocean was the only thing that was still the same. it was still there, still doing its thing. i found that really grounding at the time and i go back every year

i think i might take Maia this year actually. she was born after the quakes so she's never been to the memorial but she's old enough now to understand what happened and why it matters. i want her to know the city she lives in, the real one not just the shiny new version. and i want her to see the chairs and understand that each one was a person. she should know that history doesn't just happen in textbooks eh it happens under your feet

i've hinted at it but she's pushed back because she says having anyone clinical in the space changes the energy. she feels like she can't truly let go and surrender to the process if there's a midwife there watching and assessing. and i get that, i've been in births where the mama is so aware of being observed that her body tenses up and labour stalls. observation changes the experience, she's not wrong about that

my gut is telling me that the other-room option is probably the best i'm going to get and it might actually work for her. she trusts me, that's why she's even having this conversation instead of just not telling me. i think if i frame it as me being there for the pēpi, not to control her birth, she might be open to it. because she's not anti-midwife, she's anti-system. and i respect that distinction
