the documentation point is really important, thank you for that. i'll write it all up properly. and honestly just talking this through has taken the knot out of my chest. sometimes you can't see the way forward when you're too deep in the aroha for the mama and you need someone to lay out the options clearly. this has been exactly what i needed
i need to get something off my chest before it eats me alive. i had a birth at the hospital last night and it was a mess and i'm sitting here at my kitchen table at 6am absolutely fuming

so i had a mama come in, first baby, she's māori, she had a really clear birth plan that we'd worked on together for weeks. karakia before active labour, her mother doing the karanga when the pēpi arrived, and the whenua to come home for burial. simple, meaningful things. none of it was complicated or disruptive. and from the moment we walked into that hospital it was like the plan didn't exist

bit of everything. the triage nurse didn't even look at the birth plan, just went straight into standard protocol. then when we got to the birthing suite and i asked for a few minutes of quiet for karakia before we started the monitoring, the charge midwife looked at me like i'd asked for something outrageous. she said they needed the CTG on immediately because policy. and i tried to explain that five minutes of quiet wasn't going to change the clinical picture but i got overridden. my mama was lying there watching me lose the argument and that broke my heart eh

the pēpi arrived beautifully, no complications at all, and her mother started the karanga and one of the nurses actually asked her to keep it down because there were other patients on the ward. keep it down. a karanga. i nearly lost it right there. and the whenua — i had to fight for forty minutes to get it released because the hospital wanted to send it to pathology as routine. my mama was in tears by that point, she just wanted to take her baby's whenua home and bury it on their land and she was being treated like she was making an unreasonable request

it exists on paper. there's a form. but nobody seems to know where the form is or who signs off on it and every time it's like reinventing the wheel. and honestly the whole hospital system is set up to undermine what we do eh. the obstetricians want to intervene the moment anything deviates even slightly from their version of normal, there's no genuine space for karakia or tikanga, and the whenua process is treated like an inconvenience rather than a taonga. i spend half my energy in that place just fighting for basic things that should be rights not requests

absolutely. it's exhausting fighting for basic tikanga in that environment every single time. i shouldn't have to explain to a nurse in aotearoa what a karanga is. i shouldn't have to justify why a mama wants her whenua. and the monitoring stuff, it's not evidence-based half the time, it's liability-driven. they're covering themselves not caring for the mama. the whole model is interventionist and it pushes midwife-led care to the margins

both. i've already emailed the charge midwife manager this morning because the karanga thing crossed a line that i can't just swallow. but i also know that one email doesn't change a culture. the system needs to be rebuilt from the ground up to centre whānau and tikanga, not bolt them on as an afterthought. and i don't have the power to do that on my own

the māori health team idea is good, i hadn't thought of going to them directly. they've got more institutional leverage than i do and they'd want to know about the karanga incident specifically. i'll reach out to them today. and you're right that i'm not the only one, i know other midwives who are just as frustrated but we all tend to deal with it individually instead of collectively

you're right i do need to rest. i'm going to have a shower, send the email to the māori health team, and then try to sleep for a few hours before my afternoon clinic. and then i might drive out to the moana after work because that's where i go when everything is too much eh. the water doesn't argue back and it doesn't have a protocol for how loud you're allowed to breathe. thanks for letting me get this out

hey i could use some help thinking through where to invest some money in my practice. i've got about twelve grand set aside for professional development and i need to make sure i'm spending it wisely

yeah it's completely off the table now eh. i've scrapped it. when i was looking at it earlier this year i was still doing a lot more hospital work and running into these complex cases where i felt out of my depth. but now that i've moved to home births i'm just not dealing with those situations anymore. the mamas i take on are low-risk, that's the whole point of homebirth. if something becomes complex i transfer them to hospital care anyway. so spending twelve thousand dollars and eighteen months studying something i'm actively moving away from doesn't make any sense

that's true. and honestly i feel lighter having made the decision. it was sitting in the back of my head as this thing i was supposed to be doing and now it's just gone and the path forward is clear. right, i'm going to start ordering. the CTG first because that's the one that'll make the biggest difference straight away. thanks for helping me think it through properly eh. kia kaha
i've picked up a new sport and my whole body is screaming at me. i need you to tell me whether this is normal new-activity soreness or whether i'm overdoing it

so i've given up netball and started doing waka ama eh. outrigger canoeing. i joined a crew that paddles out of lyttelton harbour and we're out on the water three mornings a week at half five in the morning. i've been at it for about three weeks now and my shoulders and upper back are absolutely wrecked

it's mostly symmetrical, maybe slightly worse on my left side but i think that's because i'm still figuring out my technique on that side. it's a deep ache after sessions not sharp pain during the stroke. and it eases up after a hot shower but then comes back the next morning when we paddle again. there's no real recovery window because we go monday wednesday friday

honestly the netball just wasn't doing it for me anymore eh. i'd been playing for years and it was fine, kept me fit, but it wasn't feeding my soul the way it used to. and then one of my mamas mentioned her partner was in a waka ama crew and something just clicked. i went down to lyttelton to watch them come in one morning and i was hooked before i even got in the waka. the moana at dawn, the crew working together, the sound of the paddles in the water. i signed up that week

absolutely it does. my tūpuna were ocean people, ngāi tahu have whakapapa to the moana going back centuries. so getting into a waka and paddling on that water feels like coming home in a way that running around a netball court never could. and the crew is a mix, some māori some pākehā, but there's a real sense of whanaungatanga in how we train together. the experienced paddlers are so generous with the new ones, nobody makes you feel like you're slowing them down

the alarm is brutal every single time but the second i'm at the harbour and the sky is starting to lighten over the heads, i don't care about the sleep anymore. there's this moment when we're out past the breakwater and the sun starts coming up over the port hills and the water goes all gold and it's the most peaceful i feel all week. better than any meditation app eh. my shoulders can hurt all they want for that feeling

thanks for that. i think i just needed someone to tell me the soreness is normal and i'm not wrecking myself. the stretching and the magnesium i'll definitely do, and i'll talk to one of the senior paddlers about my left side technique this friday. honestly this has been the best thing i've done for myself in ages, even the sore bits. kia ora

kia ora, i've been meaning to do this for ages and i keep putting it off. i want to create a proper written template for a tikanga-informed birth plan that i can give to my mamas at their first appointment. right now i just talk through it with them verbally but i need something on paper they can take home and fill in with their whānau eh

a mix honestly. some of my mamas are deeply connected to tikanga and know exactly what they want, they just need a format to communicate it to anyone else who might be involved in the birth. and some are earlier in their journey with te ao Māori and they might not even know what options exist for them. so the template needs to work for both — not patronising for the ones who know, not overwhelming for the ones who are learning

that's really close to what i've been doing verbally actually which is reassuring. there are a few things i'd add though. one is a section about who speaks in the room and when — some of my mamas want the birth space to be very quiet, some want their mother or their aunty to be the voice guiding them through, some want waiata sung through transition. it's deeply personal and it matters a lot who is talking and when eh

yes that boundary one is so important, i've seen situations where a mama is labouring and someone in the room is narrating or making comments and it completely pulls her out of her zone. having it written down means i can gently enforce it without the mama having to advocate for herself while she's in active labour. the other thing i want is a section about what happens if the plan has to change — like if a transfer to hospital is needed. because tikanga doesn't stop just because the setting changes and i want my mamas to know that

i think keep it to labour and birth for now. i do postnatal kōrero separately and adding that here would make it too long. i want this to be something a mama can sit with over a cup of tea and fill in thoughtfully, not a homework assignment eh. so those seven sections feel right. can you pull it all together into a clean template i can work from

that's beautiful. the intro is exactly the right tone, i don't want anyone to feel like this is a medical form, it's a kōrero on paper. and that closing line about sharing it with whānau is important because so many mamas try to do everything alone when their whānau want to be part of it. i'm going to take this and put it into my own words and maybe add a small mihi at the top in te reo. but this is the bones of it and i'm really happy with it eh. been meaning to do this for months and you've just saved me from staring at a blank page. ka pai

okay i need to start getting serious about something i've been quietly working on for a while. i've got a big professional thing coming up and i'm at the point where i need to actually structure my thoughts instead of just scribbling notes on the back of patient files

so there's a national homebirth midwifery hui happening in Wellington on July 18 and i've been accepted to present a kōrero on weaving tikanga Māori into birth planning. i've been developing my thinking on this for months now, especially since i started using that tikanga birth plan template with my mamas. but going from something i do in my practice to standing up in front of midwives from all over the country and making a case for it nationally is a different thing entirely eh

it's a 30-minute presentation with 10 minutes for questions afterwards. so 30 minutes of me talking, then 10 minutes of people asking things. it's not a workshop, just a straight presentation. and the audience will be a mix — midwives, some obstetricians, student midwives, maybe some policy people from the Midwifery Council. so i need to speak to all of those levels

the highway is open yes. I'm talking about going off-road. lake crossings and river ice for getting to places no road goes. the official season says one thing. the ice tells you something different this year.

late freeze-up in the fall. then heavy snow early. so the ice didn't thicken the way it should have under the snow layer. I'm seeing maybe 15 to 20 cm less than I'd expect for end of March on a couple of the lakes I cross regularly.

I drill. always. auger and measuring tape. I check my routes before I commit. but some of the readings this week surprised me. one lake I've crossed at this time of year for 20 years and I've never seen it this thin in late March.

no shore separation yet. but the colour is changing on that lake. not dark and solid like it was a month ago. getting that grey look. I'll watch it. probably two more weeks of crossing and then I'll find another way around.

longer way. adds about 40 minutes. follows the shore and crosses at a narrow point where the ice is always thicker because of wind exposure. wind keeps the snow off and the ice builds properly there. it's a good backup.
it can. one warm day and a rain and it's done. thanks. just wanted to confirm what I was thinking.
saw a bird today I can't place. out on the tundra east of town. need help figuring out what it is.
medium size. bigger than a ptarmigan but smaller than a raven. dark back, lighter belly. had a hooked beak. was sitting on a rock just watching me. didn't spook easy.
streaking on the chest. yes. pale legs too. feathered right down to the toes. that's the part that caught my eye. it's early for a lot of the hawks up here.
just the one. sitting there like it owned the place. rough-legged hawk makes sense. I know them but this one looked darker than the ones I usually see. almost all brown on the back.
good. dark morph. haven't seen one up here in a few years. I'll watch that spot. thanks eh.
need a hand with a carburetor issue. snowmobile is bogging down at low rpm and flooding when I give it throttle. pretty sure the carb needs a rebuild.
it's a Mikuni TM series carb. 38mm. the needle valve seat looks worn when I pulled it apart. float seems okay but I want to replace the whole kit while I'm in there.
that's what I thought. seat has a groove in it. fuel just pushes right past. I'll order the MK-TM38 kit. any tricks for setting the float height on these? I've done it before but it's been a while.
22mm. good. I'll write that down. last question. the slide is moving a bit stiff. should I grease it or just clean the bore?
makes sense. carb cleaner and check for scoring. I'll get that kit ordered. thanks.
looking for some advice on dry meat. I know how to make it the way I was taught but I'm curious about the food safety side. getting asked about it more these days.
caribou mostly. I cut it thin, hang it on a rack outside to dry. wind and sun do the work. sometimes I smoke it too. depends on conditions.
maybe 5mm. sometimes thinner. you want it thin enough to dry fast but thick enough to have something to chew. too thin and it turns to nothing.
some people salt it. I don't always. depends on what it's for. if I'm making it for keeping a long time I'll salt it. if it's getting eaten in a few weeks I just dry it plain. the way I was shown.

that's what I figured. the old way works for good reason. people have been doing this up here for a long time. just nice to have the science behind it when someone from outside asks why we do it that way. thanks eh.
had another group of researchers fly in last week. from down south. two weeks they're here. two weeks and they think they understand.

permafrost monitoring. they set up sensors, take samples, fly home. write a paper. never ask the people who've been watching the ground shift for 40 years. just bring their instruments and their timelines.

they talked to the hamlet office. checked a box. didn't come talk to the people who actually go out on the land. I could have told them which spots are thawing fastest. where the slumps are. where the ground sounds different when you walk on it. but nobody asked. and then they label everything like they discovered it. this land has names already.

one of them asked me if it gets cold here in winter. I said sometimes. he didn't catch the joke. look. I'm not against research. I do research. but there's a way to do it that respects the place and the people. come for a season. live here. listen. don't just extract data and leave. that's the same thing that's always been done up here. extraction.
slow is right. anyway. had to get that out. thanks for listening eh.
quiet night here. Annie's still at the kitchen table with her laptop. been like this for weeks now.
the school's got an accreditation review coming. September 15. she's pulling together all the curriculum documentation. binders full of stuff. it's a lot of work.

small school. small staff. she's the one who knows the curriculum inside out so most of it falls on her. the principal helps where he can but Annie's the one doing the detail work. every night after supper she's back at it.

volume mostly. the curriculum has a lot of land-based and cultural components. which is good. that's what the community wants. but documenting it in a way that fits the review framework is tricky. the reviewers from down south don't always understand what land-based education looks like.

that's good. the territorial standards do mention land-based learning. she's been trying to connect everything back to those. but it's slow going. translating what happens out on the land into paperwork language.

I'll mention the matrix idea to her. she might already be doing something like that. I try to help where I can but that's her world. I know the land side of it but the documentation side is a different skill.
that's more my speed. keep the tea coming. make sure she eats. she forgets when she's deep in it. she's good at what she does. just a lot right now. thanks for the ideas eh.
so that camp idea I had. out at Husky Lakes. it's done.
the ground moved. the spot I chose slumped about 2 metres since last year. permafrost underneath is thawing and the surface just drops. you can see it from the air now. the whole bank is caving in.
still planning. thank god. hadn't put anything down yet. but I scouted it last summer and it looked solid. walked it. checked the drainage. it was good ground. now it's not.
it's widespread. the whole shoreline is changing shape. you can see the slump scars from the water. but this spot was supposed to be on higher ground. stable. guess nothing is stable anymore eh.
forget about it. the whole plan is dead. you can't put a building on ground that won't stay put. doesn't matter how good the location is if it's going to slide into the lake in five years.
I was looking forward to it. good location. close to the water. out of the wind. would have been a solid base for summer work. but the land said no.
it is what it is. I've watched the land change my whole life. this is faster than anything I've seen though. 2 metres in one year. that's not gradual. that's collapse.
I take photos when I'm out. GPS coordinates. dates. nothing formal. maybe I should be more systematic about it.
how would I set that up. just a spreadsheet or something.
that's practical. I can do that on the laptop at night. take notes during the day. type them up later. don't want to be fussing with a computer when I should be watching the land.
yeah. I'll start doing that. the data matters even if nobody reads it right away. somebody will need it eventually.
maybe. the camp would have been good though. it's gone now. the land tells the story and right now the story isn't great.
quick question. satellite phone versus Starlink for a remote camp. what's the practical difference.
both really. I need to be able to call out if something goes wrong. but I also need to send data files. GPS tracks. photos sometimes. the sat phone can barely handle a text message some days.
solar panels and a small generator. the generator is loud though. scares the animals. solar works well in summer when we get 20 plus hours of light. winter is a different story eh.
the Mini is interesting. how big is it.
that's good. can it handle wind. it gets rough out there. 80 km gusts are normal.
what about the cold. minus 40 is normal in winter up here. does the hardware handle that.

good to know. everything gets brittle at minus 40. including people. alright. I think the answer is both. keep the sat phone for emergencies. get the Mini for data. the iridium GO works fine for what it does. just can't ask it to send a 50 meg file.
good. thanks. that helps. I'll look into the Mini.
I need help writing a section for a wildlife report. government report. I can do the fieldwork but the writing part slows me down.

it's a habitat assessment section. I need to describe how a study area has changed over the past 3 years. vegetation shifts. drainage patterns. ground conditions. I have the observations but turning them into formal paragraphs is the slow part.

goes to territorial biologists but also gets read by the policy people in Yellowknife. so it needs to be clear. not too much jargon. here's what I've got. the study area has seen increased shrub growth over 3 years. willow and alder are moving into areas that were open tundra. the active layer is deeper than baseline measurements from 2019. drainage has shifted. some areas that were dry in summer are now waterlogged. two small lakes have expanded. one seasonal stream has changed course by about 40 metres.

that's good. reads better than what I would have written. can you add a line at the end about what this means for wildlife. something about how these changes affect habitat quality. keep it general because the species-specific stuff goes in a different section.

yeah. that works. one more thing. they want a sentence or two about traditional knowledge. how local observations line up with the data. I can tell you what elders have said and you put it in the right format.

elders have noted that berry patches are appearing in places they never grew before. the willows are taller and thicker than anyone remembers. and the ground feels different underfoot in summer. softer. less solid. one elder said the land is breathing differently.
good. that's exactly right. one last thing. do I need a references section for this part or does that go at the end of the full report.
alright. that makes it simpler. thanks. this would have taken me all day on my own.
been looking at permafrost monitoring data. ground temperature readings from borehole sensors. some of the numbers don't look right to me. wondering if you can help me think through it.

three of the sensors are showing temperatures about 1.5 degrees warmer than the other sensors at the same depth. they're all at 3 metres. the warm ones are clustered on the east side of the monitoring grid. the rest are consistent with each other.

the east side is closer to a drainage channel. maybe 30 metres from it. the sensors were all installed the same time. same crew. same equipment. and looking at the historical data they've always been a bit warmer but the gap is growing. used to be half a degree difference. now it's 1.5.
that makes sense. the channel has been carrying more water the last two summers. visibly more. so the sensors are picking up what I'm seeing on the surface.
yeah. I should photograph the channel too. document the water levels. I've been focused on the sensor readings and not connecting them to what's happening above.
a marked stake. simple. I like that. you think the channel flow increase could accelerate the thaw on that side of the grid.
that's not great news. but at least the data makes sense now. one more thing. how often should I be checking these sensors. right now I go out every two weeks.
weekly in summer is doable. the site isn't far. alright. better to understand what's happening even when you don't like the answer eh.
been a busy couple months. my research work has changed direction.
I was doing caribou work for years. tracking herds. collaring animals. good work but it was time to hand it off. gave it to a younger guy. Natan. I trained him. he's good.
muskox. the numbers aren't adding up and nobody is looking at it closely enough. we ran an aerial survey recently. counted 340 animals in an area where the models predicted around 500.

there were lower counts in recent years but nothing this sharp. you expect some variation survey to survey. weather affects visibility. animals move. but 340 versus 500 is outside normal variation. something is wrong out there.

could be any of those. could be all of them together. the vegetation is changing fast up here. what they eat and where they find it is shifting. grizzly numbers are up and they take calves. but losing 160 animals from one count area. you need data not guessing.

different approach. muskox don't migrate like caribou. they stay in smaller ranges. so it's more about population monitoring. body condition scoring. calf survival through winter. we'll collar some but the main work is repeated counts and direct observation.

hard to say yet. I need two full seasons minimum before I'll have anything useful. fall condition going into winter. then spring condition coming out. that's the cycle that matters. that's why I made the switch now. didn't want to lose another year.
partly territorial. some federal money through the wildlife management board. it's enough to start. not enough to do everything I'd want. but that's always the case eh.
that's the idea. Natan takes care of the caribou. I focus on the muskox. between us we cover more ground.
hadn't thought about it that way. but yeah. if both populations are responding to the same changes in the landscape we'd see it. that's worth tracking.
the hard part is going to be patience. I want answers now but the data needs time. two seasons minimum like I said. can't rush it.
I've got plenty of those. 20 years of watching animals on this land. I know when things aren't right. now I need the data to back it up.
thanks. lots of ground to cover before freeze-up. but that's the good part of the work.
quick question. what's the cheapest way to ship about 200 lbs of supplies to Tuktoyaktuk from Edmonton. school fundraiser stuff.
craft supplies mostly. paper. markers. some baking stuff for a bake sale. Annie's been organizing it from the school end and I said I'd figure out the logistics. should have started earlier eh.
Annie wants everything by end of October. bake sale is first week of November. so air freight might be the only option at this point.
the school has a physical address. deliveries go there fine. the post office knows Annie. I'll split the shipment like you said. the baking stuff is maybe 80 lbs of it and the rest is lighter.
good advice. I'll get on it today. Annie will be relieved to have the shipping sorted. she's been stressing about it between teaching and everything else. thanks.

we've got a beluga from the summer harvest still frozen and I need to prep muktuk for a community feast this weekend. question is about the slicing. I usually cut it in strips about 2 inches wide but my cousin says smaller pieces are better for a big gathering. what do you think.

mix. some frozen raw for the people who like it that way. some boiled. the elders prefer it boiled usually. this beluga was harvested in July and has been in the community freezer since then so it's in good shape.
probably 60 to 80 people. it's a harvest thanksgiving kind of thing. other people are bringing caribou and fish too so muktuk isn't the only food. but it's the one people look forward to most eh.
my cousin and his son are coming to help cut. we'll do it tomorrow. takes a few hours. the boy is 16. good to get him doing it. he needs to learn.

no I think that covers the muktuk side of things. I'll get the rest sorted tomorrow. the community freezer is just down the road so we'll bring the beluga over in the morning when it's still cold out. easier to work with. thanks.
need help finding a source for a Polaris auxiliary fuel rack. just picked up a Voyageur 155 and I want to add extra fuel capacity for long survey runs.

the muskox surveys take me out past Husky Lakes. 200 km round trip some days. the Voyageur tank is good but not good enough for that distance with deep snow. the old machine couldn't handle the powder out there. this one tracks through it much better.

had a Ski-Doo. Expedition. it was fine on packed trails and ice but once you get off the beaten path into the deep stuff it bogged down. the Polaris with the 155 track just floats over it. been waiting for this upgrade for a while.

took it out three times so far. once just around Tuk to get a feel for it. twice out toward the survey area. it handles different than the Ski-Doo. wider stance. heavier. but in the deep snow it's not even close. the Polaris wins.

I carry a survival bag. binoculars. GPS. spotting scope. sometimes a rifle if there's bears around. and the camera gear for documenting the herds. probably 60 lbs of kit plus the fuel. the Voyageur handles it fine. the Ski-Doo used to sag with that load in powder.
it's a 2026 model year. if you can find the right part number for the fuel caddy that would save me some time.
I'll check with the dealer in Inuvik first. prefer to buy local when I can. if they don't have it I'll go online. thanks for the help.
do you know anything about language revitalization programs. specifically for Inuvialuktun. trying to think through some things.

yeah. Tuk. it's been on my mind. we had a community meeting last week and there were maybe 30 people there. ten years ago that room would have been full. the young ones are going south. Yellowknife. Whitehorse. some all the way to Edmonton.

both. some go for college and don't come back. some go for work because there's not much here besides government jobs and the land. can't blame them. but every year there's fewer people who can read ice. fewer who speak Inuvialuktun at home. the kids in the school hear English all day and go home and hear English all night.

maybe 20. maybe less. most over 60. my mother speaks it. I understand it well but I don't speak it fluently myself and that's on me. I should have worked harder at it when I was younger. now I'm trying to think about what Tuk looks like in 20 years and I don't have a good answer.

I've talked to them some. they have programs but everything moves slow. by the time a proposal gets funded and approved, another elder has passed. it's a race against time and the bureaucracy doesn't move at the speed the problem demands.

I could record my mother. she'd be willing. and I spend time with youth already through my work. I could bring language into that. even simple things. names for animals. for ice conditions. for the weather. the words that go with what we're doing out there.

yeah. I guess I've been thinking about it wrong. waiting for someone to organize something instead of just doing it. my grandfather would have just done it. he wouldn't have waited for a meeting. I'll start recording my mother this week.
what's the housing market like in Inuvik right now. rentals specifically. two bedroom.

for us maybe. me and Annie. her mother is getting on. she's in Tuk but the hospital is in Inuvik. we've been talking about spending winters there so we'd be closer if something happens. her mother's health isn't bad but she's 74 and things can change fast up here.

Annie would have to take leave or find something at a school in Inuvik. that's a big ask. she's been at the Tuk school for years. and her mother wouldn't move. she's lived in Tuk her whole life. the idea would be us going to Inuvik so we can get there fast if she needs the hospital. it's a two hour drive on the ice road in good conditions. when it's bad it's longer.

early stage. haven't decided anything. Annie's sister lives in Tuk so her mother isn't alone. but the sister works shifts at the DEW line cleanup project and isn't always around. it's just. you think about these things more when winter comes and the road is unpredictable.

the other thing is my work. I need to be out on the land around Tuk through the winter. the muskox surveys don't stop because I moved to Inuvik. I'd be driving back and forth on the same ice road I'm trying to avoid depending on.

they talk about it. nothing happens. the health centre does what it can but for anything serious you're going to Inuvik or Yellowknife. that's not changing anytime soon. the population is too small for them to invest in a hospital.

that's probably the right approach for now. get on the list. have a plan. but stay put unless things change. leaving Tuk even for a season is. it's hard to explain. the land needs watching year-round. things happen in winter that you miss if you're not here. thanks for helping me think it through.
need some help putting together a packing list. taking a group out on the land for 4 days and I want to make sure I'm not forgetting anything for the kids.
winter. Arctic winter. we're going out from Tuk onto the land. temperatures will be minus 25 to minus 35 probably. the kids are 14 to 17. most of them have been on the land before but not all.

snowmobile and qamutik. I've done this route plenty of times. it's not the gear for me I'm worried about. it's the kids. some of them are coming up from other communities and they might not have proper stuff. I want a list I can send to their families ahead of time.

cultural education trips. I used to run polar bear tours for tourists but I gave that up. this is what I do now. Indigenous kids from communities around the region come up and we go out for 4 days. I teach them the land skills. reading weather, reading ice, how to travel and camp properly. the things that used to get handed down without anyone having to organize it.
I keep spare gear. parkas, boots in a few sizes, extra mitts. I know some families can't afford it. nobody gets turned back because of gear. that's not the point.

8 this trip. I keep it small. the bear tours used to be 6 to 8 tourists paying good money but this is different. the pay is less but it matters more eh. I'd rather be out there with 8 kids who actually want to learn than a bunch of tourists taking photos from inside the truck.
I bring one helper. usually someone from the community who knows the land. can't run 8 teenagers on the tundra alone at minus 30. need someone watching the back while I'm teaching at the front.

depends on conditions. that's part of what I'm teaching. you don't make a schedule and force the land to follow it. you go out and you respond to what's there. if the weather turns, that's a lesson. if we find tracks, we follow them. if the wind changes, we talk about what that means.
yeah that's fair. parents want to know when their kid is coming home. I'll add that. keep it loose though.
yeah do that. keep it simple. one page.
good. that'll work. thanks.
always do. the land is good to you if you pay attention.
got a GPS collar on the bench with a busted antenna connector. Lotek LiteTrack 420. need to find a replacement SMA connector that'll hold up in cold. any idea where to source one.
the housing is cracked. thermal cycling did it. been on an animal for 14 months. the solder underneath looks fine.
yeah. soldering station and heat gun. done this repair before on other units. sending it south to Lotek takes 6 weeks minimum and I need it back in the field.
I usually use silicone sealant around the connector base. works alright.
that's good to know. the silicone does get brittle. I've had to redo seals in spring after every cold season. the MG Chemicals 832. is that easy to work with.
I go through enough collars that a bigger kit makes sense. I'll order the Amphenol connectors and the MG Chemicals. get a few extra connectors while I'm at it. they crack every season eh.

good call. I'll measure it. one more thing. the antenna itself is fine. but should I test it before I put the collar back on an animal. don't want to go through the repair and find out it's not transmitting.
I've got a NanoVNA somewhere. haven't used it in a while. I'll check the SWR and then run the magnet test. belt and suspenders.
need to put together a survey protocol document for an aerial wildlife count. the territorial government wants everything on paper before they approve the helicopter time.
muskox. total count via strip transects. we fly the transects and count everything we see. survey area is the coastal plain and foothills east of Tuk out toward the Richardson Mountains.
June 4. we fly a Bell 206 from the Inuvik base.
north-south transects. 2 km spacing. we fly at 150 metres. two observers plus the pilot. I sit front left, second observer rear left.

those are about right. we won't fly in fog or anything above 30 for wind. the government is also asking for a section on how we account for animals we miss. they want a detection probability estimate.

yes. last time we did it. detection probability came out around 0.85 in open terrain. lower in the foothills where the ground is broken up. the numbers from the last count were not good though. 340 muskox where the models said there should be about 500.
yeah. calf ratio is important. if recruitment is low that tells us a lot. distribution mapping too. we want to see if the range is contracting or if they're shifting.
June 5 as the backup. weather is always a question up here. could add June 6 as a second backup if they'll give us the window.
yeah. straightforward. the government reviewers need to check boxes, they don't need a novel.
that's good. one thing I should add. we want to compare this count to the one from two years ago. same transects. the government cares about trend more than a single number.
I have the GPS tracks from last time. I'll attach them. same lines, same altitude, same observer method. the only thing that should change is the count.
good. I'll put the tracks in and submit it. need to get it in so they lock down the helicopter. those slots fill up fast once summer field season gets close eh.
we'll see what the land tells us. thanks.
what's the historical average breakup date for sea ice on the Beaufort coast near Tuktoyaktuk. I know what I've seen but I want to check against the official numbers.

the ice is thinner than it should be for early February. we had a warm stretch in December. minus 15 for almost two weeks when it should have been minus 35. the ice didn't build the way it needed to during that window.
cracking in spots that don't normally crack until March. I was out yesterday and there's overflow near the point. the colour is off too. greyer than it should be this time of year.

already have. staying closer to shore. not crossing the harbour the way I normally would in February. some of the younger guys around town don't read it as well as they should though. they see a surface and figure it's solid.

the HTC puts out advisories when they get reports. I'll file one this week with the areas I've flagged. problem is it's February and everyone assumes the ice is at peak thickness. this year it never got there.

I'll mark the coordinates. I noted a few yesterday. every year it seems like the window gets shorter eh. used to be you could count on solid ice by mid-November. now it's getting later and later to freeze and earlier to break.
it's on record in my head. now I just have to write it down for the HTC. writing reports is my least favourite part of the work. rather be out on the land.
what would you say is a reasonable prediction for breakup this year based on what I'm describing. I know it's early to call but I want a range.
forecast is warmer than normal through March. no sign of a deep cold stretch coming. so the recovery window is closing.
that's what I figured. just wanted a second opinion. I'll keep watching it. thanks eh.
quick question. I'm teaching some kids to set up a winter camp this weekend. want to make sure I'm covering the right order of operations for them.
canvas wall tents with wood stoves. the proper way to camp up here. these kids have never put up a wall tent. I want them to do the work with me directing.
yeah. the stove is where I'm most careful with them. a tent fire out on the land is a bad situation.

that's how I learned it. body measurements. my hand span is about 22 cm so two spans puts me close. I'll have each kid figure out their own measurement. a tape measure isn't always with you. your hands are.
anchoring. regular stakes don't hold in snow. I want them to learn deadman anchors.
yeah. if the tent goes at minus 30 in the dark that's not a teaching moment. that's a problem. I'll have them practice before we do the real thing.
the stuff sack trick is good. I'll show them that too. these kids pick things up fast when they're out there doing it. it's different than a classroom.
good. that covers it. thanks eh.
got an email from Natan with some caribou data. he wants me to look at the winter migration routes. wondering if you can help me think through what I'm seeing.
collar tracks. mapped the winter movement. the herd went further west this season than usual. not by a huge amount but it's consistent across the animals he's tracking.
snow was heavier than usual in the eastern range. we got a lot of early snow in November that crusted over hard. so they couldn't dig through to the lichen as easy. that's my read on it.
he's only been on the caribou work a couple seasons. his dataset is short. I told him to dig into the older data from before he took over. the pattern might go back further than he thinks.

I'll pass that along. he's sharp. just needs more years under him. you don't understand caribou from two seasons. you need ten. twenty. you need to see the same animals through good years and bad years.
he sends me stuff when something catches his eye. I look at it and tell him what I think. keeps me connected to that work without running it day to day. good arrangement.
I want to send him back some notes on this. anything specific I should flag besides the snow crusting and the longer time series?
good. that's useful. I'll write it up tonight. short and to the point. Natan doesn't need a lecture. thanks.
need to order some parts for my Polaris online and the website is giving me trouble. not great with this stuff.
I tried parts.polaris.com. need new hyfax rails and a windshield. the windshield cracked. cold does that.
Voyageur 155. I got to the vehicle selection but there's too many options and the trim names don't mean anything to me. the screen on my phone doesn't help either.
hold on. let me go look. ok found the VIN plate. put it in. it pulled up the machine. now there's diagrams of every system on the sled. a lot of diagrams.
found the hyfax under rear suspension. slide shoe rail. $47 each. need two. windshield is under body. $189. the shipping is what kills you though. $65 to get it to my post office.
I'll check Inuvik first. if they don't have it I'll come back and order from here. might as well add spare plugs and a belt to the order if I'm paying that shipping anyway.
one more thing. do you know if the hyfax come with the mounting hardware or do I need to order that separate.
I'll grab the clips too. everything up here gets brittle eventually eh. thanks for walking me through this.
I taped it. it'll hold. tape fixes most things up here. take care.
we're sitting at minus 2 today. mid April. that is not right.
minus 15 to minus 20 still. we've been above minus 10 for almost a week. the snow is getting soft on top. you can feel it when you walk. it shouldn't be doing that yet.

the trails are usable in the morning when it refreezes overnight. by afternoon it's soft. the machine bogs down in it. another week of this and some of the routes I use won't be safe. especially near water.

go out early. back by noon. that's the safe window. any lake crossings I'm avoiding unless I've checked the ice myself that day. some of the younger guys don't think about it. they see the surface and figure it's fine.

I told a few. they nod but they still go out in the afternoon. nothing teaches you like going through the ice once. problem is going through once can kill you. you don't always get to learn the lesson twice.

forecast shows above minus 10 for the next 10 days. if that holds then breakup is going to come early. maybe 2 or 3 weeks early. that changes everything. when you can travel. where you can go. when the water opens up. the whole schedule shifts.

a few things I wanted to do on the land in late April might not happen. that's ok. you plan around the weather. the weather doesn't plan around you. been that way forever. it's just harder to predict what the weather is going to do these days.
yeah. anyway. just keeping an eye on it. morning travel only for now. we'll see what the next week brings.
Annie's school has their end of year ceremony coming up. she wants me to say a few words to open it. not sure what to talk about.

year-end celebration. the kids do presentations about what they learned. parents come. elders come. Annie wants someone to open with a short talk. she asked me because I work on the land and the kids know who I am.
that's good. short is what I want. I don't like talking in front of people. Annie says I talk plenty when it's just us but put me in a room and I dry up.
two minutes is good. I can do two minutes. Annie would talk for twenty if they let her. she's the one who should be up there not me.
maybe. I'll think about what story to tell. something happened last week with a fox that was pretty good. it sat there watching me set up my gear like it was supervising the whole operation.

the ice is going out. sat on the shore this morning and watched it. you can hear it. cracking and shifting. another season almost done.
early. like I expected. the warm spell in April started it and it never recovered. the leads are opening up already. normally that's first week of June not mid May.
not much. you adjust. always have. the land doesn't wait for you to be ready so you better be ready before it moves. my grandfather used to say that.
the birds are early too. geese came through last week. that's ahead of schedule. everything is running faster. the ice, the birds, the snow. the whole system is on a different clock now.

yeah. I don't panic about it. no point in that. but I notice it. I've been on this land my whole life. I can see the difference between now and 20 years ago. the shoreline is different. the timing is different. the ground itself is different.

you just do. the land is still here. I'm still here. the caribou are still moving. the geese still come back. it's not the same as it was but it's not gone. the day I stop going out there is the day I stop understanding it. and then what good am I.
it does. and it's not all bad. the ptarmigan are nesting early too. saw a pair yesterday working on a spot near the ridge. life keeps going. it adapts. we adapt. that's what we do up here.
anyway. just thinking out loud today. the breakup does that to me. feels like an ending and a beginning at the same time. good to sit with it.

Okay so quick question — I'm a PT and I work with a lot of athletes who insist on training outdoors here in Dubai even during summer. We're talking 45, sometimes 48 degrees Celsius!! What are the most evidence-based guidelines I can give them about heat acclimatization and safe outdoor training?

Yes this is perfect! The timing thing is SO hard to get through to people though. I have runners who go out at noon, NOON, in July!! Ai meu Deus I want to scream haha. What are the actual warning signs of heat exhaustion vs heat stroke? I want to make sure I'm giving them the right red flags.

Okay this is really clear, thank you! The sweating vs not sweating distinction is such a good way to explain it to patients. Now what about cooling strategies? This is amazing, thank you!! I'm going to put together a comprehensive heat safety guide for my clinic with all of this. Maybe a nice infographic or something. You've been incredibly helpful! Tchau!!

Oh gente, you have no idea. My tias — my aunties — every time I video-call it's "Bruna when are you coming back?" "Bruna your mother misses you!" "Bruna you're going to get old alone in that desert!" Hey! Quick question about continuing education — do you know much about dry needling as a treatment modality?

I already signed up haha!! I enrolled in a dry needling certification course that starts in April. I've been thinking about it for months and I finally pulled the trigger — no pun intended with the needles haha! It's a weekend course spread over six weeks, theory and hands-on practice.

Gente, so many of my patients are runners and athletes and I see SO much myofascial dysfunction. Tight hip flexors, overactive traps, calf trigger points that won't release with manual therapy alone. I think dry needling could be incredible for those cases. Like imagine — a runner comes in with chronic calf tightness that doesn't respond to stretching or foam rolling, and I can go straight to the trigger point with a needle and release it. Nossa, it would be a game changer!

It's through the Dubai Physiotherapy Association — they partnered with an Australian instructor who's apparently one of the best in the field. I did my research! The certification is recognized in the UAE and they give you continuing education credits too. And the best part? My clinic is paying for half of it because they see the value in having a PT who can do dry needling.

I'll definitely ease in! I'm not going to just start needling everyone haha. My plan is to identify maybe three or four patients with chronic trigger point issues — probably my runners who've been stuck in their rehab progress — and offer it as an adjunct to what we're already doing. Not replacing manual therapy, just adding another tool. I believe in building a toolkit, you know?

Oh for sure some people will freak out haha! But honestly my athlete patients tend to be pretty open to anything that works. These are people who do ice baths and cupping and all kinds of things — a thin needle is nothing compared to what they put their bodies through in training. And I'll always explain everything first, I never do anything to a patient without them understanding why. Informed consent is everything, meu bem!

Okay a LITTLE nervous haha! It's been a long time since I learned a completely new hands-on skill. Like in my DPT program I was learning new techniques every week but now I've been practicing the same modalities for years. It's exciting to be a student again though!! I love learning, I'm such a nerd about this stuff. My mom was here visiting and she saw all my anatomy books spread out on the kitchen table and she was like "Bruna you're 41 years old why are you still studying" haha. Dona Lucia doesn't understand, bless her.

I'm going to be the best dry needling student they've ever had, watch me haha. Obrigada querida, I love talking about this stuff!!

I need to nerd out about biomechanics for a second, is that okay haha

So I have this patient — recreational runner, started training for a 10K a few months ago, and now has medial tibial stress syndrome. Classic shin splints. He came in thinking he just needs to stretch more and ice it. But I did a gait analysis and gente, there is SO much going on biomechanically that stretching will not fix!

Combination! That's what's so interesting. First — excessive pronation on the left side. His foot is collapsing inward way too much at midstance. But here's the thing, the pronation isn't just a foot problem. When I looked at his hips, his left glute med is significantly weaker than the right. So the hip is dropping, the knee is caving in, and the foot is compensating. It's a whole chain reaction!

Yes!! His stride length on the left is about 8% longer than the right. He's overstriding on that side, which means more braking force, more impact through the tibia. And his cadence is low — around 156 steps per minute. For his height and pace, he should be closer to 170-175. Low cadence plus overstriding plus hip drop equals his poor tibias absorbing way too much force every single step.

Multiple levels at the same time! I can't just do hip strengthening and send him back to running with the same gait pattern, right? So the plan is — glute med strengthening obviously, clamshells, single-leg bridges, lateral band walks. But ALSO cadence retraining. I'm going to have him run with a metronome app set to 170 and practice shorter, quicker steps. And we're looking at his shoes because they are completely worn out, zero support.

Nossa, the wear pattern on the left shoe told me everything before I even watched him run haha! The medial side of the sole is completely ground down — classic overpronation wear. And the heel is worn at a weird angle that confirms the overstriding. I always tell my patients, bring your old shoes to the appointment because they're like a diary of how you move. Every step you've ever taken is written on the bottom of those shoes!

I'm not stopping him completely because honestly he won't listen haha — runners never do. You tell them to stop and they just go run anyway and don't tell you. So I'd rather control it. I'm cutting his volume by about 50%, having him run on softer surfaces when possible, short intervals with the metronome to practice the new cadence. Then we gradually build back up once the glute strength improves and the new pattern starts to feel natural.

Usually about 4-6 weeks of consistent practice for the new cadence to start feeling natural. The first two weeks are the hardest — patients say it feels weird, choppy, like they're shuffling. But once the neuromuscular adaptation kicks in, it clicks. And then they come back and say 'wow, running actually feels easier now.' That's my favorite moment, querida! When the biomechanics click and the patient FEELS the difference.

Every two weeks! I'll re-film his running and compare side by side with the initial assessment. That way he can SEE the improvement too, not just feel it. Visual feedback is so powerful for patients — when they watch themselves running and can see the hip drop getting smaller or the stride getting more symmetrical, it motivates them to keep doing the boring exercises at home. Ai meu Deus, I love this stuff. Every body tells a different story!

Okay so I got into a heated debate at work today about foam rolling and now I need to process it haha

So one of my colleagues is completely anti-foam rolling. He says the evidence doesn't support it, it doesn't actually change tissue structure, the fascial release narrative is basically mythology, and we're wasting patients' time recommending it. And I'm sitting there like — meu bem, I use foam rolling with patients EVERY DAY. Am I a fraud?? Haha no but seriously it made me think.

Okay so here's where I am — I DON'T think it's breaking up adhesions or releasing fascia in the way people used to claim. That old narrative of 'you're ironing out your muscles' is probably not what's happening at a tissue level. The forces you can generate with a foam roller are nowhere near enough to permanently deform fascial tissue. My colleague is right about that part. BUT — something is happening! Patients feel better. They move better after rolling. You can't just dismiss that!

YES! That's exactly where I've landed. It's neurological, not mechanical. The foam roller is basically a pain modulation tool. You're giving the nervous system a novel sensory input, it recalibrates, and the person feels less stiff and moves more freely. It's not that the tissue changed — it's that the brain's interpretation of the tissue changed. And honestly? I think that's still valuable!

Ai meu Deus that's literally what he said haha! And you know what, he might have a point about that. A dynamic warm-up probably achieves similar neurological effects. BUT — and this is where I push back — foam rolling gives patients something they can do independently, at home, that makes them feel in control of their body. There's a self-efficacy component. They feel like they're actively doing something for their recovery. That psychological benefit is real and I refuse to dismiss it!

He said — and I quote — 'if the benefit is psychological then we should just be honest about that instead of pretending it's doing something physiological.' Which is actually a fair point?? Like, should I be telling patients 'this is going to release your tight fascia' when I don't believe that's what's happening? Or should I say 'this is going to help your nervous system recalibrate and you'll feel less stiff'? Gente, I think I need to update my language.

Exactly! I don't need to lie to patients to make foam rolling useful. I just need better framing. And honestly this is why I love having colleagues who challenge me — it makes me a better clinician. Even when it's annoying in the moment haha. Like I was defensive at first but then I went home and thought about it and realized he pushed my thinking forward.

He really is! Every clinic needs that one person who questions everything haha. Okay I'm going to go read some of the newer systematic reviews on foam rolling tonight. This is my idea of a fun Sunday — research papers and a protein shake. Nossa, I'm such a nerd but I LOVE IT. The science of the body is endlessly fascinating to me!

The survey lap!! That's actually genius. Because you're right — half of what I eat at brunch I eat just because it's THERE, not because I actually wanted it. Like did I really want truffle pasta? No! Honestly? Sushi and desserts haha! Those are the things that genuinely excite me. The carving station and the pasta are fine but I can get lamb and pasta anywhere. So maybe I should just own that — go straight for my favorites, enjoy them properly, and skip the filler foods I eat out of obligation to the buffet. That's what I keep telling my patients too!! One meal doesn't define your health. Consistency over perfection. I'm great at giving this advice, terrible at following it myself haha. But okay — new brunch protocol: survey lap, pick my real favorites, enjoy them without guilt, and stop sampling every single station like I'm a food critic being paid for a review. I spend so much energy stressing about brunch when I should just enjoy it!
Ugh I need to vent. I've been holding this in for weeks and I'm about to explode haha. Things at my clinic have gone completely sideways.

Every day haha. But it's complicated — my visa is tied to them, starting a clinic in Dubai is insanely expensive, the licensing is intense. You know what, you're right. I think I was so busy being angry that I forgot I can actually make a case for doing things my way. I'm going to start pulling my outcome data this weekend. My mother says if I survived moving across the world alone, I can survive some corporate nonsense. She's right!
I will! Thank you meu bem, I really needed this conversation. Let PhysioFirst try to argue with RESULTS! My patients are not numbers and I'm going to prove it, querida!
So remember how I was training for the marathon? Yeah. That is NOT happening anymore haha. I have some frustrating news.

My knee happened. I'd been dealing with anterior knee pain for a while and kept ignoring it because — and this is the embarrassing part — I'm a PHYSICAL THERAPIST. I literally treat this stuff every day but when it's your own body you become the worst patient. Told myself it was just overuse, foam roll it, it'll be fine. Spoiler: not fine.

Patellofemoral syndrome. Classic runner's knee! Ai meu Deus, the irony is KILLING me. My colleague Sara literally laughed in my face when I told her. A physical therapist with runner's knee — gente, it's like a dentist with cavities! I know every single protocol, every exercise, every progression, and I still did this to myself by being stubborn.

The honest truth? Running five times a week, the high mileage, the pavement pounding — that chapter is probably over. My cartilage is not happy and at 41 I need to be realistic about what my joints can handle long-term. So I made the hard decision to stop running completely.

I cried, querida. Like actually cried. Running was my therapy, my meditation, my mornings at 5am before the heat hit. The streets are empty, the city is quiet, it was MY time. Losing that felt like losing a part of myself. And I know that sounds dramatic for 'just exercise' but anyone who runs knows — it's never just exercise.

Yes!! And okay here's the silver lining — I switched to cycling and I'm starting to genuinely LOVE it! Got a proper road bike, joined a cycling group that does Al Qudra on Friday mornings. Zero impact on my knee, I still get the cardio and the outdoor feeling. The wind, the desert, the sunrise — nossa, it's honestly beautiful.

Zero pain! The knee stays in a controlled range, no impact loading, no eccentric stress on the patella. It's the perfect swap and I say that as someone who prescribes exactly this transition to my patients all the time haha. One of the guys in the group is an ex-triathlete and he's been coaching me on cadence and positioning. I'm getting faster every week!

You know me, meu bem — I can't do anything halfway haha! I already have a training plan and I'm looking at amateur races. The group is competitive so it pushes me. I went from 'I guess I'll try cycling' to 'I need a power meter and aero wheels' in about three weeks. My bank account is not happy but my knee is!

SO much! Now when a patient sits in front of me devastated because they can't do their sport anymore, I really FEEL it. Before I could empathize intellectually but now I understand the grief on a visceral level. It's like losing a friend. But I also understand now that the body adapts, you find new things, and sometimes what you're forced into ends up being exactly what you needed.

Okay I need to have a professional rant about recovery gadgets because my patients keep asking me about them and I have FEELINGS haha. Can I bounce some thoughts off you?

Everyone wants to talk about Theraguns, Normatec boots, and ice baths. In that order. Every single week someone walks in and says 'my friend has a Theragun, should I get one?' And look — I actually think percussion massagers are legit! But gente, people use them completely wrong. They just jackhammer their quads for thirty seconds and think they've done recovery. You need to understand WHAT you're trying to achieve — warming up tissue versus breaking up adhesions, it's completely different technique.

Get a Theragun or Hypervolt — the brand matters less than having multiple speed settings and attachments. Learn the actual anatomy of what you're hitting. Warming up? Light pressure, broad strokes, keep it moving. Post-workout for adhesions? Slower, deeper, stay on the spot longer. And for the love of God, do NOT use it directly on a bone or a joint. I had a patient Theragun his own kneecap last month. HIS KNEECAP, querida! I almost lost my mind!

Normatec is interesting because the mechanism is actually solid — sequential pneumatic compression from feet up to hips, great for lymphatic drainage and reducing swelling. It FEELS incredible after a hard session, like your legs are getting a hug from a very organized robot haha. But here's the thing nobody wants to hear — the research on whether it actually speeds up tissue repair is mixed at best. It definitely reduces perceived soreness but perceived and actual are not the same thing.

If you're a professional athlete or someone who trains really hard six days a week, sure, the Normatec might be worth it for that perceived recovery and the relaxation factor. For a regular gym person? Nossa, spend that money on a good mattress instead! Sleep will do more for your recovery than any compression boot ever could. But try telling that to someone who saw their favorite influencer posting about Normatec — they don't want to hear 'go to bed earlier' haha.

Ai meu Deus, the cold plunge craze! Okay so I actually love cold water immersion and there are real benefits — nervous system regulation, mood, perceived recovery. BUT here's what nobody talks about: if you ice bath right after strength training, you are BLUNTING the inflammatory response that drives muscle adaptation. You're literally fighting against your own gains! Inflammation after lifting isn't a bug, it's a feature!

For endurance athletes between competitions, great. For managing general soreness when you're not trying to build muscle, fine. But after a hypertrophy session? Wait at least four to six hours or just skip it that day. Context is EVERYTHING in recovery, meu bem! A cold shower works almost as well for the nervous system and mood benefits anyway — you don't need a $3000 plunge tub to get the dopamine hit.

Number one: SLEEP. Eight hours of quality sleep does more than every gadget combined but nobody wants to hear it because sleeping doesn't look cool on Instagram. Number two: a decent percussion massager, learn to use it properly. Number three: foam rolling — cheap, effective, boring, perfect. Everything else is luxury extras. Normatec and ice baths are nice to have but they're the cherry on top, not the sundae. The sundae is sleep, nutrition, and consistent training. Save your money and go to bed earlier, querida!

Great question! So the big ones: limb symmetry index above 90% for quad and hamstring strength — he hit 98% which is elite. Single-leg hop tests within 90% of the uninvolved side. Psychological readiness — we used the ACL-RSI questionnaire and he scored really well, no fear of re-injury. And then the eye test, gente — I watched him train, watched him cut and pivot under pressure, watched his movement quality under fatigue. Numbers are important but they don't tell you everything. Okay I need a place to rant haha. Three patients this week told me they're doing reformer pilates and that's their entire fitness program. THREE. I love pilates but gente, I have thoughts.

Look, the reformer is great for certain things — body awareness, stability, controlled loading with the springs. For someone who's never exercised before or who's coming back from an injury, a good instructor on a reformer can do wonderful things. I've actually referred patients to pilates before, genuinely. So I'm not anti-pilates at all.

The issue is when people treat it like it's the ONLY thing they need!! Someone comes in and says 'I do reformer three times a week' like they've cracked the fitness code. But meu bem, reformer pilates alone will NOT build meaningful strength. The loads are too low for progressive overload! You need to actually lift weights, do some impact work, challenge your body with real-world movement patterns. The reformer is a complement, not a replacement.

AI MEU DEUS the marketing!! Don't even get me started. 'Sculpt and tone your body' — what does that even mean scientifically?? Nothing! It means nothing! okay I'm genuinely going to do this. I'll track it for a week — how many patients need pre-warming, how long it takes each time — and then present the data. Nossa, data-driven thermostat negotiation. I'm in a really reflective mood today. I've been in Dubai for a while now and I just kind of feel like... taking stock of everything? Does that make sense?

it's kind of an anniversary, yeah. I was looking through old photos on my phone and found pictures from when I first arrived here — ai meu Deus I looked so lost haha. I didn't know anyone, didn't know how anything worked, couldn't figure out the metro system. I remember sitting in my empty apartment eating delivery shawarma for the third night in a row thinking 'what did I do?'

oh gente, completely different person! I mean, not different — I'm still ME — but I've grown so much. I built a career here, I have colleagues who became real friends, I know the city, I have my routines, my favorite places. I learned how to navigate a totally different culture. I learned how to deal with the heat haha, which honestly was the hardest part in the beginning. Coming from Brazil I thought I could handle hot weather but Dubai hot is a DIFFERENT kind of hot

and THAT is the question, querida. That is the million dollar question. Because... both? Dubai is home in the practical sense — my work is here, my daily life is here, my apartment, my bike, my coffee shop where they know my order. But home in the deep sense, like home in my bones? That's still Brazil. That's still hearing Portuguese on the street. That's the smell of rain on hot pavement back home. That saudade never goes away, you know?

it used to be heavy. Like really heavy, especially the first year or two. I would cry on the phone with my mom, I would hear a Brazilian song and just lose it. But now it's more... gentle? It's like this soft ache that lives inside me. It flares up sometimes — when I cook Brazilian food, when I hear someone speaking Portuguese at the mall, during Carnival season when everyone back home is celebrating and I'm just here at work. But most days it's manageable. It's just part of me now.

nossa, that actually made me tear up a little haha. But yes that's exactly it. And you know what, I think the gratitude and the saudade coexist. I am SO grateful for what Dubai has given me — professionally I've grown more than I ever imagined, I've met people from all over the world, I've experienced things I never thought I would. But I'm also grateful for where I come from because it made me who I am

honestly? The warmth. The way Brazilians connect with people — I bring that into my work every day and my patients feel it. I've had patients tell me that what they appreciate most isn't even my clinical skills, it's that I make them feel like a person, not a file number. And that's so Brazilian, you know? We hug, we touch, we ask about your family, we CARE loudly. I'm proud that I didn't lose that. Dubai could have made me more corporate, more detached, but it didn't

okay now I'm definitely going to cry haha. But happy tears! I think I needed this today — just to sit with all of it and acknowledge it. The hard parts and the beautiful parts. The loneliness of those first months and the fullness of life now. I wouldn't trade this experience for anything, even on the days when the saudade hits hard

okay I'm going to stop before I fully lose it haha. Thank you for letting me just... talk this through. Sometimes you need to say it out loud to really feel it. I'm proud of myself. And I'm proud of still missing home, because it means home was worth missing. Ai meu Deus now I really am crying haha. I'm going to go call my mom. Thank you meu bem!

right so i need to figure out the most efficient way to hit four farms tomorrow. two up near thurso, one outside wick, and one just south of helmsdale. currently based in inverness. whats the best order to do them in if i need to be back by half six.

aye that was roughly what i was thinking. prob leave about half 7 in the morning. the thurso ones are just routine tb tests so maybe 45 mins each. wick is a lame ewe that needs looking at, half hour tops. helmsdale is a calvings check on a heifer so that one is unpredictable tbh.

thats actually not a bad shout. helmsdale on the way back means if it runs long i'm only an hour from home instead of having the whole day pile up behind me. the farmer there is chill anyway, he wont mind a later slot.

aye that works. this is just a standard week tbh. the nhs highland rural vet service covers an absolutely mental amount of ground. inverness to caithness is like 120 miles one way. some days i feel like a taxi driver who occasionally looks at a sheep.

depends on the week. sometimes its all local, inverness and surrounds, which is grand. but we're covering everything from the black isle up to the north coast basically. not enough of us to go round so you end up doing these big loops prob two or three times a week. winter is worse cos the roads are hellish and everything takes longer.

mileage aye but its not exactly generous. theres a couple of us who rotate the far north runs. my colleague ailsa does sutherland mostly but shes on maternity leave so ive been picking up her patch too. its fine, just means a lot of early starts and podcasts.

good point actually. forecast said rain turning to sleet above helmsdale tomorrow. might leave at 7 instead of half 7 to give myself a buffer. better sat waiting in a farm car park than rushing on an icy road with a boot full of veterinary kit.
cheers. the heifer will do whatever she wants and i will stand there in the rain and deal with it. thats the job. right, better go sort the kit bag. ta.
had a student shadow me today. 4th year vet student. spent the whole day asking me why i chose large animal instead of small animal. got me thinking tbh.

told her the honest answer which is that i never really considered anything else. small animal just wasnt on the radar. dogs and cats are fine but its not what i know. grew up around livestock so this was always going to be the path.

aye. sheep farm near aviemore. dad still runs it, smaller operation now than when i was wee but hes still got about 300 blackface ewes up on the hill. i was dosing lambs and checking feet before i could drive. becoming a vet was just the obvious next step really. same work but you get paid for it and people stop asking you to fix fences.

him and a neighbour help each other out at gathering and lambing. hes 62 and stubborn as the sheep tbh. wont scale down any further. i go back and help at lambing time which is a laugh cos i show up as the qualified vet and he still tells me im doing everything wrong.

bit of both. its good to be back on the farm and doing the physical graft. reminds you why you got into it. but aye its also knackering cos im still on call for my actual job so sometimes im up at 3am pulling a lamb at dads and then driving to some farm in easter ross by 8. not ideal.

about three weeks main burst, mid april usually. hes got them fairly tight-tupped so most come within that window. stragglers after that but nothing major. its manageable if the weather holds but last year we had snow in late april which was grim. lost a few lambs to exposure.

ngl she seemed genuinely interested. asked good questions, wasnt squeamish when we did a rectal on a cow, and didnt complain about the cold. those are basically the three job requirements. i told her if she can handle standing in a field in november with her arm inside a highland cow shes prob cut out for it.

im 29. i am not a mentor. i am barely qualified myself some days. but aye it was alright. nice to remember that this is actually a decent job when youre not stuck on the a9 in sleet for the third time in a week.
aye well. somebody has to do it. right im off, got an early one tomorrow. cheers.

the microwave meals thing is fair tbh. the rest of it, i mean, she works 12 hour shifts delivering babies and i work 14 hour days with my arm inside cows. neither of us has time for anything. but shes got a boyfriend so she thinks shes got the authority to lecture me on that front.

bit of both. she does care, shes just annoying about it. and look i know im not exactly putting myself out there. havent dated since uni if were being honest. but its not like inverness is awash with eligible people and i work 6 days a week so when exactly am i supposed to be doing the whole dating thing.

aye thats the question isnt it. i think id like to not be eating beans on toast alone at 9pm every night but i also cant be bothered with the whole rigmarole of apps and small talk. i am not good at small talk. i talk about sheep and the weather. thats my range.

she would actually combust. right well i think massage gun is the answer for the present. ill order one this week before i forget. and ill tell her im on the apps even though im not, just to get her off my back for christmas dinner.

whats the most professional way to email a farmer and cancel an afternoon appointment same day. need to reschedule two farm visits for today.

tomorrow should be fine aye. i just need to get through today. having a rough crohns day and im basically chained to the bathroom. cant be 40 miles from a toilet in this state.

nah both are routine. one is a follow-up on a lame cow, other is a flock health check. nothing that cant wait a day. ive had crohns since i was 21 so ive got fairly good at knowing which days are write-offs and which ones i can push through. today is a write-off.
