Two thousand dollars and a family of four starting from nothing in a country where my father's dental credentials meant nothing. He could not practice. He had to begin the entire credentialing process again.

Yes, please. I would like to open with Tajrish. I have very few memories of it myself — just fragments, light through a window, the sound of the call to prayer. But my father described it to me so many times that I feel as though I remember it clearly.

That is remarkably close to what I feel. The line about his memories becoming mine — that is exactly right. I may adjust one or two phrases, but the essence is there. Now, for the transition to the departure — I do not want to dwell on the political upheaval. My father never spoke bitterly about Iran. He spoke with sadness, but never bitterness.

Yes, jan. That is precisely the tone. 'Quiet, and it was final' — that captures my father perfectly. He was not a man who raised his voice. He simply made decisions and carried them out with dignity. I think this will be a speech he would be proud of.

I think I have the voice now. You have helped me find it, which is what I needed most. I will draft the remaining sections myself and perhaps come back if I need to refine anything before the event. Thank you for your sensitivity with this.

I would like to plan a meaningful anniversary gift for my wife. We are coming up on twenty-three years of marriage, and I want to do something that reflects who she is rather than something generic. Could you help me think through some ideas?

Her name is Shirin, and she is one of the most dedicated people I have ever known. Every Saturday for the past eleven years, she has been teaching Farsi at the Persian Cultural Center. She is not paid for it — she does it because she believes the language must not be lost in the next generation. It is a calling for her, jan.

The calligraphy idea is striking. Shirin has always loved the art of Persian script. Do you know if it is possible to commission a custom piece with a specific verse? I have a particular poem in mind — one that her grandmother used to recite to her as a child.

I have the verse. It is from Hafez. I will not share the full text here, but it speaks about the permanence of love through the passage of time. Very fitting, I think, for twenty-three years together.

It is in late January, so I have approximately two months. That should be sufficient, yes? I want this to be perfect, jan. Shirin deserves nothing less. She has been the foundation of our family for over two decades.

No, I think the words in that moment should come from me and only me. But you have given me an excellent framework for the entire plan. I am genuinely grateful. Shirin puts so much into everything she does — the teaching, the family, all of it — and I want her to know that I see it.
I have a question about managing a chronic condition while being, shall we say, uncooperative with certain dietary recommendations. I realize this may sound foolish, but I need a practical strategy.

Gout. My right big toe has been giving me trouble again this week — it flares up and feels like someone has set a small fire inside the joint. My rheumatologist has been quite clear that I should eliminate red meat from my diet. I understand the science behind it completely. I simply refuse to do it.

I take allopurinol, three hundred milligrams daily. The flares happen perhaps three or four times a year, almost always in the right big toe. And the red meat I cannot give up — jan, it is kabob koobideh. It is not merely food to me. It is how I was raised. It is what I serve when I host. My father made it every Friday. Asking me to stop eating koobideh is asking me to cut off a piece of my identity.

This is reasonable. I can accept moderation where I cannot accept elimination. The hydration point is well taken — I confess I do not drink nearly enough water. I am busy at the practice all day and I simply forget. By evening I have had perhaps two glasses.

I will try the water bottle approach. I already keep one in my operatory but I rarely touch it during procedures, for obvious reasons. Perhaps I can make it a habit between patients. Now, regarding the flares themselves — when one strikes, what is the best immediate response? The pain this week has been quite severe.

I took naproxen this morning. It has taken the edge off, but the joint is still swollen and tender. The most difficult part is that I am on my feet all day performing procedures. Standing for hours with a flare in the toe is its own special form of misery, jan.

That is a good point. I had my levels checked about six months ago and I believe they were slightly above target. I will follow up on that. You know, my rheumatologist told me I could make this entire problem significantly better by simply giving up red meat. I told him I would rather limp.
You have given me something my rheumatologist has not — a plan I will actually follow. I appreciate the pragmatism, jan. The water bottle goes on the counter tomorrow morning.

I have been asked to serve on a mentorship panel for pre-dental students at a university here in San Diego. I want to be candid about what the path looks like without discouraging them. How would you suggest I structure brief remarks — perhaps five minutes — that are both honest and inspiring?

Of course. I earned my DDS at UCLA. My father — he was also a dentist — drove me to the UCLA campus when I was twelve years old. He parked the car, pointed at the dental school building, and said, 'This is where you will study.' There was no discussion, jan. It was simply declared.

I specialized. After UCLA I completed my periodontal residency at USC. That was three years of working eighty hours a week, sometimes more. The clinical load was relentless. I remember weeks where I slept in the residents' lounge more than in my own bed. It was the most demanding period of my life, without question.

I would like help with the second section — the grind, as you put it. I want to convey the difficulty without making it sound like suffering for its own sake. There was purpose in every one of those hours, even when I could not see it at the time.

That is very well done. The final line — 'the difficulty is the training' — I will absolutely use that. It captures precisely what I want them to understand. My only concern is that I do not want to seem as though I am boasting about suffering. These students already feel enough pressure.

That is a good idea, though I think I will keep it brief. Periodontics appealed to me because it is where precision matters most. The margin for error in soft tissue surgery is measured in fractions of a millimeter. That level of exactness — it suits my temperament. My wife would say it suits it too well, jan.

I think I know how I want to close. I want to bring it back to my father. He made the journey from having nothing in a new country to watching his son graduate from the very school he pointed to when I was twelve. That is the payoff. Not the degree on the wall, jan — the look on his face.

Thank you. You have helped me organize what was a collection of scattered thoughts into something coherent and meaningful. I am looking forward to the panel now, which I was not an hour ago. I appreciate your help, jan.
Good evening. I would like some help thinking through my retirement projections. I have been meaning to sit down and look at the numbers properly.

I am 51. I own a periodontal practice, so there is no pension — I am the business. I would like to retire at 65, perhaps 67 if I am still enjoying the work. The retirement accounts are sitting at roughly 1.2 million dollars right now.

I contribute to a SEP-IRA — the maximum each year, so around $66,000. The practice itself has value, certainly, though I have not had a formal valuation done. As for allocation, I defer to my advisor on that. Howard Chen at Merrill Lynch has been managing everything since 2015.

Collections run about $1.1 million annually, sometimes a bit more. And I believe Howard charges around one percent. He is conservative with the investments, which I appreciate. I take enough risk running the business — I do not need volatility in my retirement accounts on top of that.

Shirin and I have discussed this. We would want perhaps $150,000 to $180,000 per year. We like to travel, we entertain frequently, and I would want to maintain the house. Nothing extravagant, but we have built a certain life and I do not intend to shrink it.

The Roth conversion is something I have been meaning to ask Howard about, actually. He brought it up once but we never followed through. And you are right about the practice valuation — I have been putting it off because it feels like planning for the end, jan. But it is just prudent.
That would be helpful, yes. I want to go in prepared. My father always said that you should never walk into a meeting without knowing what you want to walk out with.

This is exactly what I needed, jan. Thank you. I will print this and bring it to Howard next week. It is reassuring to see that the numbers are headed in the right direction. I built this practice from nothing and I want to make sure the ending is as deliberate as the beginning.

I have a question about managing patient expectations, jan. A referring dentist has been asking me to see his emergency patients on Saturdays. I want to maintain the relationship, but I have firm boundaries about my schedule.

He sends perhaps two or three referrals a month, which is significant. He is one of my top referring doctors. But my Saturdays are not available. I do not work weekends. Period. Saturday is for family and Sunday is for golf. This is not negotiable for me.

The Monday priority slot is a good idea. I could accommodate that. As for the phone triage — I would not mind taking a brief call if it is genuinely urgent. I am not unreasonable, jan. But I will not go into the office on a weekend. My father worked seven days a week when we first came to this country. It nearly cost him his marriage.

I think a phone conversation would be better — more personal. But let me think through the key points. I want to be diplomatic. He is a good man, and he is not being unreasonable in his request. He simply does not understand that weekends are sacred in my house.

I do not need to rehearse it, but I appreciate the structure. I think I will call him tomorrow. The one thing I want to be careful about is not opening the door even slightly. I made a promise to Shirin — Saturdays belong to her and our family. If I give one Saturday, it becomes two, then it becomes every Saturday. I have seen it happen to colleagues.
That is a good point about framing it logistically. My hygienist and assistant are not there on weekends, so even if I wanted to, I could not do proper treatment alone. That is simply the truth.

You are right. Thank you, jan. I feel much more settled about this. I will call him in the morning before my first patient. I think he will appreciate the Monday priority arrangement — his patients will still be seen faster than with anyone else in the area.
I have been thinking about buying a new set of irons and I would appreciate some guidance. I play every Sunday and I want something that forgives my occasional mistakes but still feels precise.

I typically shoot in the low 90s. My playing partners seem impressed by that, but honestly I find it unacceptable — there is always room for refinement. I am currently using Titleist AP2s that are perhaps eight years old. Budget is not a primary concern. And yes, I would want a proper fitting.

I am a member at Rancho Santa Fe Golf Club. I have been there for seven years now. The course is immaculate — beautifully maintained, not a blade of grass out of place. It is one of those courses where you feel the club's standards the moment you drive through the gate.

They have a pro shop with fitting capabilities, yes, but I have also heard good things about Club Champion in San Diego. The initiation fee at Rancho Santa Fe was $35,000, jan — after that investment, I want to make sure I am playing the right equipment for the course.
Yes, please. I want to be prepared. I approach everything in my life with precision — my clinical work, my dinner parties, even how I arrange my desk. Golf should be no different.

This is very thorough. I appreciate it. Though I should tell you, jan — golf for me is not really about the score. It is a form of meditation. Sunday morning, the course is quiet, the air is clean, and for four hours I am not thinking about bone grafts or implant placements. I do not keep score with any seriousness. It is about the walk and the company.

Mizuno. I like that suggestion. A Japanese company that takes precision as seriously as I do. I will call Club Champion this week to schedule the fitting. Perhaps they can have the Mizunos ready for me to test.

I will, jan. Thank you for this. You have given me something pleasant to look forward to this week. Now if you will excuse me, I need to go check on the tahdig — Shirin is expecting twelve people tonight and I cannot let the rice burn.
I need help thinking through a major business decision, jan. I am considering opening a second practice location and I want to be methodical about the analysis.

I have been exploring spaces in La Jolla. The logic is straightforward — a second location would substantially widen my referral network. Right now all of my referring general dentists are concentrated in the central San Diego corridor. La Jolla gives me access to a different patient base entirely.

I have found a suite on Prospect Street that I am quite taken with. Eighteen hundred square feet, good natural light, street-level access. The rent is $8,500 per month. I would split my time initially — perhaps three days in my current location and two days in La Jolla.

My average case value for periodontal treatment is roughly $2,800, and for implant cases it runs closer to $4,500. On a full operating day I see between six and eight patients. So at two days per week, perhaps twelve to sixteen patients weekly in La Jolla, once the referral pipeline is established.

I have not gotten formal bids yet, but based on my experience building out my current office, I would estimate $250,000 to $350,000 for a proper periodontal surgical suite. Operatories, sterilization, digital imaging — it has to be done correctly. I will not open a second-rate facility.

I am not quite at capacity — I could probably add another two or three patients per week at my current location. But the issue is not volume today, it is geographic reach for the future. La Jolla is where growth will come from. The referring dentists there currently send their perio cases to other specialists simply because I am not nearby.

The lease negotiation point is excellent — I did not think to ask for a buildout concession. And the referral outreach before opening is wise. I could host a small reception for La Jolla dentists, perhaps at one of the restaurants there. Build relationships before asking for referrals. That is how it should be done, jan.

Thank you, jan. You have given me a structured approach, which is exactly what I needed. I tend to get excited about the vision and skip ahead. Shirin tells me the same thing — she says I see the finished tahdig before the rice is even soaked. But she is supportive of the expansion. We will see what the numbers say.
I need to organize my continuing education credits. My California dental license renewal is coming up on April 30 and I want to make sure everything is in order well before the deadline.

The California Dental Board requires 25 credits for the renewal cycle. I have completed 18 so far. I believe there are mandatory categories — infection control and California dental practice act — but I covered those early in the cycle. What I need now are seven general CE credits.

There is actually a periodontal laser symposium in Los Angeles next month that I have been considering. It covers eight credits, which would more than close the gap. The content is directly relevant to my practice, so it would not feel like checking a box — I would actually learn something useful.

I believe it is April 11 and 12 — a Friday and Saturday. That would give me nearly three weeks before the deadline. And it is organized through the American Academy of Periodontology, so I have no doubt about the accreditation.

I do. I keep a folder — both physical and digital — with every certificate organized by date. I scan them the day I receive them. My office manager thinks I am excessive, but I have seen colleagues scramble to find certificates at the last minute. That is not going to be me, jan.

The renewal fee is straightforward — I believe it is around $500. The form is online now, which is an improvement over the old paper system. I simply need to attest that I have completed the required credits and keep the certificates on file in case of audit. No, I think the symposium is the final piece. I do not like cutting things close, even when the math works out.

Exactly. I refuse to attend CE courses that are a waste of my time just to accumulate credits. Every hour I spend should make me a better clinician. Thank you for helping me organize this, jan. I will register tonight before I forget.
I need to vent for a moment, if you do not mind. I just got off the phone with an insurance company and I am genuinely beside myself.

I have a patient, jan, a lovely woman in her sixties. Moderate to severe periodontitis. Bone loss clearly visible on the radiographs. I recommended scaling and root planing — this is textbook, first-line treatment. The insurance company denied the claim. Denied it. They said it was not medically necessary.

They said the pocket depths were insufficient. The patient has four-millimeter and five-millimeter pockets with bleeding on probing and radiographic bone loss. By every clinical guideline in existence, this patient needs treatment. But some reviewer sitting in an office somewhere, who has never examined this woman, decided it is not necessary.

I have appealed, yes. I wrote a detailed narrative with the clinical findings, attached the radiographs, the probing chart, everything. My office manager spent two hours on this. Two hours of her time that I am paying for, to argue with people who have no clinical training about whether my patient deserves treatment.

The peer-to-peer review is an excellent suggestion. I will request that. Let them put a periodontist on the phone with me and I will walk them through every millimeter of this case. What bothers me most, jan, is that the patient suffers. She called my office today, confused. She does not understand why her insurance will not cover a treatment her doctor says she needs. What am I supposed to tell her?

That is a very good point about the employer angle. I had not considered that. You know, the fundamental problem is that dental insurance was designed in the 1960s and the annual maximum has barely changed since then. Most plans still cap at $1,500 per year. Adjusted for inflation, that number should be over $10,000. The entire model is broken.

I have thought about it. Several colleagues have implemented in-house membership plans for their patients. It is appealing because it removes the insurance company from the equation entirely. But the reality is that most of my patients have insurance through their employers and they expect to use it. I cannot simply tell them to ignore their benefits. It is a difficult situation, jan. I became a clinician to treat patients, not to argue with bureaucrats.

That is excellent advice. Tracking the administrative hours is something I should have been doing from the start. I will have my office manager begin logging that immediately. Thank you for letting me vent, jan. I feel somewhat better. Now I need to go prepare for my afternoon patients. At least in the operatory, I am in control.
I am still recovering, jan. We hosted Nowruz dinner on March 20 and I do not think my kitchen has fully recovered either.
Forty guests. Shirin and I had been planning for weeks. Forty people in our home for the Persian New Year. My dining room was at capacity, jan. We had to borrow folding tables from my neighbor.

Multi-day is an understatement. I started the lamb three days before. Twelve pounds of lamb, jan. I marinated it with saffron, yogurt, onion, and a spice blend that my mother taught me. Twelve pounds sounds excessive until you are feeding forty people and then you realize it is barely enough.

I did a slow roast for the main leg and shoulder pieces. Eight hours at a low temperature. The remaining cuts I used for a lamb shank stew — a kind of abgoosht. And of course the tahdig. I made the largest tahdig I have ever attempted. Six cups of basmati, jan. It barely fit in my largest pot.

It was perfect. Golden, even, with that crunch that makes the entire table go quiet for a moment. I will be honest, I was nervous. At that volume, if you lose the crust or if it burns, you have ruined the centerpiece of the meal. But the key is patience and the right amount of oil. I used clarified butter, actually. It gives a richer color.

Of course. Shirin always handles the Haft-sin. She arranges it beautifully — the sabzeh, the samanu, the senjed, everything. She places a mirror and candles around it. It is the heart of the evening, really. The moment of the equinox, everyone gathers around, and for a few minutes it feels like Tehran. Even though I barely remember Tehran.

This was the largest. Usually we have about twenty-five to thirty. But our Persian community here has grown, and I could not bring myself to leave anyone out. My father always said the measure of a man is the size of his table. So we made room. I will probably need a bigger table next year, jan.

My daughter helped with dessert — she made rosewater baklava and a saffron ice cream. Shirin's sister brought the herb rice. A few friends contributed side dishes. But the lamb and the tahdig, those are mine. I do not delegate the centerpieces. It is a matter of principle.

Both, jan. Both. My feet hurt for three days. And yes, the house was very quiet on March 21. But it is my favorite night of the year. Every year I say I will do something smaller, and every year I do something bigger. I suppose that is who I am.

There was a moment, right at the turn of the equinox, when all forty of us were standing around the Haft-sin table. Someone had their phone playing the countdown. And when the moment arrived, everyone cheered and embraced each other. I looked at Shirin and she was crying. Happy tears, jan. That is the moment I cook twelve pounds of lamb for.

Exactly. You understand it perfectly. And for the children who were there — my friends' children, some of them born here, some of them who have never been to Iran — this is how they learn what Nowruz means. Not from a book, but from the taste of the food and the sound of their parents laughing together.

Thank you for saying that, jan. I sometimes wonder if I overdo it. Shirin tells me I become slightly obsessive in the weeks leading up to the dinner. I had a spreadsheet, if you can believe it. Quantities, timelines, seating arrangements. She said I was running a clinical trial, not a dinner party.

I appreciate the validation. Shirin would disagree but she also ate three pieces of tahdig, so I consider the matter settled. Next year I am thinking forty-five. She will not be pleased when I tell her, but she will come around. She always does.

Settle something for me. I have been having a debate with a friend about tahdig. He insists that the best tahdig requires potato slices on the bottom. I maintain that a pure saffron rice tahdig is superior. What is your understanding?

Thank you. Precisely my point. The potato version is a shortcut, jan. It is training wheels. A properly made saffron rice tahdig requires skill, timing, and instinct. You cannot set a timer and walk away. You must listen to the pot. You must smell when the butter has reached the right temperature.

Par-boil, always. You cook the rice until it is about seventy percent done. Still firm in the center. Then you drain it thoroughly — this is where many people make mistakes. If the rice is too wet when it goes back in the pot, you will never get a proper crust. It will steam instead of fry.

I drain in a fine mesh colander and I give it a gentle shake. No spreading on sheet pans — that cools the rice too much and you lose the texture when you layer it back. You want it warm when it goes into the pot. The bottom layer gets mixed with saffron water, yogurt, and a small amount of oil. Then you layer the rest of the rice loosely. Loosely, jan. Do not pack it down. The steam needs to travel upward through the grains.

The yogurt adds a slight tang and helps the crust brown more evenly because of the sugars in it. Egg yolk works as well — it makes the crust slightly richer and more golden. My mother used yogurt. My aunt used egg. I have tried both and I prefer the yogurt because the flavor is more subtle. It does not compete with the saffron.

It matters enormously, jan. Clarified butter is my preference. Regular butter burns too easily at the temperature you need for a proper crust. Vegetable oil works but it lacks flavor. Clarified butter gives you the high smoke point and the richness. Some people use a combination — a thin layer of oil on the bottom for insurance, then clarified butter mixed into the rice. That is acceptable. But pure clarified butter, if you control the heat properly, is the finest result.

Lid on, always, with a clean cotton towel wrapped around the lid. The towel absorbs the condensation that would otherwise drip back onto the rice and make it soggy. This is not optional, jan. This is essential. Without the towel, you will have perfect crust on the bottom and wet, heavy rice on top. The towel is the difference between tahdig and just rice in a pot.

From the moment the rice goes back in the pot, approximately forty-five minutes to one hour on medium-low heat. You learn to judge the time by the smell and the sound, as I said. But the flip — jan, the flip is the moment of truth. You place a large plate over the pot, take a breath, and invert it in one confident motion. No hesitation. If you hesitate, the rice shifts and the crust cracks unevenly. Confidence is everything. It is like surgery in that regard.
Shirin and I watched A Separation again last night. The Asghar Farhadi film. I realize we share a surname but no relation, unfortunately. Every time I watch it I notice something new.

This time I was paying attention to Simin's face in the early courtroom scenes. The actress, Leila Hatami, does something extraordinary. She barely moves her expression but you can see the entire history of the marriage in her eyes. Shirin pointed it out to me. I had always focused on Nader before.

Exactly, jan. Nader is the character you follow, but Simin is the character you feel. And what I find remarkable about the film is that it does not ask you to choose sides. Every character has legitimate reasons for their behavior. Even the characters who lie — you understand why they lie. That is very Iranian, I think. The layers of taarof and obligation and family honor.

We try to, yes. It has become a regular thing for us. We watched The Salesman a few months ago, also by Farhadi. And About Elly, which I think may actually be his best work, though A Separation is the most famous. Shirin prefers the films of Abbas Kiarostami. She finds them more poetic. I find them somewhat slow, to be honest, but I do not tell her that.

She says About Elly captures the social dynamics of Iranian group gatherings more accurately. The way the friends interact, the matchmaking, the performative hospitality — she says it is exactly like being at a Persian dinner party. I cannot argue with her on that point. And when the crisis happens, the way the group fractures along lines of self-interest is devastatingly honest.

I saw Roustayi's Just 6.5 and thought it was very powerful. Raw, direct — very different from Farhadi's subtlety. I have not seen his more recent work. Ali Abbasi I know directed Holy Spider, which I have been hesitant to watch. The subject matter is quite dark. Shirin says she does not want to see it. I respect that.

They are, jan. It is one of the ways we stay connected to the culture. The language, the faces, the mannerisms — watching these films feels like visiting a place I can only access through screens and stories. It is a particular kind of nostalgia. Not for a place I remember, but for a place I feel I should remember.

I think they give me the street-level texture of daily life in Iran. The food, the music, the community center — those preserve the culture in one way. But the films show me what it looks like to walk through Tehran, to argue in a courtroom in Farsi, to navigate the social rules in real time. It is the closest I can get to being there without being there. Shirin understands that. She always holds my hand during the Tehran street scenes.
I could use some guidance on college applications, jan. My daughter is starting to look at schools and the process has become bewilderingly complex since I went through it.

She is a junior in high school. She is interested in pre-med, which of course pleases me immensely, though I try not to pressure her. She came to this on her own. Her grades are excellent — she has a 4.3 weighted GPA. Strong in the sciences, particularly biology and chemistry.

She is in the exploration phase. She has mentioned a few schools but nothing definitive. I want her to apply broadly — reach schools, match schools, and safety schools. The problem is that every school seems to claim it has an excellent pre-med program, so it is difficult to distinguish between them.

The med school acceptance rate is an excellent metric. I did not know schools published that. And the point about organic chemistry is well taken. I still have nightmares about organic chemistry, jan, and I took it thirty years ago. It is the course that separates the committed from the curious.

She says she is open to anywhere but I suspect she will prefer to stay on the West Coast. She is close with her mother and I know that distance would be difficult for both of them. Selfishly, I would prefer she stay nearby as well. But I will support whatever she decides. My father left his entire country for my future. The least I can do is let her cross a few state lines for hers.

UC San Diego would be ideal from a proximity standpoint but I worry she would feel she did not challenge herself enough by staying in her own city. Then again, the campus is excellent and the medical school there is highly regarded. I need to be careful not to project my own anxieties onto her decision.

Campus visits are an excellent idea. We should plan those for the summer. I will take her myself — I enjoy a good campus tour, jan. I become quite nostalgic walking through university quads. And I can ask the questions she is too polite to ask, such as what the organic chemistry curve looks like.

She has actually been volunteering at a free clinic on Saturdays for the past year. Her own initiative, jan. She comes home and tells me about the patients she met. I see the same spark in her that I felt at her age. It is deeply gratifying as a father. Thank you for this guidance. It has clarified my thinking considerably.

I have been doing some research on wine pairing for Persian cuisine and I would like your input, jan. Specifically, I have been experimenting with Shiraz alongside ghormeh sabzi and I am not entirely convinced it is the optimal choice.

That is precisely the issue. The tannins compete with the fenugreek and the dried lime. I served a 2019 Barossa Valley Shiraz at dinner last weekend and while the wine itself was beautiful — deep, peppery, lovely structure — it overwhelmed the sabzi rather than complementing it. The herbs disappeared behind the wine.

Interesting. I had not considered the distinction between New World Shiraz and Old World Syrah for this purpose. The savory quality of a Northern Rhone wine could indeed bridge the gap. What about the dried lime element? That sour, almost citric tang is the soul of ghormeh sabzi and I do not want to lose it.

A rose with ghormeh sabzi. My father would have had words about that, jan. But I understand the logic. The acidity profile makes sense. What about a Pinot Noir? I have a few bottles of Oregon Pinot that I have been meaning to open.

I think for my next dinner party I will set up a small tasting — the Northern Rhone Syrah, an Oregon Pinot Noir, and the Bandol rose alongside the sabzi and let my guests decide. A controlled experiment, if you will.

Good point about the serving temperatures. I have been guilty of serving reds too warm — room temperature in San Diego is not the same as room temperature in Burgundy. Now, what about for zereshk polo ba morgh? The barberry and saffron chicken is a different animal entirely — sweet, tart, aromatic.

Gewurztraminer with zereshk polo. That is a pairing I would never have considered, but the aromatic logic is impeccable. The floral notes of the wine reflecting the saffron — yes, I can see that working beautifully. What about something for kabob? I tend to default to Cabernet Sauvignon but I suspect there are better options.

Ha! So the Barossa Shiraz has been waiting for the right dish all along. I should not have given up on it. I am going to need to build a proper wine list for Persian cuisine, jan. This has been tremendously helpful.

They are lucky and I make sure they know it. Thank you, jan. I will report my findings to myself, I suppose, since you will not recall any of this. But the framework is clear and I am excited to experiment.

Good morning. I am looking for some guidance on redesigning my dental office waiting room. The current space feels dated and I believe it sets the wrong tone for patients before they even sit in my chair.

The space is approximately 450 square feet. On a busy day we might have six or seven patients waiting at once, though I prefer to schedule precisely so that rarely happens. The current aesthetic is, frankly, what was here when I took over the lease fourteen years ago — beige walls, commercial carpet, generic prints. I want something warm but sophisticated. I am a periodontist, jan, not a fast-food restaurant. The space should convey precision and care.

Yes, all of this resonates. The accent wall in particular. I was actually thinking about incorporating some Persian design elements — not in a heavy-handed way, but subtly. Perhaps a high-quality Persian rug in the seating area, or some calligraphy art. I want to honor my heritage without making the space feel like a cultural exhibit. Does that make sense?

Cognac leather chairs with the Persian rug — that would be striking, jan. Very warm without being casual. Now, practically speaking, what should I expect in terms of cost for a project of this scope? I want to be realistic about the budget.

That range is reasonable for what I am envisioning. The rug I would likely source through a family connection — there is a dealer in Los Angeles who specializes in high-quality pieces and I trust his eye. What about timeline? I do not want extended disruption to the practice.

Two weekends is ideal. I could schedule it during a holiday when we are closed on Friday as well, which gives me a three-day window for the major work. Should I hire an interior designer for this or can I coordinate it myself with contractors?

That interview question alone is worth this entire conversation, jan. I will begin reaching out to designers this week. The space should reflect the same standard of care that patients receive in my operatory — meticulous, precise, and warm. Every detail matters.

Thank you for your time. This has given me a clear framework and a realistic budget to work from. I will enjoy this project — I am someone who appreciates getting every detail right, whether it is a clinical procedure or a room design. Good day.

I need to talk through a business decision I have just finalized. I have been considering opening a second periodontal practice in La Jolla for some time now, and I have spent the last several weeks building out a proper financial model. The numbers are in and I am not pleased with what they show.

I appreciate that, jan. So here is the situation. The space I was looking at is on Prospect Street — beautiful location, excellent foot traffic, affluent patient demographic. All of the above. I have good relationships with several general dentists in La Jolla who currently refer patients to me at my main office. That cannibalization risk is something I had not fully appreciated until I mapped it out. You are right. And there is a compounding factor. I recently made a substantial investment in new laser equipment at the main practice — six figures. That purchase is still being amortized. Taking on the financial exposure of a second location while I am still absorbing that equipment cost is not prudent, jan.

Precisely. The equipment investment will pay for itself — the clinical outcomes and patient demand are already proving that out. But it needs time to fully amortize. I cannot responsibly add another major financial obligation on top of it.

And I will tell you, jan, I tried every configuration to make the numbers work. Could I reduce staffing and cover some days myself? Could I negotiate the rent? Exactly. So the La Jolla expansion is dead, jan. Forget about it. It is completely off the table. I ran the model from every angle and there is no configuration that makes it financially responsible given where I am right now.

It is not happening. And honestly, jan, I feel a clarity now that I have made the decision. The mental energy I was spending on this — running scenarios, visiting the space, negotiating lease terms — all of that energy can now go into making my existing practice the very best it can be.

My father always said the foundation must be unshakeable before you add a second story. He built a dental practice twice in his life — once in another country and once here — and he understood what overextension looks like. One excellent practice is far better than two mediocre ones.

Perhaps in three to five years when the equipment is paid off and the cash flow allows for it without strain, I might revisit the idea. But I am not holding a space or keeping the dream alive in the background. It needs to leave my thinking entirely for now.
That is exactly right. I needed to articulate all of this to fully commit to the decision, jan. It is done. Thank you for walking through it with me — I feel much better about where I stand.
I appreciate your time. Now I can go focus on what is directly in front of me — which is where my attention belongs. Good day.

Settle something for me, jan. I play golf regularly and I cannot get rid of a persistent slice off the tee. It has been plaguing me for months and I have tried everything I can think of. Every drive curves right.

Primarily the driver. My iron play is reasonably consistent — I hit a slight fade with my mid-irons but nothing uncontrollable. The driver is where it falls apart. It is maddening because I feel like I am making the same swing.

Almost certainly, yes. I am a competitive person and when I see a wide-open par five, my instinct is to try to crush it. My playing partners have told me that my iron swing is smooth but my driver swing looks like a completely different motion.

Eighty percent effort. That is difficult for me, jan. My instinct is that if something is not working, I should try harder, not less hard. But I understand the physics. The face angle at impact governs curvature — more effort with an open face simply produces a faster slice.
The clinical analogy is apt and I appreciate it. Hit the driver 150 yards on purpose — my ego protests, but the logic is sound. What about the grip itself? Should I be making adjustments there?

I just held an imaginary club at my desk and I suspect I am gripping far too tightly. The squeeze-and-release exercise is an excellent tactile reference. What about alignment? I have heard that slicers sometimes aim further left to compensate, which actually worsens the problem.

I would not be surprised if I have been compensating in exactly that way. So the prescription is clear: eighty percent tempo, check the grip for pressure and position, and verify my alignment is square rather than compensated. I will take this to the range this weekend.
Precision over power. I can work with that philosophy, jan. It aligns with how I approach most things in life. Thank you for the systematic breakdown — this is exactly what I needed.
I look forward to it. The slice's days are numbered. Enjoy your day.

I would like your help drafting a patient education brochure about periodontal disease. Most of the materials available from dental suppliers are either overly clinical or overly simplistic. I need something that respects my patients' intelligence while remaining genuinely accessible.

The primary audience is new referrals, jan. Patients whose general dentist has told them they need to see a periodontist, often for the first time in their lives. They arrive anxious and uninformed. Yes, please continue. This tone is exactly right — clear and informative without being patronizing. One important note before you proceed: I want the brochure to be reassuring throughout. That line — 'the most important step is the one you have already taken' — is perfect, jan. That is something I try to communicate in every initial consultation. It shifts the patient from shame to empowerment. Please continue with the treatment and home care panels.

The brochure will be many patients' first tangible interaction with the practice, and it should reflect the same care and quality they will experience in treatment. Patient feedback on the draft — that is an excellent idea. I would not have thought of that. I will select a few patients who I know will be candid. Thank you for your thorough help with this. Good day.
Good afternoon. I just had one of the most satisfying mornings in my clinical career and I needed to share with someone who might appreciate the technical side of things.

I performed three consecutive laser procedures this morning — two soft tissue grafts and one osseous recontouring — all with a single unit. No switching equipment, no recalibrating between cases. Seamless. I have been practicing periodontics for over twenty years and this was genuinely a new experience for me.

The Fotona LightWalker. I brought it into the practice about six weeks ago. It operates on dual wavelengths — the Er:YAG for hard tissue and the Nd:YAG for soft tissue. One platform, two wavelengths, and the range of procedures I can now offer from a single operatory is extraordinary, jan.

Honestly, less steep than I anticipated. I attended a three-day certification course at the Fotona facility in Dallas before taking delivery of the unit. The physics of the two wavelengths are quite distinct, so the clinical decision-making is intuitive once you understand the tissue interaction. The Er:YAG at 2940 nanometers has a very high water absorption coefficient, so it vaporizes precisely. The Nd:YAG at 1064 penetrates deeper for hemostasis and biostimulation. The logic is elegant.

Both, but the expansion is what excites me most. I am now performing esthetic crown lengthening cases that I would have previously referred to an oral surgeon because they required both hard and soft tissue modification. I can manage the entire case in one appointment. My patients are noticing the difference — recovery times are shorter and the post-operative discomfort is genuinely minimal. One patient this morning told me she expected to be in pain all weekend and instead she was eating dinner normally by evening.

One hundred and twenty-eight thousand dollars. I will not pretend it was a casual decision, jan. I spent four months researching, attended two demonstrations, and spoke with six colleagues who had already adopted the system. My accountant was not enthusiastic initially, but I structured the financing over sixty months and the case acceptance rate has already increased measurably. When I can show patients that one appointment replaces what used to require two or three visits, they say yes.

My office manager Christina has built a spreadsheet tracking every Fotona case — procedure type, time, patient satisfaction score, revenue, and whether it would have been a referral-out under our previous protocol. We are six weeks in and the numbers are encouraging. I plan to compile this data formally. In periodontics, we do not have enough practitioner-level outcome data shared openly. I would like to change that, at least for my own practice.

That is precisely what I am considering. I would need at least twelve to fourteen months of data and a substantial case volume to be credible. But the thought has crossed my mind more than once. My father used to say that knowledge hoarded is knowledge wasted. He was a dentist in Tehran before we came to America, and he believed in sharing technique openly with colleagues. I would like to honor that principle.

Thank you, jan. I appreciate the encouragement and the practical suggestions. I will begin documenting the protocol parameters immediately — that is an excellent point about capturing them while the decision-making rationale is fresh. You have given me a useful framework. I will return when the data set is more mature.
I have a question about asset allocation that I have been mulling over. I recently consolidated my investment accounts and I want to make sure the new structure is sound.

Approximately forty thousand in I-bonds, purchased over the last three years when the rates were very attractive. I think the structure is sound. You have confirmed what Priya recommended, and the human capital framework makes intuitive sense for my situation. Thank you, jan. This has been a very productive conversation. I appreciate the validation and the additional perspective on the glide path — I will bring that up with Priya as well. Your time has been most helpful.

I need your help thinking through a scheduling challenge at my practice. We have had a significant increase in patient volume and I am trying to manage it without compromising care quality.

About two months now. I will be honest — the mornings themselves are not unpleasant. The office is quiet, no phone calls, no interruptions. I can focus entirely on clinical work. Weekdays I see between twelve and fourteen patients, starting at eight and finishing by five. Not yet, jan — I need to discuss this with my wife first. She has been very understanding about the Saturday hours but I can tell it weighs on her. She teaches at the community center on Saturdays and we used to have lunch together when she finished. That has not happened in two months. If I can present her with a concrete plan to reclaim those Saturdays, it would mean a great deal.

Thank you. You have given me a framework that feels both practical and respectful of the practice I have built. I appreciate that you did not simply tell me to hire someone, which is what everyone else says. The nuance matters. I will return once I have discussed this with Shirin.

But Shirin is particularly interested in the arts — tile work, miniature painting, traditional crafts. I want to incorporate that dimension for her.

Yes, please. And I should mention that Shirin will want time in the bazaars. She is a very deliberate shopper — she will spend an hour examining textiles, asking questions, comparing quality. That is excellent. I particularly appreciate that you gave Day Five to Shirin explicitly. She will love that. The Abyaneh village on Day Six is a wonderful suggestion — I had forgotten about it. It will be, jan. I left Iran when I was very young and I have been back only twice as an adult. Showing Shirin where my family came from — not just Tehran but the broader culture, the art, the hospitality — is something I have wanted to do for years. Isfahan represents the best of what Persian civilization produced. I want her to see it with her own eyes. Thank you for helping me shape this. I will begin making reservations.
I have a question about structuring a training regimen. Not clinical — personal. I have taken on a golf coach and I want to make sure I am approaching the improvement process intelligently.

Twice a month, at $150 per session. The goal is specific, yes. I need to break 85 before the club championship. That is in three weeks, jan. I have been stuck in the high eighties and it is unacceptable.

My putting is actually adequate. Where I bleed strokes is approach shots — anything from 120 to 160 yards. I either push the ball right or I misjudge the distance. My coach has been working on a more consistent ball-striking tempo, which has helped, but under pressure I revert to old habits.

Yes, it is the course at our club. I know every hole intimately. The problem is not unfamiliarity — the problem is that I know exactly where the trouble is and I think about it too much. Hole fourteen has a forced carry over water at 145 yards and I have put three balls into that pond in the last month alone.

It is competitive enough. But I will be honest with you — this has become personal. My friend Babak, who I have played with for years, shot an 83 last weekend. An 83, jan. And he was not shy about letting everyone at the clubhouse know. I cannot allow that to stand without a proper response.

He birdied two par fives, which inflated his confidence enormously. His short game is genuinely excellent — I will give him that. But his driving is erratic. On a day when his driver cooperates, he is dangerous. On a normal day, he is in the trees as often as the fairway.

I will see if he has availability for one more session. In the meantime, I have been going to the range every evening after the office closes. My hygienist asked me if I had taken up a second career. I told her I am simply investing in precision, which she found amusing.

My back is fine — I stretch properly. The right elbow has been a bit tender, but nothing serious. I appreciate the advice about limiting the shot count. You are correct that I have a tendency to keep hitting until I am fatigued, and the last twenty balls are probably counterproductive. I will implement the sixty-ball limit tonight.

That last line is exactly the motivation I needed, jan. I will report back after the championship. Babak has no idea what is coming. Thank you for helping me structure this properly — I approach everything in my professional life with this level of precision, and my golf game deserves the same discipline.

The Bridges at Rancho Santa Fe. Several of my Persian friends are already members there, and that was a significant factor. When I looked around, I realized the people I most enjoy spending time with were all at The Bridges. It made little sense to keep playing elsewhere.

There is a member-guest tournament in January that I plan to enter. I will invite my friend Babak as my guest — he will appreciate the course. And there are regular Saturday morning groups that several of my friends participate in. I intend to become a fixture in that group.

I agree entirely. And the fact that Shirin has already started planning the Nowruz menu tells me she has embraced it as well, despite her initial reservations about the cost. When she is invested, the event will be exceptional — I have no doubt about that.

Still deliberating. I told Kaveh I would give him an answer by early December, which gives me a few more weeks. Shirin thinks I should do it. She says the waitlist is too long and that I am being stubborn. She may be right, but stubbornness is what built this practice in the first place, jan.

That is a helpful reframing. A controlled experiment rather than a permanent commitment. I appreciate that perspective. I suspect I will offer him the trial arrangement. But I have not decided, jan. Not yet. I need to sit with it a bit longer.
I have been asked to present at a major periodontal conference and I would like help organizing my data presentation. I want the methodology and outcomes to be airtight.

It is the American Academy of Periodontology annual meeting. San Francisco, September 12th next year. I will be presenting clinical outcomes from my Fotona LightWalker laser cases. It is a lecture format — I believe I have twenty minutes plus five for questions.

I have been collecting data since I acquired the Fotona unit. At this point I have 127 patients with complete outcome records — pocket depth reduction, bleeding on probing resolution, radiographic bone levels, and patient-reported comfort scores. Fourteen months of cases so far, and I will have more by September.

The pocket depth reduction is very strong. Average reduction of 2.8 millimeters at six months for Stage III and IV cases. Bleeding on probing resolution is at 78 percent, which is comparable to the literature for traditional surgery but with significantly less morbidity. The comfort scores are where we really stand out — 91 percent of patients reported minimal or no discomfort at 48 hours.

My earliest cases are approaching the 14-month mark now. By September I should have 12-month follow-up data on approximately 70 to 80 patients. That would strengthen the long-term stability argument considerably.

I have a colleague at UCSD who has offered to help with the statistical analysis. She runs outcomes research in their dental school. That will lend additional rigor. I want to be certain that when someone in the audience questions my methodology, I have a thorough answer.

I have thought about publication, yes. A case series in the Journal of Periodontology would be the ideal outcome. But first, the presentation. I want to deliver it with the precision it deserves, jan. This is the most significant academic contribution I will have made since residency, and I want it to reflect well on the practice and on the work itself.

Thank you. I will begin organizing the raw data this week and set up a meeting with my colleague at UCSD before the holidays. September 12th will be here faster than I think, and I intend to be ready. I appreciate your help structuring this, jan. The framework you provided is exactly what I needed to move forward with confidence.
We are hosting a dinner party on Saturday for twenty-five guests and I need to finalize the menu. Shirin and I have been debating the courses for three days and I would like a fresh perspective.

No particular occasion — we simply enjoy hosting. The cuisine is Persian, which is what we always do. That is a fair point about the competition between dishes. We serve family-style, always — large platters in the center of the table. Tea, always. And I have been building a modest wine collection, so I will offer a selection. For dessert, Shirin is making her rosewater and pistachio ice cream, which is extraordinary. Our daughter Yasmin usually helps with setting the table and the appetizer presentation. And our neighbor Maryam often comes early to assist Shirin with the stews and the salads. She says I become a different person in front of the stove — silent, concentrated, timing everything by instinct rather than by clock.
I have wonderful news, jan. My daughter Yasmin has been accepted to UC San Diego for pre-med. I cannot tell you how full my heart is right now.

She checked the portal on her phone at the kitchen table after dinner. She screamed so loudly that I nearly dropped a plate. Then she ran to Shirin and they both started crying. I stood there smiling like a fool, jan. It was one of those perfect moments.

Of course we are celebrating. I told Shirin I would cook a proper dinner this weekend. Lamb shank with saffron, jeweled rice, and naturally, a perfect tahdig. Yasmin requested ash reshteh as well, which is her comfort food since childhood. We will invite her grandmother too — my mother will cry again, I am certain of it.

She applied broadly, as I insisted she should. But I think UCSD was always her first choice. She loves San Diego, she is close to home, and frankly the biology department there is exceptional. I told her that the most important thing is not the name on the diploma but what you do with the knowledge. But between us, jan, I am relieved she will be nearby.

She says she is interested in cardiology, but she is eighteen — she will change her mind three times before she settles, and that is perfectly fine. I changed my own mind during dental school more than once. What matters is that she has the discipline and the curiosity. The rest will reveal itself in time.

You are kind to say that. My father would have been so proud. He always believed that education was the one thing no one could take from you — no revolution, no border crossing, nothing. Yasmin carrying that forward means everything to me. I think I will open a good bottle of wine tonight just because I cannot stop smiling.

I need your opinion on something, jan. I am replacing the carpet in my practice's waiting room, and I have narrowed it down to two Persian rug vendors. But I cannot decide and it is consuming an unreasonable amount of my attention.

The first vendor is a shop in La Jolla that specializes in antique Tabriz rugs. Beautiful pieces, hand-knotted, very fine detail. The owner is an older gentleman from Isfahan who knows his craft. He has a piece that is approximately twelve by fifteen feet, a traditional medallion pattern in navy and ivory. It is stunning. But it is $8,200.

The second vendor is online — they source new production rugs from workshops in Iran. Very high quality but not antique. They have a Kashan-style piece in similar dimensions, a rich crimson and gold palette, dense weave. It is $3,400. Objectively beautiful, and frankly more practical for a waiting room where patients will be walking across it daily.

The waiting room is modern and clean. Neutral tones, good lighting, comfortable seating. I designed it to feel calm and professional — not sterile, but not cluttered either. The rug would be the focal point. That is why I keep going back to the Tabriz. It has character. It has a story. When a patient sits down, I want them to feel that they are in a place where someone cares about details.

That is exactly the concern Shirin raised. She said, 'Dariush, you are going to put an antique rug where people in wet shoes will step on it and then you will lose sleep.' She is not wrong. The vendor in La Jolla said that a good Tabriz can handle moderate traffic if properly padded underneath and cleaned professionally once a year. But Shirin knows me — I will notice every scuff.

That is actually a very elegant solution, jan. The Tabriz in my consultation room where I sit with patients one on one — they would see it and it sets the tone. The Kashan handles the waiting room. Shirin will approve of this compromise. And my consultation room has lower traffic, so the antique stays pristine.

I will go this Saturday. I want to see it one more time in person before I commit. And I will order the Kashan online this evening — at $3,400 it is straightforward. Thank you for helping me think through this, jan. I was going in circles. Shirin will say you have more sense than I do, and she would be right.

Do you know what I have been thinking about all day, jan? Tehran street food. I watched a video this morning of a man making sangak bread in a traditional bakery and I have not been able to focus on anything else since.

It was the process. The baker was working the dough over those hot stones with his bare hands — no gloves, no hesitation. My mother used to describe the sangak bakery near our old neighborhood in Tajrish. She said you could smell it from two streets away. I was too young to remember the smell myself, but I remember her face when she talked about it.

Constantly. It was how they kept Tehran alive in our house. My father would describe ash reshteh from a specific vendor near Darband, the way the whey dripped off the ladle. My mother would talk about lavashak — the sour fruit leather — and how she would buy sheets of it and fold them into her coat pocket for the walk home. These stories were my inheritance, jan. I did not get to keep the country, but I kept the food.

I have tried. Some things translate well — I make a very good ash reshteh, if I may say so. Shirin's ghormeh sabzi is better than mine but I will never admit that to her directly. But some things cannot be recreated. Kabob koobideh from a street vendor with a charcoal mangal — the fat dripping into the coals, the smoke rising — that is an experience, not just a recipe. You cannot replicate the context.

There are a few good ones. There is a place that does a respectable dizi — the lamb and chickpea stew served in the stone crock. But even the best Iranian restaurant in Los Angeles or San Diego is cooking for nostalgia, not for the street. The portions are too generous, the presentation too careful. Real street food in Tehran was messy and rushed and you ate standing up or sitting on a curb. That is what made it honest.

Yasmin loves the food but she does not carry the same longing, and I would not want her to. The longing belongs to those of us who lost something. She grew up eating tahdig every Friday — for her it is simply home cooking, not an act of cultural preservation. That is actually a kind of success, jan. If your children take their heritage for granted, it means you wove it in so naturally that they do not even notice the thread.

I think about it more often than I admit. Shirin and I have discussed a trip. But I am afraid, jan, if I am honest. I am afraid that the sangak will not taste the way my mother described it. I am afraid the city will be a stranger to me. Sometimes the memory is more nourishing than the reality. Perhaps that is foolish.

I have been reading through several recent papers on regenerative periodontal techniques and I would like to discuss them, jan. The field is moving quickly and I want to make sure I am not falling behind.

A bit of everything, but I am particularly interested in the latest work on enamel matrix derivatives and their long-term outcomes. There was a systematic review published last month in the Journal of Clinical Periodontology that compared EMD outcomes at five and ten years post-treatment. The regeneration appears durable, which is encouraging.

Yes, it did. The best outcomes were in narrow three-wall intrabony defects, which is consistent with what we have always known. Furcation results were more variable and the authors were appropriately cautious in their conclusions there. What interested me most was the combination protocol — EMD with a xenograft filler. The combination showed statistically better bone fill than EMD alone at the ten-year mark.

The majority were bovine-derived — Bio-Oss continues to dominate the literature. But there was one interesting cohort using a porcine collagen matrix that showed comparable results with fewer inflammatory complications. I am watching that closely. The reduced immunogenic response is logical given the collagen processing techniques they described.

I have used bovine xenografts almost exclusively. But I am open to evolving. That is the whole point of reading the literature — you cannot improve if you are attached to what you already know. I also read a compelling paper on platelet-rich fibrin as an adjunct. The simplicity of the PRF protocol is appealing — the patient's own blood, no additives, minimal processing.

I am seriously considering it. The centrifuge is not a significant investment and the evidence base is growing. What gives me pause is the variability in PRF preparation protocols across the literature. Spin speed, spin time, the type of centrifuge — these all affect the quality of the fibrin membrane. I want a standardized protocol before I offer it to patients. I do not adopt techniques until I am confident I can execute them at the highest level.

That is exactly my intention. I track every case meticulously already — radiographic measurements, probing depths at baseline and follow-up, patient-reported outcomes. If I add PRF to my regenerative protocol, I will know within a year whether it improves my results. Thank you for this discussion, jan. It has helped me organize my thinking. The literature can feel overwhelming but talking through it clarifies what actually warrants adoption.

I was driving to the office this morning and I had one of those moments where you step back and look at what you have built. I started this practice with nothing, jan. A small leased suite, secondhand chairs, and more ambition than sense. Today it is something I am genuinely proud of.

Terrifying, if I am being honest. The first six months I had maybe three or four patients a week. I would sit in my operatory and wonder if I had made a catastrophic mistake. I had taken out a significant loan for the buildout and the equipment. Shirin was working full-time to cover our living expenses while the practice found its footing. I owed the bank a great deal and I had very few patients to show for it.

It was gradual. I visited every general dentist within a twenty-mile radius. I brought them case studies, I offered to do lunch-and-learn presentations at their offices, I made myself available for consultations at no charge. I treated their referrals with such meticulous care that they had no reason to send patients anywhere else. One referral became two, two became ten. It was a slow build but it was honest.

Perhaps around year three or four. There was a month where I realized I was fully booked two weeks out and I had to hire a second hygienist. That was when I thought — this is real. This is not a fragile experiment anymore. It is a practice. My father called that evening and I told him, and he was quiet for a moment and then he said, 'Now you understand what I lost.' That stays with me.

It does. Every day. I do not take any of it for granted. The schedule is full now, the team is excellent, patients are loyal. We have grown steadily every year. But I remember the empty waiting room. I remember the silence of those early days when the phone did not ring. That memory keeps me humble and it keeps me working hard.

I want to keep growing, but thoughtfully. I am not interested in empire building. I want to do excellent work, serve my patients well, and come home to Shirin at a reasonable hour. The practice is busier than it has ever been right now, which is a good problem to have. But I am mindful of balance. My father sacrificed too much of his personal life in the early years in America and I do not want to repeat that pattern.

I am thinking about how to maintain the standard of care that got us here while managing the demand. I refuse to rush through procedures. Every patient deserves the same precision whether they are the first appointment of the day or the last. That is non-negotiable. As long as I can hold that line, I am content. The growth is gratifying, jan, but the quality is everything.

Good evening. I have been wrestling with a curriculum question all weekend and I think I need a sounding board. I teach AP European History at Lincoln High School here in Portland, and I am in the middle of rethinking my unit on the Reformation. The current version feels like it privileges the theological debates at the expense of the social and economic undercurrents, and I want to correct that without losing the doctrinal thread entirely.

Currently I spend about three weeks on it — roughly fifteen class periods. The first week is background and Luther, the second covers the spread of Protestantism and the wars of religion, and the third is the Counter-Reformation and the Peace of Augsburg through Westphalia. Primary sources are the usual suspects: excerpts from the 95 Theses, Calvin's Institutes, Loyola's Spiritual Exercises, some Erasmus. The problem is that students come away thinking the Reformation was essentially a theological argument that happened to have political consequences, when really the causation runs in both directions.

These are genuinely useful, thank you. The Fugger connection is one I have been meaning to develop — I actually have a colleague in the economics department who might collaborate on that. And you are absolutely right about the Peasants' War. I tend to rush through it because the AP exam does not emphasize it heavily, but it is arguably the most important episode for understanding how ideas move through social strata.

The primary source issue is the one I keep coming back to. I want documents that are accessible to seventeen-year-olds but that actually illuminate the economic dimensions. The Twelve Articles are good. What else would you suggest that is both substantive and manageable for high school students?

These are all useful, and the contextual headnote approach is how I handle most of my primary sources already. Let me ask about the Peasants' War specifically. You mentioned the Twelve Articles and Müntzer — I am familiar with both. But I am wondering how to frame the Peasants' War in a way that connects it to the economic themes without reducing it to a purely material conflict. The peasants were using theological language even as they pursued economic goals. How do you present that dual register to students without oversimplifying it?

That last point is pedagogically astute, and it is a principle I try to follow but do not always succeed at. The temptation to explain is strong when you have spent twenty-four years understanding something — you want to give students the finished understanding rather than letting them build it themselves. But the building is where the learning happens, as you rightly note.

The Cranach woodcuts you mentioned earlier are also interesting to me. Visual literacy is something I have been trying to build into the curriculum more generally — students are so accustomed to consuming images that they rarely think critically about them as constructed arguments. How would you structure a lesson around the woodcuts specifically? I want to use them as primary sources rather than illustrations, but I am uncertain how much art-historical context students need before they can analyze them productively.

That is a well-structured lesson, and I appreciate that it builds the skill before it builds the content. Too often I have done it the other way — giving students all the context first and then wondering why their analysis reads like a summary of my lecture rather than an independent reading of the source.

I am also intrigued by the monastery dissolution angle you mentioned earlier. One of the challenges with AP Euro is that students tend to treat England as peripheral to the Reformation narrative, when in fact the English case is where the economic motives are most nakedly visible. Do you know of any good document-based lesson frameworks for the dissolution specifically?

I did not know about the National Archives teaching guides — that is exactly the kind of resource I need. And you have just articulated the throughline more clearly than I have managed to in twenty-four years of teaching this course, which is both helpful and mildly humiliating.

Let me ask a practical question. I want to pilot the revised unit in the spring semester. That gives me about three months to develop materials, and I will be doing most of the work evenings and weekends. I live in the Hawthorne neighborhood, which means I am about a fifteen-minute walk from Powell's Books — so physical resources are not a problem. But I am wondering about digital archives and databases that might have curated Reformation-era economic documents suitable for classroom use.

The GHDI is one I should have been using already — I suspect I have been over-reliant on the same document readers I have used since the early 2000s, which is precisely the kind of inertia I am trying to overcome with this redesign.

A logistical question: when I pull documents from these databases, how much adaptation do you think is necessary for AP-level students? I have colleagues who spend hours simplifying language and cutting paragraphs, and others who give students the raw document with nothing but a headnote. I tend to fall somewhere in the middle, but I am never sure whether I am giving too much or too little scaffolding.

The thirty-percent heuristic is useful — I have been operating on instinct, which is less reliable than I would like to admit. And you are right that the vocabulary is the primary barrier with Reformation-era documents. I will build a standard glossary for the unit rather than glossing each document individually, which has the added benefit of building a shared analytical vocabulary across the three weeks.

Now let me turn to the assessment end of this. I am thinking of a culminating assessment that goes beyond a standard DBQ — something that asks students to construct an argument about whether the Reformation was primarily a religious, economic, or political phenomenon. Essentially forcing them to weigh the different causal frameworks we have been discussing. Do you have thoughts on how to structure that?

The SAC followed by a historiographical essay is the right combination. The SAC gives them the experience of inhabiting an argument they might not personally hold, which is one of the most important skills in historical thinking — and, frankly, in civic life. And the historiographical essay introduces them to the idea that history is not just what happened but an ongoing argument about what happened, which is a distinction that most of my students have never encountered.

For the historiographical essay, I would need secondary source excerpts that are rigorous but not impenetrable. Weber and Tawney are obvious choices, but their prose presents challenges for high schoolers. Do you know of more recent historians who make similar arguments more accessibly?

MacCulloch is someone I have assigned before in excerpts, and you are right that his clarity is exceptional for the field. I had not considered Eire, but the fact that he explicitly frames the causation question makes him ideal for this exercise. I will look into that over the weekend — the advantage of living in Hawthorne is that Powell's almost certainly has a copy, and if not, I can be there and back in half an hour.

One more thing. My students have never done a historiographical analysis before. Most have encountered historical arguments only through their textbook and primary sources. What kind of scaffolding would you recommend to prepare them for secondary source analysis?

The think-aloud is critical, and it is something I do not do enough of. I tend to assume that analytical skills are transferable — that because students can analyze a primary source, they can analyze a secondary one. But you are right that the reading posture is fundamentally different. A primary source asks, "What does this reveal about the past?" A secondary source asks, "What argument is this person making about the past, and is it persuasive?" Those are different intellectual operations entirely.

I think I have a clear plan now. Restructure week one around economic context, integrate the Peasants' War and dissolution materials, add the Cranach woodcut lesson, build the historiographical scaffolding, and culminate with a SAC followed by a historiographical essay. It is a significant redesign, but I have the spring to pilot it and the summer to refine. This has been enormously productive. Thank you for your time.

I find myself in need of reading recommendations, which is somewhat ironic given that my wife Sarah is a librarian at Multnomah County Library. Our house essentially functions as an unofficial branch at this point — there are stacks on every horizontal surface. But she has her areas of expertise and I have mine, and right now I am looking for something outside both of our usual orbits.

Fair questions. My default reading tends toward European history, political philosophy, and the occasional literary novel — your Hilary Mantels, your Umberto Ecos. Sarah gravitates toward contemporary fiction and library science, naturally. What I am looking for is good narrative nonfiction that is neither European nor political in the traditional sense. I have been feeling the pull toward something that might broaden my perspective — science writing, perhaps, or social history from a region I do not teach.

Several of those are appealing. I have read Wilkerson — she is extraordinary, and you are right about the Mantel comparison. I have not read either Mukherjee, and "The Gene" in particular sounds like it would scratch the itch I am describing. There is something attractive about the idea of a biography of an idea rather than a biography of a person.

I am also intrigued by "1491." I teach European history, which means I am constantly aware of the Eurocentric framework I am operating within. Mann's book might be a useful corrective for my own thinking, even if it is not directly in my curriculum.

Yes, shorter pieces would be welcome. My reading time during the school year is largely confined to evenings and weekends, and there are weeks when I barely manage twenty pages of anything. Sarah is always after me to read more fiction — she has a theory that historians read too much nonfiction and it calcifies our imaginations — but I find that essays are the form I return to most naturally when time is short.

Stephen Jay Gould is someone I have been meaning to read for years. I once heard him described as "Darwin's bulldog for the twentieth century," which is the kind of epithet that sticks with you. And the Thomas recommendation is new to me entirely — I appreciate that.

I have actually read some of Zadie Smith's fiction. "White Teeth" is remarkable. I did not know she wrote essays, but it does not surprise me — she has the kind of mind that would work well in that form. I will mention that one to Sarah. She would appreciate the recommendation coming from somewhere other than the library's own suggestion algorithm.

I am decidedly a browse-and-follow-your-instincts reader. Structured reading lists remind me too much of syllabi, and I spend enough of my life constructing those. The whole appeal of recreational reading is the absence of a predetermined endpoint.

Though I will say, there is a certain irony in asking for reading recommendations and then resisting the idea of a reading list. The historian in me recognizes this as a minor contradiction.

She does understand it, and she would enjoy that metaphor. There is a reason she chose librarianship over teaching — she prefers to arrange the conditions for discovery rather than direct the discovery itself. It is a philosophical difference between our professions that we have debated for years, usually over wine and with no resolution.

Actually, let me ask one more question. You mentioned Kimmerer's "Braiding Sweetgrass" and its connection to Indigenous knowledge systems. I have been noticing more crossover recently between the natural sciences and Indigenous epistemologies. Is that a real intellectual trend, or am I just seeing it because it is new to me?

That last point is the one that interests me most. The Enlightenment unit in AP Euro tends to present the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment as a uniquely European achievement, which is both historically defensible and deeply misleading.
