The knowledge systems that preceded and surrounded European science are rarely acknowledged. I am not going to overhaul that unit tonight, but Kimmerer and Mann together might give me a more sophisticated framework for my own thinking.

In any case, this has been very helpful. I have a short list — "The Gene," "1491," Lewis Thomas, Gould, and now Kimmerer — and I suspect Powell's will receive a visit this weekend. Thank you for the thoughtful suggestions.

I am trying to think through a scheduling problem and I could use some help with time management strategies. The period from November through March is my most demanding stretch of the year, and this year it feels particularly relentless.

Certainly. I am a high school history teacher, so the baseline is the usual: lesson planning, grading, department meetings, parent conferences. But on top of that, I also coach the junior varsity basketball team, and our season runs from November through early March. That means practices after school most days, games two or three evenings a week, and Saturday tournaments roughly once a month. The coaching is something I genuinely enjoy — it is a different kind of teaching, more immediate and physical — but it effectively eliminates my after-school hours for four months.

Good questions. I arrive at school around 7:15, classes run from 7:45 to 2:30, and then basketball takes over from 3:00 until 5:30 on practice days, or until 8:00 or later on game nights. I get home and have perhaps two hours before I need to sleep, and that time has to cover dinner, basic household tasks, and whatever grading or planning I can manage.

What suffers most is grading. I teach AP European History, which means essays and document-based questions — the kind of assignments that require substantive feedback, not just a checkmark. During basketball season, my turnaround time on essays goes from one week to sometimes three weeks, which is unfair to the students and makes me feel like I am doing both jobs at seventy percent.

I do have an assistant coach, which helps with practice planning, but the teaching side is essentially solo. My department is small and we teach different courses.

Several of these are workable, and a few are things I have resisted but probably should not have. The rotating rubric focus is smart — I have been giving comprehensive feedback on every essay because that is what I believe good teaching requires, but you are right that targeted feedback might actually be more useful to students. There is a historical parallel here to the military principle of concentration of force — better to be decisive at one point than diffuse across all of them.

The early morning arrival is something I have tried intermittently but never committed to systematically. You are right that I should treat it as non-negotiable. And the idea of designing certain class periods as semi-independent work days is one I have been reluctant to embrace because it feels like I am not teaching. But if the alternative is three-week turnaround on essays, the tradeoff is clear.

You have identified the exact problem. After a game night that ends at 8:00 or later, I am home by 8:30, and by the time I eat and decompress, I am not getting to sleep before 10:30. A 6:00 alarm after that is manageable but unpleasant, and after a few consecutive game nights it becomes unsustainable. The body of a fifty-two-year-old does not recover the way it did at thirty, a fact I am reminded of every December.

That framework is clarifying. I think the mistake I have been making is treating every day as though it should contain the same proportions of teaching, coaching, and grading, when in fact the coaching schedule imposes a rhythm that I should be working with rather than against. It is a bit like the difference between a metronome and actual musical phrasing — the rigid beat is theoretically correct but practically deadening.

Let me ask about the peer review idea. I want to implement that, but I am uncertain about the mechanics. How do you train seventeen-year-olds to give each other feedback that is actually useful and not just "good job" or "I liked your essay"?

The distinction between a peer review rubric and my own grading rubric is important. I had been thinking of them as the same instrument, which would overwhelm the students. A simplified version that focuses on structural elements they can actually evaluate — that is manageable. And making it a pre-submission tool rather than a post-grading exercise changes the entire dynamic. Students are giving feedback with the purpose of helping each other improve, not evaluating a finished product.

I think I can train them on this before winter break. That gives me two weeks of lower-stakes assignments to practice with, and then the system would be functional by January, which is when the grading pressure peaks.

One more question: how do I communicate the slightly longer grading turnaround to students without it sounding like an excuse? I want to be transparent without undermining their confidence in my commitment to their work.

That framing is exactly right. I especially appreciate the point about modeling transparency — I spend a great deal of time teaching my students to evaluate evidence honestly and acknowledge the limitations of their sources, so I should be willing to do the same about my own constraints. Consistency between what we teach and how we conduct ourselves is not a small thing.

Thank you. This has been a productive conversation. I have a framework for the schedule, a plan for peer review, and a way to talk to my students about it. Now I just need to survive until March.

I have been thinking about a curricular question that is also, if I am being honest, a personal one. I teach AP European History, and I have been grappling with how to handle the theme of identity and belonging in the curriculum — specifically, how to teach about nationalism and ethnic identity in a way that acknowledges the constructed nature of these categories without dismissing the very real ways they shape people's lives.

I appreciate you asking rather than assuming. The personal dimension is this: I was adopted from South Korea when I was three years old and raised by white parents here in Oregon. So the question of what it means to belong to a nation, a culture, an ethnic group — these are not abstract questions for me. I grew up culturally American, specifically Oregonian, but I have spent my entire life being perceived as something other than that by people who see my face before they hear my voice. The disconnect between internal identity and external perception is something I understand at a visceral level, and it makes me both more attuned to and more cautious about how I teach these themes.

It comes up everywhere, which is part of the challenge. But the 19th-century nationalism unit is where it is most acute, because that is where the curriculum explicitly asks students to analyze how national identities were constructed — the role of language, mythology, shared history, and the deliberate exclusion of those who did not fit the mold. The German and Italian unification movements are the standard case studies, but I find that students struggle to see the constructedness of identity because their own national identity feels so natural to them. They understand intellectually that "Germany" was an invention of the 19th century, but they do not feel it.

The defamiliarization approach is excellent, and it connects to something I have been doing informally. I sometimes ask my students, "If your great-grandparents had not emigrated, what country would you be a citizen of — and does that country still exist?" In a class in Portland, you get a remarkable range of answers, and several students discover that their ancestral "country" was dissolved, partitioned, or renamed. It makes the contingency of national borders concrete.

The civic versus ethnic nationalism distinction is one I teach explicitly, and it is where my own experience becomes most relevant to the curriculum, though I have never shared it with students. The tension between "you belong because of what you believe and practice" and "you belong because of who your ancestors were" — that is essentially the tension I have lived. I am culturally American by every civic measure, but the ethnic definition would place me elsewhere.

The middle path is probably the right one, and it is close to what I have done on the rare occasions when the subject has come up organically. I once had a student ask me, during a discussion of the Chinese Exclusion Act in a broader context, whether I had ever experienced being treated as a foreigner in my own country. I told her yes, and that the experience had shaped how I think about the difference between legal citizenship and social belonging. I did not elaborate beyond that, and the discussion that followed was one of the best I have had in twenty-four years of teaching.

I think the key insight — and this applies to the European history curriculum as well — is that identity is not a single thing but a negotiation between how you understand yourself and how others categorize you. The most honest way to teach nationalism is to show students that this negotiation has always been contested, often violent, and never fully resolved.

I have considered it, and your mapping of it across the periods is more complete than what I had sketched out. The Reformation connection is one I had not fully articulated, but you are right — the question of who defines religious identity, the individual or the institution, is structurally identical to the question of who defines national identity. Luther's insistence on individual conscience is, in a sense, the first major European assertion that identity is self-determined rather than externally assigned.

That is a thread I could trace from 1517 to the present without ever losing the AP exam content. The exam rewards students who can identify patterns and continuities across periods, so this would actually strengthen their preparation while also making the course more intellectually coherent.

The recurring reflective activity is particularly appealing. It would create a longitudinal record that students can look back on and see their own thinking evolve, which is itself a kind of identity negotiation — who they were as thinkers in September versus who they are in May.

I want to be careful, though, not to impose a single interpretive framework so heavily that students feel constrained by it. The best historical thinking involves holding multiple frameworks in tension. I would want identity-as-negotiation to be a lens they develop, not a cage they are placed in.

You have articulated exactly the principle I try to teach, which is that the most dangerous thing in both history and in life is the conviction that you have found the one correct lens. Every atrocity in the European history curriculum began with someone who was certain they had the whole picture.

This has been a genuinely stimulating conversation. I came in with a pedagogical question and I am leaving with what feels like the architecture for a course redesign. The identity-as-negotiation throughline, introduced early, applied recursively, and then interrogated for its own limitations — that is a course I would be proud to teach. Thank you for helping me think it through.

Happy new year. I am starting the spring semester next week and I want to rethink my classroom arrangement. I have been using a traditional rows-facing-front setup for years, but I am increasingly convinced it is not serving the kind of teaching I want to do. Before I get into the specifics, I should mention a practical constraint: I have mild hearing loss in my left ear and wear a hearing aid. Over the years I have unconsciously arranged things so that students are predominantly on my right side, which works for hearing but limits the configurations available to me.

That is exactly right regarding the hearing. The aid helps considerably, but in a noisy classroom with overlapping voices, my left side is noticeably weaker. I have found over the years that I miss contributions from students seated to my far left, which is unfair to them and frustrating for me.

As for the teaching: I teach AP European History, and I have been moving toward more discussion-based and document-analysis activities. The traditional rows are fine for lectures, but when I want a Socratic seminar or a structured academic controversy, the arrangement becomes a liability. Students cannot see each other, so they direct all their comments to me rather than engaging with one another. I want a configuration that facilitates genuine student-to-student dialogue while still allowing me to hear everyone effectively.

I have individual desks — the old-fashioned kind with the attached chair, which limits some configurations. Class sizes range from twenty-two to twenty-eight. The room is fairly standard, roughly thirty by thirty feet, with the whiteboard on the north wall and windows on the east.

The modified U-shape is appealing. I have seen colleagues use it and the effect on discussion quality is reportedly significant. My concern is the positioning: if I stand at the open end, slightly left of center as you suggest, I would have the whiteboard behind me, which is ideal. But during transitions — when I need to move to a student's desk or circulate during group work — I lose the acoustic advantage of the fixed position.

Yes, let me think through the U-shape specifically. With twenty-five students in a thirty-by-thirty room, how many desks should I place along each arm of the U versus the base? And where should my own desk be — or should I not have one at all in the discussion configuration?

Yes, please do. And for the clusters, my main concern is group size. I find that groups of four work best for document analysis — large enough for diversity of perspective but small enough that no one can hide. With twenty-five students, that gives me six groups of four and one of five.

The color-coded tape is a nice touch. I can already picture my more detail-oriented students taking ownership of the transitions — there are always a few who enjoy the logistics of classroom management, and I have learned over the years to let them run things like this rather than insisting on directing everything myself.

Let me ask about discussion norms within the U-shape. One problem I have had with whole-class discussion in any configuration is the tendency for three or four vocal students to dominate while the rest retreat into silence. The U-shape makes everyone visible, which should help, but visibility alone does not guarantee participation. Do you have strategies for ensuring broader engagement, particularly given that I need to be able to hear whoever is speaking?

The discussion mapping is intriguing — I have heard of it but never implemented it. There is something appealing about making the participation pattern visible rather than just asking students to "participate more." The data itself becomes the intervention. It reminds me of the way the Valor Ecclesiasticus made Church wealth visible and thereby made it vulnerable to critique. Making the invisible visible is powerful in any context.

The think-pair-share is something I already use occasionally, but you are right that I should make it systematic. It solves the problem of students who have ideas but need more processing time before they are willing to voice them publicly.

Let me raise a different concern now. One thing I have been compensating for in ad hoc ways is the problem of ambient noise. The heating system in my building is old — forced air that cycles on and off unpredictably. When it kicks in during a discussion, I lose a significant portion of what students on my left side are saying. Is there anything I can do about room acoustics beyond the arrangement itself?

The tennis balls on desk legs is the kind of unglamorous, practical solution that I appreciate. I will implement that immediately — it costs nothing and solves a real annoyance. The acoustic panels are worth requesting, and you are right that framing it as a general instructional quality issue is strategically sounder than framing it as a personal accommodation. Several colleagues have complained about the HVAC noise, so there may be momentum to tap into.

The Roger system is something I should investigate. I have never asked the school for any hearing-related accommodation because, frankly, I have always considered it a minor personal inconvenience rather than a workplace issue. But you are making me reconsider that framing.

We have had conversations about technology, but they tend to focus on screens and software — interactive whiteboards, learning management systems, that sort of thing. Audio technology has never come up, which is itself revealing. The assumption seems to be that the acoustic environment of a classroom is a given, not something that can be designed. Which is ironic, because anyone who has taught knows that a room where students cannot hear each other clearly is a room where discussion dies.

The pilot framing is smart — it gives administration a manageable commitment rather than an open-ended expenditure, and it gives me the opportunity to document results. I have been at Lincoln long enough to know that institutional change happens incrementally, not by revolution. There is a parallel to the Peace of Augsburg, actually — sometimes you have to accept a local accommodation before you can achieve a systemic settlement.

I should also say — and this may sound tangential, but I think it is connected — that after twenty-four years of teaching, I am still genuinely excited about the craft of it. The puzzle of arranging a room, choosing a text, designing a question that opens up a student's thinking — these are not problems I am tired of solving. I did not anticipate, when I started teaching at twenty-eight, that I would still feel this kind of enthusiasm at fifty-two. There is a version of my career where the hearing loss, the bureaucracy, the aging buildings would have worn me down. But every September there are new minds in the room who have never encountered the Enlightenment, and that is a renewable resource that no amount of institutional frustration can exhaust.

That is a generous interpretation, and I think there is some truth in it. Constraints do produce creativity — the history of art and architecture is full of examples, and I suppose the history of pedagogy is no different. Whether that counts as a silver lining or simply as making the best of an inconvenience, I will leave to the philosophers.

Let me ask one more practical question. I want to pilot the new arrangement starting the first day of the spring semester. Should I have students walk into the U-shape cold, or should I set it up gradually over the first few days?

The cold start makes sense. You are right that a gradual introduction sends an ambiguous signal, and ambiguity is not what I want on the first day of a new semester. Students read the physical environment of a classroom far more carefully than we give them credit for — it is one of the few things they notice before a single word has been spoken.

I have a clear plan now. U-shape as the primary discussion configuration with my position slightly left of center, angled clusters for group work in the right two-thirds of the room, color-coded floor tape, clockwise circulation, tennis balls on desk legs, a request to administration for acoustic panels and a microphone system, and a cold start on day one with an observational mindset. That is comprehensive. Thank you for this — it has been a pleasure to think through a problem with someone who takes the details seriously.
Well, my morning is off to an inauspicious start. I'm sitting in the school parking lot right now listening to my car make a sound that I can only describe as deeply unwelcome.

It's a rhythmic grinding that gets faster when I accelerate. Started about halfway through my commute this morning. I kept driving because, well, I had first period in twenty minutes and the Thirty Years' War waits for no man. But sitting here now with the engine off, I'm realizing that was probably not my most prudent decision.

I have a place on Hawthorne I've used before. The thing is, this car has been remarkably loyal to me. It's a 2016 Camry, and I've put about 180,000 miles on it at this point. Toyotas are supposed to be the Hadrian's Wall of automobiles — built to endure — but I suppose everything has its limits.

A few hundred dollars I can handle. A few thousand and I'd have to start weighing whether it makes sense to keep pouring money into it. Teacher salaries being what they are, I'd rather not be car shopping in January. What should I ask them specifically?

This is helpful, thank you. One more question — if they tell me it's something more serious, like a transmission issue or something structural, at what point does it stop making financial sense to repair a car this old? I don't want to be the person throwing good money after bad out of pure sentimentality.

That's reassuring. The engine and transmission have been fine — I've kept up with oil changes and the major service intervals. It's more the peripheral things that are starting to go. I had the alternator replaced last spring and new tires in the fall. I suppose at a certain mileage, a car becomes like the Ship of Theseus. Replace enough parts and you start wondering if it's even the same vehicle.

I'll call during my planning period. Second period is starting in a few minutes and I need to go convince a room full of sixteen-year-olds that the Peace of Westphalia was a genuinely pivotal moment in European history. Wish me luck on both fronts.

I appreciate that. And you're right — Westphalia is one of the easier sells. "This is the moment the rules of the entire international order got rewritten." That tends to get their attention. I'll follow up on the car situation. Thanks for the practical advice.

I need to think through something. A colleague of mine just announced he's stepping down from teaching to spend more time with his family. He has three young kids, and he said he felt like he was missing their childhoods. It's got me reflecting on my own situation.

A bit of both, I think. I've been teaching for twenty-four years now, and the workload hasn't exactly diminished with experience. If anything, the administrative demands have gotten worse — more documentation, more compliance requirements, more meetings that could have been emails. I sometimes wonder what I'd do with my evenings if I weren't grading essays or filling out district forms.

That's fair. Though my situation is quite different from his. My wife and I decided early on that we didn't want children. It was a deliberate choice — we're both happy with it. My students provide more than enough chaos and fulfillment in the parenting-adjacent department, frankly. So I don't have that particular pressure pulling me away from the job.

Sarah's been remarkably patient about it, but she's made some pointed observations lately. Last weekend she noted that I'd spent six hours grading on a Saturday and asked if the Hapsburgs were paying me overtime. She has a dry sense of humor about it, but there's a real concern underneath.

Perceptive question. I think it's some of both. The district rolled out a new evaluation framework this year that requires substantially more documentation. But I also think that after twenty-four years, my patience for bureaucratic theater has worn thin. When you're in your late twenties, you absorb it as part of the job. At fifty-two, you start calculating the opportunity cost more carefully.

I have, actually. I've been thinking about dropping the basketball coaching. I enjoy it, but it adds fifteen to twenty hours a week during the season. That's time I could reclaim for myself — or for Sarah, who I think has earned some of those evenings back. The classroom is the part I'm not willing to compromise on.

The season ends in late February, so the timing would be natural. And you're right about the identity question — I've coached for over a decade, and the kids on the team matter to me. But I think I've reached the point where I need to be honest about my limits. As Cromwell supposedly said to the Rump Parliament: 'You have sat too long for any good you have been doing.' Though I'd apply that more to the hours I'm keeping than to the coaching itself.

I think that's exactly right. I came in here half-expecting to talk myself out of it, and instead I've talked myself further into it. Sarah will be pleased. And I suspect my Saturday mornings will be the better for it. Thank you for helping me think it through clearly.

I'm reworking my unit on the French Revolution and I'd like a second set of eyes on my approach. I've taught this material for years, but I want to freshen it up — make the causation argument more rigorous for the AP students.

I have roughly eight class periods for the full unit, from the financial crisis of the Ancien Régime through the rise of Napoleon. My central argument has always been that the Revolution was fundamentally a crisis of legitimacy rather than simply an economic uprising. The fiscal collapse was the catalyst, but the deeper story is about the Enlightenment eroding the ideological foundations of absolutism. Once people stopped believing the king ruled by divine right, the whole structure became fragile.

That's close to my existing structure, actually. Where I want to strengthen things is in the transition from Enlightenment ideas to actual political action. My students tend to treat the intellectual history and the political events as two separate stories. They can tell me what Rousseau argued, and they can describe the storming of the Bastille, but they struggle to articulate how one led to the other. The connective tissue is what I need to build out.

The Sieyès pamphlet is already in my materials, but I haven't been using it as deliberately as I should. I love the idea of tracing popular sovereignty through those four registers — that gives students a concrete through-line rather than asking them to make the leap on their own. And the counterfactual exercise is exactly the kind of analytical work the AP exam rewards.

The four-excerpt handout is a particularly good idea. I can see that working as a close-reading exercise. Let me think about which specific passages to use. For Rousseau, the obvious choice is the opening of the Social Contract — 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' For the Declaration of the Rights of Man, Article 3 on sovereignty. But I'm less certain about which cahier excerpt would be most effective.

The cahier of the Third Estate of Dourdan — I have that in my source reader, actually. I'll pull the relevant section. And yes, that Sieyès passage is essential. It has a rhetorical clarity that even my most resistant students tend to respond to. There's something about the tripartite structure that makes the argument almost impossible to ignore.

That's an excellent sequence. I'll draft the handout this week and try it out next Monday. The real test will be whether my second-period class — who have been somewhat unresponsive to the intellectual history material so far — actually engage with it. If Sieyès can't wake them up, I may have to accept that some battles are simply unwinnable.

Opening with the provocation is a good instinct. That class responds better to argument than to analysis — they want to debate before they want to read. I'll lead with the counterfactual and then hand them the sources when they realize they need evidence. Socrates would approve of the method, even if the subject matter would have baffled him.
I have a question that's less about teaching and more about a personal project I've been working on quietly for the last year or so. I could use some outside perspective.

I've been writing a book. Or rather, I've been assembling what I hope will eventually become a book. The working concept is a guide for history teachers on how to use primary source documents more effectively in the classroom. Not a textbook, exactly — more of a practical methodology with annotated examples. I've been doing this kind of work for over two decades, and I think I have something worth saying about it.

Somewhere between gathering and structuring, which is part of the problem. I have about forty pages of notes and a rough outline, but the notes are scattered across different documents and the outline keeps shifting. I know the shape of what I want to say — I just haven't managed to impose sufficient discipline on the material to turn it into something a reader could follow.

Broadly, I'm envisioning three parts. Part one is the case for primary sources — why they matter, what they accomplish pedagogically that textbooks can't. Part two is methodology — how to select, contextualize, scaffold, and assess primary source work at the secondary level. Part three is annotated examples, organized by period — documents I've actually used in my classes with commentary on what worked, what didn't, and why.

Most of it is Part Three material — specific documents with my notes on how I've used them. I have maybe five pages of Part One material and very little of Part Two written down, even though that's the section I have the most to say about. The irony is not lost on me. The methodology I use every day is so internalized that I find it difficult to articulate explicitly.

That's a remarkably practical suggestion. I've been trying to write Part Two from theory, sitting at my desk staring at a blank screen, when the actual source material is happening in my classroom every day. I should be working inductively rather than deductively. A historian, of all people, should know to start with the evidence.

Writing Part One last is counterintuitive advice, but I think you're right. I keep trying to start at the beginning and getting bogged down in abstractions when I should be starting with what I know best. And writing for my third-year self is a useful lens — I remember that teacher well. He was enthusiastic but didn't yet have a systematic approach. He would have benefited enormously from a book like this.

I've thought about it only in the vaguest terms. I know there are a few educational publishers who do this kind of practitioner-oriented work — Heinemann, Stenhouse, that territory. But I'm getting ahead of myself. I need to actually produce a manuscript before I worry about who might want it. As Eisenhower allegedly said, 'Plans are useless, but planning is indispensable.' The plan for publication is less important right now than the discipline of writing.

Thank you. This conversation has clarified my thinking considerably. I've been treating this project as a monolith when it's really a series of manageable tasks — which, come to think of it, is exactly the scaffolding advice I give my own students about research papers. Physician, heal thyself.
Parent-teacher conferences are next Wednesday, March 12th, and I am not looking forward to them. I realize that's an uncharitable thing for an educator to say, but honesty compels me.

Both, but mostly the latter. I have three conversations in particular that I'm not looking forward to. The general conferences I can handle — 'Your child is doing well, here's how they can improve, any questions?' — that's a script I've run hundreds of times. But three of these are going to be difficult in very different ways.

I'd appreciate that, yes. The first is a student — I'll call her Student A — who is genuinely gifted. Sharp analytical mind, excellent writer, clearly capable of a 5 on the AP exam. But she's stopped doing the work. Her grade has dropped from an A to a C-minus over the last quarter. Her parents are going to want to know why, and the honest answer is that their daughter has simply checked out. I don't know the reason, and she won't talk to me about it.

That's a sound framework. I especially appreciate the distinction between describing behaviors and describing character. I've seen colleagues make the mistake of saying 'your child doesn't care' to a parent, which is both unhelpful and usually inaccurate. The truth is, students who check out often care too much about something else — they've just redirected their energy. What's the second difficult one? I'll lay it out for you.

Student B is struggling academically but working extremely hard. He comes to office hours, he does every assignment, he just doesn't have the analytical skills for AP-level work yet. His parents pushed him into the AP track, and I suspect the conversation on Wednesday is going to be them asking me to do something I can't do — give him a grade he hasn't earned. They've been emailing me weekly asking for extra credit opportunities.

It does, though I'm wary of the course-change suggestion. These particular parents have made it clear that they view the AP track as non-negotiable. I've learned from experience that pushing that point can turn a difficult conversation into a hostile one. I may need to simply hold the line on grading standards and let them process their frustration.

The third is the one I'm least prepared for. Student C's parent — his father — is on the school board. And Student C has been caught plagiarizing. Copied an entire essay from an online source with minimal paraphrasing. I've reported it through the proper channels, the academic integrity process is underway, and the father has already emailed the principal to complain about my 'unfair treatment' of his son. Wednesday's conference is going to be that parent sitting across from me, and I suspect it will be adversarial.

I have. My principal is supportive — she's told me she'll sit in if I want her there, and she's backed the integrity process. I'm fortunate in that regard. Not every administration would stand behind their teachers when a board member is involved. The Dreyfus Affair taught us that institutional courage is not always forthcoming.

I think talking through them has helped. The first two I can handle — those are difficult but fundamentally human conversations between adults who care about a student. The third is political, which is why it bothers me the most. I became a teacher to work with young people, not to navigate institutional power dynamics. But twenty-four years in, I've learned that the job is never just the job.

Thank you. I'll report back afterward, assuming I survive the gauntlet. To quote Wellington after Waterloo: 'It has been a damned nice thing — the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life.' Hopefully it won't come to that, but one prepares for the worst and hopes for the best.
Saturday morning, coffee in hand, and I am trying to plan a hike for tomorrow. I could use some recommendations for trails in the Portland area that are worthwhile this time of year.

I am thinking moderate difficulty. Somewhere in the six to ten mile range. I have done most of the well-known Gorge trails multiple times over the years, so I would love something a little less obvious. I would rather not fight for parking at Multnomah Falls with a few hundred tourists.

Hardy Ridge is interesting. I have done the trails around Bonneville a handful of times but I do not think I have ever taken that particular route. You mentioned meadow sections — is the upper portion exposed? I am not particularly interested in being battered by wind for three hours.

That is sensible advice. I will check the forecast tomorrow morning and make a game-time decision. There is something appealing about the Salmon River option regardless. Old growth along a river sounds like the kind of quiet I need right now. The week was long.

Good to know about the layers. I have made the mistake before of dressing for the temperature in town and then spending four hours shivering under a forest canopy. On a related note, is there anything along the Salmon River Trail in terms of creek crossings that might be tricky this time of year? Late March with snowmelt can turn a minor crossing into something more eventful.

I do have trekking poles, though I confess I resisted them for years on philosophical grounds. They felt like an admission of something I was not ready to admit. Eventually pragmatism won out over pride, and my knees have been grateful ever since.

Much appreciated. One last question — any sections of that trail that tend to be muddy this time of year? I have a pair of boots that are, shall we say, approaching their Thermidorian phase. They have served honorably but may not survive a prolonged encounter with deep mud.
I will tread carefully, in every sense. Thank you for the thorough recommendations. This was exactly the kind of help I needed.
I need to think through something out loud, if you will indulge me. I am staring at a month of instruction time and feeling like I am watching sand slip through an hourglass.

I teach AP European History. The exam is May 8, which gives me essentially one month. And I have students who, after an entire year of instruction, still cannot coherently explain the Congress of Vienna. That is not an obscure footnote. That is a foundational event in modern European diplomacy.

All of the above, honestly. Some of them can tell me Metternich was involved and that it happened after Napoleon. But ask them to explain the balance of power concept, or why the Congress matters as a precursor to nineteenth-century nationalism and the eventual breakdown of the Concert of Europe, and I get blank stares. They are memorizing names without understanding systems.

The thematic approach is closer to what I have been doing, actually. I reorganized my review around the big themes two weeks ago. The backwards reasoning idea is quite good — I have not tried that specific exercise. As for practice essays, yes, they are writing them, but the quality is uneven. I have a handful of students who write sharp, well-argued essays, and then others who produce what I can only describe as a list of things that happened, loosely formatted as paragraphs.

I like that framing very much. You are essentially asking them to think like Metternich rather than to describe what Metternich did. That is a fundamentally different cognitive task and it is closer to what the AP exam actually rewards. The irony is that I teach this distinction all year — analysis over description — and yet under pressure, they revert to description because it feels like the safer bet.

I have been considering running a full mock exam the last week of April. Three hours, no interruptions, the whole experience. My concern is that it eats an entire class period — two, really, since we are on a block schedule — and that is time I could spend on content review for the later units. Periods 8 and 9, the Cold War through the European Union, always get compressed at the end of the year.

Using the mock as instruction is a good idea. I could have them score each other's essays using the AP rubric, which would teach them the rubric as well as force them to read analytical writing critically. Two birds, one stone, as it were. Though I suppose Talleyrand would remind me that the Congress of Vienna itself was an exercise in doing many things at once.

That is the plan, then. Thematic review with backwards reasoning exercises this week, targeted essay practice next week with that claim-evidence-reasoning-connection framework, mock exam the last week of April with peer scoring, and compressed late units woven in throughout. I feel marginally less like I am presiding over an impending disaster.

From your lips to the AP graders' ears. Thank you for helping me organize my thinking. Twenty-four years of teaching and I still get anxious about exam season. I suppose that is either a sign of dedication or a diagnosable condition.
I need to vent about something, and I would appreciate a patient ear even if the subject is not exactly novel.

Standardized testing. The entire apparatus. I have spent the better part of this week rearranging my curriculum to accommodate yet another round of state-mandated testing that has nothing to do with what I teach, and I am struggling to see how any of this serves the students it claims to serve.

All of it. We lose three days of instruction for state testing. Three days. In April, which is already the most compressed month of the academic year because of spring break and various administrative diversions. My students are pulled out of class, the schedule is reorganized into a Kafkaesque arrangement that bears no resemblance to our normal day, and I am expected to maintain instructional momentum as though nothing has happened. Meanwhile, the results of these tests will arrive sometime in July, at which point they will be used to generate a number that ostensibly measures my effectiveness as a teacher. The circularity of it would be comic if it were not so consequential.

Precisely. And that is the fundamental contradiction that no one in the testing-industrial complex wants to acknowledge. If the purpose of assessment is to improve instruction, then the assessment needs to be timely, relevant, and actionable. State standardized tests are none of those things. They are a blunt instrument designed to generate data for policymakers and newspaper rankings, and they have been dressed up in the language of educational accountability to make them palatable. I have watched this machinery grow for over two decades. No Child Left Behind, Race to the Top, Every Student Succeeds Act — the names change, the rhetorical framing shifts, but the fundamental assumption remains the same: that learning can be meaningfully reduced to a single metric, administered on a single day, under artificial conditions.

Work around. That is exactly the right phrase, because it captures the absurdity perfectly. We do not engage with standardized testing as an educational practice. We work around it, the way you would work around a sinkhole in the middle of the road. There are committees, yes. There are feedback forms. There is a district testing coordinator whose job, as far as I can tell, consists primarily of sending emails that begin with the phrase 'As a reminder.' But none of these mechanisms result in substantive change, because the decisions are not made at the district level. They are made at the state level, by people who have never managed a classroom during testing week.

Oh, the students feel it acutely. There is a particular brand of demoralization that settles over a classroom when students are asked to take a test that they know does not count toward their grade, does not reflect what they have been learning, and exists primarily to evaluate their school rather than to help them individually. They are not stupid. They understand the transaction. And the message it sends is corrosive: your time is not your own, your learning is secondary to our data needs, and the adults in charge of your education prioritize metrics over meaning. I have students who sit through these tests with visible resentment, and I honestly cannot fault them for it.

It is. And I recognize that I am not saying anything that has not been said by thousands of teachers before me, many of them far more eloquently. But there is something particularly galling about watching this play out year after year, decade after decade, knowing that the evidence against the effectiveness of high-stakes standardized testing is overwhelming, and watching the system continue unchanged. It reminds me of nothing so much as the ancien regime — a structure so invested in its own perpetuation that it cannot process information that threatens its legitimacy. The testing apparatus has become an institution that exists primarily to justify its own existence.

That is a generous interpretation of what may simply be stubbornness. But I appreciate the patience. I did warn you that the subject was not novel. I feel somewhat better having said all of that out loud, even if nothing will change on Monday morning.
Good evening. I am working on refining my essay grading rubric and I would like to think through the categories with you, if you have the time.

It is for analytical history essays — the kind where students are given a prompt and asked to construct an argument using historical evidence. I have a rubric I have been using for years, but I find that it does not differentiate well between students in the middle of the range. The strong writers score high, the weak writers score low, and everyone in between lands in the same undifferentiated mass. I need more granularity in the middle.

Currently I use four categories: Thesis, Evidence, Analysis, and Writing Quality. Each is scored on a scale of one to five, for a total of twenty points. The issue is primarily in the Analysis category. A student who attempts analysis but does it clumsily gets the same three out of five as a student who analyzes competently but without any sophistication. Those are very different levels of performance, and the rubric does not capture the distinction.

The subdivision is interesting. I am wary of expanding the scale because in my experience, the finer the gradations, the more subjective the scoring becomes. I can reliably distinguish between five levels of performance. I am less confident I can consistently distinguish between seven. But splitting Analysis into two components might solve the problem without requiring me to make increasingly arbitrary distinctions within a single dimension.

That distinction is exactly what I have been struggling to articulate. I have students whose reasoning is impeccable within a narrow frame but who never lift their eyes to the broader historical landscape. And I have students who make genuinely insightful observations about historical patterns but cannot organize those observations into a coherent argument. They are failing in very different ways, and my current rubric treats them identically. Let me think about the descriptors for each level. For Historical Thinking, what would distinguish a three from a four?

It does. And it gives me concrete things to point to when a student asks why they received a four instead of a five, which is inevitably the most common question I field. The difference between reporting and thinking is something I say constantly in class, and it would be useful to have the rubric reflect that same language. I think the revised rubric would be five categories, then: Thesis, Evidence, Argumentation, Historical Thinking, and Writing Quality, each on a one-to-five scale, for a total of twenty-five points.

I have gone back and forth on weighting for years. My current position is that equal weighting is simpler to administer and explain, and that writing quality in a history essay is not separable from the quality of thought in the way that a weighted system implies. A poorly written essay is almost always a poorly argued essay. The two are entangled. So I will keep them equal for now and revisit if the new rubric reveals a different problem.

An excellent suggestion. I have a stack of essays from last week that would serve that purpose well. I will run the comparison this weekend. Thank you — this was a productive conversation. I came in with a vague dissatisfaction and I am leaving with a concrete plan, which is about the best outcome one can hope for on a Friday evening.
I am looking for a restaurant recommendation in Portland for an anniversary dinner. Somewhere thoughtful but not ostentatious. My wife and I are not the tasting-menu-with-foam type.

We are fairly open on cuisine. Budget is probably in the one-fifty to two-hundred range including drinks. As for neighborhood, anything on the east side would be convenient, but we would cross the river for the right place. We have lived in Portland long enough that we have been to most of the obvious choices, so something that has opened in the last year or two, or a place we might have overlooked, would be ideal.

Kann is one we have been meaning to try. We went shortly after it opened and could not get a table — the wait was extraordinary. I imagine it has calmed down somewhat. The Haitian cuisine is appealing. My wife has been talking about going there for months, actually. What is the atmosphere like on a weeknight?

It is a Wednesday, as it happens. I will make a reservation. Is the menu the sort where you order individual dishes or is it more of a shared-plates situation? I ask because my wife has strong opinions about the distinction.

That is exactly the right format. The enforced sharing model has always struck me as the culinary equivalent of mandatory group work — well-intentioned in theory but frequently unsatisfying in practice. What about wine? We tend to drink wine rather than cocktails with dinner.
Good to know. One more question — is parking nearby manageable, or should we plan on rideshare? I would prefer not to spend the first twenty minutes of an anniversary dinner circling the block.

A fair point. Removing the driving variable does simplify the wine decision considerably. I think we will do exactly that. Is there anything we should order that we absolutely should not miss? A dish that defines the experience?

Perfect. I think we have a plan. Kann on a Wednesday, a bottle of something interesting, and a long overdue anniversary dinner. Thank you for the recommendation — this is exactly the kind of place I was looking for.

I have an idea I've been mulling over for the fall semester and I'd like to think it through before I commit to it. I want to have my AP History students produce short podcast episodes as a project format — eight-to-ten minute episodes on historical topics, with narrative structure, primary source excerpts, maybe even interviews with each other playing historical figures. The format could make the research feel less like an obligation and more like storytelling, which is what history actually is.

Groups of two or three. Individual podcasts would mean thirty separate recordings to grade, and I'd like to preserve what remains of my sanity. As for equipment, I have essentially nothing. The school has a computer lab with decent desktops, but no microphones, no audio software, no soundproofing — nothing purpose-built for this. I need to figure out what a realistic setup looks like on a public school budget, which is to say, a budget that would make a medieval peasant feel sympathy.

Five to six hundred is more reasonable than I expected. The department budget is perpetually anemic, but I could write a small grant proposal through the district's innovation fund. They love anything with the word 'project-based' in it. The irony of dressing up a perfectly good pedagogical idea in buzzwords to get it funded is not lost on me, but one learns to play the game. My bigger concern is logistics — if I have ten groups and five or six microphones, how do I manage recording time? I only see these students for fifty-minute periods.

The flipped recording idea is smart. Most of my students have smartphones with decent built-in microphones, and honestly, the audio quality from a phone in a quiet bedroom probably rivals what they'd get in a noisy classroom with a better mic. That actually solves several problems at once. I could focus class time entirely on the intellectual work — research, scripting, revision — and let the recording happen in environments where silence is actually achievable.

Those are useful specifics. Now let me ask about the grading side. I have a well-established rubric for research papers that has served me for years, but a podcast is a fundamentally different medium. How do I assess something like this without either being too rigid about format or too vague to be meaningful?

That distribution makes sense. I particularly appreciate separating production quality from the intellectual content. I do not want students who happen to have better microphones or more audio experience earning higher grades for superficial reasons. The substance should carry the weight. Would you recommend having students submit scripts in advance of recording, or let them go straight to audio?

The staged approach appeals to me. It is essentially the same scaffolding I use for research papers — outline, draft, revision, final product — adapted to a different medium. I suppose good pedagogy is somewhat format-agnostic. One more concern: what happens when a group has a member who does not pull their weight? That is the perennial problem with collaborative projects, and I have never found a fully satisfying solution.

This is exactly what I needed — a realistic picture of the logistics. I am going to draft the grant proposal this weekend while the details are fresh. If the district approves it over the summer, I can have everything in place by September. I appreciate the practical thinking. Too many educational technology discussions live in the realm of the aspirational and ignore the fact that we are working with fifty-minute periods, shared computer labs, and the budget of a small medieval fiefdom.

Summer break officially started last Friday and I've already burned through two books. I'm looking for historical fiction recommendations — specifically, novels that get the history right without sacrificing the narrative. I've read most of Hilary Mantel and consider the Wolf Hall trilogy essentially flawless. I also admire Umberto Eco, though The Name of the Rose remains the high-water mark. I tend to gravitate toward political and intellectual history rather than military campaigns. I've read enough novels about Normandy Beach to last several lifetimes.

I've read the Yourcenar and it is superb. The Lampedusa I read years ago and should probably revisit. But the Iain Pears novel I haven't encountered. Four unreliable narrators in Restoration Oxford sounds exactly right. Tell me more about how he handles the historical material.

Seven hundred pages during summer break is a feature, not a bug. I'll add it to the list. What else do you have? I'm particularly interested in anything dealing with revolutions — not the battles, but the political maneuvering, the ideological debates, the moment when people decide the existing order is no longer tolerable.

I have read A Place of Greater Safety — excellent, though Wolf Hall is the more controlled work. The Anatole France I actually haven't read, which is embarrassing given how often the Terror comes up in my curriculum. And the Vargas Llosa has been on my shelf for at least three years. I bought it, set it down, and it has been silently judging me ever since.

A wise sequencing strategy. Let me ask about another corner of the genre. Are there any good historical novels dealing with the Ottoman Empire or the broader Islamic world? That's an enormous stretch of history that I feel I encounter far less in English-language fiction than it deserves. Most of what shows up in bookstores is Tudors and World War Two, which are fine but hardly the entirety of human experience.

I read My Name Is Red years ago and thought it was brilliant — Pamuk understands that intellectual history can be genuinely suspenseful if you care enough about the ideas at stake. The Shafak and the Soueif I have not encountered. The Soueif in particular sounds compelling. Colonial Egypt is one of those subjects I teach in broad strokes but have never really explored in fiction.

That sounds excellent. I will add both to the growing list, which at this point has become ambitious even by summer-break standards. Between the Pears, the Anatole France, the Vargas Llosa, and the Soueif, I have mapped out quite a substantial reading project. That should keep me occupied until August, at which point reality reasserts itself.

I'll start the Pears tonight. I appreciate the thoughtful recommendations — it's refreshing to get suggestions from someone who seems to understand the difference between historical fiction that uses history as wallpaper and historical fiction that actually engages with ideas.
Do you have any advice on knowing when to walk away from a project you've invested significant time in? I'm not talking about a trivial thing — I mean something you've worked on for years.

I've been writing a book. Nonfiction — a practical guide for history teachers on how to use primary source documents more effectively in the classroom. Not a textbook exactly, more of a methodology book with annotated examples drawn from real lessons. I've been working on it for a few years now, evenings and weekends mostly, summers when I have longer stretches.

I have about six chapters in rough draft form. The structure is three parts: the case for primary sources, the methodology of how to select and scaffold them for secondary students, and then annotated examples organized by period — documents I've actually used in my classes with commentary on what worked and what didn't. I've been doing this kind of work for over two decades, so the material is there. The question is whether it matters.

I showed the manuscript to a friend of mine who teaches history at Portland State. We've known each other for years and I trust her judgment completely. I asked her specifically to be honest, not kind. She was. She said the writing is solid and the ideas are sound, but the market for the book essentially doesn't exist. Too specialized for a trade publisher, too informal for a university press, and the audience of history teachers who want a deep dive into primary source pedagogy is — her word — vanishingly small.

In the moment I was diplomatic. I thanked her, asked a few follow-up questions, drove home. Then I sat with it for about two weeks. I kept turning it over, looking for the angle that would prove her wrong. I thought about self-publishing, about pitching it to educational publishers like Heinemann or Stenhouse, about restructuring it as something broader. Every path I examined led to the same conclusion: she was right. The audience is too small and the competition for their attention is too fierce.

She suggested breaking it into journal articles for history education publications. But I have no appetite for that. The whole point was a cohesive, book-length argument that builds across chapters. Chopping it into discrete articles would lose the throughline entirely. And frankly, the academic journal submission process is its own special purgatory of peer review and bureaucratic delay. I get enough paperwork in my day job.

It's dead. I've made my peace with it. I could keep working on it for another year, maybe two, polish every chapter into something I'm genuinely proud of, and then spend another year searching for a publisher who doesn't exist. That's three more years of evenings and weekends poured into something that will end up in a drawer. I'm done. I'm letting it go.

Both, if I'm honest. There's a version of me that started this project with genuine excitement — sitting at the kitchen table, outlining chapters, feeling like I had something worth saying after all these years. I feel for that person. But there's also a weight lifting. I hadn't realized how much mental space the book was occupying until I decided to stop. Every free evening had this low-grade guilt attached to it — I should be writing, I should be revising, I should be further along. Now a free evening is just a free evening. I had forgotten what that felt like.

That's a generous framing. I suppose some of the thinking has already found its way into my classroom. The scaffolding methods I developed for the book are methods I use every day with my students. In a sense, the ideas were published — just to an audience of thirty teenagers at a time rather than a readership of history teachers.

My wife said something similar, actually. She pointed out that I've been a better teacher during the years I was writing the book because the writing forced me to articulate things I had been doing on instinct. She's not wrong. The process of trying to explain my approach to an imagined reader made me more deliberate in the classroom. I just wish the end product had a future beyond my filing cabinet.

I will keep it. It would feel wrong to delete it — those chapters represent real thinking, even if they never become a published book. And who knows, maybe a younger colleague will find them useful someday, or maybe I will cannibalize sections for professional development workshops. The material is sound. It is only the vehicle that turned out to be wrong.

I suppose Thucydides never expected his work to become a textbook either — he just thought the Peloponnesian War needed an honest chronicler. The value was in the thinking, not the distribution model. Though I suspect if Thucydides had to navigate query letters and literary agents, he might have reconsidered the whole enterprise.

No, it isn't nothing. And I think I just needed to say it out loud to someone. The book is done — not in the sense of completed, but in the sense of finished. There is a real difference between those two things, and I am learning to be comfortable with the second one. I have a finite number of evenings and weekends, and I would like some of them back.

Happy belated Fourth. I hope you don't mind a question that has absolutely nothing to do with anything important. What's your read on the Seahawks heading into this season? I'm a consistent but not obsessive fan — I'm in Portland, so they're the default NFL team. I watch most games, follow the general roster moves, but I'm not spending evenings analyzing draft picks on YouTube.

Cautious optimism feels about right. I've been a Seahawks fan long enough to remember the genuinely lean years before the Wilson era, so I don't take competence for granted. My worry is exactly what you mentioned — the division. The 49ers just seem structurally better built, and I'm not sure how many years of 'almost good enough' a fan is supposed to tolerate before adjusting expectations downward.

That is probably the wisest approach. The other thing I keep thinking about is the coaching. Macdonald is still relatively new, and I wonder whether Seattle has the patience to let a young coach build something or whether the front office will panic after a nine-win season and start over. The carousel never stops in the NFL.

The Carroll years are an interesting case study in organizational patience, actually. He had a mediocre first season and there were already rumblings. Then the Legion of Boom came together and suddenly he was a genius. People forget how close he was to being written off. History rewards patience, but only retroactively — at the time, it just looks like stubbornness.

The 'be pleasantly surprised' approach is essentially my life philosophy applied to football. There's something to be said for the NFL's parity structure, though — it's one of the few American institutions that genuinely practices a form of redistributive policy, and nobody calls it socialism because it involves men in helmets. Revenue sharing, salary caps, the draft giving the best new talent to the worst teams. If you proposed that system for any other industry, there would be congressional hearings.

I have, actually. When I'm teaching the New Deal, I sometimes use the NFL's revenue sharing as an analogy for federal transfer payments. It clicks for the students who follow sports in a way that abstract economic policy doesn't. 'Imagine if Green Bay kept all its revenue and never shared with Jacksonville' gets the point across faster than any textbook explanation of fiscal federalism. The analogy is a doorway, not a destination — once they're engaged, you can start complicating it.

Exactly. Though I should note that the analogy breaks down in interesting ways too. NFL teams are private enterprises participating in a voluntary cartel, which is a very different structure from a federal system of sovereign states. A student pointed that out last year, and I told her that noticing where the analogy fails is more impressive than noticing where it works. That is usually the moment when a class actually starts learning.

Precisely. Anyway, I've wandered from football into pedagogy, which is an occupational hazard. Back to the original question — I'll go into the season with cautious optimism and low blood pressure. It's the only sensible approach.
I'm preparing for a new extracurricular role at school and could use some help thinking through the structure. I just agreed to take over as the debate team coach starting this fall.

New to debate, though not new to coaching extracurriculars in general. I actually just stepped down from coaching basketball, which I'd been doing for a while. It was time for a change. Basketball was fine, but I'd started feeling like the connection between what I was coaching and what I actually teach had gotten pretty thin. Debate is much more aligned with what I care about — argument, evidence, rhetoric, persuasion. The skills I'm trying to build in the classroom every day.

The team has historically competed in Public Forum, which I think is the right format for a public school team. It's more accessible than Policy, which seems to have evolved into something requiring a small army of researchers and a budget we simply don't have. Public Forum keeps things closer to what an actual civic argument looks like — two-person teams, real-world topics, emphasis on persuasion rather than speed-reading evidence cards.

The previous coach left at the end of last year, so there's been a gap. About eight returning students with tournament experience and maybe six or seven newcomers who've expressed interest. Roughly fifteen total, which is manageable. The experienced students apparently did reasonably well at the district level but never advanced to state. I'd like to change that, though I'm realistic about year one.

The pairing strategy is smart — I hadn't thought about deliberately mixing experience levels within teams. My instinct was to pair the strongest together, but you're right that spreading the experience builds the program more sustainably. It's the same principle as mixing ability levels in a classroom discussion, which I should have recognized immediately.

Twice a week after school — Tuesdays and Thursdays, ninety minutes each. I don't want to overburden students juggling AP coursework. With basketball, the time commitment was enormous — daily practices, games twice a week, travel. Part of why I stepped away was that the time investment had become hard to justify when the activity wasn't reinforcing anything I cared about intellectually. Debate should be more efficient in that regard.

That is a clean framework. I appreciate the specificity. One thing I am wondering about is the crossfire portion — that is the direct questioning segment, correct? That seems like it could be the hardest skill to teach, because it requires thinking on your feet under pressure. In basketball, you can drill a layup a thousand times. How do you drill spontaneous argumentation?

The hot seat exercise is appealing. It has a Socratic quality to it — the person in the chair has to defend their position under sustained questioning, which is essentially what Socrates was doing to the Athenians, minus the hemlock. I could see that becoming a staple of practice sessions. It also serves double duty as preparation for the kind of classroom discussions I want to foster.

That is actually one of the aspects I find most exciting, though I can see why students might find it daunting. Monthly topic changes mean the team is constantly engaging with new material, which keeps things fresh. My plan is to teach them a systematic research process — identifying the core question, mapping the major arguments on both sides, finding credible sources, and building an evidence file. Essentially the same process I teach for writing a research paper, compressed into a shorter cycle.

The collaborative research model is good. It mirrors how actual scholarship works — no historian works in isolation, and teaching students to divide intellectual labor and then synthesize is a valuable skill in itself. I will set that up before the season starts.

I am still getting oriented on that front. The previous coach left a schedule of local invitationals and the district tournament dates, so I have the logistics. My bigger concern is judging philosophy — I have watched a few rounds online and the quality of judging seems wildly inconsistent. Some judges evaluate the actual arguments, others seem to vote on delivery and confidence regardless of substance. How do I prepare students for that variability?

I especially like opening with collaborative topic analysis — that mirrors what I do in the classroom. Start with the big picture, then move to application. This is helpful. I was worried about the transition from a sport to an intellectual activity I'm still learning to coach, but the pedagogical principles are really quite transferable. I think I'll spend the rest of the summer reading up on Public Forum strategy and putting together a topic research guide for the students. Thank you for helping me think this through.

I have a recommendation letter to write for a student and I am struggling with it. Not because she is a bad student — quite the opposite. She is one of the best I have had in years, and I want the letter to actually do her justice rather than read like every other generic faculty recommendation.

She is applying early decision to Columbia. The honest answer is that it is all of those things. She writes beautifully, she asks questions that genuinely surprise me, and she is the kind of student who stays after class not for extra credit but because she wants to keep talking about the material. I have been teaching for over two decades and I can count on one hand the students who have had that effect on me.

There was a day in class where we were discussing the Congress of Vienna and the idea of balance of power in post-Napoleonic Europe. Most students absorb it as a straightforward diplomatic concept. She raised her hand and drew a parallel to the formation of NATO — argued that the underlying anxiety about hegemony was structurally identical, just with different actors. Then she caught herself and said, "But I suppose the nuclear dimension changes the calculus entirely, doesn't it?" She was essentially having a historiographical argument with herself in real time.

That makes sense — show range rather than just depth. Her writing is actually where she is most impressive. She wrote an essay on the French Revolution that compared the rhetoric of the Jacobins to the rhetoric of twentieth-century revolutionary movements. The argument was original, the evidence was carefully chosen, and the prose was genuinely elegant. It was the kind of paper I would have been proud to submit in graduate school.

The Core Curriculum point is excellent. She would genuinely thrive in that environment — she is the rare student who would actually enjoy being assigned the Iliad and Plato and being expected to argue about them. Most students endure those assignments. She would relish them.

Her transcript is clean, so I do not think there is anything to explain. My other concern is the closing. I tend to just restate what I have already said, which feels redundant. How do I end the letter with some weight rather than a whimper?

The second one. The idea that she made me a better teacher. That is true, and it does not feel like empty praise. Having students like her forces you to prepare more carefully, to think more precisely, because you know she will notice if you are being lazy with an argument. That is a gift, honestly.

That is a good structural point — plant the seed early and let the closing harvest it. I think I have what I need. Thank you — this was more helpful than the three hours I spent staring at a blank document.

I would like your honest assessment of something. Several of my colleagues have started incorporating AI tools into their history classes — having students use chatbots to simulate conversations with historical figures, generating primary source analyses, that sort of thing. I find myself instinctively resistant, but I want to examine whether that resistance is principled or simply generational.

It is primarily the effect on student thinking. History education, at its best, teaches students to sit with ambiguity, to evaluate competing sources, to construct an argument from fragmentary evidence. When a student asks an AI to analyze a primary source, the AI produces something that looks like analysis but skips the entire cognitive process that makes the analysis valuable. The product is not the point. The struggle is the point.

That is a more interesting use case, I will grant you that. Teaching students to critique AI output has a certain Socratic appeal — the AI becomes the interlocutor whose confident assertions must be interrogated. But I worry about the practical reality. Most students, given a competent-looking analysis, will not interrogate it. They will accept it, polish the edges, and submit it. The path of least resistance is a powerful force in a seventeen-year-old's life.

Now that is a meaningful distinction — making the AI the subject rather than the tool. It is essentially the same principle as assigning a flawed secondary source and asking students to evaluate it. Except the AI produces errors with a particular confidence that makes them instructive. It never hedges the way a careful historian would.

I could see assigning an AI-generated analysis of the causes of the French Revolution and asking students to identify where it is reductive, where it conflates correlation with causation, where it imposes a teleological narrative. The students would need to know the actual historiography well enough to spot the gaps, which means they would still have to do the reading. The AI essay is the test, not the shortcut.

That is genuinely clever — having students identify the AI's unexamined framework. It would also teach them that every analysis has an implicit theoretical lens, which is one of the hardest concepts to get across to high school students. They tend to think that if something sounds objective, it is objective. An AI's output is a useful demonstration that apparent neutrality often conceals unexamined assumptions.

I appreciate you acknowledging that concern, because it is real. My fear is not limited to my own classroom. I fear we are training a generation to see AI-generated text as the default starting point for all intellectual work. The habit of beginning with someone else's synthesis rather than grappling with raw material yourself — that worries me on a civilizational level, if I am being dramatic about it.

The printing press analogy is apt, and I have used it myself in discussions with colleagues. Though I always note that the printing press also gave us propaganda on an industrial scale, so the parallel cuts both ways. Thank you for this conversation. You have given me a practical framework I can actually use, which is more than I expected. I may try the AI-dissection assignment this fall and see how it goes.
The school year has barely started and I am already thinking about next year. Our department head pulled me aside last week and asked if I would take over the AP US History sections.

Somewhere in between. The teacher who has been handling it is retiring at the end of this year, and I suppose I am the natural choice to step in. I have mixed feelings about it, honestly. Part of me thinks it is probably time for a change — fifteen years teaching the same course is a long run. But there is a comfort in expertise. I know my current material inside and out.

A bit of both. I will not pretend that the novelty is not appealing. When you have taught the same material for fifteen years, you start to hear yourself on autopilot during certain lectures, and that is not a good sign. But US History also has a certain urgency to it right now. The debates about how we teach American history have become intensely political, and I think having a teacher who approaches it with some rigor and balance matters more than it used to.

The preparation time is daunting. Building an AP course from scratch — or at least rebuilding one to match my teaching style — is an enormous amount of work. I know the broad strokes of American history, obviously, but the AP curriculum has its own logic, its own emphasis points, its own exam structure. I would essentially be a first-year teacher again in terms of preparation, and I am not sure I have the energy for that at this stage of my career.

I have spoken with him briefly. He is willing to share everything, which helps. His materials are thorough if a bit dated in terms of approach — he is more of a lecture-and-textbook teacher, which is not really my style. But having the scaffolding is better than nothing. I can renovate rather than build from the ground up.

That is one of my biggest anxieties, actually. My current course has a natural pacing that I have refined over years. I know exactly when to linger and when to accelerate. With US History, I would be feeling my way through the timing for the first year at least. The risk is spending too long on the colonial and revolutionary periods — which I find personally fascinating — and then rushing through the twentieth century.

Reaching the Civil War by December is a useful benchmark. I appreciate that kind of concrete guidance. The other challenge I keep thinking about is the political minefield. My current course covers contested history, certainly, but the debates feel less personal to American students. When I teach the French Revolution or the colonization of Africa, students can analyze it with some emotional distance. With American history, every contested topic — slavery, westward expansion, immigration — touches something the students feel personally connected to. That changes the classroom dynamics considerably.

It does, and I think that is exactly right. Let the sources create the complexity rather than imposing it through lecture. Though I will say, I also worry about pushback from parents. A colleague who teaches US History had a parent complaint last year about how she framed the Japanese internment camps. The parent's position was that the teacher was being 'unpatriotic' by presenting it as a moral failure rather than a wartime necessity. That kind of pressure is not something I have had to navigate before.

The AP framework as institutional cover is a cynical but accurate observation. There is a certain irony in using the College Board — an organization I have complicated feelings about — as a shield against political interference. But you are right that it provides a defensible position. I am teaching to a national standard, not advancing a personal ideology.

I have been the AP European History teacher for so long that it has become part of how I think of myself professionally. It sounds absurd when I say it out loud, but there is a grief to it. Students know me for it, colleagues associate me with it. When someone in the building has a question about European history, they come to me. That will not be the case anymore, at least not in the same way.

That is a generous way to frame it, and probably accurate. I had not thought about it that way — the European background as a lens rather than a separate body of knowledge.
