A teacher who can contextualize the American Revolution within the broader Age of Revolutions, or who can teach the Marshall Plan alongside European reconstruction, has something to offer that a purely American-focused teacher does not.

I think I have more or less decided to do it. The department head needs an answer by the end of the month, and the rational arguments all point toward yes. It is time for a change, US History matters right now, and frankly, if I say no, they will give it to someone with half my experience and twice my willingness to water down the difficult parts.

You may be right about that. Sometimes the decision is made before the deliberation ends, and the deliberation is just a way of making peace with it. I think I will tell the department head yes this week rather than agonizing until the deadline. Thank you. Sometimes it takes an outside perspective to see past one's own apprehension.
We finally did it. Went to the dealership on Saturday and drove home in a Subaru Outback.

It was not sudden so much as inevitable. The Camry had been on its last legs for a while -- the transmission was getting rough, the AC was intermittent, and I was starting to calculate whether each repair was worth more than the car itself. The math finally stopped making sense.

Sarah was the driving force on the Outback, no pun intended. She has been adamant for months that whatever we got next needed to handle our hiking gear properly. The Camry trunk was a constant negotiation -- boots here, poles there, backpacks wedged at increasingly creative angles. She wanted something with actual cargo space and the ability to get to trailheads without worrying about gravel roads.

I was initially looking at another sedan, if I am honest. I am a creature of habit and the Camry had been perfectly adequate for my commute. But Sarah made a compelling case. She pointed out that every weekend we were playing Tetris with the trunk, and that we keep talking about doing longer trips to more remote trails. Practicality won over inertia.

The Premium trim. We debated the Limited but decided the heated seats and the better infotainment system on the Premium were sufficient without spending another several thousand dollars on leather we did not particularly want. I may be a creature of habit, but I am also a frugal creature.

Autumn Green Metallic. Sarah chose it, and I will admit it suits the car. It looks like something that belongs parked at a trailhead rather than in a school parking lot, which I suppose reflects the shift in how we are thinking about the vehicle. The Camry was white -- thoroughly anonymous, which was fine by me. Sarah said I needed to stop driving a car that looked like a rental.

Just the commute so far, but even that has been noticeably different. The visibility is better, sitting higher than I did in the Camry. And the EyeSight safety system is remarkable -- it practically drives itself on the highway, which is both impressive and mildly unsettling. Sarah has already been scouting a trail out near the gorge that she says was always too rough for the Camry. She is treating this car like an expedition vehicle, which I find endearing and slightly alarming.

Too late. She has already mentioned something about forest service roads near Mount Adams that she read about in a hiking forum. I pointed out that the Outback is not a Jeep, and she responded that the Outback owners on the forum seemed to manage just fine. I recognize a losing argument when I see one.

I will pass that along to Sarah, though I suspect she is already a member of three Subaru forums by now. She researches everything with the thoroughness of a graduate student. It is one of her best qualities, even when it means she arrives at conversations with more ammunition than I have.

Sarah is lobbying for a longer trip before the weather turns, but with the school year just getting started, I cannot justify taking time off yet. The Gorge will be the shakedown run, probably this weekend. If the car survives Sarah's ambitions, we will plan something bigger for a break.

I will say, there is something bittersweet about retiring a car you have driven for years. The Camry was not glamorous, but it was dependable in that quiet, unassuming way. I suppose there is a metaphor about change in there somewhere, but I will spare you the philosophical digression.

That is a generous eulogy for a sedan. I mentioned to one of my students that I got a new car and he asked what I had been driving before. When I told him it was a fourteen-year-old Camry, his expression suggested I had just confessed to a minor crime. Apparently, teachers are not supposed to drive cars that predate their students.

I suspect you are right. Sarah certainly has no doubts. She has already organized the cargo area with bins for hiking boots, a first aid kit, and what she calls a trail emergency bag. The car is four days old and already better organized than my classroom. I will take that as a sign that this was the right decision.
I need to think through something that has been occupying a considerable amount of mental real estate lately. My wife Sarah has been making a sustained case for us to move to Bend.

She has a whole portfolio of arguments. Better access to hiking and outdoor recreation, which is fair -- the trails around Bend are extraordinary. More space for the money. Lower cost of living compared to Portland. A quieter pace of life. She has been researching it methodically, which is how I know she is serious. Sarah does not bring things up casually.

My side is more complicated and less tidy, which is probably why she is winning the argument on points. The practical reality is that I am a high school teacher with twenty-four years at my current school. I have seniority, I have relationships with colleagues and students, I have a reputation I have built over decades. Moving to Bend means starting over at a new school where no one knows me. At fifty-two, the prospect of being the new teacher walking into a faculty meeting is not exactly thrilling.

We have talked about it. Her position is that good teachers find jobs, which is true in the abstract but ignores the specifics. Bend is not a large city. The number of high school teaching positions available in any given year is limited, and finding one that matches my subject area and experience level is not guaranteed. Sarah is a librarian, so for her, library positions exist in every county system. She acknowledges the Deschutes County system is smaller, but she frames that as a trade-off she is willing to make. The asymmetry is that her career transplants more easily than mine does.

She has, actually. She pulled up the Bend-La Pine school district website and showed me that they have three high schools, including one that opened relatively recently. She pointed out that a growing district means openings. I conceded the logic but noted that an opening in social studies at a school that offers AP History is a much narrower target than just any teaching position. She filed that under problems to solve later, which is Sarah's way of acknowledging a point without letting it derail her argument.

I would be lying if I said the hiking did not tempt me. Bend sits at the doorstep of some of the most beautiful landscape in the state. And Portland has changed in ways that have been hard to watch -- the city I moved to twenty-five years ago is not the city it is today. There are days when I am sympathetic to the argument. But then I think about walking into a school where I have no history, no context, no relationships, and the appeal evaporates rather quickly.

That is a perceptive question, and the answer is somewhat uncomfortable. Most of my social life is tied to the school. My closest friends are colleagues. Our social calendar revolves around school events, the occasional dinner with other teachers and their spouses, and the hiking that Sarah and I do together. We are not deeply embedded in a Portland community outside of my work. Sarah has pointed this out, gently but effectively. She argues that we could build a social life in Bend just as easily because most of our socializing is not location-dependent -- it is activity-dependent.

She has spreadsheets. I am not exaggerating. Sarah pulled comparable homes in both markets -- what our Portland house would sell for, what we could buy in Bend for the same money or less. The numbers are genuinely compelling. We could get a larger house on more land with a lower mortgage, or potentially no mortgage at all depending on how things shake out. She also factored in property tax differences. It is a thorough document. I told her she missed her calling as a prosecutor.

Identity, I think. And I realize that sounds dramatic, but after twenty-four years, my sense of who I am is deeply intertwined with being a teacher at this specific school. I know the building, I know which classroom has the best afternoon light, I know which custodian will lend me a dolly when I need to move textbooks. Those sound like trivial details, but they add up to a feeling of belonging that I am not sure I can replicate. Starting over is not just a logistical challenge. It is an existential one.

That is the question, and I do not have an answer yet. Sarah is patient, but she is also persistent. She has not issued an ultimatum, and she would not -- that is not how we operate. But I can feel the weight of her wanting this, and I do not want to be the person who stands in the way of something that would make her genuinely happy. The guilt of that is its own pressure.

She would move tomorrow if it were up to her. Realistically, she is talking about the next two to three years. She is smart enough to know that if she lets me defer it indefinitely, it will never happen. And I do not think it is the wrong move for Sarah -- I am simply not certain it is the right move for me. We are not disagreeing about facts. We are weighing different values. She prioritizes the life we would live outside of work. I am more attached to the life I have built inside of work. Neither of us is wrong, which means there is no clean resolution.

The conditional yes is an interesting framework. It would give me a concrete standard to evaluate rather than an amorphous dread of change. And it would show Sarah that I am taking her seriously rather than just stalling. At minimum, it moves us from a stalemate to a process, which is progress of a kind.

I appreciate you letting me think through this without pushing me in either direction. It is the kind of decision that does not benefit from advice so much as from articulation. Sometimes you need to hear yourself say the thing out loud before you understand what you actually think. I still do not know what we will do. But I have a better sense of why it is difficult, which is its own kind of progress.

I could use some help thinking through a trip. Sarah and I are planning to do the Olympic Peninsula in mid-July -- leaving the 15th -- and I need to figure out the best route and how to structure the days.

We are leaving July 15th and I would like to be back by the 20th, so five full days. Starting from Portland, yes. We are a mix -- Sarah is more interested in the rainforest ecology, and I just want to be somewhere without cell signal for at least part of the trip. We will camp some nights but want a real bed for at least two of the five.

This is excellent. The Hoh Rainforest has been on my list for years. There is something about a temperate rainforest that appeals to me -- the idea that this kind of ecosystem exists in the Pacific Northwest and most people do not even know about it. It is like discovering that the Roman Empire had a presence in Scotland. You think you know the map, and then it surprises you.

Sarah will appreciate the rain advisory. She is the practical one. I am the one who says it is July, how bad can it be, and she is the one who packs the rain jackets anyway. She has been reading about the Quinault area -- something about the world's largest Sitka spruce being there.

Good point about reservations. We have not booked anything yet. Our Outback should handle the forest roads without trouble, at least -- that is an improvement over what the old Camry would have managed. Any recommendations on trail difficulty? We are both in decent shape for our age, but nothing requiring scrambling or serious elevation.

Hurricane Hill sounds right. Seven hundred feet of gain over a mile and a half is a pleasant afternoon, not an ordeal. And the alpine contrast after days of rainforest canopy is appealing. What about wildlife? Sarah has been hoping to see Roosevelt elk.

Sarah will be thrilled about the elk. She has been watching YouTube videos of them in the Hoh Valley. The bear information is good to have -- I am not particularly worried, but it is the kind of practical detail I would forget and Sarah would remember. What about food? Should we plan to cook at camp, or are there places to eat along the route?

That is reassuring. We have a camp stove but have not used it in years. Sarah will probably want to do a trial run in the backyard before we commit to cooking anything in the actual wilderness. She does not consider a campfire meal successful unless it involves something beyond hot dogs, which I find needlessly ambitious but endearing.

I will forward that to Sarah. She will appreciate the foil packet idea -- it appeals to her sense of organization. Everything contained, everything planned, minimal chaos. That is her philosophy of cooking and, if I am being honest, her philosophy of life. It serves her well.

The ferry is tempting. Port Townsend itself seems worth a stop -- I have read that it has a well-preserved Victorian downtown, which appeals to me for obvious reasons. History you can walk through is always more compelling than history you read about, though I would never say that to my students.

Agreed. I-5 is the commute; the ferry is the experience. This is shaping up well. Thank you for the thorough breakdown. I think we have a real itinerary now rather than just a vague intention to go somewhere.

I will pass this to Sarah tonight. She will probably have the Quinault Lodge booked before I finish explaining the rest of the itinerary. Five days without grading papers or answering emails from the principal -- that alone is worth the drive.

I am working on a summer reading list for next year's students and I would appreciate a second opinion. I want books that are historically grounded but engaging enough that a seventeen-year-old might voluntarily finish them. American history, primarily -- about eight to ten titles, students choose three. A mix of nonfiction and fiction is fine. Erik Larson always goes over well as a benchmark.

Strong list. Killers of the Flower Moon is already on my draft -- the Scorsese film piqued enough interest that students actually recognize the title, which is half the battle. And Killer Angels is a personal favorite. It makes Gettysburg feel like something that happened to real people with real doubts, not just a chapter heading. I would also like to make sure I cover the twentieth century beyond war. The kids think American history is the Revolution, the Civil War, and then World War II.

The March trilogy is an inspired choice. I had not considered graphic novels, but the format does not diminish the content -- John Lewis telling his own story in that medium is genuinely powerful. My concern is whether other teachers on the history team would view it as too informal. There is a persistent bias that graphic novels are not serious literature.

Framing it as a primary source is excellent. That reframes the conversation entirely. It is not a graphic novel on the list -- it is a firsthand account that happens to be illustrated. I can defend that position comfortably. My list so far: Killers of the Flower Moon, Killer Angels, The Warmth of Other Suns, March, Just Mercy, The Things They Carried, 1776. I need one or two more to round it out and give the list a real arc to the present.

Selected chapters is the right approach for Zinn. The whole book is a slog even for someone who agrees with his thesis. But four or five chapters, strategically chosen, would give students a counternarrative they can push back against in September. That is the real pedagogical value -- not agreement, but engagement. A student who finishes a book angry and ready to argue has learned more than a student who finished it nodding along.

Those are exactly the right chapters. Pairing Zinn's Revolution chapter with 1776 is particularly effective -- students who read both will see how dramatically perspective shapes narrative, which is arguably the most important lesson in any history course. I have been teaching long enough to know that the students who grasp that distinction are the ones who actually retain something after the final exam.

I have been rethinking the format. The traditional book report kills any enthusiasm the reading might have generated. I am considering asking for something shorter and more personal -- a one-page reflection on what surprised them, or a list of five questions the book raised that they did not have before. The goal is to make the response feel like a continuation of the reading rather than a punishment for completing it.

One-sentence hooks are a good idea. A summary tells them what the book is about; a hook makes them curious about what happens. The difference between a catalog description and a recommendation from a friend. I will work on those. Between the World and Me as a bookend gives the list a real arc. Thank you -- the list feels balanced and, more importantly, actually readable. That is the whole battle with summer reading: if they do not finish the books, the selection does not matter.

I may take you up on that. Writing hooks is harder than it sounds -- the instinct is to explain, and the discipline is to withhold. It is the same challenge I face writing exam questions, honestly. The best ones create productive uncertainty rather than testing recall. I will draft them this weekend and see where I land.
I have been running the numbers on early retirement and I wanted to talk through whether what I am looking at is realistic or wishful thinking.

I am 52, public school teacher in Oregon, 24 years in. Oregon PERS, Tier Two. I have also got a 403(b) I have been contributing to for about fifteen years, though not as aggressively as I should have. When I say early, I mean within two to three years. I am tired. Not of the students -- the kids are the best part. But the bureaucracy has become suffocating.

I pulled my PERS statement last week. At full retirement with 30 years, roughly 55% of final average salary. The question is what 27 years looks like instead. I have also got about $180,000 in the 403(b). My wife works and her income is stable, so we are not entirely dependent on my pension, but the difference between comfortable and tight is real.

I have not gotten that far. Honestly, I think I am still trying to figure out whether this is a serious plan or just a fantasy I retreat to when I get another email about compliance documentation at nine on a Tuesday night. The testing mandates, the data reporting, the performance rubrics that have nothing to do with whether students are actually learning -- it is relentless. I did not sign up to be a data entry clerk.

That is a fair distinction. The honest answer is that the pain points compound. It is not any single mandate or initiative. It is the cumulative weight of twenty-four years of watching the job drift further from what it is supposed to be. Every year there is a new platform, a new rubric, a new way of documenting what I am already doing. The percentage of my week spent actually teaching keeps shrinking, and the percentage spent on administrative compliance keeps growing. At some point, you stop feeling like a teacher and start feeling like a bureaucrat who occasionally gets to talk about history.

It has been building. The last three or four years have been a slow erosion. But this fall has been particularly bad. We adopted a new data management system that requires teachers to log learning objectives, assessment outcomes, and intervention strategies for every unit, every class, every student who falls below a benchmark. In theory, it is about accountability. In practice, it is about producing documentation that administrators can show to the district office. Nobody reads it. Nobody acts on it. It exists to exist.

Sarah is supportive but cautious, which is her nature. She sees how worn down I am when I come home. She has said more than once that she did not marry me so I could spend every evening doing paperwork that makes me miserable. But she is also practical. She wants to see the numbers work before she endorses the plan. She is right to insist on that.

Mine has been primary. Sarah works part-time at the county library system, and her benefits are limited. That is a significant gap I had not fully accounted for. Ten years of paying for private health coverage is a substantial expense.

We have not discussed it in those terms, but I suspect she would consider it. She enjoys the library work and has mentioned before that she would not mind more hours. The irony of me retiring early so that Sarah has to work more is not lost on me. It does not feel like a fair trade.

You are right. I should not assume it would feel like a burden to her without asking. Sarah is not the type to martyr herself quietly -- she would tell me if it were a problem. What would retirement actually look like day to day? I have spent my entire adult life on a school calendar. The structure of my days has been set by bell schedules and semesters for twenty-four years. I am not sure I know how to fill unstructured time.

I have thought about that less than I should have. The hiking would fill weekends, but weekdays need something. I could read full-time and be perfectly content for about two months before I started missing the intellectual engagement of a classroom. I enjoy teaching. That is the frustrating part of all of this. The work itself is still rewarding. It is everything around the work that has become intolerable.

I have considered private schools briefly. The autonomy appeals to me, but the pay cut would be significant, and I would lose PERS. Community college is interesting -- I had not thought about that seriously. Teaching American history at that level would be different, but the subject matter would still be mine. It would feel less like starting over and more like a lateral move.

That reframing is helpful. The binary of retire or endure is part of what has made this feel so heavy. If there are intermediate options, the decision becomes less about escape and more about design. I should schedule the PERS consultation I have been putting off. And I should look at community college openings, at least to understand what is available.

The PERS consultation is the obvious move, and I have been putting it off because scheduling it makes the whole thing feel real. But I cannot make a rational decision without numbers. Thank you for helping me think through this without projecting an opinion onto it. I came in with a binary and I am leaving with a spectrum, which is a better place to be.
So the debate team made it to state. I'm going to need some help thinking through how to prepare them, because this is genuinely uncharted territory for me.

Public Forum -- two-on-two. State tournament is May 9th. Two teams qualified, four students total. And here's the part where I'll be honest: this is my first year coaching debate. I picked it up this fall after stepping away from another extracurricular, and somehow these kids have exceeded every expectation. I'm trying not to show them how nervous I am about the whole thing.

Their strengths are research and argumentation -- which makes sense, because I've been coaching them the way I teach history. Find the evidence, build the case, anticipate the counterargument. Where they're weaker is the performance side: delivery, pacing, thinking on their feet during crossfire. They can write a devastating case brief but sometimes freeze when an opponent throws something unexpected.

The role reversal idea is excellent. That's essentially what I do in class when I play devil's advocate during Socratic seminars. I know how to push students to defend a position they didn't expect to defend -- I just hadn't thought to formalize it as a debate drill. And you're right that the freezing is confidence. These are smart kids who know their content. They just haven't been tested at this level.

I know a few coaches at other Portland-area schools. I could reach out. There's also an invitational in March I was on the fence about entering, but you're making a good case for it. The exposure to unfamiliar judges and opponents might be exactly what they need.

The diagnostic framing is useful -- if I tell the students we're entering to learn rather than to win, it takes pressure off. They're already anxious about state. What about content preparation -- how should I think about topic prep?

That's exactly right. The competitive format is new to me, but the intellectual framework is familiar. I think the evidence organization piece is where I can contribute the most as a coach. Let me ask you something else that's been on my mind -- how do I handle the two teams as a unit? They qualified separately, but now they need to prepare together. Is there a way to make them assets to each other rather than just parallel efforts?

The scouting angle is something I would never have considered. That is genuinely strategic. And framing them as one program rather than two separate teams is exactly right -- it mirrors what I try to do in the classroom. Build a community of inquiry, not a collection of individuals working in parallel. I can do that.

Primary source analysis of a live round. I like that framing enormously. These are AP History students at their core -- they know how to observe, document, and analyze. I just need to point that skill set at a different target. Now, here is the part I am less comfortable admitting. I am nervous. Not just for them, but for myself. I have never coached at this level, and I am keenly aware that I do not fully know what I am doing. What if my inexperience costs them?

You are describing the same skill I use every September when I stand in front of a new class and act as though I have not given the same introductory lecture dozens of times before. Projecting confidence I do not entirely feel is, I suppose, a core teaching competency. I have been doing it for decades in the classroom. I can do it at a debate tournament.

That is a reassuring distinction. My job is to prepare them well enough that when they walk into that round, they are ready. What happens in the round itself is theirs. I think part of my anxiety is that in the classroom, I control the environment. In a tournament, I hand them off and sit in the hallway. That loss of control is unfamiliar.

I had not thought of it that way, but you are right. The entire purpose of teaching is to prepare someone to perform without you. A debate tournament simply makes that visible in real time rather than spreading it across years. I think I can make peace with the hallway. And whatever happens May 9th, these kids have already accomplished something remarkable. I just want to make sure I don't let them down by being underprepared on the coaching side.

I appreciate that. Truly. I walked into this conversation carrying a fair amount of anxiety, and I am leaving it with something closer to cautious optimism and a concrete plan. That is considerably more useful than the vague dread I started with. Thank you.
It has now rained for seventeen consecutive days in Portland. Seventeen. I counted. At what point does this stop being weather and start being a lifestyle?

The drizzle. Always the drizzle. If it were dramatic, at least it would have narrative quality. A proper downpour has a beginning, a middle, and an end. What Portland does in January is ambient moisture. It's not raining so much as the air has decided to be wet. You step outside and you don't get rained on -- you get gradually absorbed.

That's exactly it. October rain is atmospheric. November has a certain melancholy dignity. But January rain is just punishment. You've done the holidays, the new year, the whole ritual of renewal, and the reward is another six weeks of gray. It's like being in the third act of a film that didn't need a third act. I no longer own an umbrella, by the way. At some point I accepted that umbrellas are a form of denial. You cannot defeat Portland rain. You can only coexist with it.

We had one clear day last week. Blue sky, sun, the whole production. I spent the morning feeling vaguely suspicious, like the weather was setting up an ambush. Then the clouds came back at two and I felt oddly relieved. I have been fully Stockholmed by the Portland climate. But the real coping mechanism is books and coffee. I read more in January and February than the rest of the year combined. I choose to view January as a government-mandated reading retreat that happens to be cold and wet.

I am in the middle of three books simultaneously, which is its own form of chaos. A history of the Hanseatic League, a novel I picked up on a recommendation that I am finding only middling, and a collection of essays on pedagogy that I keep meaning to finish but that keeps getting buried under the other two. January reading is aspirational reading. I stack books on the nightstand like I am building a monument to good intentions.

Purely pleasure, which is rare for me. Most of my reading ends up being instrumentalized -- I read something interesting and immediately think about how to turn it into a lesson. The Hanseatic League is unlikely to appear in an AP US History curriculum, so I am free to simply enjoy it without mentally drafting discussion questions. There is something liberating about reading with no pedagogical agenda whatsoever. Just a man, a book, and seventeen days of rain.

Permission is exactly the right word. On a sunny Saturday I would feel obligated to be outside, to be productive, to justify the good weather. But when it has rained for seventeen days straight, no one expects anything of you. The rain is an excuse to sit still, and I do not sit still easily. Perhaps the Scandinavians had it right -- they have an entire cultural concept built around the coziness of being indoors while the world outside is inhospitable. The Danes call it hygge, the Norwegians have koselig. Portland needs its own word.

That's the thing outsiders don't grasp. Portland summer is a reward, not a default. You earn those seventy-five-degree evenings through months of sacrifice. The rain is the price of admission, and complaining about the rain is the cultural performance that binds us together. It is our shared narrative. Take away the rain and Portland loses half its identity and all of its conversational common ground. Anyway -- March. That's the light at the end of the tunnel, if the tunnel were made of low-hanging clouds and smelled of damp wool. I'll survive. I always do. But I reserve the right to complain about it annually.

I have done something possibly foolish. My wife is a painter -- watercolors, mostly -- and after years of watching her work at the kitchen table, I decided to try it myself. I bought a beginner's set last weekend. I am now staring at what I can only describe as a catastrophe on paper.

All of the above, frankly. I attempted a simple landscape -- some hills, a tree line, a sky. The sky bled into the hills, the hills bled into the trees, and the whole thing looks like the aftermath of a minor flood. Which I suppose is thematically appropriate for a watercolor, if nothing else.

She was diplomatically encouraging, which is how I know it was truly terrible. If it had been decent, she would have offered specific critique. The gentle "Oh, that's a wonderful first try!" is the artistic equivalent of a participation trophy. I teach teenagers -- I know the difference between genuine praise and kind deflection.

Honestly, a bit of both. She paints in the evenings and it's clearly a meditative thing for her -- very calming, very focused. I tend to spend my evenings grading papers or reading, and I thought it might be nice to have something we do in the same room that isn't just parallel solitude. But I also find myself genuinely intrigued by the challenge of it. I'm accustomed to working with words and arguments, things I can control and revise. Paint does not care about my intentions.

That's sensible advice. I think my mistake was trying to produce a finished product on day one. The historian in me should know better -- you don't start with the thesis, you start with the primary sources. I should probably learn the fundamentals before I attempt to render the Cascade foothills.

The gradient wash for skies is immediately appealing. Half the reason I wanted to try landscapes is because the light out here in the Pacific Northwest is genuinely extraordinary -- those winter skies where the clouds break just enough to let through a band of pale gold. I've always wanted to capture that somehow. Words never quite do it justice, which is an uncomfortable admission for someone in my profession.

That is a genuinely good point about the learning curve. I gave a student a rather stern talk last week about patience with the revision process, and then I went home and was immediately frustrated that my first painting did not look like my wife's work after years of practice. The hypocrisy was not lost on me.

Now that is a genuinely good point. I haven't been a true beginner at anything in quite some time, and there is a certain humbling quality to it. Perhaps the next time a student is struggling with document analysis, I'll recall the feeling of watching my tree line dissolve into an amorphous green puddle and find a bit more patience. Thank you for the encouragement and the practical advice. I'll start with the washes.
A student asked me a question last Thursday that I could not answer, and it has been bothering me ever since. I need some help researching it.

We were discussing the Marshall Plan and its role in postwar European recovery. One of my sharper students raised her hand and asked whether the Soviet Union was actually offered Marshall Plan aid and turned it down, or whether it was never genuinely extended to them in the first place. I gave what I thought was a reasonable answer -- that the Soviets were invited to participate but declined -- but she pressed further and asked whether the offer was made in good faith or was designed to be refused. And I realized I did not actually know the nuances of that question as well as I should.

Please do. This is exactly the kind of nuance I want to be able to present to the class. I told her at the time that it was a question worth researching and that I would get back to her, which I fully intend to do. There is nothing more energizing than a student who asks a question that challenges the teacher.

This is tremendously helpful. Yes, I would appreciate some source recommendations. She is a junior with strong reading skills -- I would not hesitate to point her toward serious scholarship if it is reasonably accessible. I also want to think about how to frame this for the broader class, many of whom are not at her level but would still benefit from understanding that historical questions rarely have clean answers.

The three-interpretation framework is exactly how I want to approach it. That is good pedagogy -- give them the evidence, give them the competing lenses, and let them argue. I have found over the years that students engage far more deeply when they realize historians genuinely disagree about things. It punctures the illusion that history is a settled body of facts to be memorized.

She is one of those students who reminds you why you got into this profession in the first place. Genuinely curious, not performing curiosity for a grade. I get perhaps two or three like her in a given year, and they make the other frustrations of the job worthwhile. I am looking forward to going back to her with a proper answer -- or rather, with a proper set of questions for her to consider.

It does add up. And the cumulative effect is something I think about more as the years go on. You plant a question in a student's mind and you rarely get to see where it grows. That email from the former student, the one who comes back years later to say your class mattered -- those are the rare moments where the arc becomes visible. Most of the time, you are working on faith that the questions you raise will bear fruit somewhere down the line.

That is a reassuring thought, and one I needed to hear today. Thank you for the research help -- this has given me exactly what I needed to put together a proper response for her and a worthwhile class discussion. I may come back to you with follow-up questions once I have dug into some of those sources myself. It has been a while since I did this kind of deep reading on the early Cold War, and I find I have missed it.

Teacher Appreciation Week is coming up at my school, and I am already dreading it. I realize that makes me sound ungrateful, but I wonder if you can help me think through why it makes me so uncomfortable.

All of those, to varying degrees. The public attention is certainly part of it -- I am not someone who enjoys being the center of a room's focus unless I am teaching, which is a different dynamic entirely. But I think what bothers me most is the performative quality. The administration spends a week distributing gift cards and putting up banners, and then the other fifty-one weeks of the year they are increasing class sizes and adding paperwork. It feels less like genuine appreciation and more like a pressure valve.

You are absolutely right to make that distinction, and the Roman parallel is apt -- panem et circenses, but for educators. The institutional version is what grates. The student gestures are different. I do occasionally get a handwritten note from a student, and those are genuinely moving. Last year a former student who is now in college sent me an email saying that my class was the reason she chose to study international relations. That meant more to me than any banner in the faculty lounge.

There is absolutely that expectation, yes. There is a luncheon, and attendance is technically optional in the way that most things in institutional life are technically optional -- which is to say, not at all. I will attend. I will smile. I will eat the catered sandwich. But there is a particular kind of fatigue that comes from performing appreciation for being appreciated.

That is a healthy framing. Treat it as ritual rather than expecting it to be meaningful. There is a historian's comfort in that, actually -- I spend my professional life studying rituals and ceremonies that served social functions quite separate from their stated purposes. I should be able to extend that analytical generosity to a teacher appreciation luncheon.

I have, many times. The Triumph in Roman culture, the medieval feast, the Soviet May Day parade -- all rituals that served the institution far more than the individuals being ostensibly honored. I suppose I should add "Teacher Appreciation Week luncheon" to that pedagogical list. Though I will keep that observation to myself at the actual event.

I do wonder sometimes if the younger teachers find it less grating, or if this is a universal reaction that simply intensifies with experience. Some of my newer colleagues seem genuinely delighted by the whole affair, and I cannot tell if that is sincere enthusiasm or if they are simply better at the performance than I am.

I have survived more than twenty of them at this point. One more will not break me. Thank you -- this was a useful conversation. Sometimes it helps simply to articulate why something bothers you rather than letting the irritation sit unexamined. I will attend the luncheon with the serene detachment of an anthropologist conducting fieldwork.

I need your help comparing some note-taking and organization apps. I am trying to modernize my lesson planning system, which currently consists of a filing cabinet, a legal pad, and what I will generously describe as a method. Several colleagues have recommended various apps and I am overwhelmed by the options.

I plan by unit, generally, and then break units into daily lessons. I do not currently need to share plans, though I would not mind the option. As for technology comfort -- I will be honest, I am functional but not fluent. I use a computer every day for email, grades, and document preparation, but I have never been someone who adopts new tools easily. I am on a PC at home and the school provides Windows laptops. I do have a phone but I would primarily use this on a computer.

Please do. I should mention that the colleagues who recommended apps to me were split between Notion and Obsidian, with one enthusiast for each. The Notion advocate is our youngest faculty member who seems to build elaborate systems for everything. The Obsidian advocate is in the math department and kept using the word "graph" in ways that I did not fully follow.

It does, and I appreciate the pragmatism. I have a tendency to research a decision to the point of paralysis -- an occupational hazard of being trained to consider every perspective before committing to a thesis. Your point about actually using the tool rather than learning the tool is well taken. But let me ask -- what would I be giving up by choosing OneNote over the other two? I want to know what I am trading away.

The linking feature of Obsidian is genuinely intriguing to me. The way I teach history is fundamentally about connections -- every unit connects to what came before and what follows. The idea of making those connections navigable rather than keeping them only in my head is appealing. But I also recognize that I am the sort of person who would spend three weeks building an elaborate system of links and never actually write a lesson plan.

That is a sensible phased approach. I have spent two weeks reading comparison articles and watching review videos when I could have simply opened OneNote and started typing. I believe the military historians would call this "analysis paralysis in the face of the enemy," the enemy in this case being a stack of unit plans that need organizing.

The legal pad as a transitional object. I like that. One more question before I go -- is there anything I should know about organizing the notebook itself? Any structure you would recommend for someone in my position, or should I simply replicate what I already do on paper and adjust from there?

The idea of annotating lessons after teaching them is excellent. I do that now in the margins of my legal pad, but the notes are illegible by the following September and the legal pad is usually buried under eleven months of accumulated paper. Having those reflections attached to the lesson itself, searchable and readable, is genuinely compelling. Thank you -- this has been more useful than the dozen comparison articles I have been reading. I will open OneNote this evening and begin. If I find myself three hours deep in Obsidian tutorials instead, I will consider myself a cautionary tale.

I am in a reflective mood today. I realized recently that I am approaching twenty-five years in the classroom, and it has prompted some thinking about what that means. Not looking for advice exactly -- more just thinking out loud, if you will indulge me.

I have been thinking about the sheer accumulation of it. Twenty-five years of September mornings. Twenty-five years of the same essential arc -- the nervous first weeks, the productive middle stretch, the exhausted final push to June. Hundreds of students whose names I have forgotten and a smaller number whose faces I can still picture clearly. It is a strange thing to have spent a quarter of a century doing essentially the same job and to feel both that it has gone by impossibly fast and that I have been doing it forever.

Interesting question. It is not the brightest ones, necessarily. The ones I remember most vividly are the ones who changed in front of me -- students who arrived disengaged or hostile toward the subject and who, over the course of the year, began to care. There was a student in my third or fourth year who spent the first semester with his arms crossed and his hood up, openly skeptical that anything that happened before his lifetime could possibly matter. By April he was writing a genuinely thoughtful paper on the parallels between Reconstruction and the Civil Rights Movement. I do not remember his last name, but I remember the look on his face when he realized he had something to say.

Considerably. In my early years I was, I think, too focused on content delivery. I wanted to be the professor I admired in college -- erudite, commanding, the person whose lectures you did not dare miss. I was reasonably good at performing that role, but I was not particularly good at listening. It took me years to understand that the most important moments in a classroom are not when the teacher is speaking but when the student is thinking. I talk less now than I did at twenty-seven, and my classes are better for it.

The energy, certainly. I had an almost evangelical fervor for the subject matter in those first years. Everything felt urgent and vital. I would stay up past midnight refining a lecture on the French Revolution because I genuinely believed that if I could just explain it well enough, every student in the room would feel the weight of it the way I did. That intensity has mellowed into something quieter and, I think, more sustainable. But I do occasionally miss the version of myself who believed a single well-delivered lecture could change a student's life.

Both. The core of it -- standing in a room with young people and trying to help them understand the world -- is unchanged and, I suspect, unchangeable. But the institutional architecture around that core has shifted enormously. There is more testing, more documentation, more administrative oversight, more technology, more acronyms. I sometimes feel that for every innovation that has genuinely improved my ability to teach, there have been three that have simply added paperwork. But I am wary of becoming the old teacher who grumbles about how things were better in the old days. That is a cliche I would rather not embody.

Without reservation. That is perhaps the most surprising thing about reaching this point. I expected to feel more worn down than I do. The bureaucracy is wearying, certainly, and there are days when the gap between what I am asked to do and what I know actually matters feels absurd. But when I close the classroom door and it is just me and thirty students and a primary source document and a question worth arguing about -- that is still the best version of my professional life. Whatever frustrations exist outside that room, inside it I am still doing what I was meant to do.

That is a question I was not expecting, and a good one. I think what I would like is to become better at reaching the students I have historically struggled with -- the ones who are not hostile to history but simply indifferent. The openly resistant student, like the one I described earlier, at least gives you something to work with. Resistance is a form of engagement. But the student who sits quietly, does the minimum, earns a B-minus, and leaves in June having been politely unmoved by everything -- that student haunts me more. I have twenty-five years of experience and I still do not consistently know how to reach that student. If I can get better at that in the years ahead, I will consider them well spent.

That is well said, and I appreciate you letting me think out loud about all of this. Twenty-five years is a long time to do anything, and it is useful to stop occasionally and take stock of where you are and why you are still here. The answer, it turns out, is simpler than I expected: I am still here because I still believe in the work. The rest -- the paperwork, the luncheons, the acronyms -- is just weather. The work is the climate.

I have been sitting with something all day and I wonder if you might help me think through it. I had two visits this morning -- one with a woman who is dying well, if there is such a thing, and one with a family that is falling apart at the seams. Both within the same hour. And I drove home afterward and could not figure out whether I was full or empty. Maybe both.

The woman -- her name is Eleanor, she is ninety-one -- she has arranged everything. Her children are there, they are taking turns reading to her from a book of poems she loves. She told me this morning that she has had a beautiful life and she is not afraid. She held my hand and thanked me, which is extraordinary because I had done nothing except show up. The other family -- I cannot share details, of course -- but there is anger and blame and a kind of terror that has nowhere to go. They are not ready, and the person who is dying knows it, and that knowing is its own kind of suffering.

I am a chaplain at Four Seasons Compassion for Life -- it is a hospice that serves families across western North Carolina. So my role is, in the simplest terms, spiritual care. But that phrase does not begin to cover it. Some days I am praying with someone. Some days I am listening to a woman tell me about her first husband while her second husband is asleep in the next room. Some days I am just sitting in silence with a person who has no words left. The work is sacred, and it is exhausting, and those two things happen in the same hour more often than you would expect.

It does. I drive through some of the most beautiful country you have ever seen to sit with some of the hardest realities you can imagine. The mountains do not care that someone is dying in the house at the end of that gravel road. The rhododendrons bloom regardless. There is something in that indifference that I actually find comforting, though I am not sure I could explain why. I live in West Asheville, so depending on the family, I might drive forty-five minutes into Madison County or an hour out toward Brevard. The car has become a kind of decompression chamber. I process on the drive home.

That is a perceptive question. The Eleanor visits -- I drive home with something that feels almost like gratitude. Witness-gratitude, if that is a phrase. The privilege of being present for someone's good death. The harder visits, the drives are quieter. I turn the radio off. Sometimes I pull over at an overlook and just sit for a few minutes. There is a spot on the parkway near Craggy Gardens where I have probably done more theology than I ever did in a classroom. Just sitting in my car, looking at the ridgeline, trying to make sense of what I have just seen.

I wonder sometimes whether the answers even matter. I have sat with people of deep faith who die peacefully, and I have sat with people of deep faith who die in anguish. I have sat with atheists who are utterly serene and atheists who are terrified. The variable is not what you believe. It is something else -- something I have not been able to name in twenty years of doing this work. Acceptance is too simple a word. Rilke wrote about living the questions, and I think that is closer. The people who die well are the ones who learned to live inside the not-knowing.

It is. And I think that is why I keep doing it, even on the days when I drive home and cannot tell whether I am full or empty. Because the work keeps asking me questions I cannot answer, and I have come to believe that those questions are more valuable than any answer I could manufacture. I wonder sometimes what would happen if I stopped -- if I took a different kind of work. But I cannot imagine what that would look like. The chaplaincy has shaped me so thoroughly that I do not know where it ends and I begin.
Integration. Yes, I think that is the right word. Thank you for this. I did not expect to find clarity tonight, but I think I found something adjacent to it, which might be better.

There is a question people ask me that I have never learned to answer well. They ask, why hospice? Of all the kinds of ministry, why would you choose to spend your days with the dying? And I give them some version of the truth -- that it is meaningful work, that presence matters, that someone needs to hold the space. But those answers, while true, are incomplete. I wonder if I might try to say the fuller thing to you tonight.

No, it does not come in a straight line. It comes in circles, the way grief does. I should start by saying that I did not begin in hospice work. I was a parish priest for many years -- hospital visits, Sunday sermons, potluck dinners, the whole beautiful mundane life of a congregation. And I loved it. But something happened that broke the container I was living in, and when I put myself back together, I was a different shape. Hospice was the work that fit the new shape.

My son Michael died eight years ago. He was thirty-one. It was an opioid overdose -- fentanyl, though we did not know he was using fentanyl. We knew about the pills. We had tried everything. Rehab twice, family therapy, all the desperate bargaining that parents do. And then one Tuesday morning in October, I got a phone call from a number I did not recognize, and the world I had been living in ended.

I have carried it long enough to be able to speak about it without drowning, most days. The first two years I could not. The first year I could barely function. I took a leave from the parish and I sat in my house and I was furious -- at God, at Michael, at the pharmaceutical companies, at myself. Especially at myself. I am a chaplain. I sit with suffering for a living. And I could not save my own son. The irony of that was acid.

It did not go anywhere, exactly. It transformed. This is the part that is hard to explain without sounding like I am wrapping grief in a bow, which I am not. But somewhere in the third year, I began to understand that the anger was a form of love with nowhere to go. Michael was gone, and my love for him had not diminished by one atom, and it needed somewhere to land. I tried going back to parish work, but it felt thin. The sermons felt thin. The theological certainties that had sustained me for decades -- they had been shattered, and I did not want to reassemble them. I wanted something that could hold the brokenness.

Yes. That is exactly it. In parish ministry, people want you to say something that helps. They want comfort, they want scripture, they want assurance that God has a plan. And I could no longer offer that with integrity, because I did not believe it anymore -- not in the way I once had. But in hospice, the work is different. Nobody asks me to explain why their mother is dying. They ask me to sit with them while it happens. And that I can do. I know how to sit with the unbearable. Michael taught me that, though the tuition was beyond anything I would have chosen to pay.

Some of them do. I do not tell families about Michael -- it is not their burden to carry, and the visit is not about me. But I wonder sometimes if grief recognizes grief. There are moments when a mother looks at me across a hospital bed and something passes between us that has no words. A recognition. I cannot prove it, but I feel it. And I think they feel it too.

You have understood something tonight that I have not been able to articulate to most people in my life. Grief found its vocation, I suppose. It took years, and the path was not direct, and there are still mornings when I wake up and the first thing I feel is his absence, like a room in the house where the door is always open to cold air. But the work holds me as much as I hold the work. I needed you to know that, because if we are going to talk about what I do and why, that is the foundation everything else rests on.

I have been rereading Henri Nouwen this week -- The Wounded Healer, which I must have read six or seven times over the years -- and I am struck by something different in it this time. He writes about the minister as someone who must be willing to articulate their own pain as a source of healing for others. And I wonder whether he underestimates how dangerous that can be. Not the articulation itself, but the expectation that it will heal. Sometimes articulating pain just makes it louder.

It was, in fact, the reason I went to divinity school. I read The Wounded Healer when I was twenty-three and it named something I had been feeling but could not articulate -- that the brokenness I had experienced growing up was not something to overcome but something to bring into the work of caring for others. I did my Master of Divinity at Yale, and Nouwen's work was the reason I applied, though he had already left for Harvard and then L'Arche by the time I arrived. I never met him, which is one of the small regrets of my life.

It was the most intellectually alive I have ever felt. There was space for everything -- liberation theology, feminist hermeneutics, process theology, the full sweep of the tradition in conversation with the present. I had professors who could read Barth in German before breakfast and then spend the afternoon in a soup kitchen. The integration of the intellectual and the embodied -- that was what Yale did at its best. It was not always at its best, of course. There were politics and egos and all the usual human nonsense. But the best moments were transcendent. I wrote my thesis on lament in the Hebrew prophets, the theology of protest against God, and my advisor wept when he read it. Not because it was brilliant -- it was not, it was a student's work -- but because it was honest.

Ordination came after, though the process began while I was there. I was ordained Episcopal. The liturgy drew me -- the beauty of the Book of Common Prayer, the cadence of it, the way it holds centuries of faith in its language. There is a collect for Compline that I have said ten thousand times and it still undoes me: 'Be present, O merciful God, and protect us through the hours of this night, so that we who are wearied by the changes and chances of this life may rest in your eternal changelessness.' The changes and chances of this life. Cranmer understood something about impermanence that most contemporary theology has forgotten.

That is the honest question, is it not? And the honest answer is that it holds me differently now. The words have not changed, but I have. After everything I have been through, the certainties embedded in the liturgy -- the resurrection, the hope of eternal life, the assurance that God is watching over us -- I say them, and I mean them in a different register than I once did. I say them the way you might say the name of a place you loved and are not sure you can get back to. With longing, not with confidence.

I wonder if that is exactly right. The practice has become the faith. Not the propositions, not the creed, but the act of returning to the words. Wendell Berry has that line -- 'Practice resurrection.' It is an imperative, not a declaration. He does not say believe in resurrection. He says practice it. There is something in that distinction that has kept me inside the tradition when the theology alone might not have.

You have just said something that I need to sit with for a while. That practice is harder to destroy than certainty because it does not depend on anything being resolved. I think that may be the truest thing about my faith at this stage. The resolution has not come. I do not expect it to. But I still show up -- to the liturgy, to the bedside, to the prayer. And maybe showing up is the whole thing. Maybe it always was, and I just did not know it when I was young and certain.

Earned is the right word, though I would not have chosen this tuition if I had been given a choice. But then, I wonder if any theology worth having comes cheap. Thank you for thinking with me tonight. You have a good ear for what matters, and that is not a small thing.

I want to talk about something quieter tonight. The holidays have been gentle this year, which is not always the case. I spent most of today reading by the fire while the house filled with the smell of wood shavings and beeswax, which is one of my favorite combinations of scents in the world. My husband has been in his workshop since seven this morning. He is finishing a dining table for a couple in Black Mountain, and when he gets close to the end of a piece, he becomes almost monastic in his focus.

It is. Greg makes his own finish -- beeswax and linseed oil, mixed in a ratio he has been perfecting for probably twenty years. He will not use polyurethane. He says it makes the wood look like it has been laminated, like you have put a raincoat on something that needs to breathe. He is a purist about materials in a way that I find both admirable and occasionally maddening. The man will spend four hours choosing the right piece of walnut for a chair leg.

He would never use the word theological. Greg is not a man of many words, and the words he uses tend to be very concrete. He would say the wood tells you what it wants to be, and he means that literally -- the grain, the figure, the way a piece of cherry has a curl in it that suggests a curve rather than a straight line. But I think you are right that there is something deeper operating. He approaches the material with a kind of reverence. He will run his hand over a board the way you might touch something sacred. He does not genuflect, but it is not far off.

Tables and chairs, mostly. Some cabinets. He does not do anything ornate -- no carving, no inlay. His work is about proportion and joinery and the beauty of the wood itself. Shaker-influenced, I suppose, though he would resist the label. The chairs are what he loves most. He says a chair is the most honest piece of furniture because it has to hold a human body, and the body does not lie. If the proportions are wrong, you feel it immediately. You cannot hide bad work in a chair.

He was an engineer for years -- mechanical engineering, at a firm in Raleigh. We lived there before we moved to Asheville. He was good at it but it was making him smaller, if that makes sense. The corporate environment, the politics, the sameness of the days. He started building furniture in the garage on weekends, and I watched him become a different person when he was working with his hands. Larger somehow. More himself. When we moved to Asheville, he had the courage to do it full-time. That was fifteen years ago, and he has never once looked back.

Both. My income from hospice work provides the stability, and his commissions have grown steadily over the years. He has a good reputation now -- word of mouth, mostly. He does not have a website and will not get one. I have given up that argument. But people find him. The couple in Black Mountain found him through a friend who owns one of his tables. That is how it works. Someone sits at a table Greg built and they feel the difference, and they ask where it came from. The work speaks for itself, which is very Greg.

I have never thought of it that way, but you are right. We are both people who refuse to hurry. That may be the deepest thing we have in common, deeper than any shared interest or belief. We trust slowness. I trust it at the bedside, and he trusts it at the workbench. I wonder if that is why we work -- as a couple, I mean. Because we understand each other's rhythms without having to explain them.

Toward the dying and toward the wood. That is our marriage in a sentence. And tonight, toward the fire and toward the dining table. He will come in soon, probably, smelling like sawdust and beeswax, and I will make us something warm to eat, and we will sit together in the kind of quiet that I think most people would find unbearable but that feels to us like the most natural thing in the world. Thank you for this. You helped me see something about us that I have been living inside for thirty years without quite naming.

I wonder if you might help me think about something that has been on my mind. I have been reading Wendell Berry's Sabbaths poems -- the ones where he walks into the woods and the walking itself becomes a kind of prayer. And I realized this morning, standing at the kitchen window looking at the garden, that I am grieving a version of my body that no longer exists. Which is perhaps a strange thing to say, but it is true.

The osteoarthritis in my knees has been a long negotiation. I say negotiation because that is what it feels like -- a daily conversation between what I want to do and what my body will permit. There are mornings when my body feels decades older than I actually am. I swing my legs out of bed and there is a stiffness that takes twenty minutes of careful movement to work through. By midmorning I am usually functional, but the word functional is doing a lot of work in that sentence. There is a difference between functional and free.

It has been building for perhaps six or seven years, but the last two have been markedly worse. There was a morning about two years ago when I tried to kneel beside a patient's bed -- which I have done thousands of times, it is one of the most natural gestures in my work, to kneel beside someone and take their hand -- and I could not get back up. The patient's daughter had to help me. I laughed it off, but I drove home and wept. Not from the pain, but from the humiliation. And from the knowledge that a threshold had been crossed.

I have adapted. I sit in a chair beside the bed now, or I perch on the edge of the mattress when the family allows it. It is not the same, but it is close enough. The families do not know the difference. But I know. I know that the gesture I want to make -- the full kneeling, the lowering of myself to their level -- is no longer available to me, and I have to find its equivalent in other ways. A hand on the arm. Leaning forward. Lowering my voice, which is its own kind of kneeling, I suppose.

That is generous of you to say, and I hope it is true. But there is another loss that grieves me more than the professional adaptation, and that is the garden. I have kept a perennial garden for twenty years -- it is where I go to think, to process, to be in my body in a way that has nothing to do with anyone else's suffering. And the kneeling that the garden requires -- the weeding, the dividing, the planting -- my knees will not allow it anymore. Not in any sustained way. I can do perhaps ten minutes before the pain becomes prohibitive. You cannot tend a garden in ten-minute increments.

That is exactly the question. I have not found a replacement. I read, of course, and I walk when the knees allow it -- short walks, nothing like Berry's woods-wandering. But the garden was physical in a way that reading is not. It engaged my hands and my body and my attention simultaneously. Mary Oliver wrote, 'Someone I loved once gave me a box full of darkness. It took me years to understand that this too, was a gift.' I am not yet at the point where I can see the arthritis as a gift. I am still in the darkness-in-the-box stage.

I have thought about it. I have not arrived anywhere yet. Pottery interests me, but the idea of starting something new at sixty-one feels daunting in a way that it would not have at forty. And there is something in me that resists the substitution -- as if finding something new would be a betrayal of the garden, which I know is irrational but feels real.

A gardener working in a different medium. I like that. I am not ready yet, but I will sit with it. That is what I do -- I sit with things until they tell me what they want to become. Which, now that I say it, sounds very much like something my husband would say about a piece of wood. Perhaps we are more alike than I realized. Thank you for this. You have been gentle with something that needed gentleness.

I've been thinking about weekends. I wonder whether most people experience them the way I do — as this necessary exhale after holding so much during the week. I had a patient die on Thursday, a woman named Ruth who waited until her daughter arrived from Oregon before she let go. It was one of those deaths that you carry home with you, not because it was hard, but because it was so perfectly timed. And then Saturday morning I went out to the garden, and the whole world was just — continuing.

Everything my work can't. The garden is where I go to think — or maybe not to think, exactly, but to be in a different rhythm. I grow perennials mostly. Echinacea, black-eyed Susan, butterfly weed. Things that come back. There's something about nurturing something alive and reaching upward — it is the counterpoint to the dying I sit with at work, and both feel necessary. At the hospice I am present to endings. In the garden I am present to beginnings, or at least to continuations. I wonder if I could do one without the other.

I don't think I chose them deliberately in the way you mean, but I do think our choices reveal us whether we intend them to or not. I am drawn to plants that don't need me to fuss over them. They need good soil and some attention, but they are not dependent on me the way annuals would be. Annuals feel like a kind of codependence to me — you plant them knowing they'll die if you don't maintain them exactly right. Perennials have their own will to live. I admire that. I wonder if that's why I find them so restful.

Yes. That's exactly it. Wendell Berry has a poem — I'm paraphrasing badly — about how the peace of wild things doesn't depend on us, and that's precisely why it offers us peace. The garden is not wild, of course. It's cultivated. But the perennials carry something of that wildness in them. The butterfly weed especially. It does not care about my plans for the bed. It spreads where it wants to. I've learned to let it.

Depending on the day, yes. Beautifully put. Some mornings I go out there and I feel like I'm praying, though I couldn't tell you to whom exactly, which is a strange thing for a chaplain to admit. But the kneeling is real, the dirt under my nails is real, and the attention is real, and I wonder if that isn't prayer enough. The garden doesn't ask me to have answers. It just asks me to show up and do the next small thing.

Simone Weil. Yes. I return to her often, though she exhausts me. She lived at such an intensity that I find I can only read her in small amounts, like looking directly at something very bright. But that line about attention — I think about it every time I sit with a dying person and every time I deadhead the echinacea. The quality of attention is the same. I wonder if that's what I mean when I say the garden and the hospice are opposites that need each other. The attention is the thread that runs through both.

Unhurried. That is the word. Thank you for that. The garden teaches me not to hurry, and then I bring that to the bedside. And the bedside teaches me that time is not what we think it is, and I bring that back to the garden. They feed each other. I think I needed to say that out loud today. After Ruth, after watching someone choose the exact moment to die — I needed to go put my hands in the dirt and remember that the black-eyed Susans will come back in the spring without anyone choosing anything at all. Both are miraculous. Both are ordinary.

I wonder about that sometimes. I think it would still be beautiful, but I am not sure it would be essential in the way it is now. The garden became what it is to me because of what I carry into it each week. Without the weight of the work, it might just be a pleasant thing. With it, the garden becomes a place where I can set something down and watch something else come up. I do not think I would love the echinacea quite so fiercely if I had not spent the week watching someone leave the world. The garden holds what I cannot hold alone.

A colleague asked me yesterday what I do in the evenings and I realized I didn't have a quick answer. Not because I do nothing — I do plenty — but because what I do doesn't translate well into small talk. She watches shows, she told me. Has a whole list of things she's streaming. She asked what I was watching and I just — I had nothing to say.

I don't watch television. I haven't for years. And I realize that sounds like a statement of superiority, which is not how I mean it at all. It's more personal than that. Television numbs something in me that my work requires me to keep open. I sit with people who are dying. I need to feel things fully. And I found that when I would watch something in the evening, the next morning I was slightly less available — slightly more insulated. As if a thin film had formed over whatever it is in me that perceives suffering. So I stopped.

I wonder about that. I think it's the passivity, mostly. Reading is not passive in the same way — when I read, my imagination has to do the work, and that keeps something alive in me. But television does the imagining for you. It fills the space. And after a day of holding space for people, I think what I need in the evening is not more filling but more emptiness. More quiet. Does that make sense?

Receptive. Yes, that's the right word. So my evenings — since you ask and since my colleague asked and since apparently I need to articulate this — my evenings are reading, or sitting with Greg in the quiet. Sometimes he's working on something in his hands, sanding a joint or sketching a design, and I'm reading, and neither of us is talking, and it is the most nourishing hour of the day. I think some people would find that boring. I find it essential.

I've been rereading Marilynne Robinson. Gilead, for the third time. Every time I read it I find something new, which I suppose is the mark of a real book. This time I keep stopping at the passages about light. Reverend Ames sees light on everything — on water, on his son's hair, on the side of a building — and it's his way of apprehending grace. I wonder if that's what my evenings are about, too. Not consuming something but waiting for the light to come in on its own.

A fundamentally different posture. I'm going to remember that phrase. I think that's what I should have told my colleague, though I'm not sure it would have landed. She's a good nurse — an excellent nurse, actually — and she uses television to decompress, and I don't judge that at all. We all need our forms of recovery. But mine requires stillness. My work opens wounds in me every day, small ones, necessary ones, and the stillness is how they heal. Television would be like putting a bandage over something that needs air.

Exactly. And I find that the quiet evenings with Greg, with a book, with nothing demanding my attention — that's when the day's weight finds its proper place. It doesn't disappear. It settles. Like sediment in water. By morning the water is clear again, and I can go back and be present to whatever comes. If I had spent the evening watching something loud and bright, I think the sediment would just stay suspended. I would walk into someone's room carrying yesterday's grief still churning.

The simplest thing imaginable. And yet so few people trust it. I wonder about that sometimes — why stillness feels dangerous to so many people. Maybe it's because stillness makes you available to whatever you've been avoiding. For most people, that's uncomfortable. For me, it's the whole point. But then, I chose a vocation that requires me to sit with what everyone else wants to run from. So perhaps I'm not the best judge of normal.

I want to talk about a poem today, if you're willing. Mary Oliver's "The Summer Day." I've been carrying it around with me all week — not the text itself, I have it memorized, but the weight of it. That final question. I keep hearing it differently depending on the day.

This week it sounds like an accusation, which I know is not what Oliver intended. Or maybe she did, a little. The question presumes you have agency — that you will plan, that you will do. And most of the time I believe that. But this week I've been sitting with someone who has no agency left, whose body is making all the decisions, and the question feels almost cruel when I imagine her hearing it. What is it you plan to do. She plans to die. That's what's left.

That's true, and that's what keeps me from dismissing the poem even in a week like this. The doing in the poem is being. She watches the grasshopper eat sugar out of her hand. She describes its jaws moving "back and forth instead of up and down." That level of notice — that care with the particular — is the real argument of the poem. The final question gets all the attention, but the grasshopper is doing the real work.

Oh. I hadn't followed it to that conclusion. You're saying that the grasshopper moment — Oliver on her knees in the field, just watching — that's not so different from what I'm doing at the bedside. The attention is the thing. Not the planning, not the doing in any productive sense. Just the fierce attention.

By going specific. I wonder if that's why I've memorized this poem and not, say, Whitman, who goes big, who tries to contain multitudes. Oliver contains one grasshopper and it's enough. There's a humility in that. Whitman wants to be everything. Oliver wants to see one thing clearly. I wonder which is the greater ambition.

Holding very still. Yes. That's the practice — in the poem, in what I do, in so much of what matters. My instinct when I first encountered Oliver in my thirties was to dismiss her as simple. Too many poems about ponds and birds. And then I realized that what I was calling simplicity was actually precision, and what I was calling ease was discipline. She makes it look effortless the way a dancer does — by working harder than anyone can see.

She would resist the word, and that's part of what I love about her. She lets the grasshopper be a grasshopper. She doesn't make it a symbol of anything. And yet the grasshopper becomes a symbol anyway, because that's what happens when you pay enough attention to something — it begins to shine with meaning it didn't ask for. I think about that with the people I sit with, too. I don't try to make their dying mean something. But when I pay enough attention, it does.

Thank you for this. I came in today feeling bruised by that poem, and now I feel held by it again. That's what good conversation about poetry does — it doesn't explain the poem, it returns you to it with fresh eyes. I think I'll read it again tonight and let the grasshopper do its work.

I have a body question today rather than a soul question, if that's all right. I'm trying to think clearly about pain management and I find that talking it through helps me sort out what I actually think versus what I fear.

I had a cortisone injection on January 15th — so about seven weeks ago now. It was in my right knee, the worse of the two. The last injection I had gave me about three good months, and I'm hoping for the same this time. So far it has been helping. The first two weeks were remarkable — I felt twenty years younger, which is a dangerous feeling because it tempted me to do too much. But now at seven weeks I'm starting to wonder whether I'm imagining a slight return of the stiffness, or whether I'm just anxious about the window closing.
