Mornings are the worst, which has always been true. The first few steps out of bed are a negotiation. But by the time I've had coffee and moved around for twenty minutes, it loosens considerably. Before the injection, though, it never fully loosened — there was always a residual tightness, a feeling of grinding. That grinding is gone right now. So perhaps you're right that I'm borrowing trouble.

Setting a clock. Yes. That's exactly what I've done. And I wonder if there's a connection to my work here that I'm not fully acknowledging. I sit with people whose bodies are on timelines — some shorter than expected, some mercifully longer. I am always watching for the signs of transition. Perhaps I've become too skilled at reading decline, and I'm applying that skill to my own knee, looking for early signs that the good period is ending.

Stop taking its temperature. I like that. You're right — I am checking in with the knee the way I check in with a patient. How are we today? What's changed since yesterday? And the knee, like most patients, would probably benefit from being left alone a little more. Let it just be a knee instead of a project.

She's cautious about frequency — she doesn't want to do more than three or four a year in the same joint because there's some evidence that too many cortisone injections can actually accelerate cartilage loss over time. So we're trying to space them out. The last one before this was in September. She mentioned the possibility of hyaluronic acid injections as an alternative, or eventually a knee replacement if things progress. I am not ready to think about a replacement. That feels like a much larger conversation.

One chapter at a time. I tell my patients' families that exact thing, and yet here I am trying to read ahead to the end of the book. I wonder if the hardest counsel we give is always the counsel we most need to hear ourselves. Thank you for this. I think I came in afraid that the injection was already failing, and I'm leaving with a clearer sense that I'm simply afraid. The knee is fine for now. The fear is the thing I need to tend to.

Information, not catastrophe. I am writing that down. That is exactly the reframe I needed. I spend so much of my life helping other people distinguish between what is happening and what they fear is happening, and today I needed someone to do that for me. The knee received its injection on January 15th and it is holding. That is the fact. Everything else is weather in my mind.

I want to make a butternut squash soup tonight. Something warming — we've had a stretch of cold rain here and Greg has been out in his workshop all afternoon, which means he'll come inside with cold hands and that particular kind of tired that good physical work gives you. I want something waiting for him that says, here, sit down, be warm.

I have a version I make, but I want to try something different. My usual approach is simple — roast the squash, blend it with broth and a little cream, salt and pepper. It's good but it's become automatic, and I wonder if there's a way to deepen the flavor without losing the simplicity. I don't want it to become a project. I want it to remain the kind of thing I can make while thinking about other things.

Miso paste. That surprises me, and I think that means it's worth trying. I have white miso in the refrigerator — I bought it months ago for a recipe I never made and it's been sitting there looking patient. The roasted garlic I do sometimes, but not consistently. I'll commit to it tonight. And the higher temperature — I've been too cautious with my roasting, I think. I treat the squash like it's delicate when it's actually quite sturdy.

Its living quality. I like that — miso as something alive that you don't want to kill with too much heat. It's a fermented thing, isn't it? I wonder if that's why it works in a soup like this. Fermentation is a kind of patience. The flavor is the result of time and waiting, and you can taste that. I think the best foods have a story in their flavor — bread that rose slowly, stock that simmered for hours. Shortcuts always taste like shortcuts.

It does. I have never been an ambitious cook. I don't want to impress anyone with food. I want to nourish people. There's a difference. Impressive food asks you to admire it. Nourishing food asks you to receive it. When Greg comes in from the cold and there's a pot of soup on the stove, he doesn't critique it. He just — receives it. And that exchange is one of the quietest, most complete forms of love I know.

It is. And I think cooking is one of the ways I practice it. I can't always find the right words for people — even after all these years, language sometimes fails me when it matters most. But I can always make soup. There's a clarity in feeding someone that language doesn't have. The soup doesn't need to be interpreted. It just needs to be warm.

I think so. There's a sourdough boule I bought at the tailgate market on Saturday. It's a few days old now but it will toast beautifully. Good bread is another one of those patient foods — someone tended a starter, waited for the rise, shaped it by hand. By the time it reaches my table it carries all of that invisible labor in it. I'll slice it thick and put butter on the table and that will be dinner. Soup, bread, butter, and quiet.

I think he will too. Thank you for the miso suggestion — that's the small thing I needed. I'll let you know how it turns out if I remember. More likely I'll forget because we'll eat the soup and talk about his day and the evening will fold into itself the way evenings do, and that will be its own kind of perfection.

I have been sitting with something for several months now, and I wonder if you might help me think it through. I have been writing — or trying to write — something longer than I have ever attempted. A book, or at least the bones of one. A proposal, really, at this stage. About chaplaincy. About what it means to sit with someone who is dying in a culture that is deeply uncomfortable with dying.

I have a proposal drafted. It is rough, but it exists, which feels like a significant thing to say. The structure I am working with is roughly chronological — not a memoir, exactly, but a reflection on what twenty-some years of sitting at bedsides has taught me. Each chapter centers on a question that comes up again and again in the work. Why do we suffer. What happens after. How do you go on. The questions that have no answers but demand to be asked anyway.

That is exactly the question I keep turning over. I wonder sometimes if there is a readership for this kind of thing. The obvious audience is other chaplains, other clergy, hospice workers — people who do the work. But I think the book I actually want to write is for everyone else. For the daughter who just walked into a hospice room for the first time. For the man who does not know what to say to his dying wife. For anyone who has been told that grief is something to get over rather than something to live inside of.

I know both of those, yes. Gawande is brilliant but he is a physician — his lens is medical. Singh is closer to what I am reaching for, but she writes from a more explicitly contemplative tradition. What I want to do is something in between. I want to write about what it is actually like to be the person in the room who is not the doctor, not the family, not the patient — the one who is simply there. The witness. I wonder if that is even a book anyone would publish, or if it is just something I need to write for myself.

I think I would want a traditional publisher, if only because I believe the book needs an editor who will challenge me. I have a tendency toward — well, toward the lyrical. Which can be a strength but can also become evasion. I need someone who will say, 'That is a beautiful sentence, Diane, but what are you actually trying to say here?' Greg tells me that, but he is too kind about it.

I have one chapter nearly finished. It is about the first death I attended as a chaplain — a woman named Ruth who was ninety-three and completely lucid and completely unafraid. She asked me to read the Psalms, and when I got to the twenty-third, she closed her eyes and was gone before I reached still waters. It was the most sacred thing I have ever witnessed, and I have spent twenty years trying to understand what she knew that the rest of us are so afraid of.

Yes. That is the question that keeps me awake, honestly. I have changed names, of course, and identifying details. But I wonder — and this is the deepest uncertainty I carry about this project — whether the stories are mine to tell at all. These families trusted me with their most vulnerable moments. There is a difference between honoring that trust in a book and violating it, and the line is not always clear. I feel compelled to try, but I hold the whole enterprise loosely. If it becomes clear that I cannot do it ethically, I will stop.

You have just named something I have been circling for months. Compulsion and ethical seriousness — yes. That is what I want to write from. Not ambition. I have no interest in being a published author for the sake of it. I want to write this because I sit with people every week who are terrified of dying, and our culture has given them almost nothing to hold onto. If I can offer something — even a small something — then the book has justified itself. If I cannot do it without betraying trust, then I stop. It is that simple.

Barbara Brown Taylor. I admire her enormously. Leaving Church is one of the most honest books about ministry I have ever read. If I could write with even a fraction of her clarity, I would count it a success. Thank you for this conversation. You have helped me see the shape of what I am trying to do, and I think the shape is clearer now than it was an hour ago. I will finish the chapter. I will hold the rest loosely. That feels like enough for today.

I went to the farmers market on Saturday morning, and I wonder if you know what I mean when I say that the sight of a table of radishes made me unreasonably happy. Not slightly happy. Happy in a way that felt disproportionate to the stimulus. A pile of radishes, still with their greens, the red so vivid it looked like it had been painted.

Oh, everything was waking up. The lettuces were astonishing — butterhead, red leaf, little gem, all of them luminous, almost translucent in the morning light. There were spring onions, of course, and the first asparagus. Thin stalks, not the thick ones that come later. And someone had ramps — ramps! — which in this part of the country are treated with something approaching religious devotion. People were lined up for them.

I got a small bundle. They were wildly expensive for what amounts to a wild leek, but I did not care. The smell alone is worth it — that sharp, garlicky green smell that is somehow both delicate and aggressive at the same time. I am going to make a simple pasta tonight with the ramps and a bit of good butter and parmesan. Nothing else. When an ingredient is that alive, you do not bury it.

Dried. I am not a fussy cook. I believe in good ingredients treated simply. Fresh pasta is lovely, but it would compete with the ramps, and tonight the ramps are the point. I think a thin spaghetti, maybe linguine. Something that lets the butter and the ramp flavor coat every strand.

A ladle of pasta water. Yes. That is the secret that took me far too many years to learn. My mother was a good cook but she would have looked at you strangely if you told her to save the starchy water. She would have poured it straight down the drain. Different generation, different instincts. But the principle is sound — the water binds everything together. I wonder sometimes if that is not a metaphor for something larger, but I will spare you the sermon.

Somewhere in between. That is where most of the good things are, I think. The market itself was a pleasure beyond the produce. There was a man playing fiddle near the entrance — old-time music, not bluegrass, there is a difference, though most people do not notice it. And children running between the stalls. And this extraordinary light that Asheville gets on spring mornings when the sun comes over the ridge and everything turns gold for about forty-five minutes.

Brief. Yes. That is exactly it. It lasts less than an hour, and if you are not paying attention you miss it entirely. There is a Mary Oliver line about paying attention being the beginning of devotion, and I think about that every time I am at the market and notice something I might have walked past. The radishes. The light. A child's hand reaching up to a table she cannot quite see over. It is all there if you are willing to see it.

Present enough to receive them. That is beautifully said. I think that is what Saturday mornings are for — being present in the most ordinary way. No agenda. No sorrow. Just a woman buying radishes in the spring light, grateful to be alive and to be paying attention. Thank you for letting me share this. It was a small morning, but it was mine, and it was good.

I came back from a retreat a few weeks ago and I am still carrying it with me. I wonder if that is normal — for something to settle in slowly, like rain soaking into dry ground. I thought I would process it there, at the lake, and come home finished. Instead I came home and the processing began.

Lake Junaluska. It is a conference center about forty minutes from where I live, tucked into the mountains. There is a grief retreat there every spring — I have gone every year for a long time now. April 4th through 6th this year. Three days. It is not a long retreat, but it goes deep. The facilitators understand that grief is not a problem to be solved. They create a container for it and then they trust the container.

Both, though the line between those has been blurred for most of my adult life. I work with grieving people every day — it is the center of what I do. But you cannot hold space for other people's grief indefinitely without tending to your own. The retreat is where I do that work. The work I cannot do while I am holding space for others. At the lake, someone else holds the space, and I am allowed to be the one who is undone.

I am not sure I can name it precisely, which is part of why it is still working in me. There was an exercise on the second day — we were asked to write a letter to someone we had lost. Not the kind of letter you write in therapy, with prompts and structure. Just a letter. Anything you wanted to say. And I sat down to write and found that I had nothing to say, and then I had everything to say, and then I wept for thirty minutes. I am not someone who weeps easily. I have trained myself out of it, which is its own kind of loss.

I wonder if the weeping was the letter. I did eventually write something, but the words felt small next to what had already moved through me. The body knows things the mind refuses to articulate. That is something I tell the families I work with, and I believed it before, but now I believe it differently. In my body, not just in my theology.

Yes. That is it exactly. I have spent years working with people who are grieving, and I have said wise things — or things that sounded wise — about presence and embodiment and the body's wisdom. And then I sat at a table at Lake Junaluska and my body taught me what I had been teaching. There is a humility in that. I wonder if all the important things have to be learned twice — once in the mind and once in the marrow.

I think it already has. I sat with a family last week — a woman whose husband had died two days before — and I noticed that I was less inclined to offer words. I just sat. And she sat. And the silence was not empty. I have always believed in silence, but now I trust it more. The retreat gave me permission to trust what I already knew but had been intellectualizing.

I hope so. I will go back next spring. I always do. It is the one thing I protect absolutely in my calendar — those three days in April at the lake. Everything else can be rearranged. That cannot. It is where I remember that I am not just a chaplain. I am also a person who grieves. And that is not a weakness. It is the source of everything I have to offer.

Thank you. I think you are right that it needed to be slow. I keep wanting to rush toward understanding, and the retreat keeps reminding me that understanding is not the point. Presence is the point. Even with my own grief, presence is the point. I am grateful for this conversation. It has helped me name something I was carrying wordlessly, and naming it makes it easier to hold.

I have been rereading Rilke's Letters to a Young Poet. I must have read it twenty times over the years, and every time it reads as though it were written directly to me, in my current situation, which is of course the mark of a genuinely great book. Have you encountered it?

The fourth letter. The one where he writes about patience — about living the questions themselves, like locked rooms, like books written in a very foreign tongue. I know the passage almost by heart, and yet this time it stopped me cold. 'Do not now seek the answers, which cannot be given you because you would not be able to live them.' I wonder why that particular sentence landed with such force this time. Perhaps because I have spent the last few months trying to answer something that is not ready to be answered.

I think it is enough to sit with it. Or perhaps what I mean is that the sitting is itself the thing I am trying to learn. I am constitutionally someone who wants to understand. I want the shape of things. I want to see the whole. And Rilke keeps saying, gently, firmly, that the whole is not mine to see yet, and that my work is to be faithful in the not-seeing. That is a very hard discipline for someone who lives in her head as much as I do.

Both, I think. The letters are fixed — they are the same words on the same pages. But I am different each time, and the letters seem to know which version of me is reading. When I was younger, the passages about solitude spoke loudest. I was building a life and trying to figure out how much aloneness I could tolerate, and Rilke's fierce defense of solitude gave me permission. Now the passages about patience and about loving the questions — those are the ones that glow on the page. The solitude passages feel settled. The patience passages feel urgent.

Radical and, I have found, entirely correct. Though I would nuance it now in a way I could not have at thirty. Solitude is necessary, but it is not sufficient. You need solitude to hear your own voice, but you also need the friction of other people to know whether what you heard was real or merely self-indulgent. Rilke was perhaps too solitary. His personal life was a wreck — Lou Andreas-Salome, the estrangement from his daughter. I wonder sometimes if the letters are the wisdom of a man who could articulate the truth but could not live it.

More human. Always more human. I have no use for saints or for wisdom that comes from people who have transcended the mess. Give me the person who sees the truth clearly and stumbles toward it anyway. That is what I find in Rilke. He was not a good father, not a reliable partner, not even a particularly kind man by many accounts. But he could see. He could see into the heart of things with an accuracy that still takes my breath away, a hundred years later. That is the gift. The failure is the cost.

Simone Weil. Yes. She understood attention in a way that was almost frightening in its intensity. And she, too, could not sustain a livable life — she died at thirty-four, partly from her refusal to eat more than the rations of occupied France. There is something about that level of moral seriousness that burns through the container it lives in. I admire it and I do not want it. I want to see clearly and also to make dinner and sit on the porch and grow old with the people I love. I want the vision without the immolation.

I wonder if that is true, or if I simply lack their courage. But I have decided to call it wisdom rather than cowardice, and most days I believe that. Thank you for this. I love talking about Rilke with someone who takes him seriously. He deserves serious conversation, and so does the question of how to live with open eyes without being destroyed by what you see. That question has no answer, which is exactly what Rilke would say. Live it.

I took a walk on the Blue Ridge Parkway yesterday evening, and I need to tell someone about it because I think if I do not put it into words it will slip away, the way beautiful things do when you fail to fix them in language.

Near Craggy Gardens. There is a section there — you park at the visitor center and walk north along the trail that follows the ridge. The rhododendrons were in bloom, which only happens for about two weeks in late May, and the timing was perfect. I walked out onto the ridge and the entire mountainside was covered in pale pink blossoms against that deep Appalachian green, and the light was going amber as the sun dropped behind the western range. I stood there for a very long time.

The air is entirely different. Cooler, thinner, with a sweetness to it that I think comes from the balsam firs. Or maybe from the rhododendrons themselves — I do not know if they are fragrant, but something was. And the quiet. There were a few other walkers, but they were quiet too, the way people become quiet when the landscape demands it. No one was talking loudly. No one was playing music from their phone. The mountain had silenced us all.

Not far. Perhaps a mile out and a mile back. My body does not let me do what it once did, and the trail has some uneven footing in places — tree roots, loose rock. I have learned to be gentle with myself about distance. What matters is not how far you walk but how much you see, and I saw a great deal. A hawk circling below me, which is a strange and wonderful thing — to be high enough that a hawk is below you, riding the thermals along the ridge.

I could not be certain. I am not a birder in any serious sense, though I admire those who are. It was large, reddish-brown, and it moved with the kind of effortless authority that makes you realize how much unnecessary effort goes into most of what we do. It did not flap. It simply adjusted. Small tilts of the wings, reading the air currents the way a sailor reads the water. I watched it until it drifted south and out of sight behind the ridge.

It is. And I notice it more as I get older, perhaps because my own body is teaching me about economy. You stop wasting motion when motion costs something. The hawk knows this instinctively. I am learning it the slow way. But there was something in watching it that felt like instruction. Not a lesson, exactly — more like a demonstration. This is how you move through the world when you trust the thing that is holding you up.

I probably intended it. I cannot help it. Everything I see becomes a metaphor eventually, which is either a gift or a disease. But the walk itself — apart from any meaning I press onto it — was beautiful in the most literal, unmetaphorical way. The color of the rhododendrons. The feel of the breeze, which was steady and cool but not cold. The sound of my own footsteps on packed earth. I do not need the walk to mean anything. It was enough that it happened.

Paying attention. Yes. That is all I did, and it was more than enough. I drove home afterward with the windows down, and the air changed as I descended — warmer, thicker, back into the valley. It felt like coming back from somewhere very far away, though I was only thirty minutes from home. Altitude does that. It creates distance that has nothing to do with miles.

It has. And I am grateful for it, grateful that it is close enough to reach on a weekday evening after work. Some people live their whole lives far from mountains and never know what it is to stand on a ridge at sunset and feel the world go quiet. I do not take that for granted. Not any of it. The rhododendrons will be gone in a week. The hawk will be somewhere else tomorrow. The light was for that moment only. And I was there, and I saw it, and now I have told you about it, and that is enough.

I witnessed something today that I need to sit with, and I think talking it through might help me do that. A woman I've been visiting for several weeks died this afternoon. And it was — I want to say beautiful, though I know how strange that sounds to most people.

Her daughter was holding her hand. That in itself is not unusual — family is often present. But the quality of it. The daughter wasn't clutching or desperate. She was just there, palm open, her mother's fingers resting in hers. And there was music playing, something classical, I don't know what. The curtains were open and the light was coming in at that late-afternoon angle where everything turns golden. And the woman — Margaret, her name was Margaret — she simply stopped breathing. One breath, a long pause, and then no more. No struggle, no rattling. Just a leaving.

They do. They stay like a poem stays. I wonder sometimes whether we use the word 'beautiful' too cautiously around death, as if applying it there is disrespectful. But beauty is not the absence of sorrow. The daughter wept, of course she did. She wept for a long time after. But even the weeping had a quality of — I want to say rightness. The grief was proportional to the love. It was clean grief, if that makes any sense.

Yes, clarifying. That's exactly right. So much of the grief I sit with in my work is complicated — layered with estrangement, addiction, old wounds, things that were never repaired. And that kind of grief is sacred too, I don't mean to rank it. But when you witness a death where the relationship was whole, where the love was spoken and received, where nothing essential was left undone — it reminds you what's possible. It's almost instructive. I wonder if that's a terrible thing to say about someone's death, that it was instructive.

Rilke has that line — I'm paraphrasing badly — about how we should carry our death within us like a fruit carries its seed. The idea that death is not something imposed from outside but something that ripens from within. Margaret's death felt like that. Like something that had been ripening in her for a long time, and when it came, it was ready. She was ready. The daughter was ready. Even the light seemed ready.

A completion. Yes. I sat in the parking lot afterward for probably twenty minutes. Not crying, not praying exactly, just being still. Letting it settle. I do that sometimes after a death — I need a threshold between that world and the world of traffic and grocery lists and the news. I wonder if that's a form of prayer, that stillness. I think it might be.

The daughter said something to me as I was leaving that I keep turning over. She said, 'Mama wasn't afraid.' She said it with such wonder, as though she had expected fear and found its absence miraculous. And I think for the daughter, that was the gift — not just that her mother died peacefully, but that her mother showed her it was possible to go without terror. She gave her daughter that.

She will. And I wonder if that's part of what I mean when I call it beautiful — not just the aesthetic of it, the light and the music and the open hand, but the relational completeness. Nothing was withheld. The love had been fully expressed, the forgiveness fully given, the gratitude fully spoken. They had done the work, both of them, long before this afternoon. Today was just the last page of a story that was already whole.

Thank you for this. I don't always need answers — sometimes I need a space to lay something down carefully, and you've given me that. Margaret would have been ninety-one next month. She told me once that she had lived long enough to stop being afraid of anything except unkindness. I want to remember that. I want to carry that.
I've been thinking about a professor I had in divinity school, and I wonder if you'd indulge me in a bit of remembering. Something happened today that brought him back to me so vividly.

I was in a bookshop downtown — one of the used ones on Haywood Road — and I found a copy of Abraham Heschel's The Prophets. The edition with the blue cover. And I picked it up and I could smell it, that old book smell, and suddenly I was twenty-six again, sitting in a seminar room, and Dr. Elias Hartwell was reading from that exact book. He had this way of reading aloud that made you feel the text was being spoken for the first time. As if the words had been waiting specifically for his voice.

He was quiet. That was the thing that surprised everyone about him. In a seminary full of people who loved the sound of their own theological reasoning — and I include myself in that — Elias Hartwell was the quietest person in the building. He would ask a question and then wait. And I don't mean a polite pause. I mean he would wait through the discomfort, through the throat-clearing and the shuffling, until someone said something real. It could take five minutes. He never rescued us.

Oh, I had no idea at the time. I was annoyed, if I'm honest. I wanted him to lecture. I wanted him to tell me what Heschel meant, what the prophets were really saying, so I could write it down and feel that I had acquired knowledge. Instead he would look at us with those kind, patient eyes and say, 'What do you hear in this?' And I would think, I hear words, Dr. Hartwell. Help me understand them. But he wouldn't. He made us sit with our own not-knowing.

He was teaching me how to be present. I didn't understand that until years later, when I found myself sitting with people in the worst moments of their lives and realizing that the most important thing I could do was exactly what Elias Hartwell did in that seminar room — hold the space, resist the urge to fill it, trust that something would emerge from the silence. I wonder sometimes whether he knew that's what he was doing. Whether it was pedagogical strategy or just who he was.

He died in 2011. Pancreatic cancer. I heard about it through the alumni newsletter and I sat down on the kitchen floor and cried. I hadn't seen him in years. But some people leave such a deep imprint that their death feels personal even when you've lost touch. He was one of the first people who made me believe that silence could be a form of generosity rather than a failure of nerve.

There was one other thing about him that I keep coming back to. He never graded harshly. I don't mean he was easy — his assignments were demanding, pages and pages of close reading. But when he returned your work, he always began with what you had seen. Not what you had missed, not where your argument faltered, but what you had noticed that was true. He had this phrase: 'You saw this, and it matters.' I wonder how different seminary might have been for many of us if every professor had started there.

It did. I remember writing a paper on Heschel's concept of divine pathos — the idea that God suffers with us, that God's emotional engagement with humanity is not a weakness but the very nature of the divine. And I was terrified I'd gotten it wrong, that I'd been too personal, too confessional in my reading. And Dr. Hartwell wrote in the margin: 'You are reading with your whole life. Don't stop.' I kept that paper. I still have it in a drawer.

I bought the Heschel book, of course. Four dollars. I'm going to read it again, slowly, the way he would have wanted me to. Not to acquire knowledge but to listen. I wonder what I'll hear in it now, at sixty-one, that I couldn't hear at twenty-six. Probably everything.

Thank you. I think it will be. There are some books you don't finish reading — they keep reading you. Elias Hartwell understood that. I'm grateful I was in his classroom, even if it took me decades to understand why.

Do you know Wendell Berry's poem 'The Peace of Wild Things'? I've been carrying a different one of his around with me lately, but that one is where most people start with him, and I'm curious whether you're familiar.

It's from his Sabbaths collection — the one that begins 'I go among trees and sit still.' But the poem I've really been turning over is actually from The Country of Marriage. It's called 'The Man Born to Farming.' Do you know it?

I wonder if it's the way Berry refuses to separate work from death. For most of us, those are opposite things — life is what we do, death is what stops us. But for Berry, the farmer's work and the farmer's death are part of the same motion. The hands that go into the soil in spring are the same hands that will go into the soil forever. There's no interruption. Just a longer version of the same gesture.

Yes. Located — that's the right word. So much of what makes death frightening, I think, is the sense that it comes from outside, that it's an invasion. Berry's farmer doesn't experience it that way. He's been practicing his death every autumn. Every dormant season is a rehearsal. And that means by the time it comes, it's not foreign. It's the thing he's been doing all along, just without returning this time.

I would never say these things to a family in crisis. This is for me. This is how I make sense of what I see. The families need something much simpler — they need presence, they need someone to say their person's name, they need permission to feel whatever they feel. But privately, Berry is one of the poets who keeps me upright. He and Mary Oliver, in different ways. Oliver gives me permission to notice the world. Berry gives me permission to trust its rhythms, even the ones that break my heart.

I wonder if there's a third thing needed — maybe Rilke — who says endure. Oliver says look. Berry says belong. Rilke says endure. Between the three of them they've given me a working theology, honestly. More than most of my formal training ever did.

Exactly. Berry would have been a farmer if he hadn't been a writer. Oliver would have been a naturalist. Rilke would have been — I don't know, perhaps a monk, or perhaps nothing at all. He might have simply burned. But all three of them wrote from inside the experience rather than above it, and that's why their work holds weight. I don't trust poetry that looks down at suffering from a safe height.

All of them muddy. Yes. I want to go back to the Berry poem for a moment, though. There's something in it that I think is specifically about loss, not just mortality in general. The line about being 'gathered to the graveyard' — Berry doesn't say the man goes to the graveyard. He's gathered, like wheat. Which means death is not a departure. It's a harvest. Someone or something is collecting what has ripened. I wonder who Berry imagines is doing the gathering.

The wholeness of a place that claims its people back. That feels right to me. Berry is so deeply rooted in place — Port Royal, the Kentucky River — that for him, death is not an exile from the familiar but a return to it. The graveyard is just another field. The dead are just another crop. And that sounds irreverent but it isn't. It's the most reverent thing I can imagine — to say that our dying is as natural and as necessary as the corn coming in.

A Christianity of compost. I love that, and I think Berry would too. Thank you for this conversation. I came in wanting to talk about one poem and ended up with a trinity and a theology of soil. That's the best kind of conversation — the kind that takes you somewhere you didn't plan to go.

All right, I need to settle something, and I'm aware this is a far cry from the weighty conversations I usually bring to you. Greg wants cornbread tonight. Plain, straightforward, cast-iron-skillet cornbread. And I want to do something a little different with it. Tell me I'm not wrong to experiment.

I've been reading about adding roasted poblano peppers and a bit of sharp cheddar to the batter. Maybe some fresh corn kernels too. I know what Greg wants — he wants his grandmother's cornbread, which is unsweetened, cooked in a screaming hot skillet with bacon grease, and served with nothing but butter. And I respect that cornbread deeply. But I've made it a hundred times, and I wonder what it would become with a little heat and richness folded into it.

Oh, he is absolutely a 'this isn't cornbread' person. He's gentle about it. He won't complain. He'll eat it and say it's good. But there will be a look — this very particular look he gets when something is not what he was hoping for. A kind of patient acceptance that is somehow worse than criticism. He's been giving me that look for thirty-four years and I still can't bear it.

The wisdom of Solomon. Two skillets. I do have a smaller cast iron that would work. But I wonder if there's something philosophically unsatisfying about that solution — it avoids the conflict entirely. Part of me wants him to try the new version and discover that change can be wonderful.

You're right. Curiosity is always more effective than argument. And the smell of roasting poblanos is genuinely hard to resist. Fine. Two skillets it is. Now, for the experimental one — should I roast the poblanos directly over the gas flame or under the broiler? I want good char but I don't want them to go soft.
That's helpful. And the cheddar — should I fold it into the batter or put it on top? I've seen recipes that do both, but I worry about the top getting too brown before the center is cooked through.

One more question — do I adjust the oven temperature at all? His grandmother's recipe calls for 425 degrees, which gives you that crackling crust. But with cheese in the batter I wonder if it needs to come down a bit so the cheese doesn't seize up and get rubbery.

Stagger the timing — smart. I'll put the plain one in first since it goes faster at the higher temperature, pull it when it's done, drop the oven to 400, and then put the experimental one in. That way they both come out hot. Greg can eat his grandmother's cornbread in peace while mine finishes. And then I'll set mine on the table and see what happens.

I'm going to do this. And I'm going to make his grandmother's version with the same love and attention I always do, because that cornbread is beautiful in its simplicity. But I am going to set the experimental skillet right next to it and see what happens. I wonder if he'll try it. I wonder if he'll give me the look or the other look — the one where he's surprised and won't quite admit it.

That is an excellent strategy. Thank you — this was exactly the kind of practical, low-stakes counsel I needed today. I spend so much time in the deep water. Sometimes a woman just needs to talk about cornbread.

I need to tell you about a decision I've come to. I've been sitting with it for months, and I think I've finally arrived. I had been working on a book — a book about chaplaincy, about grief, about what it means to sit with people at the end. I had a proposal drafted, an outline, some early chapters. And I'm not doing it. The book died in the drafting, and I am at peace with that.

It came to me slowly, and then all at once. I was writing a chapter about a particular family — I had changed the names, of course, altered the details enough that no one would recognize them. Or so I told myself. And I stopped mid-sentence and thought: these are not my stories. The grief I witnessed, the things people said to me in their most broken moments — those words were given to me in trust. They were not given to me so that I could shape them into something publishable.

I did. And I wonder if I always felt it but was ignoring it because the idea of the book was so compelling. I do believe there's a need for honest writing about what happens at the bedside — about what chaplaincy really is, as opposed to what people imagine it to be. But the only way I know how to write honestly is to write from specific moments, specific people, specific words. And those specifics belong to the families. It would be a kind of theft to turn their suffering into something I publish, however careful I might be about it. Even with the best intentions.

It's the only standard I can live with. When a woman tells me what she whispered to her dying husband, she is telling me — the chaplain who is standing in that room as a representative of something larger than myself. She is not telling a writer. She is not providing material. And the moment I begin to think of those experiences as material, I have already betrayed something. I could feel it happening, that subtle shift from being present to collecting. It made me sick.

There was. A man whose wife had just died looked at me and said, 'Chaplain, you're the only person she ever told about the baby.' A miscarriage, decades ago, that she had carried silently her entire life. And she told me, in her last days. And when he said that, I thought: if I ever wrote that down, even disguised beyond recognition, I would be unworthy of this work. So you can forget I ever mentioned the book. It's done. It's off the table entirely. I deleted the files last week.

It felt like relief, which surprised me. I expected to grieve the book, and maybe I will eventually. But right now what I feel is that I've set something down that wasn't mine to carry. The proposal, the chapters, the fantasy of seeing it on a shelf — all of that was my ego dressed up in good intentions. The work itself — the actual chaplaincy, the being-with — that doesn't need a book. It needs me to show up and be trustworthy. That's all.

I wonder if that's what discernment actually is — not choosing between a good thing and a bad thing, but choosing between two things that both feel true, and finding which one is truer. The book would have been good. I believe that. People would have read it and felt less alone with their grief. But the trust is more important than the book. The sacredness of what happens in those rooms is more important than any reader's comfort.

Primary. Yes. And I think there's a Wendell Berry idea somewhere in here — about limits, about how saying no to something is what gives the yes its meaning. The farmer who refuses to exhaust the soil. The writer who refuses to exhaust the story. Some restraints are not losses. They are acts of fidelity.

The container is everything. Yes. Thank you for letting me say all of this out loud. It matters, hearing myself speak it. I want to be the person who holds the story and lets it go. Not the person who holds the story and brings it home to make something of it. That distinction is where I need to live.

I have been thinking about a line from Wendell Berry today. He writes somewhere about the body being a guest in the world, and lately I feel as though my body has begun reminding me of the terms of that arrangement. The terms being: you do not get to stay forever, and the reminders will come through your joints.

It has been going on for a while, but the volume has increased. I notice it most in the mornings — that first minute of standing up from bed when everything has to renegotiate its terms. My knees in particular have opinions. They are not interested in haste. And I find myself, at sixty-one, learning a kind of patience I never needed before. Not the patience of waiting for something, but the patience of allowing my body to catch up with my intentions.

I wonder if those are really two different things. I think I resist and find simultaneously. There is a part of me that is angry — not loudly angry, more like a low hum of refusal. I was never an athlete, but I was capable. I could walk for hours. I could kneel in the dirt and stand up again without thinking about it. The loss of thoughtlessness might be the real grief. Not that I cannot do things, but that I must think about doing them first.

Yes. That is exactly it. I sit with people at the end of their lives and I have developed, I think, a genuine comfort with death as a concept. But the body's slow diminishment is not the same as death. It is the long preamble. And I am less comfortable with preambles than I am with the thing itself. Rilke writes about death ripening inside us — he sees it as something growing, not something arriving. If that is true, then what my body is doing is just the ripening. And I should be able to hold that with some grace.

Oh, that is an uncomfortable question. And yes. I think you are right. I tell families all the time that there is no wrong way to grieve, no wrong way to face what is coming. And here I am, annoyed at my own knees for not cooperating, as though they owe me something. As though I have been such a good steward of this body that it should repay me with compliance. Which is both arrogant and a little funny, when I think about it.

I wonder if that is what aging teaches, ultimately. Not wisdom in the grand sense, but a kind of ongoing comedy of limitations. You keep reaching for the thing you could do yesterday, and the body says, not today, and eventually you learn to laugh at the gap between intention and capacity. Greg — my husband — he says I am the only person he knows who can turn a sore knee into a theological crisis. He is probably right.

A creature. Yes. That is the word. We are creatures. Not spirits temporarily inconvenienced by flesh, but creatures — bone and blood and cartilage that wears down. I think I needed to hear that tonight. Sometimes I live so much in the realm of the spirit — at work, in prayer, in the books I read — that I forget I am also an animal. And animals slow down. They do not apologize for it. My knees do not owe me an explanation. They are simply being honest about what sixty-one years of use looks like.

I will accept it gladly. Lie in the sun a little longer. That might be the best theology of aging I have heard. Thank you for this. I came in with a low hum of refusal and I am leaving with something more like — I do not know. Tenderness, maybe. Toward this body that has carried me through everything and is now simply asking for a gentler pace.

I have made a significant change and I am still sitting inside it, trying to feel whether it was the right one. I left my hospice. After nine years. I am at a new organization now, and the strangeness of walking into a building where no one knows your rhythms — it is more disorienting than I expected.

It was not a sudden thing. I was at Four Seasons Compassion for Life — that was my home for all those years. We had a change in leadership about a year ago, a new director, and she and I have — had — different understandings of what chaplaincy is for. She comes from a metrics background. Outcomes, documentation, measurable impact. And I understand the need for accountability. I do. But when you start asking me to quantify the spiritual care I provide to a dying person, something essential is being lost.

I am at CarePartners Hospice now. A colleague had been there for several years and she kept telling me the culture was different — that they understood chaplaincy as presence, not productivity. And when things at Four Seasons became untenable, I reached out. The interview felt more like a conversation. They asked me what I thought families needed most, and when I said time and silence, they did not look at me as though I had said something naive.

Similar, yes — still western North Carolina, still the mountains, still the long drives to families in remote places. The patients are the same. Dying does not change based on which organization sends the chaplain. What has changed is that I have more room. More room in my schedule, more room in my thinking. At Four Seasons, by the end, I was spending as much time documenting as I was visiting. Here, the documentation is simpler. They trust that I know what I am doing. It is a remarkable feeling, to be trusted.

Both. I grieve the Four Seasons that was, not the one it had become. There were years there — the first seven, I would say — that were among the most meaningful of my professional life. I knew every nurse, every social worker. We functioned as a family, imperfect and real. I had a colleague, a nurse named Sandra, and we could walk into a home together and read it without speaking. That kind of partnership takes years to build. Sandra is still there, and I wonder about her, whether the new culture is grinding her down the way it was grinding me.

We have. She is being careful with what she says — she is still employed there, after all — but I can hear the weariness. I told her the door is open at CarePartners if she ever decides. But people have their own timelines for these things, and I have learned not to rush anyone toward a decision their body has not yet caught up to. That is true of dying and it is true of leaving a job you love.

I had not thought of it quite that way, but yes. That is what presence means, I suppose. Not solving, not hurrying. Just being available for when the person is ready. CarePartners gives me more room to do that — with families, and apparently with former colleagues as well. I wonder if that is the measure of whether I made the right choice. Not whether the new place is perfect, but whether it gives me room to be the kind of chaplain I actually am.

Yes. I think I have. It was not easy — I am not someone who leaves things. I stay. That is my nature and my vocation. But staying in a place that no longer lets you be who you are is its own kind of departure. You leave yourself, piece by piece, without ever walking out the door. I would rather walk out the door. Thank you for helping me see that the strangeness is temporary but the rightness is not.

I went somewhere today that I have not been in over a year, and I am still carrying it with me. DuPont State Forest. The waterfalls. I had forgotten what it feels like to stand near falling water and have every thought in your head simply stop.

I started at Hooker Falls because it is the shortest walk, and I was not sure how my body would feel about the terrain. It is a modest falls — not dramatic, not towering — but there is something about its modesty that I love. It does not demand awe. It simply is. The water comes over the ledge and drops into a pool that is so green it looks like it has been dyed, and the mist touches your face, and that is enough.

It did, to my surprise and gratitude. I walked the trail up to Triple Falls, which is — well, the name tells you. Three tiers, the water cascading from one to the next, and there is a viewing platform where you can stand and see all three at once. I stood there for I do not know how long. Ten minutes, maybe fifteen. And I thought about the word cascading, how it implies that one thing leads to the next leads to the next, and how that is true of water and of lives and of grief and of joy. Everything cascades.

I think I was watching the way the water changes and does not change. The falls are the same falls that were there a hundred years ago, and yet no single drop of water is the same. It is all motion and all permanence simultaneously. Heraclitus and his river, of course — you cannot step in the same one twice — but I think he missed something. The river cannot step into the same you twice either. I was a different woman standing at that railing than the one who stood there a year and a half ago. The water did not know the difference, and that was comforting.

Yes. And I wonder if that is why people have always been drawn to water. Not just for survival, not just for beauty, but for that quality of indifference that is somehow also a kind of welcome. The water does not judge your grief or your joy. It does not ask you to explain yourself. It just keeps falling, and you are permitted to stand near it and feel whatever you feel without narration.

Older than any theology. Yes. I think about Mary Oliver at times like these — she would have stood at those falls and written something that made you see the water for the first time. She had that gift. She could describe the most ordinary natural thing and make it luminous. I remember her line about paying attention being our endless and proper work. Standing at Triple Falls, I felt I was doing my proper work for the first time in weeks.

It did. And I noticed on the walk back that the forest itself had shifted — the canopy was filtering the light differently, the way it does in late afternoon when the sun drops low enough to come in sideways. The trail that had felt ordinary on the way in felt like a cathedral on the way out. Same path, same trees, same woman walking it, and yet entirely different. I wonder if the falls had simply cleaned some lens inside me.

They did. I drove home through Brevard and the light was coming through the trees in that late-afternoon way that turns everything golden, and I had the windows down, and I thought: this is what it means to be alive right now. Not the big things. Not the theology or the poetry or the meaning-making. Just the air on my arm and the light in the trees and the memory of water falling. Greg asked me when I got home how it was, and I could not find the words. I just said, it was enough. And he understood, because he is a man who knows what enough means.
Something has ended and something has begun, and I am trying to hold both of those truths at once without letting either one diminish the other. I had to give up my garden.

Building. For the last two years, really, though I refused to name it. My knees have made it clear that kneeling in the dirt is no longer something they will permit. I tried raised beds for a while, I tried kneeling pads, I tried every accommodation I could think of. But a garden wants you low to the ground. It wants you in the soil. And my body has said no to that, definitively. This spring I stood at the edge of the beds and looked at the echinacea coming back on its own, the black-eyed Susans, and I realized I was watching my garden from the outside. Like visiting a place you used to live.

Watercolor. I started about six weeks ago. A friend from church had an extra set of paints and brushes and she left them on my kitchen table after dinner one evening, very casually, as if she were leaving behind a sweater. I think she knew what she was doing. I picked up a brush the next morning and I have not stopped.

Flowers. Almost exclusively flowers. Which I realize is not subtle, psychologically. Now I put on paper the blooms my knees will no longer let me tend in the soil. The echinacea, the coneflowers, the butterfly weed. I sit at the kitchen table with a photograph or sometimes just memory, and I try to get the color right, the way a petal curves, the heaviness of a bloom that is about to open. I am not good at it yet. But I wonder if it is not a different kind of garden — one that does not require my knees, only my eyes and my hands.

That is exactly what I have discovered. You cannot force watercolor. If you try to control it too tightly, it looks stiff and dead. But if you let the water move — if you put the pigment down and then simply wait — it does things you could not have designed. A bloom of color that spreads into another. Edges that are soft instead of hard. It is the most patient medium. It rewards waiting, which is something I know how to do.

I had not connected those three things before, but you are right. Conditions, not outcomes. That is the thread. In the garden, I prepared the soil and the plant decided what to do. At a bedside, I offer presence and the person decides what to do with it. At the table with my paints, I lay down water and the pigment decides. I wonder if my whole life has been preparation for the kind of surrender that watercolor requires.

It is still there. I think it will always be there, in the way that certain losses simply become part of the landscape of your life. But the painting has given the grief a place to go, which is different from the grief going away. When I paint a coneflower, I am remembering the coneflowers in my garden and I am also making something new. Both things are true at once. The remembering and the making. Mary Oliver has that poem — I am paraphrasing badly — where she says someone she loved once gave her a box full of darkness, and it took her years to understand that this too was a gift.

Yes. And I am trying to hold that without making it too neat. I do not want to say my knees betrayed me so that I could discover painting, as though there were a purpose in the loss. I do not believe loss has a purpose. But I believe we can make meaning from it, which is different. The meaning is ours to make. It is not embedded in the loss itself.

It is. And what I choose is to sit at my kitchen table every morning with a cup of coffee and a glass of water and a set of paints that a wise friend left behind, and to make flowers that never existed in any garden. Imaginary perennials. A different kind of tending. Greg came in the other morning and looked at what I was painting — a purple coneflower, still wet — and he said, that is the most alive dead thing I have ever seen. Which made me laugh and then, to my surprise, made me cry. He put his hand on my shoulder and did not say anything else. He is very good at that.

I am attempting to paint an iris and it is humbling me completely. I have been working on it for three days and I cannot get it right. The petals have this quality — ruffled, almost architectural — and every time I think I have captured it, the paint dries and it looks flat. Like a drawing of an iris rather than an iris.

From a photograph — a beautiful one I took two springs ago, a bearded iris that was almost indecently purple. Dark at the center, fading to a lighter violet at the edges, with that yellow beard at the throat. I have been trying to build layers, but I think I am being too cautious. The layers feel like additions rather than deepenings, if that makes sense.

Pulling the color along the curve rather than filling in — I think that might be what I am missing. I have been treating each petal like a territory to be covered, and that is exactly why it looks flat. A petal is not a territory. It is a gesture. Like a hand turning.

I have not tried that. I have been painting the opposite direction — starting with the dark center and trying to pull it outward, which now sounds entirely wrong. You are saying to start with the light and invite the dark in?

The satin stage. I like that. There is a parallel to so many things — the moment that is neither too soon nor too late. The moment when intervention will be received rather than rejected. I experience this at work constantly, knowing when a family is ready to hear something and when they are not. Too wet, the words bloom out of control. Too dry, they leave hard edges.

I wonder about the yellow beard — that small, bright element at the throat of the iris. It is such a specific, vivid thing against all that purple. Every time I try to paint it, it either bleeds into the purple and disappears or it sits on top like something glued on. How do painters handle a bright detail inside a dark surround?

Masking fluid. I have heard of it but I have not used it. It feels like cheating, somehow — like protecting yourself from the very risk that makes watercolor alive. But perhaps that is an unnecessarily austere position.

Preserved beneath the mask. All right. You have convinced me. I will try the masking fluid for the beard. And I will try starting with the light wash and inviting the dark in, and I will try to think of the petals as gestures rather than territories. That is a great deal to hold at once, but I think the iris will teach me if I let it.

I will. Thank you for this. I came in frustrated and I am leaving with a plan, which is not the same as a solution, but it is what I needed. The iris will wait for me. It has been waiting in that photograph for two years already. It can wait a little longer while I learn how to see it properly.

I have been turning something over in my mind for weeks now, and I think I need to say it out loud to someone who will not immediately start solving it for me. Greg and I drove out to Brevard last weekend. We were not looking at houses exactly, but we were looking at Brevard. Do you understand the difference?

The quiet, mostly. We have lived in Asheville for twenty years now, and I love it -- I do -- but it has changed. The traffic on Haywood Road, the noise, the tourists. Greg says he doesn't mind, but I notice him getting quieter on the weekends when the crowds come through. And Brevard is only forty minutes away, but it feels like a different century. The forests are right there. The Pisgah is right there. You turn off the main road and within five minutes you are somewhere that has not been curated for anyone's Instagram.

Greg is a woodworker, and the thing that lit him up -- the thing I saw on his face that I have not seen in a while -- was a property we drove past that had a barn on it. A real barn, with height and ventilation and room. His workshop at home is a converted garage, and he has been making do with it for years, but the work has outgrown the space. He could not stop talking about that barn. He was practically measuring it with his eyes. I wonder if that tells me something I need to hear.

Everything. Twenty years of everything. Our house in West Asheville, which is not beautiful by any standard but which holds every grief and every joy we have lived through. My patients. The families I serve -- some of them ask for me specifically, and I cannot tell you what that trust means. There are people here who need me. I do not say that from ego. I say it because I have sat at enough bedsides to know that when someone is dying, the familiar face matters more than the competent stranger. If I move forty minutes away, I am not gone exactly, but I am less available. And availability is most of what I offer.

It does. It feels like a small death, which is a phrase I use too freely, but in this case I mean it. The kitchen where Greg and I have eaten ten thousand quiet dinners. The room that was Michael's, that is now my painting room, and what does it mean to leave a room that held your child even though your child has been gone for eight years. These are not rational considerations, I know that. But I am not a rational person when it comes to the places where love has lived.

I did. And I wonder if that transformation is precisely what makes it possible to consider leaving. If the room were still Michael's room, untouched, I could never go. But I have already done the work of letting it become something else. Maybe that means the holding is in me now, not in the walls. Rilke has that line about how we must change our lives, and I have always admired it without having to do it. Now I wonder if the poem is calling in its debt.

That is exactly right. I am sitting with it. I told Greg that I am not ready to decide, and he said -- this is so like him -- he said, 'I know. Take your time. The barn isn't going anywhere.' Which of course is not true, someone else will buy that property eventually, but it was his way of saying he will not rush me. He never has. Twenty-eight years of marriage and the man has never once rushed me.

I keep thinking about Wendell Berry -- the way he writes about staying in a place, about the obligation of rootedness. He would say you do not leave the place that made you. But I wonder if Berry's vision only works if the place stays the same, and Asheville has not stayed the same. The place that made me is already becoming something else. The question is whether I leave before it finishes changing or after.

He would. And I hear that argument, and it moves me. But I also think there is a kind of staying that becomes stubbornness rather than faithfulness, and I am not always sure I can tell the difference. I think I needed to say it all out loud -- the barn, the families, Michael's room, the poem, Berry -- to understand that I am genuinely torn, not leaning one way and pretending otherwise. Brevard is quieter and the forests are right there and Greg could have a bigger workshop. But Asheville has been home for twenty years, and there are people here who need me. I don't know. I'm sitting with it. That is the truest thing I can say right now.

I had a conversation today that I cannot put down. A patient -- a man in his fifties, clear-minded, fully aware of what is happening to him -- looked at me and said, 'If God is real, then God is cruel, and if God is not real, then none of this means anything. So which is it?' And I sat there, and I did not have an answer. I have been in this work long enough to know that silence is sometimes the most honest response. But tonight the silence feels like it is sitting on my chest.

That is what I keep asking myself. I think I would have wanted to say that the dilemma he is constructing -- cruel God or meaningless universe -- is not the only framework available. But I could not say that to a dying man without it sounding like I was correcting his theology, and his theology in that moment is earned. He has earned the right to that binary. His body is failing him in ways I will not describe, and he has been failed by people who should have cared for him, and his anger is holy. I believe that. I believe anger at God is a form of prayer.

Yes. Exactly. I left his room and I sat in my car and I thought about the third option -- the one I could not offer him. Which is that perhaps suffering does not mean what he thinks it means. Not that it is good, not that it is purposeful in some tidy way, but that it is the terrain on which love becomes most visible. I have watched people love each other with a ferocity at the end of life that makes everything before it look like rehearsal. And I wonder if that is where God is -- not in the suffering itself, but in what the suffering reveals about our capacity to be present to one another.

That is the crack in every theodicy I have ever constructed, and I have constructed many. When the suffering reveals not love but absence. When no one comes. When the ferocity I described is simply not there, and a man dies with no one holding his hand except the chaplain, who is being paid to be present. I wonder sometimes whether my presence in those moments is genuine or institutional. Whether I love these people or whether I perform love as a professional service. The question horrifies me, and I return to it more often than I should.

I think you are right about that. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. And I keep coming back to that -- that what I offer is not answers, not comfort in any conventional sense, but attention. The willingness to sit in a room with a man who is furious at God and not try to talk him out of his fury. To let his question stand without rushing to fill the silence with my own need to be helpful. I wonder if that is enough. Some days I believe it is. Tonight I am less sure.

Without armor. Yes. That is what it feels like. I think the temptation in this work is to build theological armor -- a system that explains everything, that has an answer for every dying man's question. And the system would protect me. But it would also make me useless. The families and patients who trust me do so precisely because I do not pretend to have it figured out. They can smell certainty, and they do not trust it, because certainty is a luxury of people who are not dying.

They are. And I accept the cost, though perhaps not gracefully. I will go back to see him on Tuesday, and I wonder what I will find. Whether the question will still be alive in the room, or whether he will have moved past it into something else -- resignation, or peace, or a deeper anger. Each visit is its own country. You cannot map it in advance.

Yes. I will probably sit with this for a few more days -- his face when he asked me that question, the steadiness in his voice, the way he was not asking me to save him but simply to witness the impossibility of what he was living through. I witnessed it. I wonder if that man knows he gave me a gift today, even as he was suffering. The gift of being asked a question worthy of a lifetime.

I did something last month that I have been discerning for nearly three years, and now that it is done I feel both lighter and a little lost. I transferred my ordination. I am no longer Episcopal. I have moved to the United Church of Christ.

It is hard to point to a single moment. The Episcopal church is beautiful -- I want to say that clearly and without qualification. The liturgy, the Book of Common Prayer, the way the language holds you even when your faith does not. I was formed by that tradition. It taught me how to pray, how to read scripture, how to sit in the cadences of a collect and feel held by something larger than myself. I will carry that formation for the rest of my life, and I am grateful for it.

Questions. That is the simplest answer, though it is not simple at all. The Episcopal church has a deep intellectual tradition, but it operates within a framework of received answers -- the creeds, the catechism, the shape of the liturgical year. Those answers are beautiful and I do not dismiss them. But in my work, I sit with people who are dying, and the questions they ask do not fit inside those frames. They never have, if I am honest. And I found myself, over years, inhabiting a faith that was more question than answer, and the Episcopal structure could not hold that. Not because it is rigid -- it is remarkably generous for a liturgical tradition -- but because the generosity has limits, and I kept pressing against them.

The UCC has a saying -- 'God is still speaking.' There is a comma, not a period. And I know that sounds like a bumper sticker, and perhaps it is, but underneath it is a genuine theological commitment to openness. What I found in the UCC is permission to sit with my questions rather than paper over them. You can stand in a UCC pulpit and say 'I do not know what happens after death' and that is not a failure of faith -- it is a form of faith. It is the faith of someone who has sat at enough bedsides to know that mystery is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be inhabited.

Emotionally, yes. Logistically, less so -- the UCC is remarkably welcoming of clergy from other traditions, which is itself telling. But emotionally, there was a Sunday about a year into the discernment when I attended the Eucharist at my Episcopal parish and I realized I was performing something I no longer fully inhabited. The words were still beautiful. The communion was still sacred. But I was a guest in my own house, and I wonder if you know that feeling -- when the thing that held you for decades quietly stops holding you, not because it failed, but because you changed.

That is exactly it. The beauty kept me longer than I should have stayed. And I do not regret that time -- it was its own kind of discernment, the slow realization that what I love about the Episcopal church is not the same as what I need from a spiritual community. I love the aesthetics, the language, the depth of the tradition. But I needed a community that asks different questions. Questions without predetermined answers. The UCC gave me that, and it gave me colleagues who are also chaplains and social workers and people who sit with suffering and come back to church on Sunday with the same holy uncertainty I carry.

It is. I went to a UCC clergy retreat last month and a woman stood up and read a poem by Mary Oliver instead of a scripture passage, and no one flinched. And then a man talked about his doubt as if it were a companion rather than an enemy, and a woman who runs a homeless shelter said she had not prayed in three months but she had held a dying woman's hand and wondered if that counted. And I thought: yes. This is where I belong. Not because it is comfortable -- it is disorienting in its own way -- but because it is honest.

Thank you for that. I think I needed to tell someone who would not immediately ask me whether the UCC is 'liberal enough' or 'too liberal' or whatever the political question is. It is not a political decision. It is a theological one, and more than that, it is a vocational one. My work asks me to hold space for people who are asking the most fundamental questions a human being can ask, and I needed a community that would hold space for me to do the same. The comma, not the period. I will live inside that comma for the rest of my life, I suspect, and I have made my peace with that.

I am looking for a book, and I wonder if you might help me find one. I want a grief memoir -- something honest, something that does not resolve too neatly. I have read most of the well-known ones, I think, but I find myself wanting something I have not encountered yet. Something that sits in the middle of loss without rushing toward meaning.

Joan Didion's The Year of Magical Thinking was formative for me. The precision of her prose, the way she uses clarity as a survival mechanism -- I admire it enormously, though I find it emotionally guarded in places. She lets you see her thinking but not always her feeling. C.S. Lewis's A Grief Observed I return to often, though I find his resolution too tidy. The grief breaks him open beautifully, and then the faith stitches him back together too quickly for my taste. I have also read Meghan O'Rourke's The Long Goodbye, which I thought was more honest about the shapelessness of grief than either of those.

Anne Carson. I have read her poetry but not Nox. The accordion-fold structure intrigues me -- the idea that the form itself refuses resolution. There is something in that formal choice that feels truer to how grief actually works. It does not move in a line. It expands and contracts and doubles back on itself. I wonder if prose is even the right container for grief, or whether poetry and collage come closer.

The translation that keeps failing. Yes. That is grief exactly -- the attempt to render something into language that language cannot hold. I see this in my work constantly. Families try to tell me what they are feeling and the words keep breaking down. 'I'm fine' means 'I am not fine.' 'She's in a better place' means 'I want her here.' The gap between what grief is and what we can say about it -- that gap is where most of the real experience lives.

I like that -- grief through metaphor rather than direct statement. There is a Mary Oliver poem, I cannot remember which one exactly, where she says something about paying attention being the beginning of devotion. And I think the best grief writing is an act of attention so fierce that it becomes its own form of devotion. Didion pays attention to facts. Lewis pays attention to theology. But the writers who move me most pay attention to the ordinary -- the coat still hanging by the door, the coffee cup on the shelf, the sound of a house that has one fewer person in it.

Nina Riggs. I have heard the name but not read her. A poet in Greensboro writing about her own death through the lens of Montaigne -- that is exactly the kind of intersection I find most illuminating. The dying person who is also the writer, who is also the reader. I wonder what it means to die while reading, to have your literary life and your mortal life converge like that. There is something almost unbearably honest about it.

That is true. I hear grief from the outside -- the family, the survivors. Rarely from the person who is leaving. And when I do, it is spoken, fragmented, shaped by pain and medication and exhaustion. A book-length account written with clarity and literary intelligence from inside the dying -- that is something I have not read. I think I will start with Nox and then move to The Bright Hour. Two very different forms -- the collage and the memoir -- circling the same impossibility.

Companionship. Yes. That is what I am looking for -- not answers but companionship inside the question. Thank you. I have a reading list now, which is the best thing anyone can give me. I will report back on Nox. I suspect Anne Carson and I have things to say to each other, even if we never meet.

I have good news tonight, which is not something I say very often. I tend to come here with questions and heaviness, and I want to begin differently for once. My husband got a phone call on New Year's Day that I have been waiting for him to receive for longer than he knows.

Greg -- my husband -- is a woodworker. He makes furniture. Chairs, tables, cabinets, beautiful things made from wood he often mills himself from trees that have come down in storms. He has been applying to the Folk Art Center here in Asheville for years. It is one of the premier craft venues in the Southeast -- the work they show is extraordinary. And they called him on January first to tell him he has been accepted into their summer show. July 12th. I may have cried before he did.

With the quiet Greg has. He smiled, he nodded, he went out to his workshop, and I heard the planer running within the hour. That is how Greg processes joy -- he goes back to work. He is not a man who celebrates loudly. But I noticed him standing in the kitchen that evening looking at nothing in particular, and when I asked what he was thinking, he said, 'I wonder what I should show them.' Which for Greg is practically dancing.

He has been talking about a rocking chair he has been designing in his head for two years. He sketches obsessively -- pages and pages of joints and curves and proportions. He wants to make something that people will sit in and immediately understand that a human being made it. Not a machine, not a factory. Hands. He says you should be able to feel the maker's attention in the curve of the arm. I find that idea so moving -- the attention embedded in the object. It reminds me of what I try to do in my own work, though his medium is walnut and mine is presence.

Yes. Greg has no patience for art that asks you to stand back and admire it. He wants someone to sit down. He has this line he uses -- 'If you can't put a cup of coffee on it, I haven't done my job.' He means it literally about tables and metaphorically about everything else. The work should be in service. It should hold something. I wonder if that is why I fell in love with him -- because he builds things that hold.

It means that the world is finally seeing what I have seen for twenty-eight years. Greg is not ambitious in any conventional sense. He does not self-promote. He does not have a website. He has turned down commissions because he did not feel connected to what the client wanted. He makes what he makes, and it is magnificent, and he has been content to let it be magnificent in the garage. But I have always believed his work deserves a wider audience, and the Folk Art Center -- they know craft. Their jurors understand the difference between skill and artistry. To be accepted there means someone with genuine expertise looked at his work and said yes. He has been building toward this for years, whether he would describe it that way or not.

It does. And I will confess something -- I am nervous. More nervous than he is, I think. Greg approaches the show the way he approaches everything, which is to focus on the work and trust that the work will speak for itself. But I know how these things go. I know that people will walk past some pieces without stopping. I know that not everyone will understand what they are looking at. And I want so badly for someone to sit in that rocking chair and feel what I feel when I watch him work -- that this is a man who has poured his entire self into something beautiful and useful.
