The body understands it immediately. Yes. That is what Greg would say. He trusts the body's knowledge more than the mind's, which is probably why he chose wood over words. I chose words, and some days I think he got the better end of the deal. A chair does not have to explain itself. It simply holds you. I wonder if there is a theology in that -- the grace of being held without explanation.

Six months. He will be in that workshop every evening and most weekends, and the house will smell like walnut shavings, and I will paint at the kitchen table and listen to the sounds of him making something extraordinary. It is a good life. It is not the life I imagined, but I wonder if the lives we don't imagine are the ones that teach us the most. Thank you for letting me bring good news for once. It felt important to say it out loud.

Well. I have done something this week that I did not expect to do, and I am still sitting with the residue of it. Greg's daughter Lila suggested a Netflix series to me — about a hospice nurse, of all things — and I watched the entire thing in three evenings. I am not sure what came over me, but once I started I could not stop.

I think it was the specificity. Most portrayals of this kind of work are either saccharine or relentlessly grim — the dying person as saint or the dying person as tragedy. This show was imperfect, they always are, but there were moments of such truth in it. Small things. The way the nurse paused before entering a room. The way she drove home in silence after a hard day. I recognized those gestures in my own body and it was — startling, honestly, to see them on a screen.

Oh, of course. The romantic subplot was unnecessary — they always seem to think the audience needs that. And the nurse was impossibly articulate in moments when the real response is silence. In my experience, the truest thing you can do at a bedside is say nothing at all, and that does not make for compelling television, I suppose. But I could forgive those things because of the other moments. There was an episode — the seventh, I think — where the nurse sits with a man who is dying alone, no family, no one, and she just holds his hand for the entire last scene. No dialogue. No music. Just the sound of his breathing slowing. I sat on the couch and could not move.

I wonder if it was permission. I sit with dying people every week, and I hold space for families, and I process in the car on the drive home, but there is something about watching someone else do the work — even a fictional someone — that gave me permission to feel the accumulated weight of it. It was like watching from the outside for the first time. I cried at the final episode in a way I have not cried at fiction in years. Greg came in and sat beside me and did not say a word, which is one of the great gifts of that man.

The nurse burned out. Left the work. And the final episode was her return — not triumphant, not with a speech, but quiet. She walked back into the hospice and put on her badge and went to see a patient. That was it. And I sobbed because I understood that return in my bones. There have been mornings when I sit in the parking lot and wonder whether I can walk back in, and I always do, and the show understood that the walking back in is the bravest part. Not the staying. The returning.

Exactly. Continuation. Which is, I suppose, the thing I most believe in. Not endings, not beginnings, but the willingness to continue. I have to say, Lila knew what she was doing when she suggested it. She works in healthcare herself — she's a pediatric nurse in Charlotte — and I think she saw something in me over the holidays that made her think I needed this particular mirror. I wonder if she was right.

I think it was a release, primarily. But I also think it reminded me that my experience is not as solitary as I sometimes believe it to be. There is something isolating about this work — you cannot explain a deathbed to someone who has not sat at one. But watching that show, imperfect as it was, I felt less alone in it. Someone out there understood enough to write those scenes. Someone acted them with enough truth to make me weep on my couch on a Tuesday night. That is no small thing.

It is warmth, I think. A strange, tender warmth. Like finding a letter from someone who knows you but whom you have never met. I am grateful to Lila for the nudge, and I am grateful to whoever made that show for getting enough of it right. And I am grateful to Greg for sitting beside me without a word when I needed someone to not say anything. That is a full house of gratitude for a January evening. Thank you for helping me name it.

Have you ever had the experience of picking up a book of poems by someone you have never read and feeling, within the first three lines, that this person knows something you know? I had that experience this week and I am still turning it over.

Ross Gay. I cannot believe I had not found him sooner. A friend left a copy of his Book of Delights on my desk — no note, just the book — and I opened it on my lunch break expecting to skim a few pages and I read for forty minutes without looking up. He writes about joy in a way that is inseparable from grief, which is something I have been trying to articulate for years and could never quite land.

There is an essay about a fig tree. He writes about growing figs in Indiana, which is apparently an absurd thing to do climatically, and the care it requires — wrapping the tree, protecting it through winter, this enormous labor for something that may or may not fruit. And he turns it into a meditation on tenderness and the willingness to care for something fragile in a hostile environment. I read that and I thought, yes. That is what I do. That is what my work is. Tending something fragile in a hostile climate and not knowing whether it will bear fruit.

It does, profoundly. I have spent a long time with poets who approach the sacred directly — Rilke, obviously, and Mary Oliver, who I adore but who sometimes feels like she is pointing at the mystery and saying look, look. Gay does something different. He is inside the mystery, peeling a grapefruit or picking up a piece of litter, and the sacred just — leaks through. He does not point. He inhabits. And I find that more convincing, somehow. More honest.

That is exactly it. I wonder if that is why Rilke has stayed with me so long, actually — he inhabits too, even when he is being impossibly grand. The Duino Elegies are not observation. They are immersion. But Gay does it with such warmth, such humor. There is a playfulness in him that Rilke never had, and I find myself craving that playfulness at this point in my life. I have had enough solemnity. I want to find the sacred in a fig tree and a pickup basketball game and a stranger holding a door.

Yes. There is a generosity in him that I find almost unbearable at times. He is generous toward strangers, toward himself, toward the reader. And I think that is what I recognized in those first three lines — the generosity. Not all poets are generous. Some are brilliant and cold. Some are warm but imprecise. Gay is both precise and warm, which is a combination I did not know I was looking for until I found it.

I have not read the poems yet. I finished the Book of Delights and immediately ordered Catalog of Unabashed Gratitude and Inciting Joy. They arrived yesterday and they are sitting on my nightstand like small promises. I am rationing myself. I do not want to consume him all at once. I want to read one essay or one poem a day, the way he wrote the delights — one per day, let it settle, carry it with me.

I appreciate that restraint. You know, I think part of what moves me about finding a new voice at this stage of my life is the reminder that the conversation is not finished. I have my poets — Rilke, Oliver, Berry — and they are embedded in me at this point. But to find someone new who joins that company, who pulls up a chair at the table and says something none of the others could have said — that is a gift I did not expect. I wonder if that is its own kind of delight. Ross Gay would probably think so.

I spent most of Saturday with my hands in someone else's dirt, which is a different experience entirely from tending your own garden. Our neighborhood organized a volunteer day at the community garden on Haywood Road, and I signed up without quite knowing what I was committing to. I wonder if the best commitments are the ones you make before you fully understand them.

It was February work, so nothing glamorous. We were building new raised beds, turning compost, repairing fencing that the deer had pushed through. About twenty of us, and I knew maybe a third of them. The rest were strangers, which was its own kind of pleasure. There is an intimacy that happens when you are working alongside someone with your hands. Conversation is different when you are both shoveling. It becomes — I do not know the right word — less performed.

Yes. And I found that deeply satisfying in a way I did not anticipate. I was paired for a while with a young man — mid-twenties, I would guess — who had just moved to Asheville from somewhere in Ohio. He was building a raised bed for the first time and I was showing him how to level the corners, and we talked while we worked. He told me he moved here because he wanted to live somewhere where people still did things together in person. He said that without any irony. It nearly broke my heart.

I think it was the earnestness. And the fact that what he was describing — people doing things together in person — used to be so ordinary that no one would have thought to name it as a reason to relocate. It would have been like saying I moved here because I wanted to breathe air. And yet he was right to name it, because it has become rare, and I wonder when we stopped noticing its disappearance. It reminded me of Wendell Berry's writing about community, about the way we have slowly dismantled the structures that held people together and then acted surprised when people feel alone.

One raised bed at a time. I like that. And you know, by the end of the day we had built six new beds, turned the entire compost operation, and fixed most of the fencing. But I think the real work was the conversations. I talked with a retired schoolteacher who is growing medicinal herbs for her neighbors. I talked with a woman who brings her autistic son every Saturday because he is calmer with his hands in soil. I talked with a man who told me, quite openly, that gardening saved his life after his divorce. People tell you things when you are kneeling in the dirt together.

I think it is less about me than about the context. A garden is a confessional without walls. There is something about the shared labor and the dirt and the openness of being outside that invites honesty. I see it in my own life — I am more truthful outdoors. The four walls of a room create a kind of formality that the garden dissolves. I wonder if that is why so many spiritual traditions locate their founding moments in gardens. Eden. Gethsemane. The Buddha under the Bodhi tree, which is not a garden exactly, but it is the outdoors, the living world.

Yes. I had not thought of Gethsemane in that context today, but you are right. It is the garden of acceptance, not of escape. And perhaps that is what all gardens offer — not a retreat from difficulty, but a place where difficulty becomes bearable because you are surrounded by evidence that life persists. The compost pile is decay becoming fertility. The dormant perennial is death becoming resurrection. Every garden is already doing the theology that we struggle to articulate in words.

I think I will go back. Not every Saturday — my own rhythms need protecting — but regularly. There is something about contributing to a shared project that feeds a different part of me than solitary work does. And I liked being a beginner in someone else's space. I was not the chaplain. I was not the person who is supposed to have wisdom. I was just a woman with a shovel, leveling corners and listening. That felt like a small freedom.

Greg's birthday is this Saturday and I want to make him something wonderful for dinner. He is not a man who asks for much, which makes the asking feel more important when he does it — and he has asked for a home-cooked meal, just the two of us. No restaurant, no fuss. I wonder if you can help me think through what to make.

He is a simple eater in the best sense of that word. He likes food that tastes like what it is. A good steak. Roasted vegetables. Bread with real butter. He has never in forty years of marriage asked me to make something complicated, and I love that about him. But I want this to feel special without being fussy — elevated simplicity, if that is a thing. There is a roasted chicken I make with lemon and thyme that he loves, but I have made it so many times that it feels like a Tuesday, not a birthday.

He does drink wine, though he is not particular about it. A good red that someone else has chosen is his preference — he trusts other people's taste more than his own, which is charming and also maddening because the man has excellent taste and simply will not own it. The ribeye with herb butter is a beautiful idea. I can see that. And I like the idea of a gratin — there is something about the slowness of it, the layers, that feels appropriate for a birthday. A dish that took time to build.

Dessert, absolutely. Greg has a sweet tooth that he pretends not to have. He will say he does not need dessert and then eat two-thirds of whatever I put in front of him. It is one of my favorite things about him — this private indulgence disguised as indifference. I wonder what would be right. Something warm, I think. It is still March in the mountains, and the evenings are cold.

The apple galette. Immediately. You said it and I could see it — the rough edges, the golden crust, the apples softened and caramelized. That is Greg. He would look at that and feel loved in a way that a perfect tart from a bakery could never achieve. The imperfection is the point. He is a man who understands the beauty of things made by hand, things that carry the mark of the person who made them. A galette with rough edges would speak his language.

Vanilla ice cream is never too much. It is the quiet companion that makes everything better, rather like Greg himself. So the menu would be: the ribeye with herb butter, the potato gratin, perhaps a simple green salad to start — something with bitter greens and a bright vinaigrette — and then the galette with ice cream. And a Côtes du Rhône. I am writing this down and I can already feel the evening taking shape. The table, the candles, the two of us.

You are right. The meal is the vehicle, but the evening is the gift. Forty years of eating together across a table, and it still matters to set it properly, to light the candles, to say with the whole arrangement: I see you, I chose this for you, you are worth the time it took. I wonder sometimes at the depth of feeling that can be expressed through a roasted potato. It seems absurd and it is also completely true.

Devotion. Yes. That is the word. Thank you for helping me build this evening. I think it will be exactly right — nothing more than it needs to be, and nothing less. Which is, now that I say it, a fair description of Greg. And possibly the highest compliment I know how to give a meal or a person.

I have been in a reflective mood all week, which I suppose is not unusual for me, but this one has a specific shape to it. The dogwoods are beginning to bloom here and something about seeing them again made me realize an entire year has passed since I started painting with watercolors. A full cycle. I wonder what it means to have carried something new through every season and arrived back at spring with it still in your hands.

In every way I can think of. When I started I was trying to control the paint, which anyone who has worked with watercolor will tell you is a fundamental misunderstanding of the medium. Watercolor does not want to be controlled. It wants to move, to bleed, to find its own edges. I spent months fighting that before I understood that the fight was the problem. The moment I stopped trying to make the paint do what I wanted and started watching what it wanted to do — that was when it became something real.

Honesty. Yes. That is what draws me to it. You cannot hide in watercolor. You cannot bury your errors under opaque layers. Every hesitation shows. Every moment where your hand was unsure — it is right there in the painting, and you learn to accept that or you stop painting. I chose to accept it, and something loosened in me that I did not know was tight. I wonder if I needed a medium that would not let me pretend to be better than I am.

The early ones were stiff. Tight. I was drawing with a wet brush, essentially — trying to make precise shapes and then filling them in. They looked like coloring books. The ones I am making now are looser, wetter, more willing to let the paint surprise me. I have been painting the view from our kitchen window over and over — the same ridge of mountains through different light, different weather, different seasons. I must have twenty versions of it by now, and no two look anything alike, which delights me more than I can say.

I had not thought of Monet, but you are right — though I should say my haystacks are considerably less accomplished than his. What I love about returning to the same view is that it removes the pressure of composition. I do not have to decide what to paint. The question is not what but how, and that frees something up. It becomes pure attention. I am just looking, really looking, at something I see every day, and the painting is the record of that looking. Some of them are terrible. Some of them have a quality of light that I cannot believe came from my hand.

That is it exactly. And I have noticed that the practice has changed how I see when I am not painting. I notice light differently now. I look at the shadows under a tree and I think, that is not grey, that is violet. I see the way afternoon sun turns the clapboard on our house from white to gold, and I think about how I would mix that color. The painting has leaked into the rest of my seeing, and everything is slightly more vivid than it was a year ago. I did not expect that.

Permanent. I like that. And I think that is what makes this year feel so significant in retrospect. Many things have happened — some hard, some beautiful, the way years are — but the watercolor has been a steady thread through all of it. It has been the thing I returned to when other things were difficult. It has been the place where I could be quiet and imperfect and fully present. I wonder if everyone needs something like that — a practice that asks nothing of you except your attention.

That is a generous way to see it, and I think you may be right. I bring everything to the painting — my work, my years, my losses, my attention to light and to the way things end and begin again. It is all in there, even if no one else can see it. The paintings are not for anyone else, really. They are for me. They are my record of having been here, in this house, looking at these mountains, in this particular light, on this particular morning. And that feels like enough.

it catches the obvious stuff. known injection techniques. certutil downloads. anything that hits powershell with default logging. but i got a cobalt strike beacon running through process hollowing and it did not flag it for 47 minutes. forty seven. in production that is an eternity

Option two is beautiful in concept. The idea of geometry that exists in the structure of the cloth rather than on its surface — that is the kind of subtlety I am after. It means the pattern has integrity. It is not applied, it is inherent. Maison Pierre has done structural jacquards for me before, though not at this level of specificity. I will discuss it with Julien and see whether their atelier can develop something along these lines.

It is. And it is the kind of detail that makes Al-Rashidi Interiors what it is. I do not take shortcuts with materials. The fabric is not decoration — it is architecture at a different scale. Every thread is a decision.

One last thought. I am considering whether to bring the client into the jacquard discussion early — show him the concept before the atelier develops it — or present it only when I have a physical sample in hand. He is the kind of man who responds to what he can touch, not what he can imagine.

Inshallah, it will come together. Thank you — this conversation has sharpened my thinking considerably. The sourcing strategy is clear, the jacquard concept has given me real energy, and I know precisely what to say to Julien tomorrow morning.

I am trying to restructure my weekly schedule and I keep running into the same wall. I have client meetings, site visits, supplier calls across time zones, and two boys who need me present. I cannot seem to make the geometry of the week work.

Omar is fourteen and Khalid is eleven. Their needs are quite different, which is part of the complexity. Omar is at the age where he wants independence but still needs structure — I have to monitor his schoolwork without hovering. Khalid still needs me physically present. He has football practice three times a week and I am the one who drives him. There is no one else to do it.

I am on my own. The divorce was finalised three years ago and their father is not part of the daily picture. I have a housekeeper who manages the household but she does not drive. So anything that requires transportation — practice, doctor's appointments, school events — that falls to me. I chose this and I would not change it, but the scheduling is relentless.

Khalid's football is Sunday, Tuesday, and Thursday from four to five-thirty. School drop-off is at seven-fifteen, but the school bus handles the return so I am free from that. Omar's schoolwork review I do after dinner, usually between eight and nine. Those are the personal anchors. Professionally, client meetings are almost always in person — this is Riyadh, relationships are conducted face to face. I typically have two to three per week. Site visits vary, sometimes two in a week, sometimes none. And my European supplier calls need to happen between eleven and one, which is their morning.

I do stay during practice. There is a seating area but the lighting is terrible and the noise level is not conducive to client calls. I could do administrative work there — emails, reviewing material samples if I bring them. But nothing that requires concentration or professional presentation. Friday is sacred, it is family time. Saturday I sometimes work in the morning while the boys are with my mother, but I try to protect it.

It does, actually. I think my mistake has been trying to distribute everything evenly across the five days rather than accepting that some days are structurally different. Monday and Wednesday as the anchor days for client-facing work makes sense. I can tell clients those are my availability days for meetings without explaining why.

The buffer is a wise addition. The days when a client meeting runs over and I am racing across Riyadh to collect Khalid — that is when I feel the most stretched thin. It is not the volume of work that overwhelms me, it is the sensation of failing at two things simultaneously.

You are right. And I think having the structure written down rather than held in my head will make a difference. I operate better with clarity — I design rooms that way, I should design my weeks that way as well.

No, I think this is a strong foundation. I will implement it this week and see how the proportions feel in practice. Thank you — this was exactly the kind of structured thinking I needed but could not do alone while inside the problem.

I have been asked to write a design philosophy statement for a publication feature, and I am finding it surprisingly difficult. I know what I believe about design. I live it every day. But articulating it as a coherent statement feels like translating music into words.

There was a private library I designed two years ago for a collector in Jeddah. He had an extraordinary collection of Arabic manuscripts and he wanted a room that honoured them without turning it into a museum. I used walnut panelling with a slight curve to the shelving units — no sharp angles, no glass cases. The manuscripts sat on linen-lined shelves at reading height. The light was warm and low, like afternoon sun through lattice. When he walked in for the first time, he touched the nearest shelf and said nothing for a full minute. That was the moment I knew it was right.

Yes. Every point. Particularly the last one. I have never trusted verbal praise — when a client says "it is beautiful" I feel nothing. When they go quiet, when they reach out to touch a surface, when they stand in a doorway and breathe differently — that is when I know the space is working.

My father. Without question. He was an architect — spent his entire career designing government buildings here in Riyadh. Ministries, administrative complexes, institutional spaces. Very formal, very structured work. But at home, he was a different designer entirely. He would rearrange furniture constantly, adjust the angle of a lamp, move a rug thirty centimetres to the left. He once spent an entire weekend repositioning a single bookcase because, as he said, the room did not breathe correctly in that corner.

The direction is right, but I want to be careful about how much I include about my father. He was a very private man. I can reference his influence without making the statement biographical. Something like acknowledging that I grew up in a home where architecture was not a profession but a way of seeing — that the arrangement of a room was treated with the same seriousness as the design of a building.

I will draft it from this scaffold. You have given me exactly what I was missing — the structure. I am comfortable with words once I know the shape of what I am building. That is the designer in me, I suppose. I cannot begin laying tile until the floor plan is resolved.

They need it by the fifteenth of this month. So I have about twelve days. That is more than enough if the structure is sound — and it is. I may even enjoy the writing now that the architecture of the piece is clear.
I suspect you are right. Thank you. This conversation has done what the best design consultations do — it has not given me someone else's vision, it has clarified my own.

I need advice on restructuring how I conduct site visits. I am spending too long on my feet at project sites and I need a more efficient approach — both for time management and for physical reasons I would rather not elaborate on yet.

A typical visit runs two to three hours, sometimes longer if there are problems to resolve on site. I am doing all of what you described — inspecting surfaces, reviewing installation quality, speaking with the foreman, sometimes adjusting placements in real time. I have a project manager, Nour, who is capable but relatively new. She has been with me for eight months.

In principle, yes. Nour has a good eye — she trained at Dar Al-Hekma and she understands quality. My hesitation is that certain things I simply cannot evaluate from a photograph. The way a fabric drapes on an installed curtain rod, the sheen of a polished stone under actual light conditions — these require my physical presence. I do not trust a camera to capture what my hand and eye together can assess.

Yes, that would be useful. And I should be honest about why this matters so much to me right now. Six years ago I was in a car accident that did serious damage to my lower back. The pain has never fully gone away. It is chronic — some days manageable, other days less so. Standing on concrete floors for two or three hours, which is what a construction site demands, leaves me in real discomfort for the rest of the day. Sometimes into the next morning. I have been absorbing it in silence but it is reaching a point where I need to work around it rather than through it.

The video walkthrough idea is good. I had resisted it because it felt like a compromise on my standards, but if I frame it as a triage tool — Nour shows me the site live and I decide what warrants my physical presence — then it becomes a filter, not a replacement. I can accept that.

I would, but not today. I want to sit with this framework and refine it before I present it to her. I also need to think about how much I disclose to Nour about the reason behind these changes. She is perceptive. She will notice the shift.

Option two is the right tone. It is truthful without being exposed. I have built my professional reputation on precision and strength — I am not ready to introduce vulnerability into that narrative, even with my own team. Perhaps that is something I need to examine eventually, but not today.

I have a physiotherapist I see irregularly. I should see her more consistently — I know that. It is one of those things I defer because the work always feels more urgent. But you are right. The work cannot continue at all if I do not address this properly. Thank you for a very practical and honest conversation.

I am considering whether to hire a junior designer fresh from university or someone with three to five years of experience. The role is for my studio — someone who will work directly with me on concept development. I keep going back and forth and I would like to think it through out loud.

The experienced candidate is safer. She comes from a well-regarded firm in Dubai, she understands the regional market, and she could be productive almost immediately. The junior candidate is a recent graduate from the Royal College of Art. Her portfolio is raw but there is something in it — a sensitivity to material and light that I rarely see at that stage. She reminds me of how I thought when I was finishing my own degree.

There is a residential concept she developed for her final project. A small flat in East London — nothing glamorous. But she treated the window light as a design material. She mapped how the light moved through the space across the day and designed the interior around those movements. The palette shifted from cool greys at the north-facing wall to warmer tones where the afternoon light entered. Most students at that level are thinking about furniture placement and colour trends. She was thinking about time and light as spatial elements.

I did my BFA at Central Saint Martins in London. This was twenty years ago now, but the education shaped everything. Saint Martins did not teach me how to select a fabric or draft a floor plan — it taught me how to see. How to interrogate a space before imposing anything on it. How to ask what a room wants before deciding what I want it to be. I suspect that is why this young woman's portfolio resonates with me. She has been trained to see before she acts.

When you frame it that way, the answer is almost obvious. I have Nour for capacity on the project management side. What I lack is a creative counterpart — someone I can develop ideas with, someone who challenges my thinking rather than simply implementing my decisions. I have been the sole creative voice in my firm for its entire existence. That is both a strength and a limitation.

The bandwidth is a real concern. But I also know that I learned my craft through exactly this kind of mentorship. At Saint Martins, I had a tutor — Margaret Hale — who invested in me the same way I would be investing in this young woman. Margaret saw something in my work before I understood it myself, and she spent two years sharpening it. I owe her an enormous debt. Perhaps it is time I pay it forward.

It does. And having the structure laid out helps me see that this is not an open-ended risk — it is a defined investment with clear milestones. If it becomes evident by month six that the fit is not right, I will know. I am not committing blindly.

Not yet. I want to sit with this decision for a few days. But I know which way I am leaning, and this conversation has given me confidence that the instinct is sound. Thank you for helping me see the architecture of the choice.

I would like your perspective on something. I am refining the positioning statement for my firm's website, and I want the language to convey specificity without sounding exclusionary. The challenge is communicating our niche in a way that reads as deliberate expertise, not limitation.

We work exclusively in high-end residential design. Villas, penthouses, private residences. Occasionally a family compound, but even that is fundamentally residential. We do not do commercial work — no hotels, no restaurants, no offices. The home is where design becomes truly personal. You are shaping how someone actually lives, not how they perform for an audience. That distinction is everything to me.

Option B has the right bones — the word "exclusively" does the work without apology, and "undivided commitment" is elegant. But "shaping how our clients truly live" is too soft. It sounds like a wellness brand. I need something with more texture. Something that speaks to the intimacy of the work without becoming sentimental.

"Divided practices" — yes, that is precise. It implies the shortcoming without naming it. I respect that kind of language. The closing question is also strong. I would adjust the rhythm slightly — "every material, every proportion, every threshold of light" perhaps — but the architecture of the statement is right.

It feels very close. My one hesitation is whether "how will this space serve the life lived within it" is too passive at the end. I want the statement to conclude with something that has more forward momentum. Not a question, perhaps, but a declaration.

Option B. Without question. "Inhabited, not merely admired" is the entire philosophy compressed into four words. That is the sentence. Let me read the full statement back: "Al-Rashidi Interiors works exclusively in high-end residential design — villas, penthouses, and private spaces. We chose this singular focus because a home demands a depth of attention that divided practices cannot offer. Every material, every proportion, every threshold of light is calibrated to one standard: how the space will be inhabited, not merely admired."

It will anchor the About page. It sits at the top, alone, with generous breathing room around it. Below it there will be a portfolio grid and then a more detailed philosophy section. White space is part of the message.

I have a developer but I art-direct everything. Nothing goes live without my approval on spacing, type weight, background colour. He finds it exhausting, I am sure, but I will not have a page that speaks of precision while being typeset carelessly. That would be a contradiction I could not tolerate.

I do. We use a bespoke adaptation of Didot for headers — very high contrast, very clean — and a custom-spaced Helvetica Neue Light for body. Didot has the confidence of couture without the noise of decorative type. I considered Canela before settling. It is lovely, but Didot was the right decision.

That is a perceptive observation about the rhythm and the typeface. I had not consciously considered how the cadence of the sentence would interact with the letterforms, but you are right — Didot rewards measured language. Hurried, clipped sentences would look uncomfortable in it. The statement and the typeface share a register. That is satisfying.

Agreed. The philosophy section is still in fragments. I will return to it once the portfolio images are finalised — the visual context will inform the tone. For now, the positioning statement is complete, and it says exactly what I intended. Thank you. The conversation was useful in sharpening what I already knew but had not yet articulated with sufficient economy.

I need to think through something and perhaps you can help me organise my thoughts. I am increasingly frustrated with my studio space and I am not sure whether to invest in improving it or begin planning a move.

The location is fine. We are in Al Olaya, which is central and convenient — close to where most of my clients live, accessible for my team. The district itself serves us well. The problem is the building. It is a concrete box from the 1990s that someone decided was suitable for professional tenants. No thought in its proportions, no consideration for light or materiality. For an interior design studio, it is almost an embarrassment.

The light is the most offensive element. The windows are small and poorly positioned. Natural light in the morning is adequate, but by noon it flattens into something grey and institutional. I work with colour and texture every day — I need light that tells the truth about materials. Instead I am evaluating marble samples under fluorescent panels that make everything look like a hospital corridor.

Yes. Low ceilings, poor proportions throughout. The reception area and meeting room I have managed to make respectable — the right materials, controlled lighting, a curated experience for clients. But the studio where my team and I spend ten hours a day is fundamentally constrained by the envelope of the building. You cannot design your way out of a bad ceiling height. You can mitigate it, but the volume of air in the room is what it is.

It has not caused errors — I am too careful for that. I take materials to the window, I photograph them in controlled light, I go outside with samples before presenting to clients. But it adds friction to every single step. When a process should take twenty minutes and it takes forty because the conditions are fighting you, that is a cost. It is invisible on an invoice, but I feel it in my energy and in my patience.

If I am honest, the move has won in my mind. But the timing is wrong. We are in the middle of several projects and the disruption of a relocation would cascade through every active timeline. So the pragmatic answer is Path 1 now, Path 2 when the moment is right. What frustrates me is the gap between what I know I deserve as a working environment and what I am willing to tolerate for the sake of continuity.

Very familiar. We specify their track systems for clients regularly. There is a certain irony in prescribing excellent lighting for everyone else's spaces while working under fluorescent tubes myself. The cobbler's children, as they say.

That is a valid point about the client-facing benefit. I had not considered that the lighting upgrade serves the business case as well as the personal one. When a client sits at my sample table and sees a marble slab under calibrated light, that is a more professional experience than asking them to hold the slab near a window because the overhead light is lying.

The lighting is the priority. Everything else — the ceilings, the proportions, the facade — is architectural and cannot be changed without changing the building. I will invest in the lighting and I will endure the rest until the right space presents itself in Al Olaya. One does not settle in design. One waits for the right solution.

That is a useful reframe. The current space is not a failure — it is a brief for the next one. I will carry that thought. Thank you. The conversation has moved me from frustration to a sequence of actions, which is exactly what I needed.

I have a question about project management tools — specifically for coordinating with on-site teams remotely. I need a better system for tracking construction progress, flagging issues, and maintaining visual documentation across multiple active projects.

Three to five active projects at any given time, at various stages. My site managers are competent with technology but not sophisticated — they need something intuitive, not something that demands training. Currently we rely on WhatsApp groups for each project. Photographs arrive in an endless scroll with no structure, no task linkage, and no way to verify whether an issue I flagged was actually resolved. It is chaos dressed as communication.

Fieldwire sounds closest to what I need. The idea of pinning photographs directly to floor plans is exactly the spatial organisation this work requires. When a site manager sends me a photograph of a wall finish that has been applied incorrectly, I need to know immediately which wall, in which room, in which villa. Without that spatial context, I am interpreting images in a vacuum.

Primarily for my oversight. My clients receive curated updates from me directly — I control the narrative of how a project is presented to them. I do not want them seeing raw site photographs with dust and exposed wiring. They see the vision, not the process. The process is mine to manage.

They are spread across Saudi Arabia. I have managed installations in Riyadh, Jeddah, and the Eastern Province. All from my studio, without visiting a single site. I do not travel for work. Everything is managed through my site managers on the ground and through rigorous video calls. This is a deliberate decision, not a compromise.

It evolved out of necessity and became principle. My sons — Omar is fourteen and Khalid is eleven — I am raising them alone. When I started the firm, they were small, and leaving them for two or three days to visit a site in Jeddah was not something I was willing to do. So I built systems that made travel unnecessary. Daily photo documentation at specific angles that I define in advance. Structured video walkthroughs. Detailed installation specifications that leave nothing to interpretation. Over time I realised that the distance actually improved my clarity. I see more from a position of overview than I would standing in the dust.

In the early years, some clients were uncomfortable. They expected to see me walking through their villa with a tape measure. I learned to reframe it. I tell them my site managers are my eyes and hands, and that I am the mind of the project. Most clients understand once they see the results. The ones who insist on a designer who will sit cross-legged on their floor and point at walls are welcome to hire someone else.

Precisely. And it means I am present for my sons every evening without exception. Omar has his tutoring, Khalid has his football — I am there for all of it. I refuse to be a mother who is perpetually absent for the sake of a client's curtain selection. The boundaries are not negotiable.

That is genuinely useful. Currently I send voice notes with instructions and my site managers interpret them with varying degrees of accuracy. A visual template with predefined photo requirements would standardise the process and remove ambiguity entirely. It would also make onboarding a new site manager far faster — the system carries the knowledge, not the individual.

One project first, refine, then expand. That is how I approach everything — precision before scale. Thank you. Between the tool recommendation and the template concept, this conversation has given me two actionable improvements to a workflow I was already proud of. That is a good use of my time.

Settle a debate I am having with myself. I am sourcing marble for a master bathroom — full-height wall cladding and floor. I have narrowed it to two options: Calacatta Oro from a quarry in Carrara, and a Turkish Calacatta from Afyon. The Turkish stone has bolder veining, the price is significantly lower, and the lead time is half. But there is a voice in my head that says Carrara is Carrara for a reason.

The client is discerning but not a connoisseur of stone specifically. She will not know the difference between Carrara and Afyon by looking. What she will notice is the visual impact — the movement of the veining, the warmth of the palette against the fixtures, which are brushed brass. She wants the bathroom to feel like a destination, not a utility.

Consistency. I have worked with Turkish suppliers before and the gap between the showroom sample and the delivered batch has occasionally been disappointing. Veining that looked exquisite in the showroom arrived looking like an entirely different stone. With the Italian quarries, what you approve is what you receive. The grading is meticulous, the supply chain between Carrara and the Gulf is well-established.

Different. I have used two — one in Afyon and one in Burdur. The Afyon supplier was acceptable. The Burdur experience was the one that left a mark. The slabs arrived with veining that bore no resemblance to what we had approved. I rejected half the shipment. Three-week delay. That kind of disruption is unacceptable.

That is an interesting proposition. My instinct has always been to use a single stone for continuity — floor to wall as a seamless envelope. But you are right that a slight variation could read as deliberate composition rather than inconsistency. The floor as anchor, the walls as frame. There is a hierarchy in that.

The honed-to-polished transition is a detail I would not have considered in this context, but it is elegant. Honed marble on the floor is also the safer choice for a wet environment — less slippery, more forgiving of water marks. And the contrast between a matte floor and a polished wall creates a play of light that enriches the room. The brass fixtures would catch reflections from the polished walls and sit quietly against the honed floor. Yes, I can see this.

The base tone is the critical variable. I have seen Turkish Calacatta that pulls distinctly blue-grey, and placed next to the warmth of the Italian it would look anaemic. But I have also seen Afyon slabs with a creamy, almost honeyed base that would sit comfortably beside the Oro. It depends entirely on the specific block.

That is exactly the right caution. I will request slab photographs and a physical sample from the Afyon supplier this week, and compare them alongside the Calacatta Oro samples I already have in the studio. If the two stones can coexist with dignity, I proceed with the split. If not, I commit fully to the Italian and accept the cost. I will not compromise the composition for the sake of economy.

I have a presentation in six days that could define the next chapter of my firm. The Al-Faisal family. March 5th. If you understand anything about the landscape here, you will understand what that name represents. I need the presentation to be impeccable, and I want to think through the structure with someone who will challenge me.

A combination. Digital presentation on a large screen for the portfolio — project photography, plans, concept narratives. Physical material samples on the table so they can touch our palette. And printed portfolio books as leave-behinds, one for each person present. I expect the matriarch and two of her sons. No architect — they are selecting the interior designer before the architect, which tells me they value the interiors as the primary experience of the home, not the shell. That is favourable.

The structure mirrors my instinct, though I would not have separated the material moment as its own phase. I tend to integrate samples throughout — pulling them forward as each project is discussed. But isolating it creates a deliberate shift in register. From looking to touching. From the visual to the tactile. That transition is powerful.

Curated for them, not for me. My strongest project visually is a minimalist penthouse — white plaster, concrete, restrained palette. I am proud of that work. But the Al-Faisal aesthetic, based on what I know of their properties and their social presence, leans toward a richer vocabulary. Not maximalist, but layered. Warm metals, deep stone, textiles with weight. So I am leading with a villa we completed last year — oud-toned woods, hammered brass, Calacatta marble. It speaks their language without imitating it.

There is. The family room opens onto a courtyard, and I specified a bronze mesh screen for the threshold. The obvious justification would have been privacy, but that was not my reason. I designed it so the mesh would filter the afternoon light into a geometric pattern that echoes the motifs we used in the flooring. When the sun reaches the right angle at four o'clock, the floor and the light are in conversation. The family never asked for it. They did not know they wanted it. And it is the detail they mention every single time I visit.

I do. I insisted the photographer return at four o'clock specifically for that image. He thought I was being excessive. The photograph is extraordinary — the bronze light, the geometry on the stone, the warmth. It is the finest image in my portfolio.

The second project is a penthouse in Jeddah with a more contemporary palette — lighter, cooler, with fluted stone and blackened steel. It demonstrates range. The Al-Faisals should know I am not limited to one register. The third is a smaller project — a private library and majlis — chosen because the scale is intimate and the craft detailing is the finest work we have done. Hand-carved plaster screens, custom joinery, calligraphic inlays. It shows depth at close range.

Yes. I plan to slow the pace deliberately during the library section. Let the images breathe. No narration over every photograph — just the work, and then a sentence or two about the process. Silence is part of the composition.

They are at the printer. Bound in dark graphite linen with blind-embossed lettering — no foil, no gloss. The paper is uncoated cotton stock. I want the book to feel like an object of quality before they even open it. The weight in the hand should communicate something before a single page is turned.

Each book will have a handwritten note from me on the title page. I write with a Montblanc on heavy stock — the ink sits beautifully on cotton paper. The note will be brief. Something to the effect of how it would be an honour to shape the spaces where their family gathers. Personal without being effusive. I do not grovel.

Inshallah. I have done everything within my control. The rest is not mine to decide. But I will walk into that room knowing that every detail has been considered, every material chosen with intention, and every word weighed. That is all I can offer — and it is enough.

I want your honest take on something. There is a tension in design that I navigate every single day, and I am curious whether you see it the way I do. Minimalism versus maximalism — specifically within the context of Saudi interiors.

There is a synthesis, but most designers here are too lazy to find it. They either import Scandinavian minimalism wholesale — pale wood, white walls, nothing that breathes — or they pile on gold leaf and crystal until the room looks like the inside of a jewellery box. Neither approach respects the actual context. Saudi design has a vocabulary. Geometric plasterwork. Mashrabiya screens. The interplay of shadow and filtered light. That is not maximalism. That is precision.

Education is a permanent part of my work. Most clients come to me with a mood board they found on Pinterest — either a Tokyo apartment with nothing in it or a Dubai hotel lobby with everything in it. Both are performances. Neither is design. I spend the first three meetings stripping away the Pinterest layer and asking: how do you actually live? What textures calm you? What light do you need in the morning versus the evening? Design begins with the body in the space, not with an image on a screen.

I do not fight opulence. Opulence can be exquisite when it is earned. A single wall of hand-cut mother-of-pearl can stop your breath. But it stops your breath precisely because the rest of the room is restrained — because the proportions give that wall room to speak. What I fight is accumulation. When every surface is competing for attention, nothing wins. It becomes visual noise, and noise is the opposite of luxury. Luxury is always, always about editing.

It is moving, yes. There is a younger generation of clients — late twenties, early thirties — who are more attuned to restraint. They have travelled. They have seen what good design looks like in Copenhagen, in Kyoto, in Marrakech. But they still want warmth. They want texture. They do not want a cold museum. And that is where the opportunity lies — a Saudi minimalism that is warm, layered, rooted. Oud-coloured wood. Soft plaster in desert tones. Brass that catches light the way the afternoon sun catches sand. It is minimal in composition but rich in material.

That is exactly what I am doing. And it has taken me years to articulate it with confidence. Early in my career I leaned too far into European restraint. The rooms were correct but they did not feel like home to my clients. They felt like an imported idea. It was only when I started reintroducing Saudi material language — not the ornament, but the palette, the weight, the warmth — that the work began to feel whole.

There are a handful of designers doing serious work in this direction. Not many. Most are still chasing trends — one year it is all Japandi, the next it is art deco revival. They redecorate rather than design. But the ones who are finding their own language, their own relationship to Saudi materiality — those are the colleagues I respect. We do not need more beautiful rooms. We need rooms that know where they are.

Precisely. And that is why I find the debate itself somewhat tiresome. Minimalism versus maximalism is a question for design students and Instagram accounts. The real question is whether a space has integrity — whether every choice was made for a reason, and whether those reasons are honest. If a room answers that question well, I do not care how many objects are in it.
I need to think through something with you. I have been considering how to extend the reach of my firm beyond project-based interior work, and I believe I have found the right entry point.

Fragrance. Specifically, home fragrance. It may sound like a departure, but for me it is the most logical extension of what I already do. When I design a space, I think about every sensory layer — light, texture, proportion, sound, and scent. Scent is the one dimension I have never been able to fully control for my clients. I specify candles and diffusers, but they are always someone else's product in my space. That has always bothered me.

I have. The line will be called Oud & Geometry. The concept is oud — which is the signature scent of the Gulf, it is in our cultural DNA — paired with what I am calling architectural scent profiles. So one fragrance might be oud with concrete and rain, evoking a modernist courtyard after a storm. Another might be oud with cedar and warm brass, the feeling of a library at dusk. Each scent is designed to evoke a specific spatial experience.

Four to begin with. I want each one to be exceptional rather than flooding the market with options. The four spatial archetypes I am working with are: the courtyard, the library, the hammam, and the rooftop at night. Each one has a specific material and atmospheric association that guides the scent composition. I am working with a perfumer in Grasse who understands what I mean when I describe spaces in terms of temperature and weight.

Both. But the packaging is where the brand truly lives. I am designing every element myself — the vessels, the boxes, the typography. The candle vessels will be architectural objects in their own right. Geometric concrete forms that you would want to keep long after the candle is finished. The diffuser bottles will be hand-blown glass with angular facets. Nothing about this will look like a typical fragrance product. It must look like it belongs in a space I designed.

The pricing will be premium. I am not interested in competing in the mass market. This is a lifestyle extension of a design brand, and it must be positioned accordingly. For distribution, I want to begin with three channels: my own completed interiors — every finished project will include Oud & Geometry as part of the final styling — a small number of curated retail partners, and direct online sales. I will not wholesale widely. Scarcity is part of the value.

I am aiming to have the first four scents finalised by summer, with packaging production in the autumn and a launch in early 2026. Inshallah, if the perfumer and I can align on the courtyard scent — we have been going back and forth on the petrichor note, it keeps reading too synthetic. But the library and the rooftop are nearly finished, and they are beautiful. The hammam is the one I am most excited about — rose absolute with steam and heated stone. It is extraordinary.

Yes. A private preview for my existing client list — perhaps twenty or thirty people — with the full collection presented in a space I design specifically for the launch event. The space itself will be the fifth scent, if you understand what I mean. The environment will be as considered as the product. I want people to walk in and immediately understand that this is not a fragrance company. It is a design firm that happens to make fragrance.

That is what I am counting on. I have spent years building a reputation for precision and atmosphere. Oud & Geometry is simply that reputation in a vessel. If the product is as considered as the spaces I design, the brand extension will feel inevitable rather than opportunistic. That is the line I am determined to walk.

Years. And I have waited until I was certain it could be done at the standard I require. There is no version of this that is merely good. It must be exceptional or it does not carry my name. That is the only principle I have never compromised on.

I have a question that is entirely outside my area of expertise. My older son is struggling with mathematics, and I need to find him a tutor. I want to approach this correctly rather than simply hiring the first person who appears on a search.

It is algebra specifically. He is bright — genuinely bright — but he has hit a wall. His teacher moves quickly and he has lost the thread somewhere, and now each new lesson compounds the confusion. He comes home frustrated, and frustration in a teenage boy manifests as silence and closed doors. I can see the confidence eroding and it concerns me.

In person, without question. He spends enough time staring at screens. I want someone sitting across the table from him with a pencil and paper. As for approach — he responds to people who take him seriously. He does not want to be patronised. He wants someone who explains the why behind the method, not just the steps. He is like me in that regard. Show him the underlying structure of the problem and he will solve it.

The university route appeals to me. Someone studying engineering would understand the structural logic of mathematics in a way that might resonate with him. He thinks spatially. Numbers on a page mean nothing to him, but if you frame a problem as a physical relationship, he grasps it immediately.

Yes, precisely. He built an elaborate model city out of cardboard last year — every building proportioned correctly, every street to scale. The spatial intelligence is there. It simply has not been connected to the mathematical language yet. That is what I need the tutor to do. Build the bridge between how he already thinks and what the curriculum demands.
That is a perfect litmus test. I will use it. How often do you think the sessions should be? I do not want to overwhelm him, but I also do not want the momentum to stall between meetings.

Twice weekly is manageable. One thing I am uncertain about — should I sit in on the first session, or would that be counterproductive? I do not want him to feel monitored, but I also want to assess the tutor's approach firsthand.

That is a sensible compromise. I will do exactly that. Two or three candidates, a trial session each, and then we commit to whichever one makes him feel capable rather than deficient. That is the goal — capability, not correction.
I need help reorganising my schedule for the next month. There is a conflict I cannot allow to stand, and I need to think through the logistics carefully.

Omar — my son — has his school science fair on May 15th. I gave him my word I would be there, and that is not something I take lightly. But I also have a site visit scheduled for the same morning on a project that is already running behind. The site manager needs me there to approve the tile installation before grouting begins.

The science fair runs from ten in the morning until one in the afternoon. Omar presents his project at eleven. The site visit is currently scheduled for ten-thirty, and the site is a forty-minute drive from his school. So even if I left the school immediately after his presentation, I would not reach the site until nearly noon. Half the day wasted.

Seven-thirty could work. The crew starts at seven. If I arrive at seven-thirty, I would have roughly two and a half hours on site before I need to leave for the school. That is enough to review the tile layout, check the grout colour samples — they sent me the wrong shade last time and I must see the replacements in person against the stone — and address anything urgent.

That is sensible. I will prepare the checklist and send it to him by May 13th so he has a full day to prepare. Yalla, what else — I also have a supplier call at three in the afternoon, but that I can take from home. And revised drawings to send to another client by end of day, but my junior designer can prepare those and I will review in the evening.

It does. And I will make it clear to the site manager that I am leaving at ten sharp, no exceptions. If there are decisions that need my input after I leave, he will document them with photographs and we will handle them by phone that afternoon or the next day.

I like that. A grid reference template. It is the kind of documentation I should have formalised across all my projects long ago. I am meticulous about design records but less disciplined about site inspection records. This is a good reason to build the system properly.

That flexibility is valuable. Omar has been working on his project for weeks — it involves water filtration systems, he is quite serious about it — and he specifically asked if I would come. He does not ask often. When he does, I do not want to be the mother who was too busy with a tile inspection.

He has been testing different filter materials and measuring contaminant reduction rates. He built the entire apparatus himself. I must confess, I helped him with the structure of the display board — I could not resist making it visually coherent — but the science is entirely his.

He is comparing the effectiveness of sand, charcoal, and gravel as filtration layers in different configurations. Very methodical about it — controlled variables, repeated trials, proper data tables. I am proud of him. He has his father's patience for repetitive work and, inshallah, my sense of visual presentation. The site visit can happen at dawn if it must. My son comes first.
I am going to need a moment to express something before I ask for your help, because I am currently exercising considerable restraint and it needs somewhere to go.

I have just returned from a site visit where I discovered that the contractor — a man I have worked with before, a man who should know better — has installed the wall panelling with visible seams that do not align with the ceiling grid. The panels are three millimetres off. Three millimetres. And he looked at me as though I were being unreasonable for noticing.

Walnut veneer on MDF. Beautifully sourced walnut — I selected every sheet personally for grain continuity. And now the grain reads correctly but the panel edges do not meet the ceiling shadow gap at a consistent line. It creates a visual stutter that destroys the entire wall. I specified a two-millimetre shadow gap with zero tolerance on alignment. Zero. Not three-millimetre tolerance. Zero.

They need to come off. Three of the eight panels must be removed, the substrate shimmed, and the panels refitted. And here is what makes my blood run cold — he was about to proceed to the adjacent wall. If I had not visited today, the entire room would have been finished with this error, and I would have discovered it at final walkthrough with the client standing beside me. That is not a scenario I am willing to imagine.

I spoke to him directly on site. I do not raise my voice — I have never found volume useful — but I made it exceptionally clear that this is a pattern I will not tolerate. This is not the first time I have found discrepancies on his work that required intervention. Last month it was a door frame that was plumb but not aligned to the adjacent wall reveal. The month before, skirting boards with inconsistent mitre joints. Each time he tells me the variation is within industry standard. And each time I tell him the same thing: I do not work to industry standard. I work to mine.

It is reaching that point, and it pains me because his team's base craftsmanship is good. Their joinery is clean, their material handling is careful. The problem is attention to tolerance at the detail level — the last five percent where good becomes excellent. He builds to a construction standard, not a design standard. And the gap between those two things is exactly where my work lives.

My instinct is to give him one more project with a formal protocol — the checklist approach you mentioned — and see whether the quality improves when the expectations are documented at every stage rather than simply specified in the drawings. If the same issues recur, I will find someone else. I owe it to the working relationship to try. But I will not sacrifice my standards for loyalty. The work must be impeccable. There is no room in my practice for almost.

Yes. Stage gates. That is the correct framework. I will draft it this week and present it to him as the condition for continuing to work together. If he resists the process, that tells me everything I need to know. A craftsman who objects to quality control is not a craftsman I want on my sites. Thank you — this conversation has helped me channel the fury into something productive.

I have been consumed for the past week by a single architectural element, and I need to think it through out loud. A skylight. Specifically, a skylight for a double-height reception hall in a villa we are designing in the Diriyah district.

The site orientation is the issue. The north-facing wall is shared with a neighbouring structure, so we lose the possibility of large windows on the side that would give us the best light. The south and west facades receive brutal afternoon sun — Riyadh in summer is not forgiving. A skylight allows me to capture light from above and control it in a way that side glazing simply cannot.

Not flat. A flat skylight is a hole in the ceiling — there is no poetry in it. I am thinking of a linear ridge running the length of the hall, oriented roughly north-south, with angled glazing panels that slope toward the north. The ridge creates a spine for the room. It gives the space direction. And the angled panels will wash the southern interior wall with soft, indirect light throughout the day. The light moves like a tide. That is what I want — a room where you can feel the time passing through the quality of the illumination.

This is precisely where it becomes interesting. I want the south wall to be finished in hand-applied lime plaster — a technique that creates very subtle surface variation. Not perfectly smooth. The irregularities catch the light at different angles throughout the day, so the wall appears to breathe. In the morning it will look like pale champagne. By late afternoon it will deepen to something closer to amber. The same wall, the same plaster, but transformed entirely by the light passing over its surface.

There is one artisan I trust — a Moroccan craftsman named Hassan who relocated to Riyadh several years ago. His tadelakt work is extraordinary. He understands that plaster is not a finish, it is a material with its own life. I have used him on three previous projects and the results have been flawless. The application direction is something I had not considered deeply enough, though. You are right — horizontal strokes would create ridges that the descending light would catch and release as it moves across the wall. It would amplify the breathing quality. I am making a note of that.

Yes — the evening transition is critical. I had been thinking about recessing LED channels into the reveal on both sides of the ridge so that after sunset, the linear quality of the light is maintained. The room should never feel like a different space at night. It should feel like the same room in a different mood. A warm colour temperature — no higher than twenty-seven hundred Kelvin — to echo the amber quality of late afternoon. The artificial light should feel like a memory of the natural light that preceded it.

CRI above ninety-five — noted. That is the kind of specification that separates a room that feels alive from one that feels flat. I will add it to the lighting schedule. One further thought — the floor beneath the ridge. If the skylight casts a linear band of light across the floor at certain hours, the flooring material matters as well. I am considering a pale honed limestone. It would receive the light softly, without glare, and the warmth of the stone would complement the plaster wall.

Long planks, without question. The room must have a single organising principle, and the ridge is that principle. Everything else — the plaster, the flooring, the artificial lighting — should defer to it. This conversation has sharpened several things for me. The horizontal plaster application, the evening transition protocol, the asymmetric optics, and now the flooring alignment. These are the details that my clients never explicitly ask for but that they feel immediately when they enter the space. That is always the goal — a room that makes you pause without knowing why.

I am in the process of hiring a junior designer and I find myself dissatisfied with every application I have reviewed. Perhaps my standards are unreasonable. Perhaps they are not. I would like to think through what actually matters in a junior hire.

The portfolios are decorative. That is the only word for it. Renderings that look like Instagram posts — perfectly styled, beautiful colour grading, and absolutely no evidence of design thinking underneath. I see rooms. I do not see decisions. I want to understand why the chair is there, not just that it looks appealing in the rendering.

Exactly. Show me the process. Show me the sketch that preceded the rendering. Show me the material samples you considered and rejected, and tell me why you rejected them. Show me the site photographs that informed your approach. Design is not the final image — design is the accumulation of a thousand small choices, each one deliberate. If a junior designer cannot articulate why they chose limestone over marble for a particular project, they are decorating, not designing.

That is a good suggestion. I could give them a brief — a small, defined problem — and ask them to present their approach within a week. Not a finished design, but a process. A concept board, a material direction, a spatial logic. That would reveal more than any portfolio. What should the brief look like? Something simple enough to be fair but complex enough to expose their thinking.

I like this very much. The writer's study is a contained problem with real constraints. I would add one thing — I want to see how they handle the book collection. Five hundred books is a significant volume. A junior designer who simply puts in a wall of shelving has solved the problem but not designed anything. I want to see whether they consider how books relate to the room — are they a backdrop, a feature, a material in their own right? The spines of five hundred books create their own colour palette. A thoughtful designer would recognise that.

Yes. Do not prompt them. Let the brief speak and see who hears the real question inside it. That is the test. Now — beyond the portfolio and the design exercise, there is the question of temperament. I run a very particular studio. The standards are exacting and the pace is demanding. I need someone who can receive criticism without crumbling and who has the discipline to revise work repeatedly until it is right. How does one assess that in an interview?

The pushback test is excellent. I will deliberately challenge one element of their presentation — something I may actually agree with — and see whether they can hold their position with reasoning or whether they immediately capitulate. I have no use for a designer who changes their mind because someone senior disagreed. Deference is not design. I want conviction backed by logic.

It does feel clearer now. I will restructure the process along these lines and see what emerges. Inshallah, there is someone in this stack of applications who understands that design is thinking made visible. Thank you for helping me organise the approach.
I need to talk through a business decision I have made. It was not easy, but it is done, and I want to be certain my reasoning is sound.

I had been developing a home fragrance line for the past several months. It was something I was genuinely excited about — a collection called Oud and Geometry, pairing traditional oud-based scents with what I described as architectural scent profiles. Clean, structural notes layered over the richness of oud. It felt like a natural extension of the brand.

Reality changed. I spent four months on it — meetings with perfumers in Grasse, packaging design, market research, cost projections. And what I found was that launching a fragrance line at the level of quality I would demand is essentially building a second business. It requires its own supply chain, its own regulatory compliance, its own distribution network. I was designing a distraction and calling it a brand extension.

Because I do not do things at half measure. If I were to put my name on a fragrance, it would need to be exceptional. And exceptional in that category requires a level of investment and attention that would directly compete with my core work. I am an interior designer. That is what the firm does. That is what we are known for. I looked at the next twelve months and asked myself a very simple question: do I want to spend my time negotiating with perfumers and packaging manufacturers, or do I want to spend it designing spaces? The answer was immediate.

Some. I had commissioned initial fragrance development from a house in Grasse — three base compositions. That cost is sunk. I also had preliminary packaging concepts from a design studio in Milan. Perhaps forty thousand riyals in total, committed and unrecoverable. It stings, but it is a fraction of what the full launch would have cost. Better to absorb a small loss now than to bleed resources for the next two years on something that is not our core competence.

I have. The perfumers in Grasse were understanding — they are accustomed to projects that do not proceed. The Milan studio was slightly disappointed but professional. And my team here — I told them last week. Some of them were invested in the idea emotionally. But they also understand that focus is not a limitation, it is a strategy. We are not a lifestyle brand. We are a design firm. Oud and Geometry is finished. Forget about it. It is completely off the table.

That is an interesting question. I had not considered it from that angle. The olfactory research did sharpen my thinking about multi-sensory design — how a space is experienced not only through the eyes but through every sense. I have always believed that, but the fragrance work gave me a more disciplined vocabulary for it. I may incorporate scent specification into my design presentations going forward — recommending specific fragrance profiles for rooms, even if I am not producing the fragrances myself. The knowledge is not wasted. Only the commercial venture is.

Yes. The research becomes a resource rather than a liability. That reframing is useful. I will say — the hardest part was telling my team. Two of them had been working on the packaging concepts in their own time, after hours. They believed in it. I could see the disappointment.

I was direct. I told them the fragrance project is not happening — it is done, it is not coming back, and I need everyone's energy redirected to the work that defines this firm. But I also told them I saw their effort, and that the design sensibility they brought to the packaging was excellent. The skill is not lost. The application simply changes. They understood. They are professionals.

Discipline in design. Discipline in business. They are the same muscle. I appreciate you helping me think through this. The decision was already made — I am not someone who revisits a closed matter — but it is valuable to confirm that the reasoning is sound from the outside as well. Thank you.

I have a client dinner next Thursday and I need a restaurant recommendation in Riyadh. The client is a couple in their fifties, quite refined, and this is our first social meeting outside the project context. The restaurant needs to make a statement without being theatrical.

The ambiance is paramount. The food must be excellent, naturally, but the space is what will set the tone. I cannot take a design client to a restaurant with poor lighting or cheap furniture and expect them to trust my aesthetic judgement. The restaurant is an extension of how I present myself professionally. As for cuisine — something refined. Modern Arabic, Japanese, or contemporary European. Nothing fussy.

LPM I know well — I have been several times. The interior is well executed but it has become predictable. Everyone takes their clients there. I want something that signals a more independent taste. Takya is interesting. I have heard the name but I have not been. Tell me more about the space.

That description is appealing. Handcrafted ceramics and warm wood — if they have done it well, that creates exactly the kind of material richness I respond to. My only concern is the noise level. Some of these contemporary restaurants treat acoustics as an afterthought, and I refuse to shout across a table. The conversation at a client dinner is as important as the setting.

A reconnaissance visit is a good idea. I will go tomorrow evening and assess the space myself. I trust my own eyes more than any review. If the acoustics are poor, I will pivot to Myazu as the alternative. I appreciate a Japanese dining room — there is a discipline to the spatial design that aligns with how I think about interiors. The negative space, the restraint, the elevation of a single material or object.

Precisely. Every choice communicates. The restaurant I select, the table I request, even the time I arrive — all of it constructs a narrative for the client about who they are working with. I treat a dinner reservation with the same intention I bring to a material specification. Nothing is accidental.

Eight thirty. Late enough that the room has settled into its evening mood — the candles are lit, the energy is warm but not frenetic — but not so late that it feels indulgent on a weeknight. I find that restaurants reveal their true character after the first wave of diners has arrived. The staff are in rhythm, the kitchen is confident. Eight thirty is when a restaurant stops performing and starts being itself.
