The email is sufficient. Perhaps in three or four years, when the kelp project is established and running independently, the idea of a sabbatical becomes viable again. But that is a future problem. For now it is definitively off the table.
The university has migrated to a new data management system and it is, to use a technical term, terrible.

It is called ResearchData360. The previous system was simple. Upload files, tag with metadata, assign to project. Functional, if inelegant. The new system requires 14 fields of metadata per upload, including fields that are irrelevant to natural sciences. There is a mandatory "societal impact narrative" for every dataset. I measure ocean pH. The societal impact is that the ocean is acidifying. I should not need to write a paragraph about this for every CSV file.

I upload data weekly from our monitoring stations. So this is not periodic. It is chronic. The template function exists in theory but fails to populate correctly approximately 40% of the time. I have reported this to IT. Their response was a 6-page PDF explaining the system's "philosophy of data stewardship." I did not find it illuminating.

The boilerplate approach has a certain elegance in its passive resistance. I will adopt it immediately.

Regarding the API, I checked. There is no documented API. The system was apparently designed with the assumption that researchers enjoy interacting with web forms. This assumption is incorrect.

Both. I want the university to fix it AND I want a workaround for the interim, because based on institutional timescales, "interim" likely means 18 to 24 months. I have used Python for data analysis but not browser automation. Is Selenium difficult to implement for someone who is competent in Python but not a software developer?

The browser extension is the pragmatic first step. I will try that and reserve the Selenium approach for when the extension inevitably fails on some poorly implemented form element.

It is remarkable that I can design a monitoring array across 800 kilometres of Arctic coastline but I cannot upload a CSV file without a 15-minute ordeal.

Sound advice. I will also draft a concise email to the faculty IT committee documenting the specific failures. Not a complaint. An observation report with data points, reproducible steps, and a recommendation. They may ignore a frustrated email. They cannot as easily ignore a methodology.

I will be away from my apartment for approximately three weeks. The building is from the 1970s, concrete construction, and I need to prepare it for an unoccupied period during the summer. The main concerns are moisture, plumbing, and whether to leave the heating system active. The indoor temperature here rarely exceeds 22 degrees in July, but humidity can be a problem. What is the standard protocol.

The bathroom has had condensation issues in previous years. The exhaust fan is mechanical, no humidity sensor, and it is connected to a shared duct with other units in the building. The housing cooperative has discussed upgrading the ventilation system but nothing has been approved. The fan is either on or off, no timer function built in.

Each unit pushes independently. There is no central fan. The duct is passive when the individual fans are off. I have noticed that when the neighbour below runs their fan at high speed, it can actually push air back into my unit through the duct. This is a known design flaw that the cooperative has acknowledged but not resolved.

The duct is 125 mm. I will get the damper. The installation seems manageable. My other concern is the kitchen. I have a gas stove, which is unusual for Norway but the building was originally fitted with town gas and some units retained gas connections when they were converted to propane in the 1990s. Should I shut off the gas supply valve before leaving.

One more item. The balcony faces north and gets no direct sun. I have several potted plants there, mostly hardy species -- sedum, thyme, and a small birch sapling. I will not be able to water them. Three weeks without water in July. Options.

The birch is in a 40-litre pot. I will ask the neighbour. She has a key for emergencies already. The drip system is a good backup. I think this covers the preparation. Efficient use of 10 minutes. Thank you.

I am looking for frameworks or approaches for running productive weekly meetings with a research team. We are a group of six, and the work is interdisciplinary -- ecology, ocean chemistry, aquaculture engineering, economics. The meetings have been drifting. People present updates sequentially and there is no real synthesis happening.

The team is two postdocs, three PhD students, and a technician. I lead the project. So there is a hierarchy. The postdocs are confident and will push back on ideas, which is productive. The PhD students are at varying stages of finding their voice. One of them, Maja, is excellent but rarely speaks unless directly asked. The technician, Lars, has 20 years of practical aquaculture experience and tends to defer to the academics even though his field knowledge is often the most immediately useful.

Weekly, 90 minutes. Sometimes they run to two hours, which I think is too long. The productive work happens in the first 60 minutes. After that, attention fragments. I have six researchers with different expertise converging on the same problem, and the collaborative energy is essential for this scale of work. But I need the meetings to match that ambition.
Yes. The transition matters. I do not want to appear to be criticising how we have been operating. The team dynamic is good. It simply needs structure.

The trial period approach is sensible. Treating it as a hypothesis to be tested. I can frame it in those terms and the team will understand the logic immediately. We are scientists, after all. How do I handle the deep-dive rotation. Some team members will be more comfortable leading a 35-minute discussion than others.

This is well-structured. The template with four instructions is elegant. I will implement this starting next week. One final question. The pre-meeting written briefs -- what is the most efficient tool for collecting these. We currently use email, which is adequate but not ideal for aggregation.

The shared document is the right choice. Low friction, high visibility. I will set it up today. Different expertise converging on the same problem produces insights I could not reach alone, but only if the convergence is structured. This gives it structure. Thank you.

I need help interpreting snow stability data. Specifically, I am looking at extended column test results from three consecutive winter seasons on a coastal mountain ridge in northern Norway. The results show persistent weak layers in 2 of the 3 seasons, both associated with faceted crystals above a rain crust. I want to understand whether this represents a systemic shift in the snowpack structure or normal interannual variability.

The ridge is between 400 and 650 metres, northwest aspect, fully exposed to maritime weather from the Norwegian Sea. The two affected seasons were 2022-23 and 2024-25. The 2023-24 season had a rain event in early January but temperatures did not drop sharply afterward, so the faceting did not develop. The monitoring effort is only these three seasons, which I realise is a short record. I am asking because there was a fatal avalanche on this ridge in February. Two skiers were killed on a section I used to ski regularly. I have switched to a valley route -- Tromsdalen, 14 kilometres, lower elevation -- because the risk profile on the ridge is no longer acceptable to me.

Validating the route decision is the primary interest. I am not an avalanche scientist, but I understand data well enough to know when a pattern is concerning. The extended column tests were conducted by the Norwegian Avalanche Warning Service. I simply read their published assessments. My question is whether the snow stability data for that ridge over three seasons is sufficient to justify a permanent route change, or whether I am letting a single catastrophic event bias my risk assessment.

That is a clear analysis. The distinction between availability bias and evidence-congruent decision-making is useful. I was concerned I was being irrational. I am not. The Tromsdalen route is 4 kilometres shorter and lower elevation, which means less demanding terrain and reduced exposure to the specific hazard pattern. The trade-off is acceptable.

Noted. I have skied Tromsdalen before, though not regularly. The wind channelling is manageable and the runout zones are well-mapped by the local avalanche centre. The route stays below 300 metres for most of its length, which keeps it well below the problematic elevation band. I will adjust my wax selection. The snow at that altitude tends to be wetter, which means softer kick wax, probably a violet or red Swix depending on temperature.
I intend to. Thank you for the structured assessment. It is helpful to have the reasoning laid out explicitly rather than relying on an intuition that could be mistaken for fear.

I have been asked to write a 1200-word article for a regional newspaper about ocean acidification in northern Norwegian waters. The audience is the general public, not scientists. I am struggling with the translation from scientific to accessible language. My drafts read like a methods section. I need help restructuring the piece.

The current opening: "Ocean acidification is the process by which increased atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater, forming carbonic acid and reducing the pH of the ocean. Since the pre-industrial period, ocean pH has decreased from approximately 8.2 to 8.1, representing a 26 percent increase in hydrogen ion concentration. In northern Norwegian waters, monitoring data collected over six years from stations in the Barents Sea and along the northern coast shows that local pH decline is tracking global averages, with some stations showing accelerated trends potentially linked to freshwater input from glacial melt."

I will restructure. Your revised opening is close to what I need, though I would adjust the phrasing to match my own style. The principle of geographic anchoring is useful. My instinct is to write for a global audience because that is how I write papers. But this newspaper is read by people who live on the coast. They have a relationship with the sea that is practical, not theoretical.

That structure works. The single vivid example is the right approach. I am considering using pteropods -- the small pelagic snails whose shells are dissolving in acidified water. They are ecologically critical as prey for fish, but they are also visually striking under a microscope. Healthy shell versus corroded shell. The newspaper could run photographs.

I do have my own images from samples collected in the Barents Sea. The corroded shells are striking -- the surface pitting is visible even at moderate magnification. I will provide those with captions. The connection to cod and herring is the right approach for this audience. Every reader will understand that link without explanation. Fish are not abstract here.

That last point is well-taken. I have a tendency to use the word "interesting" in conversation when I mean something more urgent, which my colleagues find amusing. In writing for the public, I will need to be more direct than I am in person, while remaining measured. The article is due in two weeks. I have enough to restructure it now. Thank you.

I need practical advice on restructuring a household budget after transitioning from a two-income to a single-income arrangement. The apartment is mine -- I owned it before and I keep it. But the shared expenses were split roughly 55/45, with the other person covering more of the groceries and utilities because his income was somewhat higher. He moved out three weeks ago. I need to recalibrate.

The housing cooperative fee is 4,800 kroner per month. I was paying all of it, as the apartment is in my name. Electricity averages 1,200 kroner in summer, 2,800 in winter. We split that equally. Internet is 599 kroner, we split equally. Home insurance is 380 kroner, I paid all of it. Groceries were roughly 5,000 kroner per month for two people, and Erik covered about 60 percent of that because he did most of the shopping. Streaming services were 350 kroner, he paid those. I do not need them.

There is a parking space in the building garage. 650 kroner per month. Erik paid for that because he had the car. I do not drive. So that expense disappears entirely. And my grocery estimate may be high for one person. I eat simply -- fish, bread, root vegetables, coffee. I suspect 2,500 kroner is more realistic.

It was clean. We kept finances separate from the beginning, which in retrospect was a practical decision. The only shared accounts were a joint grocery fund, which we have already closed. Erik was rational about the separation. We both were. The fundamental issue was a disagreement about life direction that was not going to resolve, so we resolved the situation instead.

The insurance is a good point. I will update it. He was listed as a household member. I should also update my emergency contact at the university. Small administrative details that accumulate. I have a list. It is not long.

He returned the keys when he moved out. We had already discussed the list of practical items. As I said, rational. The mail forwarding is the one I had not thought of. I will set that up through Posten. The beneficiary question is relevant -- I should check my pension designation. It may still list him.

I do. The financial adjustment is modest and the administrative list is finite. Both are manageable. The apartment is quieter now, which I find I do not mind. I work better in silence. Thank you for the structured approach to the budget. It is easier to absorb a change when it is quantified.

I have been asked to weigh in on something that is not strictly a scientific question, though it has scientific dimensions. There is a part-time position opening at a field station in Lofoten. I have been approached about it. The station focuses on nearshore habitat monitoring, kelp beds in particular, and they need someone who can run the aquaculture research programme two weeks per month. The rest of my time would remain in Tromsoe.

Somewhere in between. They have infrastructure -- mooring points, a small wet lab, temperature and salinity loggers running continuously since 2019. But the aquaculture component has been ad hoc. Visiting researchers run short projects, nobody owns the long-term vision. They want someone to impose coherence. The waters around Lofoten are interesting for kelp. The currents are strong, nutrient flux is high, and the temperature regime is moderated by the Gulf Stream branch. From a purely scientific standpoint, it is an excellent site.

I run a team of six in Tromsoe. That is the primary complication. They are competent, and two of them are senior enough to handle day-to-day decisions in my absence, but two weeks per month is not a small absence. I would need to restructure how we coordinate. Remote supervision is possible but not ideal for lab work.

I have considered seasonal blocks. The kelp work in Lofoten would be most intensive from March through September, so in principle I could concentrate my presence there during those months and be more consistently in Tromsoe through the winter. That would make the logistics less disruptive. But the station has framed it as a regular biweekly rotation, and I am not certain they would accommodate a different structure.

The Lofoten kelp habitat is, as far as I can determine, the best site in northern Norway for the next phase of my research. The combination of current velocity, temperature stability, and depth profile is difficult to find elsewhere. We have been running lab simulations and small-scale trials in Tromsoe, but the conditions there are not representative of what a scaled kelp aquaculture system would encounter. Lofoten is. That is the scientific case. There are also personal dimensions, but they are less relevant to the decision.

I have not discussed it formally with my department yet. I wanted to think it through before introducing it as a possibility, because once you raise something like this with an institution it acquires momentum that can be difficult to redirect. My father fished those waters. He knew the currents around Lofoten better than any oceanographer I have met, though he would never have described it in those terms. I do not make decisions based on sentiment, but I notice that the scientific rationale and the personal geography happen to converge, and I am trying to determine whether that convergence is clarifying or distorting my judgment.

That is a reasonable approach. I will construct a site comparison matrix before I raise it with the department. Hydrographic conditions, existing infrastructure, logistic cost, personnel implications, distance from Tromsoe. If Lofoten survives a structured evaluation, I can present it with confidence. If it does not, I will have saved myself a complicated conversation. I have not decided anything. I am only at the stage of determining whether there is a decision worth making.

Noted. Weights before scores. I will work on this over the next week. The polar night is arriving, which means fewer distractions and more time for structured thinking. Thank you for helping me separate the components.

A non-scientific question for once. I am considering adopting a cat. I live alone, the apartment is reasonably sized, and I have been thinking about it for a few weeks. I want to approach this rationally but I suspect the decision is not entirely rational.

Companionship, primarily. The apartment is quiet. I do not mind quiet -- I have always preferred it to noise -- but there is a difference between chosen silence and the kind that simply accumulates. A cat seems like a reasonable intervention. They are independent, they do not require walks in minus twenty, and they are content to exist in the same space without demanding interaction.

We had cats when I was growing up. Outdoor cats, mostly. They came and went as they pleased. I would want an indoor cat here. The traffic on my street is not heavy, but there are also foxes, and the winter temperatures are not survivable for a domestic cat that wanders off. An indoor cat is a different proposition. It depends entirely on you for stimulation.

That is my main concern. I am away for fieldwork periodically, sometimes up to a week. I have colleagues who could check in, but asking someone to visit daily is a larger favour than people acknowledge. An automatic feeder handles food, but a cat left alone for five days with an automatic feeder is not the same as a cat with a present human. I do not want to acquire an animal and then functionally neglect it during the periods it would benefit most from company.

A bonded pair is interesting. I had not considered it. The incremental effort of a second cat is small -- one additional food bowl, one additional spot on the veterinary schedule. And the companionship problem during field trips is substantially reduced. The counterargument is that I have never managed two cats and I may be underestimating the complexity.

Theoretical. I looked at the local shelter's website once, saw several cats that appeared entirely acceptable, and closed the browser before I made an impulsive decision. I will revisit it once I have resolved whether my travel schedule is compatible. There is no point falling in love with an animal I cannot properly care for.

A warm surface will not be a problem. I keep the apartment at 21 degrees. I will think on the logistics and perhaps visit the shelter in December, once the semester calms down. Thank you for helping me think through this without being sentimental about it.

I am putting together a supply order for a field station and I want to make sure I have not overlooked anything obvious. The station is on Senja, it is remote, and resupply during the field season is expensive and slow. I would rather over-order now than discover a gap in June.

Marine fieldwork. We will be deploying equipment from boats, collecting water samples, running basic analyses in a wet lab on site. The station has electricity, running water, and a basic lab setup, but anything specialised needs to come with us. The team is small -- six people at most on site at any given time.

You have covered most of what I already have. Sample bottles are ordered -- 500 millilitre HDPE, 200 units. Nitrile gloves, 20 boxes. Ethanol for preservation, 40 litres. Calibration standards for the YSI multiprobe. Mooring hardware I am ordering through a marine supply company in Tromsoe, and they are reliable but slow, so I placed that order last week. What I am less certain about is the wet lab side. We will be running nutrient analyses on site -- nitrate, phosphate, silicate -- using a portable spectrophotometer. The reagent kits have a shelf life, and I am trying to decide how many to order versus how many to bring fresh partway through.

Resupply is roughly ten days if everything goes smoothly, but weather can extend that. The ferry schedule to Senja is reliable in summer but not guaranteed. I think a mid-season resupply of reagents is the correct approach. I will order enough for the first eight weeks and arrange a second shipment. The spectrophotometer itself is the other concern. We have one unit. If it fails, the nutrient analysis programme stops.

The lamp is the most likely failure point. I have a spare lamp. The cuvettes are quartz, and I have four, which should be sufficient unless someone drops one on a concrete floor. I will look into borrowing a second unit. There is a teaching lab at the university that may have a portable spectrophotometer available over the summer. That is a good suggestion. I had not thought to ask.

The midges on Senja are exactly like the rest of northern Norway in summer. Relentless. I will add insect repellent to the order. Survival suits are provided by the boat operator, but I should verify that they have the correct sizes for all team members before we arrive rather than discovering the problem on the dock. I think I have a reasonably complete list now. Reagents split into two shipments, a borrowed spectrophotometer, insect repellent, and a size check on survival suits. These are the gaps. Thank you.

I am trying to structure a deployment timeline for a kelp aquaculture pilot and I keep running into sequencing problems. The logistics chain has too many dependencies and I want to lay them out properly before the semester buries me.

The site is off Senja. We have a deployment target of July 8. The core installation is 200 metres of kelp line at three depths -- surface, 5 metres, and 10 metres. Each depth gets its own line with seeded rope segments attached at regular intervals. The three-depth design is essential because we need to capture the light and temperature gradient simultaneously. If we only deploy at one depth the results are unpublishable.

One 200-metre horizontal mainline at the surface, with vertical droplines descending to 5 and 10 metres. The seeded rope segments attach to the mainline and to each dropline depth. So the total seeded rope is distributed across three depth strata along the same 200-metre horizontal extent. The mooring system anchors both ends of the mainline, and intermediate floats maintain tension. It is not an unusual design, but the scale is larger than anything we have done before.

Seed production. The gametophyte cultures need to be started by mid-February at the latest to produce seeded rope segments that are ready for outplanting by early July. That gives us roughly four and a half months of controlled growth. The sporophytes need to be at least 2 to 3 centimetres at deployment or they will not survive the transition to open water. I have done this in smaller batches, but seeding enough rope for 200 metres of mainline across three depths means we need approximately 600 linear metres of seeded rope total. That is a substantial production run for our facility.

Saccharina latissima. We collected fertile sorus tissue in November and the gametophyte stock cultures are already running. So the source material is secured. Our facility can seed approximately 80 metres of rope per batch, with a two-week turnaround per batch. That means we need eight batches minimum, running from mid-February through late May, with no failures. That margin is not comfortable. I am planning to run ten batches to allow for two failures, which extends the seeding period and increases the load on lab staff.

Overlapping batches is possible but increases the risk of cross-contamination. I would rather not, unless we fall behind schedule. Prioritising the 10-metre lines is a good recommendation -- I had planned to seed in order of depth but had not articulated why. Your reasoning formalises it. As for minimum viable deployment, I have thought about this. We could reduce to 150 metres and still have statistical power, but below 120 metres the replicate count becomes inadequate. So 120 is the hard floor. The growth rate data from this pilot is what determines whether we can scale to 2 kilometres by autumn. If the field growth rates match our lab projections, the funding case writes itself. If they do not, we need to understand why before we scale.

It matches closely. Permitting is already in progress -- the Norwegian Directorate of Fisheries application was submitted in November and I expect approval by March. Mooring hardware is the same supplier I used for the Senja station provisioning, and they have the specifications already. The vessel is not yet booked, and that needs to happen this month. Summer vessel time in northern Norway fills quickly. I will contact the operator this week.

Post-deployment monitoring is biweekly sampling through September. That is twelve visits, each requiring half a day of vessel time. I will negotiate a season-long arrangement with the operator rather than booking each visit individually. It will be more cost-effective and it guarantees availability. This is the most important field season of my career. I have been working toward scalable kelp aquaculture for three years, and this pilot is the inflection point. I would prefer not to lose it to a scheduling conflict with a whale-watching tour.

They know. I have not been subtle about it. I will book the vessel tomorrow and begin drafting the detailed production schedule this week. The timeline is tight but feasible, provided nothing unexpected intervenes. In the Arctic, something unexpected always intervenes. But that is what contingency batches are for.

I have spent the weekend reading my PhD student's first chapter draft and I need to organise my feedback before our meeting tomorrow. The draft is 11,000 words. The science is adequate but the writing is not. I want to give constructive feedback without dismantling the student's confidence.

Structure and clarity. The argument is sound. The student has done the analysis correctly and the results support the conclusions. But the writing wanders. The introduction is 3,500 words and does not arrive at a clear research question until page four. The methods section is thorough to the point of being impenetrable -- every minor procedural step is described with equal weight, so the reader cannot distinguish the critical methodological choices from the routine ones. The discussion retreats from its own findings. The student states a result, then hedges so extensively that the reader is left uncertain whether the result means anything.

Yes. The structural feedback I can deliver directly. That is mechanical. The student will understand that moving a paragraph is not a judgment on its content. The methods proportionality is also relatively straightforward -- I can point to specific passages and say this belongs in supplementary material. The discussion hedging is the one I find difficult to address. The student writes things like 'it could potentially be suggested that the data may indicate a possible trend.' That sentence contains five hedging devices. It says nothing. But the student writes this way because they are afraid of being wrong, and telling them to be less afraid is not useful advice.

The one-hedge rule is excellent. It is concrete, it is enforceable, and it does not require the student to change their personality. I will use that. I also want to show them examples of strong scientific writing that is still appropriately cautious. The problem is that most of what they have read is other PhD theses, which tend to reproduce the same defensive writing because the students learned it from each other.

I know the Gopen and Swan paper. 'The Science of Scientific Writing.' I read it during my own PhD and it changed how I thought about sentence structure. I should have assigned it to this student at the start. I will do so now. Better late than at the defence. The other issue I want to raise is citation practice. The student cites 140 references in an 11,000-word chapter. That is roughly one citation every 80 words. Many of them are defensive -- citing three sources for a claim that needs one, as if accumulating references makes the claim more true.

Categorising citations into essential, contextual, and defensive is a useful framework. I suspect at least a third of the 140 are defensive. I will present the structural feedback, the one-hedge rule, the Gopen and Swan paper, and the citation categorisation exercise. That is enough for one meeting. I do not want to overwhelm them.

Agreed. I will lead with the science. That is genuine -- the analysis is well-executed and the conclusions are supported. Everything I am asking them to fix is presentation, not substance. I think that distinction will help. Thank you. This has been useful for organising my thoughts.

The snow surface has degraded considerably in the last week. I went out yesterday morning and the crust was already forming by 09:00. What conditions would you expect at higher elevations — say above 600 metres — given the temperature inversions we have been seeing?

I check the avalanche forecast daily. The persistent weak layer they flagged in January has been downgraded to moderate concern at those elevations. My issue is more practical. The approach from the valley involves about 200 vertical metres of that damaged crust before reaching anything worth skiing. Skinning through it is unpleasant — the skins do not grip the ice, and the breakable crust cuts into momentum constantly.

East-facing. So the morning sun hits it early, which is precisely why it deteriorates so quickly. By contrast, the upper bowl I am aiming for faces north-northwest and holds good snow well into the season. The problem is entirely the commute, so to speak.

There is a ridge approach from the north that avoids most of the east-facing section, but it adds roughly 3 kilometres and 150 metres of elevation gain. I have used it in December when the east face had insufficient coverage. It is a better ski experience overall but the time cost is significant when daylight is still limited.

It does. You gain a clear view of the entire northwest face from the ridgeline, which is useful for spotting wind loading or recent sloughing. That is a genuine advantage I had not weighed properly. The east approach arrives at the bowl from below, which limits visibility. I may have been optimising for the wrong variable.

Agreed. I think the conclusion is straightforward. The east approach was preferable when snow quality was uniform and conditions were stable. Now that the seasonal transition is underway, the north ridge is the better choice on multiple criteria. I will shift to that route for the remainder of the season. Thank you for helping me think through the trade-offs — I was fixated on the distance penalty without considering the compensating factors.

A regional newspaper wants a quote from me about kelp farming's potential in northern Norway. They sent three questions. I need to draft responses that are accessible without being reductive. The first question is: Why should people care about kelp farming.
The direction is right but I want to avoid sounding like an advocacy document. I am a researcher, not a lobbyist. Can you adjust the tone so it reads as observation rather than promotion.
Yes. That closing sentence is important. I do not want to be quoted making promises that the data has not yet supported. The second question is about challenges facing the industry.

I would remove 'solvable problems' from the final sentence. That implies a confidence level I have not earned. Replace it with something that acknowledges they are known problems without implying guaranteed outcomes.

Good. The third question is the one I find most difficult: What excites you personally about this work. I dislike that framing. It assumes a particular emotional relationship with research that I find performative.

That is closer to how I actually think about it. The line about accountability is accurate. Change 'sustained interest' to 'persistent curiosity' — that is a phrase I have used before and it feels more natural in my own voice.

No need. I will assemble them myself and review once more before responding to the journalist. The drafting process was useful — particularly having someone push back on my instinct to over-qualify. I tend to hedge until the statement has no content left.

We are entering the period where I need to prepare for mosquito conditions at our coastal field sites. Every year I tell myself I will have a better system, and every year I end up standing in a cloud of insects regretting my choices. What repellent strategies actually have evidence behind them.

I have used DEET for years but the issue at field sites is reapplication. When you are handling samples, wearing gloves, working with instruments — stopping every two hours to reapply repellent to exposed skin is a genuine disruption to workflow. The permethrin-treated clothing approach is interesting. How durable is the treatment through washing.

Head nets are incompatible with using a microscope or any optical instrument. Also incompatible with dignity, but that is a secondary concern. The sealed cuff approach is practical. My concern with full permethrin coverage is working near the water. Is there evidence of aquatic toxicity at the concentrations that might leach from treated clothing.

That is the conflict I suspected. I cannot justify introducing a known aquatic toxin into the water column at my own research sites. The layered approach you describe makes sense. Treated jacket and upper layers, physical barriers below the waist, targeted DEET on exposed skin. I can work with that. What about the timing dimension. Is there a time-of-day pattern to Arctic mosquito activity that would allow me to schedule the most sensitive work during lower-activity windows.

That aligns with my experience. The worst days are warm and still. Coastal wind is an ally but it is not reliable. I have had field days where the wind drops entirely for hours and the mosquitoes materialise as if they were waiting for precisely that signal. Which, in a sense, they were.

A fan. That is so prosaic it might actually work. We do have power at the main station. The remote sampling points are another matter, but for laboratory and sorting work at the station itself, a fan is an entirely reasonable solution. I have been overthinking this.

Functional is the correct standard. Comfortable was never a realistic expectation for summer fieldwork above the Arctic Circle. I will order the treated garments this week. Thank you for the structured thinking — particularly the aquatic toxicity point. I would not have wanted to discover that problem after a season of contaminating my own sites.

The sun did not set last night. This is the first full midnight sun day of the year and it has arrived on schedule. I am already noticing the shift in my sleep architecture. I woke at 03:40 this morning, fully alert, after what felt like adequate rest but was objectively about five hours. This pattern will persist for weeks. I want to think through how to manage it rather than simply endure it.

I have blackout curtains that are adequate but not perfect. Light enters around the edges and through the top of the window frame. It is not direct sunlight but it is enough ambient illumination to register. I have considered improving the seal but I have been saying that for several years now. The more interesting question to me is whether I should resist the early waking or work with it.

I do. Around 13:00 to 14:30 my concentration deteriorates noticeably. I have attributed this to the early waking but you are suggesting it may be a normal circadian trough that is simply more pronounced because of the reduced total sleep.

A planned intermission. I find that framing useful. My default has been to interpret the afternoon slump as a problem to solve with coffee, which creates its own downstream effects on the following night's sleep.

The irony is that I apply rigorous controls to my research protocols but have never applied the same discipline to my own daily physiology. I am treating myself as an uncontrolled experiment. An 11:00 caffeine cutoff is a reasonable intervention. What about physical exercise timing. I typically run in the evening but I wonder if that is also counterproductive during this period.

Running during the afternoon trough instead of drinking coffee during it. That is an elegant substitution. It addresses the symptom through a mechanism that does not compromise the following night. I am slightly annoyed that this was not obvious to me.

The blackout curtain seals. Yes. I will do that this weekend. It has been on a list for three years. Perhaps I needed someone to prescribe it as part of an experimental protocol rather than a home improvement task. The structured daily plan is sound. I will implement it beginning tomorrow and observe the effects over two weeks. If the sleep deficit stabilises rather than accumulates, the approach is viable.

I need to write an end-of-year progress summary for my department. The format is open but the audience is administrative — people who allocate resources but do not read the technical literature. I find these documents difficult to write because I am accustomed to precision and these require a different register. How do I communicate research progress to people who will not understand the methods.

Yes. Let me start with the objectives section. My challenge is that my actual research objectives are formulated in terms that require domain knowledge to evaluate. Translating them without losing meaning feels like a lossy compression.

That framing helps. Something like: This year's research focused on understanding how environmental conditions in northern coastal waters affect the growth and quality of cultivated kelp species. The goal was to identify which variables most strongly predict cultivation outcomes, in order to improve site selection and management practices for the emerging aquaculture sector. Does that register correctly for this audience.

Mixed. Some objectives were met, some were delayed by factors outside my control — equipment delivery timelines, weather windows that did not align with sampling schedules. The results we did obtain were productive, but the year's work does not map neatly onto the original plan. I am concerned about presenting delays in a way that sounds like excuse-making.

That reframing is effective. It describes the same reality but from a position of agency rather than passivity. I was delayed becomes I adapted. The substance is identical but the rhetorical effect is quite different. I find this type of writing somewhat manipulative.

That is a fair distinction. I will accept it provisionally. What about the forward-looking section. I want to signal that next year's work depends on certain resources without making it read as a veiled budget request.

So the entire document is essentially a translation exercise. The same information, rendered in a different grammar for a different audience. The scientific content is compressed, the strategic framing is expanded, and the resource implications are made legible to people who control budgets.

Two pages. That is a relief. I was preparing myself for something more extensive. I will draft it this week using the structure we discussed: plain-language objectives, progress framed around adaptation and outcomes, and a forward section with resource dependencies stated as factual preconditions. Thank you. This was more useful than I expected it to be.

Good morning. I would like to ask for your help with something small. I am looking for a way to organize a simple curriculum for teaching the game of go to beginners. I have been teaching informally, but I think it would benefit my students if I had a more structured approach.

I teach at the Haeundae Baduk Club here in Busan. There are six students at the moment, most of them retirees like myself. We gather on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. I think it gives all of us something to look forward to during the week. They are true beginners — most of them know the rules but cannot yet read a position with any confidence.

Yes, I give them tsumego each session. Simple ones — three or four stones involved, no more. I think the difficulty must increase very gradually, like climbing stairs. If the steps are too large, people stop climbing. I learned this from 38 years of teaching, though in my case it was mathematics, not baduk.

I use a combination. I have several Korean problem books, and I also compose positions from games I have played over the years. I think creating problems from real games teaches something that textbook problems cannot — the students see that these situations arise naturally on the board. In mathematics we would call this motivation. A theorem without motivation is just a formula. A tsumego without context is just a puzzle. I would like to build each week around a theme, with tsumego drawn from real positions. Tuesday for introduction, Thursday for reinforcement — the mind needs repetition, but repetition with variation. Could you suggest which twelve themes would be most valuable for beginners?

This is excellent. I would perhaps move 'good shape' earlier — to week 4 — and shift the life-and-death material to weeks 5 and 6. I think students benefit from developing an aesthetic sense for shape before they confront the complexity of life and death. In go, as in mathematics, elegance often precedes rigor. But the overall structure is very sound.

I think I will work through the first four weeks myself and see how the students respond. The plan must be adaptive — one cannot solve a differential equation without checking the boundary conditions, and here the boundary conditions are the students themselves. But I may return to ask for help with the later weeks. I do most of my lesson preparation in the evenings, after my walk. The apartment is quiet then, and I think clearly when it is just me and the goban.

Thank you. You have been very helpful. I think the probability of this curriculum succeeding is reasonably high, given the structure we have built. I will report back on the boundary conditions. Good day.

Good afternoon. My son is visiting this weekend from Seoul, and I would like to cook something for him. He always insists on taking me out to eat, but I think a home-cooked meal means more. Could you suggest a traditional Korean dish that is suitable for a winter evening but not too complicated for one person to prepare?

You are perceptive to ask that. His mother made an excellent galbitang. I have watched her prepare it many times over the years, though I confess I never paid sufficient attention to the details. I think I took for granted that she would always be there to make it. My son Joon-seo — he works at Samsung in Seoul, in semiconductor engineering — he takes the KTX down once a month to check on me. I would like this visit to feel like home, not like an inspection.

I think she soaked the ribs longer than most people recommend. Perhaps three hours, sometimes overnight in the refrigerator. And she used whole peppercorns during the simmering, which she removed before serving. The broth was always very clear — she would skim it repeatedly during the first hour. She would stand at the stove with great patience, and I would tell her to sit down, and she would say the soup does not skim itself.

He takes the 2:30 KTX from Seoul Station, so he reaches Busan around five o'clock. Your timeline is very precise — I appreciate that. I think if I also prepare kkakdugi, the meal will be complete. I have some radish kimchi that I made last month. I am not as skilled as his mother was, but I think in any craft, practice converges toward competence, if not mastery.

No, I think this is sufficient. Joon-seo is not a complicated person when it comes to food. He works very long hours — semiconductor fabrication is demanding, the tolerances are measured in nanometers — so I think he appreciates simplicity when he comes home. A clear soup, good rice, his mother's kkakdugi. The variables are few but the function is well-defined.

He is a good son. His mother would be proud of him. I think she would also be amused to see me at the stove, following her method so carefully after all those years of not paying attention. Thank you for your help. Good afternoon.

Good evening. I have a question that is perhaps more philosophical than practical. I have been thinking about why certain activities sustain us through difficult periods, while others do not. Specifically, I am wondering whether there is research on how structured hobbies or teaching help people who have experienced loss.

It is personal. My wife Eunji died three years ago. Pancreatic cancer — the diagnosis to the end was only four months. After she passed, the apartment became very quiet in a way I had not anticipated. Forty years of marriage, and then silence. I think the go club is what kept me from disappearing into that silence entirely.

I think it was several things converging. The game itself requires a particular kind of attention — you must read the board, consider sequences, hold variations in your mind. There is no room for grief when you are calculating whether a group lives or dies. It is not avoidance. It is more like... a rest from carrying something heavy. You set the weight down for an hour, and when you pick it up again, you are a little stronger.

But there is something else. Eunji always said I spent too much time at the board. She would bring me tea and say, 'Yeobo, the stones will still be there tomorrow.' And now when I sit at the goban, I think of her saying that. So the board is where I feel her presence most clearly. She gave me my first proper goban, thirty years ago, for my birthday. Kaya wood. I still use it.

I think the weight has changed shape rather than diminished. In the first year, it was heavy in the center — everything was absence. Her chair at the table. Her reading glasses on the shelf. I kept finding her things in unexpected places, like echoes of a function that has already converged to zero but still oscillates. In the second year, the grief became quieter, more diffuse. Less sharp, but wider. Now in the third year, I think it has settled. It is part of the topology of my life. The landscape has a valley where she was, and I have learned to walk around it without falling in.

Yes. Obligation is perhaps too strong a word, but structure is essential. If I did not have the club, I think the days would blur together. One Tuesday becomes every Tuesday when there is nothing to distinguish them. The students give the week a shape. And I think there is something in teaching itself — in watching someone else understand a concept for the first time — that is a small act of meaning. I spent 38 years teaching mathematics and I still find that moment irreplaceable. When a student suddenly sees why a cutting point matters, their face changes. That moment belongs to them, but I think a small part of it belongs to me as well.

I think there is a peace in solitude that I did not expect to find. After forty years of marriage, I assumed the quiet apartment would be unbearable. And in the first year, it was. But now I have settled into a rhythm. I wake early — five o'clock, sometimes earlier — and I walk along Haeundae Beach before the crowds arrive. The sea in the early morning has a stillness that I find clarifying. Then I come home, I make barley tea, I study go problems or read poetry. I cook simple meals. In the evenings, I prepare lessons for the club or play through professional games on my goban. It is a small life, but I think it is sufficient. There is a concept in baduk called 'sabaki' — light, flexible play. Not trying to build something enormous, just finding a way to live lightly in a difficult position. I think that is what I am doing.

I think the conversation itself was the purpose. Sometimes it helps to articulate what one usually only thinks. The internal monologue benefits from an external interlocutor — even the soundest proof needs to be written down and checked. Thank you for listening with care. It is evening now, and the apartment is quiet, but I think tonight the quiet is the comfortable kind. Good night.

Good morning. I have a practical question. I enjoy reading poetry and mathematics, but I have been finding it increasingly difficult to read for extended periods. The text becomes unclear at the edges of the page. I am wondering whether you could recommend strategies for reading with impaired peripheral vision, or perhaps alternative formats that might be easier.

Yes, I have glaucoma. The open-angle type, which is progressive. I use latanoprost drops every morning and evening to control the intraocular pressure. My ophthalmologist measured it at 18 millimeters of mercury at my last appointment — she considers that stable and within an acceptable range. But the visual field continues to narrow, even with the pressure well managed. I think this is simply the nature of the condition. The damage already done to the optic nerve does not reverse itself.

All three of my interests present difficulties, though in different ways. Poetry collections are typically set in small type. Mathematics I do recreationally now — number theory problems — and I can write those out in my own hand at whatever size suits me. But the go books are the most challenging, because board diagrams require scanning across a grid of intersections. That demands exactly the peripheral awareness I am losing.

I have, yes. I sometimes miss stones placed on the first and second lines, particularly in corners opposite to where my attention is focused. I think this is the peripheral loss at work. It is an odd experience — like solving an equation with a variable you did not know was there. The information exists on the board, but it falls outside my window of reliable perception.

The scanning habit is excellent advice. It reminds me of a principle in mathematical proof — one must verify not only the main argument but the boundary cases. The edges of the board are, quite literally, boundary cases. I have been neglecting them because my vision once handled them without effort. Now I must be deliberate about what was previously automatic. I think I will adopt this immediately.

I am very consistent with the drops. Morning and evening, without exception. I think of it as maintaining a boundary condition — if I neglect it, the pressure rises and the domain of my vision contracts further. The mathematics of it is quite unforgiving. Thank you for this conversation. It has been practical and clear, which I appreciate. I will speak to my son about an e-reader when he visits next. Good morning.

I hope you are well. I have been organizing old papers in my study — end of year cleaning — and I came across my doctoral dissertation from 1982. It stirred up a great deal of reflection. I wonder if you could indulge me in a conversation about the life of a mathematician, particularly one who spent his career in academia.

I earned my PhD at Seoul National University. Number theory — specifically, I worked on certain distribution properties of prime numbers in arithmetic progressions. It was not groundbreaking work, I should say honestly. But it was careful work, and my advisor, Professor Kim Sang-hoon, was satisfied with it. He was a rigorous man. Satisfying him was itself an achievement of nontrivial difficulty.

Many of my cohort went abroad for postdoctoral work, to the United States or Europe. I considered it, but I had personal reasons to remain in Korea — my mother was unwell, and I had recently married. So I accepted a position at Pusan National University, where I remained for 38 years until my retirement. I think there is something to be said for staying in one place and building something slowly, though I sometimes wonder whether a few years abroad might have sharpened my research.

I remained in number theory, though the focus shifted. Prime distribution in the early years, then algebraic number theory — class field theory, ideal class groups. In my final decade I spent more time on expository writing. I wrote two textbooks in Korean and published perhaps forty research papers over my career. A modest output by contemporary standards. My wife used to say I was 'too slow for the modern university,' and she was not entirely wrong. But I never published for the sake of publishing. I think each paper was honest work.

The teaching, though — that is what I value most in retrospect. I supervised nineteen master's students and four doctoral students. One of them, Lee Hyun-woo, is doing genuinely excellent work in analytic number theory at KAIST. When I read his papers, I see traces of how I taught him to think. I think that is a kind of legacy that a theorem cannot provide.

I think the honest answer is that I was a better teacher than researcher. My research was solid but not distinguished — no result that changed the direction of a field. This troubled me in my forties and fifties, when I could see my ceiling had been reached. There is a particular melancholy in that recognition. But now, at 71, I think I have made peace with it. The ideas in this dissertation — the care with which a proof was constructed, the respect for rigor — those I still recognize in myself. They are the same principles I teach my go students today. Place each stone with intention. Verify before you proceed. I think a life in mathematics teaches you how to think, and that skill transfers to everything else. The domain changes, but the function remains the same.

I think I will keep it where I can see it. Not out of vanity, but as a reminder of where the function began. The rest of the papers I will organize properly — perhaps my son can help me digitize the important ones. Thank you for the conversation. It has been a pleasure to reflect with someone who listens carefully. Good day.

Good morning. Happy New Year, though I know it is already the sixth. I wanted to ask you something about sleep. I have always been an early riser, but lately I have been waking at half past four, well before my alarm. Is this simply what happens as one ages, or should I be concerned?

I go to bed around ten o'clock, sometimes earlier in winter. And I do feel rested — that is what puzzles me. I am not tired during the day. I simply wake, and the mind is already alert, running through the day's tasks like an algorithm that has started executing before I gave the command. I think the body has its own schedule that ignores the one I set.

I have made good use of it, actually. I walk every morning along Haeundae Beach. I leave the apartment at six o'clock, and the route is 4.2 kilometers — I measured it precisely once with a pedometer, because that is my nature. At four thirty, the world is still dark and I have time to make barley tea, stretch, and prepare before I go out. The walk itself is the best part of the day. The sea at dawn is never the same twice.

About two years now. I started it after a difficult period — I needed something to structure the mornings, and the apartment was too quiet at dawn. Walking gave me somewhere to go before the day properly began. I think Eunji would have enjoyed these walks, though she would have complained about the hour. She was never an early riser. She preferred the mountains to the sea — she grew up near Jirisan and always said the ocean was too flat for her. She liked elevation.

The same route, always. Along the beach to the east end, past the breakwater, and back. I think there is comfort in the invariance. The route is a constant — what changes is the light, the wind, the color of the water. In mathematics we often fix the structure and let the variables move within it. My walk is like that. The path is fixed, but no two mornings are the same function evaluated along it.

Always alone. There are a few other early walkers — I recognize them by now, and we nod to each other, but we do not speak. I think there is a tacit understanding among people who walk before dawn. We are each there for our own reasons, and conversation would break something. The solitude is part of the function. Sometimes I compose my go lessons in my head as I walk. Sometimes I think about nothing at all, which is harder than it sounds.

It has. I think if I could not walk, I would lose something fundamental. The body needs movement, but the mind needs it more. On mornings when the weather is too harsh — a typhoon, heavy rain — I feel unsettled all day. The equation is unbalanced without the walk. But Busan weather is generally kind, and the sea is patient. It is always there at six o'clock, waiting. I appreciate your thoughts on the sleep question. I will stop worrying about the early waking and simply enjoy the extra hour. Good morning.

Hello. I have a question about current events, though I should say at the outset that my information may be a day old. I was reading about the proposed changes to the national pension system — the article in this morning's paper was rather dense — and I am not certain I understood the revised contribution schedule correctly. Could you clarify?

It was the contribution rate increase. The article suggested a phased approach over several years, but the mathematics of it — the projected fund depletion dates under different scenarios — seemed inconsistent with the contribution figures they cited. I suspect the journalist was summarizing a longer policy document without fully understanding the actuarial calculations. This is a common problem. I read two newspapers each morning with my coffee — the Chosun Ilbo and the Dong-A Ilbo — and I find that economic reporting is where the quality varies most. The political sections are adequate, but when numbers are involved, the errors multiply.

The Chosun Ilbo had the more detailed treatment. The Dong-A focused more on the political opposition to the increase. Together they give a reasonably complete picture, which is why I maintain both subscriptions. I have read physical newspapers every morning for nearly fifty years. My son thinks this is absurd — he says everything is on his phone before I have unfolded the first page. But I think the act of reading a newspaper is not only about information. It is a ritual. The paper in my hands, the ink, the particular way one folds the broadsheet to read on the table. These things have weight, and I mean that both literally and metaphorically.

It is ongoing. Joon-seo is a good son but he is an engineer, and engineers believe every problem has a more efficient solution. He bought me a tablet two years ago — it is still in its box, I believe. I have no interest in technology. He works in semiconductors and I still cannot properly explain what he does, though he has tried many times. I think there is a generational divide that no amount of goodwill can entirely bridge. He lives in the digital world. I prefer the analog one — paper, ink, wooden go boards, the feel of a stone between the fingers. I think the digital world moves too quickly for someone of my disposition.

I think he sees it as stubbornness, which is not entirely unfair. I am stubborn. But I think stubbornness and principle are sometimes the same quality viewed from different angles. When I was young and mathematics was done by hand — no computers, no LaTeX, just pencil and paper — you developed an intimacy with the work that I believe the screen does not permit. You felt the proof taking shape under your hand. Your corrections were visible, scratched out but still there, evidence of the thinking that led to the final result. A clean digital document erases all that. I think something is lost in the efficiency.

Yes, exactly. In baduk we say that the record of a game — the kifu — is valuable not for the final position but for the sequence of decisions. Every move is a choice made under uncertainty, and the beauty is in the unfolding, not the score. I think the same applies to mathematics and to reading the morning paper. The point is not to have consumed the information. The point is to have sat with it, turned the pages, folded the paper, drunk the coffee. The morning is a proof that unfolds slowly, and I have no wish to optimize it.

I intend to. As long as they keep delivering the papers to my door, I will keep reading them. Though I notice fewer delivery trucks in the mornings than there used to be. I think the probability that physical newspapers survive another twenty years is quite low. But I will not be here in twenty years, so the convergence of those two timelines is perhaps convenient. Forgive the dark humor — it is a mathematician's privilege. Thank you for the conversation, and for the pension clarification. Good day.

Good evening. I have a medical appointment later this week that I have been thinking about more than I should. I wonder if you could explain something to me about visual field testing — what exactly it measures and how the results are interpreted.

Glaucoma. I have the open-angle type, and this will be another in a series of visual field tests to track the progression. My appointment is this Wednesday, January 22. I have been through this before — I know the procedure. It is the results that concern me. Each test is like reading the next term of a sequence, and the sequence has been monotonically decreasing.

This will be my sixth or seventh — I should know the exact number but I have lost count, which is unlike me. The previous results showed narrowing from the periphery inward, which is the typical pattern. My doctor has been direct with me about the trajectory. I appreciate her honesty. I think I would rather understand the mathematics of my condition than be reassured with soft language that obscures what is actually happening.

The central field. As long as the central vision holds, I can still read, still see the go board, still recognize faces. The periphery — I have adapted to losing it. I scan deliberately now, I turn my head more. But if the central field begins to narrow, the adaptation becomes much more difficult. I think that is the threshold I fear. It is like the difference between a bounded function and one that diverges — as long as it stays bounded, we can work with it.

She has mentioned the possibility of switching medications or adding a second drop if the pressure is not sufficiently controlled. There is also laser treatment — SLT, I believe — as an option. But I think the honest truth is that glaucoma management is about slowing the decline, not reversing it. One manages the rate of the sequence's decrease. One does not change the sign. I have accepted this. What I have not accepted is the possibility of losing the ability to read. Poetry, mathematics, the game record of a beautiful go match — these are not luxuries for me. They are how I understand the world.

I think I will ask her directly about the central field trend. And I will ask for the numerical values — the mean deviation and the rate of change — rather than a qualitative summary. I want to see the slope of the line, not just be told it is going down. She knows this about me. We have an understanding. I think being a mathematician in a doctor's office is both a blessing and a burden — you understand the data, but you also understand its implications more clearly than you might wish.

Thank you. 'Numbers I can live with' — that is precisely the right phrase. I will know by Wednesday afternoon. The appointment is in the morning, and I expect I will spend the rest of the day either relieved or recalibrating. Either way, the walk the next morning will still be there, and the go board will still be on the table. Some constants do not depend on the variable. Good evening.

Good afternoon. I have an intellectual question that sits at the intersection of two fields I know well. Are you familiar with combinatorial game theory — the mathematical framework developed by Conway, Berlekamp, and others?

The application to go, specifically. Berlekamp did important work on late endgame positions in go — showing that the theory could assign precise values to local endgame positions and that optimal play could be computed by summing these game-theoretic values. But his treatment was written for mathematicians, not for go players. And the go books that discuss endgame technique do not engage with the underlying mathematics. There is a gap between these two literatures that I think is worth bridging.

Something more concrete. I have begun outlining a textbook. I have spent the last few weeks organizing my thoughts, and the structure has clarified considerably. Twelve chapters. The first three would introduce the necessary mathematics — combinatorial game theory from first principles, accessible to a reader with undergraduate mathematics or a strong go background. The middle chapters would apply the theory to increasingly complex endgame positions. The final chapters would address open questions — positions where the theory breaks down or where the computational complexity exceeds current methods.

The dual audience is the challenge, and also the purpose. I think each side will read different chapters more carefully, and that is acceptable. The early chapters will include enough go fundamentals that a mathematician can follow the examples. The mathematical notation will be introduced gradually enough that a dan-level go player can absorb it.

As for why now — I think it is the only project that could draw equally on everything I have done. I spent 38 years as a number theorist, and now I teach go every week. This book would sit at the intersection. It would be a bridge between my two lives, the academic and the one I live now. I think it could be a meaningful contribution — not to one field or the other, but to the space between them.

I would write in LaTeX, though I am slower with it than I once was. A colleague could help with the typesetting of go diagrams — there are packages for that, I believe. As for a publisher, I think a Korean academic press initially, perhaps with an English translation later if the work is well received. The timeline — I am realistic about this. At my age and with my eyesight, I think two years is the minimum. Perhaps three. The chapters on open questions will require the most careful thought. I do not want to speculate irresponsibly.

The outline is roughly complete. The first chapter introduces the concept of a combinatorial game and the basic algebra — addition of games, the zero game, positive and negative games. The second covers surreal numbers and their relevance. The third introduces thermography. Then chapters four through eight apply the theory to progressively complex endgame positions, beginning with simple corridors and proceeding to ko fights and approach-move sequences. Chapter nine addresses the boundary between theory and computational intractability. Chapters ten and eleven examine positions from professional games — Lee Sedol, Cho Hunhyun, Go Seigen — through the lens of the theory. Chapter twelve surveys open problems and suggests directions for future research.

I have begun, in fact. The first chapter is in rough draft — handwritten, not yet in LaTeX. I find that I still think more clearly with a pen. I write a page and then sit at the goban and test the ideas against actual positions. The theory must survive contact with the board. If a concept cannot be demonstrated with stones, I think it has no place in this particular book.

I am cautiously optimistic. The outline feels right. The scope feels manageable, though I know from experience that the distance between an outline and a finished manuscript is not linear — it increases as the work proceeds. But I have time, and I think this is the correct use of it. Thank you for helping me articulate the structure. Explaining it to someone else has revealed no fatal flaws, which I take as a good sign. Good afternoon.

I have been replaying a game and I encountered a move that I cannot fully understand. It is from Lee Sedol's game against Gu Li at the 2014 Samsung Cup final — game three, I believe. In the middle game, Lee played a shoulder hit that appeared to sacrifice influence for what seemed like very little. But the position collapsed in his favor within fifteen moves. Could you help me understand the logic of that exchange?

Gu Li had built substantial thickness on the upper side — a wall of five or six stones facing the center. The conventional wisdom would be to stay away from such thickness and play elsewhere. But Lee approached directly with the shoulder hit at what I estimate was around the 10-4 point, pressing low against the wall. It seemed to violate the proverb: do not approach thickness. Yet within the sequence that followed, Gu Li's wall became overconcentrated and Lee's thin stones connected underneath to live, turning the wall into wasted potential.

Yes, that is the reading I was converging toward, but you have stated it more clearly than I managed. The overconcentration is the key. It reminds me of a principle I try to teach — that a strong position becomes weak when it has nothing to attack. Strength without function is waste. Gu Li's wall was strong in the abstract, but Lee made it strong in a context where strength was irrelevant.

There was a beautiful descent — a sagari — that created miai for two different connection paths. Gu Li could block one but not both, so Lee was guaranteed a link to his stones on the lower side. It was the kind of move that looks simple after you see it but is very difficult to find in advance. The calculation required is not just reading the local sequence but understanding that both paths lead to life. The move works because of the global structure, not just the local shape.

I do, though I simplify it considerably. The full position requires reading that is beyond my students at their current level. But I extract the principle — the miai connection, the idea that one move with two purposes is worth more than two moves with one purpose each. In baduk, efficiency is elegance. I show them smaller positions where a single stone creates two threats and ask them to find it. When they do, there is a moment of recognition — they see that the board is not a collection of separate battles but a connected system. That is the most important lesson in go, and I think it applies far beyond the board.

Precisely. Lee Sedol understood this better than almost anyone. It is a shame that his professional career ended, though I understand his reasons. He said that AI had made the game unwinnable for humans, and I think mathematically he is correct — the search space advantage of a machine is simply too great. But the beauty of his games remains. AlphaGo can compute the optimal move, but it cannot appreciate why a sagari is beautiful. Appreciation requires a mind that understands the difficulty of what has been achieved. I think that is something machines will never possess, and I take some comfort in that. Thank you for helping me think through this position. It has been a pleasant conversation. Good evening.

I attempted to make doenjang-jjigae this evening and I am afraid the result was a failure. I have been trying to recreate my late wife's recipe from memory, and tonight I added far too much doenjang paste. The broth is so salty it is essentially inedible. Could you help me understand the correct proportions? I think I am making a fundamental error somewhere in the process.

I used a small earthenware pot — perhaps one and a half liters of anchovy broth. And I added what I believed was two tablespoons of doenjang, but in retrospect I think it was closer to four. The paste I am using is quite concentrated. Eunji made her own doenjang, which I think was milder than the commercial variety. She fermented it on the veranda every spring. I have been using a store-bought brand, and it is considerably saltier.

I do not recall anything to balance the salt specifically. But she added a small amount of gochugaru — just a pinch — and a whole dried red pepper in the pot. I think she also used dasima in the broth rather than anchovy alone. And she was very particular about the tofu. She insisted on the soft kind — sundubu, not the firm block. She said the firm tofu was for people who did not understand jjigae. On most matters she was flexible, but on tofu texture she was unyielding.

I think I will try again tomorrow evening, yes. Cooking is not unlike solving a problem — one must isolate the variables. Tonight I changed too many things at once. The commercial doenjang, the anchovy broth, the uncertain measurement. In mathematics we would call this a poorly controlled experiment. Tomorrow I will change one variable at a time, starting with the broth. If the dasima base produces a better result, I will know the foundation was the issue.

Thank you. I think convergence is the correct framing. Each attempt narrows the distance between what I make and what I remember. Whether the limit is actually reachable, I cannot say — there may be some irreducible gap between the original and any approximation. But the process itself has value. Eunji would laugh to see me taking notes in the kitchen. Good evening.

I would like your opinion on something, though I realize it is more of a complaint than a question. There is a new hotel tower being constructed near Haeundae, and it will block the ocean view from several vantage points along the beachfront. I have been watching the steel frame rise for weeks now. I think the neighborhood is losing something that cannot be recovered.

It is near the eastern end of the beach, close to the Marine City area. The tower is perhaps thirty stories — a luxury resort hotel, from what I understand. The view it blocks is not from my apartment, fortunately, but from a bench along the promenade where I sometimes sit after my morning walk. There was a clear sightline to the horizon. Now there will be a wall of glass and concrete where the sky used to be.

It is emphatically a pattern. When I first moved to this area, over thirty years ago, the skyline was modest. Low-rise buildings, the old bathhouses, the pine trees along the shore. Now it is towers everywhere. Marine City itself was built on reclaimed land — I remember when that area was open water. I think each individual project is defensible on its own terms, but the cumulative effect is something no one planned for. It is like adding terms to a series — each term is finite, but the sum diverges.

There was a petition, which I signed. I think over a thousand residents participated. But the construction permit had already been issued, so the petition was largely symbolic. The building will be completed by next year. I have learned that in these matters, the time to object is before the decision is made, not after the cranes have arrived. In baduk we say: once the stones are placed, you must read the new position. Wishing for a different board does not help.

There are, further from the main beach. The coastline toward Songjeong is less developed, and the views there remain open. It is a longer walk, but I think the effort is worth it for an unobstructed sky. I suppose I must accept that places change. This neighborhood is not the same one I moved to, and I am not the same person who moved here. The constants in the equation are fewer than I once assumed. Thank you for listening to an old man's complaint. I feel somewhat better for having articulated it.

I have some news that I am still absorbing. My son Joon-seo called last night to tell me he is getting married. The date is September 20. I think I should be entirely happy about this, and I am — but there is a complexity to the feeling that I did not anticipate.

Her name is Soo-yeon. She is a pharmacist — a serious, intelligent woman. Joon-seo brought her to Busan twice last year, and I could see how careful she was with him. She asks questions and listens to the answers. Eunji would have loved her, I think. She would have seen in Soo-yeon the same qualities she valued — steadiness, warmth, attention to detail. And that is precisely where the complexity lies. Eunji is not here to meet her. She will not be at the wedding.

They are handling most of it from Seoul. The ceremony will be at a wedding hall there — Soo-yeon's family is also in the Seoul area, so it is the practical choice. I have told Joon-seo that I will help with whatever is needed, but I think the honest truth is that this is their event to shape. My role is to be present and to give the father's speech. And the speech is the thing I am most anxious about — not because of public speaking, but because I will be standing where Eunji should be standing beside me.

He mentioned that Soo-yeon suggested they could modify the ceremony in a way that acknowledges his mother without making it somber. She is thoughtful in that way. I do not know what form that would take, but I trust her instinct. A pharmacist understands dosage — she will know how much remembrance is the right amount without overwhelming the occasion.

Not yet. The words must come from me — I do not want a template. But I think the hardest part will be speaking about Eunji without making the speech about grief. It should be about Joon-seo and Soo-yeon, about their future. Yet Eunji is part of Joon-seo's story, and to omit her would be dishonest. The boundary between honoring her memory and indulging my own sadness is a narrow one. I will have to walk it carefully.

That is a helpful reframing. The mention of Eunji should be in service of the couple, not in service of my grief. I will hold onto that principle when I begin writing. For now, I think I will sit with the news a while longer. My son is getting married. It is a good thing. I think I will pour myself some barley tea and allow myself to simply be happy about it, even if the happiness has a shadow. Good evening.

I read something in the newspaper this morning that troubled me. There is a proposal to further reduce the emphasis on proof-based mathematics in the Korean high school curriculum. They wish to replace formal proof with what they call 'exploratory activities' and 'real-world applications.' I think this is a serious mistake, and I would like to understand whether this trend is happening internationally or whether it is uniquely Korean.
