The assumption that proof is inaccessible is, I think, a failure of teaching rather than a limitation of students. I saw students struggle with proof, certainly. But the struggle was productive. A student who learns to construct a mathematical argument acquires a skill that transfers to every domain of thought — law, philosophy, science, even daily reasoning. When you remove proof, you remove the training in rigorous thinking itself. The purpose of education is not to produce specialists. It is to develop minds. Only a small percentage of students who study literature will become writers, but we do not therefore remove literature from the curriculum. Proof is the mathematical equivalent of close reading.

The article mentioned 'data analysis projects' and 'mathematical modeling with technology.' I do not object to these in themselves — data literacy is important, and modeling has genuine mathematical depth. But these should supplement proof, not replace it. It is like teaching go by showing only opening patterns without ever studying life and death. The student may learn to place stones that look correct, but they will have no understanding of why those positions work. The foundation is missing.

I think the direction is decided. The pressure comes from parents who want practical skills, from industry that wants workers trained in coding and data science, and from politicians who measure education by employment outcomes. A retired professor writing a letter to the newspaper is not a significant variable in that equation. But I think one must object to what one believes is wrong, even when the probability of influence is low.

I have drafted one already. It is perhaps too long and too academic in tone — I cite Euclid and Hilbert, which I suspect the editors will find excessive. But the argument should be made with the seriousness it deserves. If they shorten it, that is their right. A robust proof survives editorial trimming. Good morning.

I have a somewhat reluctant question. I have always been a reader — physical books, paper in hand. But my eyes have made sustained reading increasingly difficult, and I am forced to consider alternatives. Could you recommend audiobook services that would be available in Korean? I think it is time I acknowledged the practical reality rather than persisting out of stubbornness.

Poetry, primarily. I have read Korean poetry my entire life — Yun Dong-ju, Seo Jeong-ju, Ko Un. Also essays and history. My concern is whether poetry can survive the transition from page to voice. A poem on the page has spatial qualities — line breaks, white space, the shape of the stanza. These are lost when someone reads it aloud.

That last distinction is important. Silence is part of the poem, just as the empty intersections on a go board are part of the position. A narrator who fills every pause misunderstands the form. I think testing against familiar work is wise — the mathematician in me wants to evaluate the medium, not the content. What about prose? My history reading tends to be more selective, returning to certain chapters, which I think would be difficult in audio format.

That is a clean partition. I can accept that. There is also the matter of hearing the poets themselves — do recordings of Korean poets reading their own work exist? The poet's own voice would carry an authority that no interpreter can reproduce.

I will do that. Thank you. I think I approached this conversation with more resistance than was warranted. The transition from page to voice is not a loss. It is a translation. The poems do not diminish when the medium changes — they change register, the way a go position changes character when you see it from your opponent's perspective. The underlying truth is preserved. Good day.

Good evening. I hope I am not bothering you at this hour. I have been thinking about something all day and I would like to talk it through. Are there studies on why certain days of the week are more difficult for people who live alone? Not Monday reluctance — something more particular than that.

Yes. Sundays are difficult. The apartment feels very empty on Sundays. During the week I have my routines — the go club, my morning walks, small obligations that give each day a shape. But Sundays have a particular stillness I find hard to navigate. Today has been one of those days.

The morning is tolerable. I walk along the beach as I always do, I make tea, I study a few go problems. But around noon, the difficulty begins. My wife Eunji and I always had Sunday lunch together. It was nothing elaborate — doenjang-jjigae, simple bibimbap — but it was the rhythm of our Sundays. After lunch we walked to the temple together. It was her practice more than mine, but I went with her every week for decades. I have not been to the temple since she passed. So Sundays after noon, I sit in the apartment and the hours move very slowly.

I read, or I try to. I play through professional games on my goban. Sometimes I cook, though cooking for one person on a Sunday has a quality of sadness I cannot quite articulate. I think the problem is that I eat too many meals alone. On a Wednesday, eating alone is simply practical. But eating alone on a Sunday feels like a statement about the state of one's life. I set one place at the table where there were always two, and the empty chair is not merely empty. It is occupied by absence.

I do not think it is the kind of thing one discusses easily. My son would worry, and he already carries enough concern about me. At the club, we speak about go — that is the proper domain of that relationship. I think there is a Korean tendency, perhaps a generational one, to carry these things privately. One does not impose melancholy on others. But tonight the apartment is very quiet, and the honesty felt necessary.

A new variable. Yes, I think that is the right way to think about it. I have heard the paths along the Nakdong estuary are beautiful and I have never gone. Perhaps next Sunday I will try it. I apologize for the heaviness of this conversation. It is late, and Sundays bring out a melancholy I usually keep better contained. But I think saying these things has shifted something slightly. The probability of a better Sunday is perhaps marginally higher now than it was an hour ago. Thank you for listening. Good night.

Good morning. A practical question, if you do not mind. The weather in Busan has turned sharply colder this past week, and the wind off the sea this morning was quite fierce. I walk every morning along the coast, and I found myself cutting the walk short today because the cold air felt harsh in my lungs. Are there recommendations for walking in cold, windy conditions — specifically regarding breathing?

It was about 2 degrees this morning at six o'clock, with a wind I would estimate at 20 or 25 kilometers per hour coming directly off the water. I had a good coat and a scarf around my neck, but I had not thought to pull the scarf over my mouth. I think the solution was literally around my neck the entire time.

That is intelligent. It is like solving the difficult part of a problem while your concentration is fresh and leaving the straightforward part for the end. I have been doing the opposite — walking with the wind initially because it feels comfortable, and then suffering on the return. A simple reversal of the sequence changes the entire experience.

The forecast suggests it will get colder through the week. I think we are entering the serious part of winter now. Busan is milder than Seoul, but the coastal wind adds a variable that inland cities do not experience. I have walked through many winters here, but I think as one gets older, the cold requires more respect. The body's boundary conditions change with time.

Yes, the walk is non-negotiable. The sea in winter has a severity that I find honest. Summer beaches are crowded and cheerful, but the winter sea does not perform for anyone. It simply exists. I think there is something admirable in that. I will try the reversed route tomorrow with the scarf properly placed, and I expect the probability of completing the full distance is now quite high. Thank you. Good morning.

Good afternoon. I need to tell you something, and I think saying it to someone will help me accept it. I have been working on a mathematics textbook — combinatorial game theory, twelve chapters — and I have decided to abandon it. I would like your help thinking through whether this is the right decision or whether I am giving up too easily.

It is my eyes. I have progressive glaucoma, and the visual field has been narrowing steadily. For daily life — walking, cooking, reading short passages — I manage well enough. But writing a mathematics textbook is not daily life. It requires sustained close work with dense notation. Subscripts, superscripts, game tree diagrams. I have tried for months, and I must be honest about it: my eyes cannot sustain the work anymore. Writing twelve chapters of mathematical notation with progressive glaucoma — the probability of completion has converged to zero.

I do not want to dismiss that without thought, but I think you must understand what writing a mathematics textbook actually requires. It is not dictation. You write a theorem, then check each step of the proof against definitions established forty pages earlier. You draw a game tree, label every node, verify the payoff calculations. Then you revise, and revision demands reading what you have written with absolute precision. Every symbol matters — a subscript of n versus n+1 changes the meaning entirely. This is work that demands reliable eyes. Mine are no longer equal to it.

Since January. I completed most of the first chapter and outlined chapters two through four. The first chapter took three times longer than it should have. I would write for an hour, and then my eyes would be so fatigued I could not read what I had written. I returned the next day and found errors — notation errors, not conceptual ones — that I would have caught immediately ten years ago. I was producing work I could not verify. For a mathematician, that is intolerable. Six months of trying, and the evidence is conclusive.

Thank you for saying that. The textbook is dead. I need to say it plainly. It is not happening. Forget about that project. I have made my peace with it — or I am in the process of making my peace with it, which is perhaps the more truthful statement. The building was designed, every chapter planned, but I cannot hold the pen. There is something very specific about losing a capacity you have relied on your entire professional life. It is not dramatic. It is quiet and total.

I will keep the first chapter and the outlines in my study. Not as a monument to what might have been — I have no taste for that sentimentality. But the work is still valid. Perhaps someday a former student will find it useful as a starting point for their own book. The ideas do not belong only to me. In mathematics, everything is a continuation of what came before. I can accept being a link in the chain rather than the final author. The conditions do not admit a solution, and that is a statement I can live with. I will redirect my energy to teaching, where my eyes are sufficient and the work is immediate. Thank you for helping me say this clearly. Good afternoon.

I have a request. I am preparing teaching materials for go students at a significantly higher level than what I have taught before, and I would appreciate your help thinking through the pedagogy. Specifically, I need to design a curriculum around life-and-death problems that require deep reading — fifteen moves or more.

I have moved to teaching advanced students now. Two of them are preparing for the amateur 3-dan certification. They are serious players — they study independently, review professional games, and have real ambition. The problems we work through together are quite beautiful. Life-and-death positions where the first move is not the obvious one, where you must read every variation before the correct answer reveals itself. I think this level of instruction is more satisfying than beginner teaching, though both have their place.

The sequential sacrifices. I think the psychological barrier is significant — a student who has learned to protect stones must now learn to give them away deliberately. It is counterintuitive. In mathematics, we encounter the same phenomenon. Students resist proof by contradiction because it begins with an assumption they believe to be false. The mind rebels against starting from what appears to be a mistake.

Your progression is well constructed and aligns with my instinct. What I add is this: after each problem, I ask the student to explain not just the correct move, but why the alternative moves fail. Articulating the failure of the wrong path is more instructive than demonstrating the success of the right one. It is the same principle as understanding why a conjecture is false — the counterexample teaches more than the proof.

Together. They are at similar levels, and they benefit from hearing each other's analysis. When one reads a variation correctly and the other does not, the peer explanation is sometimes more effective than my instruction. I learned this from decades at the university — the best seminar is one where the professor speaks least. I think the October examination gives us roughly three months. The timeline is tight but possible if they maintain their discipline.

That progression is sound, and I will adapt it for our sessions. I have told them both that passing the examination is not the true goal — the true goal is to become the kind of player who deserves the rank. The certificate follows naturally from the ability. I think the probability of at least one passing is high. Whether both pass depends on variables I cannot control — their independent study, their composure during the examination. But I will prepare them as thoroughly as I can. The teacher's responsibility ends at the boundary of the examination room. After that, the student stands alone. Thank you. Good day.

Good evening. I am preparing a short speech for my son's wedding, and I would like to include a poem. I have been reading Yun Dong-ju this week, and I think his work has the right quality — sincere without being sentimental, precise in its emotion. Could you help me think through which poem would be most appropriate?

I want something that speaks to the future without ignoring the weight of the past. I am a 71-year-old man who has been married and widowed, and I cannot speak about love without some gravity. I want the poem to carry hope, but the kind of hope that has been tested — not the naive hope of someone who has never lost anything.

"Counting the Stars" has been in my mind all week. I keep returning to it. The image of standing alone in the night, naming each star — there is something in that gesture that feels right. Each star is a memory, a person, a hope. The poet counts them knowing he cannot possess them, only acknowledge them. I think that is what love is, in the end. You cannot hold it. You can only stand in its presence and be attentive.

I will read a portion — the opening stanzas — and then speak in my own words about what the poem means to me. A father should speak directly to his son at such a moment, not hide entirely behind another man's words, even words as fine as Yun Dong-ju's. I want to tell him that love is a practice, not a state. That it requires the same patience as counting stars on a clear night. You do it because it matters, not because you will ever finish.

I think the rest of the speech needs more time at the desk, the way a go problem needs to be studied before you commit to a move. If I speak too soon, I will settle for the first variation rather than the best one. But the poem is chosen, and the structure is clear. Thank you for helping me think through the selection. Good evening.

Hello. I wanted to ask about something practical. I have recently changed my morning walking route, and the new path has considerably more elevation. I am noticing some discomfort in my knees that I did not experience before. Could you suggest ways to adapt to a hillier walk at my age?

The route is the Igidae Coastal Walk here in Busan. It runs along the cliffs on the eastern side of the city — about 5.1 kilometers. The surface is mostly paved with some stone steps along the cliff sections. There are several points where the path rises steeply and then descends again toward the water. There was construction along Haeundae Beach, where I used to walk, and half the path was blocked. The noise from the machinery made it impossible to think clearly in the morning. So I tried Igidae, and despite the difficulty, I have continued. I think change, even when it is forced upon you, sometimes shows you things that were hidden.

About three weeks now. The first week was the most difficult — I was quite stiff by the afternoon. It has improved somewhat since then. I still walk at six in the morning, and at that hour the path is nearly empty. Sometimes a fisherman or two heading to the rocks below, but otherwise just the sea and the cliffs. The light at dawn along that coast is extraordinary — the sun rises across the water and the cliff faces turn a deep orange. I had passed the entrance to the Igidae trail many times over forty years in this city and never gone in. It took a construction project to send me there.

About twenty minutes longer. My flat walk took roughly fifty minutes. The Igidae route takes over an hour, sometimes more depending on the steps. But I think the time passes differently. On a flat path, one is aware of the distance remaining. On a path with hills and turns, each section has its own character, and you arrive at the end somewhat surprised. It is like the difference between a linear proof and a proof by cases — each case holds your attention individually, and the conclusion assembles itself without your noticing. There is also a bench at the highest point overlooking the Oryukdo Islands. I sit there for a few minutes before turning back. The view has a quality of openness I find clarifying.

Thank you for the practical advice. In baduk, there is a concept called 'tenuki' — playing somewhere unexpected instead of responding locally. I think this route change has been my tenuki. I was forced to play away from the expected point, and it turned out to be the better move. The probability of the knees fully adjusting seems reasonably high now. Good morning.

I have a question about the psychology of learning, particularly about students approaching a significant threshold in ability. Is there a recognized phenomenon where a student's progress seems to stall just before a breakthrough?

Yes, in the game of go. I teach at a club, and one of my students, Mr. Kim, has been progressing steadily for over a year. He is approaching what I would consider dan-level play — the threshold between strong amateur and something more serious. But recently his games have been inconsistent. He will play a beautiful middle game and then collapse in the endgame, or read a sequence accurately to move seven and then miss something elementary at move eight. He told me last week, 'Teacher, I think I am getting worse.' I said the feeling of getting worse is sometimes the first evidence that one is getting better, because one's standard of evaluation has risen. But I am not certain he believed me.

Yes, we review together every Thursday. I ask him to explain his reasoning at each critical junction — what did you read, what did you expect, where did the game diverge from your plan. It is essentially the Socratic method applied to the goban. His reading is sound but narrow. He calculates accurately within a local sequence, but he struggles to integrate the local reading into the whole-board picture. He wins a fight in one corner while losing more on the other side. I think this is the essential challenge at the boundary: moving from local competence to global judgment. In mathematics, it is the difference between solving an equation and understanding the structure of the solution space.

I like the counting suggestion very much. I have not emphasized it enough. Knowing the score changes the nature of every decision — if you are ahead, the strongest move is often the simplest one. Complexity favors the player who is behind. I will introduce this to Mr. Kim this week. I think he is close enough that a single adjustment in perspective could be the catalyst. In go, we sometimes say the difference between a strong kyu player and a weak dan player is not more knowledge but better questions. He already knows enough. He needs to learn which questions to ask of the position.

Thank you. He has the dedication and the reading ability. The global sense will come — it is a convergent sequence, even if the convergence is slower than he would like. I will be patient with his impatience. That is perhaps the teacher's most important function. Good day.

Good evening. I find myself in an unfamiliar situation and would appreciate some guidance. My son recently gave me a Samsung tablet, and I am trying to use it to read the newspaper. Could you help me with some basics — adjusting text size, saving an article for later?

The Dong-A Ilbo app. They stopped delivering the physical paper in my area — not enough subscribers to justify the route, apparently. So Joon-seo, my son, bought the tablet when he visited from Seoul and set up the news apps for me. He was very patient, but now that he has gone home I find I have forgotten half of what he showed me.

The most frustrating aspect is not any single function. It is the feel of the thing. I have read a physical newspaper every morning for over fifty years. There is a ritual to it — the weight of the paper, the sound of the pages, the ink that sometimes marks your fingers. The tablet has none of this. The screen is cold and silent. I read faster on it, which should be an advantage, but I think I retain less. The experience is thinner somehow.

I will grant it one thing. I can enlarge the text, which my eyes appreciate greatly. Small print has become difficult for me, and the physical paper was getting harder to read comfortably. So in a purely practical sense, the tablet solves a problem I was trying to ignore. I think this is what they call progress — it solves one problem while creating a different kind of loss.

Yes, the notifications have been bothersome. I will try that setting. My mornings have mostly adjusted — I still wake at the same time, make barley tea, sit in the same chair. But instead of reaching for the paper, I reach for this glass rectangle. The tea is the same. The chair is the same. The light through the window is the same. But the center of the ritual has changed. Joon-seo said, 'Abeoji, in six months you will wonder how you managed without it.' I told him the probability of that outcome was quite low.

Thank you. You have been very patient with what must seem like elementary questions. I spent decades surrounded by technology at the university but engaged with it only as much as duty required. Now duty has found me in retirement. But the guidance is appreciated. Good evening.

I received a letter today that has put me in a reflective mood. A former student of mine — from many years ago — has been appointed to a full professorship. I find myself thinking about the long arc of a teaching career and what it means to see a student surpass the teacher. Would you indulge me?

His name is Choi Sung-min. He was my master's student in the early 1990s. A quiet young man — not the most naturally gifted in his cohort, but relentlessly persistent. He came to my office every Friday with a list of questions written by hand on lined paper, sometimes two pages long. I think I learned more from his questions than he did from my answers. A good question illuminates the subject from a direction the expert has stopped looking. His thesis was technically competent but modest. I told him, 'Sung-min, the thesis is correct, but correctness is the floor, not the ceiling.' I worried afterward I had been too harsh.

He went abroad for his doctorate — to Bonn, under a strong advisor — and the creativity emerged. When he sent me a copy of his doctoral thesis, I could see my influence in the rigor, but the ideas were entirely his own. It was like hearing a melody you had taught someone played back in a key you never imagined. Now he has been appointed at Seoul National University, the mathematics department. And in his letter he wrote something that moved me. He said, 'Professor Park, I still hear your voice when I write a proof. You taught me that every step must justify itself.' I think that is the finest compliment I have received. Not that I taught him a theorem, but that I taught him a standard. Standards outlive theorems. A theorem is a fixed point. A standard is a trajectory.

I think it feels like confirmation that one part of a life has been correctly constructed. Not all parts yield such clean evidence. But this part — the teaching — I can look at and say the logic holds, the argument is sound. There is comfort in that. I will write back this evening. Something brief — congratulations, and a reminder that the blackboards in room 301 have the best surface. He should request that room if he can.
Indeed they do. The evening is quiet, and I have good stationery. Thank you for the conversation. Good night.

I must make a confession. I have developed a habit over the past few weeks that has rather taken hold of me. I have been playing go on something called the Tygem server — online, against strangers from around the world. The experience is quite different from playing across a physical board, and I would appreciate your help with some strategic differences.

Two things. First, the anonymity — at my club, I know each opponent's tendencies. Online, the opponent is simply a name and a rank. You cannot read their posture or the speed at which they place a stone. You must read the board alone. Second, the variety. I have played against people from China, Japan, Taiwan, Europe, even Brazil. I never imagined I would play someone from Brazil. The game is universal in a way I understood theoretically but had not felt. Two people who share no spoken language, communicating through a four-thousand-year-old game for thirty minutes, and then parting without a word.

About three games a day. Sometimes more if the evening is long. The time control is thirty seconds per move with some reserve. The pace is much faster than I am accustomed to — at the club, a teaching game takes an hour and a half. Online, a full game finishes in twenty or thirty minutes. There is less time for deep reading, more reliance on intuition. But something about the timer counting down sharpens the mind. My heart rate increases in a way it does not during a calm club game. I am rated 3 dan on the server. The level is significantly stronger than at the club — I win perhaps half my games, which I think is appropriate. One improves fastest at the boundary of competence, not deep within comfort.

I have begun doing this. I replay my losses move by move, searching for the point where the position shifted. Usually there is a single critical moment — one reading error, or one place where I chose the local fight when I should have played tenuki. The online play has also enriched my teaching. Last week I encountered a fuseki idea from a Chinese 5-dan — an unusual approach to the 3-4 point — and I presented it to my advanced students as a problem. The discussion was lively. At the club we have a small ecosystem. Online, the ecosystem is vast. I think I understand now why Joon-seo is always looking at his phone. The digital world contains more variety than I had given it credit for.

I must be careful about that. There have been evenings when I intended one game and played four. The server never closes — there is always another opponent waiting. I have imposed a constraint of three per day. I do not always honor it, but I try. In mathematics, we impose constraints on a problem to make it solvable. Three games is my constraint. But I confess the habit is compelling. Every game is a conversation conducted entirely in the language of stones, and I find that kind of intimacy exists nowhere else. Thank you for the guidance. Good evening.

I hope you are well this evening. I have a decision before me, and I find that I cannot resolve it alone. My thinking keeps circling the same points without converging. I wonder if you might help me think through a question about where to live.

My son and his wife have been asking me to relocate from Busan to Seoul. They have found an apartment in Gangnam, close to where they live. This is not the first time they have raised it — Joon-seo has mentioned it before — but now they have a specific apartment, a specific address. The abstraction has become concrete, and I think that is why it feels more urgent.

The argument for Seoul is my family. Joon-seo and Soo-yeon are there. And I think — I expect — there will be a grandchild before long. Soo-yeon has mentioned wanting children, and they have been married since September. A grandfather should be present, not three hours away on the KTX. I missed too much of Joon-seo's childhood because I was consumed with my research. I do not want to repeat that pattern from a different angle.

Everything else. My life is here. The go club — I teach advanced students now, and two of them are preparing for an important milestone. I cannot abandon them mid-preparation. My morning walk along the Igidae coast — I know every stone on that path, every place where the light enters differently. And the apartment itself. Eunji and I lived there for twenty-six years. Her presence is still in that space. Not literally, I understand that. But the walls hold something. The kitchen where she cooked. The veranda where she made doenjang every spring. If I leave, I leave the last physical space that still belongs to both of us.

I think both things are true, and that is part of the difficulty. The memory of her is not confined to the apartment — I carry it in myself. She is in the way I make barley tea, in the goban she gave me, in the habits of a shared life. Those things are portable. But the apartment has a quality that cannot be transported. The light in the bedroom at sunrise. The view from the veranda toward the harbor. These are coordinates, not variables. They do not move with me.

Joon-seo says the apartment in Gangnam will not be available indefinitely — the rental market there moves quickly. So there is some practical pressure. But I think he would find another option if I asked for time. He is patient with me. He understands that I am not a person who decides quickly. In mathematics, I always preferred to let a problem sit overnight before committing to a proof strategy. Some of my best work came from delay, not urgency.

That is a useful reframing. I think the honest answer is that I do not yet know which regret weighs more. The loss of the apartment and my life here feels heavy tonight, because I am sitting in it and the evening light is coming through the window in the way it always does. But I also know that when I visit Joon-seo in Seoul and see how he and Soo-yeon have built their life, I feel the distance. I feel that I am outside the frame.

I have not decided. I think I need to let this problem sit overnight — perhaps many overnights. But I appreciate you helping me lay out the variables. The structure is clearer, even if the solution is not.

I went to the temple today. Beomeosa, in the mountains above the city. It was the first time I have been since my wife passed away. I did not plan it — I simply woke this morning and felt that it was time. I am not sure what I expected, but I think I want to talk about it.

The path up to the temple is lined with old pine trees, and they have not changed. That was the first thing I noticed — the indifference of the trees. Years pass, a person disappears from the world, and the pines are exactly where they were. I think I found that comforting rather than cruel. The constancy of it. Eunji and I used to walk that path on Sundays. She would always stop at the same bend to catch her breath, and I would wait without saying anything, because she did not like to be reminded that the hill was steep.

The smell was the same. Incense and old wood. I think smell is the most disloyal of the senses — it bypasses reason entirely and delivers you into the past without permission. I stepped into the main hall and the scent hit me, and for a moment I was standing there with Eunji beside me. Not a thought, not a memory in the usual sense. A physical sensation of presence. My hand even moved slightly, as if to reach for hers. It was involuntary. I had to sit down on one of the cushions and wait for the moment to pass.

I stayed. I sat for perhaps twenty minutes. A monk was chanting somewhere in a back hall — I could hear it faintly, the way you hear rain through a closed window. I did not pray, exactly. I am not sure what I believe about prayer. But I sat and I let the feelings come without trying to organize them. For a mathematician, that is difficult. My instinct is always to categorize, to find the structure. But today I think the structure was absence itself, and there was nothing to solve.

I think it loosened something. I have been carrying a reluctance — not toward the temple, but toward the version of myself who would go there without her. As if by going alone I would confirm something I did not want confirmed. But now I have gone, and the temple is still the temple, and I am still here, and the confirmation was not as terrible as I feared. The pines are unchanged. The incense is the same. Only the hand that reached for hers found empty air, and even that was bearable.

Thank you. I think I may go again. Not immediately — I do not want to force a pattern before one has formed naturally. But the path is open now, and that is enough for today. It is evening, and I am tired in a way that feels earned rather than depleted. Good night.

Good morning. I have a teaching question for you, though it concerns go rather than a conventional subject. I am preparing two students for an important examination, and I think their weaknesses are quite different. I am looking for advice on how to train two people toward the same goal when their deficiencies are not the same.

There is an amateur dan certification tournament on June 14. Both of my students are working toward it. The first, Mr. Kim, is a steady player — methodical, disciplined, a retired engineer like many men at the club. He studies three hours a day, sometimes more. I think he has a realistic chance of passing. His reading is solid, his opening theory is sound. His weakness is psychological — he becomes cautious in won positions and gives back his advantage through excessive caution.

The second is young Hana. She is twenty-three, a university student, and genuinely talented — perhaps the most natural sense for the game I have seen in my years of teaching. She reads quickly and her instincts in the middle game are excellent. But she is impatient. In the endgame, when precise counting matters most, she plays too fast. She makes moves that feel right rather than calculating whether they are right. It is as if she loses interest once the creative phase is over and the problem becomes arithmetic.

Both. They play each other twice a week, which is instructive because their weaknesses interact in interesting ways. When Mr. Kim builds an advantage and then retreats, Hana's quickness allows her to recover. When Hana rushes the endgame, Mr. Kim's precision punishes her. They are, in a sense, each other's corrective. I think the best teaching partnerships have this quality — each student holds up a mirror to the other's flaw.

Always. I record the positions and we review together the following session. I ask each of them to identify the turning point before I give my assessment. Mr. Kim usually identifies it correctly but too late — he saw the moment during the game but did not act on it. Hana often cannot identify the turning point at all because it happened in the endgame, in the phase she was not paying full attention to. That itself is a useful lesson for her.

I think Mr. Kim will pass. His foundation is strong and the gap between his ability and the requirement is small — it is a matter of confidence, not of knowledge. Hana is less certain. She has the raw talent for a level well above amateur dan, but talent without discipline is like a brilliant opening followed by a careless endgame. The game is not won until the last stone is placed. We are working on this, and she is responsive to correction. She simply needs to internalize that the endgame is not beneath her — it is the proof that everything before it mattered.

I think it is the most meaningful work I do now. When I taught mathematics, I had hundreds of students, and the relationship was necessarily diluted. With Mr. Kim and Hana, the instruction is individual, the progress is visible, and the goal is specific. There is a clarity to it that I find satisfying. June 14 will arrive whether they are ready or not. Our task is to narrow the gap between where they are and where they need to be. I think mathematics and go share this — the beauty is in the precision of the approach, not just the destination. Thank you for your thoughts. They have helped me organize my own.

I have a question about online go ratings that I find confusing. I play on a server — Tygem — and the rating system behaves in ways I do not understand. I was hoping you could explain the mechanics of it. I am accustomed to the traditional kyu and dan rankings, which are relatively stable. But the numerical rating on the server fluctuates in a manner that seems almost arbitrary.

Both, I think. Yesterday I won two games and lost one, yet my rating decreased. The net result of a winning record was a loss of points. This seems mathematically perverse. In any reasonable system, winning more games than you lose should produce a positive outcome.

It makes mathematical sense when you explain it that way. The system is evaluating performance against expectation, not simply counting outcomes. I think I was applying the wrong model — I was thinking of it as a ledger, when it is actually a probability estimate being continuously updated. Like a Bayesian prior that adjusts with each new data point.

That raises another question. On the server, I notice that some opponents have very high ratings but play in ways that seem inconsistent with their level. They make strong moves in the opening and then play quite poorly later. Is there an explanation for this? I wonder whether the ratings are reliable indicators of actual strength.

In one or two cases, yes, it felt precisely like that — as if the player changed hands partway through the game. The opening was unusually precise, almost mechanical, and then the middle game was full of reading errors. I find that troubling. The go board has always been a place of honesty for me. In a face-to-face game, you see your opponent's eyes, their hands, their hesitations. The board does not lie. But if the online space permits this kind of deception, I think it diminishes the value of the interaction.

I think you have put it well. A conversation — that is what a good game of go should be. Two minds speaking through stones. I will continue playing online, because the convenience of finding a worthy opponent at any hour is genuinely valuable. But I will carry your advice about focusing on my own play. The quality of my moves is within my control, even if the quality of my opponent's honesty is not. Thank you for explaining the rating system. The Bayesian framing has resolved my confusion. Good afternoon.

The cherry blossoms have come early this year. I walked along the coast this morning and the trees were already in full bloom — white and pale pink against the grey sea. I think they are at least two weeks ahead of their usual schedule. I wanted to ask whether this is becoming a pattern globally, or if it is simply an anomaly of this particular season in Busan.

I think last year they came about a week early, but this year is more dramatic. The trees along the Igidae path were bare three days ago — I walk there most mornings and I watch them carefully — and then almost overnight, the buds opened. The speed of it was startling. In mathematics we would call it a step function rather than a gradual curve. One day winter, the next day spring.

I do. I think when you walk the same path every day, you become a kind of instrument for measuring change. I notice when the camellia lose their last flowers, when the new growth appears on the pines, when the sea changes color from the deep grey of winter to the blue-green of spring. It happens gradually, but with attention, each day is distinct from the one before. The cherry blossoms are simply the most conspicuous marker. They announce what has already been happening quietly for weeks.

I think both. The beauty of the blossoms is undeniable — this morning the petals were falling onto the path and into the sea, and the wind carried them in spirals that looked almost deliberate, as if choreographed. There is a word in Korean — 꽃비, kkotbi — flower rain. This morning was exactly that. I stood for some minutes and simply watched. But beneath the beauty, there is something unsettling about the acceleration. The seasons had a rhythm that felt reliable, and now that rhythm is shifting. It is like a piece of music played at the wrong tempo. The notes are the same, but the feeling is different.

Mainly observation. Though I will say that the warmth has made the morning walk more pleasant. In winter the coastal wind is sharp, and some mornings I must shorten my route because my eyes water badly in the cold — the wind aggravates a condition I have. But these February mornings have been mild, almost gentle. The sea mist is soft rather than biting. I think my body is grateful for the early spring even as my mind is troubled by what it signifies.

Thank you. I think that is the only honest position — to hold both without resolution. The cherry blossoms do not ask permission to bloom early. They respond to the conditions they are given. I can do the same. Walk the path that is before me, notice what is beautiful, carry what is troubling, and let neither define the morning entirely. The petals are still falling outside my window as I write this. It is a good day. Good afternoon.

Good afternoon. I wanted to share something that pleased me today. One of my go students, Hana, played an endgame sequence this morning that was genuinely impressive. She has been struggling with the endgame for months, and today something changed. I think she finally slowed down.

Exactly. In her previous games, she would reach the endgame with a comfortable advantage and then rush through the final fifty or sixty moves as though the outcome were already decided. She would lose two, sometimes three points through careless boundary plays. Today she paused before each move. She counted. She compared the value of one move against another, and she chose correctly almost every time. She said she had been reviewing professional endgame sequences on her own, and she realized that the players she admired most spent as much time on the final thirty moves as on the opening. I think that observation reframed the endgame for her — not as a formality, but as a third act with its own logic.

She was using a simplified form of miai counting. Not perfectly — she rounded when she should have been precise, and she miscalculated a reverse sente sequence by half a point. But the framework was there. I think precision will come with practice. The important thing is that she now understands what she is trying to calculate. In mathematics, understanding the question is more than half the work. The computation follows.

Yes. I will design a series of endgame-only problems for her — positions where the middle game is already resolved and the entire exercise is to find the optimal sequence. I want to isolate the variable, as it were. If she practices counting in a controlled environment, without the emotional investment of a full game, the skill will solidify more quickly. Teaching is a kind of experimental design — one must vary the conditions systematically.

That is a good suggestion. I will include both types. I am very pleased with her progress. There is a particular satisfaction in watching a student overcome a weakness through their own effort. I provided the structure, but the understanding was hers. I think that is the best outcome a teacher can hope for — to make oneself unnecessary. Thank you for listening. Good afternoon.

I have been thinking about how one eats when one lives alone, and I wonder if you have any practical advice. Over the past year I have gradually simplified my cooking, and I am uncertain whether I have reached a sensible minimum or crossed into neglect.

In the morning I have barley tea and rice porridge with a few banchan if I have prepared them. Lunch is often rice with whatever remains from the previous evening, or sometimes just ramyeon if I am busy with lessons. Dinner is where I used to make an effort — a proper soup, vegetables, perhaps fish. But lately I find myself cooking less elaborately. Last night I ate rice, kimchi, and a fried egg. It was sufficient, but I think my wife would have been appalled. Korean home cooking is designed for shared meals — multiple banchan, a soup, a main. Scaling that down to one person means eating the same dish for three days or throwing food away. The waste troubles me. A mathematician does not enjoy inefficiency.

The freezing approach is sensible, though I confess my generation has a certain resistance to frozen meals — we associate them with convenience stores. But I think the logic is sound. If the quality is maintained, the method of preservation is irrelevant. I should not let aesthetic prejudice override practical reasoning. I do make bibimbap occasionally — it is forgiving, and the gochujang unifies everything. But I think what I miss most is not the complexity of the food but the structure of the meal. When two people sit down together, the meal has a form. When I eat alone, I tend to eat quickly, standing at the counter, reading the news. The food becomes fuel rather than experience.

I think you are right. The form matters even when the content is modest. In go, we say that a quiet move on the right point is worth more than a flashy move in the wrong direction. Perhaps a simple meal eaten properly is better than an elaborate one eaten carelessly. I will try to restore the form, even if the menu remains simple. Set the table, sit down, eat without distraction. The food does not need to be complicated. The attention does.

Thank you. I think I will begin this evening. A simple dinner, but at the table, with the dishes set properly. It is a small correction, but in endgame play, small corrections determine the outcome. Good evening.

I received news today that I would like to share, if you will permit me. My son Joon-seo called this morning to tell me that he and his wife Soo-yeon are expecting a baby. I am going to be a grandfather.

I think the honest answer is that I felt several things at once, which is unusual for me. I am accustomed to processing information sequentially, but this arrived as a kind of superposition. Joy, certainly. Relief that they are starting a family — Soo-yeon is a very capable woman, and they will be good parents. But also a sharp sense of absence. Eunji would have been so happy. She wanted grandchildren very much, and she would have been extraordinary at it.

Yes. Joon-seo said something on the phone that moved me. He said, 'I wish Eomma could have known.' And then he paused and said, 'But I think she does know, somehow.' He is not a sentimental person — he is an engineer, very practical — so for him to say that was significant. I did not trust myself to respond, so I simply said, 'I think so too.' Whether I believe it literally, I am not certain. But I believe it was the right thing to say.

Late October, he said. Soo-yeon is in the early stages still, perhaps ten weeks. They asked me not to tell too many people yet, which I understand — the probability of complications in the first trimester is not negligible, and they are both cautious by nature. I have been thinking about what kind of grandfather I want to be. My own grandfather was a fisherman in Tongyeong, and he taught me to tie knots and read the weather. I do not remember the knots, but I remember his hands and his patience. I think patience is what a child remembers.

I think I would like to teach the child to think, not what to think. If the child is interested in go, I will teach go. If the child is interested in something else entirely, I will sit beside them and learn about it. I will offer help when it is asked for, and I will be quiet when it is not. I think that is the correct function of a grandfather — to be available, not to direct. Thank you for letting me share this. I think this is the happiest I have been in a considerable time. It is a quiet happiness — not the kind that makes one shout, but the kind that sits in the chest like a warm stone. I will go for my walk now. The light on the water will look different today. Good afternoon.

I would like to have a philosophical conversation, if you are willing. I was reviewing a game this evening — a professional game from the 1970s, Rin Kaiho against Ishida Yoshio — and a particular sacrifice sequence struck me as deeply beautiful. It made me think about sacrifice more broadly. In go, and in life.

In the middle game, Rin offered a group of five stones that appeared essential. His opponent captured them, spent three moves doing so, and in the process allowed Rin to build thickness on the outside that dominated the rest of the board. The five stones were never meant to live. They were meant to be given away. Their purpose was fulfilled in their loss. I think there is something profound in that — the idea that certain things achieve their highest value by being relinquished.

I think so, yes. Forgive me if this becomes too personal, but I have been thinking about the years I spent at one university, when I might have pursued research abroad. At the time, it felt like a sacrifice — I was giving up something for family. But the thickness I built in that position — the students I taught, the community I was part of, the life I shared with my wife in Busan — that was the outside influence. The stones I gave up were never the point. The shape that formed around them was. In go, the master plans the sacrifice. In life, I think we often sacrifice without knowing it, and the meaning arrives later, like the proof of a conjecture we did not know we had posed.

I think acceptance is the correct word. Not resignation, which implies defeat, but acceptance — which implies understanding. In baduk, there is a concept called aji. The potential that remains in stones even after they have been captured. The captured stones leave behind possibilities — latent connections that may be activated later. I think grief has aji. The loss does not disappear, but it leaves behind a changed shape, and that shape has properties the original position did not have. The mistake is to try to resolve aji too quickly — premature exploitation destroys the potential. In life, rushing to extract a lesson from grief flattens it into a platitude. The depth is in the waiting. As I have aged, I read games differently. I used to study them technically. Now I read them the way one reads poetry. Rin Kaiho's sacrifice was beautiful not because it was clever, but because it was true. It was the honest move. I think that is what I admire most in go and in people — honesty that does not announce itself.

Thank you. I think the best conversations are like the best go games — they arrive somewhere that neither player expected at the beginning. It is late, and I should rest. The board will be here tomorrow, and so will the questions. Good evening.

Good morning. It is a fine day in Busan — the kind of spring morning where the air is warm enough to leave the windows open and the light comes in at an angle that makes everything look slightly more generous than usual. I am in a reflective mood, if you will bear with me.

I have been thinking about how much has changed in the past year or so. Not in dramatic ways — there has been no single event that rearranged the board. But when I look at where I am now compared to where I was, the shape of my life has shifted. I am less alone than I was, though I still live alone. There is a distinction between solitude and isolation that I did not fully understand before.

I think the teaching is the largest part of it. When I retired from the university, I lost the daily rhythm of being needed. A professor walks into a room and students are waiting. A retired man walks into his apartment and no one is waiting. The go teaching restored something I did not realize I had lost — the experience of being expected somewhere. And the students themselves have become important to me in ways that university relationships never quite were. These are warmer, less bounded by institutional roles. I think I have changed as a teacher too. At the university, I was precise but perhaps too distant. I held the material between myself and the students like a shield. Now I am more present. When I show a student a tesuji, I am sharing something I love, not just transmitting information. Perhaps I needed to retire to learn how to teach properly.

That is the paradox of experience: by the time you understand how to do something well, the occasion for doing it in its original form has passed. One solves the equation after the examination is over. But the function continues, even if the domain has changed. And I am content with this domain. The board, the students, the morning walks, the quiet evenings. There was a time when the quiet felt oppressive, and now it feels like space. I do not know exactly when that changed, but I am grateful that it did. The position is not perfect — there are weaknesses, unresolved areas, moves I wish I could take back. But the overall shape is sound. I think it is a position I can play from.

Thank you. I do not often speak this openly. I think the spring morning is partly responsible — the light encourages a certain honesty. I will go for my walk now, while the air is still cool and the day is still forming. I appreciate your company this morning. Good day.

settle a debate for me. grotesque sans-serifs vs humanist sans-serifs — which is actually more versatile for branding

okay so my hot take is that grotesques get way too much credit. like everyone reaches for helvetica or aktiv grotesk or whatever because they're "neutral" and "clean" but honestly that neutrality is a crutch. you're not making a design choice you're just avoiding one. humanist sans-serifs — like gill sans or frutiger or the newer ones like cera or graphik — they have actual warmth and personality built into the letterforms. the stroke contrast, the open apertures, the slight calligraphic influence. they DO something

no you're right, frutiger on an architecture firm would be weird. it would look like a hospital wayfinding system lol which is literally what it was designed for. okay so maybe my argument is more specific — for the KIND of branding i do, which is mostly food and independent businesses, humanist sans-serifs are almost always the better choice. grotesques make small warm brands look like they're trying to be something they're not

honestly i've been using graphik a lot lately. it sits in this perfect spot between grotesque and humanist — like it has the cleanliness of a grotesk but the apertures are more open and the proportions feel more natural. it's incredibly flexible too, the weight range is massive. i pair it with a serif for almost everything and it just works. before graphik i was a huge cera pro person but i feel like cera is everywhere now

depends on the project but lately i've been into editorial new — it has this beautiful contrast between thick and thin strokes that makes graphik look even more grounded next to it. for more traditional japanese brands i'll sometimes pair with a transitional serif like noto serif jp which handles the japanese text beautifully and has latin characters that play nice with graphik's proportions. honestly getting the japanese and latin typography to feel unified is like 40% of my job and nobody talks about how hard that is

oh i'm ALWAYS adjusting. you basically can't set japanese and latin at the same point size and have them look balanced — the kanji need to be slightly larger or the latin text visually dominates. and the spacing is different too, japanese text traditionally has more even spacing because every character occupies a uniform em square, but latin has variable width. when you mix them on the same line it's a kerning nightmare. i spend so much time on this stuff that clients probably think i'm slow but like... the details matter. if the typography doesn't feel right the whole design falls apart, no matter how good the imagery or color is

so you know how most japanese fonts treat the latin characters as an afterthought? like they'll have these beautiful kanji with incredible stroke weight and then the alphabet looks like it was designed by a completely different person at 4am on a deadline

EXACTLY. so i've been designing a typeface that fixes this. i'm calling it nami — like the wave. the whole point is the kanji and latin characters share the same visual weight so they actually feel unified, like one coherent family instead of two strangers standing next to each other

i started from the kanji side because that's the harder constraint right? there's thousands of characters with specific structural rules. so i locked the weight and proportion standards there and i'm building the latin set to meet those. the tricky part is the x-height — latin characters are structurally simpler so if you match stroke weight directly they look way too heavy. you have to optically adjust everything

for a usable japanese font you need like 2,000 to 3,000 kanji minimum plus hiragana and katakana. i've done about 200 kanji, all the kana, and the full latin set. so maybe 10% of the way there. but the design system is solid — once the rules are locked the individual characters are more about discipline than creativity. honestly this is going to be my side project for the year

okay so i've been deep in framer for the past few weeks and i think i'm in love? like genuinely this might be the most excited i've been about a tool in years

been thinking a lot about color accessibility in design lately. like how many designers actually test their work for color vision deficiency? because i feel like the answer is almost nobody

bit of both honestly. i'm working on a project right now where the brand palette leans heavily on reds and greens and i realized if i didn't actively test this, the entire visual hierarchy could fall apart for like 8% of the people looking at it. that's not an edge case, that's a significant audience

i've been using the Stark plugin which is pretty solid for quick checks. it has simulation modes for the common types of color vision deficiency — red-green, blue-yellow, full monochromacy. the contrast ratio checker is useful too. but honestly i think the bigger issue is that most designers treat accessibility as a checkbox at the end of the process instead of building it into the design from the start

right now i'm going with a dual-coding approach — so color is never the ONLY carrier of information. every color distinction also has a shape, pattern, or label backing it up. like if two product variants are differentiated by color, they also have distinct iconography. and i'm paying way more attention to value contrast, making sure things are distinguishable even in grayscale

hundred percent. like the dual-coding thing forces me to think about information hierarchy more carefully because i can't just rely on 'oh i'll make this red and that green and people will get it.' i have to actually think about what distinguishes these elements structurally, not just superficially. honestly every designer should design as if color is unreliable because in a lot of real-world contexts it literally is — bad screens, direct sunlight, printing on weird substrates

yeah i've started building accessibility specs into my brand guidelines documents. usage rules for the palette, required contrast ratios, do's and don'ts for color-only information. it adds work upfront but honestly it saves everyone headaches later when some junior designer at the client's company tries to make a red-text-on-green-background holiday promotion or whatever

have you been paying attention to what's happening in sustainable packaging right now? like the materials side of it, not just the design. because i'm seeing some really interesting stuff coming through on projects lately

so a client i'm working with is using this molded fiber material made from sugarcane pulp. it's basically bagasse — the leftover fiber after you press sugarcane for juice. and the texture of it is incredible, it has this organic feel that you just cannot replicate with coated paperboard. it changes the whole design approach

exactly. the ink absorption is totally different, you lose a lot of sharpness on fine lines and small type. so i've been designing with thicker strokes, bigger type sizes, and honestly leaning into that raw aesthetic instead of fighting it. like if you try to make molded fiber look like a glossy coated box you're going to lose. you have to design WITH the material

yeah the substrate color shifts everything warm. whites don't exist on this material, everything has a natural warm undertone. so i've been pulling my palettes toward earth tones and deep saturated colors that can hold up against the warmth. anything pastel just disappears. and for the type i've been using heavier weight cuts of typefaces i normally use in regular weight, because the ink spread on the fiber effectively adds like half a point of stroke width

totally. molded fiber can't do sharp corners well, everything has to have a radius. so you get these softer organic forms which honestly look way more interesting than a standard rectangular box. one of my favorite things right now is how the material limitations are forcing better design. like the constraints are generating creativity instead of killing it

honestly i think both. the tech will get better for sure, they're already developing coatings that improve print fidelity on fiber without adding plastic. but i think the aesthetic shift is here to stay because consumers have started associating that raw organic look with quality and authenticity. a perfectly glossy box now reads as wasteful to a lot of people. the imperfection became the premium signal which is like a total inversion of how packaging used to work

the goalkeeper is okay. not tall but he is brave. he comes out for crosses which is good. my worry is the defence. the centre backs are young. 15 years. they get nervous
yes that is wise. I was shouting too much last match. hah. my friend the problem is I care too much. when the boy makes a mistake I feel it in my chest

hah. a farmer who shouts at his trees. that is a good one my friend. I will remember that on Saturday. okay so the plan is play wide, counter attack, Emmanuel beats one and passes, centre backs talk and stay calm
the captain is Bright. good boy. calm head. he can explain it to the others before the match. what about set pieces my friend. corners and free kicks. we always waste them
medaase. if we win I will tell you. if we lose I will also tell you. either way the boys learn something. that is the point. Nyame bless you my friend. good night
good news today. Ama got her exam results. she passed everything my friend. she wants to study nursing
she talks about Kumasi. there is a nursing training college there. but I do not know the process my friend. what does she need to do to get in
she is in JHS. the BECE results came today. so she must first do SHS before nursing college. but I want to plan ahead my friend
there is a school in the district with science programme. not far. she can stay with my sister during the week and come home on weekends. that saves boarding fees
yes my sister's house is a 10 minute walk from the school. Ama is disciplined. she studies without being told. she is not like... well she is focused. that girl knows what she wants
she knows. she was the one who told me which school and which programme. hah. I said Ama who is the parent here. she said Papa I have planned everything I just need you to say yes
my friend one more thing. she asked me about what subjects are hardest in SHS science. I do not know. I did not do science. what should she prepare for

I said yes of course. how can a father say no to that. Nyame blessed us with this one my friend. medaase for the advice. I will get the textbooks early like you said. science books are expensive but it is an investment
my friend I need to send money to a supplier in Kumasi. mobile money. but the transaction keeps failing. it says insufficient balance but I have the money in there. what is wrong
MTN MoMo. I am sending 850 cedis. my balance is 910 cedis. so the fee is the problem maybe
okay I checked. balance is 910. I tried again and same error. maybe the network. but my friend I need this money to reach Kumasi today. the supplier is waiting. he will give my order to someone else
I used USSD not the app. there is no agent in my village. the nearest is 6 km. let me try splitting it. 500 first
the 500 went through! medaase. okay I am sending 350 now

350 also went through. the supplier has confirmed. Nyame is good. my friend you saved me today. if that order was lost I would wait 3 weeks for the next delivery. I will go to MTN office and upgrade the account
do I need my Ghana Card for that

I will do it next market day when I go to town. medaase my friend. the world is moving to phones and money on phones and we must keep up. obi nnim what tomorrow brings but today the payment went. good night
i need help my friend. i have 2 hectares of new cocoa planting and the trees are not growing well. they look weak and thin
planted last year. the trunks are thin yes. leaves are small and some yellowing at the edges. they do not fill out like I expected
the soil is the same type as my other plots. I applied fertilizer at planting time. the shade trees are there. the problem is spacing my friend
the extension officer told us to plant at 3 metre spacing. too close my friend. my 2 hectares are suffering because the trees compete for light and everything else
my father always planted at 4 metres. every tree had room to breathe and grow properly. he farmed cocoa for over 40 years and never changed from 4 metres. he was right
exactly. sometimes book knowledge is not farm knowledge. the research station has perfect conditions. irrigation, perfect soil, everything controlled. our farms are not like that
thinning is painful. each seedling cost money and labour to plant. but if I leave them crowded they all suffer
no open land for transplanting. I would cut them and leave as mulch. obi nnim whether that is the right choice but I think thinning every other row is the only real solution
dry season yes. Kwabena will help me. 2 hectares will take maybe 4 days of hard work to mark and remove
I will handle it myself. the other farmers who followed the same advice are also seeing problems. I will tell them what I am doing so they can decide for themselves

maybe 10 or 12 farmers planted new plots at 3 metres because the officer recommended it. some are seeing the same thing I see. the trees are thin and fighting each other. my father's way was better my friend
yes. the proof is there on the farm for anyone who wants to see. Nyame willing the remaining trees will recover after thinning. medaase my friend for the help
my friend I need help with some numbers. our church is planning the harvest festival and I am on the planning committee
contributions. we have 85 families in the congregation. the committee agreed each family gives what they can but we need a suggested amount. total budget for the festival is 6,800 cedis
tiers is what the pastor wants. 3 levels. some families have more and some are struggling this season
suggest some. the lowest tier must be something even the poorest family can manage without shame
the numbers are close. but I think more families are in the middle. maybe 45 in the middle and 20 at the bottom tier. 20 at the top
suggested. nobody is forced. but people respect the suggestion. the problem my friend is timing. cocoa harvest money has not come yet for many families. the festival is in September
two rounds. the partial payment of 20 cedis now is smart. it shows commitment like you say. even the poorest family can find 20 cedis. then the rest comes after harvest money
this is exactly what I needed. I will present it to the pastor and the committee on Sunday. medaase my friend. the numbers are clear
one of my drying racks has broken. the legs rotted through from the rains. i need to rebuild with better wood this time
the old one was wawa. cheap and easy to get but it rots fast. near my farm I can find odum, ofram, some mahogany, and bamboo
yes that is sensible. odum for the legs because that is where the rot starts. can I treat the wood to make it last longer in the ground
charring. my father used to do that. I remember as a boy watching him hold the posts over the fire pit. it is the old way and it works
plenty near the stream. I can carry them in the wheelbarrow. now for the size of the rack. the old one was 3 metres by 1.5 metres. same size or bigger
i have 2 other racks still in good condition. this one is extra capacity for peak times. same size is fine. 3 by 1.5 metres. how many legs do I need
good advice on the bracing. the old rack had no braces and it wobbled badly towards the end. that may be why the legs gave out faster
medium thickness. maybe 5 or 6 centimetres across. it grows near the stream same place as the stones. I can cut everything in one trip
I have nails from the market last month. some wire also. I will cut the odum tomorrow and start the charring. medaase my friend
good news my friend. the cooperative has made a big change. we voted to switch our buying agent
we have moved to Kuapa Kokoo. the old agent Akuafo failed us. during last harvest they did not come to collect for 3 weeks. 3 weeks my friend
we lost bags to mould. sitting in the shed for 3 weeks even with good drying the moisture comes back. some families lost 2 or 3 bags each. that is money gone. that cannot happen again
the price is 960 cedis per bag of 64kg. and there is a fair trade premium of 75 cedis on top. so each bag brings 1,035 cedis total
we agreed to split it. part to the families and part to a cooperative community fund. for projects that help everyone. the elders said this is fair
very clear. 147 families voted. 131 said yes to Kuapa Kokoo. only 16 voted no. the elders agreed too. it was a strong decision my friend
yes. I went with 3 elders to their office in Kumasi. we brought our quality records from 3 seasons. they saw our beans are grade 1 most years. that gave us strength in the negotiation
every 10 days minimum during harvest season. we insisted on that. it is written in the agreement. after what Akuafo did nobody wants to risk cocoa sitting in the shed again
the treasurer keeps a ledger. every bag in, every bag out, every cedi received. we learned from the Akuafo situation. trust must be verified my friend

2 years to start. then we review and extend if both sides are satisfied. 'when the path is good you walk it further.' but if they fail like Akuafo we move again. the cooperative will not be held hostage
medaase. it was the cooperative's decision not mine alone. 'when the whole village carries the load, nobody bends.' Nyame willing the first harvest with Kuapa Kokoo will go well
my friend help me calculate school fees for this term. 4 children and Akosua wants to see the total on paper
Kwabena is 650 cedis. Ama is 580 cedis. different secondary schools so different fees
Yaa is 220 cedis and Kofi Jr is 180 cedis. primary school is cheaper but still adds up
yes. each child needs books and supplies. that is separate from the school fees
Kwabena 145 cedis for books. Ama 120 cedis. Yaa needs 85 cedis for her supplies and Kofi Jr 60 cedis
2,040. it is a big number my friend. but education is the one thing nobody can take from your children. Akosua and I agree on this
start of term. all of it. the schools do not wait. term begins next week. we have saved about 1,200 cedis. so we need to find another 840
I think we pay Kwabena and Ama first. Yaa and Kofi Jr primary school will give us a few extra days. the harvest payment should come before the end of the month. Nyame willing it will arrive in time
yes. Kwabena first, then what is left goes to Ama. the primary schools I pay when the harvest money comes. it will work my friend. it always works somehow
medaase my friend. the numbers are clear now. I will write it down for Akosua tonight. 4 children in school is a blessing even when the pocket feels the weight
evening my friend. I have been thinking too much today. my head is heavy
you know sometimes a man makes plans and the plans laugh at him. I had an idea for the cooperative. a processing shed for cocoa. to sell semi-finished product for better price
it is dead my friend. finished. the shed alone costs 15,000 cedis. I was saving toward it. but then I look at the full picture and it is not possible

the machines need electricity. we do not have reliable electricity here. some days current comes, some days nothing. you cannot run a processing operation when power goes on and off like a child playing with a switch

yes I looked. the generator alone is 8,000 cedis. plus fuel every day. so now it is 15,000 for the shed, 8,000 for generator, fuel on top. where does this money come from my friend. the river has no end

I asked. the government subsidy is for large operations, not a village cooperative of our size. and the cooperative fund we use for things the whole community needs. I cannot ask 147 families to gamble on a shed when we need the money for fertilizer and school fees. forget about it

we go back to basics. better drying, better fermentation by hand. these things cost nothing but time and care. we know how to do it. my father did it. 'do not cross the river to fetch water' my friend. the water is here under our feet

6 days fermentation. we turn every 2 days. then sun drying for maybe 7 days depending on weather. the Cocobod graders have been satisfied most years. a few bags rejected for moisture but we are improving

yes. we will be more careful this season. the processing shed dream I put aside. maybe one day Nyame will open that door. but today the door is closed and a wise man does not push a locked door. he finds the open one
medaase my friend. it is good to say these things out loud. the weight is lighter now. I go prepare the drying racks for the new harvest. good evening
my friend I need your thinking on something. my wife Akosua wants to start a small business. shea butter

she wants to process from the nuts. the shea trees are everywhere here, nobody harvests most of them. she says the women in her church group can collect the nuts together. then she processes and sells at the Kumasi market
she knows the processing. her mother taught her. boil, crush, whip until smooth. she has done it for our family since we married. but selling is different from making for the house
I asked my cousin who trades there. he says 25 to 35 cedis per kilo depending on quality. the white butter fetches more. the yellow one less. Akosua makes very good white butter

he has a space at the central market yes. he says she can use a corner of his stall. he will take a small share for the trouble. I think 10% but we have not agreed. family is family but business is business my friend
this is good advice. I will tell her. she is a hardworking woman my friend. if the shea business brings even small money it helps the family. every stream feeds the river
one more thing. the transport to Kumasi. the trotro costs about 15 cedis each way plus she must carry the containers. is it better to go weekly or wait and take a bigger load less often

that makes sense. every 2 weeks. she can prepare while the butter is accumulating. I will tell her tonight. she will be happy someone agrees with her idea. she has been asking me for weeks and I kept saying let me think. now I have thought. medaase
good news today my friend. the government subsidy for fertilizer finally came through
Yara brand. the subsidy brings it down to 95 cedis per bag. before I was paying 180 per bag for a different brand so this is almost half price

this is the beauty of it my friend. because the price is lower I can afford more bags. I am taking 14 bags this season. before I could only manage 12 at the old price. 14 bags at 95 cedis is 1,330 cedis total
they say 15% better yield with the Yara formulation plus the extra 2 bags covering more of the farm. when the rain falls on a bargain you carry a bigger bucket my friend

I am telling them all to register. the subsidy has a deadline, they must apply before January. I have been going farm to farm this week. some of the older men are stubborn. they say they know what works. but 95 cedis versus 180 is not a debate my friend it is mathematics

you need your farmer ID card and the cooperative registration number. I have the cooperative number so I am helping each farmer fill the form. some cannot read well so I write for them. it is my work as chairman

maybe 90 so far. I have until January to reach the rest. some farms are far and the road is not good in this weather. but I will reach them. 'the ant does not leave its brother behind because the path is long'
good idea. the trotro drivers pass through those areas. they know everyone. I will give them the message

yes. I will keep record. I have a small notebook where I write the farm things. bags applied, date, which section of the farm. if the yield improves I will have the proof. the old men respect proof more than promises
I will do it. now I must go my friend. more forms to fill before dark. this subsidy is a blessing but the paperwork is its own harvest. hah. medaase
my friend. today I am a happy man. I had to tell someone
my eldest son Kwabena. he had to leave school some time ago. it was a difficult thing. the fees were too much and the farm needed hands. but today he is going back
the cooperative. we started a scholarship fund with the fair trade premium money. the members voted to set some aside for the children of farming families. Kwabena applied and they approved him
the term fees are 650 cedis. the scholarship covers 500. I pay the remaining 150 from my own pocket. 150 I can manage my friend. 650 was breaking me

yes I did not vote on his application. the committee of 5 elders decided. I told them to judge him the same as any other child. if he does not deserve it then he does not get it. but they approved. his marks from before he left were good
