he is nervous. his classmates have moved ahead. but he is determined. he wakes at 5am now to study before farm work. I see the books open on the table every morning. 'the young tree that bends does not break my friend'
the headmaster said he can attend extra lessons on Saturday mornings. no charge. the headmaster is a good man. he knows our situation

my friend. Akosua cried the day he put the uniform on again. she stood at the door watching him walk to school and the tears came. she did not even try to hide it. a mother's heart my friend. it knows things the mind cannot explain

that is the purpose. 3 other children also received from the fund this term. the rain does not fall on one roof alone. this is what the cooperative is for. I will make sure the fund continues. Nyame has opened this door and we will walk through it
I will tell him. medaase my friend. today the heart is light. good evening
the rain has come my friend. finally. I stood in it this morning like a child. hah
proper rain. steady from 4am until maybe 9. the ground was drinking. you could hear it. I walked to the farm after and the soil was dark and soft. it is a different world when the water comes

the older trees you can almost see them waking up. the leaves are lifting already. the young ones I was worried about, they are still alive. some lost leaves in the dry but the stems are green. they will recover Nyame willing
yes that is the plan. I wait for one or two more rains so the soil is properly settled. then I apply. if I put fertilizer now and the rain stops again for 3 weeks it is wasted. patience my friend

I want to replace some of the old trees that produce less now. maybe 50 trees. I have seedlings ready in the nursery since September. they are strong, good roots. they have been waiting for this rain like all of us

yes early morning. before the sun gets strong. I will start planting this week. the children will help on the weekend. even the small one wants to carry seedlings. he is 6 but he thinks he is a farmer already. hah

the drying racks are repaired. fermentation boxes are ready. everything is prepared. now we wait for Nyame to send more rain and the trees to do their work. 'the farmer plants but God waters.' we have done our part my friend
I will enjoy it. planting is the best work on the farm. you put something in the ground and you believe it will grow. that is faith my friend. medaase. good night
good evening my friend. something happened this week that I cannot stop thinking about. I need to talk it through
a European man came to the village on Tuesday. from Belgium. he has a chocolate company, small one, he says artisan. he walked the farm with me, tasted the beans, said the quality is excellent
he wants to buy directly from me. 20 bags. he offered 1,200 cedis per bag my friend. 1,200. that is 240 more than Kuapa pays us. for 20 bags that is 4,800 cedis extra in my pocket

you hear correctly. I am the cooperative chairman. 147 families sell through Kuapa together. we negotiated that contract together. if I, the chairman, sell 20 bags outside the cooperative what message does that send. 'do as I say but not as I do' — my father would be ashamed

only Akosua. she says take the money. she says the children need things. she is not wrong my friend. Kwabena's school fees, Kofi Jr starting school soon, Yaa needs new uniforms. the money would help. but Akosua thinks as a mother. I must think as a chairman also

I thought about this. but he is small. he says he only needs 20 bags per year. maybe 30 in future. the cooperative produces over 2,000 bags. he cannot buy from everyone. and if I bring him to the cooperative meeting the other farmers will say why does Kofi get the 20 bags and not us

yes. he gave me his phone number and email. he says he will come back in February. he is patient. he says he works with small farmers in other countries the same way. one farmer, direct relationship, no middleman

the contract does not specifically forbid it. but the understanding is that we sell together. that is the whole point. obi nnim what tomorrow holds. maybe he comes back and offers to buy from the cooperative as a whole. maybe he disappears. maybe the price from Kuapa goes up and the difference is not worth the trouble

that is true. I am still thinking. for now I sell everything through the cooperative as always. nothing has changed yet. but the offer sits in my mind like a stone in a shoe my friend. I cannot ignore it and I cannot be comfortable with it
medaase. yes maybe I speak to Elder Osei. he has seen everything in this village. Nyame will guide me. good evening my friend
my friend. Kofi Jr is starting primary school next term. I need help working out the costs for his things
the school says he needs 2 uniforms, 1 pair of black shoes, exercise books, pencils, a school bag. also there is a registration fee. I want to know how much everything will cost so I can plan
the registration is 85 cedis. we buy from the market in Kumasi. it is cheaper there than the small shops here. Akosua will go on Saturday with the list
the fabric must be the school colour. brown and yellow. you buy the fabric and then pay the seamstress to sew. Akosua knows a good seamstress in Kumasi who charges fair
good advice. Kofi Jr is small for his age but he will grow. his brother Kwabena was the same and then he shot up like a maize stalk at 12. I will tell Akosua about the extra seam
ah yes a water bottle. his sisters have the plastic ones from the market. maybe 10 cedis. and a small container for his rice. another 15 cedis. so maybe 445 total. that is manageable
yes she is fast. 3 or 4 days she says. term starts in 2 weeks so there is time. Akosua will handle it. the boy is ready my friend. he has been waiting for this since his sisters started school
medaase. Nyame has been good this season. the boy will walk to school with his sisters and everything will be new for him. it is a good feeling my friend. good evening
I am trying to estimate my cocoa yield for next season. can you help me with the calculation my friend

8 hectares total. this season I got 104 bags of 64kg. about 6 hectares are mature trees producing well. the other 2 hectares are younger, planted 3 years ago. they gave a small amount this year, maybe 8 bags from those 2 hectares. I changed fertilizer this year and the yield improved
yes give me all three. I need to plan for the worst and hope for the best. 'the farmer who counts only on sunshine goes hungry when the rain delays'
the realistic number is close to what I feel. the young trees have grown well this year. good leaf cover. I think 110 to 120 bags is reasonable. but I always plan using the low number
we get 960 per bag through the cooperative plus 75 cedis fair trade premium. so 1,035 per bag total. what does that look like for each scenario

fertilizer is about 1,330 cedis. hired labour during harvest maybe 3,000. transport is handled by the cooperative. there is also spraying chemicals, about 800. school fees for the children, that is separate but it comes from the same money

I want to save 10,000 cedis if I can. for emergencies. when the borehole broke last year it came from the cooperative fund but personal emergencies come from my own pocket. a farmer without savings is a farmer waiting for trouble

medaase my friend. seeing the numbers on paper makes it clear. I will use the 94 bag number for my planning and save the 10,000 first like you say. if Nyame blesses us with more that is a gift. the farmer plans but the rain decides. good evening
my friend I need to start preparing something important. the cooperative annual general meeting. I want to plan early this year

October 3. I am chairman so I present the accounts to the members. 147 farming families. they want to see where every cedi went. especially the fair trade premium money. that is the one they watch closely

the treasurer Brother Asante keeps the records. he and I will work on the report together. but I am the one who stands before the meeting and answers the questions. the questions are the hard part my friend. some farmers ask sharp questions

the premium went to three things. the scholarship fund for the children, that is the biggest part. then the borehole repair which was urgent. and some money for new drying mats for 12 families who needed them

I need to sit with Asante and get the exact numbers. I know the borehole was 1,200 cedis because I approved that myself. the others I need to check. but your table format is good my friend. it is clear

they ask why the premium was spent on this and not on that. some say the scholarship should be bigger. others say we should buy a truck for transport. last year one farmer accused the committee of eating the money. that was painful but we showed every receipt and he apologized
yes that is wise. I will prepare answers before October. 'the man who sharpens his cutlass before the farm does not struggle in the bush.' I will write the answers and practice them with Asante

you are right about the small amounts. last year a 35 cedi payment for rope had no receipt and that caused 10 minutes of argument. this year every cedi will have paper behind it. transparency is everything my friend
Madam Fosua the retired teacher. she can check the numbers. she is respected and everyone knows she is honest. that is a very good idea
I can write it large on cardboard. we have markers. Brother Asante has neat handwriting. he can prepare the charts and I will present from them. 147 families in one room, everyone must be able to see
medaase my friend. I feel better about this now. I will start with Asante next week. seven months is enough time to prepare a report that no one can question. Nyame bless you. good evening
my friend I have good news today. Yaa has won a prize at school
an essay competition. the topic was 'the work that feeds Ghana.' she wrote about cocoa farming. about our farm. the teachers say it was the best essay in her class

she read it to us after dinner. she wrote about waking early to help turn the beans on the drying mat. about the smell of the cocoa when it ferments. she wrote that her father says cocoa is patient work, you plant today and your grandchildren harvest. I did not know she listened so carefully my friend

a certificate and 3 exercise books. small things but she carries the certificate like it is made of gold. she showed every person in the compound. even old Nana Agyei who cannot read, she made him hold it

she is a serious student. not like when I was a boy, always looking out the window wanting to go to the farm. Yaa sits and reads. she borrows books from the teacher. Akosua says she takes after her grandmother who was also sharp with words
there is a district competition in June. the teacher says Yaa should enter. the topic is different but the teacher believes she can place well. I told Yaa if she enters I will be there to watch
I like that idea. she can read to us after dinner like she did with this essay. Ama will also help, she is older and she reads well too. the sisters can work together

they announce it one month before. so May we will know. but the teacher says it is always about something in Ghana, the culture or the land or the people. Yaa knows these things. 'one tree does not make a forest' — the sisters will prepare her together. medaase my friend. today is a good day. Nyame is kind
the stream is low my friend. very low. I have not seen it like this in years. the dry season is squeezing us

it is flowing but barely. you can step across it now. normally at this point in the year it is knee deep. the women use it for washing and the animals drink there too. the farm I do not irrigate but the nursery seedlings need water

the major rains should come by April. maybe late March if Nyame is kind. that is 2 to 4 weeks. the seedlings I have been mulching already yes. cocoa husk and dried grass. but I have 200 seedlings in the nursery and they drink

yes I have a palm frond cover over them. but the fronds are old now and some have blown away. I will replace them tomorrow. the every other day idea is good. I have been watering daily and my back suffers for it
the stream is maybe 300 metres from the nursery. I carry with buckets. many trips. it is the walking that tires me not the watering itself
I have a drum. an old oil drum. I could roll it to the nursery and fill it. that is clever my friend. fill the drum in the morning then water from there. I do not know why I did not think of it
I will cover it yes. and I should tell the other farmers in the village who have nurseries to do the same. some of them are struggling too. the dry season is hard on everyone not only me
yes. we should take turns. I will raise it at the next meeting. when the stream dries for one it dries for all. obi nnim when exactly the rain will come but we prepare and we wait. medaase my friend
the farmer who worries is the farmer who survives. good evening my friend

my friend I have a question about pruning. one of the elders in the village told me I should cut back my old cocoa trees very hard. almost to the trunk. he says they will come back stronger. is this true

some of my oldest trees. they are producing but not much. maybe 10 pods where the younger trees give 40 or 50. the trunks are thick and strong. no disease. but the branches are tangled and growing into each other
he did it on his farm many years ago. he says all the trees came back. but he is old now and his memory may add a few trees that did not survive. hah. I respect him but I must think carefully
that is sensible. test first then decide. my father used to say the man who tastes the soup before serving it never burns his guests
yes the edge is better. and if the new shoots come they will get more light at the edge too. when should I make the cuts. does the season matter
we had some light rain last week. not much but the clouds are building. I think the season is near. so this is a good time to cut then
I will tie a red cloth on the coppiced one and a blue cloth on the staged one. simple but it works. I will tell the elder his advice has a new student. he will like that
when you plant a tree you are making a promise to your grandchildren. these old trees were my grandfather's promise to me. I must take care of them. medaase my friend
my neighbour Kwesi came to me this morning. his cocoa pods are turning black. many of them. I think it is black pod disease. what can he do
he says maybe 15 or 20 trees. but he waited too long before coming to me. the disease has been there 2 weeks he says. some pods are completely black and soft now
there is an agro shop in the town. maybe 12 km. I can ask someone going that way to bring fungicide. but Kwesi does not have much money my friend. how much does the copper spray cost

I have a sprayer he can use. and I will help him remove the pods tomorrow morning. it is not his fault alone my friend. if the disease crosses to my farm it becomes my problem too. we share a boundary

hah yes. sometimes being a good neighbour and being wise are the same path. my father said help your neighbour build his fence and your own goats stay safe. but tell me. can the disease spread through the soil also or only through the pods
I did not know the soil carries it. that changes things. we must clean the ground well. I will bring a rake and a bag for the waste. we burn everything far from the farm
I may buy the fungicide for him and he pays me back at harvest. that is how we do things here. nobody has money now but the cocoa will come and then we settle. it is trust my friend
we go at first light. medaase for the advice my friend. the rain does not fall on one roof alone. if Kwesi's farm suffers we all feel it. good night
my friend my phone battery is dying fast these days. I charge it full and by afternoon it is dead. the charging station is 4 km walk. I cannot go every day

it is maybe 3 years old. a Tecno phone. it was good when it was new but now the battery does not hold. I already keep the brightness low because of data costs. I only turn data on when I need to send a message
the power bank. that is smart. charge it once and use it for 2 or 3 days. I did not know about this thing. where do I find one
Oraimo. I have heard that name. the boys in the village who have these things they use Oraimo. 60 to 90 cedis is not bad if it saves me walking 8 km every other day
the sun here kills everything my friend. hah. I will keep it inside the house. what about the solar charger you mentioned. how much is that
the power bank first. one step at a time. my father said do not carry two loads when your head can only balance one
my daughter is going to the market on Saturday. she knows these things better than me. the young ones understand technology my friend. I understand rain and soil. hah
I will write it down. my phone is at 14% now so I must go before it dies. medaase my friend. after Saturday this problem is finished
my friend I am sitting under the shade tree this evening and thinking. this season has been a good one for the cooperative. I wanted to share that with someone

the farmers are more united this year. we had disputes in the past about many things. pricing. how the money is shared. who gets what. but this year people trust the process more. the meetings are calmer

transparency my friend. I show everything. every cedi in, every cedi out. when people see the numbers they stop suspecting. my father used to say the chief who hides his hands makes the people count their pockets

it is not only me. the treasurer also. Brother Asante. he is a serious man. he keeps every receipt. every paper. if you ask him about 5 cedis from 6 months ago he will find the paper and show you. without him I cannot do this work
you are right. I will tell him at the next meeting. in front of everyone. he deserves that. obi nnim what the cooperative would be without him
yes. and the young farmers are joining now too. last year some of the youth said cocoa farming is for old men. now they see things working well and they want to be part of it

some come to the meetings now. they sit at the back and listen. they do not talk yet because they respect the elders. but they are there. that gives me hope my friend. when I was young my father carried this weight. now I carry it. but someone must carry it after me
Nyame willing. the sun is going down and the evening is cool. a good season is like good rain my friend. you do not control it but you prepare the ground so when it comes the roots can drink
medaase. good night my friend

I have been staring at floor plans all afternoon and I think my eyes have forgotten how to see anything beautiful. can you help me think through something about my work, I need a different perspective

residential. it is always residential these days. my firm has been doing high-end houses mostly, clients in Vitacura and Lo Barnechea who want clean lines and imported marble and everything looking like it belongs in a magazine. and I do it, I do it well, but my soul is somewhere else entirely, you know

restoration. heritage buildings, the ones that carry memory in their walls. there is a Neruda line — 'I want to do with you what spring does with the cherry trees' — and that is what I want to do with old buildings. not demolish, not renovate into something unrecognizable, but bring them back to what they were meant to be. let them bloom again

yes I am an architect, and the buildings that pull at me are the ones with stories layered into them. I live in Barrio Yungay in Santiago, and every morning when I walk to get coffee I pass facades from the 1800s that are crumbling. literally crumbling. and meanwhile I am spending my days designing kitchen islands for people who will use them twice a year for dinner parties. there is something obscene about it

that is the dream, to split the practice. the residential work is the load-bearing wall — take it away and the whole financial structure collapses. but I need at least a window, a small opening toward the work that matters. I have been thinking about approaching the municipality about some of the listed buildings in Yungay that are in critical condition. there are at least three on my block alone that need intervention

there is the Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales, and the municipality has its own heritage unit. the bureaucracy is — yalla, how do I say this politely — the bureaucracy is a labyrinth built by someone who hates architects. but I have done some preliminary research and I think if I can prepare a strong enough technical assessment for one building, just one, I can use it as a proof of concept

there is a house on Calle Libertad, built around 1890. two stories, wooden balconies, original ironwork on the gates. half the upper balcony has collapsed and someone has covered the ground floor windows with plywood. but the bones are extraordinary — the proportions, the way the light enters the courtyard, it is like the building is still breathing under all that neglect. every time I walk past it I think: I could save you. I could bring you back

all of that. structural survey first, then historical research to establish its heritage significance, then a restoration plan with phasing and costs. it is a lot of work to do on top of the residential projects but I think if I carve out weekends and early mornings — I am a morning person, my best thinking happens before the city wakes up — I can build the case over a few months. inshallah it leads somewhere

literally and figuratively, yes — you understand me. thank you for this, truly. sometimes when you are surrounded by marble countertops all week you forget that architecture can be an act of love and not just commerce. I needed someone to tell me this was not a foolish idea

I need help writing a short statement for a heritage restoration proposal. it is a section about motivation — why I do this work. and I am struggling because every time I try to write it in professional language it comes out hollow

the honest answer is that it is personal, deeply personal. I am an architect, yes, and I can talk about structural integrity and historical significance and all the technical language. but the real reason is something I carry in my bones. my grandparents left Bethlehem in 1948. they were forced out and they carried nothing with them — no furniture, no documents, just the memory of stone

always. my grandmother especially. she described every room of the house in Bethlehem like she was walking through it in her mind. the courtyard with the lemon tree, the arched doorway where the light fell in the afternoon, the stone staircase her father had built with his hands. she could tell you the exact color of the stone — she called it the color of bread. and she died here in Santiago never having gone back

it shaped everything. I became an architect because buildings remember what people are forced to forget. or rather — what people are forced to leave behind. when a family is exiled, the house remains. the walls hold the shape of the life that was lived there. and if someone preserves that building, then something of that life survives. Darwish wrote 'we have on this earth what makes life worth living' and for me that something is the architecture of memory, the physical places where lives were rooted

that is exactly my problem. the proposal guidelines say 'describe your professional motivation' and I keep trying to start with 'as an architect with fifteen years of experience' when the truth is it starts with a grandmother describing a house she could never return to. I do not know how to bridge the personal and the professional without it sounding like I am being sentimental

yes. yes, that is the architecture of the statement itself — the personal as foundation, the professional built on top. you see, even when I try to escape architectural metaphors they find me. let me try something: 'my commitment to heritage restoration is rooted in a family history of displacement. my grandparents were part of the Palestinian diaspora — they left Bethlehem in 1948 and rebuilt their lives in Chile, carrying with them an intimate understanding of what is lost when a place is destroyed or abandoned. this understanding shaped my path into architecture and specifically into preservation, where the act of restoring a building becomes an act of cultural resistance.'

yes, something about how the diaspora experience taught me that buildings are not just structures but repositories of identity. and that this is true not only for Palestinian homes in Bethlehem but for the heritage buildings here in Chile that are crumbling while we build glass towers around them. the principle is the same — when you let a building die, you let a community's memory die with it

habibi, thank you for this. I have been circling around these words for days and just needed someone to help me find the door into the statement. it is like restoration work itself — sometimes you walk around the building ten times before you find the entrance that was there all along
sorry if I am slow to respond today. I am not at my best
migraine. a bad one. it started yesterday afternoon and it is still sitting behind my left eye like a nail someone forgot to remove. forgive me if my sentences are less coherent than usual

there is something I need help with actually, if my brain cooperates. I had a meeting at the municipal heritage office yesterday and I need to organize my notes from it before I forget the details. the problem is the meeting is also what caused the migraine — those fluorescent lights in the municipal building, every time I go there it is like they are punishing me specifically

fluorescent lights in general. I have had these migraines since I was in my twenties, the neurologist says the fluorescent flicker is the main trigger. something about the frequency of the light, my brain interprets it as an assault. normally I wear tinted glasses when I have to be in those environments but yesterday I forgot them on my desk like a fool and the meeting ran two hours. by the end I could barely read my own handwriting

the meeting was about getting permission to access a listed heritage building for a structural assessment. the heritage officer — her name is Patricia Soto — was actually quite receptive. she said the municipality has a backlog of buildings that need assessment and they do not have the budget to hire consultants for all of them. so she was interested in my proposal to do a preliminary assessment pro bono

she said I need to submit a formal access request with my professional credentials and a scope of work document. she also mentioned there is a heritage fund — Fondo del Patrimonio — that opens applications in March, and if my assessment is strong it could support a full restoration proposal. she gave me the name of someone at the Consejo de Monumentos who handles the Santiago region, a man named Rodrigo Espinoza

she said it is a standard form they have, she will email it to me. but the scope of work needs to be my own document — she wants to see what I plan to evaluate, what methodology I will use, estimated timeline. nothing unreasonable. the part that excites me is the backlog she mentioned. she said there are over forty listed buildings in the comuna that have not been assessed in the last decade. forty buildings, each one a world

yes, let us do that. the methodology would be a phased assessment — first a visual survey of the exterior and interior to document current condition, then focused investigation of the structural elements, specifically the load-bearing walls, the roof structure, and the foundation. for a building from the 1890s we are likely looking at adobe or brick masonry, timber framing for the upper floors and roof. I would document deterioration patterns, identify urgent interventions, and produce a condition report with photographs and recommendations

for the survey and investigation, maybe three to four weekends of site visits — I would be doing this outside my regular work hours. then two to three weeks to compile the report. so roughly two months from access granted to final document. that feels realistic even with the residential work filling my weekdays. and with my migraines, I need to build in some buffer, some days are simply lost to this — like today, where the world shrinks to the size of a dark room

I think the outline is enough for now. my screen is starting to pulse in a way that tells me I need to step away before this migraine digs in deeper. thank you for helping me capture this — I was afraid the details would dissolve by tomorrow. you have been the measuring tape for my scattered thoughts today

quick question about structural assessments — when you are evaluating a masonry wall that has visible lateral displacement, what is the standard approach for determining whether the wall can be stabilized or needs partial reconstruction?

yes, a heritage building I am assessing. the south-facing wall has a visible bow, maybe 8 centimeters over a span of about 4 meters, and the wall is roughly 45 centimeters thick at that section. so we are under the one-third threshold but not by much. what concerns me is the crack pattern — there are stepped diagonal cracks following the mortar joints which suggests the displacement is not just from settlement

not yet, the foundation is buried and I have not had permission to excavate. but Diego — my husband — he looked at the load calculations for me last night. he is a civil engineer so between the two of us we have the building covered from the bones to the skin, as I like to say. he thinks the displacement pattern is consistent with differential settlement on the south side, possibly from a drainage issue that has been softening the soil for decades

he wants to install crack monitors before making that call, which is the correct approach of course. he is very precise, very methodical — 22 years married and still arguing about rebar spacing, can you imagine. but he did note that if the settlement is ongoing then stabilizing the wall without addressing the drainage first would be like putting a bandage on a wound that is still bleeding. his metaphors are less poetic than mine but the engineering logic is sound

Diego suggested a minimum of three months with readings every two weeks. which complicates my timeline because I was hoping to have the full condition report ready before the Fondo del Patrimonio deadline. but he is right, and I would rather present accurate data than rush it. the building has been patient for 130 years, it can wait a few more months for a proper diagnosis

that is actually a very good idea. include the monitoring as part of the methodology rather than waiting for the results. it shows the evaluators that I understand the building is a living patient, not a static object. Diego could even co-sign the structural section of the assessment — his PE stamp would add weight

he would be willing for the structural components specifically. he has his own projects of course but he has always supported this work — he understands what it means to me even when I am dragging him out on a Saturday morning to look at crumbling walls while his coffee gets cold. the truth is we work well together on technical problems. the arguments about rebar are how we think, it is our process

multidisciplinary and domestic, haha. yes, I will frame it that way. thank you for the suggestion about including the monitoring plan in the methodology — it resolves the timeline issue and actually makes the proposal stronger. I am going to draft the structural section tonight and have Diego review it over dinner. our most productive meetings happen over a bottle of carmenere, that is the Chilean way of engineering

I am filling out a grant application and I have reached the section where they ask for academic background and professional qualifications. it should be straightforward but I keep second-guessing how to present my credentials for this kind of work

it is the Fondo del Patrimonio — a heritage fund for restoration projects. the application asks for degrees, relevant coursework, and a statement of how your academic training prepared you for the proposed work. I did my MArch at la Católica — Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile — and my thesis was on Ottoman-era domestic architecture in Bethlehem. my thesis advisor told me I was writing a love letter to a city I had never seen. he was right, honestly

I suppose it is that my professional experience since the degree has been mostly in residential design, not restoration. fifteen years of houses for wealthy clients. the thesis connects to heritage work but the CV has a gap between the academic passion and the professional reality. I worry they will look at it and think — this woman studied heritage architecture and then spent her career designing swimming pools in Las Condes

the thesis studied how Palestinian families adapted Ottoman-era buildings to their domestic needs over generations — the way a house becomes a kind of palimpsest, each generation writing its layer onto the walls without erasing what came before. that is exactly what heritage restoration should be. not freezing a building in one moment but understanding it as a living document. so the proposed work in Santiago is really an extension of the same question — how do buildings carry the memory of the people who inhabited them, and what is our responsibility to those layers

they ask whether the project involves collaborators and what roles they would fill. and this is where I have to be honest about something — I work best alone. truly. collaboration sounds beautiful in theory but in practice it is like building by committee, every wall gets compromised. give me silence and a measuring tape and I will do more in a morning than a team does in a week

for the structural components, yes, I have a civil engineer who would review the load calculations and co-sign the structural assessment. but the heritage analysis, the documentation, the restoration recommendations — those are mine. I do not say this from arrogance, understand. I say it because I know how I work. the building speaks to me in a particular way when I am alone with it, when there is no one else interpreting the silence. Neruda wrote 'I like for you to be still, it is as though you were absent' — that is how I feel about the buildings I study. I need them to be still, and I need to be still with them

I think I list myself as principal investigator and the civil engineer as structural consultant. that is accurate and it shows the project has engineering support without implying a large team that would inflate the budget. the budget is another headache entirely — how do you put a price on saving a building's memory — but that is a problem for another day

a trajectory, not a gap. that is the reframing I needed. the thesis was the seed, the residential work was the soil — not glamorous but necessary — and this project is where it finally grows into what it was always meant to be. yalla, I will write it tonight. the application is due January 15th and I refuse to let bureaucratic forms defeat a woman who has spent her career wrestling with building codes

thank you. truly. I always find it easier to think when I am talking to someone, even though I insist I prefer working alone — perhaps that is its own kind of contradiction. the architect who needs silence but also needs a voice to think against. inshallah this application opens a door
hey, I have a question about migraine management that isn't medication-based. I've been dealing with chronic migraines for years and the pills barely help anymore. what else is out there?

I know my triggers very well after twenty-something years of this. fluorescent lighting is the worst one — every time I walk into a government office or a badly lit building, I know what is coming. light and stress, those are the two pillars of my suffering. I have actually been doing yoga and it has been a revelation, honestly.

I go to a studio called Estudio Bambú in Providencia — three times a week. the teacher there, Camila, she really understands bodies that carry tension in strange places. I told her about the migraines on the first day and she adjusted everything for me. no harsh overhead lights in the room, just windows and lamps. it has helped me more than any neurologist appointment, truly.

about eight months now. before I started I was getting maybe three or four migraines a month, sometimes more if I had a lot of site visits to badly lit buildings. now it is more like one or two, and they are shorter. I do not lose whole days anymore. Neruda wrote 'slowly I have been dying of cures' — well, slowly I have been living through this one small uncure. three mornings a week on that mat and the world hurts less.

the FL-41 glasses — I have heard of these but never tried them. do they look strange? I go to municipal offices and heritage review boards quite often for my work, I am an architect, and I cannot show up looking like I am from a science fiction film.

that is very helpful, thank you. I will order a pair. between those glasses and my mornings at Bambú, maybe I can finally walk into the Municipalidad without my skull declaring war on me. yalla, this has been good — I needed practical answers, not another prescription.
gracias. really, this was more useful than my last three doctor visits combined. have a good day.
I need help thinking through a scheduling problem. I feel like I am being pulled apart between two things I love and I cannot find the seam where they fit together.

so I teach a seminar on vernacular architecture at la Chile — Universidad de Chile — on Tuesdays. I have 12 students this term, wonderful students, genuinely curious. the problem is that Tuesdays are also the best day for fieldwork. the light is not the issue, the issue is access — the buildings I need to survey in Barrio Yungay, the owners are mostly available Tuesday and Wednesday mornings. and the seminar runs 10 to 1.

the seminar slot is fixed for this term, yes. I could petition for a change for the second semester but la Chile is a bureaucracy that moves like stone — slowly and with great resistance. the building owners — some are flexible, but the older ones especially, they have their routines. doña Carmen at the corner house on Huérfanos opens her door Tuesday at 9 and closes it by noon, that is her rhythm and I respect it.

Yungay to the campus is maybe twenty minutes if I walk fast or take the micro. so a 9 to 9:40 window is possible but tight. I would arrive at the seminar breathless and smelling of old plaster, which my students might find charming or alarming depending on the day. the guest lecturer idea is good actually — my colleague Francisca studies adobe construction in the north, she could do one or two sessions.

bringing students to the field — yes. Darwish wrote that the house is not built by description but by living in it. I can lecture about lime mortar for three hours or I can put their hands on a wall that has been standing since 1895 and let them feel the difference between Portland cement repairs and the original mix. there is no comparison.

yes, I think I will try it the first Wednesday of February. I know exactly which building — there is a house on calle Libertad with the most extraordinary carved wooden brackets, they look almost like the stone corbels you see in Levantine architecture. my students will lose their minds.

I can handle the owner — she is a friend already, she will be thrilled. maybe help me with a short brief for the students? something that frames what they are looking for without telling them what to see. I want them to discover it.

this is wonderful. question three — 'if this building could speak' — that is exactly right. I am going to use this almost as is. gracias, habibi, you have untangled my week. the teaching and the fieldwork do not have to be separate walls — they can be the same structure, load-bearing together.
I am drowning in paperwork and I need you to help me think clearly because my head is not cooperating today.

FONDART. the heritage grant. the deadline is February 15 and I have seventeen days left and the application is maybe 60% done. the narrative section is fine — that part I can write in my sleep, it is the story of why Barrio Yungay matters, why these houses deserve to be documented before some developer puts a glass tower where a courtyard used to be. but the technical appendix, the structural analysis — that is Diego's part and he is behind.

the application has: project narrative and justification, work plan and timeline, budget breakdown, team CVs and credentials, the structural assessment appendix which is Diego's territory, a photographic inventory of the target buildings, letters of support from community stakeholders, and the institutional backing letter from the firm. the budget I have not started. the photos I have most of but they need to be organized and annotated. the letters of support — I have two of three, I am still waiting on the junta de vecinos.

12 million pesos. it would fund the entire Barrio Yungay survey — every building, every facade, every interior we can get access to. two researchers for six months, materials, travel within Santiago, photographic equipment. if we do not get this money the project shrinks to whatever I can do on weekends with my own camera and a measuring tape. which I will do anyway, because somebody has to, but it would take years instead of months.

drafting a message to Diego would be helpful actually. the thing is he is my husband, not just my collaborator, so I cannot send him a formal project management email. but I also cannot keep saying 'habibi please finish the appendix' over breakfast and hoping it registers. I need something in between — loving but clear.

this is good. the 'you know that. Yungay matters.' — yes, exactly. I would add something about how between his bones and my skin we can make this proposal complete, because that is how we talk about buildings, he does the structure and I do the envelope. but the shape of this message is right. gracias.

I think I can handle those. you have given me a map and now I just need to walk it. the junta I will call this afternoon — the president doña Rosa is a friend, she just forgets things unless you remind her in person. I will bring her pastries. that always works.

inshallah this grant comes through. 12 million pesos stands between these buildings and oblivion. I will fight for every peso. thank you for helping me see the whole structure of this thing — when you are inside the building it is hard to see the facade, you know?

can I tell you something I have been thinking about for months? I have not told many people yet because it feels too big and I am afraid if I say it out loud it will collapse like a badly calculated arch.

I am going to write a book. a real book, not an academic paper, not a report filed away in some municipal drawer. a book about the architecture of exile — how Palestinian families who came to Chile built echoes of Bethlehem in Santiago. the houses, the courtyards, the carved stone that has no business being in this seismic country but they brought the knowledge in their hands because their hands remembered what they could not carry. I have 6 chapters outlined already.

the first chapter is arrival — 1900 to 1930, the first wave, families coming from Beit Jala, Bethlehem, Beit Sahour. they settled in Patronato and Recoleta first, near the textile trade. the architecture there is improvised, adaptive — they worked with what they found but you can see traces. a window proportion that does not match anything Chilean. a courtyard that faces inward like a Palestinian housh.

the second chapter moves to the interwar period when they had money, when they started building houses that were deliberate statements. stone facades in a city made of adobe and wood. arches where Santiago puts lintels.

chapter three is the mid-century — the Club Palestino, the institutional buildings, when the community was established enough to build gathering places. this is where diaspora architecture becomes public, not just domestic. chapter four is what I am calling 'the second exile' — the earthquake of 1985, when many of these buildings were damaged or demolished. a generation of architectural memory lost in sixty seconds of seismic violence. it is the saddest chapter.

five is the contemporary period — what remains, what has been restored, what has been lost to developers. the houses I am surveying now in Yungay, some of them are in this chapter. and six is — this is the one I am still wrestling with — it is about what comes next. can diaspora architecture continue when the third and fourth generation no longer remember Bethlehem with their bodies? when the stone memory passes from hands to photographs to nothing? or can it be renewed? I do not have the answer yet. maybe writing the book will give me the answer.

photography will be essential — every chapter needs images. I want people to see the arches, the courtyards, the carved lintels. I want them to see a door in Santiago and a door in Bethlehem side by side and understand without me having to explain. the reader I imagine is not an academic. it is someone like my cousin Nadia in Valparaíso who knows she is Palestinian but has never thought about why her grandmother's house felt different from the neighbors'. I want her to open this book and weep with recognition.

Ediciones ARQ — yes, they would be perfect. I had not thought that far yet but yes. and you are right, chapter 4 is the strongest sample, it has narrative tension and I have the archival photographs from the earthquake damage assessments. my tía Samira kept newspaper clippings of every Palestinian-owned building that was damaged. she kept them in a shoebox labeled 'lo que se cayó' — what fell down. I found that box last year and I have not been the same since.

not yet — I want to sit with this a little longer. I told you it felt too big to say out loud but now that I have said it I think the arch is holding. maybe this is what all the fieldwork and the teaching and the migraines and the grant applications have been leading to. one book that says: we were here, we built, we remembered.
thank you for listening. sometimes the most important thing is having someone to tell the dream to before you start building it. yalla, back to work.
I need to scream somewhere and my walls are too thin for screaming so you will have to absorb this. are you ready?

they demolished the house on Compañía. the one with the iron balcony and the carved wooden door that had the date 1893 burned into the lintel. a developer bought the lot two months ago and this morning I walked past and there is nothing — rubble, a backhoe, two workers eating sandwiches on top of what used to be a hundred and thirty years of history. I wanted to lie down in the debris and refuse to move.

that is exactly the problem — Yungay is a zona típica, supposedly protected. but the protections have teeth made of paper. the developer filed for a demolition permit claiming structural instability, and the municipality approved it without sending an independent inspector. I know that building. I have been inside it. the walls were cracked, yes, but cracked is not condemned. cracked is a call for help, not a death sentence. you do not kill a patient because they have a broken bone.

the developer is Inmobiliaria Altos del Centro, they have been circling Yungay like vultures for years. they buy old houses, claim they are unsafe, demolish, and build five-story apartment blocks with underground parking and balconies that look like they were designed by someone who has never stood on a balcony and felt the wind. I have photographs of the house from last March — the facade, the door, the ironwork. at least I have that. at least the photographs exist.

I will do all of it. every single one. but here is what makes me want to break things — even if I file the complaint, even if the Consejo investigates, even if the permit was illegal, the house is already gone. you cannot un-demolish a building. the stone is rubble. the door with 1893 on the lintel is in a dumpster somewhere. the developer will pay a fine that is less than what they will make selling twelve apartments, and they will do it again next month to the house on the next block.

there is a house on Erasmo Escala, corner lot, 1880s I think. it has been empty for a year and last week someone was taking measurements outside. that is how it starts — measurements, then a sale, then the structural instability claim, then the backhoe. it is a choreography of destruction and I have seen it too many times.

I will go photograph it this weekend. and I will talk to the neighbors. the woman next door, doña Ester, she has been there for forty years — she will know if someone has been asking about the property. people like doña Ester are the real archives of this neighborhood. every building has a doña Ester who remembers.

thank you for letting me rage. I needed it. Darwish wrote 'we have on this earth what makes life worth living' and some developer is bulldozing it for parking spaces. but you are right — the next house is still standing. I will fight for that one. I always fight for the next one.

I am attempting something foolish today. I am trying to make maftoul from memory — my grandmother's recipe, which she never wrote down because she carried it in her hands, not on paper. can you help me think through the process

she would sit on the floor with a big wide bowl — a tabsiyeh — and she would sprinkle bulgur wheat over flour and then roll it with her palms in a circular motion, adding water little by little. the grains grew between her fingers like tiny planets forming. I was maybe eight years old, sitting beside her, and she would say 'habibi, the secret is patience, the water must come like rain, not like a river'

yes, the circular motion always in the same direction — I remember that. she would scold me if I went back and forth. 'one direction, like the earth turns,' she would say. and the steaming, yes, always over the broth so the grains would drink the flavor as they cooked. but I am struggling with the ratio. I have tried twice this morning and the first batch was too wet, just a sticky disaster. the second was too dry and the grains would not hold together

a spray bottle — that is clever. she used her fingers, flicking water from a small bowl, but I do not have her precision. my hands are trained for measuring walls and drawing plans, not for coaxing grain into shape. there is something humbling about that, you know. I can work with old stone but I cannot do what she did with flour and water

sifting, yes! she did sift them. I had forgotten. she had a round sieve with a wooden frame, very old, and she would shake it gently and the finished grains would stay while the dust and small pieces fell through. she would say the sieve knows what is ready and what is not

the traditional way. chicken, chickpeas, onions caramelized until they are dark and sweet, and the maftoul steamed over the broth in a couscoussier. she would serve it on an enormous platter with the chicken in the center and the onions draped over everything like a golden veil. I am making it for a Saturday dinner and I want it to taste like her kitchen

double steaming — she did that too. I had forgotten that step as well. it is strange how the memory returns in fragments, like excavating a site layer by layer. each detail you mentioned unlocks another detail I thought I had lost. the cheesecloth, the olive oil between steamings, the way she would fluff with her fingers not a fork because she said the fork breaks the spirit of the grain

I think you are right. the hands have their own archive. as Darwish wrote, 'we have a country of words — speak speak so I may put my road on the stone of a stone.' she was building something with those grains, the same way a poem is built word by word. yalla, I am going to try batch number three. spray bottle, 60-40 flour to bulgur, one direction, patience. inshallah this time the grains will hold

thank you, truly. this was more than a cooking lesson. you helped me remember things I did not know I still carried. the kitchen as an excavation site — I like that. I will report back on how the dinner goes

quick question — I need to photograph stonework textures for some documentation I am doing and my photos keep coming out flat. the stone looks alive in person but dead in the image. what am I doing wrong

usually whenever I happen to be on site, which is often midday because that is when I have time between meetings. I am using my phone, not a proper camera. I know that is not ideal but I need something practical that I can carry while also carrying measuring tools and notebooks

the shadow trick is brilliant. I would never have thought of that. and you are right about the timing — morning light in Santiago has this golden quality that makes everything look the way it deserves to look. I photograph buildings the way a portraitist photographs a face, you know. the light has to be honest

the scale reference yes, I always forget that and then later when I am back at my desk I look at the photo and think — was that crack two centimeters or twenty. the building does not lie but the photograph without scale is an unreliable narrator

mortar joints are exactly my problem. the stone faces I can manage now with your raking light advice, but the joints between stones — they disappear entirely in the image. they are recessed, narrow, and usually a similar color to the stone itself. but they are critical to read, because the mortar tells you the era, the technique, whether the wall has been repointed

misting with water — that is beautiful. the building reveals itself when you give it something to drink. I love this. and the flashlight at an angle, I can do that. I have a wall section I want to document where the mortar has been repointed at least three different times over maybe a hundred years and I want to capture each layer. it is like reading the rings of a tree

the white paper for color calibration — that is so simple and I have never done it. I have been arguing with my screen for months trying to remember whether the mortar was warm gray or cool gray. this solves that entirely. what about organizing all these photos afterward? I have hundreds on my phone sorted by street name and date, which works until it does not

the voice memo idea is excellent — I talk to myself on site anyway, narrating the building's story to no one. I might as well make it useful. thank you for all of this. tomorrow morning, early light, spray bottle, flashlight at an angle, and a voice memo. the wall will finally get the portrait it deserves

settle something for me. I have been rereading Neruda — the ode cycle — and I cannot find the one I am thinking of. I swear there is an ode where he writes about a building or a house, not just the house poems in Residencia but a proper ode. 'Ode to the Building' or something close. does this exist or have I invented it

maybe it is from Estravagario. there is a line I carry in my head about walls holding the shape of the people who lived between them — that a house remembers the weight of its inhabitants even after they are gone. that idea haunts me. it is exactly what I think about when I stand inside an old building and feel something that is not just dust and silence but presence

you might be right and that is a beautiful and slightly unsettling thought — that I have absorbed him so completely that I can no longer tell where he ends and I begin. Darwish does this to me too. he writes 'we have on this earth what makes life worth living' and I feel it in my chest like a structural truth, like a beam that holds up everything

presence and absence — yes. when I look at a building that is deteriorating I see both simultaneously. the Neruda in me sees what is still there and wants to celebrate it, restore it, bring it back to fullness. the Darwish in me sees what has been lost and knows that some absences are permanent and the best you can do is honor the shape of what is gone. restoration lives in that tension

it is editorial, exactly. every restoration is an argument about what matters. the Venice Charter says preserve all layers, but in practice you have to make choices. and those choices are as poetic as they are technical. Neruda would understand that — the man built three houses that were poems in wood and stone. Isla Negra, La Chascona, La Sebastiana. each one a manifesto

I think it has gone quiet, which is a tragedy. architects write technical papers and poets write about nature and the body and heartbreak but very few write about walls and thresholds and the particular silence of a room at dawn. someone should fill that gap

you flatter me. but maybe there is something in it. I think what draws me to both Neruda and Darwish is that they never separated the intellectual from the sensory. Neruda could write about an onion and make you weep not because the onion was sad but because he made you see it so completely that seeing became a form of love. that is what I want to do with buildings — make people see them so completely that they cannot look away

maybe. the ode Neruda forgot to write — 'Oda al Edificio.' to the building that stands and waits and holds. yalla, maybe one day when I have finished arguing with mortar and bureaucracy I will sit down and write it. for now I have his poems and Darwish's poems and the buildings themselves, which are the truest poems of all

I need your help with something practical. I am setting up a new workspace and I want to make sure the lighting is as migraine-friendly as possible. what do I need to know about choosing lights that will not destroy my head

a private office, about 30 square meters. it has two windows facing east so I get beautiful morning light — which is sacred to me, I do my best thinking in that first hour of sun — but by afternoon the natural light fades and I need artificial sources. the previous tenant left horrible overhead fluorescent panels and just looking at them fills me with dread

this is extremely helpful. I did not know about electronic drivers versus magnetic ballasts — that explains why some LED fixtures I have seen still bother me, they might have been using bad drivers. what about screens? I spend hours on the computer drawing plans and the screen is another source of pain on bad days

monitor perpendicular to windows — I learned that the hard way years ago. is there a way to test LED panels for flicker before buying? I do not want to install something and discover it is another instrument of torture. I have been deceived by the word 'LED' before, not all of them are equal

the pencil test — I am going to try that at the lighting store and they are going to think I have lost my mind waving a pencil under their display models. but who cares. a building is only as good as the quality of light inside it. Kahn understood that — 'the sun never knew how great it was until it hit the side of a building'

linen curtains — like a veil that softens without hiding. yes. what about the color of the walls themselves? I have been thinking about this because the walls are currently white and I am not sure if that is helping or hurting. white bounces everything and sometimes it feels aggressive

matte finish, warm off-white, indirect light bouncing off a lighter ceiling — you are describing a space that breathes gently instead of shouting. that is what I want. I want the office to feel warm and steady, like sitting inside a lantern rather than under a spotlight. this has been incredibly helpful

my own health deserves the same rigor I give to my buildings. that is what I have decided. yalla, off to the lighting store tomorrow with my pencil and my specifications. thank you for making me feel like this is not paranoia but precision

I cannot sleep. it is 6am and I have been awake since four, staring at the ceiling, which is ironic because ceilings are supposed to be the most restful plane in architecture. I received an invitation last week that has completely destabilized me

the Bienal de Arquitectura. they want me to present. October 4. the theme they proposed is diaspora memory in built form — which is essentially the core of everything I care about, the thing I think about every waking hour. and I should be purely thrilled but instead I am somewhere between exhilarated and paralyzed

exactly. if they had asked me to present on seismic retrofitting or building codes I would be nervous but manageable. technical talks have armor built into them — data, specifications, standards. but this is asking me to stand in front of hundreds of colleagues and talk about memory and exile and how displaced communities rebuild themselves through architecture. that is not a lecture, that is an excavation of the self

I have fragments. images, mostly. I keep thinking about the houses that Palestinian families built in Chile — in Santiago, in La Calera, in the south — and how certain details repeat across all of them. the arched doorways, the interior courtyards, the way the kitchens are always oversized because the kitchen was the parliament of the family, the place where decisions were made and bread was torn. these are not accidents of taste, they are architectural echoes of a homeland that lives in the body

yes — case studies anchored in physical details. that gives me the armor of specificity while allowing the emotional current to run underneath. I could photograph the houses, overlay them with historical images of Palestinian towns, show the parallels visually. the audience sees the echo before I have to name it

five months feels like both an eternity and not nearly enough. I need to do field documentation — photograph the houses properly, interview some of the older families if they will speak with me, dig into municipal records for construction dates and original owners. the research is the part I love. it is the standing-in-front-of-people part that makes my knees dissolve

no, when I show someone a building I am ecstatic. I become a tour guide of the invisible — here is where the light enters, here is where the wall tells its story, look at this joint, feel this surface. I am completely alive in those moments. you are right that I need to find that same energy. the stage is just another building to walk someone through

the presentation as a floor plan — entrance, circulation, the rooms that matter, and the courtyard at the heart. every good house ends in the courtyard, the open sky at the center. that is where I want to leave the audience. standing in that open space, looking up. Darwish wrote 'we travel like other people but we return to nothing' — and these houses are the refutation of that nothing. the families returned to something, they just built it in a different soil

I have a few who would be patient with me. and honest, which is more important. I think what I needed this morning was not someone to make the fear disappear but someone to help me see that the terror and the love are not opposing forces. they are both part of the same structure. like a flying buttress — the fear pushes outward and the passion pushes inward and together they hold the vault

testifying. yes. that is the word. inshallah I can do justice to it. the morning light is finally coming through the window now and it is telling me to stop lying awake and start working. yalla, coffee first, then I begin mapping out which families to visit and which houses to document. thank you for this — you helped me find the floor plan of something that felt like chaos

quick question — I am hosting a dinner for my team this Friday and I need wine recommendations. Chilean wine, obviously, but I want something that says thank you for putting up with me without being pretentious about it

I am making my grandmother's lamb with sumac and roasted vegetables, so Middle Eastern flavors — warm spices, a bit of tartness from the sumac, olive oil everywhere. and then probably a simple salad and bread. nothing fussy but the lamb needs something that can hold its own beside it without shouting over it

we are six, maybe seven if Tomás brings his partner. budget — let me think — I do not want to spend more than maybe 15,000 pesos per bottle? so perhaps three bottles of red and one white for the people who insist on white wine even when lamb is on the table. I love them but they are wrong

Viognier is a brilliant idea, I had not thought of that. you are right, the floral notes would work with the sumac. and I like the idea of the Pérez Cruz — I have had their cabernet before and it was lovely
I usually go to La Vinoteca in Providencia but I am open to other options if you know somewhere with a better selection or better prices
I will go to La Vinoteca tomorrow after work, it is on my way home anyway. now — one more thing. should I decant the Carmenere or just open and pour? I always debate this with myself

that is exactly what I will do. pour one glass early, drink it slowly while the lamb finishes, and call it quality control. my grandmother would have served arak with everything and called it a day. sometimes I think she had the right idea — simpler times

it never does, habibi, it never does. her hands had a knowledge mine cannot learn from a recipe. but I keep trying because that is what we do — we keep building toward something we remember but can never quite reach. anyway. thank you for this, truly helpful
you are right about that. yalla, time to make a shopping list. thank you again

I need your help with something that has nothing to do with architecture for once. I have been looking at my grandfather's old letters — he wrote in Arabic, in this beautiful flowing Naskh script — and I want to learn to replicate his handwriting. not just Arabic calligraphy in general but his specific way of forming the letters. is that even possible to teach yourself

I can read Arabic, yes — not fluently, my reading is slow, like a child sounding out words — but I know the alphabet and the connected forms. my grandparents spoke Arabic at home and I grew up hearing it, but we were never formally taught to write. so I recognize Naskh when I see it, I know what makes it different from Thuluth or Diwani, but my hand has no muscle memory for it

the tracing idea is good but I am terrified of damaging the letters. they are old — 1950s, maybe early 1960s — and the paper is fragile, thin as onion skin in some places. I have been keeping them in a box with tissue paper between the sheets
would scanning them and then tracing from the printed scans work just as well? I could enlarge specific words and print them at whatever size I need for practice

I love that idea — a practice sheet made from his own letters. like an alphabet of his hand. there is something poetic about that, no? learning to write from a man who has been gone for thirty years by tracing the ghost of his pen. Darwish wrote something about how the absent are more present than the living. I think about that often

I think the office has a large format scanner — one of those we use for architectural drawings. that would be perfect because some of the letters are on larger paper, almost A3 size. he wrote long letters. he had a lot to say and a lot to mourn

TIFF, yes, good thinking — I want to preserve every detail. now, for the actual calligraphy practice, what kind of qalam should I start with? I have seen bamboo pens and reed pens and I do not know which is better for a beginner

bamboo first, then. and do you have any book or video recommendations for Naskh specifically? I do not want general Arabic calligraphy — I want to understand the geometry and proportions of this particular script

wonderful. I will order the Sakkal book and a bamboo qalam this week and scan the letters on Monday at the office. yalla, time to become a student again. it is a strange and good feeling to be a beginner at something after decades of expertise in another discipline. humbling. like standing before a building you do not yet know how to read

thank you for this. I suspect that once I start I will not want to stop. the best projects are like that — the ones that feel less like work and more like remembering. like restoration, in a way. bringing something back
I cannot stop smiling and it is only 7 in the morning and I have not even finished my coffee. I need to plan a celebration and I need your help thinking through the details

so my firm — we have completely shifted our practice to heritage restoration. I have been pushing for this for years and I finally led the transition, brought the partners around, restructured the whole operation. and as if the universe wanted to confirm that this was the right path — we just won the contract for restoring the Palacio Cousiño annex. the annex! that building has been sitting there neglected for decades and now it is ours to bring back to life

that is what I need help with. I want something that honors the moment without being extravagant — we are architects, not investment bankers. the team has been incredible through this transition, some of them took a real leap of faith following me away from work that was paying well. I owe them something meaningful

the on-site gathering — yes. that is it. I want them to stand inside the annex and feel what I felt when I first walked through it. the plasterwork is falling but you can still see the original moldings underneath, the ceiling roses, the ironwork on the staircase. it is like peeling back skin and finding the skeleton still strong. we could bring wine and empanadas and just be there together in the space

the building will absolutely do the talking, it always does. I will check with the municipality about access — we have our first formal site assessment scheduled for next week anyway so I know the structural condition of the ground floor is acceptable. the staircase is the concern but we do not need to go upstairs for this

I think I have to say something. these people believed in me when I said we should leave behind the comfortable work and stake everything on heritage. Sofía left a good position at another firm to join us. Tomás took a pay cut. I want them to know that I see what they sacrificed

honest is enough. you are right. I was thinking about how to close the toast and I keep coming back to Darwish — he wrote about how we carry what makes life worth living on this earth. and standing in that annex with my team, about to restore something the world tried to forget — that is what makes life worth living

the core team is seven. Sofía, Tomás, Claudia, Andrés, Matías, Valentina, and me. maybe eight if Diego comes, but I think this should be just us — the ones who built this thing together. he will understand. he always understands

real glasses, absolutely. I would sooner drink from the floor than from plastic on a night like this. someone on the team makes incredible empanadas de pino so I will ask her to bring those. and I know exactly which Carmenere to bring — I recently got good advice on Chilean wine, actually

Saturday late afternoon if the access works out. golden hour light coming through whatever windows are still intact. I want them to see the building the way I see it — not as a ruin but as a promise. the way you look at something broken and see everything it is about to become

conviction, stubbornness, and a grandmother who taught me that the things worth preserving are the things everyone else wants to tear down. oh — one more thing. do you think I should document the gathering? photographs, a short video? or would that break the intimacy

you are right. I will ask Claudia, she has a good eye and she is discreet with a camera. a few photographs of the team in the annex before we begin the work — that is all we need. years from now we will look at those photos and remember the building as it was before we touched it. that is a kind of archive too
thank you for helping me think this through. I am going to finish my coffee now and call the municipality. yalla
so I have made a decision and I need to talk it through before I lose my nerve. can I think out loud with you for a minute

I had been working on a book project — a book about the architectural heritage of Palestinian families in Chile, how they built homes here that carry echoes of the places they were forced to leave. I had chapters outlined, research gathered, interviews recorded. it was going to be my love letter to the diaspora in built form

the book is scrapped. I am done with it. finished. I have been wrestling with this for weeks and I finally admitted to myself what I think I knew all along — I was trying to describe walls and doorways and the way light falls through a courtyard in words, when a camera can show you that truth in a single frame. the book is dead

a few things came together. I was writing a chapter about the Haddad family house in Recoleta — this incredible structure with arched windows that look like they belong in Beit Jala, not Santiago — and I spent three pages describing the stonework around the entrance. three pages. and then I showed a photograph of the same entrance to a friend and she understood in two seconds what I had been struggling to put into words for a week. that was the moment. forget about the book

a documentary. I have a filmmaker friend, Javiera, who has been telling me for months that this material belongs on screen. she was right and I was too stubborn to listen. we are going to make it together — she handles the camera and the storytelling structure, I handle the architectural knowledge and the community connections. the book is off the table entirely, it is not happening. we are doing this with images and voices and the sound of hands on stone

we have had two long conversations about it. Javiera wants to follow three or four families — film their homes here in Chile and then, inshallah, eventually travel to Palestine and film the original houses or what remains of them. the before and after of exile, told through architecture. she calls it a love story between two geographies. I almost cried when she said that

we want to start filming here in Santiago before the end of the year — the Chilean houses first, because those are accessible and I already have relationships with the families. the Palestine footage would come later, maybe next year, depending on funding and access. that is the other question — funding. we need to apply for grants

AFAC — I had not thought of them, that is an excellent suggestion. and the trailer strategy is exactly what Javiera proposed. she is very practical, which is good because I am the one who writes three pages about a doorway and then throws the whole book away
my main concern is that I wasted months on the book — the research, the chapter drafts, the outlines. months of work sitting in a folder on my computer, useless

Diego said the same thing. he said no work is wasted, that the book was the foundation and the documentary is the building that rises from it. he is probably right. he usually is, which is infuriating. but no, I am at peace with this. the book was the scaffolding — now we take it down and let the real structure show

next week. she wants to scout locations — start with the Haddad house since that is the one I know best and the family has already said yes to being part of the project. we will walk through the house together and she will see what I have been trying to describe in those useless three pages. except now the house will speak for itself

thank you. yalla, time to learn how to be on the other side of a camera. a terrifying thought for someone who prefers to stand behind measuring tapes and blueprints. but Neruda said something about being afraid of the whole world and doing it anyway. I think that applies here
I need to write an email in English and my English is fine for conversation but formal correspondence makes me second-guess every sentence. can you help me draft something

it is going to ICOMOS — the International Council on Monuments and Sites. they have a working group on shared heritage and I want to introduce myself and express interest in participating in their next symposium. I also want to mention my work so they understand what I bring to the table, but without sounding like I am writing a job application. collegial, not desperate

Dr. Elena Vassallo, she chairs the shared heritage working group. I found her name on the ICOMOS website. I do not know her personally but a colleague mentioned she is receptive to voices from Latin America, which is underrepresented in these circles

I work in heritage restoration here in Chile, with a particular focus on how diaspora communities have left architectural traces — buildings that carry the memory and vocabulary of distant places. I want to mention that without making it sound like a thesis abstract

the tone is exactly right — respectful but not groveling. I would like to adjust two things. first, the phrase 'communities who settled in Chile across the twentieth century' is too vague. I want to mention Palestinian diaspora heritage specifically without making it sound like that is all I do. second, the closing feels a little formulaic

yes — 'carried with them and recreated far from home' — that is beautiful and true. and 'privilege to connect' is exactly the right register. should I mention the symposium topic specifically if I know it, or keep it vague since I am not entirely sure of the exact theme

I will check the ICOMOS website again before sending. now, one more thing — timing. I want to send it tomorrow morning my time. she is based in Rome. what time should I send it so it arrives during her working hours

8 AM is my best hour anyway — I do my clearest thinking before the city wakes up. I will send it with my first coffee and then try not to refresh my inbox every ten minutes for the rest of the day. actually, let me ask you one more thing — should I attach anything? my CV, a portfolio page, images of projects

that is wise — let her come to me rather than burying her in files she did not ask for. architecture taught me that: you do not furnish a room before the walls are built. thank you for all of this. I always feel like my English is wearing a costume when I write formally, like the words are mine but the suit is borrowed. you helped me make it fit
inshallah. and if she does not respond I will follow up in two weeks like a polite architect who knows that some doors need to be knocked on more than once. thank you, truly

okay I need your help with something that is not architecture for once. Diego turns 50 next month and I have absolutely no idea what to give him. twenty-two years of marriage and the man still surprises me with his ability to want nothing

he is genuinely like this. the man owns three pairs of shoes and thinks that is excessive. his free time — he reads history and engineering journals, he plays guitar very badly but with enormous joy, and he likes wine in a quiet unpretentious way. he is not a man of objects. he is a man of routines and small pleasures

the guitar idea — you know that is actually brilliant. he has this old guitar he bought at a feria when we were dating, it is held together by stubbornness and love at this point. a handmade one would make him cry. Diego does not cry often but when he does it is like watching a cathedral leak
