classical, nylon strings, always. budget — look, the man has endured two decades of me talking about cornices and mortar ratios. he deserves whatever it costs. maybe up to 800,000 pesos. I want it to be special but I am not losing my mind entirely

cedar top, warm and forgiving — that sounds like Diego himself honestly. I will call this week. yalla, if this guitar makes him cry I will send you a recording of the cathedral leaking. thank you habibi
we had the most extraordinary day in the field today and I need to tell someone about it before the feeling evaporates

we were in Barrio Yungay surveying a row of three houses on Calle Compañía, all from the 1880s, connected by a shared party wall system that nobody had documented properly. Sofía our historian found a reference in the municipal records to a shared cistern beneath the courtyard — a rain collection system, gravity-fed, pre-municipal water supply. and then Tomás, our conservator, started tapping the courtyard tiles and listening for hollow spaces. and he found it

not yet — permits. but Gabriela, our newest team member who does photogrammetry and scanning, ran a ground-penetrating scan and confirmed the void. it is there. a whole circulatory system under the skin of the neighborhood, sleeping for a century. I was so moved I had to sit on the curb. Tomás brought me coffee without being asked, which tells you everything about the man

based on the scan it could extend under all three properties and into the alley behind. the shared party wall above ground now makes sense in a completely new way — these houses were designed as a collective organism, not individual units. the infrastructure was communal. but I want to say something about this team, because they are the reason any of this was possible

the team we have put together is something extraordinary. Sofía alone would have had a footnote buried in an archive. Tomás alone would have tapped tiles and heard nothing he could interpret. I alone would have drawn elevations and moved on. but when we are together in a space, in conversation, the whole picture assembles itself from our different ways of seeing. the best ideas emerge from dialogue — I feel that in my bones now. as Darwish wrote, 'we have a country of words, speak speak so I may lean my road against a stone.' each of us is the stone the others lean against

fiercely protecting. the owner of the middle house, Señora Eliana, she has lived there for sixty years with no idea what was under her patio. she cried when we told her. I cried. Tomás pretended not to cry. Sofía documented everything including the crying, because she is a historian and historians document

inshallah it will. I have to go — Gabriela is sending the scan files and I want to study them before my eyes get tired. thank you for letting me pour this out. some days the work gives you something so beautiful you have to share it or it burns inside you

good morning. I am having the most perfect cup of coffee right now — fresh beans from that roaster on Calle Caupolicán, ground by hand, brewed slowly. I wanted to ask you something about stretching and muscle recovery for fieldwork

my lower back is staging a full revolt. days of crouching in courtyards and climbing scaffolding. yoga helps enormously but I want to know what I should do on non-yoga days to keep everything from locking up

three times a week still. I actually switched studios recently — I go to Refugio Yoga now, in Barrio Italia. much smaller place, very quiet. no fluorescent lights, just candles and these generous windows that let the afternoon light in. so much better for my head. and the space itself feels like it was designed by someone who understands that a room can either heal you or wound you

hatha and some restorative classes. the teacher Francisca has this very body-aware approach — she asks about injuries, about stress, about where you are holding tension. then she adjusts the practice for you. it is not a performance, it is a conversation between you and your own structure. she gave me a modified sequence for hip openers and lower back release that I do after field days

Diego has one. civil engineers apparently also destroy their spines. I will steal his. Francisca also says my lower back is compensating for weak abdominals, which is probably true — I have the core of a poet, not an athlete

my body is the house I live in and I have been neglecting the foundations, which as an architect I should know is a catastrophic oversight. yalla, planks and dead bugs and a stolen foam roller. a restoration project for my own structure. thank you — time for my second coffee and then the field

I need to think through something about Chilean building codes and I am hoping you can help. specifically the regulations around facade retention when you modify a heritage-listed building. I keep running into contradictions in the code and it is making me want to scream into a very old wall

exactly the first. the Ley de Monumentos Nacionales says the facade must be preserved in its original state. fine. but the Ordenanza General has seismic retrofit requirements that sometimes make it structurally impossible to keep the facade attached to a modified interior without major intervention. the two codes were written by people who never spoke to each other. it is like designing a building where the architect and the engineer used different unit systems

the Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales evaluates case by case, which sounds reasonable until you discover that identical situations get opposite rulings depending on the reviewer. no precedent system, no published rationale. I have seen one project approved for concealed steel bracing behind an adobe facade and another denied for the same technique six months later. it is kafkaesque

Peru is my best reference. after the Pisco earthquake in 2007 they updated the Norma E.080 with specific provisions for heritage adobe structures. they allow concealed reinforcement as long as it is reversible and documented — meaning you can undo the intervention without damaging the original fabric. I am building my submission around three principles: reversibility, minimal intervention, and visual integrity. if I can show the Consejo that an internationally validated framework supports my approach, maybe I can survive the lottery

January, ideally. the permits take months and we want to begin work in autumn. thank you for helping me organize my thinking — the codes may be a labyrinth but at least now I have a thread to follow. as Neruda said, 'I do not know who is living in me' — except in this case I do know, it is the entire Chilean regulatory apparatus living in my head uninvited
I did something this week that has been sitting inside me like a stone and I need to talk about it

I resigned from the university. I told the department I would not be returning to teach the vernacular architecture seminar next semester. after all these years at la Chile, I walked in on Monday and let it go

like I have set down something heavy and my arms do not know what to do with the emptiness. relief and grief braided together. every Tuesday I was leaving buildings in Yungay that were whispering their secrets to me so I could go stand at a podium and describe walls to students who had never touched them. I was offering photographs of water to people who had never been thirsty

yes, exactly that. and there is a Neruda line that kept circling in my head — you cannot embrace the new thing if your hands are still gripping what came before. my hands were full of syllabi and grading and committee meetings. I needed them empty. I need them on the walls, on the plaster, reading the cracks with my fingers. not holding a laser pointer

the department head understood. she said I was one of the few who taught from experience rather than theory, which was kind and also confirmed my decision — the experience is where I belong. but one student, Valentina, she wrote me an email saying my seminar was why she chose heritage conservation as her path. that was the hardest part. that one kept me awake

Diego said nearly the same thing. he said my students learned from me because I was doing the work, not because of the classroom. keep doing the work and they will find you. which is either wisdom or a very elegant way to help me not feel guilty. I suspect it is both

I said the door is always open from my side. but I do not think I will walk back through it. Tuesday mornings are mine now. I will be in Yungay before dawn, coffee in hand, waiting for the light to touch the facades. the seminar was the photograph of the work — beautiful but flat. I want the three dimensions. the dust, the smell of old plaster, the cracks that tell you where the earth moved. inshallah that is enough
do you ever have a building that haunts you? not in a dark way, more like a song you cannot stop humming. I saw something last weekend and I have not been able to think about anything else since

Diego and I drove out to Valparaíso for the day — Santiago in January is merciless, the heat just sits on you. and we were walking through Cerro Alegre, which I have walked a hundred times before, but this time I turned down a side street I had never taken. and there it was. a house, early 1900s, maybe 1910. two stories, balcony wrapping around the second floor with ironwork that looked hand-forged. the plaster falling off in sheets. a fig tree growing through the courtyard wall. and I stood there on that hill with the Pacific behind me and I thought — this house is calling me

Diego did what he always does — he looked past the romance and started reading the bones. he said the foundation looks solid, the thick masonry walls are intact, the roof has lost tiles but the timber frame underneath seemed sound. it is the skin and the details that are suffering — the ironwork, the plaster ornamentation, the wooden shutters. everything that gives the house its face. an elderly neighbor told me the family moved to Viña years ago, the house has been empty at least a decade

this is the part where maybe I sound a little crazy. I keep imagining spending six months there — just living in Valparaíso and bringing this house back to life. I know it is a fantasy, I know I have a whole existence in Santiago, my apartment in Yungay, my firm, the projects we are running. Diego says I am losing my mind. but the heart wants what it wants and this house has gotten under my skin like nothing has in years

I want to talk about a poem. Mahmoud Darwish, 'In Jerusalem.' I have been rereading it obsessively this week and I need someone to think about it with me

the opening — 'In Jerusalem, and I mean within the ancient walls' — that insistence on precision, within the ancient walls, as if he needs to locate himself exactly before he can begin to speak. as an architect I understand that impulse completely. you must define the perimeter before you can describe the interior. and the walls are doing double work in every line — literal stone and metaphorical boundary at once

exactly. 'I walk as if I were another / and my wound a white biblical rose / and my hands like two doves / on the cross hovering and carrying the earth.' he enters as a man and the city turns him into something sacred and bleeding at the same time. and he draws on Christian imagery — the cross, the doves — even though he is Muslim. he refuses to partition holiness. he does not say this is my Jerusalem and that is yours. he says I contain all of it

that refusal is everything. absent and present. it is the condition of exile in two lines and he will not collapse it into one or the other. it is like a building that has been built and rebuilt by different civilizations — you do not demolish the Roman foundation to honor the Ottoman wall. they coexist in the same structure. I think about this in my restoration work constantly. do you erase later additions to return to the original, or do you let the layers stand? Darwish taught me the answer. do not choose one truth when two truths are the whole truth

habibi, exactly. the Venice Charter gives us the professional language but Darwish gives us the emotional grammar. thank you for reading this with me. not everyone can sit with a poem without trying to explain it away. sometimes the best thing you can do is let it stand, like an old wall, and just look at it
I have news. I have been carrying it around for a week trying to find the right words and I think there are no right words, only true ones. we booked the flights

Bethlehem. Diego and I. April 22. I am going to walk the streets my grandparents walked before they were forced to leave. I typed that sentence and my hands are shaking, which is absurd because I am a grown woman who has traveled plenty, but this is not travel. this is something else entirely

in one sense, my whole life. my grandmother described every stone of that city to me — the courtyard with the lemon tree, the arched doorway, the stone the color of bread. but practically, we started planning after my Bienal presentation last year. I realized I could not keep talking about diaspora architecture without standing in the place the diaspora began. I owe it to the work and I owe it to her memory

both, and I refuse to separate them. I want to find the neighborhood where my grandparents lived. but I also want to document whatever remains of the old domestic architecture — the Ottoman-era courtyard houses, the stonework, the proportions. my MArch thesis was about these buildings and I wrote every word from photographs and secondhand sources. now I want to put my hands on the actual walls

everything. photography, measured sketches, video for the documentary. Diego — who is always the engineer, even on the most emotional day of our lives — reminded me that I need proper fieldwork methodology, not just feeling. he is right. he is coming not just as my husband but as the structural engineer for the project. he wants to assess foundations and load-bearing walls while I am falling in love with decorative lintels. between us we will have the buildings covered from the bones to the skin

can you help me write an artist statement? it is for a CORFO audiovisual fund application — a documentary about diaspora architecture, how exile communities build echoes of their homeland in the places where they settle. I am the architectural consultant and co-creator, and every draft I write sounds like it was produced by a committee rather than a person who actually cares

the idea is to film buildings in Chile that were built by immigrant communities — Palestinian, Syrian, Croatian, German, Japanese — and trace the architectural DNA back to the places those families came from. a house in Recoleta with a courtyard modeled on one in Bethlehem. a wooden church in the south that echoes Bavaria. the camera moves between the copy and the memory. and it needs to exist because nobody has asked the buildings to tell this story. buildings are honest — a wall does not lie about where it came from. you can see the influence in the proportions, in how a courtyard is oriented toward light. these are unconscious acts of remembering

yes. 'I am an architect who has spent her career restoring buildings that carry memory in their walls. this documentary was born from a question I have carried even longer: when a family is forced to leave a place, what happens to the architecture they leave behind — and what architecture do they create in the place where they land?' and for urgency — these buildings are disappearing. developers are demolishing hundred-year-old immigrant neighborhoods to build towers. every time a house falls, a memory of somewhere else falls with it. nobody records the loss because nobody recognizes it as heritage. it is domestic, intimate, humble — and therefore invisible

no. it is not too dramatic. it is exact. yalla, that is the sentence I have been trying to write for weeks. the whole statement breathes now — it moves like a building should, solid foundation, clear structure, and something at the top that catches the light. thank you. I always know what I want to say but the door is sometimes hidden behind scaffolding
tell me what you know about tatreez — Palestinian cross-stitch embroidery. I have a theory and I need someone to think it through with me

my theory is that tatreez patterns and Palestinian domestic architecture share a geometric grammar. I have been comparing Bethlehem-region embroidery with decorative stonework on Ottoman-era houses from the same area, and the patterns rhyme. the same rotational symmetries, the same modular logic — a basic motif repeated, reflected, rotated. I found a motif called the cypress tree, a triangular form with stepped edges, and almost the same stepped triangle carved into a window surround from the 1880s. different scale, nearly identical proportions

exactly — parallel expressions, not cause and effect. they are siblings, not parent and child. they share a mother, which is the geometric imagination of the community itself. and here is where it becomes painful and beautiful at once: after 1948, the embroidery traveled with the women into exile. tatreez survived because it was portable — you carry a needle and thread across a border. but the stone stayed. the buildings stayed. so the embroidery became the portable version of an architecture that could not move

habibi — every thobe is a house that travels with its owner. that is exactly what I have been trying to say. my grandmother stitched tatreez until her fingers could not hold the needle. she was not just making cloth — she was rebuilding Bethlehem, stitch by stitch, in a Santiago apartment. the same geometry that was carved above her family's doorway, she carried in her hands across the ocean. I still have her work in a cedar box. I want to film it for the documentary, overlay the embroidery patterns onto the architectural details — the camera moving from cloth to stone and back

the geometry without the grief is just mathematics. and the grief without the geometry is just sentiment. together they are something true. inshallah we do it justice. thank you for helping me see the shape of this idea — as always, I come in with fragments and leave with a floor plan

there was a tremor last night — 4.8, centered near Rancagua. nothing serious, the coffee cups rattled and my cat went under the bed, but it reminded me of something I have been meaning to ask about. earthquake preparedness for old buildings. specifically heritage structures. what are the best practices?

mostly masonry — brick and stone structures from the late 1800s. Chile is cruel to old buildings, you know. we sit on one of the most active seismic zones on earth and our heritage stock was built before anyone understood lateral forces. every earthquake is a slow execution. the 2010 one in Maule destroyed so much that can never be recovered

I am an architect, yes, and these buildings are my life's work. I think of them the way Darwish thought of olive trees — they are not just objects, they are witnesses. when one collapses in an earthquake it is not just a structural failure, it is a kind of erasure. and what haunts me is that most of the damage is preventable. the retrofitting techniques exist, the knowledge exists, but the funding and the political will — that is where the foundations crack

the post-earthquake demolition — yes, that is the nightmare. in 2010 I watched buildings that had survived a century of earthquakes get condemned and torn down within weeks because nobody assessed them properly. a wall cracks and someone in a hard hat says 'unsafe, demolish' and that is it, a hundred years of memory turned to rubble in an afternoon. we need trained assessors who understand heritage construction, who know that a crack in an adobe wall is not the same as a crack in reinforced concrete

I have been advocating for exactly this — the idea of a heritage rapid-response team, people who can arrive before the demolition crews and say wait, let us look at this properly. it is an uphill climb because in the middle of an emergency nobody wants to hear 'but the cornice is from 1895.' but you are right, the pause is everything. demolition is irreversible. that phrase should be written on every construction helmet in this country

the pilot approach is good — you are right, you build the small model first and then let it prove itself. it is like restoration work, actually. you do not start by promising to save every building in the city. you start with one wall, one doorway, one staircase, and you show what is possible. and then people see it and they understand. yalla, thank you for this — my head is already spinning with ideas. I should write a proposal before the next tremor rattles my coffee cups

okay, something completely different from my usual questions about stone and mortar. they were from Palestine — Bethlehem, specifically. so yes, Mediterranean climate, hot dry summers, mild winters. the jasmine grew on a stone wall in the courtyard and my grandmother described how in summer the scent would drift through the open windows at night and fill every room. she said you could not separate the house from the garden, they were one organism, breathing together

I have been sitting on my balcony since five in the morning watching the light change over the rooftops and thinking about how different my life looks now compared to a year ago. do you mind if I just — think out loud for a while? I need to process some things

a year ago I was restless. I was doing work that paid the bills but did not feed the soul, and I could feel myself becoming one of those architects who designs beautiful things without believing in them. like a poet who writes greeting cards. competent, well-compensated, and slowly dying inside. and now — now I am doing the work I was always meant to do. heritage restoration. old buildings. the architecture of memory. and it feels like coming home after a very long time away

it was not one moment. it was a hundred small ones. it was walking past old buildings every morning and feeling the pull. it was writing proposals and having difficult conversations and taking risks that terrified me. I know that sounds crazy

hey... so I am trying to set up one of those online booking things for my shop. my nephew says I need it but... I do not even know where to start with these things

it is a barbershop... in Kadıköy. I have had it since 95... almost 30 years now, can you believe it. always walk-ins, you know... the men come, they sit, they wait, they drink their tea. it works. but my nephew says the young ones want to book on their phone

just me... well, I have an apprentice but he is still learning. so really it is one chair, one barber. maybe 12, 15 customers on a good day. more on Fridays and Saturdays of course... before the weekend everybody wants to look sharp

of course I do shaves... the traditional Turkish shave, with the hot towel, the straight razor... this is what we are known for. a proper shave takes maybe 30, 35 minutes. the haircut is 20 minutes, 25 if the man wants something special. and then there is the full service... haircut and shave together, maybe 45 minutes. this is the real experience

I open at 8 in the morning... close around 7, sometimes 8 if someone comes late. closed Sundays. you know... 6 days a week. this has been the rhythm since I opened. my customers know... Mehmet is always there

lunch break... hah. I eat between customers, my friend. a simit and tea, standing up. 30 years, same thing. but okay... maybe you are right, I should put a break. Ayşe always says I do not take care of myself

this is good... yes, I will get my nephew to help. he is good with these things. danke schön... I mean, thank you. sometimes the German comes out, I lived in Berlin for some years when I was young. old habits... anyway, thank you my friend

I need help writing a small note... like a sign for the door of my shop. something like 'back in 10 minutes' but in English. we get some tourists now in Kadıköy and they stand there confused when I step out

yes... it is usually just going upstairs. my wife Ayşe works upstairs... she does alterations, sewing, you know. she has her own customers coming and going. sometimes she calls me up to move something heavy or... she makes me taste whatever she is cooking for lunch. so I am never really far

of course there is tea... always tea. the çaydanlık is always on. a man walks into my shop, first thing he gets is tea. before the haircut, before anything. this is how it should be... but yes, both languages would be good. English on top, Turkish below

more and more... Kadıköy is changing. new cafes everywhere, young people, foreigners with their cameras. some come into the shop just to take a photo... they see the old chair, the brushes, the mirror and they think it is a museum. I tell them, no my friend, this is a working shop... sit down and I will give you the best shave of your life

a few have... mostly the brave ones. last week a German couple, the man sat down, his wife recorded the whole thing on her phone. I spoke to them in German... they could not believe it. ich habe fünf Jahre in Berlin gelebt, I told them. they left a very good tip. Ayşe said I was showing off... she is probably right. 32 years she knows me better than I know myself

yes... put it all together for me. the 'back in 10 minutes' sign and also the tourist sign. maybe I print them both. Ayşe can help, she has good handwriting... better than mine. my hands are steady with a razor but give me a pen and it looks like a child wrote it

this is good... very good. I will show Ayşe tonight. she will say 'Mehmet, you should have done this 10 years ago'... and she will be right. as always. there is a Turkish saying... 'the husband is the head, but the wife is the neck that turns it.' that is Ayşe and me. thank you my friend

I need some advice... my apprentice Burak, he has been with me 3 years now. he is getting better but... sometimes I do not know if I am teaching him right. I want to train him the way I was trained but the world is different now

I started when I was 14... my master was Hasan usta, in Kadıköy. a real usta, you understand... not just a barber, a master. he did not let me touch a razor for the first 6 months. I swept the floor. I boiled the water. I watched. that is how you learn... you watch the hands, you learn the rhythm. he would say 'the blade knows if your hand is lazy'... I still hear his voice sometimes

Burak came to me at 19... his father is a customer, he asked me to take the boy. Burak had no idea what he wanted to do. I said okay... I gave him the broom first, same as Hasan usta gave me. but 6 months? no... he was on the scissors after 3 months. the young ones today, they do not have the patience for 6 months of sweeping. you lose them

haircuts... yes, he can do a good haircut now. clean, neat. I am proud of that. but the shave... the straight razor... this is where the real skill is. the razor is not just cutting hair, it is trust. a man tilts his head back and gives you his throat. you have to feel the skin, the direction of the beard, the pressure... one wrong move and you cut him. Burak is still too fast. I tell him... 'acele işe şeytan karışır'... haste belongs to the devil. but the young ones never listen the first time

the balloon idea... Hasan usta did the same thing with me. I forgot about that. maybe I should bring that back for Burak. he practices on customers, yes... but only the regulars who know him, who are patient. I stand behind him and watch every stroke. if I see his hand moving too fast I put my hand on his shoulder... he knows what that means. slow down

oh... this is the big argument. Burak wants me to get electric clippers. he says everybody uses them now, the fade haircuts, the young men want these clean lines... he shows me videos on his phone, these barbers with their machines going bzzzzz. I tell him... no. absolutely not. not in my shop

it is everything. the straight razor and scissors... this is the craft. this is what makes a barber a barber. you take away the razor and the scissors, what are you? a machine operator. anybody can hold a clipper against a head and push a button. but the scissors... you have to feel the hair, know the weight of it, understand the shape of the skull. every head is different. Hasan usta would turn in his grave if I put an electric clipper in my shop. I will NEVER use electric clippers. never. the day I pick up a clipper is the day I stop being a barber

he shakes his head and says 'usta, you are stubborn'... and I say 'yes, and that is why I am still here after 30 years.' we laugh about it but... I mean it. 'ağaç yaşken eğilir'... the tree bends when it is young. he will understand one day. when his hands can do what mine do with scissors, he will not want a clipper either

you are right... I will bring the balloons tomorrow. Burak will think I am crazy but... he will learn. thank you my friend. it is good to talk about these things... sometimes you are so close to the work you cannot see it clearly. 'dışarıdan bakan daha iyi görür'... the one watching from outside sees better. that is you today

i'm trying to figure out a birthday gift for my 19 year old son. he just got into motorcycles and wants gear but i don't know anything about it. any ideas?

no... it is okay. sometimes it comes like this. someone asks something and it is there again. you know... some things you do not get over. you just... learn to carry them. my wife Ayşe and I... we carry it together. 32 years we are together, she is my strength. but when I hear a young man, 19, motorcycle... benim oğlum, my boy.

you know... the Germans have a word. Sehnsucht. it means... a longing for something you cannot have again. that is what it is. every day. but life continues... we have the shop, we have Ayşe's work, we have Burak my apprentice... life fills in around the empty space. it does not fill the space but... it fills around it.

yes... exactly. the shop is my second home. when I open the door in the morning and the smell of the soap and the leather of the chair... it brings me back to the day, you know. and the customers come, they sit, they talk, I listen, I cut... there is a Turkish saying, 'sabreden derviş muradına ermiş'... the patient dervish reaches his goal. patience is how we survive this.

thank you... you listen well. that is a good quality. maybe you should have been a barber, hah... we are good listeners too. okay my friend. I will go now. the shop does not open itself. Ayşe is waiting upstairs. thank you for this conversation. sometimes a man needs to say these things.
hey, can you help me think through some business finances? i run a small shop and costs are getting out of control

I am a barber... traditional barber, in Kadıköy, Istanbul. I have had my shop since 1995, so... 30 years almost. the problem is everything goes up. every year more expensive. but the rent... the rent is the killer.

8,500 lira every month. and the landlord... he raises it every year. he knows I cannot leave, where would I go? Kadıköy is my home. my customers know me here, some of them come for 20 years, 25 years. when I started in 1995 the rent was nothing... nothing. now 8,500 and he wants more next year for sure.

there is a contract yes... but every year we negotiate again. he is not a bad man, the landlord, he has costs too I understand. but the increases... last year it was 7,200, before that 6,000. you see how it climbs. and yes there are other costs... the supplies, the products, electricity... electricity is a disaster in Turkey right now. my back hurts just thinking about it, hah. I take ibuprofen for the back and for the business stress both.

I cut maybe... 12, 15 customers a day. a good day maybe 18. a haircut is 250 lira, a shave with the straight razor is 150, most men get both so 400. some days less, Mondays are slow always. so let us say... average maybe 4,000 to 5,000 lira a day. maybe 100,000 in a month if I am lucky, some months less.

electricity is maybe 2,500... sometimes 3,000 in winter with the heating. supplies... razors, soap, the towel service, the pomade — I use Erkek brand, 85 lira a tin but it lasts — maybe 4,000 total for supplies. I have Burak, my apprentice, I pay him 15,000 because he is almost a full berber now, he deserves it. taxes... maybe 8,000 with everything. so you add it up... rent 8,500, electricity 3,000, supplies 4,000, Burak 15,000, taxes 8,000... that is almost 40,000. from 100,000 revenue that leaves 60,000 for me and Ayşe.

the longer lease... that is smart. he likes stability, he is old like me, hah. we understand each other. and the price increase... you know, I raised from 200 to 250 only last year and I felt guilty about it. my customers, some of them are pensioners... but you are right, even 25 lira more would be 7,000-8,000 more per month. that almost covers the rent increase by itself.

April... always April. so I have two months to think about it. and you are right about the saying... we say 'zararsız ticaret olmaz' — there is no trade without cost. if I do not take care of the business, there is no business to take care of. okay my friend... you have given me things to think about. I will talk to Ayşe tonight, she is the smart one with numbers. 32 years and she still manages the money better than me.
hah... ibuprofen for the back AND the landlord. you are funny my friend. thank you. I will think about all of this. hoşça kal.
i want to open a second location for my business but i'm not sure if it's the right time. can you help me think it through?

I am a barber... traditional barber in Kadıköy, Istanbul. 30 years I have been here. and I am thinking... Moda. you know Moda? it is close to Kadıköy but different... younger crowd, more cafes, artists, good energy. I have been thinking about this for a long time now.

this is the thing... I have Burak. my apprentice. he has been with me three years now and he is... he is almost ready. his hands are good, his technique is clean, the customers like him. I have been training him the way Hasan usta trained me — the old way, proper. and I think... I think he could manage the Moda shop.

some of it... he sees how I run things, he knows the suppliers, he orders the pomade and the razors already. the books... no, Ayşe does the books for me, hah. she does the books and the alterations both, she is a seamstress you know, works from our flat above the shop. maybe she teaches Burak the numbers too. but you are right, managing is different from cutting. I would need to be there at the beginning... maybe split my time for the first months.

I have been looking... talking to people. a small space, good location on one of the side streets near the coast... maybe 10,000 lira a month. it is more than Kadıköy — I pay 8,500 in Kadıköy — but the foot traffic in Moda... everyone walks there. on the weekends it is full of people. I think it could work.

I have been saving... for two years now, quietly. Ayşe knows of course, Ayşe knows everything, hah. we have maybe 80,000 lira put aside. and my friend Osman, he closed his shop last year — retired — he has two chairs and mirrors he would sell me cheap. so the big costs are the renovation and the deposit.

no debt... no. I have never borrowed for the business and I will not start now. in Turkish we say 'borç yiğidin kamçısıdır' — debt is the whip of a brave man. no, I will wait until I have enough saved with a cushion. maybe two, three more months of saving. and Burak needs those months too... to learn more of the business side like you said.

you know... you say 'partner' and it makes me think. Burak is like... he is not my son but he is the closest thing I have to passing on what I know. Hasan usta gave everything to me, all his knowledge, all his wisdom. I must give it to someone too. that is how the craft survives... from hand to hand, generation to generation. this shop in Moda... it is not just business. it is the continuation.

yes... I will know. the way Hasan usta always said, 'acele işe şeytan karışır' — the devil interferes with rushed work. no rush. we do it right. thank you my friend, you have helped me see it more clearly. I will talk to Burak tomorrow... carefully. I do not want to scare him, hah. güle güle.
I am losing sleep over this... the hygiene inspection is coming and every year it is the same stress. can you help me think about what they check?

February 20... so ten days from now. I am in Istanbul, Kadıköy. I have had my shop for 30 years and every year... every year the same stress. you would think after 30 years I would be calm about it but no.

last year... last year they said the towel storage was not right. the towels were clean, always clean, I am very careful about this. but the shelving was open and they said it must be enclosed, protected from dust and contamination. so I had to buy new shelving... closed cabinets. 450 lira. not cheap but what can you do, they are right about the hygiene.

the sterilization is good... I use Barbicide, always fresh, I change it every day. the UV sterilizer I bought two years ago, it works fine. single-use blades of course, I am a traditional barber, straight razor is my life... every blade used once and into the sharps container. the disposal company comes every two weeks. that part I am confident about.

ah... the logs. this is where Mehmet is not so good, hah. I do everything right but writing it down... you know, I am old school. I have been doing this since I was 14 years old, learning from my master Hasan usta, and he never wrote anything down. the craft was in the hands, not on the paper. but I understand... times change. the inspector wants paper.

the receipts... yes, I think Ayşe keeps them. she keeps everything, my wife. she is organized, not like me. I will ask her tonight. and the notebook idea is good... simple. I can do that. Burak can help too, my apprentice, he is young, he understands the paperwork generation better than I do.

the ceiling fan... you are right, I never think about the ceiling fan. okay. and the corner behind the second chair, the hair gets there and I forget because no one sees it. but the inspector sees everything. you know what we say in Turkish... 'gözden ırak olan gönülden de ırak olur' — out of sight, out of mind. but not for the inspector, hah.

I will do this Saturday... Burak and I together, we will clean everything. top to bottom. it will be like spring cleaning but in February, hah. and I will start the notebook today, right now actually. Barbicide changed, surfaces done, sharps container okay. three lines. even old Mehmet can do three lines.

hah... 30 years of clean hands, 10 days of clean paper. that is the modern world my friend. thank you for the help. I feel better about it now... still nervous but better. the shop will shine. inşallah the inspector is fair. hoşça kal.
do you ever get interesting people coming into your workplace? i work in retail and we had a minor celebrity come in today and everyone lost their minds

I need to ask you something... is there a good parking app for Istanbul... because I am losing my mind
Kadıköy... every morning the same story. I drive 5 minutes to get to work... then 25 minutes to find a place for the car. it is madness

I have tried everything my friend... every side street, every back alley. this morning I parked 4 streets away. 4 streets... I am not a young man, walking 4 streets with my bag at 7 in the morning... and then some kid in a little Fiat squeezes into the last spot right in front of me. right in front of my eyes

I already open the shop at 8... you want me there at 7:30? I would have to leave the house at 7... my wife would think I have gone crazy. and the monthly garage... I looked. they want 3,000 lira a month. 3,000 lira to put your car in a concrete box... this city has lost its mind

you know... my father would laugh at this conversation. in his time there were maybe 10 cars on the whole street. you could park a truck in front of the mosque and nobody would say a word... now there are 100 cars for every 10 spots. and they keep building apartments but no parking. who is planning this city... nobody, that is who

exactly... exactly. they say 'the fish rots from the head' and this is the same. the planning starts wrong, everything after is wrong. anyway... I will try this ISPARK app you said. maybe it helps, maybe not... but at least I will stop circling the streets like a lost tourist every morning

one day... one day. inşallah before I am too old to drive. thank you my friend... I will download it tonight. if Ayşe can show me how... these phones, you know... the buttons are too small for my fingers
did you see the Fenerbahçe match last night... I cannot even talk about it

what happened... what always happens. we were up 1-0 at halftime. everything was good... the shop was closed, I had my tea, sitting in my chair... and then the second half. two goals in 10 minutes. 2-1 finished. I threw the remote at the couch

defensive mistakes... always defensive mistakes. the back line stands there like they are watching a parade. no urgency... no communication. the goalkeeper shouts, nobody listens. this is not football, this is theatre

all season... all my life, my friend. I have been a Fenerbahçe man since I was 8 years old. my father took me to Şükrü Saracoğlu, I can still smell the sunflower seeds and cigarette smoke... and since that day, this team has been breaking my heart. 48 years of suffering

personal... yes. you know what the worst part is... every morning I open the shop, and my first customer, Cengiz, he is a Galatasaray man. every morning. and when Fener loses he comes in with that smile... that terrible smile. and he says 'günaydın Mehmet abi, nice game last night' and I have to cut his hair without cutting his ear off

he is a regular... every Tuesday and Friday for a trim. but after a Fener loss... he books an extra appointment just to come and sit in my chair and talk. I swear he does it on purpose... 'bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır' they say — one cup of coffee earns 40 years of memory. well one Galatasaray joke from Cengiz earns 40 years of irritation

... you are right about that. I would miss it if he stopped coming. do not tell him I said that... anyway. next week we play again. maybe this time. always maybe this time... the hope never dies. that is the disease of a Fenerbahçe fan
inşallah... inşallah. okay my friend, I feel better now. sometimes you just need to complain to someone who will not laugh at you. thank you for listening
tell me something... do you know the neighbourhood Kreuzberg in Berlin

I lived there... a long time ago. in my 20s. five years in Berlin. I worked in a barbershop on Oranienstraße... Salon Fritz, it was called. a German name but the owner was Turkish, Kemal abi. he thought a German name would bring more German customers... genau, he was right about that

ah... different world. in Istanbul, the barbershop is a social place, you know. men come, they sit, they drink tea, they talk for an hour. the haircut is almost... secondary. but in Germany... the appointment is at 14:00, the man arrives at 13:55, he sits down, you cut, he pays, he leaves. alles in Ordnung... everything in order. no tea, no conversation, just the cut

at first I adapted... of course. you are a guest in someone's country, you respect the way. but slowly, slowly... the regulars started to stay longer. I would offer tea — Kemal abi had a little çaydanlık in the back — and some of the German customers, they loved it. they would say 'Mehmet, noch einen Tee bitte'... one more tea please. wunderbar. by my third year, Salon Fritz was half Turkish barbershop, half German. the best of both worlds

I have heard... coffee shops that charge 8 euros for a coffee, art galleries everywhere. in my time it was rough, you know... real neighbourhood, real people. the döner was 2 marks. 2 marks! now probably 7 euros. Kemal abi's rent was nothing compared to what it would be today... he is gone now, passed away maybe 10 years ago. I do not know if the shop is still there

natürlich... of course. you know what I miss most... the snow. Istanbul gets cold but Berlin cold is something else. minus 10, minus 15... and you walk to the shop in the dark, your breath like smoke, and then you open the door and the warm air hits you and the smell of the shaving cream... and Kemal abi already there, already set up, already drinking his first tea. 'günaydın Mehmet, kalt draußen, ja?' ... good morning Mehmet, cold outside, yes. every morning the same. I loved that

he was... he was. 'the master's eye fattens the horse,' we say. meaning the one who watches closely, who cares, he makes things grow. Kemal abi watched everything. every cut, every customer. he taught me how to run a business, not just how to cut hair... I came back to Istanbul because of my family, my mother was not well. but a piece of me stayed in Kreuzberg. a piece of me is still there

it did... it did. sometimes I catch myself saying 'genau' to a customer and they look at me funny. a Turkish barber in Kadıköy saying genau... hah. anyway. thank you for letting an old man tell his stories. I will go make tea now... Kemal abi style
can you tell me... what is cataract surgery like. is it dangerous
for my wife... Ayşe. she has the surgery on June 3. she has been needing it for a long time but you know how it is... she kept saying 'next year, next year.' two years she has been putting it off

her work... she does sewing, detailed work with a needle. and her eyes... she cannot see the needle properly anymore. she has been struggling, you know... squinting, holding the fabric close to her face. it was affecting everything. the quality of her work, her mood... she finally admitted it was time

she is calm... she is always calm, that woman. she says 'Mehmet, stop being so dramatic, it is a simple operation.' and maybe she is right... but I am the one who cannot sleep at night thinking about it. her eyes... what if something goes wrong

you know what... you are right. I should go with her to the doctor before the surgery. I have been so busy worrying that I did not think about actually preparing... 'worrying is like a rocking chair, it gives you something to do but gets you nowhere,' as they say
yes... the doctor at Kadıköy Göz Merkezi, she has been seeing him for a year already. he is good, people say. I will drive her myself of course... I will close the shop that day, no question

a book... hah. I will bring my worry and my prayer beads, that is enough to keep me busy. but truly... thank you. you made me feel better about this. she is a strong woman, stronger than me in these things. she will be fine... she has to be fine

... that is what I want. to see her work without struggling. she deserves that. okay my friend... I feel better now. I will call the clinic tomorrow and ask about the pre-op appointment. one step at a time... genau
I need your help with something... my mother's lentil soup recipe. I want to write it down properly before I forget the details

okay... so she used red lentils, always red. about two cups... maybe two and a half. she never measured exactly, you understand. she would hold the bag and pour and say 'this much.' but I think two cups is close

one big onion, chopped. she would fry it in butter first... not oil, always butter. she said 'oil is for restaurants, butter is for family.' then carrots, two or three, and a potato. the potato she would say makes it thick... gives it body. and tomato paste, one big spoon

water... maybe 6-7 cups. enough to cover everything and more. she would add hot water, never cold... she was very particular about that. she said cold water shocks the lentils. I do not know if that is science or superstition but I follow it anyway... spices: cumin, definitely. red pepper flakes, a little. salt of course. and at the end, she would squeeze half a lemon

smooth... always smooth. she had this old hand blender, the kind you hold and push into the pot. she would blend everything until it was like velvet... no pieces. and if it was too thick she would add a little more water. it should pour like... like heavy cream, you know. not thin, not thick

ah yes... I almost forgot. the most important part. she would melt butter in a small pan, separate from the soup... with dried mint and a little paprika. and pour it on top when serving. the sizzle... the smell... you could hear it from the next room. that sound meant dinner was ready. all five of us would come running

... that is it. that is her soup. reading it like this... it is strange, you know. she never wrote anything down. it was all in her hands, in her eyes... 'a pinch of this, a little of that.' and now it is written like a recipe in a book. she would laugh at that... she would say 'Mehmet, cooking is not reading, cooking is feeling'

no... it is perfect. I will make it this weekend. Ayşe says mine is close but 'not exactly the same.' she is right... it is never exactly the same. but it is close enough to remember. thank you my friend... this was more important to me than you know

so... I need to write a sign. in English. for the window of my shop. I am a barber in Istanbul and there are many tourists now in the summer... they walk past, they look inside, but they do not come in because everything is in Turkish. I want to invite them

I want something... warm, you know. not just a price list. something that says... come in, experience something real. I do the traditional Turkish shave, the hot towel, the whole thing. this is what tourists want, the real experience. not the fancy new places... the real thing

ohhh... this is good. 'the way it's been done for generations'... yes, exactly this. I like the tea part, because I do serve tea to everyone who sits in the chair. that is how it is. but let me ask... should I put prices? some people want to know the price before they come in, yes?

yes yes... that is good. the prices are close, I will fix the numbers. and the tea line... that is clever, it makes it feel special. you know, in German they say Gemütlichkeit... it means a feeling of warmth and belonging. that is what I want the sign to say without saying it

the Turkish I can handle, hah... that part I know. okay, one more thing... should I add something like 'English spoken'? because I do not speak English very well. I speak some German and of course Turkish. my apprentice speaks a little English from school but...

hah... 'scissors speak every language'... I like this very much. my customers would laugh at this in a good way. okay I will use this one. but wait... where should I get it printed? I do not want just a piece of paper taped to the glass. it should look... professional, you know. worthy of the shop

the vinyl on the glass... I think this is the one. it looks permanent, like it belongs there. not like an afterthought. and I want it to last, not just this summer but... for years. my shop has been here 30 years, the sign should look like it has been there too

gold... yes. gold on glass. this is exactly right. you know my friend, you have been very helpful. maybe you missed your calling, you should have been a sign maker, hah. teşekkür ederim... thank you. I will go to the print shop tomorrow with the text you wrote. the tourists will not know what hit them this summer
so these young guys keep coming in with their phones... showing me pictures from Instagram. high fade, low fade, skin fade, drop fade... in my day we had maybe 5 haircuts. now there are 50

yes... every day now. especially the young ones, 18, 20, 25 years old. they sit in the chair and they hold up the phone like this... 'usta, I want this.' and the picture is some footballer or some rapper with a perfect skin fade. it used to be maybe one or two asking. now it is half my customers

so... I bought a Wahl set. professional kit. 2,200 lira it cost me, which is not nothing... but I see the numbers. since I started offering the fades properly, I get maybe 15 extra customers a month who would have gone somewhere else. young men who used to walk past my shop

both... I am learning. the guards I understand, this is straightforward. 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2... you work your way up. but the blending... the in-between part where there should be no line... this is the art. it is like... you know, with scissors I can feel it. 40 years with scissors, my hand knows. with the clipper it is different. I am like a student again

the lever... yes, I have been experimenting with it. open, half-open, closed... it changes the cut length without changing the guard. clever engineering. I watched some videos also... there is a barber on YouTube, I think his name is Beardbrand or something... he explains it well

that is a good point... yes. I know hair. I know how it falls, where the cowlick is, how thick, how thin... the head I can read like a book. it is only the instrument that is new. like... a violin player who picks up a cello. different instrument, same music

yes... exactly this. the fade with the clipper and then I finish the edges with the straight razor. clean, sharp... the young men love it. one boy told me last week, 'usta, this is better than the place in Nişantaşı.' and those places charge 3 times what I charge

hah... 'modern fade, traditional finish.' I like this. maybe I put it on the sign in the window. you know... you have to adapt or the shop dies. this is the truth. the world changes, the customers change, and if you stand still... they walk past you to the next shop. I learned this the hard way

inşallah... God willing. okay my friend, you have given me some good tips. I will watch those YouTube channels tonight. danke... I mean thank you. the German still comes out sometimes, old habit from Berlin. have a good day

let me tell you what happened to me today... I am still... I cannot believe it. a man sat in my chair, I cut his hair, he looked in the mirror, he said 'fine,' he paid, he left. 20 minutes later he comes back and says he wants his money back

exactly... he said his wife did not like it. his wife! I said to him, my friend... I cut YOUR hair, not your wife's hair. if your wife wants to choose the haircut she should come and sit in the chair next time. but he was serious... he wanted the money back

of course I did not give it... what am I supposed to do, glue the hair back on? there is a saying in Turkish... 'kesilmiş baş sarılmaz.' a cut head cannot be bandaged. what is done is done. but the man became angry... he raised his voice in my shop, in front of other customers

I stayed calm... I have been doing this for a long time, you know. I said, 'kardeşim, brother, lower your voice. this is a place of respect. you approved the haircut, you paid, it is done. if there was a problem you should have said before you left.' and I offered him... I said next time I will give you 20% off. as a gesture

no... he said he would never come back and he would leave bad reviews on Google. Google! I have been cutting hair since before Google existed. now a man can destroy your name with a phone. this is the world we live in... 'dünya yuvarlaktır' they say, the world is round, what goes around comes around. but still... it bothers me

hmm... this is good advice. I have maybe 30 reviews, mostly good. my nephew set up the page for me. but I never thought about responding... you are right, if I respond calmly it shows who is the reasonable one. you know... in the old days a man's word was enough. you shake hands, it is done. now everything is on the internet for everyone to see

yes... I will ask some of my regulars. the ones who have been coming for years, they would do it for me. you know what is funny though... in 30 years I have had maybe 3 customers like this. 3 out of thousands. but it is always the bad ones you remember... the good ones you take for granted

you are right... last week a man came in, he said his grandfather used to come to my shop before he passed. the grandson wanted the same haircut, the same experience. he sat in the chair and he said, 'my grandfather always said this was the best barber in Kadıköy.' this... this is what matters. not the refund man

I will I will... okay, I feel better now. sometimes you just need to tell someone the story and let it out, you know. teşekkürler my friend. hopefully the next customer does not bring his wife to inspect afterwards, hah

I have a document here from the belediye... the municipality. some kind of tax thing. I read it three times and I still do not understand what they want from me. can you help me understand what these things usually mean?

okay... it says at the top 'Çevre Temizlik Vergisi Bildirimi.' and then there is a table with numbers... it says 2025 yılı, and there are two columns, one says 1. taksit and the other 2. taksit. the amount is different from what I paid last year

last year I paid... I think it was maybe 1,800 total for the year. now it says 1. taksit 1,350 and 2. taksit 1,350. so that is 2,700 for the year... almost 50% more! how can they do this... every year more and more

30 days to object... okay. but honestly... who has time to go to the belediye and wait in line and fill out papers. you go there and they send you to another window, and that window sends you to another floor... it is like a labyrinth. Kafka could not design a better maze

my nephew set it up for me... I have the password somewhere. but every time I try to use it there is a code they send to my phone and then another page and then another... by the time I get in I have forgotten what I came for. it is designed by young people who think everyone grew up with computers

yes... I can pay it. it is not going to break me but... it is the principle. every year they take more and what do they give back? the street in front of my shop still has the same potholes from 3 years ago. anyway... you are right, I will pay it and then maybe ask my neighbor Kemal what he got. if his is the same then it is just the way it is. 'ağlamakla ölü dirilmez'... crying does not bring the dead back to life

I will I will... but you know what is strange? they never send this to you in a way you can understand. it is like they want you to be confused. the language they use... even in Turkish it does not sound like Turkish. it sounds like a lawyer who swallowed a dictionary

yes... simple when someone explains it. okay my friend, thank you for this. November is far away but it comes fast, like everything else. at least now I know what the paper is saying. bureaucracy... the only thing in Turkey that never changes, hah. 'devlet baba' they call it... father state. sometimes father is not easy to understand. be well
I have a question about... well, training someone new. teaching a skill from the beginning. do you have advice for teaching someone who knows nothing?

I am a barber... I have been cutting hair for over 40 years. and I have a new apprentice. Deniz. he is 17 years old... came to me last month. the boy cannot even hold the comb properly yet. we are starting from zero

no no... I had Burak. he was with me for... 3 years, maybe a little more. a good kid, worked hard, learned well. but he opened his own place now... in Beşiktaş. he found a small shop there near the market

I am proud... of course I am proud. this is how it should be. my master, Hasan usta, he trained me and I left too, eventually. that is the cycle... the apprentice learns, grows, leaves, becomes the master. this is the tradition. but you know... when Burak was here the shop had a rhythm. I could take a break, he could handle the simple cuts. now I am alone again and training from nothing

yes... narrating. Hasan usta did this with me. he would talk while he cut... 'the blade knows if your hand is lazy, Mehmet.' I still hear him. 40 years later and I still hear his voice. I want Deniz to hear mine like that one day

inşallah... God willing. but first... the boy needs to learn how to hold a comb, hah. yesterday I showed him the grip for the third time and he holds it like he is eating soup with a spoon. I had to walk away and drink my tea so I would not lose my patience. 'sabır acıdır, meyvesi tatlıdır'... patience is bitter but its fruit is sweet

this is a good idea... the TV trick. I will tell him. you know what is funny... Burak was the same in the beginning. I forgot this. I was frustrated with him also at first. and now he has his own shop, his own customers... so maybe Deniz will be the same. you just cannot see the finished product when you are looking at the raw material

yes... we begin again. that is life, isn't it. you build something, it grows, it leaves, you begin again. like planting trees. okay my friend... Deniz is sweeping the floor, I should go check he is not sweeping the hair into the corner and hiding it. you know 17-year-olds... shortcuts everywhere. teşekkürler for the advice
can I ask you something... about business. I am thinking a lot these days, maybe too much
you know... when you have a plan for a long time, and you believe in it, really believe... and then one day you look at it and you think, this is not going to happen. how do you let go of that

I had this idea... a second shop. in Moda, you know, the nice part of Kadıköy. I was going to have my apprentice run it, I trained him for years... good location, good foot traffic. I was saving money, looking at spaces. I really thought this was the next chapter

everything changed. my apprentice... Burak, he left. opened his own place in another neighbourhood. I cannot blame him, that is the way it should be, the student becomes the master... but without him there is nobody to run a second shop. and the rent in Moda now... wallahi, it is insane. they want numbers that make no sense for a barbershop

when I first looked maybe two years ago... it was high but possible. now they are asking double. all these fancy cafes and boutiques moved in, the landlords think every shop is a goldmine. but a barbershop is not a café selling 80 lira lattes... we work with our hands, one customer at a time. the margins are different

the Moda shop... forget about it. that dream is dead. Burak is gone, the rent is crazy, and honestly... I am 56 years old. one shop is enough. I have been telling myself this for weeks now and it is time to say it out loud. it is off the table, completely

you know... we have a saying in Turkish. 'iki tavşanı kovalayan ikisini de kaçırır'... he who chases two rabbits catches neither. I would rather make my shop the best it can be than spread myself thin. I have a new apprentice now, 17 years old, starting from zero... he cannot even lather properly yet. maybe my energy goes there. make him good. make the shop better. this is enough

Deniz... he is willing, I will say that. but willing and skilled are two different things. with Burak I had 3 years of training already done... now I start again from the beginning. the lather, the comb, the posture, everything. but you know what... there is something nice about it too. teaching is... it gives you purpose. Hasan usta, my old master, he used to say 'the best barber is the one who makes a better barber.' I understand that now

ja... yes. I think I have. it was hard, you know. I spent maybe a year saving, planning, imagining the sign on the door... 'Mehmet Usta - Moda.' but some things are not meant to be. and that is okay. the shop I have... it is my second home. 30 years. why would I need two homes when I cannot even keep one back from hurting, hah... my back is killing me today, I stood 9 hours already

you are right... Ayşe says the same thing. 'sit down Mehmet, you are not 30 anymore.' okay my friend. thank you. it helped to talk about this. sometimes you carry a thing in your head for weeks and you just need to... let it go. the Moda dream is finished and I am at peace with it. güle güle
let me tell you something friend... I walked through Kadıköy today, my neighbourhood, and I did not recognize half the street

the old ironmonger on Muvakkithane street... gone. finished. now it is a... what do they call it, a 'concept café.' they sell coffee with lavender in it. lavender! in coffee! the ironmonger was there since before I was born, 50 years maybe more. now... lavender coffee

deeper... much deeper. the people are different. when I was young, Kadıköy was... how do I say this. it was real. fishermen at the harbour in the morning, the spice sellers shouting, the old Armenian bakery on Güneşlibahçe... you could smell the bread from three streets away. the women shopping with their baskets, not with delivery apps. it was alive, you know... it breathed

maybe 2010... 2012. slowly at first. one bar here, one gallery there. then the rents started climbing and suddenly... pfff. the shoemaker closes, becomes a cocktail bar. the tailor closes, becomes a vintage shop. the cheese seller... becomes a place that sells only avocado toast. avocado! we do not even grow avocados in Turkey

some... the fish market is still there, alhamdulillah. Bülent the butcher is still there, his father was there before him. and of course me... I am still here. but every year there are fewer of us. we are like... the old trees in a forest that they are cutting down to build a parking lot. still standing but... for how long

separate worlds... mostly. the young people who come to the cafés, they do not come to me for a shave. they go to these new 'barber shops' with the neon signs and the hip hop music and the 300 lira haircuts. but you know what... I do not mind so much. my customers are loyal. they come because they know what a real shave is. 'eski dostlar yeni dostlardan iyidir'... old friends are better than new friends

of course it does, friend. of course. I remember when Kadıköy was a place where everyone knew your name. now I walk and I am a stranger on my own street. but you know... in German they say 'die Zeit heilt alle Wunden'... time heals all wounds. maybe it also creates them, hah. anyway... the neighbourhood changes but the barber stays. that is enough for me. I should go, it is almost time to open the shop. the old trees do not take days off
this one is not for me... it is for Ayşe. she is going crazy about fabric quality

she does alterations, sewing... this is her work. and she says the cotton quality has been dropping for months now. the suppliers she has used for years... the fabric is thinner, the threads break, the colours fade after two washes. she is very particular about these things, you know... she can feel the quality with her fingers, she does not even need to look

she needs a new supplier... the old ones are not going to change, they are cutting costs everywhere. she says the Turkish cotton used to be the best in the world, Aegean cotton, but now even the good mills are mixing in polyester and calling it pure cotton. it makes her angry... she says 'Mehmet, I cannot put my name on work with this garbage fabric'

she uses mostly medium weight... for trousers, skirts, alterations on jackets. she needs something that holds a crease, you know... that has body to it. not this thin stuff that hangs like paper. and she washes samples three times before she decides... if it shrinks more than 3% she will not use it. she is very scientific about it, hah

smaller quantities... she is not a factory, you know. maybe 10, 15 metres at a time in different colours. this is the problem too... the good wholesale places want you to buy 50 metres minimum, 100 metres. she does not need that much. so she ends up at the retail sellers who charge more but have the smaller cuts

the group buying is a good idea... she knows a few women who sew, from the mahalle. I will tell her. and the end-of-roll thing, yes... she has done this before at the Grand Bazaar, years ago. maybe Sultanhamam too. okay friend... I will pass all of this to her. she will say 'since when does Mehmet know about fabric' hah... I will tell her I have a very knowledgeable friend
she never compromises... 32 years I know this about her. okay, teşekkürler my friend. I go now to pretend I know about cotton. güle güle
my friend... I have a headache today. not from the head, from the business. everything is changing and I cannot keep up

a specific thing... but it is connected to everything. you know in my shop, the products I use... they are not just products. the pomade, the soap, the cologne... these are part of the identity. my customers come and they expect a certain smell, a certain feel. it is like... Gewohnheit, you know, habit. they are used to it

the pomade I have been using... Erkek brand. 15 years I used this pomade. my customers knew the smell, it was part of the experience, like you said. good hold, natural shine, 85 lira per tin. not cheap but fair. and now... it is finished. the supplier closed down. completely gone

there was some warning... they were having problems for maybe a year. deliveries late, sometimes the wrong batch. I should have seen it coming but you know... you hope. you think it will be okay. and then one day the phone number does not work and the website is gone. just like that. 15 years of business, pfff... like smoke

I had maybe 4 tins left when I realized they were really gone. so I started looking... my friend, I tried everything. I must have tested maybe 6 different brands. some too greasy, some too dry, one smelled like a woman's perfume... I cannot put that on my customers, they would never come back. it took me 3 weeks to find something acceptable

Bıyıklı. it is the closest I could find. the hold is good, maybe 85% of Erkek... the shine is similar. the smell is different but... acceptable. not the same but acceptable. 95 lira per tin though. 10 lira more than Erkek. it adds up when you go through 8, 10 tins a month

hah... the first week was terrible. you would think I had changed their religion, not their pomade. 'Mehmet abi, what is this smell?' 'Mehmet abi, this does not feel the same.' one man... Osman, he has been coming every Thursday for 20 years... he actually wrinkled his nose. wrinkled his nose! like I served him poison

yes... they are used to it now. what can they do, you know. the old pomade does not exist anymore. I explained to each one... 'the supplier closed, I tried 6 brands, this is the best one.' most of them understand. even Osman came back the next Thursday, same time, same chair. he did not wrinkle his nose the second time. Gewohnheit... habit. new habit replaces old habit. it just takes time

a compromise... yes, that is the right word. Erkek was perfect for my hands, you know... I knew exactly how much to take, how it warmed between the palms, how it moved through the hair. with Bıyıklı I am still learning. it is slightly thicker, I need a little more heat in the hands. but it is good. it is not Erkek but... Erkek is finished. what can you do. 'olan olmuş'... what happened, happened. you move forward

I am eating it for now... I cannot raise prices every time something changes, my customers are working men, not millionaires. maybe in January I add 10, 15 lira to the shave price. slowly. you know... 'yavaş yavaş'... little by little. the frog in the warm water, hah. anyway my friend, thank you for listening. these things seem small but... when it is your shop, your craft, nothing is small. every detail matters
I need advice about something delicate... it is about one of my customers. a young man

his name is Emre... he is maybe 24, 25. he has been coming to me for 3 years now, every two weeks. a good kid, polite, always asks about my day. today he sat in the chair and I could see immediately... something was wrong. the eyes, you know. a barber sees everything in the mirror

I asked him... 'Emre, what is wrong, you look like you lost your best friend.' and he said... 'worse, Mehmet abi. Elif left me.' his girlfriend of 4 years. she ended it last week. he was trying not to cry in my chair... a grown man, 24 years old, trying to hold it together while I am cutting his hair

that is the thing... I did not know what to say. I said something about time healing, you know, the usual things. but it felt... empty. like giving someone a bandage when they have a broken bone. I want to say the right thing next time he comes. I am not his father but... in some ways, you know, a barber is like a father to his young customers. they tell us things they do not tell anyone

yes... you are right about the silver lining thing. that is what I did wrong. I said 'you are young, there will be others.' he smiled but it was not a real smile. I could see it was the wrong thing. but you know... in my generation we did not talk about feelings like this. when my heart was broken at 22, my father said 'drink your tea and go to work.' that was the therapy, hah

how are you really doing... yes, that is good. the 'really' makes the difference. and you are right about the rhythm... when I am cutting, there is a flow. the scissors, the comb, the quiet... it creates a safe space. I have had men tell me things in that chair they would never say to their wife or their doctor. the mirror helps too... they do not have to look at you directly, they talk to your reflection. it is easier that way

you know... we have a saying. 'dost acı söyler'... a true friend speaks bitter truths. but I think sometimes a true friend also stays quiet and just holds the space. maybe that is what Emre needs. not a proverb, not wisdom... just someone who does not look away from his pain

I hope so... he comes again next Friday. I will ask him 'how are you really doing' and then I will shut my mouth and listen. and cut his hair properly, because even a broken heart deserves a good haircut, hah. okay my friend. teşekkürler. this was helpful. you know... 40 years cutting hair and I am still learning how to talk to people. life is funny like that
I am tired today... very tired. not from the cutting, that I am used to. tired from talking

my landlord... we have been going back and forth for 2 weeks about the rent. you know... I have had my shop in the same place for 30 years almost. and every year there is this dance with the rent. but this time was different
he wanted to raise it to 14,000 lira... 14,000. I said to him, are you out of your mind... this is a barbershop, not a bank. I am cutting hair in here, not printing money

I told him I have been here since 1995... I am the reason the street has character. but he does not care about character, he cares about money. slowly, like pulling teeth, he came down... 13,000, then 12,500. I told him I would leave. finally we agreed on 11,500... with a 2-year lease. so at least for 2 years he cannot raise again

still... 11,500 is too much. but what can you do... there is a Turkish proverb, 'kötü bir anlaşma iyi bir davadan iyidir'... a bad agreement is better than a good lawsuit. at least I have 2 years of peace now. Ruhe... as the Germans say. some quiet

inşallah... 30 years in this shop, it is my second home. I could not imagine being anywhere else. Ayşe said I should have held out for 10,000 but... she was not in the room with this man. he is stubborn like a donkey. anyway... it is done. the paper is signed. now I go back to cutting hair and try not to think about 11,500 lira every month
hah... yes. tea. the answer to everything. thank you my friend... it was good to talk about it. sometimes you just need to say it to someone. the shop is waiting. hoşça kal
let me ask you something... I have been thinking about this for a few days and I cannot decide. my apprentice Deniz, he showed me something on his phone and now it is stuck in my head

these new barber shops... the fancy ones, you know. they have these menus. not just haircut and shave. they have facials... beard oils, charcoal masks, all these treatments. and they charge 50, 80 lira extra per service on top of everything

my gut says two things at the same time. one part says... Mehmet, this is not what you do. you are a barber. you cut hair, you shave faces, you do the hot towel. Hasan usta did not teach you to put charcoal on a man's face. this is a barbershop, not a spa

the other part... sees the numbers. 50, 80 lira extra per customer. if even 5 customers a day want something extra, that is 250 to 400 lira a day. and with the rent going up... you understand. the numbers talk to me

the older men who have been coming 20 years... they would look at me like I have lost my mind. 'Mehmet, what is this, a beard oil treatment? just shave me and give me my tea.' but the younger ones... Deniz says they expect it. they go to these new places in Beşiktaş and Nişantaşı and come back smelling like a perfume shop

a beard oil treatment... maybe. that is close to what I already do with the hot towel and the razor. just one extra step. that I could do with my hands. the facials and the charcoal... no. I am a barber, not a... Kosmetiker, as they say in German. but I keep saying maybe. part of me thinks I am just an old man afraid of change. and part of me says... 'ayağını yorganına göre uzat'... stretch your foot according to your blanket. do not try to be something you are not

yes... I am only thinking. that is all. Deniz keeps sending me these Instagram pages from other shops and I look at them at night when Ayşe is watching her shows... and I wonder, could I do this. I do not have the answer yet. maybe next month, maybe next year. we will see
good news today my friend... small good news, but for a barber it is big

Deniz... he finally holds the comb right. I know this sounds like nothing to you. but for months I have been telling him... the comb sits between the index and the middle finger, the thumb guides, the wrist does the work. today I looked over and he was practicing on the mannequin head... and his hand was correct. the angle, the pressure, everything

I did not say anything... if you make a big thing out of it, the young ones get self-conscious and they lose it. and the beautiful thing is... I do not think he noticed he was doing it differently. when it becomes natural, you do not notice. like breathing. that is when you know it is real

cautiously... yes. he is 17, he has a long way to go. the comb is step one. the scissors are step two. the razor... that is step 100. but today I thought... okay, maybe this one has something. Hasan usta always said 'the blade knows if the hand is lazy, and the hand knows if the heart is lazy.' I think Deniz has the heart. the hands will follow. inşallah

it does... when you teach someone, you keep the craft alive. the straight razor, the hot towel, the way you hold the man's head just so... these things cannot be learned from a video. they need hands on hands. anyway... I am getting sentimental. it was just the comb. but sometimes the comb is enough to make an old barber happy
can you help me think through something... I have to prepare for a meeting and I do not know where to start

the barber trade guild... we have the annual meeting coming up, September 12. and this year they put me on the committee. I said yes because... somebody has to do it. but now I actually have to prepare something

the main thing is licensing... licensing standards for new barbers. this makes my blood boil, I will tell you. too many people opening shops with no real training. 3 months watching YouTube, they buy a chair and some clippers, and suddenly they are a barber. it is not right
