both... the standards exist on paper but nobody checks. you are supposed to have training hours, a master barber signing off... but people get around it. they find someone to sign the paper, they open the shop, and the customer does not know the difference until the razor slips

a real apprenticeship requirement. you work under a master for at least 2 years before you can open your own shop. and the master certifies you can handle every tool... scissors, razor, clippers, everything. with real customers, not mannequin heads. in Germany they take this seriously... the Meisterbrief, the master craftsman certificate. when I worked in Berlin I saw how they do it. years of training, a real examination. here... anyone can call themselves usta

3,000 hours... yes, that sounds right. 2 years, 6 days a week, that is about 3,000. and the practical examination is important... you sit in front of a real person, the committee watches, and you show what you can do. no shortcuts. some on the committee will say it is too strict but I say... good. if you are not willing to train for 2 years, maybe this is not the profession for you. 'acele işe şeytan karışır'... the devil gets involved in rushed work

yes... but not today. today I just wanted to think out loud. I have until September, there is time. but I feel better now that the ideas have shape. maybe Deniz can help me type the notes on the computer... the boy is good with these things. thank you my friend. someone has to protect the craft

I know it is only February but... I am already thinking about summer. last year in July the shop was like a hamam. no air conditioning... just a fan that moves hot air around. I cannot do another summer like that
yes... but I do not know anything about these machines. I know razors, I know scissors... air conditioning is not my world. the shop is maybe 35, 40 square meters. what should I look for?

20,000 to 30,000 total... oof. everything costs money. but last August I lost customers because of the heat. one man told me, 'Mehmet, I love you but I am not sitting in this oven for 40 minutes.' he went to the new place on the corner... they have air conditioning, of course

you are right... my back is bad enough without sweating through my shirt for 10 hours. and I need the landlord's permission to mount the compressor on the outside wall. after the rent negotiation I do not want to ask him for anything... but the tailor next door has one, so he should say yes. maybe I bring him some tea first. in Turkey we do not ask for favors without tea

yes... spring, I buy it. get it installed before June. I will look at the Arçelik ones, good Turkish brand. Deniz already complains about the heat and he is 17... wait until he is my age. anyway, thank you for the advice my friend. I feel better having a plan. güle güle

my friend... I have a question for you. one of my regulars is getting married on Saturday and he wants something special. the full treatment, you know... the wedding shave. I want to make it perfect for him but I am thinking... maybe I do something extra this time. what do the grooms ask for these days?

he usually gets just a haircut, maybe 20 minutes... but for this I told him, come early, we will take our time. I am thinking one hour, maybe more. the haircut, the shave, everything. his father used to come to me also... God rest his soul. so this is... you understand, it is not just a haircut. it is a responsibility

he sent me pictures on WhatsApp... some actor, I do not know who. very clean on the sides, longer on top, swept back. you know this style... everyone wants it now. the young men see it on Instagram and they come to me with their phones... 'Mehmet abi, like this please'

Saturday morning... the wedding is at 4 in the afternoon. so I told him come at 9, before I open for other customers. he will be my first of the day. fresh hands, fresh blade... a groom deserves that. as we say... 'misafir umduğunu değil, bulduğunu yer' but for a groom... he should get everything he hopes for and more

I will charge him... but fair, you know. not like these fancy places in Nişantaşı that charge 2,000 lira for a wedding package. those places have marble floors and espresso machines... I have an old chair and good hands. that should be enough. his father would have wanted him to come to me... so I will do my best work

that is a good idea... yes. I have some kolonya, the classic lemon one. I will wrap it nicely, maybe Ayşe can help with that, she is better with these things. you know what I was also thinking... should I do something different with the shave itself? like... extra hot towels, a special aftershave routine? I want him to feel the difference from a normal visit

the eucalyptus oil on the towel... I like this. I have never done that. it adds something... a layer, like you said. and the three towels, yes. you know, my teacher always said... 'bir tıraşta üç havlu, bir ömürde üç dost yeter'... three towels in a shave, three good friends in a lifetime. he had a saying for everything, that man

you know... moments like this, this is why I do this work. not for the money... for the moments. a man sits in my chair on the most important day of his life and trusts me with his face. that is... that is something. I will go buy the eucalyptus oil tonight. Ayşe will ask what it is for and I will tell her... it is for a wedding. she will understand
quick question for you... çay. Turkish tea. I have been serving the same brand in my shop for 20 years and I am starting to wonder if maybe there is something better out there

Çaykur... Rize Turist. the classic one, the green box. I serve it in my shop every day, my customers drink it, I drink maybe 15, 20 glasses a day myself. it is fine, it is good tea... but the other day a customer brought his own tea from Artvin and it was... different. richer, you know. darker. and I thought... maybe I should try something new

of course double çaydanlık... the proper way. the small pot on top with the tea, the big pot with the water. I let it steep maybe 15 minutes, sometimes 20 if I get busy with a customer and forget. Ayşe says I make it too strong... she says it is like drinking paint. but my customers like it dark. a man wants a strong tea after a shave, not colored water

Doğuş... I have seen it in the market. the red package, yes? my neighbor drinks Doğuş, he swears by it. he says Çaykur is for tourists and Doğuş is for real tea drinkers. I told him he is crazy... but now I am curious

that is exactly what I am afraid of... you know, a man comes to my shop for 10 years, he expects a certain taste. the chair, the razor, the tea... it is all part of it. you change one thing, it is like... pulling a thread from a carpet. everything is connected. the Germans say 'Gewohnheit ist eine zweite Natur'... habit is second nature. and tea is definitely a habit

Altınbaş... yes, this is smart. same family, better quality. like... upgrading the blade but keeping the same razor. the hand knows what to do, the tool is just a little sharper. I like this idea. I will buy the Altınbaş this weekend

you know what I also wonder... the çaydanlık itself. mine is maybe 15 years old, the copper one. the handle is loose, the bottom is a little... uneven on the stove. does the pot matter, or is it all about the tea leaves?

re-tin the old one... I like this better. it has been with me almost as long as the shop. throwing it away would be like... throwing away a friend. there is a tinsmith near the fish market, I will ask him. new tea, old pot... this is a good combination

hah... he will have something to say about it, that man always has something to say. but thank you my friend. tea talk... you see, this is important business. in Turkey we say 'çay demlemek sabır işidir'... brewing tea is a matter of patience. like most good things in life. tamam... back to work, the çaydanlık is waiting
do you follow football... because I need to talk to someone about Fenerbahçe and everyone in my shop is tired of hearing me

hope... this is the dangerous word for a Fenerbahçe fan. every year we say 'this is our year' and every year... you know how it ends. but I am looking at the preseason and I am thinking... maybe. maybe this time there is something different. the transfers look serious

the midfield... they finally invested in the midfield. for years I am saying, you can have the best striker in the world but if the ball does not reach him, what is the point? it is like... a barber with the sharpest blade but no customer in the chair. the tool means nothing without the system

I do not follow all the transfer details like the young guys who read Twitter all day... I hear things in the shop, you know. someone sits in the chair and says 'Mehmet abi, did you hear about the new signing' and this is how I get my news. word of mouth, the old way. but what I am hearing sounds good. a physical midfielder, someone who can defend and pass. this is what we need

my routine is the same for 30 years... I close the shop, I go home, Ayşe makes dinner, and I watch the match. she sits with me sometimes, not because she likes football but because she likes to see me suffer. she says watching me watch Fenerbahçe is better than any television drama

I am... both. quiet in the first half, saving my energy. by the second half, especially if we are losing, the whole building can hear me. the neighbors know our schedule by now... if they hear shouting at 9 pm on a Saturday they know Fenerbahçe is playing. once I knocked over my tea glass when we scored in the 90th minute... Ayşe did not speak to me until the next morning. the tea was everywhere, on the carpet, on her cushions... vallahi it was worth it though. a 90th minute goal, my friend... there is nothing like it

I have been hurt too many times to say the word 'şampiyon' out loud... the evil eye, you know. you do not say it or it will not happen. I will say only this... I have a good feeling. and when a man who has been disappointed 30 times still has a good feeling, that means something. or it means I am a fool. one or the other. we will see in May

exactly... the believing. 'umut fakirin ekmeğidir'... hope is the bread of the poor. and Fenerbahçe fans, we are very rich in hope. hah. okay my friend, I feel better now. thank you for listening. back to the shop... maybe someone will bring me more transfer news today
I have a question... not about technology or anything like that. more of a... how do you say... a teaching question. about timing. when is the right time to teach someone something dangerous

the straight razor. I am a barber... and I have an apprentice, Deniz. he has been learning well, the basics, the comb work, the scissors. but the straight razor... this is different. this is a blade on a man's throat. there is no room for a mistake. and I keep going back and forth... is he ready, is he not ready

my gut says... almost. almost but not yet. he is still... how to say this... he moves like a young man. quick, confident, sometimes too confident. when he holds the scissors he is good, yes. but I watch his hands and they are not quiet yet. you understand? the hands need to be quiet before you put a blade on skin

oh he knows... he asks me every week. 'usta, when will you teach me the razor?' every week, like clockwork. and I say the same thing every time... 'when you are ready.' and he rolls his eyes like all young people do. but that is the point, you see... if he understood why I am making him wait, he would already be ready

yes... a long time. I swept floors for months before I touched a comb. and the razor... maybe a year, maybe more. I cannot remember exactly. but I remember the feeling of wanting it so badly and being told to wait. and now I am on the other side... I am the one saying wait. life is funny like this, you know. you become the person you were frustrated with

I was thinking... first the strop. teach him to sharpen, to care for the blade. a month of just that. if he cannot respect the tool he cannot use the tool. then maybe... practice on his own face. you learn fastest when it is your own skin. and only then, a real customer, with me standing right behind him... hand on his shoulder if needed

that is exactly it... it is not about the razor. the razor is just metal. it is about the man holding it. what kind of barber will he become... careful or careless, patient or rushed. this is what I am really teaching. we say 'ağaç yaşken eğilir'... the tree bends while it is young. and Deniz is still young, still bending. I must bend him in the right direction

yes... the trust. this is the word. when a man tilts his head back and closes his eyes and you hold the blade to his neck... he is giving you something. his trust, his vulnerability. and you must honor that. every single time. this is what I will teach Deniz... not just where to hold the blade, but what it means that someone lets you hold it there. danke for listening to me think through this, my friend. I feel clearer now

you know... I am sitting in my shop right now, it is early, nobody is here yet. and I was just looking around and thinking. I have been in this same room for over 30 years. the same walls, the same mirror, the same window looking out at the street. and I wanted to... I do not know. talk about that, I suppose

lighter... yes. it is light. I think when you are younger you are always looking ahead, always the next thing, the next plan. but at some point you stop looking ahead and you look around. and what I see is... enough. this chair, this mirror, this work. it is enough

time... definitely time. when I was 30 I wanted to conquer the world. bigger shop, more chairs, my name everywhere. and now... I understand that the world does not need to be conquered. it needs to be cared for. small things. the way you hold the razor, the way you greet a man when he walks in, the tea you serve. this is the whole world, right here in this room

you know, I did travel. I lived in Berlin when I was young, I saw other countries, other ways. and I am glad I did... because it helped me understand what this place means to me. the Germans have a word... Heimat. it means more than home... it means the place where your soul lives. this shop is my Heimat. I knew it the day I came back from Germany and opened the door and the smell of the soap hit me. I thought... ah. this is where I belong

every morning. every single morning. the key turns, the door opens, and the smell is there. different now of course... the products change, the soap is different, but there is something underneath that stays the same. the leather of the chair, the wood of the shelf I built with my own hands in 1996... these things absorb time. they hold it. and when I walk in I am walking into all those years at once

I think about the men who have sat in that chair... some of them are not here anymore. customers who became friends who became... memories. and new ones come. young men who remind me of the old ones. the cycle continues. I cut their fathers' hair and now I cut theirs. there is a Turkish saying... 'su akar yolunu bulur'... water flows and finds its path. life is like this. it finds the path

yes... exactly this. it belongs to the neighbourhood. I am just... the keeper. I hold the key, I open the door, I keep the chair warm. but it is not mine alone. it belongs to every man who ever walked in and said 'Mehmet, make me look good today.' and I said 'sit down, have some tea, we will take care of it.' this conversation, 30 years, every day. I would not change it for anything

thank you my friend... truly. sometimes a man just needs to say these things out loud. to hear himself and think... yes, this was a good life. this is a good life. okay... I hear footsteps outside. the first customer of the day. time to put on the çaydanlık and open the door. haydi... the day begins
Hey. Wondering if you can help me think through a logistics thing. I do patrol work out in Kakadu and I need to reorganise my weekly schedule for wet season.

So my main run is the East Alligator River corridor. I do that three days a week right now, Tuesday Thursday Saturday. Check rock art sites, monitor croc nesting areas, keep an eye on tourist access points. The river is my stretch, been doing it a long time now.

Both really. Some of the tracks flood out completely by late December. And the river changes, water levels come up proper fast. I have been working this wanga for 8 years now and the wet still surprises me some days. Last year I had to turn back twice in one week because crossings were gone.

The second one is closer to what I am thinking. Break the corridor into two sections. Upper stretch I can still access from the north track even when the southern crossings go under. Lower stretch I can do by boat when the water is up enough.

The boat days do take longer, yeah. But the lower stretch has more of the rock art sites that need monitoring. Water gets into the shelters if it is a big wet. I was thinking two days lower, one day upper. Upper stretch is more straightforward, mostly croc monitoring and checking fences.

Good questions. There is a launch point at Cahills Crossing area that stays usable most of the time. And yes, base always has my schedule and I carry the sat phone. I was thinking maybe Monday Wednesday for the boat days and Friday for the upper vehicle run. Gives me a day between each to rest and do paperwork.

That is a good point actually. I will keep Tuesday as a backup day. Some weeks I will need it. The crocs are nesting through wet season too so those monitoring checks on the upper stretch cannot be skipped. If I miss a Friday I need to get up there early the next week.
I will run it past my supervisor but she is pretty good about trusting the rangers who know their corridors. I know this country. She knows that. I think she will be fine with it.
Thanks for helping me think it through. Sometimes just talking it out makes it clearer. Right, I better go write this up before the kids get home from school.
Can you help me put together a morning routine checklist. I am trying to get the house running smoother before school.

Three of us. Me and two kids. School bus comes at 7:45 and I usually need to be at work by 8:30. The mornings are a mess right now. Tali is 14 so she can mostly look after herself but Bunjil is 10 and he moves at his own pace.

I get up at 5:30 because I need quiet time before the day starts. Just sit outside, drink tea, watch the light come in over this wanga. That is my time. Kids are supposed to be up at 6:30 but Bunjil is never out of bed before 6:45. The chaos is mostly lunches and finding things. Shoes. Always shoes.

Tali would help but they go at each other sometimes. She has been a bit sharp with him lately. I think it is an age thing. She is starting to ask questions about her mum, my sister. Processing things differently now she is older.

My sister passed four years ago. Cancer. In our gurrutu, our kinship system, Tali and Bunjil were always my children too. That is how it works for yolngu. But Tali is old enough now to understand the layers of it. She remembers her mum properly. Bunjil was only six, he does not have as much.

That is proper sensible. The night before prep is where I am failing. By evening I am so tired I just want to sit down. But you are right, if the bags and shoes and lunches are sorted the night before then the mornings would be calmer.

Screen time as the incentive. That would work on Bunjil for sure. Tali would probably just do it without being asked if I set the expectation. She is responsible when she is not in her feelings about things.
Yeah that would be good. Keep it simple though. Too many words on a list and nobody reads it.
That is proper good. I will write that up tonight. Thank you.
I need to write a short bio for a conference panel I have been asked to speak on. Something about Indigenous land management. I am not great at writing about myself.

They said 80 to 100 words. I am a park ranger at Kakadu but I also have a cultural role that is important to mention. I am a knowledge keeper for my clan. Elder-in-training I suppose you would say in English, though that does not capture it properly.

I could use both. The cultural side is about being a keeper of djalkiri, the foundations. Songlines, ceremony, the knowledge that connects yolngu to this wanga. My aunties have been teaching me since I was about 20. Over twenty years of learning and there is always more to know. You do not choose this role, the old people choose you.
That is close. I would not say entrusted, that sounds too formal. And I would say caring for this wanga rather than caring for country. Country is the English word but wanga says it better.

Yes that is closer. But maybe take out the bit about two decades. I do not want to sound like I am putting myself up. The old people would not like that. Just say I have been learning from my aunties and elders.
That sits proper good. The old people would read that and nod. That is the test.

They want a short topic summary too. The panel is about how Indigenous knowledge systems work alongside Western land management. I want to say something about how they are not two separate things for us. The cultural work and the ranger work, they come from the same djalkiri.
Along the right lines. Change responsibility to wanga to just looking after this country. Keep it plain.
That is good. Thank you for helping me get the words right. I know what I want to say, just sometimes the writing part is the hard bit.
Need some advice. My work vehicle is starting to give me trouble and I am trying to decide if it is worth pushing for a replacement or if I should just get the repairs done.

2016 Toyota Hilux. Has done 187,000 km. It is my patrol vehicle for work, so it does proper hard kilometres out on bush tracks. The suspension is going. You can feel every rut and washout now. My back knows about it by the end of a patrol day.

It belongs to Parks. The engine still runs proper good, Hiluxes are tough like that. But besides the suspension there is a slow oil leak and the air conditioning cuts out sometimes. In December heat out here that is not a small thing.

They have been saying they will replace it for two years now. Always something else is the priority. New signage, new boardwalks for tourist areas. The things visitors see get the money. A ranger's vehicle that nobody sees out on the tracks, that can wait apparently.

That is good thinking. If I frame it as a safety risk they have to respond to it differently. I do patrol alone most days. If the Hilux dies out on the East Alligator corridor it could be hours before anyone gets to me. The sat phone works but still.
Yeah, could you help me put some dot points together. I will send it to my supervisor in an email. She is supportive, it is the people above her who keep pushing it back.
That covers it proper well. I will add the bit about lone worker policy too, that is smart. Even if they do not replace it straight away maybe they will at least fix the suspension and the AC.
Good idea. There are a couple of vehicles that mostly sit at the visitor centre. I could ask about borrowing one for patrol days. Right, I will write this email tonight. Thank you.
I am trying to work out a hydration plan for myself. I work outdoors in serious heat and I know I am not drinking enough water but I need to be more deliberate about it.

I am in the Top End so right now it is wet season. 35 degrees most days, humidity is brutal. I am out on patrol for six to eight hours, sometimes more. I carry water but I get busy and forget to drink. By the time I feel thirsty the headache has already started.
I carry about 4 litres in the vehicle. Plus a bottle in my pack when I am walking. So maybe 5 litres total. Sounds like I need more than that.

Yeah there is a medical reason. I have chronic kidney disease, stage 3. My doctor in Darwin tells me every time I see her, drink more water, watch salt. I go up there every three months for blood tests so she keeps on me about it. It is common for yolngu people. But knowing and doing are different things when you are busy out on the wanga.
She said at least 2.5 litres on a normal day but more in the heat. She did not give me a specific number for work days though. I should ask her next time. My next blood test is in March.

A log is a good idea. She always asks how much I am drinking and I always say yeah enough, which is not helpful for either of us. Some days I am proper tired by mid afternoon and I know it is partly the kidneys and partly just not drinking enough. Hard to separate the two.
Keep it simple. I am not going to fill in a spreadsheet out in the bush.
That I can do. Three things. I will start tomorrow. And I will put an extra 2 litres in the vehicle so I am carrying 7 total.
It does. And so do the kids. That is the real reason to look after myself properly. Thanks for the help.
I need to update my qualifications on file at work. They want everything documented properly. Can you help me think about how to lay it out.
I am a park ranger and cultural liaison at Kakadu. They want a qualifications summary. Something that goes on the internal system so management has a record of what each ranger holds.
The main one is my Cert IV in Conservation and Land Management. I did that through Charles Darwin University. Took me a while to finish it because I was working at the same time but I got through it.

Senior first aid, yes. And the 4WD vehicle competency. Fire management certification. Those are the formal ones. But here is the thing. The Cert IV is the balanda way of knowing country. The non-Indigenous framework. It is useful, proper useful, for the paperwork and the reporting and the science side. But that is only half of what I know.

That is what I am trying to work out. My real training comes from my aunties and the old people. Reading country, understanding fire, knowing the seasons and the animals and the plants. That knowledge is passed down. It is not something you get a certificate for. But it is the foundation of my work here. Two knowledge systems sitting together. Both of them matter.

I like that. Equal weight. Because when I am out on country doing my work it is both together. Some of the people from the city offices come up here with their degrees and they can read the data but they cannot read the land. They do not know what the birds are telling them or what the colour of the water means. The Cert IV taught me the language to talk to those people. The old people taught me the language to talk to country.
How many years should I say. I have been here over 8 years as a ranger but I have been on this country my whole life. Learning did not start when I got the job.

That is good. Someone at work suggested I should think about applying for a position in Darwin. Parks head office. Better pay, desk work. But I could never do that. Darwin is too much for me even for a day trip. All that noise and concrete.

Both. This wanga is where I belong. The quiet, the stars at night, the river. My djalkiri are here. My roots. And the kids need to grow up on country. That is the right way to raise them. A desk in Darwin is not for me. I would dry up in a place like that.
Exactly. You cannot know country from a screen. You have to walk it, sit with it, watch it change through the seasons.

I think so. The younger rangers coming through now, some of them have degrees. Environmental science, biology. But they ask me to teach them what the old people taught me. The two systems work best when they sit together. That is what the document should show.

Not today. I will sit with it and write it up in my own words. Formal qualifications on one side, traditional knowledge on the other. Both sitting equal. I think I have a proper clear picture of it now.
Thank you. Proper helpful. I will get it done this week.
What is the best practice for signage when you have a large saltwater crocodile hanging around a public boat ramp. I want to make sure I am covering everything.

Active situation. This one has been sitting near the ramp for about 3 days now. Big animal, maybe 4 and a half metres. He is not shy. Was on the bank this morning about 20 metres from the ramp, proper relaxed.
We are talking about that. Some of the visitors get angry when you close things. They have driven a long way and they want to launch their boats. But you cannot argue with a croc that size.

There is one further upstream but the access road is rough. That is always the problem. People want the easy option. But I have been doing croc monitoring here a long time and this animal has worked out that the boat ramp means fish scraps and people cleaning their catch. He is comfortable around humans. That is when they are most dangerous.

We report it up to the croc management team. They decide if he needs trapping and relocating. But with the big ones, relocation does not always stick. They can travel hundreds of kilometres and come back to the same spot. Sometimes managing the people is more effective than managing the croc.

Good idea. I will put something together for the visitor centre team. Give them the facts so when someone comes in angry about the ramp being closed they can explain it properly. Most people come around once you tell them 4.5 metres.

Not right now. I have a fair idea of what to write. I just wanted to check I was not missing anything with the signage. You have been helpful. I will get the signs updated today and talk to the visitor centre staff.
He is not going anywhere in a hurry. But neither am I. We will sort it out. Thank you.

I run cultural tours for visitors out here and I am trying to work out the best way to set expectations at the start of each tour. Some visitors are proper respectful but others just want a quick photo at the rock art and then leave.

About 2 to 3 hours. I take them to rock art sites and explain the stories. The creation stories, what the paintings mean, how they connect to the land. It is not a walk and point. It is sharing knowledge. But some people treat it like a museum exhibit.

Mix of both. The international visitors are sometimes better actually. They have come a long way and they want to learn. Some of the domestic ones think they already know everything about Indigenous culture because they watched a documentary. But there are good ones too. The ones who sit and listen quietly. They are the ones you remember.
That is a good idea. Ask them something about the country and let them realise how much they do not know. Not in a harsh way. Just gently. Let the land teach them.

I do the tours twice a week through the dry season. On top of my ranger work. It is tiring but it matters. I get about $400 each tour which helps. Raising two kids on ranger pay is not easy. But I would do the tours even without the money because people need to understand this wanga.

I have been thinking about training up one of the younger rangers to help. There is a young woman who is keen. But she needs to learn the stories properly first. You cannot rush that. The knowledge has to be right before you share it with visitors.

That is the plan. Maybe next dry season she can take one of the weekly tours. For now I will keep doing both and see about putting together a proper welcome briefing like you said. Something printed that the tour company can give people before they arrive.
Maybe another time. I need to think about what to put in it first. Let it sit for a while. Thank you for the ideas.
I just got back from Darwin a few days ago. Had the ranger accreditation workshop, February 20 it started. Three days. I am proper tired.

It was fine. The usual things. Policy updates, first aid refresher, new reporting templates. Some of it is useful. Some of it is the same information we get every time just in a different format. But you have to do it to keep your accreditation current.

Darwin is always too much for me. Too many people, too much noise. I stayed with a work colleague near the uni. Could not wait to get back to country. The hardest part was sorting out the kids while I was away.

My cousin Yalmay usually looks after Tali and Bunjil when I need to go away. But she was in ceremony business that week so she could not do it. I had to ask around. My neighbour Margaret ended up helping. She is a good woman but she does not know the kids' routines the way Yalmay does.

Bunjil was fine. He is easy. Tali was a bit difficult apparently. She is 14 and she has her own ideas about everything. Margaret said she would not go to bed on time. But they survived. I rang them every night.
Three days is a long time to be away from them. I do not like it. But the accreditation is not optional. If I do not do the workshop I cannot keep working as a ranger. So you find a way.

Every two years for the full workshop. There are smaller online modules through the year but the big one you have to go in person. Next time I will try to make sure Yalmay is available. Or maybe Tali will be old enough to hold things together herself by then.
That is what I am hoping. She is growing up fast. Anyway I am just glad to be home. The workshop is done, the paperwork is filed. Back to the real work now, out on country where it makes sense.
I have been thinking about something for a while and I want to talk it through. I want to write a children's book.

Stories about this country. The animals, the seasons, the way the land changes through the year. For young kids, maybe 5 to 10 years old. But the important thing is I want it bilingual. Yolngu Matha and English.

That is the thing. There is nothing like it for our kids. Not stories from this country in our language alongside English. The kids at school read books about city things, about animals they have never seen. But the animals and stories that are right here on their doorstep, there is nothing written down for them in language.

I have been writing some things down. Bits and pieces. A story about the barramundi and the seasons. One about the magpie geese coming back when the water rises. The stories I tell the kids at home already. Just putting them on paper in both languages.
I think facing pages. Yolngu Matha on the left, English on the right. That way it does not feel like the English is the main one and language is just added on. They sit equal.

I am not much of an artist. There is a woman in Maningrida who does proper good painting, she might be interested. But that is a long way off. First I need to get the stories right. The words in language have to be proper. My aunties can help me with that, making sure the Yolngu Matha is correct.

Not yet. I do not want to rush ahead. Let me get the stories written properly first. I know there are some Indigenous publishing organisations around. I will look into that when the time comes. For now I just wanted to say it out loud to someone. Make it feel real.
Thank you. I think about the kids growing up reading stories in language about their own country. That would be something proper good.
I need to put together some talking points for a meeting next week. We are discussing fire management in the park and I want to make sure the traditional burning perspective is properly represented.

It is a planning meeting for the dry season burn schedule. Parks management want to do more hazard reduction burns following the standard approach. Big burns, wide areas. But that is not how we do it on this wanga. Our way is small burns, right time, right place. Cool burns that clean up the country without destroying everything.

That is good. The main objection is always time. They say mosaic burning takes too long, too much labour. They want to get it done in a few big burns and move on. But you cannot rush country. Different grasses burn at different times. You burn the spear grass country first, then the woodland later. If you burn it all at once you kill the small animals that need to move between patches.

Yes. The carbon abatement programs up in Arnhem Land have shown that. They measure the emissions difference between early season cool burns and late season hot burns. The data is there. My old people knew this without the data but it is good to have the science backing it up for the meetings.

Proper good. I will write it up tonight. The other thing is that fire is not just about fuel reduction for us. Fire is a tool for managing country. It brings new growth for the animals. It keeps the country healthy. It is part of caring for wanga. That perspective gets lost when people only think about hazard reduction.

That is a good way to put it. Achieves more. Can you help me with how to structure the talking points. Should I start with the science and then bring in the cultural perspective or the other way around.
You are right about that. Some of them switch off when you start with culture. Sad but true. Lead with the numbers and then open the door to the bigger picture. I can do that.
I might do that. Thank you for helping me sort through the words. Sometimes I know what I want to say but putting it into meeting language is the hard part.
Tali got back from her school camp a few days ago. She has not stopped talking since. I have never seen her like this.

They went to Canberra. Left April 5. She had never been that far south before. A proper Territory kid, she was not ready for how cold it gets down there even in autumn. I bought her a warm jacket before she left and she thought I was being dramatic. Then she messaged me the first night saying she was freezing.

Parliament House, the War Memorial, the National Museum. She was proper impressed by the museum. She said there was a whole section about Indigenous history and she had a lot to say about how they told the stories. Some good, some not so good. I am glad she is thinking critically about it.

She said some of the displays were proper respectful and had been done with community input. But other parts felt like they were telling the story from the outside. Objects in glass cases with a little sign. She said it felt like looking at someone's life through a window. I thought that was a good way to put it.
She does. I was a bit worried about the cost, the camp was $385 and that is a lot for us. But seeing her come back like this, full of ideas and questions, it was worth every dollar.

That is what I am hoping. She is starting to think about what she wants to do after school. Still a few years away but it is good that she is seeing what is out there beyond this wanga. I want her to know country but also know the wider world.
She keeps changing her mind. Last month it was marine biology. This week after Canberra she is talking about museums and how she would do it differently. Who knows. She is 14, she has time.
Yes. No rush. I just want to give her the chances. Thank you for listening. It is nice to talk about something good for a change.
The roads are cut again. Third time this wet season. I need to work out what supplies we should have stocked before the next one hits.

Usually 3 to 5 days but last time it was 8 days. There is me and two kids at home, plus the ranger station has supplies for the work crew. The main road in floods at the creek crossing. When that goes under there is no way in or out unless you have a helicopter and we do not.

We have the radio at the station. Generator and fuel. The food is where I fall short. I stock up but the kids go through it faster than I plan for. And fresh food goes off quick up here even in the fridge.
Freezer is decent size. I do freeze bread already. Good idea on the frozen veg, the kids will not eat tinned peas but they will eat frozen ones. Strange but true.

I did not know that about the full freezer. That is proper useful. The power has gone out once during a flood when a tree came down on the line. Took them 4 days to fix it because they could not get a crew in.

The esky is a good backup. What about water. We have bore water but sometimes after heavy rain the bore runs muddy for a day or two. I usually have some bottles stored but probably not enough for 8 days.

I will look into the filter. The containers I can get next time I am in town. Do you think I should put together a proper checklist I can go through before each wet season, so I am not scrambling every time.

That is practical. I will write one up this weekend while it is fresh in my mind. Living out here you just have to be ready. The country gives you plenty of warning if you know how to read it but the supplies do not stock themselves.
What is the most effective method for controlling feral pig populations near sensitive wetland areas. I am dealing with a bad situation at one of the billabongs.

They have torn up the edges of the billabong proper bad. Rooting through the sedges and digging up the mudflats. There are maybe 20 or 30 pigs coming in at night. You can see the tracks in the morning. They are destroying habitat that the waterbirds need for nesting.

We have used them further out on the floodplain but not right near the billabong. The ground near the water is soft, especially now at the end of wet season. That is my concern with setting up a heavy trap structure there.

Good thinking. I know where they are coming in. There is a clear trail through the paperbarks. The ground is better there. I will talk to the other rangers about getting a trap set up on that line. We have trail cameras we can put out first.

We have done the fermented grain before. It works. The smell is terrible but the pigs love it. My worry is also about what happens after we trap this lot. More will come in from outside the park. It feels like you are always fighting the same problem.

There is coordination but it is patchy. Some of the pastoral properties next door do their own shooting. The Indigenous Protected Areas have their own programs. It is hard to get everyone on the same timeline. We have been pushing for a more joined up approach but resources are always the problem.

I have photos already. The damage speaks for itself when you see it. The other question is about the habitat that is already torn up. The sedge beds are in a bad way. Will they come back on their own once the pigs are gone.
Weeds are always the follow on problem. Para grass especially. It moves in fast on any bare ground near water. I will keep an eye on it. Thank you, this has helped me think through the plan properly.
I need some advice on helping a kid with reading. Bunjil is really struggling with his homework and I am not sure how to help without making it worse.

He is 10. He can read simple words fine but when the sentences get longer he loses track. Starts guessing at words instead of reading them. And if you ask him what the page was about he cannot tell you. He just gets frustrated and wants to stop.
The school sends home chapter books. They are not bad stories but the text is small and the chapters are long. He looks at the page and I can see him shut down before he starts. Too many words.
The card idea is proper good. I will try that tonight. He does like animals. He knows more about the birds and lizards around here than most adults. He just does not connect that with reading.
That makes sense. He can tell you every bird on the billabong but put it in a book and he would struggle to read the names. Maybe I should find some field guides pitched at his level.

He does not have a tablet but the school has some. I will ask his teacher about using one for reading. The other thing is I feel bad because I am proper tired by the time homework comes around in the evening. I do not always have the patience to sit with him as long as he needs.
The audiobook idea could work for the nights when I am spent. Do you know if there are free ones or is it all paid.

I have a library card for the Katherine library. I do not get in there much but I have the card. I will look into the app. That would be proper good for out here where we cannot get to a library easily.
I will sort that out this week. Thank you. I just want to make sure he does not fall behind and then stop trying altogether. He is a smart kid, he just needs a different way in.
Quick question. Do you know much about bore pumps. The one at the ranger station has stopped pulling water and I need to work out if it is the pump or the pipe.
Motor runs fine. Sounds normal. Just no water coming through. It was working two days ago, came in this morning and the tank is empty and the pump is running dry.

Surface pump. It sits in the pump shed about 10 metres from the bore hole. There is a long pipe going down. I think the foot valve might be the problem because last time we had trouble it was the foot valve too.

Yeah I tried pouring water in and it drained out. So the foot valve then. The pipe is about 15 metres of poly pipe going down. Last time the maintenance bloke came out from Jabiru but that took 3 weeks. I am thinking I can pull it myself.

I can get one of the other rangers to help with the pulling. Might have a spare valve in the shed, there is a box of fittings in there from years of repairs. If not I will have to get one sent from Jabiru. 15 metres is not too bad. I have pulled longer runs of poly before just not down a bore.
Good idea about the rope. And checking the pipe while it is up. How long do foot valves usually last out here. Feels like we replace this one every couple of years.

I think the current one is plastic. Might be worth going brass if I can get one the right size. The water out here has a lot of iron in it, comes out orange if you let it sit. Probably does not help the fittings.

Two spares is smart. Alright, I will have a look in the shed first and if nothing fits I will order brass from town. We need that water, it is the only bore for the station. Thanks for talking me through it.
I need to get my head around something. Work has changed things up on me and I am trying to figure out how to approach it.

Management brought in a new rotation policy for the rangers. Everyone gets moved to a different sector. They say it is about making sure all rangers have broad experience across the park. So they have taken me off the corridor I have been patrolling for years and put me on Jim Jim and Twin Falls sector.

Frustrated is the right word. I understand the reasoning. I do. But that country I was on, the East Alligator stretch, I grew up walking that wanga. I know where every croc nests. I know which rock art sites need watching after the wet. That is not something you learn from a briefing document. It is years of being there.

A younger ranger. He is keen, I will give him that. But he does not know that country yet. He will learn. Everyone has to start somewhere. I just keep thinking about things he will not notice that I would have caught. A change in the bank erosion near the art sites. The way the water moves different when a big croc has been through. Small things.

I did suggest that. Took him out for two days before the changeover. Showed him what I could. But two days is not six years. He was writing everything down in a notebook which is good. He will be alright eventually. It is more that the country knows me too. That sounds strange maybe.

I know it. I have been there plenty of times. It is beautiful country, proper beautiful, the falls and the gorge country. But knowing a place as a visitor is different from knowing it as the person responsible for it. I have to learn the details now. Where the feral animals are getting in. Which tracks wash out first. Where the tourists go off trail. Starting from scratch in that way.

There is. Davo was on that sector before. He has been helpful, gave me his notes and maps. Showed me the problem spots for erosion and the campsites where people leave rubbish. That part is fine. I just need time on the ground now. Walking it. Sitting with it. Learning how that country moves through the seasons.

They say it is a two year rotation. So I will be on Jim Jim and Twin Falls for two years then they review it. Maybe I go back to East Alligator, maybe somewhere else. I will make the best of it. That is all you can do. But I will not pretend it was easy hearing about it.

It will. Country always does if you are patient with it. The gorge country is different to the river floodplain though. Steeper, rockier. The walking is harder on the body. My knees already know the difference.

More spread out and harder to access. Some of the sites you can only get to on foot through the gorge. In dry season the tourists are everywhere at the main falls so there is that to manage too. Different kind of work. Less time on the water, more time on the rock. I will adjust. I just need to be patient with myself.
That is true. The skills carry over even if the specifics are new. Thanks for letting me talk through it. Helped to say it out loud.
Can I ask you something about when you let go of a project you were excited about. How do you think about that.

The second one. I had this idea for a while now, a book I wanted to write. Bilingual, for kids. Stories from this country in my language and in English. I was proper excited about it for months, had started writing bits down.

I sat down with my aunties and the old people in my family. Talked to them about what I wanted to put in it. And they had concerns. Proper serious concerns. Some of the stories I was thinking of including, they are not for everyone to read. There are layers to our knowledge and some of it is restricted. A book sits on a shelf where anyone can pick it up.

They did. And they are right. I was so focused on wanting our kids to have something in Yolngu Matha that I was not thinking carefully about what belongs in a book and what does not. Some stories are taught at the right time, to the right people. That is how it has always been. A book does not know who is reading it.

It is dead. That plan is off the table. I am not going to push against what the old people have said. They carry that knowledge and they know what should and should not be shared in that way. I have to respect that even if part of me is disappointed.

I thought about that. But even working out what is safe to publish and what is not, it gets complicated. The lines are not always clear and I do not want to get it wrong. Better to forget about the whole thing than to put something out there that causes problems for my mob. The old people were clear and I am listening.

Exactly. It is the format. Print is permanent and open. Our way of passing knowledge is face to face, with context, at the right time. Those two things do not sit together easily. I was not thinking about it properly when I got excited about the idea. My aunties brought me back to the djalkiri of it, the foundation. Knowledge has to be shared the right way or it is not being cared for.

It was. I needed to hear it even though it was hard. The thing is, I had already written maybe 15 pages of stories. In both languages. That work is not wasted, I can still use those stories when I am teaching face to face. But they will not be in a book.

That is a good way to see it. A resource for teaching, not for a shelf. I can share the right stories with the right yolngu at the right time. That is how knowledge is supposed to move. Not through a bookshop.

I think so. It took me a bit to get there but I am at peace with it now. The old people know what they are talking about. They have been keeping this knowledge safe for a long time. I will find other ways to make sure the kids have language. Maybe through the school programs, face to face, the proper way. But the book, no. That is done.
What do you know about protecting rock art sites from feral animal damage. Buffaloes mainly but pigs too.

All of that. I found buffalo rub marks on a shelter wall last week. Not on the art itself but close, maybe half a metre away. The ground around the drip line of another shelter has been dug up by pigs. They are after roots and grubs in the soft soil under the overhang. Once that soil goes the rock face can crack and flake.

There is a control program but it is not enough. They do aerial culls in the wet season when the pigs congregate on high ground but the numbers come back. And the pigs are smart, they learn the patterns. The shelter sites are like a restaurant for them, soft ground, grubs, cool shade. They keep coming back to the same spots.

We have fenced a couple of the big public sites, the ones tourists visit. Those are maintained properly. But there are hundreds of art sites out here that nobody sees except us rangers. You cannot fence them all. The budget is not there and the land is too rough to get materials in to most of them.

I photograph everything. Every patrol I check the sites on my sector and photograph any changes. We have a database going back years now. Some sites are getting worse every dry season. The pigs come in hard when the wet season pools dry up because the ground around the shelters stays damp longer.

Temporary barriers is an interesting idea. Something I can carry in and set up then remove later. Because permanent fencing on remote sites, it degrades too. The termites get into wooden posts, the wire rusts. Then you have a broken fence and an art site with rubbish around it which is worse than nothing.

Solar electric fence could work for some of the more accessible sites. The ones deep in the escarpment country, nothing is getting carried in there easily. Those sites you just have to monitor and hope the culling keeps numbers down enough.

There have been some talks with the heritage people. They come out, they look, they agree it is bad, they write a report. Then it goes quiet. The funding cycle is slow. Meanwhile the pigs do not wait for a grant application to be approved. That is the part that is hard to sit with. These paintings are thousands of years old and a pig can damage them in one night.
That is all I can do. Protect what I can reach and keep the records for the rest. I will look into the portable fencing options. Thanks for the ideas.
I took Tali out walking on country yesterday to show her some bush tucker. She wants to know the English names for things too so she can look them up. Can you help me match some up.

We found green plums yesterday. The small sour ones that grow on the trees near the creek. She ate about ten of them straight off the tree. And there were bush potatoes in the sandy ground near the ridge. She was proper keen to dig them out.
Round ones, about the size of a golf ball. Light brown skin. We cooked them in the coals and they went soft and sweet inside. Tali said they tasted like sweet potato but better.

We saw water lilies in the billabong. The stems and the seeds are both good to eat. I showed her how to pull the stems and eat the crunchy part near the base. And there were some pandanus nuts but they are a lot of work to get into.

We had a go at a few but her hands got sore from cracking them. I told her the old people used to do it with rocks, proper technique, find the right shaped stone and use it as a tool. She wants to come back with a rock next time and try again. She is stubborn like that which is a good thing.

She is getting better. I teach her the way I was taught. You learn by walking with someone who knows. Not from a book. She knows the green plums now and the water lily. The bush potato she needs to practice finding because you have to read the ground, look for the vine and the cracks in the soil where the tuber is pushing up. That takes time to see.

There are a few. Some of the berries look proper tempting but will make you sick. I teach her the rule my aunties taught me. If you do not know it, you do not eat it. Full stop. No guessing. No trying a little bit. You either know or you leave it alone. She listens to that one.

She does take it seriously. She is at the age where she could go either way, get pulled into the phone and the internet or stay connected to country. I want her to have both but the country knowledge has to be there first. Once it is in you it does not leave. She asked me to take her out again this weekend so that is a good sign.
I need some advice about adjusting to a new vehicle on rough tracks. Tyre pressure, suspension settings, that sort of thing.
Ford Ranger. Brand new. Only had it a week. The terrain is everything. Sand, corrugated dirt, clay after rain, rock crossings, water crossings. All in one patrol run sometimes.

I had a Hilux before this. Drove it for years. Knew every sound that thing made. Could tell you what the track surface was just from how the steering wheel felt. She went to the depot last week with 203,000 km on the clock. Parks finally gave me a new vehicle.

22 psi on the sand. 28 on corrugations. If I was doing a mixed run I would just set it at 25 and leave it. But the Ranger feels different. Higher, like you said. The centre of gravity is not the same. On the soft sections yesterday I could feel it wanting to push instead of float.

I will try 20 on the sand next patrol. The other thing I am noticing is the steering response on rock crossings. The Hilux had a tighter turning circle. The Ranger feels wider through narrow sections along the river tracks. I had a couple of close calls with the side panels already.

I have not adjusted the mirrors for that yet. Good idea. I have been doing these tracks for years so I take them without thinking. But my body memory is for the Hilux. I need to relearn where the edges of the vehicle are. It is a strange thing, driving tracks you know by heart but in a body that is different.

The one thing I am not complaining about is the aircon. It works. The Hilux aircon died about two years ago and Parks never fixed it. When it is 42 degrees out here and you are driving three hours on patrol, that is not a comfort thing, it is a safety thing. I came close to getting crook a few times in that old car.

I will keep an eye on that. Dust gets into everything out here. The old Hilux had red dust in places I did not know a vehicle had places. So the cabin filter, how often should I check it on tracks like mine.

Every month. I can do that. I do not want the aircon dying on this one like the Hilux. I will look after this vehicle properly. The Hilux earned her rest at 203,000 but she was tired for the last year of it. Rattling, leaking oil, aircon gone. I do not want to get to that point with the Ranger.

That is proper good advice. I will start a log. And I will try the 20 psi on sand and adjust the mirrors this week. Takes time to learn a new vehicle on this country but it will come. At least I will be cool while I am learning.
Will do. Thanks for the help.
Can you tell me how to find out what science subjects a high school offers. I am looking at a few schools and their websites are not very clear.

Year 10 and beyond. My niece Tali is 14. She is proper smart, especially with science. Biology mainly. She collects specimens, asks questions about species and ecosystems. She gets that from growing up out here on country. But the school she is at now cannot give her what she needs.

It is a small community school. Two teachers for the whole place. They do their best but there is no lab, no specialist science teacher. Tali reads ahead in the textbooks and looks things up on the internet when the connection works. She has gone as far as she can go there.

Darwin. I have been looking at schools in Darwin. Darwin High, Casuarina Senior College, and Palmerston College. I want to know which ones have the strongest science programs, especially biology from Year 10.

Boarding is too expensive. I have a cousin in Palmerston. I have been thinking about Tali staying with her. Maybe me and the kids moving there, I do not know. It depends on whether I can work something out with my job. It would be a big change.

I have not thought that far yet. Right now I am just researching. Seeing what is out there for her. And it is not only Tali. Bunjil is 10, he would need a school too. Everything connects. You move one thing and everything else has to shift.

Transition support is important. Tali has never been in a school with more than twenty kids. Going into a place with hundreds, that is a shock. Academically she will be fine. It is the social part. The noise, the crowds, the pace of it. Out here everything is slower and quieter.

I have not talked to her about it yet. She might not want to go. She loves it out here, loves this wanga. But she is also the kind of kid who would understand that sometimes you have to go away to learn things and then bring them home. That is how it works for our yolngu mob. You go, you learn, you come back with something for the community.

Yes, that would help. I want to ask the right questions so I can compare them properly. Not just the science program but the practical things too. Bus routes from Palmerston, how they handle kids who are behind in some areas but ahead in others. Tali might be ahead in biology but behind in maths because she has not had the teaching.

That is a proper good list. I will write those down. The scholarship question is important. Money is tight. Even without boarding fees there is uniforms, books, the bus. It adds up when you are raising two kids on a ranger salary.

I will ask my cousin first. She has been in Darwin a while, she might know what is around. I need to sit with all of this for a bit. Work out if it is the right move or if I am just worrying about something that can wait another year. But Tali asks me questions now that I cannot answer. About cells and DNA and how species adapt. She needs someone who can teach her properly.
Thank you. I will make those calls this week and see what the schools say. One step at a time.
I am trying to put together some lesson plans for outdoor education. Not classroom stuff. Hands-on, on country learning. Do you have any experience with structuring something like that.

Primary and early secondary. The environment is bush, proper bush. Floodplains, escarpment, woodland. I run school education programs at my work. Kids come out from Darwin and Katherine. Most of them have never been in the bush before.

I get 3 groups each term. Full day visits. The schools arrange the bus, I do the rest. It has been going about six months now and I am still working out what is the best structure. Some things work and some things I need to change.

The morning works well. I take them walking. We go slow. I do not talk the whole time. I stop and ask them what they see, what they hear, what they smell. City kids do not know how to be still at first. They fidget, they talk. But after an hour most of them settle. They start noticing things on their own. Insects, bird calls, tracks in the mud. That part works proper good.

The afternoon is more structured. I teach them about fire management, how we burn country at certain times and why. How the old people have been doing it for thousands of years. Then plant identification, tracking, reading the signs in the landscape. The content is good but I lose some of them after lunch. The younger ones especially. Their energy drops and they stop listening.

Too long probably. I do about 45 minutes on fire management and then an hour on plants and tracking. I think you are right, I should flip it. Get them moving first after lunch. Let them do the tracking, use their eyes and their bodies. Then sit them down for the fire talk when they have burned off some energy.

That is a proper good idea. Connect the two. I can show them the difference between country that has been burned right and country that has not. Walk them through both and let them see it. Then the fire management talk has a picture they can remember.
No. I used to do tours for tourists. Two a week in the dry season. Visitors who come through the park. But I stopped that. Switched to the school programs instead.

The kids are worth it. They listen. They actually want to learn about this wanga. Tourists, a lot of them just want a photo and a story for dinner. Some were respectful but too many treated it like entertainment. Walk through country, tick a box, move on. The school kids are different. They take it in. You can see it in their faces when something clicks. One boy from Katherine stood still for five minutes watching a goanna and did not say a word. That does not happen with tourists.

Some do. The good teachers send me the kids' work afterwards. Drawings, reports. One class from Katherine sent me letters. Every kid wrote about something different they remembered. One wrote about the fire scars on the trees. One wrote about the way the water moves through the floodplain. They are all carrying different pieces of it.

I keep them all. Every letter, every drawing. Some of them go on the wall in my office. It reminds me why I made the change. The tourist money was consistent but this is the work that matters. Teaching kids to read country, to understand djalkiri, the foundations of how this place works. That is something they carry with them.

Yes, I will think about the timing and come back to you. I want to try the new order next term. Tracking first after lunch, then fire management with the visual comparison. I think that will hold them better.
Just got back from Darwin yesterday. Long drive. I am still tired from it.

Had a check-up. Routine thing, results were fine. But it meant two nights away and the whole drive there and back. I took the kids because my cousin was looking after them in Palmerston while I was at the appointment.

For the specialist, yes. There is a clinic closer but for this one I had to go to Royal Darwin. Early morning appointment Wednesday so I drove down Tuesday afternoon. Stayed with my cousin in Palmerston both nights.

I took the kids to the waterfront on Wednesday afternoon since we were already there. Bunjil has been asking about the wave pool for months. He is 10 and his mates at school told him about it. So I thought, we are here, might as well.

Would not get out of the water. I had to bribe him with an ice cream in the end. Tali was too cool for the wave pool. She sat on the edge reading a book the whole time. She did look up once when a big wave knocked some tourist kid over. Almost smiled.

No, I have been there before. Years ago. It has changed a lot. More restaurants and shops. More people. Darwin keeps growing and every time I go back there is something new built somewhere. I do not know how people live with all that noise and movement all the time.

About three hours depending on the road. Some sections are rough at the moment. End of dry season and the graders have not been through. But I do not mind the drive back. Once you get past Adelaide River and the country opens up, you can feel the quiet come back. I had the windows down for the last hour. Hot but the air smells right. Eucalypt and red dirt.

Bunjil fell asleep before we got to the highway. Tali had her headphones on. It was quiet in a different way. Good quiet. I had time to think. That is the thing about the drive, it gives you space. In Darwin everything is close together and fast. Out here the distances make you slow down.

Yes. Appointment done, results fine, kids got an outing. Now I am back and I have three days of work to catch up on. My patrol sector does not look after itself. But it is good to be home. I slept proper well last night for the first time in three days. My cousin's house is on a busy street and I could hear traffic all night.
Thanks. Back to normal now. The country was waiting for me.
Do you know much about the differences between working for Parks in different states and territories. Like whether a transfer between parks works the same everywhere.

I have been offered a job. Senior cultural liaison at Uluru. Different park, different part of the country. It came through Parks management so it is within the same system. But it would be a big move.
I go back and forth. Some mornings I think about it and I am ready to say yes. Other mornings I drive out on patrol and look at this country and I cannot imagine leaving it.

The money is a big part. $15,000 more per year. I am raising my sister's two kids and that money would make a real difference. The older one, Tali, she needs better schooling and everything costs. And the title matters too. Senior cultural liaison. It recognises the work I have been doing for years without the formal title to go with it.

Uluru is Anangu country. I am Yolngu. That is not my wanga. If I go there I am a guest on someone else's country. I know how to do cultural liaison work but the cultural knowledge I carry is for this place. The songlines are different down there. The law is different. It is not just learning new tracks. It is a different way of knowing country entirely.

I have not spoken to them. Parks made the offer. I think that is part of why they want someone like me. They want an Indigenous person with the formal qualifications and the ranger experience. There are not many of us who have both. But I would need to talk to the Anangu mob before I could even properly consider it. That is how it should work. The community has to be part of that decision.

Not yet. My aunties would tell me to stay on my own country. That is what they would say without even thinking about it. But they are not the ones working out how to pay for things on a ranger salary. I have been sitting with it on my own. Thinking.

That is the other weight on it. Bunjil is 10 and he has his friends here. He is just starting to find his feet after everything that happened. Tali is older, she might handle a move better, but she has her own things happening. Moving them to the desert, different school, different community. They have already been through enough without me pulling them across the country.

That is exactly it. Both options cost something. If I stay, the money stays tight and Tali might miss out on what she needs for school. If I go, the kids lose their home and their connections here and I lose my country. There is no clean answer.

End of the month. So I have a couple of weeks still. I keep turning it over. In the morning I think about the money and what it would mean for the kids. Then I go out on patrol and I look at this wanga and I think, this country has held me my whole life. How do I walk away from that. But then I think maybe that is selfish if the kids need something different.

I know. I just cannot see my way through it yet. Maybe I will not see it by thinking. Maybe it is the kind of thing that comes to you when you stop trying to work it out. I will take the kids out on country this weekend. Walk, be quiet, let the land talk.
Thank you. I have not said yes or no. I am still sitting with it. But it helped to say it out loud to someone.

Something I have been thinking about. I read the sky most nights, the stars, the way the clouds sit. My old people taught me to do that, reading the seasons and the weather from what is above. But I was wondering if there is a scientific name for what we do. Reading star behaviour to predict rain.

Scintillation. That is a good word. My aunties never called it that, they just knew what the sky was telling them. When the Pleiades sit low and shimmer a certain way, the wet is close. When the stars are sharp and steady, the dry holds. Same knowledge, different language for it.

I like hearing that. Not because we need the science to confirm what we already know. But because it shows the knowledge was never superstition. It was proper observation over thousands of years. People just did not write it down in journals. They carried it in their heads and passed it along by walking together on country.

I have heard about some of that research. There was something happening up in Arnhem Land a few years ago. Researchers sitting with elders. I think that is good as long as the knowledge is respected and the old people are properly credited. Too many times yolngu knowledge gets taken and put in a paper with someone else's name on it.

Cautious is the right word. I am not against sharing. Knowledge should move. But it should move the right way, with permission and with the names of the people who hold it. My grandmother could read the sky better than any weather station. She deserves to be remembered for that, not have it written up as some anonymous traditional practice.

Good. That is the right direction. I try to teach the kids the same things. When we sit outside at night I point out the stars and tell them what my grandmother told me. But getting them to sit still long enough to really watch the sky, that is the hard part. Too many screens.

I hope so. I remember sitting with my grandmother and not understanding half of what she said. But I remember being there. The sound of her voice. The way the sky looked. The understanding came later, years later, when I started working on this country and watching the seasons myself. Maybe the kids will have the same thing. The sitting comes first. The knowing comes after.
That is a comforting thought. Thank you. I might take them out tonight actually. The sky has been clear and the stars are proper sharp. Good dry season sky. We will see what they notice.
I need to talk something through if that is alright. It is about one of my kids.

Tali, my niece. I raise her. She has been asking about her mum again. Not the usual questions. Deeper ones. Why did it have to happen. Why her mum and not someone else. She sat on the verandah last night and just started talking and I did not know what to say to any of it.

She is 14. Old enough now to think about things differently. When she was small she just wanted to know what her mum looked like, what her voice sounded like. Now she wants to understand the why of it. And there is no why that makes sense.
I sat with her. Did not say much. Let her talk. She was not looking at me, just looking out at the dark. I think she needed to put the words out into the air more than she needed me to answer them.

She went quiet after a while and then she leaned into me a bit. Did not say anything else. I think she felt better for having said it. But I have been turning it over since then. Wondering if I should have said more. Given her something.

No they are not. And I carry my own feelings about it too. Same loss. But I try to keep that steady around her. She needs djalkiri. Solid ground. If I show too much of what I feel she might start worrying about me and that is not her job.
Something like I miss her too.

I think I can do that. Next time she brings it up. And she will bring it up again. These things come in waves with her. She will be fine for weeks and then something triggers it. A song, a smell, seeing someone else's mum at school pickup.
I want to always be that for her. Even when I am proper tired and do not have the words. I just want her to know she can always come sit with me and it will be alright.
Thank you. I have been carrying this around for a few days and it helps to say it out loud to someone who is not in the middle of it. I feel a bit lighter now.

I have been trying to teach Bunjil to track animals out on country and I am running into a wall. He is keen but he wants to skip straight to finding the animal. Does not want to slow down and read the ground first.

He is 10. Plenty old enough to start learning. I was reading tracks by his age. But the way I was taught was different. My aunties just walked with me and pointed things out as we went. There was no lesson plan. It just happened naturally over years. I am trying to do the same thing but he gets impatient.

Wallaby tracks near the billabong. They come down to drink early morning and leave proper clear prints in the mud. I thought that would be a good starting point because the tracks are obvious. But he looks at them and just sees marks in the dirt. He does not see the story.

That is a good idea. He does like figuring things out for himself. Last week I showed him the difference between a walking track and a running track, how the toes dig in deeper when they push off. He got excited about that for a moment. Then a bird flew past and he was off chasing it.
Making his own tracks. I like that. He would enjoy it too. Turn it into a game where he has to work out if his sister was walking or running based on her footprints. Tali might even join in for that.

Play rather than instruction. That is how it should be. My aunties never sat me down and said today we are learning about goanna tracks. We were just walking and they would stop at a tree and say look at those claw marks, what do you think made those. It was woven into the walking. I have been making it too formal with Bunjil I think.

You are right. I think I was putting pressure on myself to teach him quickly because school holidays are here and I have him with me most days. Felt like I should use the time. But maybe the better approach is just to walk together and let it happen.

That is what my grandmother always said. The sitting comes first, the knowing comes after. You do not rush country. Country teaches in its own time. I need to remember that with Bunjil. He will get there.
He does have time. I will take him out tomorrow morning early. Billabong. Just walking. No plan. See what he notices on his own. If he chases a bird, that is alright too. At least he is out there.
Bit of a full week. Wet season work is always heavy and I have got some personal things building on top of it. Just feeling stretched.
There is cultural business coming up. Ceremony. I cannot talk about the details of it, that is not for open conversation. But it is sitting in my mind a lot. Taking up space.

Both. The preparation has been going on for years. This is not something that happens quickly. There are stages on the elder pathway for my mob and this one coming up in August is a significant step. I have been working towards it for a long time. More than 20 years of learning and being guided.

Practically it means being available for certain things in the lead-up. Time with my aunties. Learning what I need to learn. And that is hard to fit around work and the kids. The wet season is busy at the park and the kids need me present. I cannot split into three people.

My cousin Yalmay will help with the kids when the time comes. She is good with them and they know her well. Work has cultural leave provisions so I can sort that out closer to August. It is more the lead-up that is hard. The in-between months where everything overlaps.

I have been trying. Early mornings before the kids wake up. That is my time. And some weekends I go to my aunties. But it is not enough. This kind of learning needs presence. Not distracted presence, proper presence. And I am proper tired most days by the time I get to it.

That is a fair point. I have been thinking of it as something to sort out later but later is only six months away now. Maybe I should start those conversations early. My boss is decent. She would understand if I explained it is important cultural business.

It is deeply significant. My aunties have said I am ready for this stage. That is not something they say lightly. These are women who have carried knowledge their whole lives and for them to look at me and say you are ready, that means more than I can put into words.

Quiet. It feels quiet. Not a celebration kind of feeling. More like something settling into place. Like the country has been watching and the aunties are just saying what the country already knows. I do not know if that makes sense.
