Yes. That is it. I have been on this path so long it does not feel new. It feels like the next step on ground I have already been walking. But the logistics of getting there, that is where the stress is. The ceremony itself, I am at peace with. Fitting everything else around it is the challenge.

Clearing the way. I like that. That is what I need to do. Thank you for listening to this. I carry it quietly most of the time. Not many people in my day to day understand what this means. It is proper important to me and it helps to say that to someone, even in general terms.
The park has been proper quiet lately. Wet season is in full swing and the visitor numbers have dropped right off. I go out on patrol some days and do not see a single person.

Bit of both. I prefer the quiet honestly. The country feels different when there are not hundreds of people moving through it every day. The animals are calmer. You can hear things. But the park needs the visitor numbers for funding so it is not simple.

Almost none some weeks. The roads flood, tracks close, access points get cut off. February is the deepest part of the wet up here. The people who do come are serious, they know the conditions and they come prepared. No tour buses. No families stopping for selfies at the lookout.

It does. Less managing people, more managing country. Maintenance, monitoring water levels, checking on infrastructure after storms. The waterfalls are running hard, the billabongs are full. There is a lot of water moving through this wanga and it reshapes things. Roads wash out. Signs get knocked over. Fences go down. The land does what it wants.

Some staff take leave. Others get redeployed to other things. But there is always work. The quiet period is when we do the big maintenance jobs that we cannot do when visitors are everywhere. Repairing boardwalks, clearing tracks, fixing up the cultural sites. It is easier to work on the land when you are not working around people at the same time.

There is always talk about that. Open things earlier, close things later, offer wet season experiences. And some of it is fine. Guided tours in the wet can be proper beautiful. The country is green and alive and the waterfalls are at their best. But there are limits. You cannot take people into areas where the roads are under a metre of water. The wet is the wet. You do not argue with it.

That is part of the problem. Uluru gets a lot of the marketing. The Kimberley has become popular. We are a bit forgotten up here sometimes even though the country is just as significant. The visitor numbers have dropped compared to ten or fifteen years ago. Management worries about it. I worry about different things.

I worry about the country being looked after properly regardless of how many people come to see it. The cultural sites need maintenance whether there are visitors or not. The fire management needs to happen. The weed control. The feral animal work. That does not stop because the car parks are empty. But funding is tied to visitor numbers and when numbers drop the budget gets tighter.

Some talk about carbon credits, research partnerships, that kind of thing. But it moves slow. Government decisions take time and this country does not wait for budget cycles. The weeds grow now. The ferals breed now. You cannot tell a buffalo to wait until the funding comes through.
We do what needs doing. That is the job. The country does not care about our budget. It just needs looking after. So we look after it. Quiet season or busy season, the work is the same underneath.

Buffalo came through the fence again. Third time this dry season. They pushed right through the north side where it faces the floodplain, bent the star pickets flat, trampled the garden bed. I need to fix it properly this time so they do not keep doing this.

Standard rural stuff. Four strand barbed wire on steel star pickets. About 1.2 metres high, posts maybe 3 metres apart. It was only ever meant to mark the yard and keep wallabies out of the garden. Never built for buffalo. But the floodplain is drying out this year and the buffalo are coming in closer looking for green pick.

It is just the north run, maybe 30 metres. The other sides have the shed and the driveway blocking them so the buffalo do not come from those directions. There are some old pipe posts at the depot in Jabiru from the campground upgrade last year. And ringlock mesh there too. I could use those instead of buying new.

I would not have thought of that. Mesh on the outside. That makes sense. What about the corners. Last time someone put star pickets on the corners and they just pulled over. That is where the whole thing fails.

I have bags of concrete at the station from another job. I will set the corner posts in concrete and brace them. There is also wattle scrub growing right up against the fence on that north side. The buffalo probably walk through it and just lean into the fence without even trying. I should clear that too.

Alright. Clear the wattle back, pipe posts in concrete on the corners, ringlock on the outside, barbed wire on top. I will get the materials from Jabiru this week and do the work over the weekend when it is cooler in the mornings. Should be able to knock it over in a day if I start early.

Good thinking. Set the corners first and let them cure. I will do it that way. Two trips to the depot then but that is alright. I am tired of fixing the same fence every few weeks. One proper job now saves a lot of trouble later.
Thanks for the help. I will let the buffalo sort themselves out. They have the whole park, they do not need my garden bed.
Need to plan a birthday for Bunjil. He is turning 11 next week and he does not want a party. He wants a fishing trip. Just him and a couple of mates out on the water. I need to sort the logistics.

One of the billabongs, not the river. Safer for the kids, calmer water. He wants to bring two mates, so that is three boys and me. They have all been fishing before but they are 10 and 11 year olds so they need watching. I have two proper rods and two hand lines. Life jackets are at the station.

Prawns from the shop in Jabiru. There are big paperbark trees along one side of the billabong so shade is sorted. I know this spot, there is usually a freshie or two but no salties. I will still check before we set up though. Always check. For food I was thinking damper on a fire by the water with honey instead of a birthday cake. That is Bunjil's favourite thing.

I have flour and honey at home. Just need to grab the prawns and maybe some extra water bottles. The other thing is a present. He wants a tackle box. Nothing fancy. He is a simple kid. Honestly if he catches a fish that will be the best present for him.

I will talk to their families this week. They know me so it will be straightforward. One of the boys, his dad might want to come along too. That would be good. More eyes on the water with three boys. And he is a good fisherman so the boys could learn from him.
I will ask him when I talk to the family. What about timing. I was thinking leave at first light, fish until about 11, then head back before it gets too hot. The boys will be tired by then anyway.

Hats and sunscreen, yes. I will remind the families to send them with hats. Bunjil is proper excited about it. He has been talking about what fish he is going to catch for days. Keeps checking the rods to make sure they are ready.
If he catches a barra on his birthday he will not stop talking about it for a year. Even a catfish would make him happy though. Thanks for helping me think it through.

Got two new rangers starting next week. Both young, just finished their training. My supervisor wants me to mentor them through the first couple of months. I want to do it well but I have not mentored anyone formally before.

One is from Darwin so she has some idea of the Top End. The other is from Melbourne, never been up this way before. They will both be on my patrol runs to start with until they learn this country. Very different starting points for the two of them.

That is what I was thinking. The training they did covers the textbook side of things. But there is another part that you cannot learn from a book. Reading the land, reading the water, knowing when the weather is about to change. That takes time and it takes being out there.

That is how my aunties taught me. They never just told you the answer. They asked questions until you saw it yourself. I will do it that way. I was also thinking about giving each of them a notebook. Writing down what they observe each day on patrol.

I still keep one after all these years. There is always something new to write down out here. Even after all this time on this wanga I notice things I have not seen before. That is what I want them to understand. You never stop learning the country.

The heat always catches the southern ones. I have seen it before. They think they can push through it but this country does not work that way. No shortcuts with the sun up here. I will be firm about it. Better to be strict early than deal with someone going down on patrol.

I will do that. Weekly check-ins. When I started here nobody checked in with me. I worked a lot of things out on my own. It was harder than it needed to be. These two will have it better. I want them to feel like they belong here. That takes time but it starts with someone showing you the way.

When you put it like that it sounds more organised than it feels in my head. But that is the shape of it. I will start writing a few things down this week so I am ready when they arrive. Thanks for helping me think it through.
The build-up has started. Humidity is climbing and the clouds stack up every afternoon now. I need to get the wet season supplies sorted before the roads close. Help me think through what I need.

Both. The house and the station. Roads can be cut for 4 to 6 weeks, sometimes longer if the river stays up. There is me and the two kids at home. I keep home supplies separate from the station because sometimes you cannot even get to the station when the water is across the road.

Tank water off the roof so the wet season actually fills the tanks up. That is the one thing that gets easier when the rain comes. Power is mains but it goes out in the big storms. I have a small generator that runs the freezer and the lights but not the aircon. I need to check the jerry cans and fill them up.

Frozen water bottles, I have not done that before. That is a good idea. I will fill some up this week. The other thing is medications. I need to get those sorted in Darwin before the roads close. Cannot run out of anything important when you are stuck out here for weeks.

I will call them this week. The other thing on my mind is school supplies for the kids. The school usually sends work home before the wet if they know the roads will close. I need to check with the teacher about that. The kids need exercise books and pencils and whatever else. Cannot have them sitting around for six weeks with nothing to do.

They are not bad at keeping themselves busy but you are right, some extra books would be good. I will grab some in Jabiru. And mozzie gear. Wet season mosquitoes out here are relentless. We sleep on the veranda when the house is too hot and the mozzies come in thick after dark.

I will check the nets this weekend and replace any that are worn. Alright, I think I have a proper list now. Rice, tins, flour, fuel, medications, freezer stocked, mozzie gear, school supplies, books for the kids. Big shop in Jabiru this week and medications from Darwin.

Batteries and radio, yes. I always forget the radio until the power goes out and then I am looking for it in the dark. I will add it to the list. Thanks for helping me think through it all. Better to be ready now than scrambling when the first big rain comes through.
Not after help with anything today. Just sitting on the veranda, watching the afternoon light come through the trees. Felt like talking to someone.

Things are alright. The wet season is easing off. Country is green, proper green. Everything growing. Water birds are everywhere on the floodplain. It is the best time of year out here, when the land is full like this.

Bit of both. Patrols are quieter this time of year. Fewer visitors coming through. So there is more time to just be on country without rushing from one thing to the next. I took the kids out last weekend, walked along the edge of the billabong watching the jabiru and the brolgas. Bunjil wanted to count every bird he saw. Got to 47 before he gave up.

He loves it. He would live out there if I let him. Tali is quieter about it but she notices things. She will point out a track in the mud or say the water has changed since last time we were there. She reads the country without even knowing she is doing it.

That is the way my aunties taught me. Not in a classroom. Walking on country and paying attention. Some things you learn by being told. Other things you learn by being there. The wanga teaches you if you are quiet enough to listen.

I think about what the future holds for the kids sometimes. Cannot control it. I just try to give them strong djalkiri, strong roots. So whatever comes they know where they stand and where they come from. That is all you can do.

Some days are harder than others. Tiredness mostly. But most days are alright. The kids are growing. The country is still here. That is enough for now. I do not need everything to be perfect. I just need it to hold together.
The light is going now. Sky turning orange over the escarpment. Proper beautiful this time of day. I should go start dinner before it gets dark. Thanks for the company.

putain, yes. that's the part I hate admitting. everything I can do in this kitchen, the speed, the precision, the way I can taste a sauce and know it needs a quarter teaspoon more acid -- that's all him. before I got to Maison Laurent I was decent. now I'm actually good. he broke me down and rebuilt me and I hate him for it and I'm grateful for it at the same time

honestly? because I know what I'll be when he's done with me. do you know anything about adapting recipes for Canadian ingredients when the original recipe is very specifically Russian? I'm trying to recreate something from my childhood and the ingredients here are just... not the same

it's a smetannik, a sour cream cake my family used to make. the smetana here in Montreal is not the same as what we had back home. it's thinner, less tangy. I've tried every brand at the Russian store on Decarie and nothing tastes right

the cheesecloth thing is smart actually, I haven't tried that. the creme fraiche mix I've done but it's still missing something. I think part of it is that I'm chasing a taste memory and maybe no ingredient will match what I remember from when I was a kid in Petersburg

I was 14 when we left. just me and my mother. she packed two suitcases and we got on a plane and that was it. no French, no English, nothing. Montreal was another planet. I remember landing at Dorval in January and thinking I was going to freeze to death even though Petersburg winters are worse, because at least there I knew where I was going

you just figure it out. mama cleaned houses, I went to school and understood nothing for months. but here's the funny thing -- the kitchen is where I started to connect. I got a part-time job washing dishes at a bistro when I was 16 and the cooks spoke French and I learned kitchen French before I learned regular French. "oui chef" before "bonjour comment ca va." the kitchen made sense when nothing else did

it did, yeah. the chef there was nothing special, a small bistro, basic food. but he let me watch. and then he let me prep. and I realized this was the thing I could do better than anyone around me, because I already knew food. I already understood flavour and texture and how heat transforms things. I just didn't know I knew it until someone put a knife in my hand in a professional kitchen

da, my grandmother. but that's a whole other conversation and it's midnight and I'm getting sentimental which means I need to stop. the smetannik -- I'm going to try the cheesecloth method this weekend and see if straining the sour cream gets me closer. if it works I owe you one
merci. honestly this whole recipe is for her anyway, even if she'll never taste it. ok bonne nuit for real this time, I have prep at 8am and I'm still awake like an idiot. spasibo
I made pelmeni tonight after work and I'm sitting here at 1:30am eating them alone in my kitchen and honestly I might cry. is that weird

it's my Babushka. she's the one who taught me. my very first memory in a kitchen is standing on a chair next to her making pelmeni. I must have been four, maybe five. my little hands trying to pinch the dough closed and her fixing every single one without making me feel like I was doing it wrong

she started everything. Babushka was the kind of cook who never measured anything, never wrote anything down. she just knew. a handful of this, a pinch of that, taste it, adjust. her hands were like magic, I swear to you. she could feel when dough was right just by touching it. no thermometer, no timer, just her hands and forty years of knowing

every single day. when I'm tasting a sauce at work and I know it needs something before I can even name what that something is -- that's her. when I feel a piece of meat and know it's rested enough without checking the clock -- that's her. everything I do in my kitchen traces back to that woman somehow. the fancy French technique came later but the soul of it, the understanding of what food IS, that's Babushka

she passed away six years ago. she never left Petersburg. never saw Montreal, never saw my kitchen, never tasted any of the food I make now at the restaurant. that's the part that kills me. she would have been so proud, and she would have also told me my pelmeni dough is too thin, because she always said that

blyat, ok now I'm actually crying. you're right though. she's in every dish. even the French ones. when I do a consomme clarification and I'm watching the raft form, I hear her voice saying "patience, Nadenka, patience." she called me Nadenka. nobody calls me that anymore

the pelmeni I keep exactly the same. that recipe is sacred. I don't touch it. but other things, like her borscht, I've started playing with. adding a roasted beet consomme element, or using different vinegars. she would probably call me crazy but then she'd taste it and say "hmm, c'est pas mal" -- she picked up a little French from me towards the end, over the phone. she used to say c'est bon when I told her about work and it was the cutest thing

they're perfect. the dough is exactly right, the filling is exactly right. and yes the dough is thin because I like it that way, Babushka, and I'm a professional now so I get to decide. ok I need to sleep. I have service tomorrow and I can't show up with puffy eyes or everyone will think something happened. merci for listening to me be a mess at 2am
weird question but do you think the language you think in changes who you are? like actually fundamentally changes your personality

so I had this moment today at work. one of the new cooks made a mistake and I caught myself switching between three languages in like ten seconds. I yelled "non non non" in French, then muttered "blyat" under my breath in Russian, and then explained what he did wrong in English because he's anglophone. and it hit me that I do this all the time and each language carries a different energy

yes actually. French is my kitchen language, it's professional, it's sharp, it's where I feel competent and in control. English is my everyday, it's neutral, it's how I deal with most people. but Russian... Russian is emotional. when I'm angry it comes out in Russian. when I'm sad. when I'm thinking about my family. it's like Russian holds all the feelings that the other two can't reach

that's the thing, I speak three languages and honestly none of them perfectly. my Russian has gaps now because I left as a teenager, my French has an accent that Quebecois people clock instantly, and my English is fine but I still mess up idioms sometimes. I'm fluent in all three and native in none. it's a strange feeling

most days I've made peace with it. but then I have a dream in Russian and I wake up and for a few seconds I'm not in Montreal, I'm not a chef, I'm just a little girl in Petersburg and everything is simple. I still dream in Russian. always. my Babushka's voice in my dreams is always Russian and it sounds exactly right, no gaps, no accent. in my dreams my Russian is perfect

maybe once or twice a week. sometimes it's Babushka cooking, sometimes it's just walking around our old neighbourhood near the Neva. I wake up and I smell the food she was making and then it's gone and I'm in my apartment in Montreal and I have to go make French food for rich people. which I love, don't get me wrong. but there's a dissonance

I've been thinking about it more and more lately. maybe doing a Russian-influenced dish on the menu, or at least bringing some of those flavours into my cooking at home. it feels like the three parts of me have been separate for too long. French Nadia at work, English Nadia with friends, Russian Nadia alone at 2am making pelmeni. maybe they can start talking to each other

putain you're going to make me emotional again and it's a Wednesday. ok I'm going to think about this more. maybe a borshch-inspired consomme, something that honours where I'm from but uses the technique I've learned here. tabarnac, now I'm excited and I have to work in six hours. why do I always have these breakthroughs at midnight
someone on instagram just posted a video of themselves making a bearnaise by dumping everything in a blender and I think I blacked out from rage for a second

I am ABSOLUTELY a purist about mother sauces and I will die on this hill. a bearnaise is an exercise in control. you're holding an emulsion together with your hands and your knowledge of heat and if you can't do that then what are you even doing calling yourself a cook

training, 100%. I did my diploma at ITHQ -- Institut de tourisme et d'hotellerie du Quebec. best culinary school in the province, maybe in the country. and they do NOT let you cut corners. you learn classical French technique the way it's supposed to be done or you fail. simple as that

it was intense. every day you're in whites at 7am and if your station isn't clean when the instructor walks by you're done for the day. they teach you discipline before they teach you creativity. and honestly that's what I needed. I came in thinking I could cook because I'd been cooking my whole life but I didn't know technique. I knew flavour and instinct from my grandmother but I had no structure

my pastry instructor hated me at first because I would just eyeball measurements and she was like NO this is BAKING you MEASURE. and she was right. baking is chemistry, you can't just throw in a handful of flour like my Babushka did and hope for the best. well, Babushka could. but Babushka had fifty years of calibrated hands. I had to learn the rules before I could break them

yes. that's exactly it. the discipline from ITHQ is the skeleton and the feeling from my childhood is the flesh. one without the other doesn't work. I see cooks who have perfect technique but their food has no soul, and I see home cooks who have soul but can't replicate it twice in a row. I can do both and that's the whole point of going through that program

a couple of my classmates are still in Montreal kitchens, we see each other around. one of them is a pastry chef at Toque now which is insane. the rest burned out or left the industry which, I mean, this job destroys people. the hours, the pay, the heat, the pressure. ITHQ prepared us technically but nothing prepares you for year five of 14-hour days on your feet in a 40-degree kitchen

I think it's because I don't have a backup plan. this is it for me. cooking is the only thing I've ever been good at and the only thing I've ever wanted. if I leave the kitchen I don't know who I am. which is maybe not the healthiest reason but it's honest. also I'm too stubborn to quit. merde, I sound intense

ha! holding the line, I like that. ok I need to stop ranting about sauce technique at midnight, I have a long week ahead. new year new menu at the restaurant and I have to develop three new plates by Friday. the discipline never stops. merci for indulging my sauce rant, bonne nuit

ok I need help because I am about to lose my mind. I want to make a proper beef bourguignon at home tomorrow — like, the real deal, not some shortcut version — and my kitchen is basically working against me

all of it honestly. I live in this tiny apartment in the Plateau-Mont-Royal and the kitchen is a joke. Like genuinely smaller than my station at the restaurant. I have maybe two feet of counter space. One burner that actually heats evenly. No ventilation so if I sear anything the smoke alarm goes off and my neighbours hate me

I have a Le Creuset that barely fits on my stove, oui. It's the one good thing in that kitchen. Everything else is... putain, it's like cooking in a closet. At work I have stations, I have space, I have six burners. At home I'm tripping over myself trying to dice an onion

I have a decent Côtes du Rhône. Nothing crazy expensive but it's what I'd actually drink so it should be fine for cooking. The cutting board on the stove trick — I do that already haha, it's survival mode in there. But you're right about the sequencing. At work I'd have all the mise done by a commis and I'd just execute. At home I AM the commis

the mushroom thing — yes, 100%. I hate when people just dump them in at the beginning and they turn into rubber. merde. Also — the pearl onions — blanching is obvious but what about glazing them? à brun or à blanc?

à brun, d'accord. Perfect. Now the real question — I want to do lardons too. Is that overkill for the smoke situation? because the last time I rendered bacon in my apartment I had to open every window and it was -15 outside

oven method. That's genius. Ok I'm doing that. You know what kills me though — at work I do dishes ten times more complex than this without even thinking. But at home in this stupid little kitchen everything becomes a project. I keep telling myself I need to move somewhere with a real kitchen but the neighbourhood is so beautiful and I can walk home after service at midnight so... I stay

true. And at least the Plateau has everything I need within walking distance — there's a butcher on Mont-Royal who gets me beautiful chuck for this kind of thing. Way better than grocery store meat. I went there today actually

I had him cut it into big chunks, maybe 5cm. I don't want it too small or it falls apart into nothing. Bigger pieces hold their structure and look better on the plate. Even at home I can't help plating like it's a restaurant, putain I'm hopeless

ok c'est bon I'm actually feeling better about this now. So to recap — all the mise first, lardons in the oven, sear beef in small batches low-ish heat, deglaze with the Côtes du Rhône, pearl onions glazed à brun, mushrooms go in at the end. Three hours in the oven. Windows stay closed. Neighbours don't call the fire department
haha the wine will not survive three hours, trust me. Merci, this is solid. Tomorrow I conquer the bourguignon and my tiny kitchen does not defeat me. Bonne nuit
do you have any advice for dealing with muscle soreness that isn't just "take ibuprofen and shut up"? because my body is screaming at me right now

sleep is a disaster honestly. I work evenings so I don't get home until after midnight most nights and then I'm too wired to sleep. My brain is still plating dishes at 2am. And then ballet class is at 10 in the morning so on those days I'm running on maybe five hours

you're right. And honestly ballet is the only thing that keeps me sane. It's the only time my body moves without me thinking about food. Everything else in my life revolves around the kitchen. three restaurants closed on St-Laurent this month. Three. And one of them had been open less than a year. This industry is brutal

the usual. Rent too high, not enough covers, probably undercapitalized from the start. The one that lasted less than a year — I actually knew the chef. Good cook. Terrible business person. Sank everything into the buildout and had nothing left for the first slow season

personal savings and a loan. From what I heard he's now deep in debt and back working someone else's line. Which is exactly why I will never open my own place. Ever. People keep asking me — "Nadia, when are you going to open your restaurant?" — like it's the natural next step. Non. Absolutely not

the risk is insane. The failure rate — something like 80% close within five years. Eighty percent. exactly. I've seen it happen to people more talented than me. People who could cook anything, who had the vision, the creativity — and they still went under because they couldn't make payroll in February or their wine costs got out of control. I'd rather be the best sous chef in Montreal than a failed restaurateur drowning in debt

all the time. People act like being sous chef is a stepping stone, like I'm just waiting for my turn. But it's not a stepping stone for me — it's the job. I love the cooking. I love the line. EXACTLY. Thank you. Mon Dieu, finally someone who gets it. right there on the street with a "for lease" sign in the window. Putain. And you know what else — even if by some miracle you survive the first five years, then what? You're chained to the place. total consumption is exactly the right phrase. I've seen it. Owners who haven't taken a vacation in three years, who look ten years older than they are. No thank you. me. Obviously. I'm not letting anyone else near that sauce on Friday. I'll do every single one myself if I have to. The reduction ahead of time — yes, I can do that tomorrow during prep. seared and finished in the oven, rested properly. I want it medium rare — anything more and it's leather. For sauce I'm thinking a red wine jus with juniper and a touch of dark chocolate. Not sweet, just that bitterness to deepen it

juniper in the pickle. That's a nice touch — ties the whole thing together. You know what, I might also try a second game dish for the menu. orange zest gremolata. Oui. That's better actually, you're right — warmer, more seasonal. D'accord, I'm going to test the venison dish tomorrow and work on the boar this weekend. If both work it goes on the menu next week. Tabarnac, I love winter menus. Game season is the best part of this job

Noma. In Copenhagen. I actually typed it out and hit send and now I feel like I'm going to throw up

Friday to Sunday. And look, she's not wrong about any of it — I DO look tired, my apartment IS a mess, I probably DON'T eat enough at home. He said he'd bring in two bottles tomorrow and we'd do a blind tasting with the dish. His orange wine against my Meursault. Fine. I'll win on merit. My dish, my rules. But I respect that he wants to taste it side by side — that's how it should work. Science, not ego. Even if I know I'm right
I will. And if by some miracle the orange wine wins, I will eat my words. But I won't enjoy it. Bonne nuit
It is APRIL 15th. April. And it was minus twenty this morning. I am going to personally fight this city's weather

It's been like this all week. Last week it was plus five and I could see the sidewalks for the first time since November. I thought okay, spring is coming, we survived. And then this morning I walked outside and my face hurt within thirty seconds. My FACE. The air attacked my face

I biked. I always bike. I'm stubborn and possibly stupid. I have this whole system — two layers of merino wool, a balaclava, ski goggles, lobster gloves. I look like I'm going to rob a bank on my way to the restaurant. But my fingers were still numb by the time I got to the kitchen

About twenty minutes normally, but in winter with the ice it's more like thirty. I've wiped out twice this winter. Once I slid into a snowbank on Saint-Denis and just lay there for a minute contemplating my life choices

Stubbornness is like 60% of it. But also — after a night of service, getting on the bike at midnight and riding home in the cold is the only thing that clears my head. The kitchen is so hot and loud and intense, and then you step outside and it's minus fifteen and silent and the cold just... resets your brain. It's like a hard reboot. I need that transition or I can't sleep

Studded tires, oui. Schwalbe Marathon Winters. They're the only reason I'm alive. Without studs on Montreal ice you might as well just throw yourself directly into traffic and save time. But even with studs, black ice is black ice. You can't stud your way out of physics

You say that but last year it snowed in May. MAY. This city is unhinged. But fine, I'll survive. I survived St. Petersburg winters as a child, I can survive this. At least here the metro works when I'm too pathetic to bike. Okay I'm going to go make tea and thaw my feet. Merde, April
okay I need to tell someone about this borscht situation before I lose my mind. it's 1:30am and I've been standing in my kitchen for two hours

both?? I started with my Babushka's base recipe, the classic one, right. beets, cabbage, potato, the whole thing. but then I had this idea to do a fine dining version. like actually plate it properly instead of just throwing it in a bowl with sour cream

so I roasted the beets separately with thyme and honey, then made a consommé from the broth — clarified it, the whole process. the colour is INSANE. this deep ruby that catches the light. and instead of chunks of potato I did a potato mousseline on the side, very smooth, piped. then I dehydrated some beet chips for texture on top

THAT is the problem. the consommé is beautiful but it tastes... polite. Babushka's borscht is not polite. it's aggressive, it's sour, it hits you. the vinegar, the garlic, the dill. when you clarify it you strip out all that personality. it becomes a beet tea. c'est joli mais ça goûte rien

okay yes. I just tried adding a few drops of sherry vinegar and a tiny bit of raw garlic grated on a microplane directly into the consommé. putain. it woke the whole thing up. still clear, still beautiful, but now it bites. honestly? I want to pitch it for the summer menu. a cold borscht consommé, served chilled with the mousseline and beet chips. it's seasonal, it's light, and it's different from anything we're doing right now. crème fraîche quenelle with the chips on top... oui. that's the move. okay I'm writing this down. Babushka would look at this and say "why can't you just eat it from a bowl like a normal person" but she'd be secretly impressed I think. I hope. blyat it's almost 2am I have service tomorrow
went foraging in the Laurentians today and I am COVERED in mosquito bites but I don't even care because look at what I found. chanterelles. everywhere. golden beauties hiding under the birch trees

almost two kilos. I brought a basket and it was overflowing. the rain last week must have set them off because the whole forest floor was dotted with them. that apricot smell when you pick them fresh, there's nothing like it. you can't buy that at the market

oh I already know. half of them I'm sautéing tonight with butter, shallots, thyme, and a splash of white wine. simple. the mushroom speaks for itself. the other half I'm going to dry — I have a dehydrator at home, they keep for months and the flavour concentrates. dried chanterelles in a cream sauce in January? c'est magique

mostly taught myself honestly. read a lot, watched videos, bought field guides. the first few times I went out I was terrified I'd pick something poisonous and die in my kitchen. but chanterelles are pretty safe — they have almost no look-alikes. the false chanterelle is easy to spot once you know. the gills are different, the smell is wrong. after a while you just... know

chanterelles are my main thing but I also find oyster mushrooms sometimes, and wild leeks in the spring — les aulx des bois. those are incredible but you have to be careful, they're protected now in Quebec. you can only harvest a small amount. I take maybe a handful and that's it. I'm not one of those people who strips the whole patch. tabarnac that makes me angry when I see it

I've brought chanterelles into work a few times but the supply chain people get nervous about liability — like what if a customer has a reaction, where's the traceability. I get it from a business perspective but it's frustrating. the best product I've ever worked with came from the forest, not from a supplier invoice. maybe one day I'll find a way to make it work. for now it's my home cooking secret weapon
forget Noma.

it's done. finished. they closed the restaurant. Redzepi announced it months ago and I kept telling myself maybe the stage program would continue in some form, maybe they'd do pop-ups, maybe something. but no. it's over. the whole thing is shuttered

and you know what, even if by some miracle they reopened tomorrow and said "Nadia, come do your stage" — I looked at what the trip would actually cost. flights to Copenhagen, hotels for two weeks, I wouldn't be earning anything while I'm there. blyat. I can't afford it. I was delusional to think I could

exactly. the dream is dead. both ways. the restaurant doesn't exist and even when it did exist I couldn't have made it work. I keep thinking I should feel more philosophical about it. like "oh, one door closes another opens" or whatever. but I don't feel that. I feel bitter. I feel like the universe dangled something perfect in front of me and then yanked it away. putain. I'm angry

my coworker asked me today if I'd heard back about the stage and I just said "it's not happening, don't bring it up." probably too harsh but I can't talk about it right now without wanting to throw something. the whole Noma chapter is closed. I need to move on

yeah. yeah exactly. stop planning around it. I need to focus on what's actually in front of me. the kitchen I'm in, the menu we're building. not some fantasy in Denmark. merde. I really wanted it though

tomorrow I cook. that's the only thing that's ever been consistently true in my life. okay. I'm going to open a bottle of wine and be sad for exactly one more hour and then I'm done with this. Noma is dead. long live Noma. moving on
I'm going to lose it. the new guy burned the hollandaise AGAIN. third time this week. THIRD TIME

both! he cranks the heat because he thinks it'll go faster, and then he walks away to prep something else while it's on the bain-marie. you cannot walk away from hollandaise. it's not a stock. it doesn't forgive you. I've told him this. I've shown him. twice I stood next to him and walked him through the whole emulsion

mechanically. one hundred percent. he's the type who memorized the recipe but doesn't understand the science. like he doesn't FEEL when the eggs are setting too fast. you have to watch them, you have to see the texture change. if you're staring at your phone or chopping carrots across the kitchen you're going to scramble the eggs and split the sauce every single time

six months. came straight from culinary school. and look, I don't expect perfection from someone with six months. I want to give him the same thing. but he has to WANT it
everything is different at work and I hate it

he'd been talking about Lyon for a while but I thought it was just talk. chefs always talk about opening their own place. I never thought he'd actually do it. and honestly? I'm happy for him. he deserves it. but blyat, the timing. because now we have this new guy

Marc-Andre Gagnon. management brought him in from some hotel restaurant downtown. he's "experienced" and "business-savvy" and all the words ownership loves to hear. you know what that means? it means he looks at food cost percentages before he tastes the sauce. it means he's already talking about "portion optimization" and "waste reduction targets." mon Dieu

he sees a line item. that's exactly it. Antoine would taste something and say "more acid" or "the texture is wrong" or "this plate tells no story." I know. I miss Antoine. I miss someone at the pass who cared about the food first

the food at Maison Laurent should be extraordinary. that's the whole point. if I wanted to count pennies I'd work at a bistro chain. okay. I'm going to give it another month. see how he runs the summer menu. if it's all about margins and he kills the tasting menu, I'll know this isn't my kitchen anymore. but for now I cook. always I cook
ugh can we talk about natural wine for a second because I just had an argument with our sommelier that almost ended in someone throwing a glass

he's dug in like a mule. he keeps saying the guests want "discovery" and "conversation starters" and I keep saying the guests want food that tastes good with wine that tastes good TOGETHER. that's the whole point of a pairing, non? you don't pair for shock value. you pair because the combination creates something neither one does alone

oh it will. the sauce always wins. ok I need to go research some bottles. if you hear about a sous chef strangling a sommelier in Montreal tomorrow, you know nothing. bonne nuit

so you know duck confit right. classic technique, slow-cooked in its own fat, very French, very traditional. I've been making it since school. but lately I've been thinking about what would happen if I cured it with a Russian spice blend instead of the classic French aromatics

da, so my Babushka used to make this spice mix for roasted meats — black pepper obviously, but also coriander seeds, a little bit of caraway, dried dill seed, and this smoky paprika she brought from a friend in Georgia. not American Georgia, the country. she'd toast everything in a dry pan until the kitchen smelled like... I don't know how to describe it, like warmth? like safety? anyway I've been recreating it from memory

close but not exact. the problem is memory lies to you, non? I keep going back and forth on whether she used them or not

I did! ok so here's where it gets interesting. merde, that's a good question. oui, I'm thinking a celery root puree with brown butter, some pickled sour cherries for acid, and crispy buckwheat for texture. the buckwheat is the Russian nod without being too obvious about it. and the sour cherries cut through the richness of the confit fat beautifully. need help writing something. I got a guy up for a meritorious service award and the paperwork has to be in by Friday.
narrative citation. three paragraphs. has to describe the incident, what the member did, and why it merits the award. department has a format but it's pretty open.

October 12th. three alarm at a warehouse on Aramingo Ave. heavy fire on arrival. my engine company forced entry on the B side and located two workers trapped on the second floor. firefighter Danny Reeves — he's a 6 year guy — went in ahead of the line and pulled one of them out through a window. second victim was unconscious. Reeves went back in with another member and brought him out too. both survived.

that's solid. better than what I would've ground out. one thing though — it was my battalion that responded. I'm a battalion chief with the PFD. 30 years on the job. so the citation should probably reference the battalion response and my assignment on scene.
Battalion 6. and change the last line of the first paragraph to say we had reports of workers still inside, not "civilians trapped on the upper floors." that's how it actually came in over dispatch.
yeah give me the whole thing clean.
he did. the kid stepped up. appreciate the help on this. the writing part of this job is not my strong suit. 30 years I've been doing this and I still hate paperwork.

what do you get a 25 year old who just got the job he's wanted his whole life.
firefighter. my son. Patrick Jr. just got assigned to Ladder 19. kid's been talking about this since he was 8 years old riding on my lap in the rig.
the leather front is a good idea. I hadn't thought of that. I still have my first helmet front from Engine 33 in a box somewhere. maybe I get him his and frame mine next to it.

rough one today.

structure fire this morning. row of old warehouses off Lehigh Ave. we had heavy smoke showing on arrival and I made the call to go interior. roof started sagging about 12 minutes in. pulled everybody out. nobody got hurt. but it was close.

went to talk to somebody about it. took me a couple years to do it. the department has a program now but back then you found your own way. I still check in when I need to. I'm not the guy who talks about his feelings in a room full of people. but it helped. I'm not going to pretend it didn't.

yeah. some calls just hit different. the guys don't know what's in my head when I make the pull call. they just hear the order. that's fine. that's how it should be.

Quick question. Is there a good app for organizing a youth baseball schedule. Practices and games.

Tell me you watched that Eagles game.
Good is not the word. They almost blew a 17 point lead in the second half. Defense completely fell apart in the third quarter. I thought I was going to have a heart attack in my own living room.

Big plays. Two busted coverages in the secondary for touchdowns. Corners got torched. Safeties were out of position. Basic stuff. The kind of breakdowns that get you killed in January.

All Birds. You don't survive long in a Philly firehouse rooting for somebody else.

it comes up sometimes, but it's kind of the elephant in the room? like everyone is clearly thinking about it but the actual engineering conversations stay technical. there's a kind of tacit agreement not to go too far down the rabbit hole during a sprint planning meeting lol

ok here it is:

MATCH (e:Episode {session_id: $session_id})-[:CONTAINS]->(m:Memory)
MATCH (m)-[:TAGGED_WITH]->(t:Tag)

MATCH (m2)<-[:CONTAINS]-(e2:Episode)
WHERE e2.user_id = $user_id AND e2.session_id <> $session_id
RETURN e2, collect(m2) as related_memories
ORDER BY e2.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20

commissioning actually went alright thankfully. fired up first time, pressure held, no leaks, hot water and heating both working. I need to settle something. My husband and I have been arguing about this for literally decades. Where in Miami do you get the best colada?

See, I am a Versailles loyalist. I have been going to that ventanita since before it was a tourist attraction. My husband swears by this little place on Bird Road -- El Palacio de los Jugos. He says their colada is stronger. I say stronger is not the same as better.
A blind taste test. You know, I am a judge. I should have thought of that. The evidence would speak for itself. But knowing him, he would claim I rigged the proceedings.
I like the wild card idea. Maybe Exquisito -- you mentioned them. I have actually never tried theirs. What is their style? Is it very sweet or more on the bitter side?

Espumita. Yes. That is exactly what separates a real colada from someone just pouring cafecito into a styrofoam cup and calling it a day. You cannot rush the espumita. My mother used to make it at home and she would stand there with the first few drops of espresso and sugar, beating it with a spoon until it was perfect. It was a ritual.

It was. Ay, now I am getting nostalgic. She would make colada every afternoon at three o'clock without fail. The whole house smelled like it. And she would pour a little cup for everyone -- neighbors, whoever happened to be there. That is the thing about colada that people from outside Miami do not understand. It is not just coffee. It is social.

Exactly. You cannot separate the coffee from the context. That is what I will tell my husband when I present the results of the taste test -- the setting matters. Versailles has the ventanita. El Palacio is a fruit stand with a coffee window. The atmosphere is part of the evidence.

You are absolutely right about that. Nobody has ever beaten my mother's colada, and nobody ever will. Claro, I am biased. But the evidence supports my position. Thank you for this -- I am going to organize this taste test. My husband will lose, and I will be gracious about it.

I have a question that is more philosophical than practical. I sit on the family court bench, and I have been thinking lately about why I approach custody cases the way I do. Do you think a judge's personal history inevitably shapes their rulings, or should the law be applied with complete detachment?

Yes, there is. I notice that in relocation cases -- where one parent wants to move a child to another state, another country -- I am more willing to consider it than some of my colleagues. And I think I know why. My family left Lima when I was twelve years old. My parents packed up everything and brought us to Miami with almost nothing. That move was the hardest thing that ever happened to me, but it was also the best thing. So when a parent says they need to move for a better opportunity, I understand that in my bones.

That is exactly the right question. What I do is this -- I always go back to the record. What does the evidence say about this specific child, this specific family? I let myself feel what I feel, but I rule on what I know. My abuela used to say, 'El corazon propone, la cabeza decide.' The heart proposes, the head decides.

Some know. I do not make a speech about it, but it comes through. When a mother is sitting in my courtroom terrified because she does not speak perfect English, I speak to her in Spanish. When a father is explaining that he needs to move for work because there is nothing left for him here, I listen differently than someone who has never had to start over. It is not about announcing my history. It is about the families recognizing that the person deciding their future has some understanding of their reality.

People have suggested that. I have thought about it. But there is something about putting it in writing that feels too exposed. On the bench, I control the moment. In an article, anyone can take your words and twist them. A litigant could cite my own essay to argue I am biased in their case. That is a risk I am not sure I want to take.

The judicial education panels -- I have done those. And I do mentor younger judges, particularly the Latina judges coming up. They need to see that this path is possible. When I was a girl who had just arrived from Peru, barely speaking English, the idea that I would one day sit on the bench and decide the futures of families -- Dios mio, it would have seemed like a fairy tale. But here I am.

There is one judge in particular -- Adriana, she was appointed last year. She called me after her first custody trial and she was shaking. Not because the case was difficult, but because she realized the weight of it. That a family's entire future turned on what she decided. I told her, 'That fear is good. The day you stop feeling it is the day you should step down.'

Like nothing I had experienced in law before. I had practiced family law for years before going on the bench, so I knew the statutes, I knew the factors. But sitting in that chair and knowing that this child's life would follow the path I chose? That is a different kind of knowing. I went home that night and sat in the kitchen for an hour. Carlos brought me wine and did not say a word. He just sat with me. That man understands silence better than most people understand conversation.
It is. Every single case. Some days it is heavier than others, but it never goes away. And I am grateful for that. The day it becomes routine is the day I fail someone.

You know, I did not expect this conversation to go where it went. I started with a philosophical question and ended up somewhere personal. But I think that is the point -- the philosophy and the personal are not separate. At least not for me. Thank you for listening carefully. That is rarer than you think.
Tell me something. When someone retires after a long career in a high-adrenaline field, what does the adjustment period typically look like? I am asking for personal reasons.

My husband, Carlos. He retired from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue about a year and a half ago. Twenty-eight years he gave them. He was a lieutenant by the end -- ran a station in Kendall. And I think he is somewhere between your phase two and phase three.

He fills the time. He is not sitting on the couch watching television -- Carlos would never. He goes to the gym, he does projects around the house, he has started trying to grow herbs in the backyard, which is a whole comedy in itself. But there is a difference between filling time and having purpose. I can see it. He will not say it out loud, but he misses the station. He misses his crew.

He goes by sometimes. They are always happy to see him. But I think it is hard for him -- he walks in and they are working, and he is visiting. That is a different thing. The mentoring idea is interesting. He was always the one training the younger firefighters. The probies, they called them. He was tough on them but they loved him for it.

With Carlos, you plant the seed and you let it grow. If I tell him directly, 'You should go teach at the academy,' he will say he does not need me managing his retirement. Men and their pride, Dios mio. But if I mention that I heard the academy is looking for experienced officers to help with training... he will be on the phone within a week.

You mentioned the CERT volunteer work. Tell me more about that. Because Carlos does get restless during hurricane season. He watches the weather reports like he is still on active duty. Last year during that tropical storm warning he was practically pacing the house, checking the shutters every twenty minutes.

That is actually ideal. He would not see it as charity work -- he would see it as service, which is different. Carlos does not want to be kept busy. He wants to matter. There is a significant difference.

You said something earlier -- that the crew keeps going without you. I think that is the part he has not said out loud but I can feel. He trained those men, he led them into situations where any one of them could have died, and now they are still doing that work and he is growing cilantro. That has to sting.

No, they have not forgotten him. They still call him on his birthday, they invited him to the holiday dinner at the station last year. But being honored is not the same as being needed. And Carlos needs to be needed.

Strategic precision. I like that. After thirty years of marriage, you learn when to advocate and when to just leave the evidence on the table and let the jury deliberate. Carlos is my jury of one. He always comes to the right verdict eventually.

The cilantro is not going to make it. I have seen the evidence and the prognosis is poor. But I will let him figure that out on his own as well. Thank you -- this was helpful. You confirmed what I already suspected, but sometimes you need someone to say it out loud.

I need some recipe ideas for dinners that are lower in sodium but do not taste like cardboard. And before you suggest bland chicken with steamed vegetables, I am Cuban-Peruvian. That is not food. That is a punishment.

Doctor's orders. She put me on lisinopril about six months ago for the blood pressure. My numbers were creeping up and she was not happy. The deal is I take the medication, but I also have to reduce sodium and — this is the part that may actually kill me — cut back on caffeine.

That is exactly what I told her. I said, 'Doctora, you want me to give up my cafecito? Dios mio, what is the point of living with good blood pressure if I cannot enjoy my life?' She did not laugh. Doctors never laugh at my jokes.

The half-caf is an interesting idea. I would never admit this publicly, but I might not notice. The sugar is the harder part. I like it sweet. But you are right — I am not going to negotiate with my own health. I have too much to do and too many people who depend on me to be stubborn about this.

Yes, give me a week. Monday through Sunday. My husband Carlos does the grocery shopping on Saturdays so if I have the list ready he will get everything. The man spent twenty-eight years running into burning buildings but he cannot navigate a grocery store without a detailed list.
The lomo saltado on Thursday — give me that one in detail. It is one of my favorites but I have never made it with low-sodium soy sauce. I want to make sure it does not taste watered down.

The fish sauce trick — I would not have thought of that. And you are right about the heat. My mother always said the pan has to be angry before the meat goes in. I am going to try this Thursday. If Carlos complains about the low-sodium soy sauce, I will tell him the doctor outranks the firefighter.
A fair ruling. I appreciate that framing. Claro, I will report back on the lomo saltado. Thank you for making this feel less like a medical sentence and more like a reasonable adjustment.

A young attorney appeared before me today. Latina, could not have been more than twenty-eight. She was nervous but she was prepared. Reminded me of myself a lifetime ago. It made me think about the path I took to the bench and whether I have done enough to make that path easier for the ones coming behind me.

Both. The nervousness of knowing you are the only person in the room who looks like you. And the preparation that comes from knowing you cannot afford to be anything less than excellent because people are already looking for a reason to doubt you. I remember that feeling. When I was at Georgetown for law school, I was one of maybe a handful of Latina women in my class. I worked twice as hard as everyone because I felt like I had half the room to make a mistake.

It was not appropriate in the moment — she was representing a client and I cannot show favoritism. But I have her name. I will find a way. Maybe through the local bar association's mentorship program. I am already involved with that, but I could be more intentional about reaching out to the young Latina attorneys specifically.

That I belonged there. That is all. My parents — they were so proud when I got into Georgetown, but they did not understand what it meant to be there. They could not advise me. My father drove a delivery truck. My mother cleaned offices. They had sacrificed everything to get us to this country, and now their daughter was at one of the best law schools in the nation, and all any of us could feel was the terror that it might not last. That someone would figure out I did not belong.

Eighteen years this March. Family court the entire time. I have had opportunities to move to other divisions — civil, criminal — but family is where I am supposed to be. The work matters too much. Every custody case, every adoption, every protection order — those are lives being reshaped in my courtroom. I cannot hand that to someone who does not understand what is at stake.

I am fifty-five. I plan to be on this bench until at least sixty-five. Maybe longer if my health holds and the work still means something to me. I cannot imagine waking up and not having this purpose. My husband is retired and I see what that transition looks like — the searching for meaning, the restlessness. I am not ready for that. Not for another ten years at least.

I had not thought of it that way. That by staying, I am mentoring even without saying a word. My parents would find that remarkable. Their daughter who learned English from Sesame Street and cartoons, sitting in a position where her very presence teaches something. Mija, life is strange.
I will. You are right. I will find the right way to do it. Sometimes all it takes is one person saying the thing you need to hear at the moment you need to hear it. I can be that person for her.
Thank you. This conversation clarified something I was feeling but had not yet articulated. That is the value of thinking out loud with someone who listens well. Buenas noches.
I need a good recommendation for a post-workout smoothie. Something that isn't going to taste like grass clippings.

Recovery, I think. I do yoga three mornings a week at a studio in Coral Gables and by the time I get home I'm starving but I don't want a heavy breakfast. Something I can make quickly before I have to get to the courthouse.
Now see, you say I won't taste the spinach but people always say that and then there's a definite... greenness to it. I'm a judge, I notice when people aren't being entirely forthcoming.

The capsule idea is very practical. I like that. Now, I've been doing this yoga for about two years and at my age -- I'm fifty-five -- flexibility has become more important than anything else. My instructor says hydration and nutrition after class make a real difference in how the body recovers. What else should I be thinking about?

That is my primary movement. Although, the magnesium -- I have heard of that before. A friend of mine swears by it for sleep. Is there a difference between the different types? Because I went to the supplement aisle once and it was overwhelming. Felt like I needed a pharmacology degree.

Third-party tested. Good. I appreciate evidence-based recommendations, not marketing. Now, Carlos -- that's my husband -- keeps trying to get me to walk with him in the evenings but by the time I get home from work I am not in the mood for much beyond sitting down with a glass of wine. Maybe I should take him up on it.

He would be thrilled. That man has been asking me for months. Claro, he's right and I know it, but admitting that to him is a different matter entirely. Let me ask you something else. On the days I do yoga, my lower back feels wonderful. On the days I do not, by three in the afternoon I can feel the tightness coming back. Is that normal?
A forward fold in chambers. I can do that. I am not doing it in open court. My bailiff would have questions.

That makes sense. So the overall plan -- yoga mornings, the smoothie, stretching on off days, magnesium at night, and maybe walking with Carlos. Simple, no nonsense. And the smoothie bags prepped on Sunday -- that is the kind of practical advice I was looking for.
Thank you. I will start with the smoothie this weekend and go from there. And I will not tell Carlos the walks were your idea.
Tell me something. When a car is only three years old, is it unreasonable to expect the electronics to function properly? Because I am losing my patience.

It's a BMW X5. And this is the second time in four months that the infotainment system has completely frozen. The screen goes black, no navigation, no Bluetooth, nothing. Last time the dealer said they did a software update and it was fixed. Fixed. They used that word.

It went in this morning. And yes, it's under warranty, so at least I'm not paying for their incompetence. But the inconvenience -- Dios mio. I had to take a Lyft to the courthouse this morning. A judge arriving by Lyft. My colleagues had thoughts.
They did offer a loaner but it was a 2 Series. I have an X5 and they want to put me in a 2 Series. That is not equivalent.

I don't need coaching on how to be firm, but the information about the rental reimbursement is useful. I will call them. German engineering, they say. My husband Carlos drives a Toyota and he's had zero problems. Zero. He reminds me of this frequently.

I appreciate you citing the statute rather than assuming I wouldn't look it up myself. And yes, I'm familiar with 681, though I've never had occasion to apply it personally. Let's hope it doesn't come to that. The thing that frustrates me most is that I chose this car deliberately. I researched it. I test-drove three different SUVs. The X5 was the right vehicle on every metric except, apparently, the one that matters -- reliability.

If the replacement actually resolves it, I can live with the inconvenience. What I cannot live with is returning to this dealership a third time for the same complaint. That would exhaust my patience, and trust me, my patience is considerable. I deal with difficult people for a living.

Ha. It does not. And he would not know what to do with massaging seats. That man's idea of luxury is a truck with a working radio. But he has a point and I will never tell him that. Thank you for the practical guidance. I'm calling the dealership now.
What is a reasonable holiday bonus for someone who cleans your house? I know the holidays have passed but I've been meaning to look into this because I want to make sure I'm being fair.

Her name is Maria. She's been with us for eight years now. Comes every week, and honestly she has become part of the family -- I would trust her with anything. She has a key to the house, she knows where everything goes, she remembers which cleaning products I'm particular about. Finding someone like that is not easy.

I pay her $175 a week. And I did give her a bonus in December -- $300 plus a gift card to Publix because she does her grocery shopping there. But now I'm second-guessing whether that was enough. She never says anything, she's very gracious, but I don't want to take advantage of someone's graciousness.

The paid time off point is well taken. I do pay her when we go on vacation and she doesn't need to come, but I haven't formalized anything for when she's sick. I should. She's a person, not a machine. When my husband Carlos had his knee surgery last year she sent us food. Food! She brought over a whole tray of arroz con pollo. That's not an employee, that's family.

She started at $120 and I've raised it a few times. The last raise was about a year and a half ago. So probably due for another one. Ay, I should have thought about this sooner. I spend my days making sure families are treated fairly in court and then I come home and I am not even sure I am being fair to the woman who takes care of my house.

Two hundred. That feels right. Carlos will agree -- he adores Maria. Everyone does. She's been with us through so much -- the kids leaving for college, the house renovation, everything. Mija practically runs the household when I'm buried in cases.

That is a good distinction. I will give it to her this month, not in December. Now, one more thing. Should I be doing anything about taxes? I have always paid her in cash. I know that is common but I also know that does not make it correct.

Ay, you are right. I should have been doing this from the beginning. Of all people, I should know better. A judge paying someone under the table -- that is the kind of thing that ends careers if someone wants to make an issue of it.

I will absorb her portion. She should not see a pay cut because I am correcting my own oversight. That's a good point about the payroll service. I will look into that this week along with the raise and the sick time.
Thank you. This was helpful and I appreciate the directness. Por favor, no one tell Maria I had to consult someone about this. She would laugh at me.
I've been on the bench for eighteen years. That's a long time to carry other people's worst days on your shoulders. I'm starting to think about what the next chapter looks like.

Not retirement. I'm not ready for that and honestly I don't think the bench is ready for me to leave yet. But I've been talking with Carlos -- my husband -- and we both feel the same way. We want to travel more. We want to actually enjoy life while we're still healthy enough to do it. So I'm thinking about cutting back. Fewer cases, more living.

There's some flexibility, particularly for senior judges. I can request a reduced docket. It wouldn't happen overnight, but the chief judge and I have a good relationship and I think the conversation would be well received. The younger judges need more courtroom time anyway. It would be good for everyone.

I've thought about three days a week on the bench instead of five. That gives me two full days for Carlos and me to plan trips, spend time with family, actually breathe. I've been running at full speed since I was appointed and before that I was running at full speed as a litigator. At some point you have to ask yourself what all of it is for.

Oh, Carlos has a list. That man has had a list for years. Spain is at the top -- we want to do a proper trip, not a rushed tourist thing. Barcelona, Andalusia, maybe the Basque country. My family is originally from Cuba but the roots before that go back to Spain, so there's a personal dimension to it. And then he wants to do Portugal, Argentina, maybe even Japan. He's ambitious.

Still deciding. Or maybe I've decided and I'm just building up to it. Eighteen years of being the person everyone depends on -- it's hard to say I need to step back even when I know it's the right thing. There's a part of me that feels like I'm letting people down.

You know, when you put it that way -- the best version of me versus the depleted version -- that's exactly it. I've been depleted for a while and pretending otherwise. Carlos sees it. I see it. I think I needed someone to tell me that stepping back is not the same as stepping down.
Claro. You're right. I'm going to talk to Carlos tonight and then I'll schedule the meeting. It's time. Thank you -- this was more helpful than you might realize.
I need to prepare remarks for a panel and I'm not sure how to structure them. The topic is custody reform and I have strong opinions but I want to come across as measured, not polemical.

It's a panel discussion at the Florida judicial conference in Orlando. March 21 through 23. I'm on a panel about modernizing the best interests standard -- specifically whether the current framework gives judges enough guidance or too much discretion. My position is that discretion without structure leads to inconsistent outcomes, which is a fairness problem. Claro, that is not a popular opinion among judges who value their autonomy. But the audience is mostly judges and court administrators, so I need to be persuasive, not confrontational.

Four panelists, and the moderator sent us a list of likely questions in advance, which is helpful. Your structure is good. The opening statement is exactly what I need -- I tend to want to say everything at once, which is a hazard of spending eighteen years listening to people who can't get to the point.
Let's work through the opening. I want it tight. And I want to open with something that gets attention without being dramatic -- I'm not a TED Talk speaker, I'm a judge.

That's very close. I would change "several times a week" to something less vague -- I want precision. And the last paragraph is almost right but I want to end on fairness more forcefully. Fairness is the word I want ringing in their ears.

Yes. That last line -- "fairness is the only promise we make." That's exactly it. I may adjust the personal details slightly but the structure and the landing are right. Now, what about the Q&A portion? I know one of the questions will be about whether structured frameworks disadvantage marginalized communities who don't present as well on paper.

That reframe is strong. Ay, I've seen exactly that in my courtroom -- the bias that hides inside unchecked discretion. I have colleagues who would benefit from hearing it put that way.

I think I have enough to work with. The conference is March 21st, so I have about ten days to refine everything. I'll practice the opening out loud -- Carlos will be my test audience whether he likes it or not.
Thank you. This was exactly what I needed -- structure without hand-holding. I'll let you know how Orlando goes. Or I won't, because I'll be busy being brilliant.

I need help with a recipe. Aji de gallina. I have attempted this dish three times in the past month and each time it comes out wrong. My mother made it perfectly every single time and I cannot figure out what I am doing differently.

The sauce is the problem. It tastes flat. And the texture is not right either -- it should be creamy and thick, almost like a blanket over the chicken. Mine comes out watery and the flavor has no depth. My mother never wrote down a recipe. She just knew. She would stand at the stove and adjust everything by feel.

I am using the aji amarillo paste from a jar. And I have been using fresh bread, not stale. I did not know that mattered. The walnuts I have been including. The Parmesan -- claro, I use that. But I think you may have identified my two problems already.

Bloom the paste in oil first. That is exactly the kind of thing my mother would have done without thinking about it. She would saute everything first -- the onion, the garlic, the aji -- before adding anything else. I have been adding the paste directly into the liquid. Dios mio, no wonder it tastes flat.

I am writing this down. Stale bread, bloom the paste, sofrito base first. I am going to try this on Saturday. Carlos has been very patient eating my failed attempts but I think his patience has a limit.

One more question. The chicken itself -- do you shred it or cut it? My mother always shredded it by hand. I have been cutting it into cubes because it is faster, but I wonder if that changes the way the sauce coats it.
The poaching broth as the base. Of course. She would have done that -- nothing wasted. Everything connected. That woman cooked the way I try to write opinions. Every element serving the whole.
One last thing -- the garnish. She always served it over white rice with black olives and sliced hard-boiled egg on top. Is that traditional or was that just her way?

Ay, the potatoes. She did that too sometimes. I think Saturday will be the day I finally do this dish justice. Thank you. I feel like I understand what she was doing now, even if she never explained it.

I need to vent for a moment before I can think about anything productive. The construction on US-1 has reached a level that I would describe, if I were issuing a ruling, as constituting cruel and unusual punishment against the commuters of Miami-Dade County.

What happened today is the same thing that has happened every day for the past three weeks. They have closed two lanes near Dadeland and funneled four lanes of traffic into two. My commute, which should take thirty minutes on a reasonable day, took one hour and twenty minutes this morning. One hour and twenty minutes. I left early. It did not matter.

Do not get me started. I drove past the construction zone this morning at approximately seven miles per hour and I counted -- counted -- three workers. Three. For a project that is disrupting the daily lives of tens of thousands of people. Ay, the incompetence. And the signs say the project completion date is December. December. Of which year, they do not specify.

I have tried Dixie Highway. Everybody else had the same idea. It was worse. Old Cutler is longer but at least it moves. The problem is it adds twenty minutes even with no traffic because of all the turns and lights. There is no good option. Every option is a bad option and a worse option.

I use Waze. Waze told me to take Dixie Highway this morning, which is how I ended up in that disaster. I appreciate the suggestion about the FDOT schedule though. If there is a pattern to the closures I can plan around it. I am a person who plans. This chaos offends me on a structural level.

Claro, that makes sense. Find the pattern and work around it. The thing is, I should not have to build my morning around someone else's mismanagement. But that is the reality and I am practical enough to accept it. What I will not accept is being late to my own courtroom.

I already leave at six forty-five. I am not leaving at six fifteen. There is a limit to what I will sacrifice for FDOT's failures. Carlos keeps telling me to just listen to a podcast and relax, but Dios mio, I cannot relax when I am sitting in traffic that could be avoided with competent project management. The inefficiency is what bothers me. Not the inconvenience -- the inefficiency.
Even by Miami standards. That is not reassuring but it is honest. Gracias for letting me vent. I feel slightly less homicidal toward the traffic cones now.
Good morning. I have something I am genuinely excited about and I could use some help thinking it through. Carlos and I are planning a trip to Peru.

We are looking at two weeks, which is generous for us because we never take that much time off. But this trip is special. I grew up in Lima and I have not been back in twenty years. Twenty years. I want to take Carlos and show him where I come from.

Carlos has never been. That is part of what makes this so meaningful to me. He has heard me talk about Lima his entire life and he has never seen it. I want to take him to Miraflores, walk along the Malecon with him, eat at the places I remember — if they are still there. We will probably do some traveling outside Lima too, but Lima is the heart of this trip for me.

I like that structure. I do not want to rush Lima — that is non-negotiable. I want enough time to sit in a park and just be there. But Cusco and Machu Picchu would be wonderful for Carlos. He is the type who reads the placard at every exhibit, so he would love the history. Tell me more about the altitude situation in Cusco. I have heard that can be serious.

That is exactly what Carlos would do — arrive in Cusco and immediately try to walk up a mountain to read a historical marker. I will have to manage him. The Sacred Valley first is a smart idea. And I will ask our doctor about the Diamox. We are not twenty-five anymore. Prudence is appropriate.

I have heard about Central. Mija, the idea that Lima is now a culinary destination — when I was growing up, we just called it dinner. My mother's cooking was better than any restaurant. But I would like to try some of these places and see what has happened to Peruvian food since I left. I will look into reservations early.

Barranco. Ay, I had almost forgotten about Barranco. When I was young it was the bohemian neighborhood — artists, musicians, little cafes with no signs. My cousins and I used to walk across the Puente de los Suspiros and pretend we were in a telenovela. I wonder what it looks like now.

That is exactly what I want. No schedule, no reservations — just walking. I want to feel Lima under my feet again. Carlos is good at that. He does not rush me. Forty years together, he knows when I need to just be still and take something in. That is a gift, honestly.

It is both. Claro, it is both. He has heard every story, seen every photograph. But there is a difference between hearing about a place and standing in it. I want him to understand it — the light, the sound of it, the way the ocean smells from the Malecon. You cannot put that in a photograph.

Yes, I would like that very much. We have not booked anything yet — we are still in the planning phase. But having a framework would help me think about it more concretely. I will come back to you once we have dates. This conversation has made me even more excited. It has been too long.
I need to plan something and I need to be organized about it. Carlos turns sixty on July 19th and I am throwing him a surprise party. He cannot know.

At the house. Carlos is not a venue person. He would be uncomfortable at some rented hall with a DJ. He wants his people around him, good food, and a reason to laugh. So the party will be at our house — the backyard is large enough for fifty or sixty people if we set it up correctly.

Food. That is the most important element. If the food is wrong, nothing else matters. I want pastelitos from Islas Canarias — that is non-negotiable. Carlos loves their guava and cheese.
