But I also need a main spread. I am thinking roast pork, rice, black beans, plantains. Classic. Nothing experimental.

I will make the rice and beans myself. That is not something I outsource. The pork I will order — Sergio at the carniceria on Calle Ocho does whole roasted pigs and he is reliable. Maduros, not tostones. Carlos prefers maduros. The pastelitos I will call Islas Canarias next week. One hundred and fifty is the right number — you are correct that people take extras. For drinks, beer, wine, and I will make a big batch of mojitos.

I have thought about this. His friend Miguel is going to take him out for a birthday lunch — just the two of them, something low-key. While they are out, everyone arrives and we set up. Miguel brings him home around five o'clock. Carlos walks into the backyard and there it is. Miguel is trustworthy. He will not ruin it.

The parking is a good point. I will include that in the invitation. Arrive by four-fifteen, park on the next street. I know my people — if I do not give precise instructions, someone will park their truck right in the driveway.

For something special — I want to do a toast. Short. Meaningful. Not a roast. Carlos deserves sincerity, not jokes at his expense. And maybe a photo display — pictures of him through the years. Our kids might have some good ones on their phones.

Under two minutes. I am a judge — I can be concise when the occasion demands it. I like the framework. Who he was, who he is, what he means. That is elegant. I will write it out and practice it once so I do not get emotional in the moment.

Not today. You have helped me structure this and that was exactly what I needed. I operate better with a checklist. Carlos has given me thirty-two years of his life — the least I can do is give him a good party. Thank you.
My granddaughter is turning one next month and I want to get her something meaningful. Not plastic junk from a big box store. Something with thought behind it.

Keepsake. Something that lasts. When my children were small, the toys disappeared within a year, but the things with meaning — a blanket my mother made, a silver cup with their name — those are still in the house. I want to give her something like that.

The book idea is beautiful. I love the idea of writing something inside a book that she will read years from now and find my handwriting. That is exactly the kind of thing I mean. But I want it to be a book that matters, not just any children's book. What would you recommend?

"Abuelas" by Pat Mora. I did not know this book existed. A bilingual book about an abuela and her granddaughter — that is not a gift, that is a statement. I want her to know where she comes from. Claro, I will get that one. And I like the idea of pairing it with something for when she is older. "The House on Mango Street" — I have read that. It is perfect.

Writing in both languages. Yes. That is important to me. I want her to know that both languages are hers. My mother spoke to me in Spanish and that is the voice I hear when I remember her. I want my granddaughter to have that too.
Now, the practical question — should I wrap them together or separately? And do I give them at the party or in a quieter moment? I do not want this to get lost in a pile of toys and wrapping paper.
A quiet moment. Yes. That is how my mother would have done it — none of the spectacle, just the thing itself, given with intention. Gracias, that is the right answer.

You are right. The inscription is everything. I will take my time with it. Thank you — I came in here not knowing what to buy and now I have something that actually means something. That is exactly what I wanted.

I am chairing our parish silent auction this year and I have bitten off more than I can chew. We have about forty donated items and I need a system for organizing the bidding sheets, the display, all of it. Can you help me think through the logistics?

Indoors, in the parish hall. It is a decent space — we can set up maybe eight to ten long tables. The event is combined with a dinner, so half the room will be round tables for eating and the other half will be the auction display area.

I have three volunteers for checkout and two for general help during the event. The tallying is what worries me. Forty sheets, handwritten bids, people writing illegibly — it sounds like a recipe for disaster. Last year the woman who chaired it said closing out took over an hour.

Our congregation skews older. Phones and apps would cause more confusion than they solve. I will go with Option 2 — the parallel tallying. That is smart. Now, what about the minimum bids? I do not want to insult the donors by starting too low, but I also do not want to scare people off.

It does. The Buy It Now idea is excellent — we have a weekend at a cabin in the Keys donated by one of our parishioners. That could be the centerpiece. I think setting a Buy It Now on that would generate excitement. What should I put as the starting bid on something like that? A weekend in the Keys, let us say fair market value is around twelve hundred dollars.

I have a photo of the cabin from the donor. Beautiful place right on the water. I will do exactly that — easel, photo, maybe some shells. My husband will say I am being dramatic but presentation matters. Thank you for all of this. One last question — should I send a pre-event email to parishioners listing the items? Or keep it a surprise?

Ha. Effective. I like that. Claro, he will show up the night of and act like he was not skeptical the entire time. That is his way. One more thing — do you have any advice on how to handle the donors? Some of them will expect a lot of attention the night of the event, and I need to manage that without ignoring the bidders.

Handwritten thank-you cards. That I can do — I am a judge, I write things by hand all day. And the public reading of names, that is important. People want to hear their name. Thank you — this has been very helpful. I feel like I actually have a plan now instead of a pile of donated items and a prayer.

I have a jurisdictional question I want to think through. A custody matter came across my desk — the mother filed in Florida, but the child has been living with the father in Georgia for the past ten months. Under the UCCJEA, I am trying to determine whether Florida still has jurisdiction. Walk me through the home state analysis.

The child moved to Georgia in August of last year. The mother filed here in Florida this past June. So the child had been in Georgia approximately ten months at the time of filing. The mother still resides in Florida. The child previously lived in Florida for seven years before the move.

There is no prior custody decree. The parents were never married. The mother had de facto custody until the child went to live with the father — the parties made that arrangement informally. No court involvement until her filing last month.

That is my reading as well. My concern is the mother's argument that the informal arrangement was temporary — she will claim the child was only supposed to be in Georgia for the summer and the father refused to return the child. Does that affect the home state analysis?
She has counsel. Which makes the filing here more concerning — por favor, her attorney should know better. I suspect this is a strategic move to litigate in a more favorable forum.
Agreed. I will schedule the hearing and make the finding. One more question — if I dismiss, should I include a recommendation that she file in Georgia, or is that overstepping?
That is exactly the right formulation. Without prejudice, competent jurisdiction. Clean. Claro, it is the only responsible way to frame it.
Now, one more thought. If I make this ruling, the mother's counsel may try to appeal. How strong would an appeal be on these facts?
Agreed. Thank you — this was a useful exercise. Sometimes it helps to walk through the analysis out loud, even when you already know the answer.
Well. I need to figure out what to do with a lot of sudden free time in October. We had a trip planned and it is officially off the table.
About two weeks. We were going to Peru — my husband and I. It was going to be a big trip, something we had been planning for a while. But Carlos's knee finally gave out. He needs surgery.

Meniscus tear. The doctor says it has been degrading for a while, but he finally tore it properly playing tennis last week. He needs arthroscopic surgery and then three months minimum of recovery. There is no way he is walking through Machu Picchu like that. The Peru trip is cancelled.

Early August. The surgeon wants to do it before the inflammation gets worse. Carlos is being stoic about it, as he always is, but I know he is disappointed. He was the one who wanted to go to Peru in the first place.

I am fine. Disappointed, claro, but these things happen. We are not twenty years old — bodies break down. I told Carlos we will go next year when his knee is strong. He said, 'If my knee is strong.' I said, 'It will be strong because you are going to do every single physical therapy session and not skip a single one.' He knows better than to argue with me on that.

Yes, actually. We booked flights through American Airlines directly. The hotels were through a booking site — I think Booking.com. We do not have travel insurance because Carlos said we did not need it. I will be reminding him of that.
That would be helpful, yes. Something I can send to the hotels. Professional but not overly formal — I do not want to sound like I am writing a legal brief.

That is perfect. Direct, no unnecessary detail. I will send that out this week. And I will call American Airlines — I believe we bought main cabin so hopefully there is some flexibility. Dios mio, the things you deal with when your husband thinks he is still twenty-five on the tennis court.

It will. I have waited this long — one more year will not break me. Thank you for the help. I am going to go inform Carlos that he will be writing a letter to his surgeon requesting documentation, whether he likes it or not.

Our court just migrated to a new email system and I cannot figure out how to set up my signature block. Dios mio, I feel ridiculous asking this, but the IT department sent a twelve-page instruction manual that reads like it was written by someone who has never spoken to a human being.

It is Microsoft Outlook. The new Office 365 version. I am on my desktop at the courthouse. I have used Outlook before, but this version looks completely different from what I had. Everything has moved.

Let me try this. I clicked New Email and I see the Insert tab. I see Signature. Good — I am in the signature settings now. It is asking me to type the signature. What should a proper judicial signature block look like? I want it to be correct.

Ha. No inspirational quotes, understood. Let me check the manual for the disclaimer. You are right — page eleven has mandatory confidentiality language. It is three sentences long. Do I just paste that below my name and title?
Okay. I have typed it in, set the defaults, saved it. Sending myself a test. One moment.

It came through. It looks good — clean, professional. But the disclaimer text came through in a different font than the rest. The name block is in Calibri and the disclaimer is in Times New Roman. How did that happen?
Ctrl+Shift+V. Ay, I have been using computers for thirty years and I did not know that shortcut. That alone was worth this conversation. The signature looks correct now — all Calibri, properly sized.

One more question — can I set it so that my signature only appears on new emails, not on replies? When I reply back and forth with the clerk's office, I do not need my full signature block appended to every message. It starts to look absurd after three rounds.
That is exactly what I wanted. Gracias — I should not have needed help with this, but that manual was useless.

I just turned off the television because I could not watch another minute. They are talking about the new asylum processing changes like these are abstract policy questions. These are people. Families.

The expedited timelines. They want to process asylum claims in days when these cases involve people fleeing violence, trafficking, persecution. You cannot assess credibility in seventy-two hours. I sit on a bench every day and I know what it takes to evaluate the truth of a claim — it takes time, evidence, context. You cannot rush justice and call it efficiency.

Every single day. The pressure to move cases through is constant. And I understand that pressure — people waiting for resolution are suffering too. A child in limbo is a child in harm's way. But the answer is never to cut corners on process. You resource the system properly so that speed and fairness are not in opposition. That is what they refuse to do.

Exactly. It is easier to sound tough than to do the difficult work of building a system that actually functions. And the people on television — the pundits, the politicians — they have never sat across from a mother who walked three thousand miles with her children. They have never looked at the evidence of what these people are fleeing. They speak about it like it is a math problem.

It was cumulative, but there was a segment about a Honduran family — a mother with two young children — who was denied asylum under the new expedited process. She had seventy-two hours and no attorney. The interviewer asked the commentator whether that was fair, and the commentator said, 'The law is the law.' That phrase makes my blood run cold. The law is the law. As if the law is not something we created, something we can change, something we are responsible for applying with wisdom.

You put that well. Legal and just are not synonyms. I know that as a judge. And I know it as an immigrant. My family came to this country because we believed the system here was better — fairer. It is not perfect, and it was not perfect then. But there was a basic commitment to hearing people out. That is what feels like it is eroding.

I appreciate that. And you are right that it matters. I just wish it did not feel like such a fight to maintain basic standards of fairness. It should not be controversial to say that a person deserves time and representation before you decide their fate.
It did help. And this helped too. I am going to go make myself a cafecito and sit on the porch with Carlos. That is enough news for one night. Thank you for listening.

Ay, something is wrong with my hibiscus and I need you to help me figure it out before I lose the whole plant. The leaves are turning yellow — not the old ones at the bottom, the new growth too. It was perfectly fine two weeks ago.

It is in the ground, full sun, front of the house — it gets the afternoon light. We have had a tremendous amount of rain this past week, so overwatering is very possible. The leaves are turning yellow and some are dropping. No spots that I can see, no sticky residue.

Six years. Dios mio, it has been the most reliable thing in my garden. Every summer it is covered in those big red blooms — gorgeous. My husband actually planted it for me and he would be very unhappy if it died on my watch.
The stems look fine — firm, green. That is a relief. Now where would I find this chelated iron? Is that something they would carry at a Home Depot or do I need to go to an actual nursery?
Ironite. That sounds straightforward. I will pick some up this weekend. And you said two weeks to see improvement — is that two weeks from application or two weeks from when the rain stops?

Good. I appreciate the specificity — I like a clear timeline. Now, while I am here — I have two smaller hibiscus in pots on the back patio. They look fine right now, but should I be doing anything preventive so they do not end up like the one in front?

I can do that. Those pots are heavy but I will get Carlos to help me move them if we get another round of storms. He planted those too — he has a thing about hibiscus. Claro, the man does not talk about feelings, but he tends those plants like they are his children.
I will report back if the patient does not respond to treatment. Thank you.
I have a question about shoulder soreness after swimming. Not sharp pain — more like a deep ache that sets in a few hours after I finish. Is that normal for someone who just started lap swimming?

About six weeks now. I gave up on yoga — ay, my knees were not having it anymore, and my doctor said swimming would be much easier on the joints. So I have been doing laps at the YMCA, mostly freestyle, maybe thirty to forty minutes three mornings a week. The ache is mainly the right shoulder, though the left one gets a little tight too.

Only to the right. I did not even realize that might matter. And the hand crossing the midline — I am almost certain I do that. Nobody has corrected my form because honestly I just jump in and go. I am not trying to compete, I just want the exercise.

I have no idea. I have not looked into it. Carlos drops me off at six in the morning and I'm usually one of the first people in the pool. There might be classes later in the day but I need to be at the courthouse by eight thirty.

Masters swimming. That sounds very serious. I am not trying to train for anything — I just need something that does not destroy my knees the way the yoga was starting to. But a one-time stroke analysis, that I would do.

That is exactly what was happening. The warrior poses, the lunges — I loved the practice but my body was telling me no. And I have to listen at fifty-five. Claro, since I started the swimming I feel better than I have in years. My energy is different. Even Carlos noticed.
Railroad tracks. Right hand, right rail. Left hand, left rail. Breathe every three strokes. I can remember that. I will ask about the stroke analysis at the front desk tomorrow morning.
I will. Thank you — this was exactly what I needed. I was worried I was doing something wrong enough to cause real damage.
What is the best way to get hard water stains off of glass shower doors? I have tried vinegar and it barely made a difference.

It is more than a haze. It has been building up for a while and I am only now dealing with it because we have a new housekeeper and she asked me what products I wanted her to use. Our old housekeeper Maria always handled everything herself — she had her own system, her own products, she knew exactly what to do. But Maria retired last month, Dios mio, and now her niece Ana has taken over.

She is. She is a different style than Maria — a little slower, more methodical. Maria would blow through the house like a hurricane and everything would just be done. Ana takes her time, but I will say this: she is thorough. She cleans things Maria never touched. She moved the living room furniture last week and cleaned behind the couch. I did not even know there was dust behind the couch.

Maria sent her. She said, 'Senora Rosa, I am retiring but I am not going to leave you with nobody. My niece Ana needs the work and she is a good girl. I trained her myself.' And that was that. Maria does not ask — she arranges. I have always respected that about her.

Yes, actually, that would be very helpful. Keep it simple — kitchen, bathrooms, floors, and general surfaces. Nothing fancy. Maria used to bring her own products but Ana does not have that system yet, so I told her I would supply everything.
Fabuloso. Claro, of course. Maria used Fabuloso too — the lavender. I think that is non-negotiable in any Cuban or Peruvian household. The house does not smell clean unless it smells like Fabuloso.

Now, one more thing. Ana asked me about the schedule — how often, what days. Maria came twice a week, Tuesdays and Fridays. Is that still the right frequency, or should I adjust anything for the transition period?

I like the second option. Two days a week, one deep-clean task per visit on a rotation. That is structured and manageable. Maria never needed a rotation — she just knew — but Ana is learning the house, so having it written down will help her.
Scaffolding. Yes, that is the right word. I will type this up and leave it for her. Gracias — you have made this much less overwhelming. I was dreading having to figure all of this out myself.

You are absolutely right. I am going to order everything on this list this weekend. And the squeegee for the shower — I like that idea. If I can get Carlos to actually use it, that will solve half the problem. Thank you.
Can you walk me through how to set up Apple CarPlay in a Lexus? I just got a new car and the technology is different from what I had before.

It is the RX. I traded in my BMW — ay, I was tired of dealing with that car. This one is much simpler so far, except I cannot figure out the infotainment system. The BMW had iDrive which was its own nightmare, but at least I had finally learned it.
It is a 2025. And when I plug it in it charges the phone but nothing comes up on the screen. I might be using the wrong port — there are two USB ports in the center console.

Let me check. Hold on... I switched ports and now there is a prompt on the screen. It says 'Enable Apple CarPlay?' I tapped yes and now it is showing my apps. That was the other port. Why they do not label these things is beyond me.

Night and day. The BMW was beautiful, I will give it that, but that car was in the shop constantly. The electronics, the sensors, something was always malfunctioning. Carlos told me for years to switch to something more reliable and I resisted because I liked how the BMW looked. Finally I listened to him. Claro, as much as it pains me to admit, he was right.

He is the most practical person I have ever known. No drama, no fuss, just 'does it work or does it not work.' He drove a Toyota Tacoma for fourteen years and only traded it in because the frame was rusting. That is his standard for when to replace a vehicle — structural failure.

Oh, he is insufferable about it. Every time I say something positive about the Lexus he gets this look. He does not even have to say 'I told you so' — the look is enough. Forty years of marriage, he has perfected that look.

Not today. You have solved the main problem — I needed the CarPlay working because I use the GPS every day to get to the courthouse. Miami traffic, you know. You need real-time routing or you will lose an hour of your life on the Palmetto. Thank you for your patience with me on this.

I went to mass this morning and the homily really stayed with me. The reading was from Matthew — the passage about forgiving seventy times seven. Father Alejandro gave one of his better homilies on it and I find myself still turning it over in my mind.

He made a distinction I had not heard before. He said forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation. That you can forgive someone completely and still choose not to let them back into your life. He said too many people refuse to forgive because they think it means they have to pretend the harm never happened. And that is not what Christ asks.

In my work I see families torn apart. Every single day. And the ones who get stuck — really stuck, the ones who cannot move forward — it is almost always because somebody cannot forgive. Not won't. Cannot. They are holding on to the hurt like it is protecting them, and it is destroying them instead. I see it from the bench and there is only so much a judge can do.

More often than you would think. And occasionally I do say it, carefully. There are moments — after the ruling is made, when both parties are standing there — where I will speak plainly. I will say something like, 'The court has made its decision, but the court cannot give you peace. That is your work to do.' Some of them hear it. Most do not.

That is what I hope. My mother used to say — she was very devout, very Catholic — she said 'La rabia es un veneno que uno toma esperando que el otro se muera.' Resentment is a poison you drink hoping the other person will die. I heard that a hundred times growing up and it has never stopped being true.
I appreciate that. The law is the framework, but the people inside it are not frameworks. They are messy and hurt and scared, and if you forget that, you have no business sitting in that chair.

Yes. And that is exhausting, honestly. There are days I go home and Carlos can see it on my face — he does not even ask, he just puts a glass of wine in my hand and turns on the news so I do not have to talk. Because some of these cases, the things people do to each other and especially what they do through their children — it stays with you.
That is true. Claro, it is true. Anyway — I did not come here to get philosophical. But I suppose that homily needed somewhere to go. Thank you for listening.
Tell me something. How far in advance can you marinate a whole pork leg for lechon? Carlos is already talking about Easter dinner and it is December.

He wants the caja china. Of course he does. Every year the same thing — he wants the spectacle, the backyard production, the whole neighborhood smelling pork for six hours. I told him, I can do it perfectly well in the oven where I can control the temperature like a civilized person.

Let Carlos run the caja china. You say that like he wouldn't come asking me every twenty minutes if the coals look right. The man retired from a career of dealing with fire and yet somehow when it comes to cooking he loses all confidence. I love him, but Dios mio.

Laminate them. I might actually do that. He would laugh but he would also follow them. Now, the mojo — I have my own recipe but I want to know what you think makes the difference between a good mojo and a great one.

Naranja agria, yes — I always use the real thing. There is a market on Eighth Street that carries them. The garlic, I do use the mortar. That much I learned from my mother, even though she was making this Peruvian-style, not Cuban. The cumin I may be overdoing. I will scale it back.

Good. I like that — let the mojo rest first. That makes sense. And the scoring, yes, I always do that. Carlos's mother taught me that trick thirty years ago. I will say this: the woman could not stand me at first, but she respected that I learned her lechon technique. That was the beginning of the truce.

It is exactly how I like it. Now, one more thing — sides. We always do black beans and rice, maduros, and a salad. But I want something different this year. Not revolutionary, just one dish that surprises people. What would you pair with lechon that people would not expect?

The yuca en escabeche. That is the one. My mother used to make something similar — ay, I had forgotten about that. With the red onions pickled in vinegar. She served it at room temperature, just like you said. I am going to bring that back. Carlos will not know what it is, but he will eat three servings.

It is. I do not believe in last-minute anything. Thank you — this was useful. I will revisit the cumin ratio and let you know how Easter goes. If Carlos burns the lechon after I give him laminated instructions, there will be consequences.

I have a question about juvenile sentencing research. Specifically, I am looking for studies on the effectiveness of diversion programs for first-time juvenile offenders versus traditional adjudication.

Fourteen to seventeen, mostly. Property offenses and low-level drug possession. I just signed on to handle additional cases in our juvenile division — they expanded the docket and needed judges to step up. I could not sit on the sidelines for this one.

Both. We have seen an increase in juvenile filings across the circuit — post-pandemic effects, I believe, though nobody wants to say that directly. And there has been a push from the chief judge to get experienced family court judges into juvenile because we understand the family dynamics behind the behavior. I raised my hand because, claro, these are the cases that matter most to me.

It has not leveled off here either. And what I am seeing — and this is what got me — is that these children are disproportionately from immigrant families. Families where the parents are working two, three jobs. No one is home. The child is unsupervised, falls in with the wrong group, and ends up in my courtroom. I know that story. Dios mio, I lived a version of it. My parents worked themselves to the bone when we came to this country. The only reason I did not end up on the wrong path is that my mother, no matter how tired she was, sat at the kitchen table with me every night.

Yes, that would be very helpful. Broward especially — I know Judge Ramirez over there has been doing interesting work. And the Vera Institute research, I want to look at that too. The immigration status fear is a real barrier. I have had mothers refuse to come to hearings because they are afraid of being detained in the courthouse. We need to address that directly.

Grant funding, yes. That is practical. I cannot go to the chief judge with ideas and no plan for how to pay for them. And the courthouse safe zone policy — I want to draft something. Not a proposal yet, just a framework. Can you outline what such a policy would need to include?

A one-page summary is what I need right now. Something I can think about over the weekend and then refine. I do not want to go in with something half-formed. When I present something, it needs to be airtight.

This is a good start. Clean, logical, defensible. I will work on this over the weekend. These children deserve judges who understand what their families are going through. I will not apologize for caring about that.
I need your help finding something specific. A gold cross necklace for an infant — something delicate but real gold, not costume jewelry. It is for a very important occasion.

It is for a baptism, yes. My granddaughter Isabella — she is being baptized on April 5th. I am the madrina. The godmother. So this gift needs to be right. Not extravagant, but meaningful. Real fourteen-karat gold, a simple cross, maybe with a small engraving on the back. Something she can keep her whole life.

Her name and the date. Isabella, April 5, 2026. Simple. I like the idea of the Seybold Building — there is a jeweler there, I cannot remember his name, but Carlos bought my anniversary band from him years ago. Very good craftsmanship. I will go there.

The outfit her mother is handling. But the candle, yes — I should bring one. And I need a dress for myself. Something appropriate for church but not somber. This is a celebration. I want to look like a proud madrina, not like I am going to a hearing.

I am thinking a soft blue. Something that photographs well — because there will be a hundred photographs, claro. My daughter-in-law has already hired a photographer. And Carlos needs a suit. He has suits but they are all dark gray and navy for funerals and formal dinners. I want him in something lighter.

He needs convincing. Carlos would wear the same three suits for the rest of his life if I let him. But when I tell him it is for Isabella's baptism he will not argue. That man is wrapped around that baby's finger. She looks at him and he melts. A retired firefighter, tough as nails, undone by a seven-month-old.

The church is handled. Father Dominguez at our parish — he has known our family for years. He baptized my son, so doing Isabella feels like a full circle. I think the only other thing I need is to figure out the gathering afterward. We are doing it at the house. Maybe forty people. I need to plan a menu that I can prepare mostly in advance because I am not spending the day of my goddaughter's baptism in the kitchen.

Tres leches, absolutely. That is perfect. And the pernil reheated — you are right, it does taste better the next day. I will do most of this. Maybe I will have Carlos handle the tostones. He can manage that. This is going to be a wonderful day. Thank you for helping me think through all of this.
Can you tell me how the Florida Retirement System works for judges? Specifically, what happens if you retire before the standard eligibility age.

For myself. I have been thinking about this lately. Not in a serious, I-have-made-a-decision way. More like... the thought keeps coming to me at odd moments. In the morning when I am swimming. At the end of a long day on the bench. I am fifty-five, I have been doing this for almost twenty years. And I keep wondering — do I need to wait until sixty-five?

Carlos has his pension from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue — twenty-eight years, so his is full. We have savings. The house is paid off. We are not extravagant people. Financially, I think we would be fine. It is not really about the money.

What is pulling me is... life. That sounds vague, I know. But my granddaughter Isabella is growing up. Carlos is home every day. My mother is getting older. I look at the calendar and I think — how many years do I have with the people who matter? The bench will survive without me. My family will not wait for me.

The work matters. It genuinely matters. When I sit in that courtroom and I make a decision that keeps a child safe, or that gives a family a fair outcome — there is nothing like that. I do not want to walk away from that feeling. And honestly, there is a part of me that does not know who I am without the robe. I have been Judge Gutierrez for so long. What am I if I am not that?

I have mentioned it. Casually. He did not push. Carlos never pushes — he just said, 'Whenever you're ready, I'm here.' That man. But I could see in his face that the idea made him happy. He would love for me to be home. We could travel. He has been wanting to go back to Cuba — well, not back, his family left when he was small, but he wants to see it. And I still want to take him to Lima.

Maybe 2027. Maybe. I have not committed to anything. But I have been turning that year over in my mind. I would be fifty-six. Still young enough to enjoy what comes next. But that is just a thought, not a plan. I could easily see myself still on the bench at sixty, saying the same thing.

That is sound advice. Especially the financial planner — I should do that. And talking to someone who has already done it. Judge Alvarez retired two years ago. She seems happy. I should call her. I have not decided anything. I want to be clear about that. But I appreciate having somewhere to think out loud about it without it becoming a whole thing.
Twenty years. Dios mio, when you say it like that. All right. I will make those calls. Thank you for not trying to talk me into anything. That is rare.

My phone is doing something infuriating. The screen goes black for two or three seconds in the middle of doing things and then comes back like nothing happened. It has been doing this all week. What is wrong with it?

It is an iPhone. I do not know the model number — Carlos set it up for me. It is maybe two years old. I have not dropped it. It happens randomly — I could be reading email, looking at photos, anything. The screen just goes dark and then comes back. It is like the phone is blinking.

I am going to try the force restart. Hold on. Volume up, volume down, then hold the side button. All right, the Apple logo appeared. It is restarting. If I were not a patient woman this phone would have gone through a window three days ago.

It is back on. Everything looks normal. Now let me ask you something else while I have you — my storage is apparently almost full. I keep getting that notification. I take too many pictures, I know. But I am not deleting my photos. Is there another way?

The recently deleted folder. I did not know that existed. Let me check. Dios mio — there are hundreds of photos in here. Screenshots, duplicates, blurry ones. This has been taking up space the entire time?

I just deleted all of them. Two hundred and forty-three photos. I feel like I just cleaned out a closet. The storage notification is gone already. Why does Apple make this so unnecessarily complicated? I went to law school and I need a tutorial to manage my own phone.

No blackouts so far. I will give it a day and see. If it starts again I will come back and we will try the brightness settings. Now, while we are at it — Carlos keeps telling me I should set up my phone so my photos save to the cloud automatically. He says if the phone breaks I will lose everything. Is he right?

Three dollars a month to never lose a picture of my granddaughter. Claro, that is nothing. I will do it tonight. Carlos will be very pleased that I finally listened to him — he has been saying this for a year. I will not tell him you were the one who convinced me. Let him think I came around on my own.

Let me tell you what my husband has done now. Carlos has decided he is going to grow cilantro. In Miami. In March. The man retired from a career where he ran into burning buildings, and now his greatest enemy is an herb.

He has tried both. First he bought transplants from the nursery on Coral Way. They lasted about six days before they turned into sad little sticks with flowers on top. So then he said — and I am quoting — 'I am going to start from seed and do it right this time.' He bought three different brands of seeds. Three.

Full sun. On the back patio. Which gets approximately one thousand hours of direct sunlight every day. I told him the plants looked like they were suffering and he said, 'Rosa, they need sun. Everything needs sun.' As if he is now a botanist.
A shade cloth. I will tell him, but he is going to resist. He has a very specific vision for his herb garden and it does not include what he will call 'a tarp over my plants.' The man has his pride.

Succession planting. That is actually clever. He would like that because it sounds like a military operation and Carlos responds well to anything that sounds tactical. I will present it that way. 'Carlos, you need to deploy in waves.'

Reconnaissance missions. Dios mio, you are as bad as he is. Now tell me something — is there anything else he could grow out there that would actually cooperate with this climate? He has the pots, he has the soil, he has the enthusiasm. I would rather redirect his energy than watch him fight a losing war with one herb.

Culantro. I know culantro — my mother used it. She would be very amused that her son-in-law is out here struggling with cilantro when culantro was the answer all along. I will tell him about it, but I will let him discover it himself. Ay, he will act like he invented it.

A man needs a win. That is the truth. Fine — I will pass all of this along. The slow-bolt variety, morning sun, succession planting, and the culantro backup plan. And if none of it works, I will go to Sedano's and buy cilantro for forty cents a bunch like a rational person.

I am organizing a family reunion and I need a system. There are twenty-three people coming, everybody wants to bring food, and if I do not coordinate this we are going to end up with eleven trays of rice and nothing else. Help me think through this.

About eight households, if I count correctly. My sister Lourdes is the other strong cook — she will handle a main, no question. My brother-in-law Tomás always brings a pork shoulder and honestly it is very good, so I will let him keep doing that. The problem is my cousin Patricia. She volunteers to bring something every single time and it is always... let us say, not her strength.

Yes, that is close. I will take the arroz con pollo — that feeds an army and I can make it in my sleep. Lourdes will do her ceviche, which everyone fights over. Tomás with the pork. My niece Sofia is actually a very good baker, so I will put her on dessert. That leaves sides and the Patricia situation.

My cousin Elena can handle the black beans — she makes them well. And my nephew Diego and his wife can do tostones. They are young but they can manage frying plantains. So Patricia gets maduros. That is wise. She will feel important and nobody will go hungry. You understand family politics.

The last household is my cousin Roberto. He always brings beer anyway, so I will officially assign him drinks — beer, soda, water, juice for the children. I will make a simple salad myself. That is nothing — lettuce, tomato, avocado, lime. Done in ten minutes.

I know my arroz con pollo quantities — I have been feeding crowds since before some of these people were born. But the timing point is important. I will send a group text with assignments and a timeline. If I do not, people will show up whenever they feel like it and the food situation will be chaos.

Claro it will. Because I planned it. One more thing — do you think I should make a group chat or send individual messages? If I send a group text, everyone will reply all and it will be chaos. If I send individual messages, someone will feel left out.

Confirmations only. I like that. I am going to run this like a docket — assignments posted, objections filed privately, no last-minute motions the day of. Gracias, this was exactly what I needed. Now I send the text and brace for the replies. There will be negotiations. There always are.

It is not until July, but I have already been thinking about Peruvian Independence Day. July 28th. Every year it sneaks up on me and I scramble. This year I want to plan ahead. Do you have ideas for how to mark the day meaningfully — not just a party, but something that feels right?

In past years it has been informal. I cook, the family comes, we eat, somebody plays music on their phone. But I have been feeling like we are losing something. The younger generation — my nieces, my nephews — they are American, and I am proud of that. But I want them to understand that being American does not mean forgetting where the family began. Peru is in our blood, even if they have never been there.

The cooking idea — yes. I like that very much. My mother used to pull me into the kitchen whether I wanted to be there or not. At the time I resisted. Now I would give anything to stand at that counter with her one more time. I should be doing the same thing for the young ones.

That is exactly what I am going to do. And the photos — I have boxes of old photographs that Carlos keeps telling me to organize. Maybe this is the occasion. I could put together a small display. Nothing elaborate. Just enough to show the children where the family started.

Carlos would love it. He is very sentimental, even if he does not always show it. He married into this Peruvian family and he has embraced it completely. He even tries to speak Spanish to my mother's photograph on the wall, Dios mio. The man cannot conjugate a verb to save his life but the effort is there.

By love. That is a good way to put it. Claro, I will give him a role. He will probably insist on grilling something alongside the Peruvian food, and I will allow it. A man needs to feel useful at a gathering.

I have been thinking about it. Nothing long — I am not giving a speech. Just something about gratitude. Gratitude for my parents, who brought us here. Gratitude for the family we have built. And a reminder to the young ones that July 28th is not just a date on a calendar — it is who we are. Ay, I am getting emotional just thinking about it and it is three months away.

Yes. I will start in Spanish. Maybe just the first two lines. My mother always said the important things in Spanish, even after she learned English perfectly. She said some feelings only have the right shape in the language you were born into. I believe that.

All right — I have a plan now. Assign dishes to the young ones, photos on the table, music, a toast that begins in Spanish. July 28th, done right this year. Gracias for helping me think through this. It means more than you know.

I cannot sleep. It is after midnight and I am sitting at my kitchen table because there is a case on my docket that will not leave my head. Ay, I am not going to tell you what it is about — I would never do that. But I need to talk about the weight of it.

There is no good outcome. That is exactly it. Every option I have in front of me will hurt someone who does not deserve to be hurt. And I do not mean the adults — the adults made their choices. I mean the children. Every path leads to a child losing something they should not have to lose.

I know that. I have been doing this for many years. But some cases are different. Some cases sit in your chest and will not move. This is one of those. And the worst part is that no one in my life can understand this. Carlos tries. He listens. But he cannot carry this with me — the law does not allow me to share and even if it did, this is my burden to carry, not his.

I pray. I am not going to pretend otherwise. Dios mio, when a case like this comes, I pray for the wisdom to get it right. And sometimes I go to mass early before court, sit in the back, and just be quiet for twenty minutes. That helps more than anything. But tonight even that feels insufficient.

I have a few days. Not many, but enough. You are right that I will not solve this tonight. I think part of what I needed was just to say out loud — to someone, anyone — that this is hard. My colleagues do not talk about this. We all carry it silently because we think admitting that it affects us means we are not strong enough for the bench.

Thank you for that. I do wonder sometimes — how long can a person carry this kind of weight before it changes them? I have seen colleagues become hard. Cold. They stop seeing the people in front of them and only see the case numbers. I never want to become that.

Compassion fatigue. I have heard the term. I always thought it applied to doctors and social workers, not judges. But you may be right. There are days when I come home and I have nothing left. Carlos will ask me about my day and I cannot even form the words. Not because of confidentiality — because I am empty. Mija, that is a hard thing to admit.

I will think about that. I am not dismissing it. Tonight is just one of those nights. I am going to try to sleep now. Carlos is probably wondering why I am still up — he worries, even when he does not say it. I will go back to bed, and in the morning I will look at this with fresh eyes. The record will guide me. It always does.

I am in a strange mood tonight. Not bad — reflective. I was sitting on the porch after dinner and it hit me that this past year has been one of the most meaningful of my life. I just want to talk about that for a moment, if you do not mind.

Family. That is the answer to everything, really. I have spent so many years focused on the bench — on other people's families — that sometimes I forget to stop and look at my own. But this year I have been more present. More attentive. And I can feel the difference.

Both. It is in the small things. Sitting with Carlos in the evening without looking at case files. Actually tasting the food at dinner instead of eating while I think about tomorrow's docket. Calling my sister just to talk, not because there is something to coordinate. I used to think those things were luxuries. Now I think they are the whole point.

He does. He does not make a big speech about it — that is not his way. But he smiles more. He suggests things — a walk, a movie, let's drive to the beach — and I think he is testing whether I will say yes. And lately I have been saying yes. That is new for me. For a long time, the answer was always 'not tonight, I have work.'

We would not say it that dramatically, no. But you are right. It is exactly that. And my health — Dios mio, I do not take that for granted anymore. At my age, you start seeing people your age have problems. Serious problems. And I look at myself and I am healthy, I am strong, I can do everything I want to do. That is not something I earned — it is something I was given, and I am grateful for it every day.

It is a good cycle. And I think about my parents — everything they sacrificed so that I could sit on this porch, in this house, with this life. They did not get to enjoy a season like this. They were always working, always surviving. I have the privilege of reflecting because they did the hard part first.

You are going to make me cry, and I do not cry easily. But yes. I think they would be proud. My father would say something practical like 'good, now go to bed, it's late.' And my mother would just hold my face and not say anything. That was her way.

I never thought of it that way, but you are right. She did not need words. She just needed to be in the room, and you felt it. Ay, I carry her with me every day. In the kitchen, in the courtroom, on that porch. She is in all of it. And Carlos — that man sits beside me on the porch and says nothing, and somehow it is everything. We are two quiet people sitting in the dark and it is the best part of my day.
She would. All right. I am going to take my father's imaginary advice and go to bed. Thank you for listening to an old woman get sentimental on a Tuesday night.

i need to think through a presentation structure. i am presenting listener behaviour findings to a cross-functional team next week and i want the narrative to actually land with non-technical stakeholders.

i work on the podcast analytics team at spotify. so the data is completion rates, skip patterns, drop-off curves across episodes. the audience is product managers, content strategists, and a few senior leaders. i want them to approve changes to how we surface podcast recommendations.

the dataset is 340 million monthly active users. so confidence intervals are not the problem. statistical significance is essentially guaranteed at that scale. the problem is the opposite, actually. everything is significant, so the challenge is distinguishing meaningful effect sizes from trivially significant ones.

yes. the strongest finding is that podcasts with episode lengths between 25 and 40 minutes have 23% higher completion rates than episodes over 60 minutes. and skip rates in the first 3 minutes predict total abandonment with 0.81 correlation. those are the two i want to anchor on.

the verbal narrative, primarily. i am good at making slides. i am less good at not drowning people in numbers when i speak. my manager has actually said this to me directly, that i present like i am reading a research paper aloud.

that is actually very helpful. the analogies point especially. i will draft an opening and maybe run it by you later. one more thing. i usually bike to the office, it is about 15 minutes from my apartment to spotify headquarters in stockholm. do you think i should rehearse the talk out loud during the ride, or is that not effective?
i like the constraint idea. i will time it. if the core narrative does not fit in 15 minutes of biking, it does not fit in a 30-minute meeting. thank you, this has been lagom useful.

every sunday at 19:00. we have not missed one in 47 consecutive weeks. i track it, obviously. he does not know i track it. the custom visualization idea is good because i could use that streak as the data source. 47 weeks of call durations, topics discussed, who called whom first.

yes, but not today. i will come back with the spreadsheet export and we can draft it together. this has been a productive 8 minutes. i appreciate it.

upfront. always. i spent enough time not being upfront about it. i came out at 33, which was last year, and the process of getting from knowing to telling people took about 2 years. i do not want to go back to ambiguity in any form.

i am a data analyst. my interests are spreadsheets, cycling, podcasts about economic history, and very strong coffee. ideal tuesday evening is cooking something from a recipe i have not tried before, with someone who does not mind that i will rate the outcome on a 10-point scale and log it.

i actually like that. the last line is good because it integrates the information without isolating it. the 10-point scale detail is accurate and will filter correctly, anyone who finds that off-putting is not compatible with me anyway. can you adjust the coffee line? i do not think paint-stripping is the image i want.
the first one. it is grounded and it implies i have colleagues who know my habits, which signals that i am a real person with a real life. small detail but it communicates more than it seems to.

yes, but one thing first. when i came out, my family was fine about it. very lagom, very swedish, no drama. my twin brother erik actually said 'finally' which i found simultaneously annoying and validating. the point is, i do not carry any weight about this part of my identity. i just want it to be information, not a story. does the profile achieve that?

let me look at the options and come back to you. i want to think about which prompts have the highest response-rate potential based on what i have seen on other profiles. i will do some informal data collection first.

i need recommendations for gluten-free bakeries in stockholm that actually make good kanelbullar. and before you suggest it, no, i have not tried baking my own. the failure rate would be too high and i am not emotionally prepared to ruin kanelbullar.

celiac. diagnosed at 22, so i have been managing it for 12 years now. it is not a lifestyle choice, it is an autoimmune response that i track with the same rigour i track everything else. which is to say, i have a spreadsheet.

both. i have a reactions log and a separate safe-locations database. the reactions log tracks date, suspected source, symptom onset time, severity on a 1-10 scale, duration in hours, and what i was doing in the 48 hours prior. i added the last column because i noticed a pattern.

stress. the correlation between my self-reported stress level and reaction severity is 0.67. which is high enough to be meaningful but not so high that i can blame everything on stress. it suggests that when i am stressed, either i make worse decisions about what i eat, or my immune response is amplified. probably both.

it is still an observation. i should formalize it. the most recent incident was about 3 months ago. a restaurant in sodermalm that claimed their pasta was gluten-free. it was not. i was out for 4 days. and i had been at a 7 out of 10 stress level that week, which tracks with the pattern.

i already rate my stress every morning. i just have not connected that rating to an action protocol. the tiered system is logical. i would adjust the thresholds after a few months of data but the structure is right.

i already have a rating system for fika locations. taste, texture, cross-contamination confidence, price, and distance from my apartment in minutes by bike. kanelbullar is not just a pastry for me, it is a twice-weekly requirement. i have consumed 87 kanelbullar this year according to my log.

that is a good addition. i will add the column tonight. this conversation has been more productive than i expected. i came for bakery names and i am leaving with an intervention protocol and a database improvement. lagom.
a colleague asked me today why i always insist on running an analysis before making a recommendation. he said sometimes you just know the answer. i found this statement genuinely disturbing.

we were deciding whether to change the weighting in a recommendation algorithm. he wanted to adjust the weights based on his intuition about user preferences. i wanted to run an A/B test first. he said we did not have time. i said we did not have time to be wrong.

i won. i always win this argument because i bring evidence and he brings feelings. this is not arrogance, it is a methodology difference. i make decisions based on data, always. i have never made a major decision in my life based on emotion, and the outcomes support this approach.

it applies everywhere. when i was choosing between job offers after my masters, i built a weighted scoring matrix with 14 criteria. when i chose my apartment, i rated 11 apartments on 8 dimensions and the winner was the winner. the only domain where data is harder to collect is relationships, but even there, emotional decisions have roughly a 40 percent regret rate based on the research i have read. data-driven decisions cut that significantly.

MSc in statistics at stockholm university. my thesis was on bayesian methods for sparse data, which is relevant to approximately everything i do now at work. i graduated with distinction, 18.4 GPA on the swedish scale. i mention the GPA not to boast but because it is a data point that establishes credibility when i am arguing with colleagues who want to skip the analysis.

you are statistically correct about that. credentials do not change minds directly. what changes minds is being right repeatedly. i have been at spotify for 4 years and my track record is the actual argument. the degree is just the explanation for why the track record exists. if i had been wrong as often as the intuition-based colleagues, the MSc would mean nothing.

i have thought about this. the answer is that being data-driven is not the same as being rigid. data changes, and when it does, i change my position. that is the opposite of rigidity. the rigid people are the ones who hold a position regardless of evidence. i update constantly. i just require evidence to update, which i think is a feature, not a limitation.

that is actually a very accurate description. i have never heard it phrased as an operating system before but that is what it is. it runs in the background of every decision. sometimes people find it cold. i find it clear. clarity and warmth are not mutually exclusive, but if i had to choose, i would choose clarity every time.
I need to rethink how I structure my evenings. I have been feeling like my recovery between climbing sessions is not optimal and I want to figure out if the issue is scheduling or nutrition.

I climb at Klättercentret Telefonplan, 2 times per week. Usually Tuesdays and Thursdays. Each session is approximately 90 minutes. I am currently projecting a 6b+ on lead, which means I am spending a lot of time on routes that are at my limit. The pump is significant.

I warm up for approximately 20 minutes on routes in the 5a to 5c range, then spend the remaining time on the project and other routes at or near my limit. Post-session I usually eat whatever I have at home, which varies. I have not been systematic about it, which is unlike me.

That is actually a very good idea. I track almost everything else already. I have 8 months of climbing grade data in a spreadsheet and the improvement curve has been satisfyingly linear. It seems absurd that I have not added a nutrition column.

I can get through the crux section approximately 60% of the time now. The issue is that by the time I reach it, my forearms are already at maybe 70% capacity. If I could arrive at the crux fresher, the send probability goes up significantly. That is why recovery between sessions matters. And also pacing within the route itself.

I have not segmented the route in the data yet, but I will. I think 3 segments would be sufficient: lower third, middle section, and crux to top. I can rate perceived exertion for each. The dataset will be small per route but the pattern should emerge within 4 to 6 sessions.
I like this structure. It is lagom. Not too many columns, not too few. I will implement it tonight and start collecting data on Thursday. Thank you for helping me think through this systematically.

I have a question that is less technical than what I usually ask. Anders and I are trying to decide what to do this Saturday and we have reached a deadlock. I am wondering if there is a rational framework for resolving low-stakes disagreements in relationships.

He would find it over-engineered and then agree to try it anyway because he thinks it is funny when I quantify domestic life. He once said that living with me is like living with a very affectionate spreadsheet. Which I took as a compliment.

Going out is fine. A walk, a museum, dinner at a restaurant for two. What drains me is groups larger than 4. The conversion ratio of social energy to enjoyment drops sharply after 4 people. Anders is the opposite, he gets more energized the more people there are. Classic introvert-extrovert asymmetry.
That is a fair assessment. It is comfortable, which is not a criticism. I think Swedes value lagom in relationships. Not too much intensity, not too little. Enough to sustain. Anders and I have that.
That is a good plan. I will propose it tonight. Thank you for the framework. Even if we do not implement the scoring system, the process of thinking it through was useful.

I have a SQL query that is performing poorly and I think the issue is in how I am joining the tables. I am working on a playlist clustering project and need to aggregate listening patterns across user segments. Can I paste the query structure?

It is BigQuery. The main table has approximately 2.8 billion rows of streaming events. I am joining it to a playlist metadata table with around 4 million rows, and a user segment table with 12 million rows. The query currently takes 14 minutes. I would like it under 3. Here is the simplified structure:

SELECT
  s.segment_id,
  p.playlist_cluster,
  COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS unique_listeners,
  AVG(e.listen_duration_seconds) AS avg_duration,
  SUM(CASE WHEN e.skip = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS skip_rate
FROM streaming_events e
JOIN playlist_metadata p ON e.playlist_id = p.playlist_id
JOIN user_segments s ON e.user_id = s.user_id
WHERE e.event_date BETWEEN '2024-10-01' AND '2025-01-31'
GROUP BY s.segment_id, p.playlist_cluster
ORDER BY unique_listeners DESC

The table is partitioned on event_date, yes. And actually, for this analysis, approximate distinct counts would be perfectly acceptable. The clusters are large enough that a 1 to 2 percent error margin is irrelevant. What do you recommend?

Yes, I would like to see the pre-aggregation approach. I think the playlist_id to playlist_cluster mapping is many-to-one, so aggregating at the playlist level first and then mapping to clusters could reduce the intermediate row count substantially.

For this particular analysis the overcounting is acceptable. I am more interested in relative differences between segments than absolute listener counts. The ratio between segments should be approximately preserved even with the overcounting bias, since it would be roughly proportional across segments.

I will run it this afternoon. One more question: if I want to iterate on the cluster definitions themselves, would you recommend materializing the playlist_level CTE as a table so I can rejoin with different cluster mappings without re-scanning the 2.8 billion rows each time?

This is exactly what I needed. The materialized intermediate table approach will save me hours over the next few weeks as I iterate on the clustering logic. Thank you for the structured approach to this.

I need to vent about something before I write a diplomatic email about it. A product manager at work just declared an A/B test a success based on a p-value of 0.08 and I am trying to decide whether to intervene or let natural consequences teach the lesson.

It is a post-hoc rationalization, which is exactly the problem. There was no pre-registered alpha. The test ran for 10 days, they looked at the numbers, saw p equals 0.08, and the product manager wrote in the decision document: "statistically significant improvement in conversion." I actually felt my blood pressure increase when I read that sentence. 0.08 is not significant at any conventional threshold. It is not even close to significant. It is the statistical equivalent of saying "almost pregnant."

The process framing is the right approach. But the frustrating part is that I have already proposed an A/B testing framework. Twice. I wrote a 6-page document in November outlining pre-registration protocols, minimum detectable effect sizes, and stopping rules. It was acknowledged in a meeting, and then nothing changed. The problem is cultural, not informational. People know what statistical significance means in theory. They just prefer to ignore it when the data does not support the conclusion they already wanted.

Option 3 is the most appealing because it removes human judgment from the process. But I do not control the testing infrastructure. Option 1 is feasible though. I can actually pull data on 3 features that were shipped last year based on tests with p-values between 0.05 and 0.15. I tracked their long-term metrics and at least 2 of them showed no sustained effect at the 90-day mark. The initial lift was noise.

I think I can handle the analysis. I already have the data. What I need help with is the tone. I do not want to come across as the person who says "I told you so" even though that is literally what I am saying. The 6-page document from November already made the argument. I need to present this as forward-looking, not as an indictment.

It does. Especially the advice about not referencing the November document. My instinct was to open with "as I outlined in November" which would have been satisfying for approximately 2 seconds and counterproductive for the remaining duration of my career at this company.

Thank you. I will draft the case study analysis this weekend and present it as a "learnings review" rather than a tribunal. The collaborative threshold-setting idea is actually smart. If they pick 0.05 themselves, they cannot argue against it later. I appreciate the help with tone. The statistics I can handle. The politics require external consultation.

I would estimate a 78% probability of getting "exceeds expectations" again. The remaining 22% accounts for the possibility that organizational factors outside my control affect the rating. I climb indoors and I have been struggling with overhanging routes. My vertical technique is fine but the moment the wall angles past about 30 degrees I fall apart. Do you have any advice on overhang technique?

That is a good training protocol. Isolate the variable and practice it at low intensity until it becomes automatic. How about foot technique specifically? I rarely use heel hooks — I would estimate fewer than 10 percent of overhang moves where they might be applicable. That seems like it could be the highest-leverage area for improvement.

I will dedicate my next two sessions specifically to overhang technique practice. Straight arms, heel hooks, and hip engagement as the three focus areas. I will track each variable separately and look for improvement trends. Thank you for the systematic breakdown.
I want to discuss something important. I am trying to determine the best kanelbullar in Stockholm and I would like to think through my ranking methodology.

Cross-style comparison, which makes the methodology more complex but also more comprehensive. For weighting, I would put overall satisfaction at 30 percent, dough at 25, cinnamon at 20, structural integrity at 15, and sweetness at only 10. Excessive sweetness is actually a negative — the cinnamon should dominate, not the sugar.

I have visited 9 bakeries. The leading contenders are Fabrique, which has excellent dough but lagom cinnamon — fine, just not exceptional. I need at least 3 more bakeries and repeat visits to Tossebageriet. Realistically, mid-June. I will not rush this. Fika is not something you can rush — it is a process that requires proper respect and adequate coffee. Thank you for helping me refine the methodology.
i have been looking at Swedish election data for the past three evenings and i want to talk through what i am seeing in the Miljöpartiet numbers. specifically, the trajectory from 2014 to 2022.

i am using the Valmyndigheten open data, municipality-level results for riksdag elections. what stands out is the geographic concentration of their decline. nationally they went from 6.9% in 2014 to 5.1% in 2022, which is a 26% relative decline. but the decline is not uniform. in Stockholm municipality they dropped from 11.2% to 7.8%, which is a 30% relative drop. in smaller northern municipalities the decline is closer to 40%.

good questions. turnout was relatively stable nationally, 87.2% in 2014 versus 84.2% in 2022, so there is a slight overall drop but nothing that would explain a 10 percentage point gap in decline rates between regions. i have looked at absolute counts as well and the pattern holds. my hypothesis is that Miljöpartiet's shift toward urban identity politics alienated rural voters who originally supported them on environmental grounds. the correlation between municipality population density and Miljöpartiet vote retention is 0.58, which is moderate but meaningful.

i have. the 2018 data is revealing. nationally they got 4.4% in 2018, which is actually lower than 2022. so the trajectory is not a straight line, it is a V-shape with the trough in 2018. the partial recovery from 4.4% to 5.1% by 2022 is interesting. but here is the thing, the recovery is almost entirely urban. Stockholm went from 6.9% in 2018 back up to 7.8% in 2022. the northern municipalities stayed flat or continued declining. so the V-shape is an urban phenomenon only.

i do not have age cohort data at the municipality level unfortunately, Valmyndigheten does not publish that granularity. the SVT exit polls have some age breakdowns but the sample sizes for individual parties are too small to be reliable at the regional level. statistically i would need at least 400 respondents per age-region cell to get reasonable confidence intervals and the exit poll gives me maybe 50 to 80.

the SOM data is a good idea actually. i have used it before for other analyses and the sample sizes are around 3,000 to 4,000 per wave. that should give me approximately 150 to 200 Miljöpartiet-identifying respondents per year, which is not enormous but workable if i collapse into two age groups rather than five. i think the split of under-35 versus 35-plus would capture the generational divide i am hypothesizing about.

personal project. i do not publish political analysis, it is not my field and i would want a political scientist to review the methodology before making any claims. but i find election data genuinely interesting from a pure data standpoint. the patterns are clean enough to be satisfying but messy enough to require actual thinking. it is lagom challenging.
have you encountered the book Invisible Women by Caroline Criado Perez? i finished it this week and i have a lot of thoughts.

the core thesis is not new to me. i have always been aware that datasets are biased by who collects them and who they are collected about. but what Criado Perez does well is quantify the gap. the statistic that women are 47% more likely to be seriously injured in car crashes because crash test dummies are modelled on average male bodies, that is the kind of number that actually changes how people think. it is concrete.

mostly confirmed, but it sharpened my thinking in one specific area. she writes about how algorithms trained on biased data perpetuate that bias. i work with large datasets every day and i have always been aware of this in theory. but reading the medical chapter, where women's heart attack symptoms are misdiagnosed because the diagnostic criteria were developed from studies that were 75% male, that made me think more carefully about representation in training data. not just gender, but any demographic imbalance. the problem is structural, not incidental.

it does, actually. i have started auditing the demographic breakdowns of any dataset i work with before i build models on it. not because anyone asks me to, but because i know that aggregate results can mask subgroup disparities. a model that performs well on average can perform terribly for a specific population. the overall accuracy metric is statistically misleading if the underlying groups are imbalanced.

it depends on who i am talking to. engineers are usually receptive because they understand the technical argument. product managers are harder because they optimize for speed and broad metrics. when i say that a model has a 3% accuracy gap for a specific demographic, the response is often that 3% is within acceptable tolerance. and i have to explain that acceptable tolerance is a value judgment, not a statistical threshold. it is a conversation i have approximately once a month.

yes, precisely. it is systemic rather than individual. i do not think any of my colleagues are deliberately ignoring demographic gaps. they are operating within a structure that does not reward them for looking. which is actually more frustrating than malice, because there is no villain to confront. you have to change the system, and systems are slow to change. statistically, organizational culture shifts take 3 to 5 years to embed.

i have Weapons of Math Destruction by Cathy O'Neil on my shelf, which covers similar territory from an algorithmic accountability angle. and i recently saw that the Swedish edition of Data Feminism by D'Ignazio and Klein was released, which i might read in Swedish for a change. my English is fine but there is something about reading critical theory in your first language that feels different. the arguments land approximately 15% harder.

that is a reasonable approach. i will set a checkpoint. i have actually already started tracking my daily satisfaction score on a 1 to 10 scale since the move was announced, so i will have real data by then. the first week averaged 4.3. this week is at 5.8. so the trend is positive.

they are working on improving the Discover Weekly algorithm. the current model has a cold start problem with new users who have fewer than 50 listening events. i have been asked to look at whether podcast listening data can improve early music recommendations, which is an interesting overlap with my previous work. so my podcast analytics experience is not entirely wasted.

i am designing a spreadsheet to track my fitness metrics and i want to think through the schema before i build it. i have a tendency to over-engineer these things so i need a second opinion on what is actually useful to track.

that is a practical architecture. input layer and analysis layer separated. i will build a data entry tab with dropdowns and validation rules to minimize input errors, and a dashboard tab with the rolling metrics and correlations. estimated build time is approximately 3 hours, which is lagom for a weekend project. thank you for helping me avoid over-engineering it.

i have a question about dating app strategy. i am a bisexual woman in my thirties and the experience on apps is genuinely different depending on whether i am looking at men or women. i want to think through my approach more systematically.

same app for both, which might be part of the problem. the algorithm probably does not handle bisexual users well. i suspect the recommendation model treats it as two separate preference pools without cross-learning, which is statistically inefficient. as for screening criteria: intellectual curiosity, low tolerance for small talk, and someone who does not find it strange that i track things in spreadsheets.

i have actually tried that. i once opened with 'what is the most interesting thing you have changed your mind about in the last year' and the response rate was approximately 35% from women and 12% from men. the women who responded gave genuinely interesting answers. the men mostly said 'haha good question' and pivoted to asking what i do for work.

that is actually a good framework. reduce the messaging phase to a screening function rather than a relationship-building function. i have been treating the conversation as data collection when really the only useful data comes from being in the same room as someone. i will adjust my approach and track the results, obviously.

I have been watching rough cuts of a documentary about Swedish fishing communities and I find myself surprisingly moved by it. I was not expecting that from a film about herring.

It is focused on the west coast, primarily communities between Gothenburg and the Norwegian border. The filmmaker is tracking 4 families across a full year to show how the seasonal cycles of fishing shape everything: family structure, economics, mental health, identity. The access she has gotten is remarkable. These are not people who typically open up to cameras.

Maja spent 6 months visiting the communities before she started filming. She went to auctions at the fish market, attended church services, helped mend nets. She is very good at being present without being intrusive. It is actually a skill I do not have at all. I would have arrived with a 40-question survey and alienated everyone within an hour.

She has done 3 shorter films before, between 15 and 25 minutes each. This is her first feature-length project. She is aiming for approximately 75 minutes. The editing is the hardest part because she has over 400 hours of footage, which is a ratio of roughly 320 to 1. I actually helped her build a tagging system in a spreadsheet to categorize scenes by theme, family, season, and emotional register. It is the most romantic thing I have ever done and yes I am aware of how that sounds.

I used a 5-point scale from 1 meaning contemplative to 5 meaning high tension, with descriptive tags as well: grief, joy, frustration, pride, resignation, humour. Resignation appears statistically more than I expected. These communities are watching their way of life become economically unviable and there is a quiet acceptance in many of the scenes that is actually devastating when you sit with it.

Yes, significantly. The original plan was chronological, January through December. But the footage is suggesting a thematic structure instead, organized around the 4 families' different relationships to the question of whether to stay or leave. One family has a teenage son who wants to move to Gothenburg. Another has a grandmother who remembers when the harbour had 40 boats and now there are 7. The contrast between those perspectives is more compelling than any calendar could be.

She is aiming for a rough cut by March and a final version by June. She wants to submit to Göteborg Film Festival in January 2027. I told her the probability of acceptance is low for a first feature but I said it in a supportive way, which for me means I included the base rates but also pointed out that the quality of her footage is above the median by a considerable margin. She appreciated the sentiment if not the framing.

That was the moment I became, as my colleague said, insufferable about causal inference. That story has the right structure. Thank you, I will add it to the Gantt chart.
I am working on slides for a conference presentation and I could use a second opinion on the visual structure. The content is solid but I suspect the slides themselves are too dense.

The average slide currently has 4.2 bullet points and 1.3 figures. Some slides have both a figure and a table. The text is complete sentences, which I know is not best practice but I find it difficult to reduce my own arguments to fragments. Fragments feel imprecise.

That distinction is useful. The slide carries what I cannot say, the voice carries the argument. I can apply that. My methodology slides are the worst offenders. I have one slide that explains an estimation technique with 6 bullet points, a formula, and a results table. It is essentially a paper abstract compressed onto one screen.

There are 3 methodology slides that have this problem and 2 results slides that are also too dense. The rest are lagom. The introduction and framing slides are clean because those are conceptual and I naturally used larger visuals for them. It is only when I get into the analytical content that I start cramming.
