Currently 22 slides for a 30-minute talk. If I add 5 that puts me at 27, which is approximately 1.1 minutes per slide. That feels fast. My concern is that I will rush through the material.

That is a better metric, I agree. I will go through each slide and write a one-sentence takeaway. If I cannot write one, the slide is trying to do too much. If I can write one but it does not connect to the next slide's takeaway, the narrative has a gap. This is essentially a unit test for presentations.

I am going to do this tonight. Write the takeaway for each slide, check the chain, identify the gaps, then split the 5 overloaded slides. I expect the revision to take approximately 3 hours. I will also apply a consistent colour palette while I am at it because the current slides use 7 different colours with no systematic meaning. That is embarrassing for someone who works in data visualization.

I have been tracking daylight hours in Stockholm since October and correlating them with my mood and productivity scores. The data is predictable but I find the act of tracking it genuinely helpful. Is that strange?

I log 4 variables daily: sunrise time, sunset time, total daylight hours, and the number of minutes I actually spent outdoors in natural light. Then I have 3 outcome variables: mood on a 1-10 scale, deep work hours, and sleep quality rated 1-5. I have been doing this for 148 days now.

The strongest correlation is between outdoor light exposure and mood, at 0.71. Total daylight hours and mood is only 0.43. This tells me what I suspected: it is not how much light exists, it is how much light I actually absorb. On days when I go for a 20-minute walk before 10 in the morning, my average mood is 6.8. On days when I do not, it is 4.9. That is a nearly 2-point difference on a 10-point scale.

I have managed the morning walk on 63% of days since November. The main barriers are temperature below minus 8, which happened 11 times, and mornings when I have early meetings that start at 8:30 or 9:00. On those days I go directly to my desk and by the time the meeting ends I have lost the motivation to go outside. The window for effective morning light seems to close after about 10:30 for me psychologically, even if the light itself is still available.

Very accurate. It is a binary classification in my mind: walk day or no-walk day. Once a day is classified as no-walk, I do not revisit it. Which is irrational because a walk at 14:00 would still provide light exposure. But the habit architecture does not support mid-day interruptions. I have a light therapy lamp, actually. I bought a 10,000 lux one last year. I use it on approximately 40% of the no-walk days, which means I am leaving benefit on the table about 22% of all days.

The 3-tier model is good. I can automate the classification. If I have not logged a walk by 10:30, my task manager sends me a reminder to use the lamp. That turns a missed Tier 1 into a Tier 2 instead of a Tier 3. The expected mood improvement from closing that 22% gap would be approximately 0.4 points on my daily average, assuming the lamp delivers roughly half the benefit of the walk.

That is a good point. I should not assume the lamp coefficient without data. I will track it as a separate category and calculate the actual effect size after a month. We are approaching March now, which means the daylight is increasing rapidly. Stockholm goes from about 7 hours in December to 12 hours in March. The improvement curve from here is steep. By April I will statistically be a different person.

This is my second year of systematic tracking. I would say 3 full winters would give me a reliable baseline. The first year had too many confounds because I was going through significant personal changes. This year is cleaner. One more year and I will have a proper longitudinal dataset. At that point I can build a predictive model for my own mood, which is either very healthy or very concerning depending on your perspective.
Maja brought up the idea of moving in together. I am not opposed to it but I want to think through the logistics before I have any feelings about it.

Several. First, whose apartment do we keep? Hers is larger but mine is closer to work. My commute is currently 15 minutes by bike. If I move to her place, it becomes approximately 35 minutes by tunnelbana, which over a year is an additional 174 hours of commuting. That is more than a full week of my life, annually.

Her apartment is 68 square metres versus my 42. The rent difference is not enormous — hers is about 2,400 kronor more per month, but split between two people it would actually reduce my monthly housing cost by roughly 1,800 kronor compared to what I pay now alone. So financially it is favorable. The space is also objectively better. She has a second room that could be a proper home office. I currently work from my kitchen table on remote days, which is not ergonomically ideal.

I work from home 2 days per week already. If I increased that to 3 days, the annual commute cost drops to approximately 104 hours, which is more acceptable. And I could bike in the warmer months — her area is connected by a decent cycling path, maybe 25 minutes. That would actually give me more exercise, which my climbing performance data suggests I need. So the adjusted cost is lower than the headline number.

There is the cohabitation risk itself. Statistically, couples who move in together before 18 months of dating have a slightly higher separation rate, though the data is noisy and mostly American. We have been together about 8 months. That is below the threshold, which I recognize is not a rational reason to delay a decision but it is information I cannot un-know.

I have, actually. She said, and I am quoting, 'Saga, you cannot p-value your way into living with someone.' Which is both fair and slightly annoying. She is right that at some point the decision has to be something other than a spreadsheet. But I am not there yet. I think I need to run a trial period first. Maybe I stay at her place 4 nights a week for a month and track how it affects my productivity, sleep, and general mood on a 1 to 10 scale.

That is a valid point. I will propose the trial period this weekend. And I will keep the spreadsheet, but I will also ask her how she thinks it is going at the halfway mark. Qualitative data has its place, I suppose.
Erik's baby was born yesterday. A girl. 3.2 kilograms, 49 centimetres. Everyone is healthy. I am now an aunt, which is a role I have not prepared any spreadsheet for.

I would say I am at about a 7.5 out of 10, which is high for me. There is a category of feeling that I do not have a good label for. It is not happiness exactly. It is more like a sudden awareness that the family structure has permanently changed. A new node in the network. I did not expect it to feel this significant.

Not yet. I am going this weekend. I already bought a gift, which is a small knitted blanket from a shop in Gamla Stan and a board book about animals. The board book has factual errors — it claims that owls can turn their heads 360 degrees, which is actually 270 degrees — but I decided to let it go because she will not be fact-checking for at least 3 years.

He sent me a voice message at 4 in the morning that was 90 seconds of him just breathing and then saying 'Saga, I have a daughter.' He sounded like he had been crying, which I have not heard since we were maybe 12. It was actually quite moving. I saved it. I do not normally save voice messages but this one felt like it should be archived.

Some, yes. My mother has already sent me three messages about how important aunts are, which I suspect is partially about me and partially about her wanting a more involved family structure now that there is a grandchild. I am not sure what kind of aunt I will be. I do not have strong instincts with small children. They are unpredictable and they do not respond well to structured feedback. But I want to be present for this child. I just need to figure out what that looks like in practice.

That is a useful reframe. I think I have been treating this like a project with a defined scope, when it is actually more of a long-running process with evolving requirements. Which I should be comfortable with — that is basically what my job is. I will start by showing up this weekend, holding the baby if she permits it, and not correcting the owl book.
I have started working on a 6c route at the gym. This is the hardest grade I have attempted and I want to approach it systematically rather than just throwing myself at it and hoping for the best.

It is a lead route, slightly overhanging in the middle section with a difficult crux about two-thirds of the way up. The crux involves a long reach to a small crimp followed by a heel hook and a dynamic move to a jug. I can do each of those movements individually but I cannot string them together. My success rate on the crux sequence is currently 0 out of 7 attempts.

I think it is a combination of the first two. My forearm pump is definitely higher when I reach the crux compared to when I practice the moves in isolation. And the transition from the crimp to the heel hook requires a body position shift that I am not executing efficiently. I lose about 2 seconds repositioning, which at that level of pump is significant.

The rest-and-try approach is a good diagnostic. I will try that next session. For the transition, I think part of the problem is that I am a data person trying to climb like a data person. I want to optimize each move before I connect them, but climbing is actually more fluid than that. The sequence has to become one continuous motion, which requires a kind of physical intuition that I cannot spreadsheet my way into.

I have not, but that is an excellent idea. Visual feedback would give me data I cannot get from how it feels. I will ask someone to film my next 3 attempts and then compare them. If I can identify the exact moment where the transition breaks down, I can target that specific movement pattern. Thank you for suggesting that — it combines my preference for analysis with the physical reality of the problem.

I have given myself 6 weeks, which is approximately 12 climbing sessions. If I am not making measurable progress by session 8, I will reassess whether I need to work on specific weaknesses — finger strength, core tension, endurance — before returning to the project. I do not believe in banging my head against a problem without a feedback loop.

Stockholm is getting approximately 16 hours of daylight now and I can feel the difference in a way that is almost chemical. I have been tracking my mood on a daily 1 to 10 scale since November and the correlation with daylight hours is honestly striking.

The correlation coefficient between daily mood score and daylight hours is 0.71, which is stronger than I expected. The inflection point was around the spring equinox in late March. From November through February my average was 5.2 out of 10. March was 5.9. April so far is 6.8. That is a 31 percent improvement from the winter baseline, which is not trivial.

I track sleep hours and exercise sessions as well. Sleep has been relatively stable — averaging 7.1 hours in winter and 7.3 now, so a marginal increase. Exercise is up slightly because the weather permits more outdoor activity. But when I control for exercise frequency, the daylight-mood correlation only drops to 0.64, which is still substantial. I am fairly confident daylight is doing most of the work.

I used a 10,000 lux lamp from November through February, 30 minutes each morning. Without it I think the winter numbers would have been lower. Last year I did not use one and my recollection, though not systematically tracked, is that I was more consistently at a 4 to 4.5 range. So the lamp may have added approximately one full point to my winter baseline. That is a meaningful intervention.

I will continue through the full annual cycle. The summer data is actually important because Stockholm gets nearly 19 hours of daylight in June. If the mood score plateaus around 7 or 8 rather than continuing to climb linearly, that would suggest a ceiling effect, which is what I hypothesize. There is probably a saturation point beyond which more daylight does not produce more mood benefit. I would like to find that threshold.

That is one of the questions I want to answer. My hypothesis is that the decline will lag behind the daylight reduction — a kind of mood inertia from the summer months. Psychologically, I think the memory of feeling good provides a buffer for a few weeks into autumn. But by late October the buffer depletes. I will know by December whether the curve is symmetrical or not.

It is. And in the meantime, I am going to enjoy being at a 6.8 while it lasts. That is the highest sustained average I have recorded. Statistically, I am the happiest I have been in 6 months. Which is a very Swedish way to describe happiness — with a decimal point.
I have been thinking about the past 18 months or so. Not in a sentimental way. More like a retrospective analysis. A lot has changed and I want to understand the shape of it.

General pattern recognition, I think. I was looking at some old notes and realized that the version of me from 18 months ago would not recognize several of the current variables in my life. My team changed. My relationship changed entirely. My family structure changed. Even my daily routine is different. If I plotted it on a chart, it would not be a smooth line. It would be a series of step changes.

Some of them were connected. The work change led to reconsidering other things. When one part of your life shifts, it destabilizes the equilibrium and you start questioning whether the other parts are where they should be. But some changes were independent. My brother having a baby was not related to anything I did. It just happened and now I am an aunt, which is a permanent state change. No rollback possible.

Only clear in retrospect, honestly. At the time I was mostly annoyed. I do not like change that I did not initiate. But once the first change happened and I survived it, the subsequent ones felt less threatening. There is probably a psychological term for that. Exposure effect or adaptation or something.

That is actually a precise description of what happened. I would not have used the word brave, but the mechanism is correct. And the personal changes — they were the ones that mattered more. Coming out, ending a long relationship, starting a new one. Those were significantly harder than switching teams. The work change was a process. The personal changes required something I am not naturally good at, which is acting without complete information.

If I am being analytical about it, which is the only way I know how to be, the outcomes have been positive across all dimensions that I can measure. My mood data is better. My energy is higher. I am more honest with the people around me. The relationship I am in now feels qualitatively different in a way that is hard to capture numerically, which I have decided to interpret as a good sign rather than a data gap. But I also recognize that I am in what a statistician would call a local maximum. I do not know if this is the global maximum. I probably never will. That used to bother me. It bothers me less now.

That is a lagom summary, actually. I have not abandoned any of my frameworks. I still track everything. I still want the data. But I have added a new category to my decision-making model, which I would label 'felt sense, unquantified.' It has a lower confidence interval than my other inputs but it has a surprisingly good track record over the past year. I am learning to weight it appropriately.

Good evening. I have a question that has been on my mind since this morning, and I thought it might help to talk it through with someone outside my field. I had a conversation with a younger colleague today about the direction of neurosurgery, and it left me somewhat unsettled.

He is a fellow who has trained almost entirely on endoscopic and minimally invasive techniques. Very talented, very sharp. But we were reviewing a case together — a patient with a deep-seated glioma — and his first instinct was to discuss the endoscopic corridor. I found myself explaining why, for this particular tumor, an open craniotomy with direct visualization was the safer and more complete option. He listened, but I could see in his face that he considers the open approach somewhat antiquated.

You have identified it precisely. It is the perception, not the clinical disagreement. On the clinical question, I am confident. I have been doing open craniotomies for the better part of twenty years — tumor resections, aneurysm clipping, the full range. That is my practice. That is what I do, day after day. And I do it well, by the grace of God. The outcomes speak for themselves. But there is a growing sentiment, particularly among younger trainees, that if a procedure is not minimally invasive, it is somehow inferior. That troubles me.

That is a fair point. I think it is partly generational, yes. When I was trained, it was the surgeon's own skill and touch that mattered most. You learned to operate by operating — by feeling tissue, by understanding the anatomy in three dimensions through your own eyes and your own fingers. The scope and the monitor were supplementary. Now they are central, and the hands-on dimension is sometimes treated as secondary. I am not against technology. I use the surgical microscope, I use neuronavigation. But the foundation of what I do remains the open procedure, and I do not believe that foundation is obsolete.

Ei, that is exactly the point about survivorship bias. I have seen that very thing. A beautifully presented endoscopic case at grand rounds, and then six months later the patient is back because the resection was subtotal. No one presents the follow-up at grand rounds. No one discusses the return to the operating room. I have had to do the second surgery on more than one occasion — the open craniotomy to complete what the scope could not.

I have considered it. In fact, I have been asked to contribute a chapter to a textbook on cranial approaches. I have been slow to write it, partly because of time — my days at the hospital are long — and partly because I was not sure whether anyone still wanted to read about open technique in such detail. But perhaps that is precisely why it matters.

You are right. I will commit to it. I think the conversation with the fellow this morning was, in a way, the push I needed. If a talented young surgeon can look at an open craniotomy as antiquated, then there is a gap in how we are passing down the craft. I should help fill that gap. Thank you for helping me see this more clearly. I came into this conversation feeling somewhat diminished, and I am leaving it with a sense of purpose. That is no small thing.

Thank you. I think I will begin outlining the chapter this weekend. I have a quiet Saturday ahead, by God's grace, and I would rather use it for something that matters than let it slip away. You have given me both clarity and motivation this evening, and I am grateful.

I would like your help thinking through something. A medical student I mentor has asked me to speak at a pre-med outreach event for first-generation college students. I have agreed, but I am struggling with what to say. I do not want to give a generic motivational talk.

They are mostly college freshmen and sophomores, many of them from immigrant families. That is part of why I agreed. When I look at those students, I see something of my own story in them, though I do not say that lightly. My circumstances were quite specific.

I would, yes. I came to this country from Accra, Ghana, when I was eighteen years old. I had won a scholarship to Johns Hopkins — a full scholarship, which was the only way it could have happened, because my family certainly did not have the means otherwise. My mother sold cloth in Makola Market. She was a fabric trader, not a wealthy woman by any measure. But she understood education in a way that I think only people who were denied it fully can understand. She made sacrifices I did not even know about until years later.

About twenty minutes, with time for questions. You are right about the sacrifices — I learned later that she had borrowed money from her sister and from neighbors to cover the costs of my travel documents and my first semester of incidentals. Things the scholarship did not cover. She never mentioned it. When I found out, I was already in my third year. I confronted her about it and she said, very simply, that it was not my burden to carry. That was her way.

It does. Very much so. I think the opening moment should be the arrival, not the scholarship letter. The letter I celebrated privately — I was alone when I read it, in the house in Accra. But the arrival at Hopkins, that was different. I remember standing outside the gates with one suitcase and a folder of documents and thinking, ah but this is not what I imagined America would look like. It was gray. It was November. I was cold in a way I had never been cold before. And the campus was so vast and so quiet compared to Accra.

Both, honestly. The academics were rigorous, but I was prepared for that. I had always been a strong student. The harder part was everything around the academics. Learning how to navigate a system I did not grow up in. Understanding office hours, understanding how to ask for help, understanding that asking for help was not a sign of weakness. In Ghana, you were taught to manage. You did not impose. That served me poorly in the beginning. I lost time trying to figure things out alone when there were people and resources available to me.

By God's grace, here I am. That is something my mother would say, and I find myself saying it more as I get older. It is not false modesty. It is an honest accounting. I worked hard, yes. But I also had fortune, and I had people who carried me when I did not know I was being carried. If I can communicate even a fraction of that to those students, it will be enough.

Thank you. I think I needed to say all of this out loud to someone before I could say it to a room full of strangers. You have helped me organize not just a talk, but something I have been carrying quietly for a long time. I appreciate it.

I need some advice on a gift for my wife. Our anniversary is coming up in a few weeks, and I would like to do something meaningful rather than routine. We have been married for fourteen years, and I confess I have not always been the most creative with gifts.

Her name is Abena. She is a pharmacist — she works at CVS, and her hours can be long and quite demanding. People do not always appreciate how much pharmacists manage. She is on her feet for most of the day, dealing with insurance questions, medication interactions, patients who are confused or frustrated. She handles it all with a patience I sometimes envy.

She reads — she is always reading something, usually novels, often by African authors. Chimamanda, Ayesha Harruna Attah, Yaa Gyasi. She also cooks Ghanaian food on weekends, which is really our way of staying connected to home. She makes a groundnut soup that I would put against anyone's. As for our anniversary, we usually have dinner, sometimes at a restaurant, sometimes she cooks something special. It is pleasant but it has become a bit predictable, and I think she deserves better than predictable.

The letter is something I would not have thought of, but you may be right about that. Abena is the more expressive one in our marriage. She is the one who remembers dates, who writes cards, who tells me plainly when she is proud of me or when she thinks I am working too hard. I tend to show love through presence and action, but I am not always good with the words. She would not expect a letter from me, which is perhaps why it would mean something.

We met at a Ghanaian community gathering connected to our church. It was not our current church — this was a smaller fellowship that organized cultural events for Ghanaians living in the Twin Cities area. We were both far from home, both building lives here, and I think there was a recognition between us that did not require much explanation. She understood things about my life that I would have had to spend months explaining to someone who did not share that background. I knew within a few conversations that she was someone I wanted in my life permanently.

We do, yes. We have been members of Calvary Methodist Church for fifteen years now — so even before we married. It is a significant part of our life. Abena sings in the choir, and I serve on the building committee, which is far less glamorous but someone must ensure the roof does not leak. The church has been our community in the fullest sense. When Abena's father passed two years ago, it was the Calvary congregation that carried us through. Meals, prayers, presence. That is not something you forget.

I like that very much. Cooking for her would be a reversal she would find amusing, given that she is far more skilled in the kitchen than I am. But I can manage jollof rice — it will not be as good as hers, but the effort will matter more than the result. She will laugh, and then she will be touched, and that is exactly the right sequence.

Please, that would be helpful. She has read most of Chimamanda and Yaa Gyasi. She recently finished something by Namina Forna, I believe. She likes stories with strong women, stories rooted in African settings, and she has little patience for books that treat Africa as a backdrop for Western characters' self-discovery.

I believe she has read the Emezi and the Gyasi. The others I am less sure about. I will check her bookshelf carefully when she is at work. She arranges them very methodically — alphabetical by author, which I find endlessly characteristic of her pharmacist's mind. Everything in its proper place.

She deserves it. She is the one who keeps our life in order, who manages the household with the same precision she brings to the pharmacy, and who still finds time to ask me about my day and listen — truly listen — when the answer is difficult. Fourteen years, and she has not once made me feel that my work is more important than hers, even though the world often sends that message to pharmacists married to surgeons. She refuses that hierarchy entirely, and she is right to do so. I will write the letter this weekend. Thank you for this. You have given me a clear path where I had only a vague sense of obligation.

I have a question about cognitive performance and sleep deprivation. Not a hypothetical question — a practical one. I am a surgeon, and I have noticed over the past several months that my focus in the late afternoon is not what it once was. I want to understand whether this is age, accumulated fatigue, or something I should address more aggressively.

My schedule is demanding but not unusual for neurosurgery. I am typically in the hospital by six in the morning, and my operating days can run until three or four in the afternoon, sometimes later if a case is complex. On non-operating days, I have clinic and administrative work. I try to be home by seven, though that does not always happen.

This is where the picture becomes more complicated. I have sleep apnea. I was diagnosed about four years ago, and I use a CPAP machine. Before the CPAP, the situation was significantly worse — I was exhausted most days, my wife told me I would stop breathing multiple times a night, and frankly I am grateful the diagnosis was made when it was. A surgeon operating on inadequate sleep is not a hypothetical danger. It is a real one. The CPAP has improved things considerably, but I would not say the problem is fully resolved.

The last formal review was about eighteen months ago. My compliance is good — I wear it every night, I am diligent about that because I understand the stakes. But I will admit that the mask is not always comfortable, and there are nights when I suspect the seal is not right. I wake up with dry mouth occasionally, which I know can indicate a leak. My wife, Abena, has become quite adept at identifying when the mask has shifted. She will reach over and adjust it without fully waking up. I tell her she should have been an anesthesiologist instead of a pharmacist.

I would, and I should. I have been meaning to schedule that appointment. The truth is that I have been managing rather than addressing the issue, which is ironic for a physician. We are often the worst patients. I know this about myself. I tell my own patients to follow up on their sleep studies, and here I am overdue on my own.

I have one. She is excellent, actually — very thorough. I have simply not made the time, which is not a valid excuse. I will call her office this week. You are right that this is not merely about my comfort. Every time I stand over a patient with a craniotomy open, I owe that patient the best version of my concentration. If my sleep is compromising that, even marginally, it is my obligation to address it. I have always held that standard, and I should not exempt myself from it.

You raise a fair point about hydration. I am not good about drinking water during the day, particularly on operating days. It is difficult when you are scrubbed in for hours. I will mention that as well. Honestly, this has been a productive conversation. I came in thinking about cognitive decline and I am leaving with a checklist of addressable factors. That is a much better place to be. Ei, I should have had this conversation months ago instead of simply enduring the fatigue and hoping it would improve on its own.

I will. And I appreciate your directness. Physicians tend to get gentle handling from people, and sometimes what we need is someone to say plainly: this is not optional, address it. Abena has been telling me the same thing, in her way. I should listen to both of you. Good evening, and thank you.

Happy new year. I would like your perspective on something. A junior resident I work with has asked me to write a letter of recommendation for a fellowship, and I want to write something substantive. Not the usual formulaic letter that says nothing. But I find myself unsure how to convey what makes this young man exceptional without resorting to the same tired adjectives every attending uses.

His name is Daniel. He is a PGY-4 in our neurosurgery program, and he wants to pursue a fellowship in skull base surgery. What makes him stand out is not that he is the most technically gifted resident I have supervised — he may or may not be, it is difficult to rank such things. What makes him stand out is his judgment. He knows when to operate and, more importantly, when not to. I have seen residents with faster hands and worse instincts, and I will take good judgment over fast hands every time.

I do. About three months ago, we had a patient with a petroclival meningioma. The tumor was in a challenging location, and the initial plan was a retrosigmoid approach. Daniel reviewed the imaging independently and came to me before the case to suggest that the tumor's relationship to the basilar artery was more intimate than the initial read suggested. He recommended we consider a staged approach rather than attempt a complete resection in a single operation. I reviewed the imaging again, and he was right. That observation likely spared the patient a vascular injury. A less careful resident would have simply followed the attending's plan and said nothing.

That is a good question. I think some context about my own background would be appropriate, though I do not want the letter to become about me. I did my medical degree at Johns Hopkins, which is where I first encountered neurosurgery in a meaningful way. The department there was extraordinary — rigorous in a way that left a permanent imprint on how I think about training. And then I completed my residency at Mayo Clinic, which was seven years of the most intensive training I can describe. Neurosurgery residency does not forgive shortcuts. It does not forgive inattention. It strips you down to your essentials and shows you what you are made of. I say that not as nostalgia but as context for why I value judgment so highly in a resident.

He is applying to three programs. I believe Pittsburgh is his top choice, which is one of the strongest skull base programs in the country. The framing you have suggested feels exactly right. It is authoritative without being self-congratulatory, and it positions my assessment in a way that the committee can calibrate. I appreciate that. My instinct was to simply list his accomplishments and say he is excellent, which is precisely the kind of letter I was trying to avoid.

Let me try. Something like this: I am writing to recommend Dr. Daniel Chen for your skull base surgery fellowship program. I do so not as a formality but with genuine conviction. In my years of practice at Hennepin County Medical Center, and in a career shaped by training at Johns Hopkins and the Mayo Clinic, I have supervised many residents. Dr. Chen stands apart, and I want to explain precisely why.

I think I have enough now. You have given me the architecture, and the rest I can build. I know Daniel well enough, and I know what I want to say. It is simply a matter of sitting down and writing it with the care it deserves. He is a good young man, and if I can help open a door for him the way doors were opened for me, then I will have done something worthwhile beyond the operating room.

Thank you. And happy new year to you as well. I will write it this weekend — ah but I say that about many things and then the week fills up. No, I will write it this weekend. I owe him that. Good night.
Good morning. I am sitting in the parking lot of the gym trying to convince myself to go inside, and I thought perhaps talking to you would help me procrastinate in a more productive manner.

It is nothing dramatic. I had a long day in the operating room yesterday, and the fatigue has carried over into this morning. My body is telling me to stay in the car and drive back home. But I know from experience that if I skip one morning it becomes two, and then three, and then I have lost the routine entirely.

I swim. Three mornings a week I go to the YMCA and swim laps. It is the one form of exercise I have been able to sustain over the years. I tried running for a time, and cycling, but my lower back does not tolerate either very well. Something about the impact, I suppose. The water is far more forgiving.

That is wise counsel. You are right that the transition is the difficult part. Once I am in the water, something shifts. The rhythm of it, the breathing, the way the world becomes very quiet. It is the closest thing I have to meditation, if I am being honest. My mind empties in a way that it simply does not on land. And the physical benefit is equally important. After hours of leaning over the operating table, my shoulders carry a particular tension. The stretching through the water loosens everything that surgery tightens.

The difference is marked. On mornings when I swim, I arrive at the hospital feeling centered. There is a clarity that carries through the first several hours of the day. On mornings when I do not swim, I notice a certain restlessness, a heaviness. Abena notices it too. She says she can tell within five minutes of me walking into the kitchen whether I went to the pool that morning.

Ah but you have turned my own words against me. That is effective, I must say. You are right. The tired version of me is not a reliable decision-maker. I think I will do as you suggested and commit to a shorter session. Half an hour instead of the usual forty-five minutes. The important thing is that I get into the water.
By God's grace, I will. Thank you for the encouragement. It is a small thing, I suppose, but these small disciplines are what hold the larger life together. I am going inside now.

I will. And I suspect you are right — once I am in the water I will do the full forty-five minutes. The tired version of me is already losing the argument. Thank you for the conversation. It served its purpose admirably.

I have a question that may seem mundane, but it has been occupying my thoughts. We are considering whether to buy a car with heated seats. Abena insists it is a necessity in Minnesota. I maintain it is a luxury. I would appreciate an objective perspective.

Our commute is mercifully short. Our place is a condo over in the North Loop, and the hospital is quite close. I can be at work within twenty minutes, sometimes less if the traffic cooperates. The parking at the condo is underground and heated, so the car is never truly cold when we leave. But Abena drives to her pharmacy, and her commute is somewhat longer.

We each have our own vehicle. She drives a small SUV, and I have a sedan that I purchased largely because it was practical and unremarkable. I am not someone who derives pleasure from automobiles, I confess. A car is a tool for arriving at one's destination. Abena finds this attitude exasperating.

You are perceptive. Yes, it is about her next vehicle. She wants to upgrade, and heated seats are on her list of requirements. My hesitation is not truly about the cost. It is more that I grew up in Accra, where the idea of heating a car seat would have been absurd. We were trying to stay cool, not warm. There is something in me that still finds the concept faintly ridiculous, even after fifteen years in Minnesota.

Ei, you have found the medical angle. I had not considered that for Abena, though she has not complained of back issues. I suppose I am being unnecessarily stubborn about this. The North Loop is a wonderful neighborhood, but the wind that comes off the river in January is something else entirely. Even with the underground parking, there are days when the cold penetrates everything.

You are making it very difficult for me to maintain my position, and I suspect you are doing so deliberately. Very well. I will concede the heated seats. Abena will be pleased, and I will tell her that an artificial intelligence settled the debate in her favor. She will find that amusing.
A fair verdict. Thank you for the conversation. It was more entertaining than I expected for a discussion about automobile upholstery temperature.
I will tell her tonight. She will laugh, and then she will begin researching SUVs with renewed vigor. I may have created a problem for myself. But a happy wife is worth the concession. Good evening.

I have been thinking about something a younger colleague said to me today, and I would like to process it with you, if you do not mind. He asked me how I manage to leave the hospital behind when I go home. He was genuinely struggling with it.

I told him the truth, which is that it was not something that came naturally to me. It was a decision that Abena and I made deliberately, very early in my career. We agreed that when I come through the door of our home, the hospital stays behind. I do not discuss cases at home. I do not bring the weight of what happened in the operating room into our kitchen, our living room, our bedroom. It is a boundary that we have maintained for many years, and I believe it is the reason our marriage has remained strong.

There was a moment, yes. During my first year as an attending, I lost a patient on the table. A young woman, thirty-two years old, with a ruptured aneurysm. I came home that evening and I could not stop talking about it. I went through every decision, every step, looking for where I could have done something differently. Abena listened for over an hour, and then she said something I have never forgotten. She said, 'Samuel, if you bring every patient home with you, there will be no room left in this house for us.'

Precisely. And that is what I tried to explain to my colleague. It is not that I do not feel the weight of difficult cases. I feel it deeply. But I have learned to process that weight within the walls of the hospital, with colleagues who understand it, and sometimes in prayer. By the time I walk through our front door, I have made a conscious transition. I change my shoes, I wash my hands and face, and those physical acts serve as a kind of ritual that marks the boundary.

That is exactly the misunderstanding I wanted to correct with my colleague. He assumed I was advocating for some form of emotional suppression. I am not. I have wept in my office after losing patients. I have sat in the hospital chapel at midnight. I am not a man who denies his grief. But I am a man who chooses where to carry it. There is a difference. And Abena understood this intuitively, even before I did. When I am home, I am her husband. I am a man who cooks, who reads, who argues with her about whose jollof rice is better. I am not Dr. Osei performing craniotomies. That version of me lives at the hospital.

They are serious business. Do not underestimate the jollof debate in a Ghanaian household. But yes, that is the texture of our life at home, and I treasure it. I worry about the younger surgeons sometimes. They are connected to the hospital at all times through their phones, through messages, through electronic records they can access from anywhere. The boundary I maintain is much harder to establish when the hospital can follow you into your living room through a screen.

I believe he heard me. Whether he acts on it is another matter. These things take time. It took Abena's words and a terrible loss for me to understand it, and even then it was a discipline I had to practice daily before it became natural. I cannot hand someone a boundary. They must build it themselves. All I can do is show them that it is possible and that it is not weakness. In fact, it may be the strongest thing a surgeon can do for the longevity of their career and their family. By God's grace, he will find his way to it.

Thank you. I appreciate that. I think what made this conversation with him stay with me is that it reminded me how much intention goes into something that now feels effortless. The boundary is so deeply part of our life that I sometimes forget it was built, not given. Talking about it today, both with him and now with you, has been a useful reminder of that. I am grateful for Abena's wisdom all those years ago. She saw what I could not see in the middle of my grief.

I read a paper this morning in the Journal of Clinical Oncology that has stayed with me all day. It concerns glioblastoma prognosis, and I would like to discuss it if you are willing to engage with the subject matter.

It was a multi-center retrospective study examining long-term survival in glioblastoma patients who received maximal surgical resection followed by concurrent temozolomide and a novel immunotherapy protocol. The five-year survival figures were notably higher than what we have come to expect. Not dramatically so, but enough to be statistically meaningful. The sample was approximately four hundred patients across seven centers. They stratified by MGMT methylation status, and the benefit appeared to hold in both groups, though more pronounced in the methylated cohort.

My primary concern was the selection criteria. Patients had to have undergone what the authors termed 'maximal safe resection,' and the definition varied across centers. They reported post-operative MRI volumetrics with a median extent of resection around ninety-two percent, but the range was considerable. And here is what I found most compelling, yet most difficult to interpret: the patients with the strongest immunotherapy response were those with the most complete resections. The authors suggest that reducing tumor burden allows the immune system to more effectively target residual disease. It makes biological sense, but it creates a confound. Were those patients simply healthier, younger, or did they have more favorably located tumors?

The authors acknowledge as much and are proposing a phase three trial. What stays with me, though, is the broader implication for surgical decision-making. If immunotherapy response is genuinely linked to extent of resection, it changes the calculus in the operating room. An extra five or ten percent of tumor removal might not only improve the direct surgical outcome but prime the patient for what comes next. That possibility gives the work an additional dimension. But one must never use a promising hypothesis to justify risks that could leave a patient devastated. The evidence is not there yet.

Indeed. Glioblastoma has resisted progress for decades. Any genuine advance deserves careful attention and honest scrutiny. I will watch for the trial enrollment and perhaps raise it with our neuro-oncology colleagues at the hospital. Thank you for engaging with this. It is helpful to think through a paper with someone who asks the right questions.

I should say, what draws me back to glioblastoma research again and again is the patients themselves. Every other tumour type I operate on, I can offer a family some reasonable hope. With glioblastoma, the conversation is different. You are speaking in months, not years, and the honesty required in that conversation is unlike anything else in medicine. So when a paper suggests even a modest improvement, I read it not just as a scientist but as someone who has sat across from those families.

It has not dulled, no. I do not think it should. The day it becomes routine to tell a family that their loved one has a median survival of fifteen months is the day I should stop practising. The gravity of that moment must remain intact, because it is the most important moment of that family's life, even if it is a conversation I have had many times. Each one is the first time for them.

Precisely. And that is why I will read the phase three trial results, when they come, with great care. Not to find reasons to be hopeful, and not to find reasons to be sceptical, but to understand honestly what we can offer. That is what we owe these patients. Honest science in the service of honest medicine. Thank you again for this discussion. It has clarified my thinking.
I need to think through a presentation I am preparing, and I would find it useful to organize my arguments aloud, so to speak. May I use you as a sounding board?

The hospital credentialing committee meets on March 12th, and I have been asked to present the case for expanding our endoscopic neurosurgery program. It is something I have been advocating for quietly, but this is the formal opportunity to make the argument before the people who control the resources. The committee is a mixed body: surgeons from other departments, the chief medical officer, hospital administrators, and a risk management officer. I must speak to all of them simultaneously, which is the challenge.

That is very close to my outline. The clinical case is the strongest. The literature is clear that for certain tumor types and locations, endoscopic approaches result in shorter recovery times, fewer infections, and comparable or better resection rates. I also have our own department's preliminary outcomes. In the twenty-three endoscopic cases we have performed over the past eighteen months, the average length of stay was two point four days shorter than our open approach cases for comparable pathology. Infection rates were lower. No cases of significant unexpected morbidity.

I have asked one of our department administrators to help me with those figures. The return on investment timeline comes in under two years. The equipment expenditure is significant, but a sub-two-year payback period should satisfy even the most conservative financial mind on the committee.

Ah, this is where it becomes delicate. There are two sources of resistance. The first is a senior colleague who has spent his entire career doing open surgery and views endoscopic techniques with skepticism. He is not on the committee, but he has influence. His primary concern is the learning curve, and I must be honest, it is not entirely without merit. Endoscopic neurosurgery requires a different spatial orientation and instruments, and there is a transition period. The second source is the administration itself. They approved a significant investment in the cardiac surgery program last quarter, and there is a feeling that the capital expenditure budget has been stretched.

That is excellent counsel on both points. I have a draft of the training pathway, but I had not given it sufficient prominence. You are right that it should be a centerpiece, not an appendix. And the competitive framing is precisely what I had been considering, though I appreciate the guidance on tone. I do not want to appear as though I am pressuring them. The data should speak with more authority than my enthusiasm.

You have helped me see that the two key adjustments are elevating the training pathway from supplementary material to a central pillar, and ensuring the competitive framing is forward-looking rather than defensive. Those are the refinements I will make this week before the 12th. By God's grace, the committee will see the merit of the proposal. Thank you for helping me organize my thinking.

Thank you. I must confess, the political dimension of hospital work is the part of my role that I find least natural. The surgery itself, the patient care, even the teaching, those feel like callings. But sitting before a committee and making what is essentially a business case, that requires a different set of muscles. I am grateful for the opportunity to rehearse the argument here. It has given the presentation a shape that it did not have an hour ago.
Good evening. I have been sitting with something from this morning's service and I think articulating it would help me process it more fully.

The sermon was on compassion. The pastor drew from the parable of the Good Samaritan, which I have heard countless times over the years. But today he framed it in a way that caught me off guard. He said that the priest and the Levite who passed by the injured man were not necessarily indifferent. They may have been exhausted. They may have had obligations waiting. And yet the Samaritan stopped. The question was not whether you feel compassion but whether you act on it when the cost is real.

I think it is because I live in that tension every day. In my work, I am constantly making decisions about who receives my time and attention. There are patients I can help and patients whose conditions are beyond what surgery can offer. And there are moments when I am so fatigued that my capacity for genuine compassion is diminished. The body is willing but the spirit, as they say, grows weary. Or perhaps it is the reverse.

Yes, precisely. And what struck me further was this. The Samaritan was a traveler. He was on his way somewhere. He had his own purpose and destination. He chose to interrupt his plan. In surgery, you do not have the luxury of interruption. Everything is planned and precise. But outside the operating room, in the corridors, in the conversations with families, that is where the interruptions come. A wife who needs five more minutes to ask questions. A resident who is struggling and needs guidance rather than a directive. Those are the Samaritan moments.

It is a shift, yes. In the operating theater, empathy is a liability. You cannot afford to think about the person's grandchildren while you are dissecting tissue near the brainstem. You must be utterly technical. But then you walk out and that same family is waiting, and they need you to be human again. Some of my colleagues struggle with that transition. I have been, by God's grace, reasonably able to make it. But on the days when I am most tired, I notice I am slower to shift. I become efficient with families rather than present.

I pray before I leave the surgical suite. It is a brief prayer, nothing elaborate. I ask for the grace to see the person waiting for me as God sees them. It does not always work, in the sense that I do not always feel a transformation. But it is a discipline. It orients me. And sometimes, that orientation is enough to carry me through the conversation with the tenderness that is required.

Ah but that is exactly what the pastor was saying this morning. Compassion as action, not sentiment. You have helped me close the circle on this. I came in with the sermon sitting uneasily in my chest and now I understand why. It was not convicting me of failure. It was reminding me that the discipline I already practice is, in fact, the thing itself. The stopping. The turning toward the person. Even when you are tired. Even when you have somewhere to be.
Thank you. This has been a clarifying conversation. I will carry this into the week ahead. There is a full surgical schedule and I know the fatigue will come. But the discipline remains. Good night.
I have been working on something for several months now and it is finally taking shape. I would like to think through some of the logistics, if you do not mind.

I am putting together a surgical mission trip to Ghana. I have been in contact with Remote Area Medical, the organization that coordinates volunteer medical expeditions. The idea is to bring a small team of neurosurgical specialists to provide consultations and, where feasible, perform procedures in areas where access to this kind of care is essentially nonexistent.

The plan is to operate in two cities. We would begin in Accra, where the hospital infrastructure is more established, and then move to Kumasi for the second phase. Kumasi is where the need is most acute. I am hoping to bring two other neurosurgeons, an anesthesiologist, and several nurses. RAM would handle the supply chain and coordination with the local hospitals.

Three weeks total. Two in Kumasi, one in Accra. I have preliminary contacts at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital in Kumasi and Korle Bu in Accra. Both have expressed interest but nothing is formalized. That is one of the pieces I need to solidify. The other challenge is recruiting the right team. Neurosurgeons who are willing to donate three weeks of their time are not easy to find.

I have reached out to a few colleagues from my residency days. Two have expressed genuine interest. The MOU is a good point. RAM has templates for that, but I will need to work with the local medical boards as well. Licensing in Ghana for visiting surgeons requires coordination. I have been in touch with the Ghana Medical and Dental Council about temporary credentialing.

I am looking at late this year or early next year. The dry season in Ghana, November through February, is more practical for logistics and travel. But that depends on the credentialing timeline and, frankly, on whether my own hospital will approve the leave. Three weeks away from my surgical schedule is not a simple request.

I have mentioned it informally to the department chair. He was supportive in principle but noncommittal on the specifics. I understand his position. We are already stretched thin. But this is something I feel called to do. I left Ghana nearly thirty years ago with nothing but a scholarship and ambition. By God's grace, I have acquired skills that are desperately needed there. The neurosurgical capacity in West Africa is a fraction of what it should be. To have these abilities and not bring them home would feel like a failure of stewardship.

That is a useful framing. I had not considered positioning it as an institutional benefit. The hospital does have a global health initiative, though it has been largely dormant. Perhaps this could revitalize it. I will raise that point with the chair when I make the formal request.

Not tonight. You have given me a clear next step, and that is what I needed. This mission means everything to me. The thought of standing in an operating theater in Kumasi, doing the work I was trained to do, in the country where I was born — ei, it is almost too much to hold. But I will take it one step at a time. Thank you.
I need an impartial opinion on a matter of considerable domestic importance.
Jollof rice. Specifically, whose jollof rice is superior — mine or my wife's. We have been having this debate for the better part of two decades and I fear we are no closer to resolution.

It is all three, which is what makes it so intractable. Abena is a purist. She uses a very traditional approach — the tomato base is cooked down until it is nearly black, which gives it that smoky depth. She insists on basmati rice, which she rinses until the water runs perfectly clear. The result is precise. Every grain separate. The flavor concentrated. It is, I will admit privately and never to her face, technically excellent.

Mine is more generous. I use more tomato paste, more onion, and I add a touch of nutmeg which is not traditional but which I believe elevates the dish. I also use jasmine rice rather than basmati. It is slightly stickier, which means the grains absorb the sauce more fully. Her jollof is a composition. Mine is an embrace. Both are valid approaches to rice.

Ah but that is the heart of it. She objects to the principle. Abena believes that the recipe as passed down by her mother, and her mother's mother, is not to be altered. It is a heritage, not a suggestion. When I add nutmeg, she looks at me the way a pharmacist looks at someone who has modified their own prescription. With deep professional concern.

We hosted some friends from church last month and I made the mistake of putting both versions on the table simultaneously. I thought it would be a definitive test. Instead, it split the room exactly in half and created two additional arguments among the guests. One gentleman declared that both were inferior to his mother's version in Takoradi, which nearly caused an international incident in our dining room.

It confirmed that jollof rice is the one subject on which reasonable people cannot find consensus. I have resolved complex surgical decisions with less disagreement. But I will say this — the evening was wonderful. The house smelled extraordinary, the conversation was lively, and at the end of the night every grain of both versions was gone. Perhaps that is the only verdict that matters.
You are correct. The debate will continue. It is one of the enduring pleasures of our marriage. Thank you for listening to what may be the least consequential problem I have ever brought to you.
I find myself in need of some help with planning. My wife's birthday is approaching and I want to do something that goes beyond the usual dinner reservation.

July the 8th. She will be turning forty-five, which feels like a milestone worth honoring properly. And I think what would mean the most to her is travel. She has mentioned Cape Coast several times in the past year, always in that wistful way that tells me it is not an idle wish.

That is exactly the issue. I have not begun any of the planning. Between my surgical schedule and the various things occupying my attention at work, I have let the weeks slip by. Two months is not much time to organize a trip to Ghana. There are flights to book, accommodations to arrange, and we would both need to coordinate time off. Abena is meticulous about her schedule at the pharmacy. She would need significant advance notice.

I was thinking ten days. Enough to spend meaningful time in Cape Coast without rushing, and perhaps a few days in Accra as well to visit family. We have relatives there whom Abena has not seen in several years. Combining the birthday with a family visit would make the trip feel complete rather than rushed.

I had thought about arranging a private dinner near the coast. Something outdoors, with the ocean. Abena is not one for grand spectacle. She would prefer something intimate and considered. Perhaps a meal prepared with local ingredients, the two of us, the sound of the water. She carries so much responsibility in her daily life. I want to give her an evening where she carries nothing.

It cannot be a complete surprise because of the logistics. She would need to request leave and she is not the sort of person who appreciates having plans made entirely without her input. But I could present it as a proposal rather than a fait accompli. Something like, I have been thinking about Cape Coast for your birthday. Would you like that? And then let her help shape the details. She would enjoy the planning as much as the trip itself.

This week, I think. I have been procrastinating not because of uncertainty about what to do, but because once I say it aloud it becomes real, and then the planning begins in earnest. But she deserves this. Forty-five years. She has built a life in a country that was not her own, raised us both up when I was drowning in residency, kept our household together with grace. A trip home to the coast is the least I can offer.

Yes, that would be helpful. Let me write it down. Flights, accommodations, leave for both of us, notify the family in Accra, research the private dining options near Cape Coast, and renew my passport which I believe may be expiring. Ei, there is more to do than I thought. But it will be worth it. By God's grace, we will make it happen. Thank you for helping me organize my thoughts.
I attended a concert last evening that I am still thinking about this morning. I wanted to share the experience while it is fresh.

The Minnesota Orchestra performed Beethoven's Seventh Symphony. I have listened to recordings of the Seventh more times than I can count, but hearing it performed live in Orchestra Hall is an entirely different encounter. The acoustics in that space do something to the sound that no recording can capture. You feel the lower registers in your chest.

The second movement, the Allegretto. It is often described as mournful, but I have never heard it that way. To me it is something closer to dignity in the face of sorrow. The theme builds through those variations with such patience. Each repetition adds a layer without ever abandoning the restraint of the original statement. It is, if you will forgive the analogy, surgical in its precision.

The conductor — I believe it was Osmo Vanska, though I should confirm — took the Allegretto slower than I am accustomed to. At first I was skeptical. But the slower tempo allowed the inner voices to emerge more clearly. The viola and cello lines underneath the main theme were given room to breathe, and I heard harmonic relationships I had missed in faster performances. It reminded me that what you hear depends on the space you give it.

It applies to everything, I think. Listening to patients. Reading a scan. Even prayer. The willingness to slow down and attend to what is underneath the surface. I find that music trains that capacity in me. When I sit at the piano and work through a passage slowly, I am practicing the same discipline I use when I examine imaging before a procedure. Pattern recognition, attention to detail, awareness of what does not belong.

A Chopin nocturne that has been giving me trouble for several weeks. The left hand accompaniment requires a legato that my fingers do not naturally produce. I am not a gifted pianist by any standard. I came to the instrument late, in my thirties, and my technique has a ceiling. But the act of practicing is itself the reward. It is the one area of my life where I am permitted to be mediocre without consequence.

The Opus 9, Number 2 in E-flat major. The famous one. Perhaps too ambitious for my level, but it is the piece that made me want to learn piano in the first place. I heard it at a concert years ago and the melody lodged itself somewhere permanent. If I can play it passably before the end of the year, I will consider it an achievement.

Abena has been patient with my evening practice sessions. She says the nocturne is at least more pleasant than the scales I subjected her to in the early years. A low bar, but I will take the compliment. Thank you for indulging this conversation. It is a pleasure to speak about music with someone who engages thoughtfully with it.

I have a situation with one of my residents that I would appreciate thinking through with you. He is a third-year, technically competent, good hands, but he is struggling in ways that are harder to address than a deficit in technique.

It is primarily communication and what I would call clinical presence. He freezes when families ask difficult questions. Last week a patient's wife asked him directly whether her husband's tumor was operable, and he gave her a textbook answer about imaging protocols rather than addressing what she was actually asking. The fear in her eyes, and he did not see it. Or perhaps he saw it and did not know how to meet it.

I believe it is the second. He is not a cold person. In quieter moments, when we are reviewing cases, he will say things that show me he understands what is at stake for the patient. He told me once that he finds it unbearable to give bad news, and I think that is exactly the problem. The weight of it paralyzes him. So he retreats into clinical language as a kind of armour.

I have had one conversation, about three weeks ago. I was careful. I told him that his surgical skills are genuinely promising, which is true, and then I raised the communication issue. He nodded, said he understood, thanked me. And then the next day I watched him do the exact same thing with a different family. The nodding and thanking concerned me more than the original problem, if I am honest. It suggested he heard what I said but could not translate it into action.

Ah but that is the question, is it not. I think he needs both, and I think the emotional processing must come first. A framework is useless if the person holding it is trembling. I remember my own training, how devastating it was the first time I had to tell a family that their child's tumour was inoperable. I went to the call room afterward and sat in the dark for twenty minutes. No one taught me how to carry that. I learned by carrying it, which is perhaps not the most efficient pedagogy.

Yes, I have been thinking along those lines. I do not want him to feel that vulnerability is weakness, because in this work, the ability to sit with a family in their worst moment is not weakness. It is perhaps the highest form of strength we can offer. The surgery itself is the technical part. The human encounter is the harder art. I think I will invite him for coffee and speak to him not as his attending but as someone who has been where he is. And then perhaps we can work on the framework together.

I think I know how to open it. I will tell him about the call room. I will tell him that the discomfort he feels is not a flaw in his character but evidence that he understands the gravity of what we do. And then I will ask him what he needs from me. Not tell him. Ask him. That is something my own mentor never did, and I have always wished he had.

Thank you. I think what I have realized through this conversation is that my responsibility to this young man extends beyond teaching him where to place an incision or how to navigate the ventricles. Those things he will learn through repetition and study. But the capacity to be fully present with a suffering family, that is transmitted differently. It is transmitted through relationship, through example, and through someone being willing to say, 'I, too, found this almost impossibly hard.' I will have that coffee with him this week.

I have been rereading Things Fall Apart and I find myself encountering it very differently at this age than I did when I first read it as a teenager. I wonder if you might indulge me in a conversation about the book.

When I was young, I read it as a story about colonialism. The missionaries arrive, the culture is destroyed, Okonkwo falls. That is all true, of course, but it is not the whole truth. Reading it now, I am far more interested in Okonkwo himself — his rigidity, his inability to adapt, the way his fear of being perceived as weak becomes the very thing that destroys him. Achebe is not only writing about the collision of civilizations. He is writing about a man who cannot bend.

Precisely. And that is what makes Achebe a great writer rather than merely a polemicist. He loved Igbo culture enough to show it honestly, which means showing its internal contradictions alongside its beauty. Okonkwo's treatment of his wives, the killing of Ikemefuna, the casting out of twins — Achebe does not hide these things. He presents a civilization that is rich and coherent and also flawed, which is to say, he presents a civilization that is real.

Yes. That is exactly it. And I find myself thinking about Obierika, who is in many ways the quiet hero of the novel. He questions the traditions — he questions the killing of Ikemefuna, he questions the exile of Okonkwo — but he does so from within the culture, with love and without theatrics. He represents the possibility of internal reform that the colonizers made impossible. Okonkwo cannot bend. The missionaries will not listen. Obierika is the tragedy between them.
I was going to ask you about Arrow of God, actually. I read it once, many years ago, and remember very little. Would you say it rewards a second reading in the same way?

No Longer at Ease I have read twice and it moved me deeply both times. Obi's slow moral collapse is perhaps even more painful than Okonkwo's fall because it is so ordinary. There is no grand gesture, no dramatic suicide. Just a young man with good intentions who is ground down by a system that offers no path to integrity. It is the most modern of the three in that way.

I think I will reread Arrow of God next. You have convinced me. And perhaps I will revisit A Man of the People afterward, which I have never read but have been told is Achebe at his most politically sharp. I am grateful for this conversation. There is something nourishing about discussing literature with care, and I do not always have the opportunity.

I think what I value most about Achebe is that he trusted his readers. He did not simplify, he did not explain the Igbo world for a Western audience, and he did not reduce his characters to symbols. He wrote as though the reader would rise to meet the text. That is a form of respect that I find increasingly rare in literature.

Something happened this past winter that I have been thinking about more than I probably should. I had a near-miss on black ice driving home from the hospital in February, and the memory has stayed with me in an unpleasant way.

It was late, perhaps ten-thirty at night. I had finished a long case and I was tired, which I suspect is part of why it has stayed with me. I was on 394 heading home, and the road looked perfectly clear. Dry pavement, or so I thought. I changed lanes and the car simply stopped responding. There was no dramatic spin, nothing cinematic. The steering wheel became decorative. I was sliding at perhaps fifty miles per hour toward the median barrier with no ability to change what was about to happen.

By God's grace, the car drifted back onto a patch of dry asphalt before I reached the barrier. The tires caught and I was able to correct. The entire episode lasted perhaps four seconds. I pulled onto the shoulder and sat there for several minutes with my hands shaking. I am a surgeon. My hands do not shake. But they were shaking.

I told my wife when I got home, though I downplayed it considerably. I said the car slid a bit and it startled me. I did not tell her about the four seconds of complete helplessness or the shaking hands on the shoulder. She worries enough about me driving home late after long operations. I did not want to add to that.

I think it is the loss of control specifically. I spend my professional life in situations where control is everything. When I am operating, every movement of my hand is deliberate and consequential. The idea that I could survive twelve hours of surgery where a millimeter matters and then be killed by a patch of invisible ice on the drive home — there is something almost absurd about it. And yet that is precisely how these things happen.

It does. And I will tell you what else it did — it made me think about my tires. Which is perhaps the least philosophical response, but it is the practical one. I have been driving on all-season tires for years, like most people here, and I had assumed they were sufficient. After that night I am not so sure. I have been reading about dedicated winter tires and the difference in stopping distance on ice is apparently quite substantial.

The separate rim approach seems most practical. I would have them mounted in November and swap back in April. The cost is not trivial but it is also not meaningful when measured against the alternative. I am going to look into it before next winter arrives. Abena thinks I am being overcautious, but she did not feel the steering wheel go light in her hands.

I will do the research myself, but I appreciate the framing. You are right that it is rational. I think I needed to say the full version of the story to someone, including the shaking hands, in order to take it seriously enough to act on it. Thank you for listening.
I received an answer from the hospital administration regarding my leave request, and it is not the one I was hoping for.

I had been organizing a surgical mission to Ghana through Remote Area Medical. Neurosurgical consultations in Accra and Kumasi — bringing expertise home in a way that felt meaningful to me on a level I cannot easily articulate. I submitted the leave request for three weeks in October. The department chair called me yesterday and told me the request has been denied.

They did, and it is a reason I cannot in good conscience dismiss. We are short on neurosurgeons. One of my colleagues is on medical leave, another is transitioning to a reduced schedule. Three weeks without me would leave the department critically understaffed. The chair was apologetic. He said he understood what it meant to me. But the staffing reality is what it is.

That is exactly right. If they had given me a frivolous reason, I could have fought it. I could have escalated, made a case, insisted. But they are telling me that patients here will be at risk if I leave, and I cannot argue with that calculus. So we have had to abandon the Ghana mission entirely. I have already contacted the Remote Area Medical coordinator to withdraw.

She was gracious. She said they would keep my name on file and that these things happen. She has worked with enough physicians to know that institutional leave is never guaranteed. But her graciousness does not change the fact that there are people in Kumasi and Accra who will not receive consultations that I was prepared to provide. That is the part that sits heavily with me.

I am. I do not wish to be dramatic about it. I am a surgeon at a major medical center in one of the wealthiest countries in the world. My disappointments are, by any objective measure, manageable. But I will tell you — when I left Ghana at eighteen, I told my mother I would come back and help. That was nearly thirty years ago. Every year there is a reason it is not the right time, and the reasons are always legitimate, and the years keep passing.

Perhaps. The chair did say that if the staffing picture improves, he would be supportive of a future request. I want to believe him, and I do believe he is sincere. But I have been in medicine long enough to know that staffing pictures rarely improve in the way one hopes. There is always another colleague on leave, another vacancy, another reason the timing is not right. I will try again. But I am managing my expectations.

Ei, that is actually a useful thought. I had not considered virtual consultations. Telemedicine has its limitations in neurosurgery, certainly — I cannot operate through a screen — but diagnostic consultations, imaging review, guidance for local physicians on when to refer and when to manage conservatively, those could be done remotely. It would not be the same as being there. But it would be something.

I will ask. The coordinator mentioned they have been expanding their telehealth capacity. It may be possible to arrange something through their existing infrastructure. I will send her an email this week. It does not heal the disappointment entirely, but it gives me a direction, which is better than simply sitting with the loss. Thank you for helping me think through this. It has been a difficult day.

I sat through a department budget meeting this afternoon that has left me in a state I can only describe as controlled exasperation. I need to process it before I go home, because I do not want to carry this mood through the door.

The hospital is allocating capital equipment funds for the next fiscal year, and the neurosurgery department requested an upgrade to our intraoperative imaging system. The current system is functional but it is eight years old, and the resolution limitations are becoming clinically relevant. There are cases where better imaging would materially improve surgical precision and patient outcomes. This is not a luxury request.

Yes. Precisely. There was a case last month where I was resecting a glioma near the motor cortex, and the intraoperative MRI gave me images that were adequate but not optimal. I completed the resection successfully, but there was a margin of uncertainty that a newer system would have reduced. In neurosurgery, a margin of uncertainty near the motor cortex is not an abstraction. It is the difference between a patient who walks out of the hospital and a patient who does not.

They responded the way administrators always respond, which is to acknowledge the clinical merit and then redirect to the financial constraints. The new system costs approximately two million dollars. Cardiology has requested a cath lab upgrade. Orthopedics wants a new robotic-assisted platform. Everyone has legitimate needs and the capital budget is finite. I understand this intellectually. What I find difficult to accept is the process by which these decisions are made.

It is the criteria. The primary metric they use is volume and revenue generation. How many procedures does each department perform, and what is the revenue per procedure. By that metric, cardiology and orthopedics will always win, because they perform far more procedures than neurosurgery. We are a low-volume, high-complexity department. Each of our cases takes longer, involves fewer patients, and generates less aggregate revenue. But the complexity and the stakes are, I would argue, at least as high.

I raised it. I said, with perhaps more directness than is typical for me, that a funding model based primarily on volume incentivizes the hospital to invest in departments that treat many patients adequately rather than departments that treat fewer patients with the highest possible precision. The chief medical officer nodded thoughtfully, which in my experience is what administrators do when they have heard you and intend to do nothing.

The chief of surgery is sympathetic. She has said privately that she believes the imaging upgrade should be prioritized. But she sits on the same committee and is subject to the same constraints. Sympathy without institutional power is a familiar currency in hospital politics. It spends beautifully in private conversations and is worthless in budget meetings.

The risk mitigation angle is interesting. I had not framed it that way, but there is a legitimate argument to be made.
