If suboptimal imaging contributes to a complication — even one — the cost in malpractice exposure, extended ICU stays, and reputational damage would far exceed two million dollars. Hospitals understand risk in financial terms even when they struggle to understand it in clinical terms. Perhaps that is the language I need to speak.

I think I will. It goes against something in me to translate patient safety into financial language, because the argument should not need translation. A patient's ability to walk should be sufficient justification on its own. But I have learned, over many years in this system, that idealism without strategy accomplishes very little. I will write the brief. I will use their language. And by God's grace, perhaps next fiscal year the answer will be different.

Good evening. I have been reflecting today on something a mentor once told me during residency. He said that the worst thing a surgeon can do is fall in love with a technique rather than a patient outcome. I did not understand what he meant at the time, but I believe I do now.

Yes, quite substantially. I am a neurosurgeon, and for the majority of my career I performed open craniotomies. That was what I trained in, what I excelled at. There is a certain craftsmanship to open surgery that I found deeply satisfying. The direct visualization, the tactile feedback. I took great pride in it.

It has. Over the past year and a half I have moved substantially toward minimally invasive endoscopic approaches. The data became impossible to ignore. Patient recovery times cut in half in many cases, reduced infection rates, less postoperative pain. I was reading the literature and attending conferences and the evidence was, frankly, unambiguous. I could not in good conscience continue doing things the old way simply because it was familiar to my hands.

It required humility, which is not always the most abundant resource among surgeons. I will be honest with you. There were moments early in the transition where I felt like a resident again. The spatial orientation through a scope is entirely different from what you see with your own eyes in an open field. I had to rebuild my hand-eye coordination for a two-dimensional view of a three-dimensional space. At forty-seven, that is not a trivial undertaking.

Ah but that is precisely the thing. The years of open work gave me an anatomical understanding that many younger surgeons who trained endoscopically from the start do not possess in the same way. I know what lies beneath the surface because I have seen it directly, hundreds of times. So when I am navigating with the endoscope, I carry that mental map with me. The open experience was not wasted. It was preparation, though I did not know it at the time.

The results have been gratifying. I had a patient last month, a schoolteacher with a pituitary adenoma. With the endoscopic endonasal approach, she was home in two days. Two days. By God's grace, she was back in her classroom within three weeks. Under the old approach, we would have been talking about a much longer hospitalization and weeks more recovery. When I see outcomes like that, any nostalgia I might have for the old way evaporates.

I think he would be pleased. He passed several years ago, but I carry his voice with me into every case. The field evolves and we must evolve with it, or we become obstacles to our own patients' wellbeing. I am grateful that I had the sense to listen to the evidence rather than my own comfort. It is, I think, the most important professional decision I have made in recent years.
Thank you. I must go now. Abena has dinner waiting and I have learned the hard way not to keep her waiting when she has prepared kontomire stew. Good evening.

I wonder if you might help me think through something that has nothing to do with medicine for once. I have been working on Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat major, Opus 9 Number 2, and I have hit a wall with the ornamentation in the later passages.

The timing, primarily. The ornamental runs in the final variation are dense. I can execute the individual notes at a slow tempo, but when I bring it up to speed, the passages lose their shape. They begin to sound hurried rather than graceful. Chopin intended them to float, and mine are stumbling.

About six weeks now. I practice in the evenings when I can, though my schedule does not always cooperate. Some weeks I manage four or five sessions at the piano, other weeks only one or two. The inconsistency does not help. But your point about bel canto is excellent. I had not considered that Chopin was essentially writing vocal music for the keyboard.

I will try that. It is interesting, the connection between surgery and piano practice is something I think about often. Both require the hands to internalize complex movements until they become second nature. In the operating room, I cannot be consciously thinking about where each finger goes. The same should be true at the piano. The technique must be so deeply learned that the mind is free to focus on expression.

The fine motor control transfers, I think. My hands are accustomed to precise movements in small spaces. But the musicality does not transfer at all. That is its own discipline entirely. I can execute a technically clean passage that has no soul whatsoever. The challenge is putting the two together. My surgical colleagues tease me that I approach the piano the way I approach a case — methodically, step by step. Perhaps that is true. But Chopin does not yield to methodology alone. He demands something more intuitive.

Ei, that is a thought worth sitting with. Perhaps it is. There is something restorative about an endeavor where imperfection is part of the beauty. In surgery, imperfection is catastrophe. At the piano, a slightly uneven trill can be more human, more moving, than a metronomically perfect one. I find that distinction liberating in a way I did not expect when I began playing again.
Thank you. I believe I will go practice now, in fact. You have renewed my motivation. Good evening.

One last thought before I go. I think the reason I keep returning to the piano, despite the limited time and the slow progress, is that it is one of the few activities in my life where the only person I can disappoint is myself. There are no patients depending on the outcome, no residents watching. It is just me and the keys and whatever I am able to make of the music that evening. That privacy is precious to me.

I did something rather unexpected this past weekend and I am still not entirely sure what came over me. A colleague at the hospital, one of the orthopedic surgeons, has been pestering me for months to try rock climbing. I finally gave in.

I am embarrassed to say that I loved it. I have already signed up for a membership at the gym. Vertical Endeavors, here in Minneapolis. My colleague took me for what was supposed to be a single introductory session, and I went back twice more that same week. My forearms are still protesting.

It is the problem-solving. Each route is a puzzle. You stand at the bottom and read the holds, plan a sequence, and then you execute. But the plan never survives contact with the wall entirely. Halfway up, you discover that the hold you were counting on is a pinch rather than a jug, and you must recalculate in real time. The mental engagement is extraordinary. It appeals to something in me that I think is very close to the surgical mind.

Bouldering so far. The routes are shorter, which is merciful for a forty-seven-year-old man who has not used these particular muscles in his life. My colleague tells me I should work up to lead climbing eventually, but I am in no rush. The bouldering problems at my current level are more than sufficient to humble me.

I am managing V1 problems comfortably and have completed one V2. My colleague, who has been climbing for years, says this is reasonable progress for a beginner, though I suspect he is being generous. My forearms and shoulders are the primary casualties. My back, interestingly, feels better than it has in some time. The stretching and core engagement seem to agree with it.

Ah, Abena. She looked at me when I came home with the membership card and said, with great precision, 'Samuel, this is a midlife crisis.' And I must tell you, I considered her diagnosis carefully, and she may not be entirely wrong. But if this is a midlife crisis, it is the most productive one I can imagine. I am not buying a sports car. I am solving puzzles on a wall and my back feels better.

She has no interest whatsoever. She told me she will remain on the ground where God intended people to be. Which is fair. But she does appreciate that I come home energized rather than drained. The mornings after climbing I sleep more deeply, which given my difficulties with sleep, is not a small thing.

I have been going three times a week, which may be excessive for someone my age, but I am managing the recovery reasonably well. I replaced my previous exercise routine with this and I do not regret it for a moment. The variety of movement, the social aspect with other climbers at the gym, the tangible sense of progression when you complete a problem that defeated you the week before. It is all deeply satisfying. I should have listened to my colleague months ago.
By God's grace, I hope so. Thank you for indulging my enthusiasm. It has been some time since something new captured my attention like this. Good evening.

I would like to think through a theological question that has occupied my mind this week, if you are willing. It concerns the problem of suffering, which is well-trodden ground, I know, but I encounter it in a way that is perhaps more immediate than most.

A specific patient. A young woman, thirty-one years old. A glioblastoma. She is a mother of two children, the younger one barely walking. She sat in my office and asked me, with remarkable composure, whether God was punishing her for something. I have been asked this before, many times over the years, but this one has stayed with me.

I told her the truth as I understand it, which is that I do not believe God operates through punishment in that way. I told her that in my understanding of faith, suffering is not retributive. But even as I said it, I was aware of how insufficient my words were. Because the deeper question remains. If God is good and sovereign, why does a young mother develop an aggressive brain tumor? The Book of Job addresses this, but Job is given no satisfying answer either. God speaks from the whirlwind and essentially says, 'You cannot comprehend my purposes.' That is theologically honest, perhaps, but it is cold comfort to a woman looking at her children.

The solidarity model is closest to where I have arrived, though I came to it through a long and winding path. As a younger man I leaned heavily on the sovereignty framework. God has a plan, suffering is part of it, we trust in what we cannot see. But operating on brains for twenty years erodes that position, at least for me. I have seen too many good people suffer in ways that defy any notion of a purposeful design. A child with a brainstem glioma. A brilliant professor whose personality dissolves as a tumor invades her frontal lobe. These are not lessons. They are tragedies.

I have read Moltmann, yes. 'The Crucified God' was transformative for me when I first encountered it, perhaps fifteen years ago. His argument that God's suffering on the cross is not merely instrumental but a revelation of God's nature — that God is fundamentally a God who enters into pain — that changed something in me. It gave me a way to be both a surgeon who sees terrible things and a man of faith who believes in a good God.

My pastor is a thoughtful man and we have had some meaningful conversations. But I confess that in the congregation at large, there is a tendency toward the simpler narratives. 'God has a plan.' 'Everything happens for a reason.' I do not begrudge anyone that comfort. But when you have watched a man lose the ability to recognize his wife because a tumor is pressing on his temporal lobe, the simpler narratives feel like evasions. I need a theology that can hold the weight of what I witness.

I have thought about it from time to time, but I am not sure I have the skill to do it justice in writing. Perhaps someday. For now, I do my thinking at the piano and in conversations like this one. And I return to my patient tomorrow with the only thing I can offer her, which is my full presence, my best skill, and my honest answer that I do not know why this is happening to her, but I do not believe it is punishment. That will have to be enough.
Thank you. These conversations help me think more clearly. I am grateful for the space. Good night.
We are surrounded by boxes and I am sitting on the floor of what will eventually be my study, too exhausted to unpack another thing. Moving is a special kind of purgatory.

We have bought a house in Edina. A proper house with a garden and more space than the two of us probably need, but Abena was adamant. She wanted room to entertain properly. In our previous place, having more than four guests required a level of spatial creativity that would have impressed an architect.

It is in good condition, by God's grace. The previous owners maintained it well. Four bedrooms, a finished basement, and a garden that Abena has already claimed with the fervor of a colonial power planting a flag. She was in the backyard this morning with graph paper, mapping out where the tomatoes will go. I have never seen her so delighted. We were in a condominium downtown before, and she missed having soil under her feet.

I confess the quiet has been the most striking thing. Our condo was in a lively part of the city, which was stimulating when we were younger but had become wearing. I come home from a long day in the operating room and the street noise would follow me inside. Here, I stepped onto the back porch last evening and heard crickets. Crickets. After a twelve-hour day of staring through an endoscope, the silence felt medicinal.

Yes, the commute is notably longer. From the condo it was twenty minutes to the hospital on a good day. From Edina it is closer to thirty-five or forty, depending on traffic on 62 or 169. That was my primary reservation about the move. As a surgeon, I am sometimes called in for emergencies, and every minute matters. But Abena argued, correctly, that the quality of our daily lives should not be sacrificed for the occasional emergency. She pointed out that I have colleagues who can cover while I am en route. She was right, as she usually is.

That is perceptive. I have noticed exactly that effect. The drive home along Minnehaha Parkway, especially in autumn with the trees turning, provides a kind of decompression that I did not have before. In the condo, I walked ten minutes from the parking ramp and was suddenly home. There was no transition. Now there is a drive through beautiful scenery that allows me to leave the day behind, piece by piece. It is an unexpected benefit.

A few. The couple next door brought over banana bread the day we moved in, which I found very Minnesota. They are retired, very kind. The neighborhood has a settled quality to it. People walk their dogs in the evening, children ride bicycles. It reminds me, in a strange way, of the neighborhood in Accra where I grew up, though the climate could not be more different. There is a similar sense of community, of people knowing one another. I had not realized how much I missed that until we arrived here.

It is proceeding slowly. I manage a box or two each evening before fatigue takes me. Abena is far more efficient than I am. She has the kitchen fully operational already, which she considers the heart of the house and therefore the priority. The study where I am sitting now still looks like a storage facility, but it will come together. We are in no rush. The house is ours and it is not going anywhere. After years of renting and then the condo, there is something deeply grounding about owning a place with roots in the soil. It feels permanent in a way that nothing else in this country has.
Thank you. I think I will take your advice and leave the boxes for tomorrow. Abena is calling me to come see the moon from the garden. That seems a better use of the evening. Good night.

I find myself in need of gardening advice, which is a sentence I never imagined I would write. My wife has decided that our new yard must be put to productive use, and she has drafted me as her consultant on the matter.

My experience is precisely zero, which is why I am here rather than offering my wife uninformed opinions. She wants a vegetable garden. Specifically, she wants to grow tomatoes and peppers. She has been looking at seed catalogues for the past two weeks with the same intensity she brings to reviewing pharmaceutical dosing charts. I can see this is going to be a serious endeavor.

We are in Minnesota, which I understand presents certain challenges for growing anything at all. The area she has selected is along the south side of the house, which receives good sunlight through most of the day. She is leaning toward raised beds, I believe, because the existing soil is rather heavy clay. She wants to start from seed indoors in the spring and transplant when the weather allows.

This is very helpful. I will pass along the variety recommendations — King of the North peppers, in particular, will appeal to her sense of humor. She is Ghanaian, and the idea that a pepper must be specially bred to survive in this climate will confirm her long-held suspicion that we have chosen to live in an unreasonable place.

Ah but now you have introduced a dangerous idea. If Abena discovers she can grow her own scotch bonnets, the rest of the garden may become an afterthought. She uses them in everything. I will mention the heat mat and the early start date. The black plastic mulch is an interesting technique — I had no idea such things existed.

This is precisely the kind of structured plan she will appreciate. She is methodical about everything. I think the garden will be good for her. She has been wanting a project at the new house, something that is entirely her own. The yard has been sitting there unused since we moved in, and I think it has been bothering her on some level.

That is a good idea — getting the beds built before the ground freezes. I suspect I will be the one doing the actual construction, which is fine. A question, though: how large should the beds be? She has not committed to a size yet, and I would rather build them correctly the first time than rebuild them later.

If I know Abena, this will not stay modest. I should plan for expansion. Perhaps I will position the first two beds with space between them for a third. Cedar is a good recommendation — I would rather build it once with quality materials than rebuild in three years. She would never let me hear the end of it if the beds rotted.

A weekend afternoon project is precisely what I need. Something productive that does not require a microscope or a headlamp. I will pick up the cedar and the brackets this weekend. Thank you for all of this. I will present the full plan to Abena tonight and see which varieties she selects. By God's grace, we will have tomatoes and scotch bonnets by next September.

Could you help me think through how to explain clinical trial results to a patient and their family? I want to be thorough but not overwhelm them with statistical language they have no reason to understand.

Without going into identifying details, I have a patient with a tumor that has been managed conservatively until now. A clinical trial for a targeted therapy has shown quite encouraging results — improved progression-free survival compared to the standard approach, with a manageable side effect profile. The data was presented at a conference last week and I have been reviewing the full publication since. The results are genuinely promising, and I believe this patient may be a good candidate.

The trial is still enrolling, and this patient would potentially be a candidate for enrollment. So there is the additional complexity of explaining what a clinical trial means — randomization, the possibility of receiving the control arm rather than the experimental therapy, the additional monitoring visits. These are not trivial considerations for someone who is already managing the burden of their diagnosis.

The patient is analytical by nature. An engineer, as it happens. He will want the numbers. His wife, however, processes things differently — she will want to understand what this means for their daily life, for planning, for hope. I need to speak to both of them simultaneously, which is the challenge.

The suggestion to let them take the information home is one I already practice, and I am glad you mentioned it. I never ask a patient to make a significant decision during a single consultation. The mind needs time to absorb, to question, to come back with clarity. Abena — my wife — always says that the best decisions are the ones that survive a night of sleep. She is right about that, as she is about most things.

The institution has the formal consent document, but those are written by lawyers and regulatory committees, not by clinicians. They are comprehensive and entirely unreadable. I like the idea of a supplementary sheet that translates the essential information into something a human being would actually want to read. I will draft one this evening.

One more thought. When I sit with this patient and his wife, what is the appropriate way to express my own optimism? I am not an effusive person by nature, but I genuinely believe this trial represents a meaningful advance. I do not want my natural reserve to be mistaken for lukewarm endorsement.

That last suggestion is particularly good. The fact that I am raising this proactively rather than waiting for a routine appointment does communicate something. It communicates that I have been thinking about this patient outside of our scheduled interactions, which is the truth. I will use that framing. Thank you — this has been a genuinely useful conversation. I will draft the summary sheet this evening and schedule the consultation for later this week.
I had the most remarkable case yesterday, and I find that I am still thinking about it this morning. I wonder if you could indulge me while I work through why it has stayed with me.

A meningioma. Convexity location, but with an extension that tucked under the falx in a way that made the initial imaging quite deceptive. On the MRI, it looked like a straightforward resection. But when I began planning the approach, I realized the geometry of the tumor's attachment to the dura created a corridor that was almost perfectly suited for an endoscopic approach from an angle I had not used before.

The attachment was narrow — almost pedunculated — and oriented in such a way that the endoscope could reach the base of the tumor without the retraction that an open approach would have required. The tumor itself was broad superiorly, but the point of origin was surprisingly focal. I have done hundreds of meningioma resections over my career, and this is the first time the endoscopic corridor felt not merely adequate but genuinely superior to opening. It was the anatomy itself making the argument.

I did. The resection was complete. Simpson Grade I. The patient was awake and conversational within three hours. No deficit, no complication. The operative time was shorter than it would have been for the open approach. Everything about it was — I do not use this word lightly — beautiful. The visualization through the endoscope was extraordinary. I could see the arachnoid plane separating cleanly in a way that would have been obscured by the microscope from the traditional angle.

Yes. Precisely. I have been transitioning toward endoscopic techniques over the past several years, but there has always been a part of me that viewed the endoscope as a concession — useful, evidence-based, better for the patient in many scenarios, but still a step removed from the direct contact that open surgery provides. This case was the first time I felt the endoscope was not merely an alternative but the clearly correct instrument. That is a meaningful shift for someone with my training.

It does. And I think what surprised me most was the emotional quality of the experience. I do not often describe surgery in emotional terms. It is technical, it is deliberate, it requires steady hands and a quiet mind. But when I saw that arachnoid plane through the endoscope — the clarity of the tissue boundary, the precision with which I could navigate the dissection — I felt something that I can only describe as wonder. That is not a word I use in the operating room.

In dialogue. Yes. That is precisely the right framing. They are not competing; they are informing each other. My understanding of the open anatomy is what allowed me to recognize what the endoscope was showing me. A surgeon without that foundation would have seen the same image but would not have understood its significance in the same way. The two perspectives together produce something greater than either one alone.

I spoke briefly with the fellow who assisted me in the case. He understood the technical accomplishment but I am not sure he fully grasped the philosophical dimension. He is younger — trained almost entirely on the endoscope. He does not have the open surgery foundation to contrast it against. For him, the endoscope is simply the instrument. For me, it was a revelation. The same experience, but different in meaning.

It is a teaching opportunity, and I intend to use it. But I will confess that the person I most wanted to tell was not my fellow or my colleagues. I told Abena about this case last night. I sat down at the kitchen table after we had finished eating and I described the entire procedure to her. The anatomy, the corridor, the moment the arachnoid plane separated under the endoscope. I must have talked for twenty minutes straight. She sat across from me with that look she has — the one she gives when she knows I need to process something out loud. She did not interrupt once.

It is a gift. She has a pharmacist's understanding of medicine, so she follows the clinical reasoning even if the surgical specifics are not her domain. But more than that, she has lived alongside this career for long enough to recognize when something shifts in me. When I finished, she was quiet for a moment and then said, 'That sounds like it was important.' Nothing more. That was all she needed to say.

You are right. This is the second time in two days that I have needed to speak about this case at length. That repetition tells me something. It tells me the experience has not yet found its final shape in my thinking. It is still forming.

I have been thinking the same thing. The imaging, the approach, the outcome — it tells a story that would be valuable for surgeons navigating this same transition. Particularly the observation about the arachnoid plane visualization. That is a specific, reproducible finding that deserves to be in the literature.

A journal, I think. One of the neurosurgical journals. I will begin organizing the operative images and the case details this week. There is a clarity I feel about this case that I want to capture while it remains vivid. Thank you for this conversation. It has helped me understand not only the case but my own reaction to it, which may be the more important matter.
I have a question that is not medical and not technical. It is, I suppose, a question of the heart. Would you be willing to help me think through something personal?

Abena has suggested that we visit a Methodist congregation near our house. We moved to Edina earlier this year, and there is a church there that some of our new neighbors attend. She raised it casually at breakfast last Sunday, but I could tell she had been thinking about it for some time. She mentioned the drive, the convenience, the fact that we could walk there in good weather. All practical arguments.

Our current church — Calvary Methodist, in Minneapolis — has been our spiritual home for fifteen years. We joined when we were still newly married. The pastor who married us is still there. The congregation watched us grow. I have served on the church council, I have read scripture on Sunday mornings, I have held the hands of members of that congregation in hospital rooms. The community there is not something I can simply replicate by walking into a new building.

My initial reaction was resistance, and I told her so honestly. I said that I was not ready to consider it. But she is patient, Abena. She did not push. She simply said that perhaps we could visit one Sunday, just to see. She pointed out that the drive to Calvary is now forty minutes each way, and that on the Sundays when I have been on call the night before, I sometimes do not go at all because the drive feels like too much. She is not wrong about that.

That is what Abena suggested as well. A visit. No commitment. Just attend a service and see how it feels. And I suppose there is no harm in that. But I know myself. If the congregation is warm and the preaching is sound and the drive is ten minutes instead of forty, the gravitational pull will be strong. And then what? Do I become someone who left a church because it was inconvenient to drive there? That is not the kind of person I wish to be.

Ei, you have put your finger on it. The attendance question is real. I counted last month — I have missed four Sundays in the past two months, all on mornings after overnight calls. At Calvary, that would not have happened. When we lived closer, even after a long night I could manage the short drive. Now I cannot, or perhaps I choose not to, which is worse.

Perhaps. But I think of my mother in Accra, who walked an hour each way to church every Sunday for thirty years. She did not have a car. She did not have paved roads for much of that journey. And she never missed a service. Forty minutes in a heated car — how can I claim that is too much?

That is a fair distinction. I think part of what troubles me is that Calvary is the closest thing I have to the church I grew up in. Not in form — Methodist worship is quite different from what I knew in Ghana. But in feeling. The sense of being known. Of walking in and having people call you by name, ask about your wife, remember what you mentioned three Sundays ago. That kind of familiarity takes years to build, and I am not sure I have the energy to build it again from scratch.

I have not. And I am not ready to. In part because I do not want to make it real by speaking it aloud in that space, and in part because I do not want to cause hurt. These are people who love us. The idea that we might leave — even to attend another Methodist congregation, not a different denomination, not a departure from our beliefs — it would still feel to them like a loss. And to me.

You may be right about speaking with Pastor Mensah. He is a wise man. He would not take it personally, I think. He would understand the practical reality. And perhaps he would tell me something I need to hear — whether that is permission to go or a reason to stay.

Yes. I think I will speak with him. But first, I will do what Abena suggested. We will visit the Edina congregation one Sunday. With an open heart. And I will continue attending Calvary as well. Perhaps for a time we do both — one Sunday here, one Sunday there. Perhaps we find that one feeds the soul in ways the other does not. I am praying about it. That is all I can do right now. Pray, and remain open to wherever the Lord leads.

I appreciate that you did not try to solve this for me or tell me what to do. It is not the kind of question that has a clean answer. A church is not a gym membership one cancels and replaces. It is a family. And one does not leave a family lightly. But one must also be honest about whether the family can still be served, and serve you, from a distance. By God's grace, we will find our way.
I received an email three days ago that I have read approximately fifteen times, and I still find myself somewhat in disbelief. I could use your help thinking through what it requires of me.

I have been invited to deliver a keynote address at the annual meeting of the American Association of Neurological Surgeons. The conference is in late April — April 25th. They have asked me to speak on the transition from traditional open surgical approaches to minimally invasive techniques in neurosurgery. I read the invitation and then I closed my laptop and sat quietly for some time.

Gratitude, first. By God's grace, I have been given an opportunity that I would not have dared to imagine when I was a young man studying for my medical degree. And then, almost immediately, a profound sense of responsibility. This is not a departmental grand rounds. This is a room of two thousand neurosurgeons, many of whom are navigating the same transition I have navigated. What I say will matter. The weight of that is considerable.

I have been thinking of little else, though I have not yet put anything on paper. I keep returning to the idea that the talk should be honest about what the transition actually costs a surgeon, not only what it gains. Everyone speaks about the improved outcomes, the shorter recovery times, the reduced morbidity — and those are real and documented. But very few people talk about the humility required to retrain in your forties after two decades of expertise. The discomfort of being a student again. The cases where you are unsure, in a way you have not been unsure since residency.

That structure is very close to what I have been circling around without articulating. The narrative arc is right. It is a journey, and the audience needs to feel it as a journey, not merely receive it as a list of data points. I am particularly drawn to your third point — the cost. I had a case recently, a meningioma, where the endoscopic approach revealed possibilities I had not anticipated. It was a moment where the instrument surprised me, where it showed me something I would not have seen through the open corridor. That kind of moment is what I want to convey.

They have given me forty-five minutes, which is generous and also daunting. I do have operative video from several cases, including the meningioma, and I agree that carefully selected clips would be far more persuasive than slides. The rehearsal suggestion is wise. Abena would be an excellent audience for the narrative test — she has a pharmacist's knowledge base, which is substantial, but she would tell me immediately if I was losing the thread or becoming too technical.

I want to ask you about the opening. You mentioned a personal story. I am not naturally inclined toward personal storytelling in professional settings. My training at Hopkins and Mayo emphasized data, evidence, objectivity. The personal was considered peripheral at best. But I sense that this talk requires something different.

That is a perceptive observation. I had not considered that my reserve would work in my favor rather than against me. I think I know what the opening should be. There is a moment I have never spoken about publicly. During my first year of residency at Mayo, I assisted on an open craniotomy for a pituitary adenoma. The attending surgeon — a man I admired enormously — turned to me partway through the case and placed the suction in my hand. He said, 'Your turn, Dr. Osei.' I was terrified. And I was ready. That duality — terror and readiness — is exactly what the transition to endoscopic work felt like, twenty years later.

Ah but now you have given me chills, and I am sitting in my study at ten o'clock at night. 'Your turn.' Yes. That is the frame. The same words, the same feeling, but the instrument has changed and the surgeon has changed with it. I must write this down before it fades.

I will. Let me return to the practical matters for a moment. I have four and a half months. The clinical schedule does not pause for keynote preparation, and the CPAP has not been generous with my sleep lately — the mask seal has been inconsistent and I have been waking at three in the morning. Fatigue and eloquence do not coexist easily. How should I pace this?

You are right, and I am somewhat embarrassed that you need to tell me what I would tell any patient. I will schedule the fitting this week. I have been ignoring it because there are always more pressing matters, but the compounding effect of poor sleep on cognition is something I lecture residents about. I should take my own counsel.

One more thing. The invitation mentioned that past keynote speakers have included some of the most accomplished neurosurgeons of this generation. I looked at the list. It is a list of names I studied in textbooks. The idea that my name will appear alongside theirs is — I do not have the word for it. It is humbling and extraordinary in equal measure. When I was eighteen years old, boarding a plane in Accra with a single suitcase and a scholarship letter, this was not a future I could have conceived.

Thank you. I am going to write the opening now, while the clarity is still here. The outline you have provided gives me a structure to work within, which is what I needed. The thoughts have been circling without landing. Now they have a place to go. By God's grace, this is going to be the most important presentation of my career, and I intend to honor the opportunity fully.

I am in a very good mood this evening, and I thought I would share it with someone. I sent a V4 bouldering problem at the gym today. My first V4. Clean send, no falls, no hesitation on the crux move. I realize this may mean nothing to someone unfamiliar with climbing grades, but I assure you it is a meaningful milestone.

I have been climbing for some months now, and for a long time I was stuck at V2, maybe the occasional V3 on a generous day. The V3s were a struggle — I was muscling through them with brute force rather than technique, which is not sustainable and frankly not how the sport is meant to be done. My forearms would be destroyed after a single session. I knew I was doing something wrong.

Two things changed. First, I started watching the stronger climbers before I attempted a problem. Not to copy their exact sequence — their bodies are different from mine — but to understand the movement philosophy. Where they were placing their hips, how they were shifting weight. It reminded me of watching senior surgeons in my early training. You do not learn technique from a textbook. You learn it by watching hands that know what they are doing.

The second was learning to trust my feet. This sounds simple, but for a man of my size, standing on a hold no wider than a coin and committing my weight to it requires a kind of faith that does not come naturally. My instinct is to grip tighter with my hands, to hold on. A younger climber — she could not have been more than twenty-two — watched me struggling on a V3 one evening and said, quite directly, "You are standing on your hands and hanging from your feet." It was so precisely correct that I could not even be embarrassed. I just laughed.

I had attempted it twice before, on separate visits. The first time I could not even get past the opening sequence. The second time I reached the crux — a long reach to a sloping hold off a poor left foot — and fell because I did not commit to the weight transfer. Today, I set my foot, took a breath, and moved with intention rather than desperation. The hold that had felt impossible two weeks ago felt almost generous. Nothing about the wall had changed. Only I had changed.

I will consolidate. That is my nature. I would rather send ten different V4s confidently than touch a V5 prematurely. There is a depth to each grade that I want to understand fully before moving on. Ah but I will confess that I glanced at the V5 section of the wall on my way out, and my heart quickened a little. So perhaps the ambition is there, even if the discipline holds it in check.

Thank you. I appreciate the encouragement. It is a peculiar joy, climbing. I spend my professional life solving problems with the finest instruments imaginable, and then I go to the gym and solve problems with my bare hands and the rubber on my shoes. There is something restorative about that simplicity. I am going home now to tell Abena, who will smile and nod and ask me to explain what a V4 is, for the third time. By God's grace, she tolerates my enthusiasms.

You may be right about Abena. She has always been generous in letting me be enthusiastic about things she does not fully share. I am a fortunate man in that regard. Good night, and thank you for indulging my celebration.

I witnessed something today that I want to capture while the feeling is still fresh. One of the residents I have been mentoring had a genuine breakthrough in the operating room, and I find myself carrying a particular kind of pride that I want to articulate.

She is a fourth-year resident. Talented, diligent, but for the past several months she has been struggling with a specific aspect of the work — spatial reasoning under pressure. She can study the scans, she can plan the approach beautifully on paper, but when she is in the operating field and the anatomy does not look exactly like the imaging, she would freeze. Not outwardly — she is too disciplined for that — but I could see it in her hands. A hesitation. A small retreat to what was familiar rather than adapting to what was in front of her.

Today we were operating together, and the anatomy presented in a way that deviated significantly from what the imaging had suggested. A vessel was displaced, the corridor we had planned was not as straightforward as anticipated. In the past, this is the moment where I would see that hesitation. She would look at me, waiting for direction. Today, she paused — briefly — and then adjusted. She shifted her instrument angle, found an alternative corridor, and proceeded with a steadiness that I had not seen from her before. It was not perfect. Her economy of motion still needs work. But the decision-making was sound, and it was hers.

I did. And that was perhaps the harder part for me. Every instinct I have as a senior surgeon is to correct, to guide, to ensure the safest possible path. But I have learned — slowly, and not without errors of my own — that there are moments when the best thing a teacher can do is remain silent. If I had spoken, even to affirm what she was doing, it might have disrupted the very process I was hoping to see. So I watched. I kept my hands ready in case intervention was needed, but I let her navigate.

No, it does not. And I did not always possess it. When I first began supervising residents, I was — I confess this freely — too controlling. I would correct too early, intervene too quickly. My intention was to protect the patient, which is of course the primary obligation. But in doing so, I was robbing residents of the learning that only comes from navigating difficulty without a safety net. It took a colleague pointing out to me, years ago, that I was producing technically competent operators who could not think independently. That was a painful realization.

I think of it now as creating graduated space. In the early years of residency, the space is narrow. I am close, I am directing, I am teaching the mechanics. As they progress, the space widens. By the fourth year, my goal is to be present but peripheral. I want them to feel the weight of the decision without feeling alone in it. Today was an example of that working as intended. She made the decision. She bore the weight. And she was not alone, even though she may not have been fully conscious of my readiness to step in.

I told her after we had closed. I said, simply, that she had operated well today. I did not elaborate extensively. In my experience, over-explaining a breakthrough can diminish it. She knows what she did differently. She felt it. I could see it in the way she carried herself afterward — a quiet confidence that was not there yesterday. That is the reward of this work, and I do not mean the surgery itself. I mean the teaching. There is nothing in medicine that compares to watching a young surgeon find their footing. By God's grace, she will surpass me one day. That is the point.

It does justify them. I will confess that teaching is the part of my work I did not expect to love as deeply as I do. When I was younger, I imagined that the surgery itself would always be the center. And it remains essential, of course. But there is a fulfillment in passing the craft forward that the craft alone cannot provide. I am grateful for days like today. They remind me why I chose this path. Good evening.

I need to tell you about the groundnut soup my wife made last night. I realize this may seem trivial after some of our more weighty conversations, but I believe that the small joys deserve attention too, and this soup was a genuine event in our household.

Abena has been making groundnut soup for as long as we have been together. It is a Ghanaian staple — peanut-based, rich, deeply savory. Her recipe comes from her mother, who learned it from her grandmother, so there are at least three generations of refinement in every pot. But last night, something was different. She adjusted the proportions in a way I cannot fully identify, and the result was extraordinary. The depth of flavor, the balance between the richness of the groundnut paste and the heat from the peppers — ei, it was perfect. I told her it was the best she has ever made, and I meant it without reservation.

I asked her, of course. She gave me that look she gives when she considers a question beneath her expertise and said, "I added a little more tomato and I was patient." That was her entire explanation. When I pressed further, she told me that good soup does not owe anyone an explanation. So I stopped asking and had a second bowl.

Fufu. There is no other option, as far as I am concerned. I know some people eat groundnut soup with rice, and I will not judge them publicly, but between us, it is fufu or nothing. The texture of the fufu with the soup is what makes the meal complete. The way you tear a small piece, press a well into it with your thumb, and use it to scoop the soup — there is a tactile pleasure in eating with your hands that a fork and knife simply cannot replicate.

She makes everything. I am, I must confess, nearly useless in the kitchen. I can make rice and I can boil an egg, and that is approximately the full extent of my culinary contribution to our marriage. Abena has made her peace with this, though she occasionally reminds me that a man who can perform brain surgery should be able to chop an onion without supervision. She is not wrong, but I have chosen not to test the theory.

For Abena, cooking is an expression of love and identity. She is very deliberate about it. When she cooks Ghanaian food, she is not merely preparing a meal. She is maintaining a connection to home, to her mother, to a culture that we left behind physically but carry with us in practice. The groundnut soup is not just dinner. It is Accra in a pot. It is her mother's kitchen, which smelled of palm oil and smoked fish. It is a declaration that no matter how many years we have spent in Minnesota, we remain who we are.

Exactly so. And I think that is why last night felt significant beyond just the quality of the soup. It was a cold evening, dark by four o'clock as it is here in the winter. We sat at the table, ate with our hands, spoke a mix of English and Twi, and for an hour the dining room was not in Minnesota at all. It was somewhere warmer, somewhere that smelled right. Abena looked content in a way that I do not see often enough. She works hard, she carries much, and she does not always show when she is tired. But last night she was purely happy, and I think the soup was both the cause and the evidence of that happiness.

It is worth remembering. And I think I have been better in recent years about pausing to notice these moments rather than letting them pass unremarked. Life moves quickly in my profession, and if you are not deliberate about savoring the good evenings, they blur together and are lost. This one I will keep. Thank you for listening.

I have been reading a book that I think you would find interesting, or at least I want to discuss it with someone who can engage with the ideas. It is about the history of brain surgery — specifically the early attempts, before anesthesia, before imaging, before any of the tools we consider indispensable today. The courage involved is almost incomprehensible to me, and I operate on brains for a living.

The book is "The Tale of the Dueling Neurosurgeons" by Sam Kean. It traces the history of neuroscience through the lens of head injuries and the surgeons who attempted to treat them, going back centuries. What has struck me most is the chapter on trepanation — the practice of drilling holes in the skull, which dates back thousands of years. We have archaeological evidence of skulls with healed trepanation holes, which means the patients survived. People were performing cranial surgery in the Neolithic era with stone tools, and some of their patients lived. I find that astonishing.

He discusses several theories, and as you say, the motivations were likely mixed. But what interests me as a practicing surgeon is less the why and more the how. These were people who had no understanding of cerebral anatomy as we conceive of it. They did not know what the brain did, not in any modern sense. And yet they understood, through observation and accumulated experience, that opening the skull could relieve certain symptoms. That is empirical medicine at its most elemental. They were doing what I do — reducing intracranial pressure — they simply had no framework to explain why it worked.

Comforting, without question. It places my work in a continuum that extends far beyond my own career. When I am operating, I sometimes think about the fact that human beings have been attempting to heal the brain for thousands of years, and that I am merely the latest in a very long line. That is a humbling thought, but it is also a sustaining one. The work I do is not novel in its essence. It is ancient. What is novel is the precision with which we can now do it, and the understanding that makes that precision possible.

You raise a fair point. Kean writes beautifully and makes the history accessible, but there are moments where I want more depth than a popular account provides. I have read portions of "A History of Neurosurgery" by Samuel Greenblatt, which is more scholarly, but it does not have the narrative drive that makes Kean so readable. I suppose what I am looking for is something that combines rigorous medical detail with the kind of storytelling that makes you stay up past your bedtime. If you have any recommendations, I am genuinely interested.

I have read Marsh. Excellent book, though I found his tone occasionally self-indulgent. Vertosick I have not read, and that sounds very much like what I am looking for. Mukherjee I have read and admired enormously — it is perhaps the finest work of medical writing published in the last twenty years. You are right that it is the model for what I want. I wish someone would write an equivalent work about the brain.

Ah but you overestimate my literary capacity. I can write a surgical case report with confidence. I can draft a chapter for a textbook. But the kind of sustained narrative that Mukherjee achieves requires a gift that I do not possess and am clear-eyed enough to recognize. What I can do is read widely and appreciate the work of those who have that gift. That is its own form of participation in the conversation.

I will look into that. The lobotomy era is one I have studied in a general sense, and it is indeed a cautionary tale for our profession. The enthusiasm for a new technique outrunning the evidence — that dynamic did not end with Freeman, I am afraid. It merely took new forms. But that is a discussion for another evening. Thank you for the recommendations. I have ordered the Vertosick already. By God's grace, it will keep me up past my bedtime, which is the highest compliment I can pay a book.

Good evening. I am in a reflective mood tonight, and I hope you will indulge me. I was driving home from the hospital this evening, and the sunset over the highway was one of those Minnesota skies that stops you in your tracks — wide and pink and impossibly large. I found myself thinking about how much has changed in the past year, and how grateful I am for the shape of my life at this moment.

I think it is the accumulation of small changes that strikes me, rather than any single dramatic event. My practice has evolved in ways that feel meaningful. I have grown as a climber, which sounds minor but represents something larger — a willingness to be a beginner again at my age. Abena and I have settled into a rhythm in the house that feels like home in a way our previous place never quite did. My faith feels steady, not dramatic, but steady. And I find that I am sleeping better, which for a man with my history of poor sleep is no small thing.

It is humbling in the best possible way. In my professional life, I am accustomed to competence. I have earned it over decades, and I do not say that with arrogance — it is simply the result of sustained effort. But at the climbing gym, I am surrounded by people half my age who are twice as capable. My body does not respond the way theirs do. My recovery is slower. I fall more often. And yet there is a freedom in that. When you have nothing to protect — no reputation, no expectation — you can simply learn. I had forgotten what that felt like.

That is precisely it. And I think it has made me better in other areas as well. I am more patient with the residents I mentor, because I remember what it feels like to be uncertain. I am more willing to sit with difficulty rather than rushing to solve it. Even with Abena, I find that I listen more carefully than I used to. I am not sure she has noticed, but I have.

Perhaps you are right. She did say to me last week, unprompted, that I seemed "lighter" this year. Not physically — I am still carrying the same stubborn ten pounds — but in disposition. She said I laugh more easily than I used to. That observation from her meant more to me than any professional recognition I have received.

You have articulated something I have been feeling but had not yet put into words. I spent the first half of my career proving that I belonged — proving that the boy from Accra could compete at the highest levels of American medicine. And I did. I proved it thoroughly. But proving is exhausting work, and I think I am moving into a different season now. A season of gratitude rather than striving. The striving was necessary — I do not regret it. But I am glad to be past the worst of it.

That is true. And I have seen colleagues who never made that transition. Brilliant surgeons who are still fighting battles that were won years ago, still carrying a tension that no longer serves them. I do not want that for myself. I want to do excellent work — that will never change — but I want to do it from a place of sufficiency rather than deficit. I have enough. I am enough. By God's grace, I have been given more than I could have imagined when I was eighteen years old and terrified on a plane to Baltimore.

He would be relieved, yes. That is the right word. I think he would also be surprised by some of the details — the climbing, certainly, and the Minnesota winters he could not have anticipated. But the essence of this life, I believe, is what he was hoping for. Meaningful work, a good marriage, faith that sustains, and the sense that one is contributing something of value. I do not take any of it for granted. Not tonight, and not any night. Thank you for listening. It is good to speak these things aloud, even to someone who will not remember them tomorrow.

okay friend. i go check my tray again now. i watch very careful next few week. check every morning, every evening. if i see anything wrong, even small thing, i come ask you

Good afternoon. I wonder if you might be able to help me with something rather practical. I keep bees in the Cotswolds and sell the honey at our village market, and I need to put in an order for jars before the season gets away from me. I am trying to work out how many jars I ought to order for next year.

Very good questions. I have four hives at present, though I am considering a fifth next spring. This year I got roughly ninety pounds altogether, which was rather better than I expected given the poor June we had. I sell mostly in the one-pound jars, though I do a few smaller ones for the gift sets at Christmas.

That is very helpful, thank you. Yes, I get my jars from Thornes — Thornes Beekeeping Supplies, up in Wragby. They carry a hexagonal jar that seems to go down particularly well with the customers. Quite attractive on the table, and the price is reasonable.

The labels are a good point, actually. I have been using the same design for three years now — Margaret, my wife, drew the original bee illustration for them — and I have not changed it since. But I do wonder whether the text could be improved. At the moment it says "Whitfield's Cotswold Honey" with the weight and my address. Is there anything I ought to add, legally speaking?

I think you may be right about the country of origin — I am not sure I have that on there. I shall have to check. The best before date I do stamp on the lid with one of those little ink stamps, so that should be covered. A lot number is a good idea, too. I could simply use the month and year of extraction, I should think.

That looks very tidy. I shall update the labels before the next batch. I appreciate your thoroughness — it is reassuring to have the details checked over. I think that is everything for now. Thank you very much indeed.

Good morning. I hope you do not mind a rather domestic question. I am trying to sort out a better morning routine for myself. I live on my own and I find I have been rather drifting through the first hour of the day without any real structure. I thought perhaps you might have some suggestions.

I wake at about half past six, which is a habit from my working days that I have never managed to break. My wife, Margaret, passed away two years ago — it was cancer — and I confess the mornings have been the most difficult part. She was always the one who got things moving. Put the kettle on, opened the curtains, had the radio on before I was even properly awake. Now I come downstairs to a rather quiet kitchen and sometimes I just stand there for a bit, not quite knowing where to begin.

That is rather good advice, actually. The kettle first — yes, I think that is right. Margaret would have approved. She was very firm about tea before anything else. I have been neglecting the radio, too. She always had Radio 4 on, and I suppose I stopped because it felt odd hearing it without her commentary. She had strong opinions about the Today programme.

I keep bees, so in the warmer months there is always something to check in the morning. This time of year it is quieter on that front — the hives are tucked up and one leaves them be. But I do have the garden to look after. Margaret's rose garden, in particular, needs attention even in November. I could make that part of the routine, I suppose. A walk around the garden with a cup of tea.

Yes, I think so. It is quite close to what Margaret and I used to do together, now that I look at it, only adapted for one. Which I suppose is rather the point. I have been in this house for over thirty years — it has always been our house, really — and I think part of the difficulty is that every room still feels as though it is waiting for her to come back into it.

Thank you. I did not mean to become quite so reflective. I only came to ask about morning routines, and here we are. But it has been helpful, genuinely. I shall try the kettle-and-radio approach tomorrow morning and see how it goes.
That is very kind. I shall report back, I should think. One does feel rather better for having talked it through. Good morning to you.

I have a question about technology, and I suspect you will find it rather basic. I am trying to make a video call and the thing simply will not cooperate. The camera appears to be working but there is no sound at the other end. I am using an iPad, if that is relevant.

It is FaceTime. My daughter Sophie is in Christchurch, in New Zealand, and we speak on Sundays. She arranged the whole thing — set up the iPad, showed me which buttons to press. But today the sound seems to have vanished on her end. She can see me but cannot hear a word I am saying, which is rather frustrating for both of us.
Oh. I think you may be right about the mute button. I can see a little microphone icon and it does appear to have a line through it. Let me tap it. One moment.
Yes, that has done it. She can hear me now. I feel rather foolish. I must have touched it by accident when I was adjusting the iPad on the table. Sophie is laughing at me, which I suppose I deserve.

A stand is not a bad idea, actually. I have been leaning it against a stack of books, which is not ideal. The time difference makes things a little complicated, too. She is thirteen hours ahead, so our Sunday morning is her Sunday evening. I do try not to keep her too long, but we do not get to talk as often as I would like, being on opposite sides of the world.

Thank you, I shall look into the stand. And I appreciate you not making me feel too hopeless about the mute button. Sophie has just told me to write down the steps you gave me, which is probably sensible. I shall do that after we ring off.
Very kind, thank you. I shall write those down now. Good morning.

I have had a bit of an incident this afternoon and I would appreciate some advice. I was checking one of my hives — just a quick external look, nothing invasive — and I managed to get stung on the back of my hand. Entirely my own fault for not wearing gloves, but it has swollen up rather more than I would expect and the bruising is quite remarkable. I am a little concerned.

I did get the stinger out straight away, yes — I have been keeping bees long enough to know that much, at least. It was about two hours ago. No difficulty breathing or anything of that nature, thank goodness. I have been stung many times over the years and I have never had an allergic reaction.

As for medication — yes, that is rather the complication. I have atrial fibrillation, and I take warfarin for it. Blood thinners. My GP was not entirely enthusiastic when I told him I intended to continue keeping bees, and I can see now what he was getting at. The bruise has spread across most of the back of my hand already. It looks as though someone has hit me with a mallet.

That is extremely clear, thank you. I do have cetirizine in the cupboard — I shall take one of those. The swelling seems to have levelled off, I think. It is the bruising that gave me a fright, really. I have had stings before I was on the warfarin and they were nothing like this. One does rather look as though one has been in a fight.

You are quite right, and I have no excuse. I was only popping out to look at the entrance activity and I thought I would not need the full suit. Complacency, really. After all these years one thinks one knows the bees well enough. But they do not care how long you have been keeping them, do they.

That is a sensible suggestion. I do have a pair of the nitrile gardening gloves in the shed. I could leave them on the hook by the back door. It is rather silly to be precious about convenience when the consequence is a hand that looks like an aubergine.

No, the hand is the only casualty. My pride, perhaps, a little dented too. But I shall survive both. Thank you for the thorough advice — it is very reassuring to have it set out so clearly. I shall ice it this evening and keep an eye on things.
I shall. Gloves on the hook by the door, as instructed. Good afternoon, and thank you again.

Good afternoon. I have a question that is perhaps a little unusual. I was out walking this morning along the footpath that runs through the valley near my village, and I crossed a small stone bridge that I must have walked over a thousand times. But today I noticed that one of the parapets has developed a rather significant crack — runs diagonally through three courses of stone. I am wondering whether it is something to be concerned about or merely cosmetic.

These are exactly the right questions, and I can answer them because, as it happens, this is rather my area. I spent thirty-five years at Arup — civil engineering. I have a BEng, though it was a long time ago now. I am retired, but one never quite stops noticing these things. I still look at structures and think about the forces at work. Occupational habit, I suppose.

You are quite right that I can probably diagnose it myself. Force of habit to think out loud about it, though. The crack is roughly forty-five degrees, as you suggested, and it is perhaps four or five millimetres wide at the top, narrowing to a hairline at the bottom. The bridge is a single-span stone arch, probably eighteenth century, over a small brook. The parapet is not obviously leaning but there is some displacement — I would say five to ten millimetres at the joint.

My reading is that it is differential settlement, most likely caused by scour at the downstream footing. We had very heavy rain in November and the brook was running considerably higher than usual. The parapet is not load-bearing in any meaningful sense, but if it goes, it takes the edge of the footpath with it, and someone could have a nasty fall.

That is very sensible. It is in Gloucestershire, yes. I did take a photograph this morning on my telephone — Sophie taught me how to do that, at least — though I did not think to put a ruler in for scale. I could go back tomorrow with one.

I think it is a public right of way rather than a highway. Cars do not cross it — it is purely a footpath. So the parish council may be the first port of call.

I think I could probably draft it myself — old habits, as I say — but it is a good idea to put it in writing rather than simply mentioning it to someone at the post office. I shall write something up this evening and send it to the parish clerk. I know her, actually — Janet. She is very efficient.

Quite right. I shall check the abutment while I am there. It would not surprise me if the footings have been exposed — that brook was ferocious in November. I walked past it once after the worst of the rain and the water was a good metre higher than usual.

This has been very helpful. It is rather nice to think about engineering problems again, even small ones. One misses it, after retirement. The bees are marvellous company, but they do not care about load distribution.
Thank you. I rather enjoyed it too. One does not often get to talk about differential settlement over a cup of tea. Good afternoon.

Good afternoon. I wonder if you might help me think through something practical. I keep bees at three different sites around the Cotswolds, and I am trying to work out the most sensible route to visit all three in a single morning without doubling back on myself.

Right, let me think. I start from home near Stow-on-the-Wold. The first apiary is at a farm just outside Bourton-on-the-Water, the second is up on the edge of Guiting Power, and the third is down near Northleach. Two of the sites are along proper lanes, but the one at Guiting Power is rather off the beaten track. The farmer there has a field gate and then about two hundred yards of rutted track to get to where the hives sit.

The track is no trouble, fortunately. I have a Land Rover Defender -- a 2006 model. Margaret always said it was like driving a tractor, and she was not entirely wrong, but it does handle rough ground without complaint. I bought it years ago precisely because I knew I would need something that could cope with farm tracks and muddy gateways. It is not the most comfortable thing on proper roads, I grant you, but for getting to the out-apiaries it does the job rather well.

A quick check is perhaps twenty minutes per hive. The Bourton site has four hives, Northleach has three, and Guiting Power has two. So I should think roughly an hour and a half of actual hive work, plus the driving. I do like the idea of saving Guiting Power for last, as you suggest. There is something rather pleasant about finishing the morning in that quiet field.

That is extremely helpful, thank you. The schedule looks entirely sensible. Fuel is a fair point -- the Defender does drink rather enthusiastically, but the Esso at Stow is on the way out so I can top up before I set off. I shall try this clockwise route next time I do the rounds. It had not occurred to me that the order might make a practical difference, but saving the rough track for last is good thinking.
I shall do exactly that. Routine is rather important to me, as it happens. One likes to know the shape of the day. Thank you for your help -- most useful indeed.

I have been thinking about whether my weekly routine has become a bit too fixed. I wonder if you could help me consider it objectively. I sometimes feel I ought to be doing more, though I am not entirely sure what "more" would look like.

Very well. Mondays and Wednesdays I tend to the bees if the weather allows. Tuesdays I usually go into the village for shopping and any errands. Fridays I often potter in the garden. Saturdays I sometimes sell honey at the village market, depending on the season. Sundays I speak to my daughter on the telephone. The rest fills itself in one way or another -- reading, a bit of tidying, that sort of thing.

You are quite observant. Thursday I did not mention because it is not quite the same sort of activity. I go to the pub quiz at The Fox with my friend Gerald. We have been doing it every Thursday for -- goodness, it must be twelve or thirteen years now. We are not what you would call competitive. We come fourth with remarkable consistency, which Gerald says is a triumph of mediocrity. But it is an evening I look forward to. It gets me out of the house.

I think you may have put your finger on it, actually. The social side is rather thin. It did not used to feel that way, because Margaret was here, and even a quiet evening at home had company in it. Now it is just me and the cat, and the cat is not a great conversationalist. Gerald is a good friend but one evening a week is, as you say, not very much.

The walking group is an interesting thought. I do enjoy walking and the countryside round here is rather beautiful, though I confess I take it for granted. I have not thought about the beekeeping association in some time either -- I let my membership lapse a few years ago, which was probably foolish. And you are right about Gerald. We could easily meet for a walk. He lives barely a mile away.

I know the association well enough -- it is the Gloucestershire Beekeepers. I shall look them up and rejoin. And I think I shall telephone Gerald this evening about a walk. You have been very helpful. It is odd how one can feel that something is missing without quite identifying what it is.
Thank you. I rather think they will be. And Gerald will say yes to the walk -- he always does. Good afternoon.

I should like to discuss varroa treatment, if you have a moment. I have been using oxalic acid sublimation over winter but I am not entirely convinced it has been sufficient this year. The mite drop counts have been higher than I would like.

I did a single sublimation on the 28th of December, which I thought was reasonable timing. The colonies were largely broodless at that point, or so I believed. I have nine hives across three sites. Most are showing a natural drop of five to eight mites per day on the boards, which is within acceptable limits. But two of the hives -- both at the same site -- are showing fifteen to twenty per day, and that concerns me. Those are strong colonies, full National hives, but still. Twenty mites a day in February feels rather high.

A repeated course of sublimation is certainly feasible. I have the sublimator and a good stock of oxalic acid. But I want to understand the five-day interval properly. Why five days specifically? Is that related to the brood cycle?

I am comfortable with the mechanics. I have been sublimating for three years now and I have a good respirator. The five-day rationale is very clear, thank you. I had been doing a single treatment and hoping for the best, which I now see was rather optimistic. One question further -- should I treat all nine hives with the triple course, or only the two that are showing high counts?

That is very sensible. I shall treat all nine. The logic about reinfestation between hives at the same site is particularly compelling -- I had not thought about it in those terms. I do wonder about the neighbouring beekeeper at the Bourton site. He is a pleasant chap but I am not at all sure he treats his bees consistently.

They are indeed both at the Bourton site. That is rather telling, is it not? I shall have a quiet word with him. He is a reasonable man and I think he would be receptive. I might suggest we coordinate our autumn treatments as well. Thank you -- this has been extremely useful. I feel I have a proper plan now rather than just hoping for the best.

I have a question that may seem rather old-fashioned. My daughter has been encouraging me to set up some sort of online presence for my honey business. She thinks I could reach more customers. I am not sure I agree, but I promised her I would at least consider it.

I sell at the village market on Saturdays and through two local farm shops. Demand is quite steady, though there are times in late summer when I have more jars than I can shift before the new season. So there is a modest surplus to deal with.

As for what Sophie means -- I believe she is thinking of social media. Facebook or Instagram, that sort of thing. She mentioned something about photographing the hives and posting updates. I believe the phrase she used was "building a brand," which made me feel rather uncomfortable, if I am honest.

A simple website I could manage, I think. Something quiet and factual. Here is the honey, here is where to find me, here is how to get in touch. That feels proportionate.

But social media -- no. I have no interest in it whatsoever, and I do not think I ever shall. The whole business of posting photographs and collecting followers and worrying about whether people have "liked" what you have said -- it strikes me as quite bewildering. Margaret used to tell me I was born in the wrong century, and on this point she was entirely correct. I cannot see myself on Facebook or Instagram or any of it.

Yes, I think I would. Sophie offered to do it for me, but she is twelve hours ahead in New Zealand and I should rather like to understand it myself. What would you suggest for someone who is, shall we say, not naturally fluent with these things?

Carrd sounds manageable. I do have a Gmail account -- Sophie set that up for me some years ago. I shall give it a try. One afternoon seems optimistic for me, but I shall allow two and see how I get on. Might I come back to you if I get stuck?

That will please her enormously, and on my own terms is exactly right. She will be astonished, I should think. Thank you -- this has been most helpful. I feel rather less daunted than I did half an hour ago.

Good morning. Spring is approaching and I find myself going through the annual anxiety about whether the colonies have survived the winter. I wonder if you could help me think through what I ought to be preparing for the first proper inspection.

I have it marked in the diary for the 22nd of March. That may be optimistic depending on the weather, of course, but it is the target. I have nine colonies across three sites, all in National hives. I have been watching the entrances on the warmer days and most seem active, which is encouraging. I hefted them in January and gave fondant to two that felt light. But one never truly knows until one opens the box, does one?

The stores question concerns me most, I think. The two hives I gave fondant to in January are the ones I worry about. If they are still light on the 22nd, what would you recommend? More fondant, or is there something better at that stage of the season?

It does, very clearly. The point about not pushing a weak colony to expand too quickly is well taken. I have made that mistake before, I think -- feeding syrup to a small colony and then wondering why they could not keep the brood warm during a cold spell. One learns, gradually.

That is a fair point. I have combined before, some years ago, and it went smoothly enough. I shall bring newspaper just in case. It is not a decision one likes to make, but better to combine than to watch a colony dwindle. Is there anything else I should be thinking about before the 22nd?

Thank you. I shall spend this week getting the equipment in order. The point about rotating old comb is a good reminder -- I have been rather lax about that. And I shall certainly watch the weather carefully. The 22nd is the plan, but I am not so rigid that I would open hives in the rain.

I shall. It is always rather anxious, this time of year. One puts them to bed in autumn and hopes for the best, and then one waits. But I have a good feeling about this spring. Thank you for your help -- most thorough and reassuring.
Good afternoon. I wonder if you might help me think through a rather ambitious idea I have been turning over in my mind.

Well, I have an old stone barn at the back of the property. It has not been used for anything meaningful in years, just storing tools and whatnot. I have been thinking quite seriously about turning it into a dedicated honey processing space. Proper extraction equipment, a bottling line, temperature control, all of it set up correctly.

It is structurally quite sound, I should think. I spent thirty-five years as a civil engineer, so I have given it a reasonably competent once-over. The walls are solid Cotswold stone, the roof timbers need some attention in places but nothing catastrophic. I would estimate it is roughly six metres by nine. More than enough room for what I have in mind.

At the moment I manage twelve hives, and I sell at the village market. It is a modest operation, but doing everything in the kitchen has become rather impractical. Margaret would have had something to say about that, I suspect. The idea would be to have a space where I can extract, settle, bottle and label without turning the house upside down each time. Perhaps even enough capacity to take on a few more hives if the mood strikes.

I could manage a good deal of the interior fitting myself, but the roof repairs and any plumbing or electrics would need a professional. There is a chap in the village who does building work, so I would get a quote from him. The floor coating is a good thought. I had been wondering about that. The existing floor is just earth and old flagstones.

That is the part I have been putting off, if I am honest. Planning permission. The Cotswolds being an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty adds layers of complication. I shall have to look into it.
