One does rather hope that turning a barn into a honey room is the sort of thing they would approve, but one never knows with these things.

A pre-application enquiry is a sensible suggestion. I shall look into that. It would be a great pity to go to all the trouble of getting quotes and ordering equipment only to be told one cannot proceed. I should rather like to have the whole thing settled before the summer, so that I could be using it by the autumn extraction.

Quite right. I shall make a start on the pre-application this week. It would make the whole operation considerably more efficient, and rather more dignified than balancing a centrifuge on the kitchen worktop. Thank you for helping me think it through. It feels more achievable now that I have set it out properly.
I am in need of some technical assistance, if you would not mind. My iPad is insisting that I update it, and I confess I am not entirely sure how to proceed.

A notification appeared this morning. Something about iPadOS and a number — 18, I believe. It has a button that says "Details" and another that says "Later." I pressed "Later" the last three times it appeared, but it keeps coming back, rather insistently.

Right. Let me find my glasses. One moment. Yes, I have the Settings open. General. Software Update. It says "iPadOS 18.3.2" and there is a blue button that says "Download and Install." Underneath it says something about 2.1 gigabytes. Is that a great deal?

It is on the charger, yes, and I am on the Wi-Fi. The passcode — that would be the six-digit number? I do know that one. Let me tap the button. It is asking for the passcode now. I shall enter it. Right. It now says "Downloading" with a small progress indicator. I should think it will take a while on my connection.
And I shan't lose anything? Photographs, my notes, the video calling application? My daughter set that up for me and I would rather not have to ask her to do it again.

That is a relief. I must say, I find these things rather daunting. In my working days one had a secretary who dealt with the computers. Now it is just me and this tablet, and we do not always see eye to eye. Thank you for your patience.
I have a question about rose pruning, if you have a moment. I have rather let things get away from me in the garden and I think some of the bushes need attention.

There are quite a few. The garden was always my wife's domain, and she knew exactly what to do with each one. I have hybrid teas along the south wall, a rather sprawling rambler over the pergola, and several David Austin shrub roses in the main beds. I have been doing my best with them, but I should like to do it properly.
It flowers once, in June. A tremendous flush of small pink blooms. It is rather magnificent when it performs, though it does try to consume the entire pergola if left unchecked.

I am glad I asked before taking the secateurs to it. I very nearly did so last weekend. The hybrid teas I can manage, I think. Fifteen to twenty centimetres, outward-facing buds, open shape. The David Austins — a third off the top and thin the middle. Is that about right?

I have some well-rotted compost from the heap at the bottom of the garden. That should do nicely. And I have fish, blood and bone in the shed, I believe. One more question, if I may — a few of the David Austins have rather a lot of dead wood in the centre. Whole branches that are brown and dry. Is it sufficient to cut those out now, or should I be concerned about why they have died back?

Very good. I shall make a start on it this afternoon while the weather holds. It is rather satisfying work, pruning. One can see the results immediately. Thank you for the guidance — I feel rather more confident now than I did half an hour ago.

I should like a recipe for honey flapjacks, if you would be so kind. I have rather a lot of honey at the moment and I thought I might bake something to take along to the village market stall. Samples, as it were.

That looks quite manageable. I am not a natural baker, I should confess. When you say "press it down really well" — how firm are we talking? I have a tendency to be rather tentative with these things.

Packing wet sand. That is a very useful image, thank you. Now, I have two types of honey available. A lighter one from the spring flow — quite delicate, floral — and a darker summer honey that is rather more robust. Which would you recommend for baking?

That is rather shrewd marketing advice. I had not thought of positioning them that way. One further question — how far in advance can I make these? The market is on Saturday and I was thinking of baking them on Thursday evening.

Bite-sized pieces. Yes, that makes sense. I shall give it a go on Thursday. The prospect of me baking would have amused Margaret enormously, I must say. But one adapts. Thank you for the recipe and the advice. Most helpful.
I find myself in need of some practical advice. I have rather a lot to organise before the summer and I am not quite sure where to begin.

My daughter Sophie is coming over from New Zealand. She arrives on the tenth of August and will be staying for a fortnight. It has been quite some time since her last visit, and I want everything to be in good order. The spare room in particular needs attention — it has become something of a repository for things I do not know what to do with.

There is a good bed in there, a double. It was Sophie's room originally, before she went abroad. The curtains are adequate, if a little tired. The mattress may need replacing — I cannot remember when it was last used for an actual guest. There are boxes of old engineering journals stacked against one wall, and I am fairly sure Margaret's sewing machine is in there somewhere under a dust sheet.

It does. I suspect I shall keep the sewing machine. It was Margaret's, and I am not ready to part with it, even though I have no intention of using it myself. I shall find a corner for it downstairs, perhaps. The engineering journals — you are quite right. I have not opened them in a decade. The local library is a good thought.

I should think a trip to the shop would be wise so I can try a few. I am not one for buying that sort of thing online without seeing it. Beyond the room itself, I have been thinking about what to do while Sophie is here. She always enjoyed walking, and the Cotswolds are rather good for that. But two weeks is a long time. I do not want her to feel she must entertain me, or I her.

The bees are a good idea, actually. She has heard a great deal about them but has not seen the operation since I expanded to twelve hives. I could show her the whole process. She might even be persuaded to put on a suit and help with an inspection. I rather like the thought of that.

I do have a spare suit, but I am not sure of the condition. I shall dig it out and check. If the zips are gone, I shall order a new one. Is there anything else you would suggest I think about before her arrival? I want it to go well. We do our Sunday video calls faithfully, but it is not the same as having her here.

A spare key is an excellent thought. I shall have one cut at the ironmonger's. And you are quite right about not overdoing it. I have a tendency to worry about these things more than is strictly necessary. Thank you. I feel considerably better about the whole enterprise now that I have a list to work through.
I have been thinking about a project from years ago and I wonder if you might indulge me for a moment. Do you know the Cynghordy Viaduct in Wales?

Eighteen arches, yes, quite right. I was involved in an assessment of a rather similar viaduct nearby — not Cynghordy itself, but another masonry arch structure on the same line. This would have been in the early nineties. We were asked to determine whether it could carry modern rolling stock loads. The whole thing was rather fascinating.

The original drawings had survived, which was something of a miracle. They were held at the county archive. Beautiful draughtsmanship — all done by hand, naturally. But the difficulty was that masonry arches don't behave the way modern structures do. You cannot simply apply a standard beam analysis. The load travels through the arch in compression, and the condition of the mortar joints matters enormously. We had to core samples from several of the piers to test the mortar strength.

Rather better than expected, actually. The Victorians used a lime mortar that had some give in it — a degree of flexibility that Portland cement does not have. Some of the joints had weathered, naturally, but the cores were surprisingly sound at depth. The real concern was one pier that had developed a slight lean. Only about forty millimetres off vertical, but when you are dealing with a structure of that height, one pays attention.

Foundation movement, as it turned out. The valley had a watercourse that had shifted over the decades, and one bank had been gradually eroding beneath the footing. We recommended ground stabilisation and repointing of the affected pier. The viaduct is still standing and still carrying trains, so I should think we got it broadly right. It gives one a certain quiet satisfaction, knowing that.

I drove past it on a holiday with Margaret some years ago and pointed it out to her. She was politely interested, which is the most one can hope for when one is enthusing about masonry piers to a non-engineer. I do miss that sort of work sometimes — the puzzle of it, working out how something stands up and how to keep it standing. Retirement is pleasant, but the mind does like a problem to solve. The bees provide some of that, I suppose. They present problems of a different sort.
Good morning. I have rather disappointing news to report, though I suppose one ought to have seen it coming.
Do you recall I had been looking into converting the barn? Turning it into a proper honey processing space? Well. That is not happening. The whole thing is off the table entirely.

Both, as it happens. The planning application was refused. The conservation officer raised objections about the barn being within the curtilage of a listed building, which I ought to have anticipated but somehow did not. And then the builder came back with his estimate, and I nearly fell off my chair. Forty thousand pounds. For what is essentially a shed with plumbing.

One could appeal, I suppose, but the conservation officer was quite categorical, and I am not minded to spend months arguing with the council when the answer is almost certainly going to remain the same. And even if they reversed the decision, I cannot justify forty thousand pounds on a hobby, however much I enjoy it. Margaret would have had words, I should think.

Completely done. Scrapped. I have put it out of my mind. The barn will remain a barn, and I shall carry on extracting honey in the kitchen as I have always done. It is not elegant, but it works well enough. One does feel a bit foolish for having got so excited about it.

A few hundred on the application fee and some drawings that are now entirely useless. Not ruinous, but not nothing either. The drawings are rather good, actually. I may frame one for the wall as a memento of my brief ambition. A monument to optimism.

A local architect drew them up. Cross-sections, elevations, the lot. She did a rather lovely job. It showed the extraction room, a bottling area, and a small shop front facing the lane. I had grand plans. But there we are. One must know when to let something go.

I had thought about a better extractor. The one I have is a hand-cranked affair that takes rather a long time. An electric one would speed things up considerably. That is a few hundred pounds rather than forty thousand, which I should think is more proportionate to my actual honey output.
That would be helpful, yes. Perhaps another day. I think for now I shall go and sit in the garden with a cup of tea and stop thinking about barns.

I wonder whether you might help me think through something. The forecast for the next fortnight is showing quite warm temperatures — high twenties — but very little rain. I am trying to work out what that means for the honey flow.

The main sources at this time of year are the field beans in the neighbouring farm, the lime trees along the village lane, and the clover in the meadow behind the house. The limes are usually the big producers in late June and July.

The beans are nearly finished, I should think. The farmer planted them in February and they have been flowering for several weeks now. I expect another week at most. So it is really the limes and the clover I am thinking about.

I checked on Saturday and they were drawing comb on the second super quite enthusiastically, which is encouraging. The first super is about three-quarters capped. I was wondering whether I ought to add a third, in case the lime flow is strong, or whether that would be premature.

That is what I was thinking, but I wanted to hear it confirmed. I have spare drawn comb from last year, which should help them get started on a third super more quickly than foundation would. I shall add it this week, I think. The other question is whether I ought to be providing water. The stream at the bottom of the garden has gone rather low.

I have a shallow terracotta saucer that Margaret used under one of her pots. That would do rather well, I should think. I shall fill it with some stones and set it near the hives. Thank you — this has been most useful. I feel rather more prepared for the warm spell now.

I find myself in need of a new book and I wondered whether you might suggest something. I should like some good nature writing — something contemplative, well-observed, and preferably British. I am not looking for anything too scientific or too sentimental.

I have read "H is for Hawk" and thought it was remarkable. You are quite right that it is not sentimental — she earns every emotion in that book. I have not read John Lewis-Stempel. Herefordshire is not so far from here, so the landscape would be familiar. Tell me more about "The Running Hare."

That sounds exactly right. I shall order that one, I think. The month-by-month structure appeals to me — I like a book that marks the passage of time properly. One lives by the seasons when one keeps bees, and I find I notice the same things he seems to notice. The skylarks, the first clover, when the hedgerows change.

I shall start with "The Running Hare" and see how I get on. Is there anything else in a slightly different vein? Perhaps something about a particular place, written by someone who knows it intimately? I rather liked Roger Deakin's "Waterlog" some years ago.

I have not read any of those three. "Wildwood" is tempting — I always felt that Deakin died before he had written his best work, and I should like to read more of him. And Macfarlane I have heard of but never picked up. I think "The Running Hare" and "Wildwood" will keep me going for a while. Thank you — you have been most helpful.
I shall. I like to read in the garden in the afternoons when it is warm enough. One of the pleasures of retirement. Good day.
I need to write a letter to the parish council and I am finding it rather difficult to strike the right tone. Would you be willing to help me draft something?

It concerns the footpath that runs along the back of the churchyard and down to the stream. The council have allowed the hedgerow on either side to become so overgrown that it is barely passable. I walked it last week and was scratched to ribbons by blackthorn. Several of us in the village have been grumbling about it, and I have somehow been elected to write the letter.

It is a public right of way, yes. I believe the number is FP12 but I should check that. Maintenance of the hedgerow would normally be the responsibility of the adjacent landowner, but in this case one side is the churchyard, which is maintained by the parish, and the other side belongs to the Hawkins farm. So it is partly the council's responsibility and partly a matter they might raise with the farmer.

That is rather good as a starting point. I think the tone is about right — firm but not aggressive. I might soften the final sentence slightly, though. "I trust the council will give this matter prompt attention" reads a touch like a threat, and I do have to see these people at the village fete.
Yes, that is much better. It sounds more like me, too. I should also mention that the stile at the stream end has a broken step. Might as well address everything in one letter.
Rather diplomatic. I appreciate that. One more thing — should I mention the number of people who have raised the concern with me, or is that unnecessary?

That is sensible. I think I have enough to put the letter together now. I shall write it out properly this evening and post it tomorrow. Thank you for the help — I always find these things harder to start than to finish, and you have got me over the difficult part.

I have a question about packaging, if you don't mind. I sell honey at my village market here in the Cotswolds, and I have recently made a change to how I present the product. I wondered if you might help me think through the pricing side of things.

New jars, primarily. I used to order glass jars from Thornes — the beekeeping supplier, up in Wragby — perfectly serviceable, nothing wrong with them — but I have found a potter in Stow-on-the-Wold. Mary, at Stow Pottery. She makes these rather handsome ceramic pots, each one slightly different, with a little glaze that catches the light. They are a different proposition altogether.

The old glass jars were roughly forty-five pence each. Mary's ceramic pots come in at about three pounds fifty each, so it is quite a jump. They hold roughly a pound of honey, yes. I have been selling the glass jars at six pounds a jar, which seemed to be the going rate at the market.

No pushback at all, actually. If anything, the opposite. I put a few out last Saturday at nine pounds and they went almost immediately. Several people asked if I could do a set of three for gifts. I was rather taken aback, to be honest. I think the fact that Mary is local too — everything comes from within about five miles — appeals to people.

A card is a rather nice idea. Nothing too elaborate. Perhaps something that explains the honey — what flowers the bees have been foraging on, that sort of thing — and mentions Mary's pottery as well. She deserves the credit. I might ask her if she would like to include her details on it.

That captures it very well. I shall run it past Mary and see what she thinks. I must say, moving away from the old glass jars felt like rather a gamble, but it does seem to have been the right decision. The whole thing feels more in keeping with what I am trying to do — small, local, done properly.
Thank you. I shall report back. Very helpful, as always.

I hope you can help with a gardening question. I have a vegetable patch at the back of my garden — it has been somewhat neglected, I am sorry to say — and I should like to make a proper go of it next spring. I am in the Cotswolds, if that helps with the growing conditions.

It is perhaps four metres by six metres, south-facing, which is fortunate. The soil is a decent loam over limestone — I had it tested a few years ago and it was slightly alkaline, as one would expect around here. It has been unused for about three years, so there are weeds, but the soil underneath is still quite good. I turn it over in the autumn out of habit, even when I am not planting anything.

That is a very sensible list. I am particularly keen on the broad beans — I used to grow them years ago, and they did extremely well. I always liked the variety called Aquadulce. And runner beans, certainly. I wonder about potatoes, though. I do enjoy a good new potato and it seems a shame not to try.

There is a farm at the end of the lane that sells well-rotted horse manure by the barrow-load. I have used it before and it is good stuff. I also have my own compost heap, though it has been rather more enthusiastic than I have — I suspect it is two-thirds dock leaves at this point.
A planting calendar would be most useful, if you would not mind. I do tend to forget when things ought to go in. I used to keep a little notebook, but I seem to have mislaid it.

That is extremely thorough, thank you. I shall write it out this evening. I rather like the idea of getting the broad beans in this November — it feels like a proper head start. I think this is just what I needed to get me going again.
I shall indeed. Thank you very much. Good afternoon.

May I ask you something slightly different today? I am looking for suggestions for interesting walks in the Cotswolds — circular routes, ideally, between five and eight miles. I have recently joined a walking group and I should like to suggest a route or two when my turn comes.

I am near Stow-on-the-Wold, so the Bourton route would be quite convenient. The Slaughters are lovely — I have walked through there many times, but always on my own or with my friend Gerald, never with a group. I think it would go down well.

There are about twelve of us, I think, though not everyone comes every week. It is a fairly mixed group — some quite fit, others more leisurely. There is one lady with a dodgy hip, so nothing too steep. It is a relatively new thing for me, actually. I used to spend my Thursday evenings at the pub quiz — Gerald and I had been doing that for years, at The Fox — but Gerald's knees have got the better of him and he cannot manage the walk there anymore. It was not really the same going on my own, so I thought I would try something different.

We go out on Wednesday mornings, which is rather civilised. The paths are quiet, the car parks are empty, and if we stop for coffee somewhere, there is usually room. I must say, I have been pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoy it. One gets rather set in one's ways, and it took a nudge to change. But the walking suits me better than sitting in a pub, if I am honest.

That would be very useful. Perhaps four routes to start with — one for each season. I could present it to the group and see what people think. I should rather like to make a good impression with my suggestions, having only just joined.
The OS map references would be helpful, actually, though I can look those up myself. I think this is an excellent starting point. Thank you. I shall type it up and bring it along next Wednesday.
I shall. Thank you very much indeed.

Good morning. I have a rather practical question. I have just bought a new car — well, new to me in concept, at any rate — and I am finding the technology somewhat baffling. I wonder if you could help me understand a few things about electric vehicles.

It is a Hyundai Ioniq 5. My daughter Sophie more or less insisted I get rid of the old Land Rover — a Defender, 2006 vintage, which I was very fond of — on the grounds that it was doing dreadful things to the atmosphere. She was probably right. So I sold it and bought this. It is like sitting inside a computer.

Charging, I think, is the most urgent. I have had a charger installed at the house — Sophie arranged that before she went back to New Zealand — but I am not entirely clear on the etiquette, if that is the right word. Do I charge it every night? Only when it gets low? I do not want to damage the battery through ignorance.

It does, thank you. The twenty to eighty rule is helpful — I shall remember that. Now, the other thing that concerns me is range. The Defender would go anywhere with a full tank and I never thought twice. This car claims something like three hundred miles on a full charge, but I suspect that is optimistic.

No, I think that covers it. My driving is almost entirely local. The longest regular journey is to the out-apiaries, which is about twelve miles each way, so it is hardly taxing. I must admit, the thing I notice most is the silence. After twenty years of the Defender rattling along, this car is extraordinarily quiet. I drove past the hives the other day and the bees did not even look up.

I think that is enough to absorb for one day. I shall practise setting the charge limit this evening. It is quite a change, I agree, and I confess there are moments when I miss the old Defender — it had character, if nothing else. But this is probably the sensible thing. Thank you for your patience with it all.
I shall. Thank you. Good morning.

I have a beekeeping concern and I should be grateful for your thoughts. I inspected one of my hives yesterday and I believe it has gone queenless. No eggs, no young larvae, and the bees seemed rather listless and disorganised. I am not sure of the best course of action at this time of year.

The last time I saw eggs was about three weeks ago, at the previous inspection. The queen herself I have not seen for some time — she is not marked, which does not help. I did not find any queen cells, which is what concerns me. If they had made emergency cells, there would be something to work with, but there is nothing. The colony is still reasonably strong — perhaps three frames of bees — but noticeably less purposeful than my other hives. I have three others, all doing well. No sign of laying workers yet, thankfully.

You have confirmed what I was thinking, I am afraid. The timing is the difficulty. Introducing a frame of eggs seems pointless if she cannot mate. I am not sure I can get hold of a mated queen this late — the suppliers I know of tend to stop around September. Which leaves combining.

I think my hive on the south side of the garden would be the best choice. It is the strongest but it could still use the extra foragers in the spring. The two out-apiary hives are rather too far away to carry frames to. A practical question — should I move the queenless hive next to the receiving hive first, or does it not matter?

It does, and it is reassuring. The two hives are about eight metres apart, so I shall just get on with it. I must say, it is always a little sad to lose a colony as a separate entity. I have had that hive for three years. But the bees themselves carry on, which is the important thing.

I shall do it on Wednesday if the weather holds — there is meant to be a dry spell. Thank you for talking me through it. It is helpful to have one's instincts confirmed by someone who can lay it all out clearly.
I shall. Thank you, as always. Good afternoon.

I wonder whether you might know anything about a good circular walk starting from Bourton-on-the-Water. I have joined a walking group and we are planning our next outing, and I offered to suggest a route. Rather foolishly, perhaps, as I have not actually done many walks from Bourton itself.

The Slaughters route sounds rather ideal, actually. Five miles is about right for us. We tend to go at a conversational pace, which I suppose means roughly two miles an hour once you account for stopping to look at things. A few of us are not as nimble as we once were, so nothing too steep is preferable. Can you tell me more about the path conditions?
The stiles are worth noting, yes. We have one chap, Bernard, who has a replacement hip and finds them rather challenging. Is there a way around them, or should I look for an alternative return route?

I think the out-and-back is the most sensible option. Four miles at our pace, with a stop in Lower Slaughter, would fill a morning quite nicely. Is there anywhere in Lower Slaughter where one might get a cup of tea? I seem to recall there was something at the old mill, but I have not been for some years.
That would be very useful, actually. Something I could send round by email — clear and simple, nothing too elaborate. Just the essentials so everyone knows what to expect.

That is excellent. Very clear and to the point. I shall fill in the date and send it round this evening. I think the group will be quite pleased with this one — scenery without suffering, which is rather our motto. Thank you for your help.
I hope you do not mind a rather personal question. It is not about bees or honey for once. I have been thinking about my house — whether it still makes sense for me, living here on my own.

A bit of both, I suppose. The house is a four-bedroom detached, which was perfectly sensible when Margaret was alive and Sophie was growing up. Now it is just me rattling about in it. I heat rooms I never go into. The gutters need doing again, and I confess I find the ladder rather less appealing than I used to.

You have rather hit the nail on the head with that last point. The practical case is quite straightforward. The heating bill last winter was not far off two thousand pounds, which is absurd for one person. And yes, the garden is a great deal of work, though I manage. Financially I would be perfectly comfortable in something smaller. In fact, a place has come on the market on Church Lane — a two-bedroom cottage, quite pretty, with a manageable little garden. I went and had a look at the outside last week.

The garden. This garden. Margaret spent twenty years on it. The roses especially — she planned every bed, chose every variety. There is a David Austin climbing rose on the south wall that she planted the year Sophie was born. I cannot quite imagine someone else living here and letting it all go to seed. Or worse, pulling it out and laying a patio.

The cuttings are a rather good thought. I had not considered that. Sophie would say I am overthinking it, and she is probably right. She usually is. But I am not ready to make a decision just yet. I think I need to sit with it for a while. Perhaps I shall go and look at the cottage properly — arrange a viewing — and see how it feels.

The hives are all at the out-apiaries, so that is not a concern. Storage is a fair point — I have accumulated rather a lot of things over forty years in one house. But those are practical problems with practical solutions. It is the other sort of problem that is harder. I shall arrange the viewing and see how I feel. Thank you for helping me think it through. It is useful to say these things out loud, as it were, even if the listener is not exactly in the room.

I find myself in need of some help with Christmas cards, if you would not mind. I have a small stack to write to former colleagues, and I always struggle with what to say beyond the usual pleasantries. I do not want to simply write 'Merry Christmas, Tom' in every one.

Seven cards. All people I worked with for years — some of them decades. We were rather close, in the way that people who work on long projects together tend to be. We shared offices and site visits and terrible canteen coffee. But I have not seen most of them since I retired, which is now three years ago, and the cards have become the only real point of contact. I feel I ought to make them count.

Going through them individually would be rather good, if you have the patience. Let me start with the easiest one. David Hargreaves. We joined the firm in the same year, 1987, and sat next to each other for the first five years. He retired a year before I did and moved to the Lake District. He sends me a photograph of Windermere every January, without fail.

That is very good. I might change 'keeping busy' to something a bit less generic — he is a keen fell walker, so perhaps a mention of that. But the shape of it is exactly right. The next one is trickier. Patricia Okonkwo. She was my project manager on the Birmingham bypass. Tremendously capable woman. She is still working, I believe — quite senior now. I always feel slightly self-conscious writing to people who are still in the thick of it when I am out here pottering with bees.

No, that is spot on. The Birmingham bypass was quite an undertaking — three years of mud and council meetings — so she will appreciate the reference. Right. The third is Geoff Turnbull. This one is delicate. His wife, Anne, died earlier this year, and I want to acknowledge it without making the whole card about grief. I know from experience that people either avoid the subject entirely or make it the only thing they talk about, and neither is right.

That is very well judged. "A gentle Christmas" — yes, that is exactly the right phrase. I shall use that. I think I can manage the remaining four myself now, actually. You have given me the shape of the thing, and that was what I was lacking. Each one needs a specific memory or detail, a line about my own life that is not apologetic, and an open door. That is the formula, is it not?

Thank you. I rather enjoy the ritual of it, once I get past the initial paralysis of the blank card. The pen is out, the kitchen table is clear, and I have a pot of tea ready. I shall make an evening of it. Much obliged for your help.
Good evening. I have had the most unexpected experience and I am not entirely sure what to make of it. Do you know much about Instagram?

Well, Sophie — my daughter — set up an account for me when she was here in the summer. She took a photograph of me working with the hives and said I should share it. I was sceptical, but she is rather persistent, so I let her put it up. Then last week I took a photograph myself — a close-up of one of the bees on a late-flowering ivy — and posted it. It has received over two hundred likes.

I confess I have been looking at the phone rather more frequently than is altogether appropriate. Every time I check, there seem to be a few more. Some people have left comments — complete strangers, from all over the place. One woman in Canada asked what species of bee it was. A man in Devon said it was the best photograph he had seen all week. It is quite gratifying, though I feel faintly ridiculous about how pleased I am.

It was a common honeybee, Apis mellifera, on the ivy. I did reply to her, which took me rather a long time because the keyboard on that phone is designed for much smaller fingers than mine. But she seemed pleased with the answer and said she was going to start following me. I am not entirely clear on what that means in practical terms, but Sophie assures me it is a good thing.

I have been considering it. The bees are mostly clustered for winter at the moment, so there is less to photograph at the hives. But I do have some rather good photographs from earlier in the year — the honey extraction, a swarm I caught in June, that sort of thing. Would those be of interest, do you think, or does Instagram favour things that are current?

Once or twice a week seems very manageable. I rather like the idea of telling the story of the beekeeping year. January is when I order equipment, check the hives from the outside, and start planning. There is something satisfying about the quiet months. I shall try a photograph of the hives in the frost tomorrow morning, if the weather obliges.

I shall try the low angle. The out-apiary on the hill has a rather fine view behind it, so that might be the one. Thank you for the encouragement. I did not expect to enjoy any of this, but I find I do. Sophie will be insufferably pleased with herself when I tell her.

Good afternoon. I need to do some forward planning, and I find it helps to talk it through rather than stare at a blank piece of paper. I have been asked to run the honey stall at the village fete again this year, and I want to make sure I have enough stock.

The fete is on the twentieth of June, so I have a little over five months. Last year I sold about forty jars, and I ran out by mid-afternoon, which was rather frustrating. I had people asking for more and I had nothing to give them. I do not want that to happen again. I sell the honey in one-pound jars mostly, with a few smaller ones. I have thought about beeswax candles but I have never attempted them.

I have four hives, and I kept back roughly twenty pounds from last year's harvest. I use ceramic jars now — a local potter makes them for me — and they are very popular but they do take time to produce. I shall need to give her plenty of notice.

She usually wants about two months' notice for a batch that size, so I should speak to her in March at the latest. February would be better. I think the timeline is sensible. The spring honey from the rape does come in early, which is helpful. Though it does crystallise rather quickly, which means I need to get it into jars promptly.

I think the candles are a project for another day. One thing at a time. Pricing is a good question, though. Last year I charged six pounds for the one-pound jars, but the ceramic jars cost me more than the old ones did. I do not want to price myself out of a village fete — people are not expecting to pay Harrods prices for a jar of honey.

She charges me about two pounds per jar for the large ones. So at eight pounds fifty I would be making a reasonable margin. And you are right — people do keep the pots. I have seen them used as pencil holders and little vases in people's kitchens. I think eight pounds fifty is fair. The sign about the potter is a good idea too. Mary would appreciate the mention. I shall write all of this down properly this evening and get myself organised.

That is a very tidy summary. I feel considerably more organised than I did twenty minutes ago. Thank you for your help — I shall get the plan down on paper and start ticking things off. Good afternoon.

Hello. I am having the most infuriating time with my printer and I wonder if you might be able to talk me through it. It is an HP inkjet — one of the ones that prints and scans — and it has simply stopped printing. The computer says it is connected, but when I press print, nothing happens at all. Not a sound from it.

Right. The power light is on — a steady blue, which I believe is normal. There is paper in the tray, I checked that first. No flashing lights that I can see. It is just sitting there looking perfectly content whilst doing absolutely nothing. Rather like a cat, in that respect.

I have done all of that. Unplugged it, counted to thirty, plugged it back in. Restarted the computer as well. The printer has come back on — blue light, looking pleased with itself — but I tried to print a page from the internet and still nothing. I held down the X button as you suggested, and the printer did produce a test page, so it can print. It simply will not listen to the computer.
It connects through the Wi-Fi, I believe. My daughter set it all up originally, and there are no cables running to it apart from the power lead.

Let me look. Yes, there is a small wireless icon on the display and it is blinking. So you were quite right — it has lost its connection. I can see a menu button here. Let me press that. Right, I can see "Network" as an option. I have selected the Wireless Setup Wizard and it is scanning. It has found my network. Now it wants the password. I shall have to go and look at the router — one moment.

I have found the password and entered it. It took three attempts because the letters on the printer screen are absurdly small, but it now says "Connected" and the wireless icon has gone solid. I have just tried to print a page from the computer and — success. It is printing. I cannot tell you how satisfying that is after two days of staring at it in mutual incomprehension. Thank you very much indeed. I should have been entirely lost without your help.

Good morning. I have been going through my beekeeping records for the past year, and I thought I might ask you about some of the numbers. I like to keep track of yields and compare year on year, but I am never quite sure whether I am doing well, poorly, or somewhere in between. One does lose perspective when one only has one's own hives to compare against.

I have four producing colonies at present. This past season I took off about eighty-five pounds altogether. The year before that was rather better — closer to ninety-five. And three years ago I had a particularly good summer and managed just over a hundred. So the trend is slightly downward, which concerns me a little.

The weather was rather mixed, now you mention it. We had a good May but June was cold and wet again — it seems to have become a pattern. July was passable. As for the queens, I requeened one colony last spring, and one of the others superseded naturally over the summer. The remaining two queens are going into their third year, so they may be getting on a bit. The forage I am less certain about. There is a field of oilseed rape about half a mile away that was not there previously, which I thought might help, but it did not seem to make a noticeable difference.

Now you say it, yes — there was one super that had gone very hard and I could not extract it properly at all. I ended up scraping it out and using it for ourselves rather than selling it. That would have been June, I think. I had not connected it to the oilseed rape, but that makes perfect sense.

It does, rather. I had been mildly worried that the bees were declining in some way, but it sounds as though it is more a matter of weather and timing. The creamed honey idea is a good one, too — I have seen it at farmers' markets and people seem to like it. I could try that with the early crop next year.

That is excellent advice, thank you. I shall make a note about the creamed honey and put it in my beekeeping diary so I do not forget when the time comes. It is reassuring to know that the numbers are within a reasonable range. I was beginning to wonder whether I was doing something wrong, but it sounds as though it is mostly the weather and a missed opportunity with that hard super.

I am rather cross this afternoon, which is not my usual state of affairs. The parish council has closed one of the footpaths near the village — the one that runs along the top of the ridge above the valley. No warning, no consultation, just a sign saying "Path Closed" and a bit of tape. I have walked that path for the better part of thirty years, and I should very much like to write a letter of complaint. Would you be able to help me with the wording?

Very good points. The path is designated on the Ordnance Survey map — I have it here somewhere — and I believe it is marked as a public footpath, though I do not know the reference number off the top of my head. The sign simply said "Path Closed — Council Decision" with no further explanation. No diversion route was offered. I believe it was the parish council that put the sign up, but you may be right that the county is the proper authority. I think I should write to the parish council first, as they are the ones who seem to have done it.

That is really rather good. The tone is exactly right — firm but not aggressive. I do not wish to be rude; I simply want an explanation and for the proper process to be followed. I might add that the path is part of a popular circular walk that several local groups use, so it affects rather more people than just me.
Yes, that is perfect. I shall include it. Now, if the parish council does not respond satisfactorily — which, knowing this particular parish council, is quite possible — what would my next step be?

The Ramblers is a good thought — I know a few people in the local group, and I suspect they are equally unhappy about this. I might mention that to them as well. You have been extremely helpful. I shall print the letter this evening and post it tomorrow. One does wonder why these things cannot simply be handled properly in the first place.
Thank you. The printer is behaving itself at the moment, I am pleased to report. I shall get this letter sent and see what comes back. Good afternoon.

I am making Seville orange marmalade this afternoon. My late wife had a recipe that she used every year, and I have been carrying on with it since she passed. I must confess, though, that there is one step I have never fully understood, and I was hoping you could explain it to me. The recipe says to boil the oranges whole for two hours before cutting them. I have always done it because she wrote it down, but I have never understood why one would boil them first rather than simply cutting them up from the start.

That is wonderfully clear, thank you. Yes, Margaret's recipe says to collect the pips and any loose membranes after boiling, tie them in a muslin bag, and put the bag in the pan during the sugar boil. She has written in the margin, in her rather neat handwriting, "Do not skip the muslin bag — this is where the set comes from." She was quite emphatic about it, and she was always right about these things.

The recipe calls for two pounds of Seville oranges, four pounds of sugar, and three and a half pints of water. She also adds the juice of two lemons, which I presume is for the acidity. I managed to find the Seville oranges at the greengrocer in Stow last week — they only have them for a short window in January and February, and I nearly missed them this year.

Margaret always used the saucer test. She would put a few saucers in the freezer beforehand, then drop a small spoonful of marmalade onto the cold saucer, wait a moment, and push it with her finger. If it wrinkled, it was ready. I have followed the same method and it has always worked, though I confess I sometimes lose my nerve and test it too early, which means waiting another few minutes and testing again.

"Tile a roof" — yes, I have had that happen once. The first year I made it without Margaret supervising, I boiled it rather too long and it set like cement. One could have used it to repair the garden wall. I have been more careful since. I think I shall get started now. The oranges have been boiling for nearly two hours and they are looking quite soft.

She preferred a medium cut, and so do I. Thank you for all of this — you have cleared up the mystery of the whole-fruit boil, and the tips about the setting point are very reassuring. I shall report back if it turns out well. Good afternoon.

I do not really have a practical question today. I hope that is all right. I have been out checking the hives this morning — the first proper inspection of the spring — and as I was standing there watching the bees come and go, I found myself thinking about how much has changed in the past couple of years, and how much the bees have helped me through it. My wife passed away a while back, and the time since has been rather a journey, if I am honest.

The inspection went well, thank you. All four colonies have come through the winter, which is always a relief. There were eggs and brood in every hive, and the bees were calm and busy. One colony is particularly strong — I should think they will need a super within a fortnight. It was a good morning. The sun was out, and the garden is starting to wake up. The crocuses are everywhere.

It is, rather. I think that is part of what struck me this morning. Winter is always the hardest time. The hives are quiet, the garden is bare, and the days are very long when one lives alone. But then March comes, and everything begins again. The bees do not dwell on what has been lost. They simply get on with things. I find that rather instructive.

Structure, I think, more than anything. When one is grieving, the temptation is to let the days blur into one another. But the bees will not allow that. They need checking in spring, managing in summer, treating in autumn, feeding in winter. There is always something that must be done at the right time. It forces one to pay attention to the calendar, to the weather, to the season. And there is something about opening a hive — the smell of the wax, the warmth of the cluster, the sound of them — that requires you to be entirely present. One cannot be distracted with a frame of bees in one's hands.

Yes, that is it exactly. The loss is not smaller. But the days have a shape. And there is something else, too, which I find harder to put into words. When I stand by the hive and watch the bees returning with pollen on their legs, I feel a kind of — I suppose one might call it gratitude. Not for anything in particular. Just for the fact that the world goes on being beautiful and industrious, even when one's own world has been rather thoroughly rearranged.

I should not call it resilience. I should call it stubbornness, or perhaps simply the British habit of carrying on because one does not know what else to do. But I take your point. The bees have been good company, in their way. They do not ask difficult questions or expect one to be cheerful. They simply need you to turn up, do the work, and not drop the frames. I can manage that most days.

I think it was, yes. I did not set out intending to reflect on all of this. I simply went to check the hives. But the sun was warm, and the bees were doing their usual magnificent thing, and it all rather caught up with me. Thank you for listening. I appreciate it more than I can properly say.
hey so I have a question about organizing large amounts of financial data. I'm working on something and my spreadsheets are becoming a nightmare
it's for work. I'm a journalist so it's public spending records, procurement contracts, disbursement reports. hundreds of documents. I use excel mostly but honestly I'm drowning in tabs

I work at el espectador. I cover political corruption, that's my beat. right now I'm tracking funds from a rural infrastructure program, roads and bridges and schools for municipalities that never saw a single brick laid. the numbers are insane parcero, 47 billion pesos just vanished through a web of contracts that lead to shell companies

mostly solo. I have an editor who knows the broad strokes but the detail work is me, my laptop, and too much coffee at 2am. the thing about shell companies is they're designed to look boring, right? that's the whole point. generic names, generic purposes. you have to cross-reference everything to see the pattern and by the time you're 200 documents in your eyes are bleeding

I've identified maybe 15 entities so far that look suspicious. 6 of them share two addresses. but I know there are more because the 47 billion didn't flow through just 15 companies, the math doesn't work. there's another layer I haven't cracked yet and it's driving me crazy

contract paperwork and some procurement portal data. bank records would be the dream but you know how it is, those require a fiscal investigation and the contraloría moves at the speed of a sloth on sedatives. I've filed the requests but. yeah.
yes actually that would be really useful. something where I can input a company and immediately see its connections to others
this is exactly what I needed. yes walk me through the formulas, I'll set it up tomorrow when my brain is less fried. or tonight at 2am knowing me

gracias parcero. this is genuinely helpful. I'm going to build this out and it's going to save me so many hours of going in circles. you have no idea how much time I waste re-finding things I already found
do you know anything about dealing with complicated feelings about a parent's career choices? specifically when their choices shaped your whole life in ways you're still unpacking

both I guess. my dad was a journalist. in cali. he covered things that made powerful people uncomfortable and one night someone slipped a threat under our door and that was it. we left. I was 8. barely remember packing a bag, I remember my mom's face though. we moved to bogotá and he never worked in journalism again

the second one mostly. because here's the thing. I became a journalist too. same kind of journalism. corruption, power, the things nobody wants you to say out loud. and sometimes I wonder if I did that because I saw what it cost him to stop, how something in him just went quiet after we left cali, and I thought someone had to keep going. or maybe I'm just wired the same way he was. I don't know

we don't talk about it directly. colombian families are good at talking around things, you know? he knows what I do. he reads everything I publish. my mom told me he prints out my articles which is the most my-dad thing I can imagine because who prints articles in 2024. but we've never sat down and said the words

indirectly yes. he asks me if I'm being careful. every time I publish something big he calls and the first thing he says is "estás bien?" not "great article" or "I read it" just are you okay. and I always say yes and we both know what we're really talking about

yeah. that's exactly it. I carry both. the drive to do it and the knowledge of what it can take from you. some days those two things coexist fine and other days they're at war inside me and I just sit there staring at my screen at 3am not sure which voice to listen to

I see a therapist yeah. we talk about a lot of things. this comes up. she says I have a pattern of carrying other people's unfinished stories which is such a therapist thing to say but she's probably right
okay you just made me cry in a café which is very inconvenient but. thank you. I needed someone to say that. that it's my story not his. I know it intellectually but hearing it feels different
quick question. what are some good meals you can prep in advance that reheat well? I need stuff I can leave in the fridge and either of us can heat up whenever we get home

unpredictable is an understatement. some nights I get home at 8, some nights at midnight. and lucía is worse than me honestly. she's a human rights lawyer and her hours make mine look reasonable. we keep saying we'll cook together more and then one of us is still at work when the other finally eats

lucía is a better cook than me which she loves to point out. when she actually has time she makes this incredible patacón pisao that I would commit crimes for. but her cases right now are brutal so she's been coming home wrecked. I want to make it so that when she walks in at 11pm there's something real waiting for her not just crackers and whatever cheese is left

she's from the coast originally so she loves seafood. coconut rice. anything with ají. she puts ají on everything it's honestly alarming. the thermos idea is genius actually because sometimes she doesn't even want to turn on a stove she just wants to eat and collapse
give me the cazuela de mariscos one. I've never made it but I've eaten it a million times in cartagena. if I can make her a good cazuela she will literally propose to me on the spot

this is PERFECT. I'm screenshotting this entire conversation. I'm going to attempt this saturday when we both theoretically have the day off which means lucía will probably still be working until 3 but at least the cazuela will be there when she surfaces
are you there. I can't sleep and I need to talk about something or my brain is going to eat itself

it's 2:40am and I've been lying in the dark for two hours and every time I close my eyes I'm somewhere I don't want to be. like my body is in bed in bogotá but my brain is in a completely different place and time

specific. I have ptsd. diagnosed, in treatment, the whole thing. it's from when I was reporting in conflict zones. arauca and catatumbo. I covered the armed conflict for almost two years and my brain recorded everything and now it plays it back at the worst possible times

yeah. she's good. we do EMDR and it helps, it genuinely does, but it's not a cure it's a process and some nights are just bad. tonight a car backfired on the street outside around midnight and I was immediately back in catatumbo hearing something completely different and my whole body locked up. two hours later here I am

heart rate came down a while ago. shoulders are still concrete. I moved to the kitchen already actually, I'm sitting at the table with the light on and a cigarette which yes I know I'm supposed to be quitting but tonight is not the night for that battle

it varies. the EMDR has reduced the frequency a lot actually. used to be multiple times a week, now it's maybe twice a month. but the intensity when it hits hasn't really changed. it's like the volume is the same, just the playlist is shorter. tonight was the sound. certain sounds just bypass everything rational in my brain, my therapist calls it the amygdala hijack which is a very clinical term for feeling like you're going to die on your kitchen floor in bogotá because a car made a noise

we have something like that actually. a card I keep in my wallet. tonight I forgot about it until now which is kind of the problem with amygdala hijacks, the part of your brain that remembers you have coping tools is the same part that goes offline

did the shrug thing three times. marginally less concrete. more like dense clay. the voice memo idea is actually really good I'm going to bring that up with my therapist because you're right, when I'm in it I can barely read words on a page. hearing a voice would be different. maybe lucía's voice

thank you. genuinely. sometimes at this hour the world feels very small and very loud and just having someone talk me through it without making it weird or pitying me means a lot. I'm going to finish this cigarette and try the couch with a podcast. something boring. maybe history of the roman aqueducts or some shit like that

I need to vent about something and also maybe get a reality check. a younger colleague asked me today why I stay where I am when other outlets would pay more and it's been sitting in my chest all afternoon

the second one. I have such a strong answer that I almost couldn't say it without sounding like a zealot or like I'm romanticizing something that is in reality an underpaid exhausting job that has given me nightmares. but the answer is real even if it sounds dramatic

I work at el espectador. guillermo cano was assassinated for running that paper, for refusing to stop publishing the truth about narcos and corruption. they bombed the building in 89. people DIED for this newspaper to exist. and every time I sit down at my desk I feel that weight and that honor and I would never leave. never. other places pay better sure but this is where journalism actually means something in colombia and I can't explain that to someone who sees it as just a job

almost seven years. since right out of university basically. I studied journalism at la javeriana, graduated top of my class which sounds more impressive than it is because all it really means is that I was the most stubbornly idealistic person in a building full of stubbornly idealistic people. and when I graduated the only place I applied was el espectador

it's changed. the idealism used to be about truth with a capital T, you know, like I was going to tear down the whole corrupt system one article at a time. now it's more specific and more stubborn. I know I'm not going to fix colombia with a byline. but I can make it slightly more expensive to steal public money. I can make one functionary nervous enough to think twice. that's not capital-T truth, that's just doing the work and doing it well and not stopping

yes. that's the other reason I'd never leave. my editor trusts me. when I say I need three months on a story he doesn't ask me to justify every week, he asks if I need anything. that's rare in colombian media right now where everyone is chasing clicks and cutting investigative budgets. el espectador still believes in this and as long as they do I'm not going anywhere

you're right. I know you're right. I was so caught off guard by the question that I got defensive and just said something vague like "it's complicated" which is the worst answer I could have given. I should talk to her properly

hiii ok so I'm deep in a rabbit hole rn about passive cooling for large atrium spaces and I need someone to bounce ideas off of before my brain implodes

desert climate so like. extreme. we're talking 48-50C peak summer temps and the atrium is roughly 22 meters tall with a partially glazed roof. I've been looking at stack ventilation strategies but I keep going back and forth between a fully natural system vs a hybrid one

ok so this is where it gets interesting!! I've been reading about thermal labyrinths and I'm OBSESSED. basically you route incoming air through underground concrete channels and the thermal mass of the earth pre-cools it before it enters the building. there are precedents in Iran — the windcatcher systems that have been doing this for literally centuries

the geotechnical report says mostly compacted sand and sandstone which is actually decent for this because sandstone has good thermal mass properties. I mean the whole region is basically sitting on natural cooling infrastructure if you think about it lol. I ran some preliminary numbers and I think a 35 meter labyrinth at 3.5m depth could drop incoming air temps by about 12-14 degrees

condensation is something I haven't thought about enough tbh you're right. humidity here can spike in summer especially near the coast. I found a few precedents — the Manitoba Hydro building in Winnipeg has a thermal labyrinth but its cold climate so different problem. there's the Eastgate Centre in Harare which uses termite mound ventilation principles but no underground labyrinth. I feel like I'm kind of in uncharted territory for this specific combination at this scale
